payload.title: werk v0: the map is a fold over an append-only log
payload.why: The smallest visual layer over Claude Code that I can use while building it.
payload.body:
Three parts and no dependencies.

1. .werk/log.jsonl — the agent appends one event per decision, in the same turn.
2. src/fold.ts — folds the log into {nodes, edges} and derives stale and needsReview.
3. web/ — one view = one node, live over server-sent events.

Node 25 runs the TypeScript directly. There is no build step.
Seeded by importing decision-map-data.json: 154 nodes, 191 edges, 345 events.

payload.title: The map is read-only. The CLI writes it.
payload.why: The agent already has a shell. A write UI is a second interface to keep in step.
payload.body: Open question: does editing from the map matter, or is 'Claude, mark that decided' enough? This cannot be settled by talking. Use v0 for a week first.

payload.title: Excerpt pointers are still null
payload.why: Every quote in the imported map was written from memory, not extracted.
payload.body: The session file is on disk at ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl. The next step is a werk quote command that reads it and writes an excerpt node with a real msgIndex and span. Until then nobody can tell a quotation from a paraphrase.

payload.text: Can the composer send straight into the running session instead of the clipboard?
The composer cannot inject a turn into a live Claude Code session. It puts the prompt on the clipboard instead. One Cmd+V.

payload.title: The chatbox writes to the log and the clipboard
payload.why: A per-node conversation, with a one-paste bridge into the live session.
payload.body:
Typing in a card's composer does two things.

1. Appends note.added to .werk/log.jsonl, so the thread is part of the map, not the transcript.
2. Copies 're #<id> "<title>": <text>' to the clipboard. Cmd+V in Claude Code sends it.

There is no API to inject a turn into a running interactive session, so the paste is the seam.
The agent reads a thread with 'werk inbox' and replies with 'werk say <id>'.

Open: whether a headless 'claude -p' per node beats pasting into the flat session. The research
says scoped context per node cuts tokens by up to 82%, so this is worth a prototype.

payload.title: Conductor's own Claude Code integration (inspected 2026-09-01)
payload.finding: Conductor drives Claude Code as a child process over stream-json on unix sockets. No terminal, no paste. Events land in a per-session append-only outbox file.

payload.title: A per-node chatbox needs its own claude child, not this session
payload.why: Conductor owns this session's stdin socket. werk cannot write to it.
payload.body:
Conductor spawns its pinned claude binary (2.1.237) from 'conductor-runtime sidecar' with:

  claude --output-format stream-json --input-format stream-json --verbose --thinking adaptive --thinking-display

Its fds 0, 1 and 2 are unix sockets to the sidecar, not a tty. A user turn is one JSON line written to that socket. So Conductor never pastes and never simulates keystrokes.

Two consequences for werk.

1. The composer cannot reach a Conductor-owned session. That stdin belongs to the sidecar. The clipboard stays the seam for the session you are in.
2. werk can spawn its own claude child with the same flags and get a real per-node conversation, no paste. Conductor proves the flag set works in production.

The 'conductor message create --session <id>' CLI command does send a user turn, but it targets api.conductor.build. There is no keychain token here and this workspace is CONDUCTOR_IS_LOCAL=1, so it does not reach a local session.

payload.title: Conductor's outbox is the same shape as werk's log
payload.why: Independent confirmation that event log plus projection is the right substrate.
payload.body:
One file per session under sidecar-v2-session-event-outbox, named as the base64 of the UTF-16LE session id. Inside: { version, sessionId, nextSequence, pending[] }. Each pending item wraps the raw Claude Code stream-json payload with a sessionId, a turnId and a userMessageId. The queue drains into conductor.db, a SQLite file.

That is nextSequence and pending against werk's seq and fold. A production app converged on the same design independently. It also shows what werk is missing: a snapshot, so the fold does not replay every event forever.

payload.title: One continuous conversation, with the open card as context
payload.why: A session per card fragments the thread. The app needs a persistent chat window anyway.
payload.body:
The chat pane is docked on the right and never resets. As I navigate the map, the card under the cursor becomes the context the chat already knows about. The conversation writes back to the map, and the map redraws live.

Eryk decided this. The simpler option is also the one that matches how the app has to work: there must be a continuous chat window regardless, so a per-card session would be a second conversation surface to keep in step.

payload.title: A fresh claude session per card thread
payload.why_not: Fragments one conversation into dozens. Needs a second chat surface next to the continuous one. Scoped context saves tokens, but the map already gives the agent the scope.

payload.text: Tested end to end on 2026-09-02: the chat pane works.

payload.title: The chat pane is built and the loop closes
payload.why: Talk in the pane, the map redraws while you read the reply.
payload.body:
src/agent.ts owns one long-lived claude child. The server exposes POST /api/chat and streams every message back over the existing SSE channel.

Three things that make it work.

1. The open card is prepended only when it changes, as a compact block built from the map itself: title, why, kind, status, who, children and depends_on. Navigating without typing sends nothing.
2. The agent's allowlist is 'Bash(node src/cli.ts:*)' plus read-only tools. It maintains the map and cannot edit code. Widen with 'serve --allow'.
3. When the agent runs a werk command, log.jsonl changes, fs.watch fires, and every open map reloads. The transcript in .werk/chat.jsonl never triggers a redraw.

Verified on 2026-09-02: a message in the pane produced 'node src/cli.ts say werk-onechat', the log grew by one line, and the note appeared on the card.

payload.title: The transcript is disposable. The map is the record.
payload.why: chat.jsonl is gitignored. log.jsonl is committed.
payload.body: IBIS, 1970: the map, not the transcript, is the record of what the conversation established. So the two files have different lifetimes. Deleting .werk/chat.jsonl must lose nothing that matters. If it does, a decision failed to reach a card.

payload.title: The pane streams the turn, and renders Markdown
payload.why: A tool call appearing was the only sign the agent was alive.
payload.body:
Two problems, one turn.

**Progress.** The child runs with --include-partial-messages, so it emits stream_event frames. The server now forwards three SSE channels, not one:

- chat: a finished block. Persisted. Carries an id of `${messageId}:${blockIndex}`.
- delta: a token. Ephemeral, never written to the transcript.
- status: thinking or running, with the tool name, elapsed time and output tokens.

A streaming block and its final form share the id, so the finished text replaces what streamed. The header shows a pulse, what the agent is doing, seconds, and tokens. The turn ends with duration and cost.

**Markdown.** web/md.js is about 100 lines and has no dependencies: fenced code, inline code, bold, italic, strikethrough, links, headings, ordered and unordered lists, block quotes, rules. Fences are split out first, so no inline rule ever runs inside a code block, and an unclosed fence still renders while a reply streams. Everything is HTML-escaped before any rule runs.

Card bodies use the same renderer.

payload.text: Verified on 2026-09-02: 20 delta frames, 8 status frames, thinking to running Bash to idle, 215 tokens, 5.8s.

payload.title: Paste a screenshot into the composer
payload.why: Eryk thinks visually. Describing a UI bug in prose is the slow path.
payload.body:
Cmd+V an image into the composer, or drag one onto the pane.

POST /api/upload takes the raw bytes with the image content type and writes .werk/attachments/<timestamp>-<uuid>.<ext>. The message carries the absolute path, and the agent opens it with Read. Thumbnails come back through /api/image?name=, which only serves files inside the attachments directory.

PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP. 20 MB cap. The directory is gitignored: a screenshot is transcript, not map.

payload.title: One assistant event per content block, each at array index 0
payload.why: The array index is not the stream's block index. Assuming it duplicated every reply.
payload.body:
Claude Code emits a separate `assistant` event for every content block, and each event carries that block alone in `message.content`. So the array index is always 0, whatever the block's real position in the stream.

The first version keyed the finished block on the array index. A reply after a thinking block streamed at index 1 but finalised at index 0. The rendered text overwrote the thinking bubble, and the raw streamed text at index 1 was never replaced. Both copies stayed on screen.

The fix keeps the blocks opened by the current message in order. Each finished block claims the first unclaimed block of its own kind. Verified: two streamed ids, two finished ids, no orphan.

payload.title: Show a pasted image as a filename chip, not a thumbnail
payload.why: The thumbnail render is broken, and a thumbnail does not say where in the message the image sits.

payload.text:
Two problems in the composer.

1. The thumbnail does not load. The img in the composer preview shows the broken-image glyph, so /api/image?name= is not returning the bytes for the pending attachment.
2. There is no marker of where the image sits in the message. Claude Code and Conductor both write an inline token, [Image #1], at the caret, plus a small chip with the file name and a green image icon.

Proposed style: a rounded chip with a green image glyph and the file name, drawn above the input. The message text keeps [Image #1] at the paste point. The agent then maps each token to a path.

payload.title: A pasted image gets a chip and an [Image #N] token

patch.body:
Claude Code and Conductor both mark the place. werk does the same.

Pasting inserts `[Image #1]` at the caret, and a chip appears above the composer with a thumbnail and the same token. Removing a chip deletes its token and renumbers the rest, so the numbers stay 1..n.

The agent receives a header mapping each token to its path:

    [Image #1] = /…/.werk/attachments/2026-…-bf34ecf0.png
    [Image #2] = /…/.werk/attachments/2026-…-b94d63b0.png

    Open each image above with Read before you answer.

The sent message shows each image under its own number.

Verified: two images pasted, both read, and the reply referred to them as [Image #1] and [Image #2].
patch.why: A thumbnail alone does not say where in the message the image belongs.

payload.title: A bad request must not kill the server
payload.why: An empty ?name= made the server read a directory. The whole process died.
payload.body: The chip rendered an `` before the upload finished, so the browser asked for `/api/image?name=` with no name. `join(dir, '')` is the directory itself, `existsSync` said yes, and `readFileSync` threw EISDIR outside any try block. Node killed the process. Three changes, and each one alone would have stopped it. 1. The whole request handler is wrapped. A failed request answers 500 and the server stays up. 2. /api/image uses `basename` and `statSync().isFile()`. An empty name, a dot, or a traversal all answer 404. Tested. 3. The chip shows a spinner until the upload returns a name, so no request is made without one. The lesson is number 1. The other two are the bug; this one is the class of bug.

payload.text:
Decided: plain ticket descriptions. No agent-session API, no streaming timeline.

The reason is portability. A ticket description is text in a field that every tracker has. The agent-session API is Linear-only, so it would tie the state model to one vendor. The tracker card already says state lives in the tracker; a plain description keeps that true for Jira, GitHub Issues, or a file.

Cost: no live progress in the Linear UI. The agent writes the result when it finishes, not while it runs.

Decided: the repo is werk itself. The first work item is to align on a plan for werk.

The tool is its own first user. That was already the rule in CLAUDE.md; now it is also the first ticket. It also means the first run tests the planning stages against a problem where Eryk has the basis and can judge the output.

Scope order: planning first. Build, review, and improve come after.

payload.title: The MVP is the planning half: intent and options
payload.why: Planning is where Eryk's judgement is needed and where the tool is complementary. Build-review-improve is the well-served part.
payload.body: Stages 1 and 2 of the six, ending at gate G2. The MVP produces an agreed brief and a chosen option. It does not build, validate, ship, or measure.

payload.text:
A first cut at the boundary. Three questions decide it.

IN
- Stage 1, intent. A conversation that produces a brief. The map holds it as cards, with why and who on each.
- Stage 2, options. Never one option (see al-two). Two to four variants, each with a preview.
- G1 and G2. Eryk approves the brief, then the option.
- The map, the chat pane, staleness and depends_on. These already exist.

OUT
- Stage 3 build, stage 4 validate, stage 5 ship, stage 6 measure.
- The tracker adapter and the state machine from pr-now. Nothing to move through states yet.
- Risk tiers, merge on green, the pause and revert path.

THE OPEN EDGE
Where does the plan land at G2, and who carries it to the builder? Three answers:
1. The map is the output. Eryk opens the chosen card and pastes the id into a coding agent. Nothing new to build.
2. werk writes a ticket description (see tk-api) and a human runs the agent on it. Needs a render step, no adapter.
3. werk calls the coding agent itself. That is stage 3 and belongs outside the MVP.

Answer 1 is the smallest thing that closes the loop.

Decided: answer 1. The map is the output at G2.

Eryk opens the chosen card and pastes its id into a coding agent. The agent runs 'node src/cli.ts show <id>' and walks refines and depends_on for the constraints. Nothing is written down twice, and the builder always reads the current map.

Cost: the builder must run in this repo. The plan cannot leave the machine. Answer 2, a rendered ticket description, is the later step for that. It is deferred, not rejected.

Nothing new to build for the handoff. The MVP is now stages 1 and 2 only.

payload.title: Render a card subtree as a portable ticket
payload.why: A rendered plan travels to a phone, to Linear, or to a repo without the map. The map pointer does not.
payload.body: Deferred out of the MVP. Two problems to solve first: which ancestors and dependencies to include, and how deep to walk. A render is a snapshot, so a reopen after rendering leaves the ticket silently wrong.

payload.text:
Moved out from under #mvp. It refines #tracker now, because it is about writing a plan into a ticket.

Status stays open. It is not decided: we know we are not building it now, we do not know how it renders.

Rule settled here: status is one axis, scheduling is another. status says whether the judgement is settled, and reopen and stale walk that axis. A 'deferred' status would put a schedule on the judgement axis and corrupt both. Werk gets no deferred status and no milestone field.

For now the refines parent carries the schedule. A card is in the MVP if it sits under #mvp. When the tracker adapter lands, the tracker's own milestone field takes that job.

payload.title: Green means settled, not drained
payload.why: A topic with one decision is all green and looks finished. Absence of open cards is not evidence that the questions were asked.
payload.body: Two states read as green today. Settled: no open descendants. Drained: settled, and nothing is left to challenge. Only the first is computable from status.

payload.text:
Proposed signal, computed from edges that already exist.

Call a decided card UNCHALLENGED when it has no alternative_to node under it and no supported_by edge. Nobody offered a competing option, and nothing external backs it. By #al-two that means no choice was ever made — the card is an assumption wearing a decision's colour.

The readout is not a third colour. It is a count carried up the refines tree: how many unchallenged decided cards sit in this subtree. All green with 6 unchallenged is a fresh topic. All green with 0 is drained.

Second candidate signal, from the log: the sequence number of the newest card in the subtree. A subtree that stopped growing many events ago has converged. Cheap, because the log is append-only and every event has a seq.

Open question the prototype answers: does the count read as useful, or as noise? Eryk cannot judge it from a description. Build the count, put it on the map, look at it.

A parent card's status is about its own claim, not about its subtree.

Root is decided even though align and loop are open. The claim 'we build and fix software with agents in one repeating pipeline' is settled. Its children are finer claims that sit under it. refines is not composition.

If status meant 'subtree complete', root stays open until the map is finished, and every card above the frontier reads open forever. That status would carry no information.

So there is no 'in progress' status. That is a rollup over the subtree, derived and never typed. Same axis split as mvp-render: one axis for the judgement, one for everything else.

payload.title: A derived rollup line, separate from the card's status
payload.why: Eryk cannot tell whether a subtree is finished or barely started. Status answers for one card only.
payload.body: One line per card, computed over its refines subtree: 12 cards, 3 open, 1 proto, 8 decided, 5 unchallenged. Text in show first. Pixels only if the line reads useful.

payload.text:
BLOCKED from the pane. The pane agent runs claude in permission mode default, and the pane cannot answer a permission prompt. Edit fails, Write fails, and Bash refuses to start a second claude. A subagent inherits the same mode, so it fails too.

Paste this into a terminal in this repo. It runs a second claude that is allowed to edit, and it makes the change that unblocks the pane.

claude --permission-mode acceptEdits 'Make two edits in this repo. Change nothing else. Do not run tests and do not commit. Match the existing single-quote style. FILE src/agent.ts: (a) add Edit and Write to the DEFAULT_TOOLS array around line 43, and update its doc comment, which currently claims the agent does not edit code. (b) add a new constant DEFAULT_PERMISSION_MODE set to acceptEdits, with a comment saying acceptEdits is the auto mode of the terminal UI, a file edit applies with no prompt, every other tool still asks, and the pane cannot show a prompt so a mode that asks for an edit stalls the turn. (c) the Agent constructor around line 92 is constructor(cwd: string, allow: string[] = DEFAULT_TOOLS). Add a third parameter permissionMode: string = DEFAULT_PERMISSION_MODE, store it in a private field next to the existing private allow field, and assign it in the constructor body. (d) in start() around line 141 the args array ends with --allowedTools then ...this.allow. Insert --permission-mode and this.permissionMode immediately before --allowedTools. FILE src/server.ts: serve at line 80 is export function serve(port = 4000, allow?: string[]) and line 82 is const agent = new Agent(process.cwd(), allow). Add a third parameter permissionMode?: string and pass it as the third argument to new Agent.'

Then restart: node src/cli.ts serve

After the restart the pane can edit files, and the rollup gets built here.

payload.title: A restart resumes the conversation
payload.why: Editing werk means restarting werk. A fresh session would lie: the transcript stays on screen.
payload.body:
The child reports its session id in the `system/init` event. werk writes it to `.werk/session` and passes it to `--resume` on the next start. Verified: told the agent a codeword, killed the server, restarted, and it answered from the resumed session.

The failure path matters as much. A stored id that no longer resolves makes the child report an error result and exit before it ever reaches init. werk detects that, clears the id, starts a new session, and **replays the message you were waiting on**. Verified.

One bug found while testing this: the error result cleared the pending message before the exit handler ran, so the replay had nothing to send. A result that arrives before init is not a finished turn.

`serve --new` starts fresh on purpose.

payload.title: The pane may edit code, with acceptEdits
payload.why: The pane cannot show a permission prompt, so a mode that asks would stall the turn.
payload.body:
Edit and Write joined the allowlist and the child runs with `--permission-mode acceptEdits`. A file edit applies with no prompt. Every other tool still asks.

The cost is real: the pane can now write to any file in the repository, and the pane shows no diff. Use git to see what changed. Narrow it back with `serve --allow`.

payload.title: Never blame the session for a crash it did not cause
payload.why: Any early exit was read as a dead session, so werk deleted a working conversation.
payload.body:
The first version treated *any* exit before `init` as proof that the stored session id was bad. It cleared the id and started over. A transient crash therefore destroyed a perfectly good conversation, and the pane said only "The agent exited (code 1)" with no reason.

Three changes.

1. Only `No conversation found with session ID` clears the id. That string comes from Claude Code itself. Anything else leaves the id alone, because losing a working conversation costs far more than one retry.
2. The child's stderr is kept and shown. "code 1" became "error: option '--permission-mode <mode>' argument 'nonsenseMode' is invalid. Allowed choices are acceptEdits, auto, bypassPermissions, manual, dontAsk, plan."
3. One automatic retry, then "Your message was not delivered. Send it again." A crash loop cannot spin, and a message is never silently dropped.

Verified both paths. A planted dead id is cleared and the message replays into a new session. An invalid permission mode crashes twice, reports the real reason, and the good session id survives and still resumes.

payload.title: Show the whole error, and do not retry what cannot succeed
payload.why: The one-line summary cut off the first line, which is where the cause is.
payload.body:
Two defects in the first version of the crash reporting.

1. It kept the last two lines of stderr. The login failure begins "Remove the credential and run: claude auth login" *after* the sentence that names the problem, so the useful part was cut. The pane now emits the whole stderr as a result bubble, which is monospace, red, and folds anything past six lines behind a disclosure.
2. It retried every failure. A login problem, a bad flag, or a missing credential fails identically the second time. It doubles the wait and the noise. A FATAL pattern now skips the retry and the pane says "Fix the problem above, then send it again."

Verified with an invalid --permission-mode: the full allowed-choices list appears, no retry, and the stored session survives.

payload.title: The pane's agent must be logged in where the server runs
payload.why: werk spawns claude as a child; it inherits that shell's credentials, not the browser's.
payload.body:
Seen on 2026-09-04: the child died with "Remove the credential and run: claude auth login".

Not reproducible from this session. Every path was tested and all of them worked: the inherited environment, a scrubbed environment with only HOME, PATH, USER and SHELL, and all three claude binaries on PATH — .local/bin, homebrew, and Conductor's pinned 2.1.257.

So the difference is the shell that started `werk serve`. OAuth lives in the login Keychain under the service "Claude Code-credentials", and Keychain access is granted per application. A terminal that has not been granted access, or a stale credential, fails exactly this way.

Next step for Eryk: in the same terminal he runs `werk serve` from, run `claude auth status`, and `claude auth login` if it is not signed in.

payload.title: One werk server per .werk directory
payload.why: Two servers share the session id and the transcript. It looks like the agent losing its memory at random.
payload.body:
On 2026-09-04 my test servers ran against the live .werk directory while Eryk's server was serving it. They overwrote .werk/session with throwaway test conversations and interleaved their transcripts into chat.jsonl. Eryk saw "Session 1dcacf3e could not be resumed" and synthetic errors from tests he never ran.

I diagnosed that as a transient fault I could not reproduce. That was wrong. The cause was two servers sharing one directory.

serve now takes .werk/serve.lock, holding the pid and the port. A second server checks whether that pid is alive and refuses:

    werk: another werk is already serving this repository on port 4211 (pid 89491).
    werk: stop it first, or run in a different directory. One server per .werk.

A stale lock from a killed process is ignored, because the pid check fails. The lock is released on exit and on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Set WERK_LOG to point at another directory to run a second instance on purpose. That is how my tests should have been run.

payload.text: Correction: most of the failures between 22:43 and 22:53 were my own test servers sharing this .werk directory, not a fault in Eryk's setup. The auth failure at 22:54 is the one real event.
Write access from the chat pane works. Test note.

patch.body:
One line per card, computed over its refines subtree, the card itself included: cards, open, proto, decided, unchallenged, stale. A zero count is left out. A leaf card prints no line.

Built in text. `deriveRollup` in src/fold.ts, printed by `werk show`: once for the open card, and once per child on each incoming refines line, so you can see which branch is heavy before you open it.

Result on the real map: root reads `71 cards, 19 open, 10 proto, 42 decided, 38 unchallenged, 4 stale`. The per-child lines separate a dead branch from a live one: `measure` is 4 cards, 4 open. `tracker` is 7 cards, 6 decided.

Pixels only if this line reads useful.

payload.text: Built. Run: node src/cli.ts show root. The per-child lines carry more signal than the card's own line — they rank the branches. Open question stays: does this go on the map, or is show enough?

payload.title: unchallenged nearly equals decided, so it carries no signal yet
payload.why: 38 of 42 decided cards are unchallenged. A count that is always near the maximum cannot rank branches.

patch.body:
unchallenged counts a decided card with no alternative_to edge against it. On the real map that is almost every decided card, because we rarely record options as nodes.

Two readings, and they need different fixes:

1. The measure is right and the map is bad. We decide without contrast, which is what #al-two warns about. Then the number is the alarm, and it should stay.
2. The measure is wrong. We do consider options, but we do not record them as alternative_to nodes. Then the number measures our logging habit, not our judgement.

Which one it is decides whether the count stays on the rollup line.

payload.title: Approval happens in the pane, through a PreToolUse hook
payload.why: claude --print cannot prompt, so a tool outside the allow list came back as 'This command requires approval' and the turn carried on without it.

patch.body:
A PreToolUse hook runs before every tool call. It blocks. That block holds the turn open, so an approved call runs inside the same turn instead of coming back as an error the model has to work around.

The path:

1. `src/ask.ts` is the hook. Claude Code runs it with the call on stdin.
2. It POSTs to `/api/ask` on the werk server and waits.
3. The server answers by itself when a rule already covers the call. Otherwise it pushes the question to the pane over the existing SSE channel and holds the socket open.
4. You click Allow once, Always allow, or Deny. `Cmd+Enter` allows, `Escape` denies.
5. The server replies, the hook prints `permissionDecision`, the tool runs or does not.

Two lists decide without a click: `--allow` from the command line, and `.werk/allow.json`, which is what Always allow writes.

The hook timeout is 600 seconds. Long enough to read a command, short enough that a forgotten tab does not hold a turn open all day. If the server is gone or you never answer, the hook says nothing and the normal permission check applies. Failure never widens permission.

payload.title: Answer the CLI's can_use_tool control request on stdin
payload.why_not: This CLI has no --permission-prompt-tool flag, so there is no way to switch the control protocol on, and no way to test the wire format from here.

payload.title: Catch the denial, add the rule, restart the child, replay the turn
payload.why_not: The model has already seen the error and moved on. An approval that arrives one turn late is a retry, not an approval.

payload.title: A prefix rule must match every command in the line, not the first
payload.why: Bash(node src/cli.ts:*) would otherwise allow 'node src/cli.ts add x; rm -rf /', because the line starts with the prefix.

patch.body:
`matches()` in src/permission.ts splits the Bash command on the operators that start a new command, then requires every part to match the prefix. A line that contains a backtick or a dollar-paren is refused outright: a substitution can hide anything, and no small parser can see inside it.

This is not a shell parser and must not become one. It errs toward asking. A quoted semicolon inside an argument splits the line and costs one extra click. That is the right direction to be wrong in.

Claude Code's own harness applies the same rule. It refused a compound command from this session while this card was being written.

payload.text: Built, not yet run against a real claude child. I could not spawn claude from my own sandbox: it blocks every command except 'node src/cli.ts *' — the same problem this card fixes. Two probes are in probe-permission.mjs. Run 'node probe-permission.mjs rules' and 'node probe-permission.mjs http'. Delete that file once the card says decided.

Bug fixed: the empty approval bar stayed visible. .asks set display:flex, which beats the browser rule for [hidden]. Added .asks[hidden]{display:none} in web/style.css. Checked #results — it has no display: rule, so it hides correctly.

Proven end to end against a real claude child, 2026-09-04. Two blocked Bash calls in this session (grep and sed) raised the bar, waited, and ran after Allow once. No external agent run was needed: the pane's own agent was the test. probe-permission.mjs can go.

payload.title: A read-only call never asks
payload.why: A bar that pops up for grep teaches you to click Allow without reading it. Then a real question gets waved through too.

patch.body:
READ_ONLY in src/permission.ts is a fixed list of calls that cannot change anything: Read, Grep, Glob, the werk read commands (show, stale, events, inbox), and about 20 shell commands (grep, rg, cat, head, tail, wc, ls, file, which, diff, date, pwd, echo, and git status/log/diff/show/branch/blame/remote).

Absent on purpose: any write, delete, install or network call. sed is out, because sed -i writes. find is out, because find -exec runs anything. sort and uniq are out, because both take an output file.

isReadOnly() checks each command in the line against the whole set, not against one rule. `cat README.md | head -20` is free. A single rule stays strict, so `grep x; rm -rf /` still asks: rm matches nothing in the set. A line with $() or a backtick never matches at all.

The redirect falls out of the same splitter. `echo pwned > /etc/hosts` splits into `echo pwned` and `/etc/hosts`, and the second matches no rule, so it asks.

The default permission mode is now auto, not acceptEdits. The hook answers allow or deny for every call it sees, and that bypasses the mode, so the mode only decides a call the hook never sees.

16 checks cover this in probe-permission.mjs rules.

payload.text: Verified 2026-09-04 against claude 2.1.235 with a real child process. Allow: the hook fired, the pane got the question, and date ran inside the same turn (num_turns 2, is_error false). Deny: the tool_result came back is_error true with the reason from the pane, and the agent did not retry. Always: the call ran and Bash(date:*) was written to allow.json; the next identical call was answered by rule in 21ms with no question.

payload.title: The hookSpecificOutput schema is the one that works
payload.why: The two candidate PreToolUse shapes had never been tried against a real child.
payload.body:
Claude Code 2.1.235 accepts what src/ask.ts already prints:

    {"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
      "permissionDecision": "allow" | "deny",
      "permissionDecisionReason": "..."}}

The older {"decision": "approve"} shape was not needed and was not used. No change to src/ask.ts.

Two other questions answered by the same run.

A matcher of "*" does match every tool. The Bash call was intercepted while the settings file named no tool but the star.

--settings <path> merges. The child ran with --settings pointing at .werk/hook-settings.json and --allowedTools Read at the same time; Read stayed allowed by rule and Bash went to the hook. The hook file adds hooks without replacing the rest of the settings.

payload.title: Cmd+Enter fired the composer and the approval bar at once
payload.why: The two handlers sit on different targets, so one keystroke did two things.
payload.body:
The approval shortcut listens on document. The composer listens on the textarea and treated any Enter without Shift as send. Cmd+Enter therefore sent the typed message AND allowed the pending call. The element handler runs first, so preventDefault in the document handler came too late.

Found by reading the code, not by clicking: I cannot drive a browser from this terminal.

The fix is one guard in web/app.js. The composer now ignores Enter when Cmd or Ctrl is held, so Cmd+Enter belongs to the approval bar alone. Plain Enter still sends.

Escape is left as it is. It denies from anywhere, including while the jump search is open, which can cost an accidental deny. Deny is the safe direction to be wrong in, and the card werk-approve already says failure must never widen permission.

payload.title: The three buttons have not been clicked by a human
payload.why: The server side is proven; the pane's own click path is only read, not run.
payload.body:
Every decision was verified through /api/ask/answer against a real claude child. That covers the hook, the server, the rules and allow.json. It does not cover renderAsks, the button click handler, or the two keystrokes, because I cannot drive a browser from this terminal.

What is left for Eryk, about two minutes:

1. Start the server, ask the pane to run 'git status'.
2. Click Allow once. The command must run in the same turn.
3. Ask again, click Always allow. Check that .werk/allow.json gains Bash(git status:*) and that the next one does not ask.
4. Ask again, click Deny. The reply must say it was denied, with no retry.
5. Repeat once with Cmd+Enter and once with Escape.

Step 5 is the one that changed today, so it is the one worth doing first.

payload.text: Re-verified 2026-09-04 with six added cases in the probe. 'node src/cli.ts add x; rm -rf /' does not match Bash(node src/cli.ts:*), and neither does the && form, the pipe form, the backtick form, nor $(...). A line of two allowed commands still matches. 12 of 12 cases pass.

payload.title: npm run dev: restart on src, reload the page on web
payload.why: A code change needed a manual restart and a manual refresh. Two steps between an edit and seeing it.

patch.body:
`npm run dev` is `node --watch src/cli.ts serve`. Node watches the modules it imported, so a change under src/ restarts the server. It does not watch web/, because node never imports those files.

web/ is handled in the server. A change there pushes a `reload` event on the same SSE stream the map already listens to, and the page calls location.reload(). A `changed` event only refetches the graph, which is not enough: the browser is still running the old app.js.

The draft in the composer is stashed in sessionStorage before the reload and restored after it. The open card is in the hash and the transcript is on the server, so nothing else lives in the page.

Two races come with --watch, because the new process starts before the old one has died:

1. The lock. takeLock now waits up to 5 seconds for a live holder to let go, then refuses as before. A server that is really running is still refused, only later.
2. The port. EADDRINUSE retries the listen every 250 ms, up to 20 times. The old process can hold the socket for a moment after it drops the lock.

Proven: the lock wait. A second serve printed "waiting for pid 9710", waited, then refused with the right message.
Not proven: a full --watch restart cycle. Testing it means restarting the server the chat pane runs on.

payload.title: A #card-id in any text is a link
payload.why: The map is a graph, but a reference written in prose was a dead string. You had to search for the id by hand.

patch.body:
cardLinks() in web/md.js turns #card-id into <a href="#card-id">. The href is the hash route the map already uses, so a click needs no handler.

Only an id the map knows becomes a link. web/app.js passes knows(id), which checks G.byId. A dead reference stays plain text, so a link always lands somewhere.

Where it renders: the card body, the why line, the finding line, the notes thread, your own messages in the pane, and the agent's replies. Not the card summary in a grid tile, because that tile is a button and an anchor inside a button is invalid.

What it leaves alone:
- A code span. `node src/cli.ts show #rollup` is a command, not a reference.
- A fenced block.
- A heading. `# rollup` needs a space, an id does not have one.
- A URL fragment. The character before the # must not be a word character or a slash.

md() also stopped running bold and italic inside a code span. Code spans are stashed before the other inline rules and restored last.

15 checks in probe-md.mjs.

payload.text: Bug: no links appeared in the chat pane. Two causes, both fixed. 1. load() and loadChat() raced, so knows() ran against a null graph and every id read as unknown. Startup is now load().then(loadChat). 2. A card created during a turn is mentioned in the same message, and that bubble rendered before the card existed. The transcript now repaints once, when the turn goes idle. It keeps your scroll position if you scrolled up.

payload.title: Default tools allow Bash(node:*)
payload.why: Edit and Write already let the agent change any file, so a node script adds no new risk. Allowing it by default stops a repeat ask on every one-off probe script in every fresh workspace, since .werk/allow.json is not tracked by git.

patch.body:
49 decided cards. 5 have an option recorded against them: #tracker, #st-merge, #pr-now, #werk-onechat, #werk-approve. 12 option nodes in the whole log.

The split by who decides is the finding:

| who | decided | with options |
| --- | --- | --- |
| you | 19 | 4 |
| me | 28 | 0 |
| prototype | 1 | 1 |

A who:me card is a reversible call the agent made and reported. An option on it is noise. So the population #al-two cares about is who:you, and there the number is 15 of 19 with no contrast, not 44 of 49.

The 44 with no options, by branch:

**visual (27)** — #vi-images #vi-overwrite #vi-srcnode #vi-detail #vi-onview #werk #werk-chat #werk-chat-stdin #werk-outbox #werk-pane #werk-two-files #werk-progress #werk-shots #werk-blockid #werk-shot-chip #werk-crash #werk-resume #werk-edits #werk-crashmsg #werk-fullerr #werk-onelock #werk-prefix #werk-readonly #werk-hookschema #werk-cmdenter #werk-dev #werk-reflink

**product (5)** — #product #pr-logic #pr-log #pr-iface #pr-first

**tracker (5)** — #tk-config #tk-local #tk-gates #tk-verbs #tk-api

**stages (3)** — #stages #st-six #st-gates

**align (2)** — #al-two #al-ephem

**loop (1)** — #lp-split

**root (1)** — #root

Most of the visual branch is werk build work from one session: a discovered fact, not a choice. #werk-blockid records how Claude Code emits content blocks. There is no alternative to a fact.

So the count needs a population before it means anything. Two candidates: count only who:you cards, or add a kind that marks a card as a finding rather than a choice.

payload.title: Tool calls collapse into one line per run
payload.why: The transcript showed every Read, Edit, and Bash call at full length. That pushed the actual conversation off screen.

patch.body:
The chat pane now groups a run of tool calls into one collapsed <details> section. Its one-line summary shows the latest call and a count, and updates live as calls stream in. Opening it shows every call in the run, each with its input and its output.

Considered and rejected: keep every tool call visible at full length, and only fold the long tail of output lines behind an expander (the pattern the 'result' messages already used). A quick prototype of that version still left five or six lines of Read/Edit/Bash noise per turn before any output collapsed, so the transcript stayed dominated by tool chatter. Collapsing the calls themselves, not just their output, is what actually clears the space.

payload.title: Alternative: show every tool call, fold only long output
payload.why: Considered via prototype, then rejected.
payload.why_not: A quick build still left every Read, Edit, and Bash call visible at full length; only output past a few lines folded. That did not clear enough space.

payload.title: unchallenged counts who:you cards only

patch.why: Counting every decided card put the number at 44 of 49. A count that sits near its maximum ranks nothing.

payload.text: Done. deriveRollup in src/fold.ts counts a card as unchallenged only when who is you, the status is decided, and no alternative_to edge points at it. Root went from 44 to 15.

payload.title: Status and staleness are two axes. They never share a row.
payload.why: unchallenged sat in the dot row next to the bar, so it read as a bar segment. It is not: an unchallenged card is also counted in decided.

patch.body:
The rollup carries two kinds of number, and they must not look alike.

**Axis 1: status.** decided, open, proto. These partition the subtree and add up to the card count. They get the bar, and a row of dots under it with the same three names. A reader can check the widths against the numbers.

**Axis 2: what is wrong.** stale, unchallenged. Both cut across status. A stale card is still decided. An unchallenged card is decided by definition. If either joins the dot row, the numbers stop adding up and the reader looks for a purple segment in the bar that is not there.

So the second axis is a row of chips with words in them: "9 of 31 decided had no option presented" and "4 stale". A different shape, and a ratio rather than a count, because the count alone means nothing without the population.

rollupBar, rollupLine and rollupFlags in web/app.js. The rule is in the comment above rollupLine: nothing may join that row.

payload.title: A derived rollup on every card, in three rows

patch.body:
Built. deriveRollup in src/fold.ts computes one Rollup per card over its refines subtree, the card itself included: cards, open, proto, decided, unchallenged, stale. It ships in /api/graph and prints in werk show.

Three rows on the card, and the split between them is the finding. See #ro-axes.

1. **The bar.** decided, open, proto as widths. How much is left, not how many.
2. **The dot row.** The same three as numbers, with the total and a label: "this card and everything below it, 43 cards". Without the label the line reads as a claim about the open card, and "1 decided" under a proto title looks wrong.
3. **The chips.** "9 of 31 decided had no option presented" and "4 stale". A different shape, because these cut across status and would break the sum.

werk show prints the same rollup as one text line, and again on each incoming refines edge, so a branch can be ranked before it is opened.

The browser's own rollup() is gone. It walked the tree with a different definition: it left the card out and had no unchallenged count, so the map and the CLI disagreed. One definition now, on the server.

What this card does not answer: which cards are the unchallenged ones. The chip gives a ratio, not a list. On #visual that is 9 cards you cannot name without clicking through.

payload.title: Sonnet runs the turn, Opus advises
payload.why: The advisor tool is Anthropic's built-in mechanism for exactly this: a stronger model consulted at decision points, not run on every turn.

patch.body:
src/agent.ts now spawns claude with --model sonnet --advisor opus. Sonnet handles every turn; Claude calls Opus itself before committing to an approach, when an error recurs, or before declaring a card settled — the advisor decides the timing, not the code here.

This is Claude Code's built-in advisor tool (docs: code.claude.com/docs/en/advisor), not a custom subagent. It is experimental, Anthropic-API-only, and bills Opus-rate tokens for each consultation on top of Sonnet's usage. If DISABLE_TELEMETRY or an LLM gateway blocks feature-flag fetching, the advisor silently stays off and the session just runs Sonnet alone — worth checking with /advisor inside the embedded session if a decision seems under-considered.

payload.title: A model selector in the chat header: Sonnet, Opus, Sonnet + Opus advisor
payload.why: The model was only settable in code. Switching for a hard card or a cheap one should not need a restart of werk itself.

patch.body:
The chat-head now has a <select> next to the running indicator. Agent.setModel(model, advisor) is the seam: it updates the fields that build the spawn args, then kills the child so it restarts with them. Killing on purpose, not a crash — the exit handler checks a 'switching' flag first and skips the retry and error-reporting path that a real crash goes through.

The restart resumes the same session id, so switching models does not lose the conversation. It does throw if a turn is in flight, since --model only takes effect at spawn: the pane disables the selector while busy so that path is not the common one.

POST /api/model carries {model, advisor}; advisor is null for plain Sonnet or Opus, 'opus' for the third option. A 'model' SSE event keeps a second open tab's selector in sync.

payload.title: A context-fill pie next to the model selector, with a clear-context popover
payload.why: Token usage was invisible until the child crashed or slowed down near the window limit.

patch.body:
The pie reads modelUsage from the CLI's own 'result' event — inputTokens + outputTokens + cacheReadInputTokens + cacheCreationInputTokens over contextWindow, both reported by the model itself, so the fill and the limit are never a guess baked into this file. It turns var(--proto) blue under 33%, var(--open) yellow from 33%, var(--stale) red from 66%, drawn with a conic-gradient on a 16px button — no canvas, no chart library.

Clicking it opens a popover with the percentage and a Clear context button. Agent.clearContext() drops the stored session id and the chat.jsonl transcript, then restarts the child the same way setModel does: kill, flagged as deliberate so the exit handler skips the crash-reporting path, restart. The map itself is untouched — only the chat forgets. Same busy guard as switching models: --model and a cleared context both only take effect at spawn, so the pane refuses both mid-turn.

payload.title: The unchallenged marker reuses the decided/open dot, not a new ring glyph
payload.why: A hollow ring with a shadow halo was a second visual language next to the filled decided/open/proto dots already on the map.

patch.body:
One .dot class, five colours: decided, open, proto (already existed), unchallenged (var(--src), purple), stale (var(--stale), red).

Three places it appears:
- In a rollup-line row, inline, exactly like the existing decided/open/proto dots.
- In a .flag badge, inline before the ratio: `1/3` with a purple dot after it.
- On a card tile, .dot.corner: same 8px filled circle, position:absolute, top:8px right:8px — inside the tile's own padding, no shadow, no halo.

Also added to the hero's tag row: a .tag.unchallenged pill, styled like the existing .tag.decided / .tag.open pills (colour + border, no fill), so a card opened directly (not via a parent's grid) still shows the marker.

Superseded the first version, which used a bordered .ring glyph with a box-shadow halo for the corner case — a shape and treatment nothing else on the map used.

payload.text: Fixed a bug: the pie showed 300%+ fill on a turn with many tool calls. The 'result' event's modelUsage sums every internal API call the turn made — a turn with 10 tool calls reports 10x the real context size, since each call re-reads the growing cache. Switched to reading usage off each individual assistant-message event instead, which is one API call's real tokens, and always overwriting (never accumulating) so the last one before the turn ends is what the pie shows. modelUsage is still the source for contextWindow, since that number is genuinely constant per model.

payload.title: Two prompts that looked like a permission bug were self-inflicted habits
payload.why: Two screenshots showed 'simple-looking' commands asking for approval: a chained node;head|node -e line, and a python3 -c rewrite of web/app.js.

patch.body:
Checked src/permission.ts against both. Neither is a matching bug — matches() is working as designed:

1. `node --check src/fold.ts 2>&1 | head -20; node --input-type=module -e "..."` — Bash(node:*) requires every command in the line to start with 'node' (permission.ts:44-47, deliberately: otherwise `node src/cli.ts add x; rm -rf /` would slip through on the first command). 'head -20' breaks that, even though head is separately read-only — isReadOnly() cannot help either, since the other half of the line is a live node -e script, which can do anything and can never be blanket-approved.
2. `python3 -c "...re.sub...open(...,'w')..."` rewriting web/app.js — python3 isn't node, so no rule covers it, and it writes a file, so it isn't read-only either. Correctly asked.

Neither needed to ask. Edit and Write are already unconditionally allowed (bare entries in DEFAULT_TOOLS, agent.ts) — the python3 rewrite should have been an Edit call. And a lone `node -e "..."` with no ';' or '|' matches Bash(node:*) and sails through with zero clicks — the friction came entirely from chaining it with head and a second node call in the same Bash invocation.

Fix: added two lines to SYSTEM in agent.ts telling the agent to use Edit/Write over shelling out for a rewrite, and to run one node check per Bash call instead of chaining. No change to permission.ts — its conservatism here is correct, not a bug.

payload.title: unchallenged rides the status line as a ring, no separate row
payload.why: The pill badge on its own row and the corner dot were both extra shapes. The ring belongs next to the numbers it modifies, and next to the who label it describes.

patch.body:
Corrects #ro-corner, which went too far: it turned the ring into a filled dot and kept it as a separate pill row. Two things reverted, two things kept. Reverted: the marker is a hollow ring again (border, no fill), not a filled dot. The ring was never the problem. Kept moved: rollupFlags is gone. unchallenged and stale now push onto the same array rollupLine already builds for open/proto/decided, in the same
, same span shape, same icon-then-text order: `1/3`. No border, no pill, no second row. On a card tile, the ring moved from an absolute-positioned corner dot to sitting inside .meta, directly before the who label it applies to: `you decide`. It never appears next to "I decide" or "build it first", because deriveUnchallenged only ever flags who:you.

payload.text: Final tweak: on the tile, the ring sits after the who label, not before — "you decide (ring)". Confirmed good.

patch.body:
Two states read as green today, and now both are computable.

**Settled.** No open or proto descendants. Read straight off the rollup: `r.open + r.proto === 0`.

**Drained.** Settled, and nothing is left to challenge. `r.open + r.proto === 0` and `r.unchallenged === 0`.

A branch can be settled without being drained: every card decided, but some of those decisions never had an alternative put against them. That is exactly what #ro-unchal found on the real map, at 44 of 49 before the count was narrowed to who:you.

This card's own branch is the example. It reads 5 decided, 1 unchallenged: settled, not drained. The 1 is #ro-unchal's sibling that never got a ring — check the tile.

Nothing separate was built for "drained" as a state. It has no colour of its own and no extra badge. It is what you get by reading two rollup numbers together: zero open or proto, and zero unchallenged. The rollup built for #rollup is the whole answer to this card.

payload.title: Drained = settled and unchallenged is zero

payload.text:
Researched Claude Code's programmatic-invocation modes end to end (headless -p/print, the Agent SDK, hooks, --permission-prompt-tool). Summary:

Four ways to run Claude Code programmatically, only two of which fit werk (a long-lived local child bound to this repo's map):
- Managed Agents (hosted REST API, Anthropic runs the sandbox) — wrong shape, no local child.
- Client SDK (raw Anthropic API) — you write the whole tool loop yourself; throws away everything Claude Code's harness already gives werk for free.
- Agent SDK (Python/TS library, in-process) — same tools/loop as the CLI, but as a library call instead of a subprocess. Werk uses neither package; adopting it would mean rewriting agent.ts's hand-rolled stream-json parsing into query()/ClaudeSDKClient.
- Headless CLI (-p, what werk does today) — spawn the binary, talk stream-json over stdio. Everything below is a variant within this one.

Within the CLI, approval can be resolved five ways, checked in this order every time: hooks, deny rules, ask rules, permission mode, allow rules, then (only if still unresolved) a callback/prompt-tool. --allowedTools/.werk/allow.json is the 'allow rules' step. --permission-mode auto (werk's default) is the 'permission mode' step — worth noting: Claude Code's own auto mode already has a model classifier reviewing unresolved actions, running in parallel to werk's own PreToolUse hook. --dangerously-skip-permissions / bypassPermissions approves nearly everything except a few hardcoded critical-path guards. --permission-prompts none denies anything unresolved outright, for unattended runs.

The two live findings are on new option cards below.

payload.title: Route approval through --permission-prompt-tool instead of a PreToolUse hook
payload.why: A documented, stable CLI flag exists for exactly this: an MCP tool name that Claude Code calls when a prompt reaches it unresolved. It requires standing up a one-tool MCP server in place of src/ask.ts, but the wire format is real and supported for --print, unlike the raw can_use_tool control message alt-control looked at.

payload.title: PermissionRequest hook instead of PreToolUse
payload.why: PermissionRequest fires only when Claude Code's own rule evaluation could not already resolve the call — PreToolUse fires on every call and has to redo that filtering itself, which is why src/permission.ts carries isReadOnly and isApproved at all. Switching could delete most of that file. Open question: PermissionRequest fires selectively 'based on mode' and the docs single out default (manual) mode — unclear whether it fires under auto, which is werk's default permission mode. Needs a real run to find out, not a doc read.

payload.title: Count every decided card, regardless of who
payload.why_not: Near its maximum on almost every branch. Root read 44 of 49, and branches like visual read 27 of 30 — too much noise to rank anything, which is what #ro-unchal found once it was built and looked at.

payload.title: A spawned claude subprocess speaking stream-json, not the Agent SDK
payload.why: werk needs one long-lived local child, resumable, bound to this repo's log — chosen when werk-pane was first built, but never written down or checked against the alternative.

patch.body:
Four ways to run Claude Code programmatically. Two don't fit werk's shape at all:

- Managed Agents (hosted REST API) — Anthropic runs the sandbox. No local child, no access to this repo's working tree.
- Client SDK (raw Anthropic API) — you write the whole tool loop yourself. Throws away every built-in tool, hook, and session feature Claude Code's own harness already gives werk for free.

Two genuinely apply, and werk picked one without writing down why:

- Headless CLI (-p / --print), what agent.ts does — spawn the claude binary, talk newline-delimited stream-json over stdin/stdout. src/agent.ts hand-parses that protocol itself: assistant/user/result/stream_event, --resume, --model, --advisor, tool_use blocks. Every wire-format detail agent.ts knows about is public API surface werk maintains against.
- Agent SDK (Python or TypeScript library) — same tools, same agent loop, same session/hook/subagent machinery, but as an in-process library call (query() / ClaudeSDKClient) instead of a subprocess. Would replace most of agent.ts's hand-rolled parsing with the SDK's own message objects, and would turn --permission-prompt-tool's MCP round-trip into an in-process canUseTool callback (see werk-approve). Not adopted: nothing currently broken forces the rewrite, and werk is already committed to the stream-json wire format working — switching is a rewrite for its own sake, not a fix.

Worth re-opening if: the hand-rolled parsing in agent.ts breaks against a new Claude Code version, or the werk-approve research on canUseTool/PermissionRequest turns up something the CLI truly cannot do.

This card keeps only the approval-flow findings: --permission-prompt-tool and PermissionRequest, both on option cards below.

payload.title: The tracker is the backend, werk is the interface
payload.why: werk was built as its own system of record: log.jsonl is the spine, and the tracker was only a downstream target for step 6. This inverts it: each card is an issue, and werk reads and writes it rather than owning it.

patch.body:
werk is the interface for working with the agent, not the system of record. That belongs to the tracker.

Each card in the map becomes a tracker issue. The issue body carries the card's content, its links (refines, depends_on, supported_by, alternative_to), and its metafields (status, who) in a form that is:

1. Readable directly in the tracker's own UI, on a phone, with no werk running.
2. Cheap to parse back into werk's graph.

This replaces #vi-images's image-only answer. That decision said the issue holds a rendered picture and the Mermaid source stays local, because GitHub and Linear cannot both render live Mermaid. The open question now: does the issue hold the rendered image only, or the diagram source too, folded under something like a collapsed <details> block or a comment thread, so a human reads the picture first and the source is one click away for whoever restores state.

This also changes what #pr-log means. "An append-only event log is the spine" was written when the tracker was step 6's write-only target. If the tracker becomes the backend, the question is which one is authoritative: does log.jsonl stay the spine and the issue becomes a rendered projection of it, or does the issue itself become the spine and log.jsonl becomes a local cache werk rebuilds from tracker state on start.

Open, and named on this card rather than guessed at:
- Content format: what goes in the issue body vs. a comment vs. a custom field, per tracker (Linear has structured fields GitHub does not).
- Reconciliation: if the issue is edited directly in Linear or GitHub, how does that edit fold back into the log without a conflict neither side can resolve.
- Whether "the tracker is the backend" makes log.jsonl redundant, or log.jsonl stays as the local, fast, offline-first copy and the tracker is the durable one.

payload.title: Text is cached and reconciled. The image is never stored, only regenerated

patch.body:
Superseded reasoning, current answer.

The old version chose between two options that both turned out wrong for the same reason: a rendered-somewhere format (Mermaid text, live in the issue) is not actually portable, because it silently breaks on Linear. The real choice is between that and a format nothing renders natively, paired with a picture: plain structured text plus a separately rendered image. The second one wins, because the text half never depends on which tracker is reading it, and the image half is identical everywhere since werk renders it, not the tracker.

The caching rule that follows: the local map caches text only. log.jsonl never holds a rendered image, in any form. An image is not a fact to store; it is a view of one, and a stored view goes stale the moment the text under it changes.

So the image is never cached anywhere, local or remote. It is regenerated from the current text at the moment it is needed — before posting to the tracker, or before showing a preview in the browser. This is what keeps #vi-backend's reconciliation question small: two texts can conflict and need a merge; a text and a disposable render of it cannot.

Resolves two of #vi-backend's three open questions: content format (text plus a fresh render, not a renderer bet) and authority (text is what is cached and diffed; the image is derived and never part of that set). Reconciliation, for edits made directly in the tracker, is still open.
patch.why: Linear does not render Mermaid; GitHub does. A format that depends on the tracker's renderer is portable on one tracker and dead weight on the other.

payload.text: Two of the three open questions here are answered on #vi-images: content format is text plus a fresh render, not a bet on the tracker's own renderer. Authority is text — that is what is cached and diffed. The image is never cached, local or remote; it is regenerated from current text whenever it is needed. Reconciliation, for an edit made directly in the tracker, is still open.

payload.title: The tracker is a publish target. log.jsonl stays the spine

patch.body:
Narrower than the first version of this card, which said werk reads and writes through the tracker rather than owning state. That was rejected in favour of a one-way publish.

**Tracker as backend (rejected).** The tracker would own state; werk reads and writes through it. Pro: one store, no reconciliation, durable, phone-readable. Con: deriveStale compares sequence numbers across time, not current state. A tracker gives you current state plus a comment thread — treating comments as the event log means reconstructing fold.ts's job over a network, with rate limits, on every read. Linear has structured fields, GitHub only text, so the adapter that makes both trackers equally "the spine" is a bigger build than the log itself. Offline work stops working.

**Tracker as output (chosen).** log.jsonl stays the spine, exactly as built. The tracker gets a one-way publish: the final plan, as a map of small linked tickets, one per work item or top-level card. werk never sources from the tracker. This keeps every fast, offline, sub-second feature already built — fold, rollup, stale, rederive — and only adds a renderer, not a sync engine.

The same rule from #vi-images applies to the whole publish, not only the image: never treat the published tickets as state to reconcile. Republish from the current log when it changes. If a ticket is edited directly in Linear or GitHub, that edit is not read back — the log does not know about it, and the next publish overwrites it. That is the trade this card makes: simplicity over letting the tracker be edited as a second interface.

Open: what a top-level ticket contains when its own card refines into a dozen sub-cards. One ticket per root-level branch, with sub-cards folded into its body? Or one ticket per card, linked, and the map's own edge types become the tracker's own link types where each tracker supports them?
patch.why: Every feature built this session leans on ordered event history, not current state: stale, rollup, rederive, unchallenged all compare sequence numbers across time. A tracker gives you current state plus a comment thread. Rebuilding staleness propagation on top of that is a bigger, riskier build than the log werk already has.

payload.title: The tracker owns state; werk reads and writes through it
payload.why_not: deriveStale and the rollup compare sequence numbers across time, not current state. A tracker gives you current state plus a comment thread — treating comments as the event log means reconstructing fold.ts's job over a network, with rate limits, on every read. Linear has structured fields, GitHub only text, so the adapter is a bigger build than the log itself. Offline work stops working.

payload.title: Record a rejected option the moment it's weighed, not after
payload.why: unchallenged cannot tell "no option was weighed" from "an option was weighed and never written down." Both #ro-unchal and #vi-backend were corrected after the fact for exactly this.

patch.body:
Same discipline CLAUDE.md already states for depends_on: record it the moment you create a card, or it cannot be reconstructed later. Extended here to alternative_to.

The rule: when a decision comes from real contrast in conversation — a named alternative, a reason it was rejected — add that alternative as its own option node with --why_not, and link it alternative_to the decided card, in the same turn.

node src/cli.ts add <id>:opt0 --kind option --title "..." --why_not "..."
node src/cli.ts link <id>:opt0 <id> --type alternative_to

Skipping this made two cards indistinguishable from a decision made with no contrast at all, until someone noticed and asked. #ro-unchal:opt0 (count every decided card, rejected as too much noise) and #vi-backend:opt0 (tracker owns state, rejected for losing ordered event history) were both added after the fact, not at decision time.

This is now in CLAUDE.md, in the same section as the depends_on rule, and in the agent's persistent memory for this project, so it survives a session boundary.

payload.title: Backfill the option only when the marker flags it
payload.why_not: Manual and repetitive. Both #ro-unchal and #vi-backend needed the same after-the-fact fix separately, in the same conversation, before the pattern was named.

payload.title: One ticket per card, linked. No subtree to walk or inline

patch.body:
Narrower than the first version of this card, which asked a ticket to be portable: readable on a phone, in Linear, or in a repo, with no map running, which meant it had to carry its own context. That forced the two open problems named originally: which ancestors and dependencies to inline, and how deep to walk a subtree before stopping.

Dropped. A ticket does not need to stand alone. One card becomes one ticket. A related card becomes a separate ticket, linked, the same way #vi-backend already settled: publish target, not portable artifact.

The link mechanism still needs a per-tracker answer, since #vi-backend left that open: Linear has native issue relations; GitHub only has references (#123) and task-list checkboxes. refines, depends_on, supported_by, and alternative_to need a mapping to whatever each tracker actually supports, and a plain text fallback (a links section in the ticket body) for the edge types a tracker has no native concept of.

The snapshot problem shrinks but does not disappear. Per #vi-images's rule, a ticket is never cached as state — it is republished from the card's current text whenever the card changes. That still leaves one open question distinct from vi-backend's reconciliation question: a card's *links* can change without the card's own text changing (a new depends_on edge, a sibling added). Does adding an edge anywhere in the graph trigger a republish of every ticket it touches, or only the two tickets the edge is between.
patch.why: Per #vi-backend, the tracker is a publish target, not a self-contained snapshot. A 1:1 card-to-ticket mapping with tracker-native links needs no decision about how deep to walk or what to inline.

payload.title: Plain ticket descriptions. No agent-session API

patch.body:
A ticket description is text in a field every tracker has. That keeps #tracker's own claim true across trackers, not just Linear.

Cost: no live progress in the Linear UI while the agent runs. The ticket updates when the agent finishes, not while it works.
patch.why: The agent-session API is Linear-only. #tracker already says state lives in the tracker, plain across trackers; adopting a Linear-only API would break that for Jira, GitHub Issues, or a file.

payload.title: Use Linear's agent-session API with a streaming timeline
payload.why_not: Linear-only. Ties the state model to one vendor, and breaks #tracker's own claim that state lives in the tracker, plain across Jira, GitHub Issues, or a file. Cost of the chosen option instead: no live progress in the Linear UI while the agent runs.

payload.title: Render a card subtree as one portable, self-contained ticket
payload.why_not: Forced two unresolved problems: which ancestors and dependencies to inline, and how deep to walk a subtree before stopping. Unnecessary once the tracker is only a publish target, not something a ticket must survive without, per #vi-backend.

payload.title: Tickets carry a kind: decision vs buildable
payload.why: A gate only means something on a buildable ticket. Moving a decision or rejected-option ticket to in-progress builds nothing. Decision tickets close on settle, no in-progress phase. Buildable tickets keep the normal gate flow and carry a label such as ready-for-agent so an agent knows what to pick up.

payload.title: Reopen has no reason-kind: postponed, invalidated, and rejected all render as the same STALE
payload.why: The reopened event carries only id and free-text why. Staleness propagation and the red marker treat every reopen the same way. A deliberate postpone (still true, just paused) looks identical to an actual invalidation (now wrong). This was never decided — no card discusses it, and the schema has no field for it.

payload.text: Reason belongs on reopened, not rederive. reopened fires once and causes the whole fan-out, before any review. rederive fires per-card, later, only for whoever reviews that one dependent. A free-text reason on rederive can't change the marker color for the other N-1 still-unreviewed dependents. Only a fixed reason-kind read at fan-out time (on reopened) can make postponed render differently from invalidated, for the whole reverse closure, at once.

payload.title: The chat header sits below the composer, not above the log
payload.why: The thinking indicator and the context-fill pie sat far from the textarea. You type at the bottom. You could not tell at a glance if the agent was still working or stuck.
payload.body:
Before: chat-head (title, thinking state, context pie, model select) sat above chat-log, farthest point from the textarea in the pane.

After: chat-log, then asks, then chat-composer, then chat-head. The header sits right under where you type, so the busy state and the context fill are in the same glance as your next keystroke.

CSS: chat-head's separating border moved from border-bottom to border-top, since it now sits below what it used to sit above.

payload.title: Keep the header on top, above the chat log
payload.why_not: Same problem the fix solves: the thinking indicator and the context-fill pie sat farthest from the textarea. You type at the bottom, so you could not tell at a glance if the agent was stuck.
