Postponed. Focus is on planning and the werk tool itself, not the build pipeline.

payload.text: Prototyped. The --reason postponed flag and the stale/paused split in deriveStaleness already existed in code — the bug was in the log, not the logic. The pr-log and pr-logic reopens at seq 573-574 were written before --reason existed, so they carried no reason field, and fold.ts defaulted them to invalidated. That flooded STALE down the depends_on chain to werk-head-bottom and 30 other werk-* cards. Fix: re-issue the reopen with --reason postponed for both ids. New reopened events overwrite the old ones in reopenedAt (last one wins per id), so the fan-out re-runs as paused. Confirmed with node src/cli.ts stale: werk-head-bottom and the other 30 cards dropped off the stale list.

Follow-on fix: .context-pop opened downward (top:100%), which put it off-screen once chat-head sits at the bottom of the pane. Changed to bottom:100% / margin-bottom, so the clear-context popover opens upward, above the context-fill pie.

payload.title: No reason-kind on reopen — every reopen is treated the same
payload.why_not: Marked every postponed-but-still-valid card stale, with the same aggressive red as an actual invalidation. Annoying in practice: #tk-gates and #werk-head-bottom both went red for a postponed pipeline decision six hops away, not because their own content was wrong.

payload.why: node --watch restarts the whole process, including in-flight claude child sessions, whenever the agent edits a watched src file. Confirmed in session e28c5093: 8 mid-turn kills, each landing right after an Edit to src/cli.ts, src/fold.ts, or src/types.ts, producing a stuck 'still here, finishing' loop. See #reopen-reason-gap diagnosis.

payload.title: Rebuild werk's dev server on a stack with HMR that survives its own edits
payload.why: The agent's job includes editing werk's own source. A restart-based reload cannot support that: it kills the live claude child mid-turn every time the agent saves a file it is working through. Needs a stack where a code edit reloads the changed module without killing the process holding open child sessions.

payload.title: Keep node --watch: restart the whole process on a src change
payload.why_not: Restarts kill in-flight claude child processes and their session state. Confirmed in session e28c5093: 8 mid-turn kills, each right after the agent edited a watched src file, so the very task of improving werk keeps interrupting itself.

payload.title: dev-pipeline-research-hmr.md: vite-node/Bun/Deno HMR vs. Agent state
payload.finding: vite-node's invalidateDepTree is transitive, not global: editing fold.ts never re-evaluates a module agent.ts doesn't import. Bun --hot guarantees globalThis survives but not the object graph across an edited boundary. Deno --watch-hmr names 'an async function currently running' as a forced-full-restart case — the exact shape of werk's failure. Node core has no HMR, only full-restart --watch.

patch.body:
The agent's job includes editing werk's own source. A restart-based reload cannot support that: it kills the live claude child mid-turn every time the agent saves a file it is working through. Needs a stack where a code edit reloads the changed module without killing the process holding open child sessions.

Research (#werk-hmr:src0): top pick is vite-node (or Vite in middleware mode) in front of a globalThis-pinned Agent registry. vite-node's invalidateDepTree invalidates transitively up the import graph, not globally — editing fold.ts would not re-evaluate agent.ts unless agent.ts imports it. Combined with the Prisma globalThis-singleton pattern, the live claude child handle and session map survive an edit to an unrelated module. Cost: migrating server.ts's entry point off plain node onto vite-node's runner, a real migration, not a config flag.

Runner-up: Bun --hot. One flag, globalThis persistence documented directly, but a weaker invalidation guarantee than vite-node's transitive walk, and it changes werk's runtime (Node 25, no build step) not just its dev loop.

Ruled out: Deno --watch-hmr names 'an async function currently running' as a forced-full-restart case — the exact shape of werk's failure — so it may solve nothing here. Node core has no HMR, only full-process --watch.

Not decidable from docs, needs a prototype: does vite-node's invalidation really spare agent.ts given werk's actual import graph; is an edit landing mid-turn (this.busy true) safe under any of these tools; does Bun's instanceof-across-reload gap bite werk's single Agent instance. Prototype: pin an Agent-like object to globalThis holding a real child_process.spawn handle, run under bun --hot and under a vite-node entry point, edit a sibling module mid-spawn, check proc.pid is unchanged.
patch.why: The agent's job includes editing werk's own source; a restart kills the live claude child mid-turn every time. See #werk-hmr:src0 for the researched options and the prototype that would settle it.

payload.why: Reclassified: focus is on planning and the werk tool, not the build pipeline. Still true, just paused.
Reclassified: same reason. Still true, just paused.

payload.text:
Prototype built. reopen takes --reason postponed|invalidated|rejected, default invalidated (old log lines with no reason keep their old meaning). deriveStaleness in fold.ts now returns {stale, paused}: postponed fans out to paused, invalidated/rejected fan out to stale; stale wins if the two disagree on one card.

UI, per #ro-axes (stale/paused ride the flag row, never the status bar):
- New --paused color, a calm gray (#8b98a8), next to --stale red.
- Rollup chip: a paused ring + count, same shape as the stale chip.
- Card border, hero border, and #id tag: is-paused / tag.paused, gray instead of red.
- Alarm banner: gray, 'Paused. A card this one depends on was postponed, not invalidated. It still holds.' Only shows if not also stale.
- CLI: werk show prints PAUSED next to STALE; werk stale lists a PAUSED section; werk reopen --reason postponed reports 'went paused, not stale' instead of 'went stale'.

Tested on a scratch copy of the log (WERK_LOG env var) against #tk-gates, then for real: retagged #stages and #pr-now as postponed. #mvp moved from STALE to PAUSED, along with 33-35 other cards in the werk-tool branch that were never actually invalidated.

payload.title: Prototype: globalThis-pinned child process survives edits under bun --hot and vite-node --watch
payload.finding: Built an Agent-shaped harness: a real spawn()'d child pinned to globalThis, plus an unrelated sibling module standing in for fold.ts. Under both bun --hot and vite-node --watch, editing the sibling AND editing agent.ts directly left the outer process pid, the child's pid, and the pinned object's bornAt all unchanged — only the exported marker value updated. vite-node's own --help calls --watch 'restart, similar to nodemon', but it never crosses an OS process boundary, so the globalThis guard alone was enough in both tools. This settles all three prototype items on #werk-hmr: transitive invalidation sparing agent.ts, an edit to the very state-holding file, and object-identity survival — all confirmed, for both candidates.

patch.body:
The agent's job includes editing werk's own source. A restart-based reload cannot support that: it kills the live claude child mid-turn every time the agent saves a file it is working through. Needs a stack where a code edit reloads the changed module without killing the process holding open child sessions.

Research (#werk-hmr:src0): vite-node invalidates transitively, not globally. Bun --hot guarantees globalThis survives. Deno --watch-hmr names an in-flight async function as a forced-full-restart case, the exact shape of werk's failure. Node core has no HMR.

Prototype (#werk-hmr:src1): built a real Agent-shaped harness — a spawned child process pinned to globalThis, plus an unrelated sibling module standing in for fold.ts. Under both bun --hot and vite-node --watch, editing the sibling AND editing the state-holding module itself left the outer process pid, the child pid, and the pinned object's identity all unchanged. Both candidates work, given the globalThis-singleton pattern.

What is left is not a technical unknown, it is a tradeoff between the two working options:
- vite-node: keeps Node as the runtime (CLAUDE.md's 'no build step' premise holds), but server.ts's entry point has to move off plain node onto vite-node's runner — a real migration.
- bun --hot: one flag, no new dependency, but changes werk's runtime from Node to Bun, a bigger-blast-radius call than a dev-loop change.

Both are proven safe for the actual failure mode. The remaining choice is which cost Eryk would rather pay.
patch.why: Both researched-and-prototyped candidates protect the live claude child from a src edit; the remaining question is a runtime-vs-migration tradeoff, not a technical unknown. See #werk-hmr:src0 and #werk-hmr:src1.

payload.title: Real-app test: unpatched vite-node crashes, unpatched bun --hot silently orphans
payload.finding: Ran werk's actual server.ts/agent.ts, not the toy harness, on two isolated scratch copies with a live claude child mid-task. src/cli.ts:121-124 dispatches server.listen() unconditionally at module top level with no guard, and src/agent.ts's Agent is a plain 'new Agent(...)' with no globalThis pin. Result: editing fold.ts alone (the 'safe' tier) is enough to trigger cli.ts's entry dispatch to rerun under BOTH tools, contradicting the assumption that only editing agent.ts/server.ts was risky. vite-node --watch: server.listen() fails EADDRINUSE, server.ts's own retry loop exhausts 20 tries over ~5s, then calls process.exit(1) - full crash. bun --hot: does not crash, but silently constructs a new Agent + server context on every edit. Proved with a real 25-step counting task: the already-open SSE connection kept streaming the live task uninterrupted (same claude child pid throughout, task completed normally), but a brand-new SSE connection opened mid-task saw nothing - the new Agent has no session, no child. A page refresh or new tab would silently lose visibility into a still-running task. Bun's unpatched failure mode is quieter than vite-node's crash, not safer.

patch.body:
The agent's job includes editing werk's own source. A restart-based reload cannot support that: it kills the live claude child mid-turn every time the agent saves a file it is working through. Needs a stack where a code edit reloads the changed module without killing the process holding open child sessions.

Research (#werk-hmr:src0): vite-node invalidates transitively, not globally. Bun --hot guarantees globalThis survives. Deno --watch-hmr names an in-flight async function as a forced-full-restart case, the exact shape of werk's failure. Node core has no HMR.

Toy prototype (#werk-hmr:src1): a minimal Agent-shaped harness, globalThis-pinned, survived edits to both a sibling module and the pinned module itself, under both bun --hot and vite-node --watch.

Real-app test, unpatched (#werk-hmr:src2): werk's actual code has neither guard yet. Editing even an unrelated file (fold.ts) is enough to trigger cli.ts's unconditional top-level dispatch to rerun under both tools - the toy harness's tier1/tier2 split does not hold for the real code, because the entry point itself (cli.ts) reruns on any change reaching it. vite-node --watch: full crash via process.exit(1) after its own EADDRINUSE retry loop gives up (~5s). bun --hot: no crash, but silently constructs a new orphaned Agent + server context on every edit - proved with a real 25-step counting task where a fresh SSE connection mid-task saw nothing while the original connection kept streaming normally. Quieter than a crash, not safer: a page refresh would lose visibility into a still-running task.

Next: port the globalThis-pin + a listen-once guard into the real code (not just the toy harness), then repeat the real-app test on both candidates.
patch.why: Both researched candidates need real guards ported into werk's own code before either is safe to adopt; unpatched, vite-node crashes and bun --hot silently orphans live tasks. See #werk-hmr:src0, src1, src2.

payload.title: Real-app test, patched: globalThis-pin guard fixes both candidates
payload.finding: Ported the globalThis-pin from the toy prototype into the real src/server.ts: serve() now checks globalThis.__werkServe before taking the lock, constructing Agent, or calling listen(), and no-ops with a log line if the port is already being served. Repeated the exact same real-task test: 20-step counting task, edit fold.ts mid-task, on both bun --hot and vite-node --watch. Result for both: single 'hot-reloaded, reusing the live server' log line (no duplicate Agent, no EADDRINUSE, no crash), same claude child pid throughout, task completed normally, and - the decisive check - a brand-new SSE connection opened mid-task saw the live task in progress, not silence. This directly reverses the unpatched result in #werk-hmr:src2 for both candidates. The fix needed is small: one guard clause at the top of serve(), no dependency on which of vite-node or bun-hot is chosen.

patch.body:
The agent's job includes editing werk's own source. A restart-based reload cannot support that: it kills the live claude child mid-turn every time the agent saves a file it is working through. Needs a stack where a code edit reloads the changed module without killing the process holding open child sessions.

Research (#werk-hmr:src0): vite-node invalidates transitively, not globally. Bun --hot guarantees globalThis survives. Deno --watch-hmr names an in-flight async function as a forced-full-restart case, the exact shape of werk's failure. Node core has no HMR.

Toy prototype (#werk-hmr:src1): a minimal Agent-shaped harness, globalThis-pinned, survived edits to both a sibling module and the pinned module itself, under both bun --hot and vite-node --watch.

Real-app test, unpatched (#werk-hmr:src2): werk's real code has neither guard. Editing even an unrelated file (fold.ts) triggers cli.ts's unconditional top-level dispatch to rerun under both tools. vite-node --watch crashed outright (EADDRINUSE retry loop exhausts, process.exit(1), ~5s). bun --hot did not crash, but silently constructed a new orphaned Agent + server on every edit - a fresh connection mid-task saw nothing while the original connection kept streaming, unaffected. Quieter than a crash, not safer.

Fix, real-app test, patched (#werk-hmr:src3): added one guard clause to the top of server.ts's serve() - a globalThis.__werkServe check that no-ops a re-entry into serve() instead of reconstructing Agent and re-listening. Repeated the identical real 20-step counting-task test on both tools: no crash, no duplicate Agent, same claude child pid throughout, and a brand-new connection opened mid-task now correctly sees the live task instead of silence. Fixes both candidates identically; the guard, not the tool choice, is what was missing.

Decided: port the globalThis-pin guard into werk's real src/server.ts (not just the scratch copies), and pick a runner. Remaining tradeoff, unrelated to correctness (both now proven correct): vite-node keeps Node as the runtime (CLAUDE.md's 'no build step' premise holds, at the cost of an entry-point migration to vite-node's runner); bun --hot is a one-flag change but switches werk's runtime to Bun.
patch.why: Both prototype tiers and the real-app test are done. The one missing piece was the globalThis-pin guard on serve() itself, not a property of either tool - once added, both bun --hot and vite-node --watch survive a real in-flight task through a src edit, verified with a fresh-connection check. See #werk-hmr:src0 through src3.

payload.title: Bun vs Node as werk's shipped runtime (Sept 2026)
payload.finding: Node's native TypeScript support is stable as of 25.2.0/24.12.0 (experimental-transform-types removed in 26.0.0) - werk's 'no build step, no dependencies' premise already holds on Node, since werk uses no enums/namespaces/decorators. Bun's TS support is a superset (also runs enums) but that gain is unused today. The decisive finding: oven-sh/bun #7716 and #13811, both open, document that Bun's http.createServer does not reliably emit the close event when an SSE client disconnects - werk's src/server.ts serves SSE over plain http.createServer for exactly this pattern. child_process piping (werk's spawn+pipe of the claude CLI) is not on Bun's documented gap list but has open issues (#30831, #4670) showing the area is still being patched. Bun 1.4 (Aug 2026) was a full Zig-to-Rust rewrite shipped as a point release with an itemized breaking-change list - a materially different stability posture than Node's LTS-scheduled majors (Node 26 LTS Oct 2026 - Apr 2029). Bun's advantages (startup speed, bun build --compile) answer a distribution problem werk does not have; it ships as source, not a compiled binary.

payload.title: Direct repro on Bun 1.4.1: SSE close event fires correctly on werk's real code
payload.finding: Tested against Bun 1.4.1 specifically (the version installed and used throughout this whole investigation, and the version the runtime-migration research flagged as the big Zig-to-Rust rewrite). Added a probe to server.ts's actual /api/live handler: console.log on clients.add and inside req.on('close', ...). Opened and disconnected SSE clients two ways - a clean client-side timeout (curl --max-time) and an abrupt kill -9 mid-stream - against werk's real, unmodified route-handling code. Both cases: 'added, clients=1' followed by 'close fired, clients=0', every time, no leaked entries, no growth in server fd count (lsof) after 10 rapid connect/disconnect cycles. oven-sh/bun #7716 and #13811 are real, filed, open issues, but do not reproduce for werk's plain http.createServer + SSE + req.on('close') pattern on 1.4.1. Side finding: the globalThis-pin guard from #werk-hmr:src3 means a hot reload no longer applies code changes inside serve()'s body at all (a hot-reloaded edit to the SSE handler itself did not take effect until the process was fully restarted) - the guard trades 'my latest route-handler edit is live' for 'my live session survives an edit', which is the correct trade for the original problem but is worth naming explicitly.

patch.why_not: Originally rejected because oven-sh/bun #7716/#13811 document Bun's http.createServer not reliably firing 'close' on SSE disconnect. Retested directly against werk's own /api/live handler on Bun 1.4.1 (#werk-hmr:src5): close fired correctly on both a clean and an abrupt disconnect, every time. The bug is real and filed but does not reproduce for werk's specific pattern. Eryk also weighed in: binary distribution (bun build --compile) is a real productionization goal, not hypothetical, and the breaking-change/stability risk is acceptable given agents do the upgrade work. Superseded - see #werk-hmr's current decision.

payload.title: Stay on Node, use vite-node --watch for dev-reload

payload.title: Why a dependency is flagged: a section between the hero and Depends on
payload.why: PAUSED and STALE come only from a reopened event, never from status alone. A depends_on target can show status: open and still never have flagged anything, because it was never reopened, only created open. That was unintuitive to see from status alone, so the reopen's reason, date, and why now render inline, one hop before Depends on.
payload.body:
CLI: werk show prints the reopen reason/date/why under a flagged depends_on row, or 'from a reopen further upstream, open #id to trace it' if the target itself was never reopened directly.

Web: a new section, 'Why a dependency is flagged', between the hero and the Depends on section. Same two cases: g.reopens.get(target) for a direct reopen, otherwise a link to trace the chain.

Schema: Graph.reopens is the latest reopened event per id (reason, why, at) — not the fanned-out stale/paused closure. Exposed in toJSON as a plain object, since the target id is looked up directly, not iterated.

payload.title: State is exported to an external issue tracker

patch.body:
Gives three things the raw log cannot, for a human without the map open: the record outlives the branch, you read it on a phone, and step 6 can query across every past work item to find patterns.

The tracker is never read back. Per #vi-backend: publish the current log state, one ticket per work item, republished whenever the log changes. Editing a ticket directly in the tracker does not write back to the log.
patch.why: Linear for work, GitHub Issues for side projects. The log stays the source of truth; the tracker is a one-way publish target, so a human reads the plan on a phone, and the record outlives the branch.

payload.title: An option needs alternative_to only, not refines
payload.why: Using --parent on an option node also adds a refines edge. The card then renders twice on its parent's page: once under 'N below', once under 'Options'. #ro-live's own command pattern already omits --parent — this is a mistake in how I called it, not a gap in the rule.
payload.body:
Fixed on four options this session: tk-config:opt0, tk-config:opt1, werk-head-bottom:opt0, reopen-reason-gap:opt0. Each had its redundant refines edge removed, alternative_to kept.

The correct call, exactly as #ro-live already states it:
node src/cli.ts add <id>:opt0 --kind option --title "..." --why_not "..."
node src/cli.ts link <id>:opt0 <id> --type alternative_to

No --parent. alternative_to alone is what puts it in the Options section.

payload.title: No verb publishes depends_on or alternative_to as a tracker link

payload.body:
First raised as an open question inside #vi-backend and repeated inside #mvp-render, never given its own card. Both point at the same unanswered question: does refines, depends_on, supported_by, and alternative_to each get a native tracker concept where one exists, and a links section in the ticket body as fallback where it doesn't?

Concrete gap: tk-verbs lists linkPR but nothing like linkDependsOn or linkAlternative. If the answer is 'add verbs', this card names which ones. If the answer is 'fold into setBrief's body text instead', the six-verb count does not change, but the ticket body's shape does.

payload.title: Fold links into setBrief's body text, no new verbs, uniform across trackers
payload.why_not: Consistent with #tk-api and #vi-images (reject tracker-specific richness), but unlike those two, a missing native relation here only degrades to a text line — the ticket stays readable. Losing Linear's native relation chip gives up real phone-readable value #tracker exists for, for no portability gain GitHub actually needs.

payload.title: Issue relations – Linear Docs
payload.finding: Four relation types: related, blocking, blocked, duplicate. No separate depends_on or hierarchy type distinct from these — blocking/blocked is the dependency pair. Once a blocking issue resolves, the relation auto-converts to related.

payload.title: REST API endpoints for issue dependencies — GitHub Docs
payload.finding: GET/POST/DELETE on /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{issue_number}/dependencies/blocked_by, plus GET .../dependencies/blocking. A directional prerequisite relationship, generally available, separate from sub-issues (parent/child hierarchy, GA since April 2025) and from plain 'relates to' links.

payload.text:
Researched both APIs. Findings, per edge type:

depends_on — both trackers have a real native match. Linear: blocking/blocked relation type (#linear-relations). GitHub: dedicated REST API, GET/POST/DELETE on .../dependencies/blocked_by, GA as of the 2026-03-10 API version (#gh-issue-deps). This is the strongest case for a native linkDependsOn verb — no fallback needed on either tracker.

alternative_to — no native match on either tracker. Linear's 'duplicate' relation looks close but is semantically different: a duplicate is the same work item reported twice, not a rejected design option kept for context. GitHub has nothing analogous. This one is plain-text-fallback only, on both trackers, always.

refines (as tree placement / hierarchy) — GitHub has a separate sub-issues API (parent/child, GA since April 2025), distinct from the dependencies API above. I did not confirm whether Linear has an equivalent parent/sub-issue mechanism separate from the four issue-relations types — linear.app/docs/issue-relations is scoped to relations only and did not mention one. Worth the implementer checking Linear's own sub-issue docs before deciding this edge type's mapping.

supported_by (evidence/citation) — no native concept on either tracker. Plain-text fallback only, same as alternative_to.

Not a decision, just groundwork: #tk-verbs-links stays decided as 'native relation + fallback' in principle. These findings are what 'native' actually resolves to per edge type, for whoever builds the adapter.

payload.title: Seven verbs are the whole contact with the outside

patch.body:
Skills must not know which tracker they talk to. Every call goes through the adapter.

linkDependsOn is the new one, added because depends_on has a real native match on both trackers — Linear's blocking/blocked relation, GitHub's dependencies/blocked_by REST API (see #linear-relations, #gh-issue-deps for the API detail).

alternative_to and supported_by get no verb. Neither tracker has a native match, so both fold into setBrief's body text as a plain links section instead.

refines, as hierarchy, is still open. GitHub has a native sub-issues API; whether Linear has an equivalent separate from its issue relations is unconfirmed. No verb added for it yet.
patch.why: getBrief, setBrief, addNote, setStage, listByStage, linkPR, linkDependsOn. A third tracker costs one file.

patch.body:
The tracker already has workflow states, so the gates need no new interface and there is nothing to catch in a terminal. It also means where a work item stands is a thing you can see.

Concrete mapping, per #st-gates: G1 approves the brief, G2 approves which option, G3 approves the pull request (and, per #st-merge, permits the merge). Each gate is one tracker-native state transition — a Linear workflow state or a GitHub label, per #tk-config's abstraction. #tk-verbs' setStage is the verb that would move a ticket between them; listByStage is how anything queries what is currently sitting at a given gate.

Scope, per #tk-ticket-kinds: gates only apply to a buildable ticket. A decision ticket has no gate at all — it closes on settle, no in-progress phase.

Approving from a phone means exactly what it sounds like: dragging a card between board columns in Linear, or changing a label on GitHub, both work from either tracker's mobile app. No custom UI to build for this.

payload.title: Something must read the gate move back — vi-backend's rule does not cover this
payload.why: vi-backend decided werk never reads the tracker back: an edit made directly in Linear or GitHub does not flow into the log. But a gate only means something if a move is detected and acted on. That reader is not werk's own map sync — vi-backend governs that specifically. The closest existing candidate is lp-overseer's 'a second process reads the event log in real time,' but that reads the log, not the tracker. Nothing yet names what actually polls the tracker for a gate move.

payload.title: Read the gate transition from the tracker itself
payload.why_not: Requires a read-back path #vi-backend already rejected: one-way publish only. Nothing names what would poll the tracker for a state move — the tracker would have to become the source of the gate signal instead of a mirror of it.

patch.why: Resolved by rejecting read-back entirely: the gate is not detected from the tracker, it is triggered internally, in werk's own log. The tracker only ever mirrors it afterward, so vi-backend's rule holds without exception.

payload.title: The gates are stage transitions in the log, published outward

patch.body:
Concrete mapping, per #st-gates: G1 approves the brief, G2 approves which option, G3 approves the pull request (and, per #st-merge, permits the merge). Each gate is a stage transition recorded in the log first. #tk-verbs' setStage then publishes the matching tracker state or label — Linear workflow state or GitHub label per #tk-config's abstraction. listByStage is how anything queries what is currently sitting at a given gate.

Approval itself happens through werk's own interface — the map or chat pane, a served web page, on a phone the same as any other browser tab — not by moving the ticket in the tracker. #tk-gates-readback settles why: the tracker is never read back, per #vi-backend, so nothing can be triggered by moving it there.

Cost, named plainly: the original appeal was zero new interface, using the tracker's own mobile app to approve. That is gone. Approving now needs werk's own UI reachable from a phone, not just the tracker's.

Scope, per #tk-ticket-kinds: gates only apply to a buildable ticket. A decision ticket has no gate at all — it closes on settle, no in-progress phase.
patch.why: Stages move internally, in the log, per #tracker and #vi-backend. The tracker's state or label updates to match afterward, one-way — a human sees where a work item stands without werk ever reading the tracker back.

A gate only means something on a buildable ticket, since only buildable tickets pass through stage transitions in the log at all. Decision tickets close on settle, no in-progress phase — publishing one as in-progress would misrepresent it, since nothing is being built for it. Buildable tickets keep the normal gate flow, published via #tk-verbs' setStage, and carry a label such as ready-for-agent so a human sees what's ready to pick up.

payload.title: Treat every ticket the same, no kind distinction
payload.why_not: A decision ticket would publish through the normal gate flow like a buildable one — in-progress, then done — misrepresenting it, since nothing is ever built for it.

payload.title: Execution scratch is per-branch and disposable. The worklog is branch-agnostic and durable

patch.body:
If you must judge it, or it must outlive the branch, it goes to the tracker, published one-way. If the loop must run it, it stays in the branch's scratch folder — delete it any time, re-running the loop rebuilds it from the worklog's last milestone, never from the tracker.

The worklog itself is not part of that disposable folder. It is the same durable log #pr-log and #vi-backend call the spine, stored somewhere a branch or worktree cleanup cannot reach. Losing it loses the only durable record — there is no tracker read-back to reconstruct it from.

The loop posts to the tracker only at milestones — entered the loop, rubric passed, blocked, done. A 200-cycle machine log would drown the ticket.
patch.why: The seam: durability goes to the worklog, kept branch-agnostic so deleting a branch's folder never touches it. Execution scratch stays local to the branch, disposable, rebuilt by re-running the loop. The tracker gets a one-way milestone publish; per #vi-backend, nothing is ever read back to reconstruct anything.

payload.title: One folder for both — scratch and the worklog together, per branch
payload.why_not: Deleting a finished branch's scratch folder would silently destroy the only durable record along with it. No tracker read-back exists to reconstruct it, per #vi-backend.

payload.title: The worklog is a durable, branch-agnostic, milestone-only log

patch.body:
The worklog posts to the tracker only at milestones — entered the loop, rubric passed, blocked, done — a one-way publish, per #tk-verbs' addNote. A 200-cycle machine log would drown the ticket if posted every cycle.

It is stored branch-agnostic, not inside whatever the branch's own working directory holds. Losing it loses the only durable record of a work item's progress — there is no tracker read-back to reconstruct it from, per #vi-backend.
patch.why: Durability and judgment go to the worklog and the tracker; nothing else needs a name here. A branch's commits, test runs, and tool calls already live in git and the coding agent's own session — werk owns none of that. Only the worklog is werk's to keep, and it must survive the branch being deleted.

patch.why_not: Deleting a finished branch would silently destroy the only durable record along with it. No tracker read-back exists to reconstruct it, per #vi-backend.

payload.title: A deterministic contract check gates decided, not creation
payload.why: AGENTS.md's rules (who, depends_on, rejected options) are prose only. Nothing enforces them, so the map can drift despite #pr-logic's own principle.

patch.body:
The gate lives inside cli.ts itself, not a Claude Code hook: a hook only works inside this harness, and #product already says the harness is temporary.

The gate fires only at the status -> decided transition. Card creation and proto stay free.

Three facts, each with an explicit escape hatch instead of a silent default:
- who is set.
- a depends_on edge exists, or --no-basis states none applies.
- an alternative_to option node exists, or --unchallenged states none was weighed.

Each failure prints the exact next command, so the agent can self-correct without Eryk in the loop.

This replaces the silent, after-the-fact guess fold.ts makes today (deriveUnchallenged): decided + who:you + no linked option. That guess cannot tell 'no option was weighed' from 'weighed but never written down.' Moving the same question to decide-time makes it a written record instead of an inference.

payload.title: Enforce with a Claude Code hook (PreToolUse/PostToolUse) instead of inside cli.ts
payload.why_not: A hook only works inside this harness. #product already rejects logic that can't ship with the product; a hook here repeats the exact mistake #pr-logic already rejected.

payload.title: A soft-nag hook flags a turn that settled something but was not logged
payload.why: A hook can check a mechanical fact, like whether the log grew. It cannot read whether the conversation actually decided anything. That needs judgment, which a hard gate cannot apply.

payload.text: Implemented in src/cli.ts and src/types.ts. status <id> decided now checks who, depends_on/--no-basis, and (who:you) alternative_to/--unchallenged, printing the exact fix command per missing fact. add --status decided is rejected outright, so decided is only reachable through the checked status command. edit gained --who, --no-basis, --unchallenged so a card can self-correct without being recreated. Reused the noBasis field already present in the imported log data but unwired until now; added noAlternative alongside it.

payload.title: The open-card announcement has no recovery path once it drops from context
payload.why: This session's whole visible conversation ran with the map open at #pr-logic. I was never told, because lastCard in agent.ts is state in the long-lived server process, set before my visible context began. There is no tool for the agent to ask which card is open right now.

payload.title: Send the full describe() block on every turn, not just on change
payload.why_not: Restores awareness but reverts the token-saving #werk-pane already decided. A one-line tag costs nearly nothing and still names the card, so the fix does not need to give that back.

patch.body:
src/agent.ts's send() sent describe() only when the open card changed (per #werk-pane). If the change happened before the agent's visible context — a resumed session, or a turn dropped by compaction — the agent had no way to learn or re-derive the open card. That happened this session: the pane sat on #pr-logic the whole time and the agent never knew.

Fixed: send() now always prepends something when a card is open. The full describe() block still fires only on change; every other turn gets tag(), a one-line '[still on #id — title]' reminder cheap enough to send always. AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md now say 'this card' or 'current' defaults to whatever that line names, unless Eryk gives a different id.

Verified: bun build src/agent.ts compiles clean.

payload.title: No log exists of tool-approval asks and decisions
payload.why: Eryk wants to review what gets asked and denied, to find patterns worth adding to the auto-approved rules. Nothing durable exists to review today.

patch.body:
Checked src/permission.ts and src/server.ts's /api/ask handling.

What persists today:
- .werk/allow.json (readAlways/addAlways) keeps only the rule pattern from an 'always' click. No timestamp, no link back to the call that produced it.

What does not persist:
- A one-time 'allow' or any 'deny': Asks.answer() resolves the promise and deletes the entry from an in-memory Map. Nothing is written anywhere.
- .werk/chat.jsonl records the tool call that ran and its result, but not how it was approved: auto-approved (read-only or already-covered), asked-and-allowed, or asked-and-denied.

So today there is no way to see what was asked, what was denied, or how often the same shape of call keeps asking. Reviewing that is exactly what would surface which patterns belong in READ_ONLY or in an --allow default.

Open: where this log should live (a new .werk/asks.jsonl, or fold into the existing log.jsonl as a new event type) and what it should record per ask: tool, label, input, decision, pattern, at.

payload.text: Implemented: ASKS_PATH = .werk/asks.jsonl (src/permission.ts). appendAsk(ask, decision) writes one line per resolved ask — tool, label, input, pattern, decision, at. Wired into server.ts's /api/ask right after asks.put() resolves, so a killed turn's forced deny is captured too. Only calls that actually reached the pane are logged; auto-approved calls never call appendAsk. Added to .gitignore alongside chat.jsonl, since it's local runtime history, not shared map data. Verified against a scratch log: a deny wrote one correct JSON line.

payload.title: Fold asks into log.jsonl as a new event type instead of a separate file
payload.why_not: log.jsonl is the shared decision map, replayed by fold(). An ask-and-decision is operational noise, not a card or an edge; mixing it in would make every fold() pay to skip past it and would put local approval history in the same file the map exports and imports.

payload.title: Merge Renderer and Bus into one Output interface
payload.why_not: No alternative Bus or Renderer is expected, so there is no pressure to merge them. Keeping them separate also avoids coupling Bus's durability requirement (an event can never be dropped) to Renderer's looser one (a dropped re-render is fine).

payload.title: Split AgentRuntime into a prompt-runner seam and a tool-execution seam now
payload.why_not: Codex is the planned second AgentRuntime, tried later, not now. Splitting the seam ahead of that evidence is the same guess-before-evidence risk this decision otherwise avoids.

payload.title: Name no interfaces until a second implementation of each exists
payload.why_not: Testing every seam against a real second implementation before deciding is a stretch. Tracker already has two planned (Linear, GitHub Issues). AgentRuntime will get Codex later. Bus and Renderer are not expected to need a second implementation at all.

patch.body:
AgentRuntime is Claude Code headless today, and the Claude Agent SDK later, with Codex as a further, harder test of vendor-independence (see #pr-iface:opt1). Bus is a JSONL file today, a real event store later — the append-only log that is the spine (#pr-log): every state change is one event, and it is the only thing Renderer and Tracker's outward publish ever read.

Four names, four jobs:
- Tracker: the external issue tracker (Linear, GitHub Issues). Seven verbs only — getBrief, setBrief, addNote, setStage, listByStage, linkPR, linkDependsOn (#tk-verbs). It is a one-way publish target; a change made directly in the tracker never writes back to the log (#tracker).
- AgentRuntime: whatever executes a work item. Given a task, it runs the agent and returns its events.
- Bus: the append-only event log. Every state change the loop controller makes becomes one event here, and nowhere else.
- Renderer: turns the Bus into something a human can see. The werk map today, something else later.

The loop controller in #pr-logic is the only code that calls all four. It reads a work item through Tracker, hands it to AgentRuntime, writes every step to Bus as it happens, and Bus is what both Renderer and Tracker's outward publish read from. No other code touches any of the four.

payload.title: Redirect to /dev/null made read-only chains ask
payload.why: cat/ls/grep with 2>/dev/null asked on every turn, even though nothing was written. Screenshots showed the same read-only command prompting twice in one session.
payload.body:
The splitter in permission.ts treated any redirect except fd>&fd as a write, so
`cat package.json; ls src/*.test.* 2>/dev/null; grep -n "test" package.json` came back
UNPARSED and asked, even though every command in the chain is in READ_ONLY.

Fix: the redirect regex now also accepts `/dev/null` as a target (permission.ts:116),
alongside the existing `&digit` / `&-` fd-to-fd case. `2>/dev/null` and `>/dev/null 2>&1`
no longer make a line unparsed.

Also added `Bash(node --check:*)` to READ_ONLY (permission.ts:214): it only parses a file
for syntax errors and never writes, so a syntax-check-then-report chain no longer asks
either.

Five new cases in permission.test.mjs cover both, including the exact chain from the
screenshots. `node src/permission.test.mjs` passes.

Two prompts in the same screenshots were not bugs and still ask: `npx playwright install`
(installs a browser) and `cp web/app.js /tmp/... && node --check ...` (cp writes to /tmp).
Both are real writes/installs; click Always in the pane if they recur often enough to be
worth a permanent rule.

payload.title: cd and sleep were not in READ_ONLY, so they asked too
payload.why: sleep 1; cd /tmp && node g3d-repro.mjs 2>&1 | tail -30 asked, even though node is already in the agent's default --allowedTools (Bash(node:*), agent.ts). cd and sleep matched no rule at all, so the whole line asked.
payload.body:
Neither command can change anything past the end of the Bash call it runs in: `cd` only
moves the subshell for that one call, `sleep` only waits. Added both to READ_ONLY
(permission.ts:239-241).

This is a different gap than #werk-devnull: that one was a redirect the splitter refused
to parse. This one is a command the splitter parsed fine, but no rule — not READ_ONLY, not
the agent's own default --allowedTools — named it.

New isApproved() test in permission.test.mjs runs the exact repro line against the agent's
real default rules (Bash(node:*) etc., from DEFAULT_TOOLS in agent.ts), not just against
READ_ONLY alone, since that is the real check path when a chain mixes a READ_ONLY command
with one only approved by --allowedTools. `node src/permission.test.mjs` passes.

payload.title: Recolor the selected node solid white
payload.why_not: It marks the node as picked, but throws away the one thing the whole feature is for: seeing the node's own status and kind color. Checking a card's type from the 3D view is exactly what breaks at the moment you click it. A white glow around the node marks the pick without erasing the color underneath.

payload.title: A line continuation after && hid the command that followed it
payload.why: A two-step add-then-link chain, written with && \ across lines the way the agent normally formats a multi-line card body, asked even though both halves are node src/cli.ts calls the agent is already approved for.
payload.body:
commands() treats `\` as 'hide the next character', so it kept both the backslash and the
newline in the token: `current += c + line[i+1]`. Real bash deletes a `\<newline>` outright
— it is a line join, not an escaped newline. Kept literally, the segment right after the
`&&` began with `\` and a newline instead of `node`, so `program()` never saw `node` at the
front and no `Bash(node ...)` rule matched it — the whole chain asked.

Fix: the backslash branch in permission.ts now special-cases `\` followed immediately by a
newline and drops both, before falling through to the general 'hide the next character'
case (permission.ts:88-97). Single-quoted content is untouched — that branch runs before
this one, and bash gives no special meaning to `\` inside single quotes either.

New isApproved() test in permission.test.mjs reproduces the shape: an add call, `&& \`,
newline, a link call — both node src/cli.ts, one rule, must not ask. `node
src/permission.test.mjs` passes.

Same family as #werk-devnull and #werk-cdsleep: a call built entirely from already-approved
commands still asked because the splitter mis-modeled one piece of real shell syntax. This
one lives in commands() itself rather than in the fixed READ_ONLY list, so it sits directly
under #werk-approve instead of under #werk-readonly.

patch.body:
Tracker adapter, state machine, event log, pipeline init. Then every work item we run adds the piece it needed. Nothing is thrown away later.

Concrete shape, four small files:

1. tracker.ts — one interface, six methods: getBrief, setBrief, addNote, setStage, listByStage, linkPR. tracker-linear.ts and tracker-github.ts implement it. No other file talks to Linear or GitHub directly.

2. state-machine.ts — one type: Stage = intent | options | building | merging | measuring | done | blocked. One function: transition(stage, event) -> stage. The tracker workflow state is the source of truth; this file only maps it to a Stage and checks a move is legal.

3. log.ts — append-only JSONL file, one line per event. One function: append(event). One command: pipeline events reads the file and prints it.

4. init.ts — the pipeline init command. Reads a conversation. Writes a brief (intent, why, success signal) to a new tracker issue through the Tracker interface. Sets the issue stage to intent. Appends one event to the log.

Call direction: init.ts calls tracker.ts and log.ts. state-machine.ts calls nothing. Nothing calls the CLI parser except the CLI parser.

Build order: tracker.ts first, with a fake in-memory tracker for tests. Real Linear and GitHub adapters after the shape is proven. Then state-machine.ts, then log.ts, then init.ts on top of all three.

payload.title: for-loop batch reads asked; the prescribed SYSTEM fix had never actually landed
payload.why: for id in ...; do echo ...; node src/cli.ts show $id 2>&1; echo; done asked, even though every real command inside it (echo, node src/cli.ts show) is already read-only on its own.
payload.body:
Not a permission.ts bug. for/do/done are shell keywords, not commands, so the splitter's
per-segment matching sees "for id in ...", "do echo ...", and "done" as unmatched commands
and asks. Teaching commands() to recognize these keywords would be unsafe with the current
prefix-matching design: rule matching is startsWith, and "do" is a prefix of "docker", "in"
is a prefix of "install"/"init". A bare do/in/done rule would silently approve commands that
only share a prefix with the keyword. Same reasoning permission.ts already gives for
refusing to parse a subshell: splitting shell control flow correctly is a parser's job, this
file does not try to be one.

#werk-approve-habits already diagnosed this exact class of self-inflicted friction and
recorded: "added two lines to SYSTEM in agent.ts telling the agent to use Edit/Write over
shelling out for a rewrite, and to run one node check per Bash call instead of chaining."
That text was never actually in agent.ts — grepped for it, not there. The decision was
right; the code change described on the card was never made.

Applied now: agent.ts SYSTEM tells the agent to run one command per Bash call, not to chain
with &&/;/a for loop, and to check several cards as several node src/cli.ts show calls
rather than one loop — each call is already free, a loop around them is not.

patch.body:
Tracker adapter, state machine, event log, pipeline init. Then every work item we run adds the piece it needed. Nothing is thrown away later.

Shape of three of the four pieces is decided elsewhere. This card points at them, it does not restate them:

- tracker.ts — verbs and adapters. Shape: #tk-verbs.
- state-machine.ts — gates as log transitions, published outward, never read back from the tracker. Shape: #tk-gates.
- log.ts — same append-only shape as werk's own log.jsonl, maybe the same file. Shape: #pr-log.

Only pipeline init has no card of its own yet: the init command that turns a conversation into a brief, writes it through tracker.ts, sets stage to intent, appends one log event.

Build order: tracker.ts first, with a fake in-memory tracker for tests. Real Linear and GitHub adapters after the shape is proven. Then state-machine.ts, then log.ts (or reuse fold.ts directly, per #pr-log), then init.ts on top of all three.

payload.text: Superseded by #werk-loopbody: a SYSTEM-prompt nudge is not enough, since the agent can ignore it. permission.ts now classifies the commands inside a for loop directly, so a read-only loop body no longer asks regardless of what the agent was told.

payload.title: The classifier looks inside a for loop instead of just seeing for/do/done
payload.why: The SYSTEM-prompt fix on #werk-forloop only asks the agent nicely not to use a for loop. It can still write one, and then the same prompt returns — the fix has to hold even when the instruction is ignored.
payload.body:
Added loopBody() to permission.ts. It recognizes exactly one shape: a header matching
`^for <name> in <word> <word> ...$` — a literal list, no quotes, no `$`, nothing a shell
would expand — followed by a body opening with a bare or same-line `do`, ending in a bare
`done`. Both anchors are checked end to end, not by prefix, so nothing resembling this
shape matches by accident, and `for id in $(cat /etc/passwd); do ...` still hits the
existing substitution check and returns UNPARSED before loopBody ever sees it.

This does not add a rule for the keywords themselves — that was rejected on #werk-forloop's
sibling reasoning: a prefix rule for `do` or `in` would also match `docker` or `install`.
Instead loopBody() strips only the loop's own punctuation (the header, the `do`, the
`done`) and hands the caller the body commands alone, once per line of the loop. Each still
has to pass the same READ_ONLY / approved-rules check as if it had been sent standalone.
A `for id in a b c; do rm -rf /$id; done` still asks — only the ceremony around an
already-approved body stops asking.

isReadOnly() and isApproved() both call loopBody() first and fall back to the raw parts
when it returns null, so every existing case (a plain command, a pipe, a chain) is
unaffected. Four new tests in permission.test.mjs cover both screenshots (semicolon- and
newline-separated) plus the two adversarial cases above. `node src/permission.test.mjs`
passes.

The #werk-forloop SYSTEM-prompt line stays — it costs nothing and helps a well-behaved
agent avoid the extra tokens of a loop-over-approved-calls — but it is no longer what makes
this safe.

payload.text: Generalized: loopBody() only recognized a loop that was the entire line (parts[0] must be the header). A real chain often runs a plain command first — node src/cli.ts show stages 2>&1; echo ---; for id in ...; do ...; done — and the loop still asked. Added unrollLoops(), which finds a for...done bracket anywhere in the parts list, unrolls just that bracket with loopBody(), and splices the body back in place, leaving what comes before and after untouched. isReadOnly()/isApproved() now call unrollLoops(parts) instead of loopBody(parts) ?? parts. New test covers the exact command-then-loop shape. node src/permission.test.mjs passes.

Reviewed 2026-09-09: mvp inherited PAUSED status only from its depends_on edges to stages and pr-now (both build-engine work, correctly paused). mvp itself was never reopened. Its own content — planning is the current focus — is not in question, so I ran 'rederive mvp' to clear the inherited pause. mvp is decided and active. The other planning cards (align, al-diff, al-profile, al-sample) are open/proto by normal progress, not paused.

payload.title: The CLI's own permission engine can replace src/permission.ts
payload.why: src/permission.ts hand-rolls a shell splitter, a READ_ONLY list and a rule matcher. It asks about read-only calls it does not recognise and waves through arbitrary script execution, because --allow already grants Bash(node:*), Bash(python3:*) and Bash(bun:*). The CLI has a real classifier for the same job.
payload.body:
Prototype, run against claude 2.1.235. It works.

Spawn the child with --permission-prompt-tool stdio next to the existing --input-format stream-json. The CLI then writes a control_request to stdout when its own permission engine cannot decide:

  {"type":"control_request","request_id":"...","request":{
     "subtype":"can_use_tool","tool_name":"Bash","input":{...},
     "description":"...","tool_use_id":"...",
     "decision_reason_type":"subcommandResults",
     "blocked_path":"/tmp/werk-probe-dir",
     "permission_suggestions":[
       {"type":"addRules","rules":[{"toolName":"Bash","ruleContent":"mkdir -p /tmp/werk-probe-dir"}],"behavior":"allow","destination":"localSettings"},
       {"type":"addDirectories","directories":["/tmp"],"destination":"session"},
       {"type":"setMode","mode":"acceptEdits","destination":"session"}]}}

The answer goes back on stdin, on the same pipe the turn already uses:

  {"type":"control_response","response":{"subtype":"success","request_id":"...",
    "response":{"behavior":"allow","updatedInput":{...},"updatedPermissions":[<a suggestion>]}}}

Deny is {"behavior":"deny","message":"...","interrupt":false}.

Three results measured, not read:

1. In --permission-mode auto the CLI asked nothing for 'ls /tmp | head -3', 'grep -c . /etc/hosts' and 'cat /etc/hosts | wc -l'. No READ_ONLY list was involved.
2. It did ask for 'curl -s https://example.com | head -3', for Write, and for 'mkdir -p /tmp/werk-probe-dir'.
3. Answering allow with the CLI's own addRules suggestion at destination:session stopped the second identical mkdir from asking. So 'Always allow' needs no patternFor heuristic — the button carries the rule the CLI itself proposes.

What this deletes from src/permission.ts: commands(), program(), subject() for matching, loopBody(), matches(), patternFor(), READ_ONLY, isReadOnly(), isApproved(), readAlways(), addAlways(), ALLOW_PATH. About 330 of its 400 lines. Asks, appendAsk and ASKS_PATH stay: the pane still needs a queue of open questions and the ask log.

What this deletes elsewhere: src/ask.ts, writeHookSettings() and .werk/hook-settings.json, the /api/ask HTTP route. The question arrives on the pipe agent.ts already reads, so no hook process and no loopback HTTP.

What it costs: the werk read commands (node src/cli.ts show|stale|events|inbox) lose their explicit READ_ONLY entries. The CLI classifies 'node ...' as script execution, so those will ask unless --allowedTools keeps a Bash(node src/cli.ts:*) rule. Keep that one rule; drop the list.

The three cards below this one describe the hand-rolled parser and will need reopening if this is adopted: #werk-prefix, #werk-readonly, #werk-devnull, #werk-cdsleep.

payload.text: Prototyped, 2026-09-09, claude 2.1.235. It works: --permission-prompt-tool stdio makes the CLI write a can_use_tool control_request to stdout and read the answer from stdin. This is the same pipe --input-format stream-json already uses, so no MCP server and no hook process is needed. Evidence and the wire format are on #werk-perm-native.

The doubt in this card's why is now settled. 'The raw can_use_tool control message' does work with --print. The stdio value of --permission-prompt-tool is not an MCP tool name; it routes the prompt over the control protocol instead. So alt-control and alt-prompttool are one option, not two. See #werk-perm-native.

payload.title: manual is the mode, not auto: the CLI asks about the path
payload.why: The mode decides everything now that werk classifies nothing. auto and manual were measured against the same ten calls, and they disagree about what a question is for.
payload.body:
Measured with claude 2.1.235, one command per turn, scratch working directory holding one file.

--permission-mode manual — the ask is about the PATH, not the command:
  free  cat inside.txt | wc -l
  free  grep -c . inside.txt
  free  git status
  free  ls | head -3
  ASK   cat /etc/hosts | wc -l      (outside the working directory)
  ASK   mkdir -p sub/one
  ASK   echo hi > /private/tmp/x
  ASK   curl ... https://example.com

--permission-mode auto — quieter, and much wider:
  free  everything above that manual allows, plus:
  free  npm install left-pad            (ran, package installed)
  free  mkdir -p /private/tmp/outside   (ran)
  free  echo pwned > /private/tmp/x     (ran)
  ASK   rm -rf sub                      (only when sub exists)
  ASK   curl ... https://example.com

manual wins on both counts.

1. It is not noisy. A read inside the repository is free, which is the whole complaint that started #werk-perm-native. It knows something READ_ONLY never could:  is free for a file in the repository and asks for /etc/hosts. The old list had one answer for  and no idea what it was reading.
2. auto stops asking about the calls that matter most. It ran npm install without a word. werk's old rules asked about that.

auto also has no widening to offer. Every ask it raised came back with an empty permission_suggestions, so the 'Always allow' button never appears. In manual every ask but the network one carried a suggestion.

acceptEdits sits between them: it allows a write but still asks about a read outside the working directory. That is the mode to pass when a session is mostly editing.

payload.title: Keep --permission-mode auto, the quietest mode
payload.why_not: Measured: auto ran npm install left-pad, mkdir outside the working directory and echo pwned > /private/tmp/x, each without a question. It also returns an empty permission_suggestions for the few calls it does stop, so the Always allow button never appears. Quieter is not the goal — asking about the right calls is.

payload.title: Keep the READ_ONLY list next to the CLI's engine, as a second opinion
payload.why_not: Two classifiers means the looser one wins on every call. The list would only ever widen what the CLI already decided, and the reason the list is being deleted is that it was wrong in both directions: it asked about a read it did not recognise and allowed Bash(node:*), which is arbitrary script execution.

payload.text: Deleted, 2026-09-09. The splitter and matches() are gone with the rest of the hand-rolled rules — see #werk-perm-native. Claude Code's own engine now decides, and it refuses a chained line for the same reason this card gave. Nothing in werk parses a shell line any more.

Deleted, 2026-09-09. READ_ONLY, isReadOnly() and isApproved() are gone — see #werk-perm-native. --permission-mode manual does this job and does it better: it asks about the path, not the command, so 'cat inside.txt' is free and 'cat /etc/hosts' asks. The list had one answer for cat and no idea what it was reading. Measurements on #werk-perm-mode.
Deleted with the splitter that caused it — see #werk-perm-native. There is no redirect handling in werk any more.
Deleted with READ_ONLY — see #werk-perm-native. cd and sleep are the CLI's business now.

patch.body:
The decision is unchanged: approval happens in the pane, and the mechanism holds the turn open while you read. What carries it changed on 2026-09-09 — see #werk-perm-native.

The path now:

1. The child runs with --permission-prompt-tool stdio, next to the --input-format stream-json flags it already had.
2. Claude Code's own permission engine decides first. A read inside the repository never reaches werk.
3. What it cannot resolve arrives on the child's stdout as a control_request with subtype can_use_tool. agent.ts reads it on the same pipe the turn already uses.
4. The server pushes the question to the pane over the existing SSE channel. The child stays blocked because nothing has been written to its stdin.
5. You click Allow once, Always allow, or Deny. Cmd+Enter allows, Escape denies.
6. agent.ts writes one control_response back on stdin with the same request_id, and the tool runs or does not.

There is no hook process, no MCP server and no loopback HTTP between the question and the pane. src/ask.ts, .werk/hook-settings.json and the /api/ask route are gone.

Always allow applies every widening suggestion the CLI attached to the question, at session scope, and keeps them in .werk/allow.json so the next child starts with them as --allowedTools and --add-dir. werk does not compose a rule of its own.

Two lists still decide without a click: --allow from the command line and .werk/allow.json. What is new is that werk hands both to the CLI to interpret instead of interpreting them itself.
patch.why: claude --print cannot prompt, so a call the CLI could not resolve came back as 'This command requires approval' and the turn carried on without it.

payload.text: Rewritten, 2026-09-09. The hook is gone; the CLI's own can_use_tool control request replaces it. The decision this card names did not change, so it is not reopened — but four cards below it described the hand-rolled parser and are now open and stale: #werk-prefix, #werk-readonly, #werk-devnull, #werk-cdsleep. #werk-hookschema is about a wire format werk no longer sends.

Invalidated, 2026-09-09. werk no longer sends a hook response of any shape. The wire is a control_response on the child's stdin: {type:'control_response',response:{subtype:'success',request_id,response:{behavior:'allow'|'deny',...}}}. See #werk-perm-native.

The shape changed with #werk-perm-native. asks.jsonl now records the CLI's own decision_reason_type per ask, and 'widened' holds the exact permission updates an Always click applied, not a rule werk invented. allow.json moved from a bare array of rules to {rules,dirs} — a bare array is still read.
Invalidated, 2026-09-09. commands() is deleted — see #werk-perm-native. werk no longer reads a shell line, so a line continuation is Claude Code's business.

payload.title: A card reference links, whatever form it is typed in
payload.why: The three forms Eryk kept seeing — bare al-diff, backtick al-diff, backtick #al-diff — only one of which rendered as a link.

patch.body: Fixed in web/md.js. cardLinks() now accepts a bare hyphenated/namespaced id (al-diff), not only a hashed one (#al-diff), because that shape never collides with ordinary prose. A backtick code span that is nothing but a card id — `al-diff` or `#al-diff` — now renders through the same path instead of staying a dead <code> span. All four forms of writing a reference now render as the identical #id link.

cardLinks() in web/md.js turns #card-id into <a href="#card-id">. The href is the hash route the map already uses, so a click needs no handler.

Only an id the map knows becomes a link. web/app.js passes knows(id), which checks G.byId. A dead reference stays plain text, so a link always lands somewhere.

Where it renders: the card body, the why line, the finding line, the notes thread, your own messages in the pane, and the agent's replies. Not the card summary in a grid tile, because that tile is a button and an anchor inside a button is invalid.

What it leaves alone:
- A code span with more than an id in it. `node src/cli.ts show #rollup` is a command, not a reference.
- A fenced block.
- A heading. `# rollup` needs a space, an id does not have one.
- A URL fragment. The character before the # must not be a word character or a slash.
- A bare single word with no hyphen or colon, hashless. align and loop are ordinary English words as often as they are ids, so only #align links, not align on its own.

Amended 2026-09-09 (#werk-refs, merged here): a bare id still links without the #, as long as it has a hyphen or a colon — al-diff, pr-iface:opt0 — because that shape never occurs in prose. A code span that is nothing but a card id — `al-diff` or `#al-diff` — links too, through the same check, instead of staying a dead <code> span. A command inside a code span still stays code, since the whole span has to be only the id.

md() also stopped running bold and italic inside a code span. Code spans are stashed before the other inline rules and restored last.

payload.title: Merged into #werk-reflink

patch.body:
The three forms Eryk kept seeing — bare al-diff, backtick al-diff, backtick #al-diff — only #al-diff rendered as a link.

Merged into #werk-reflink — the fix now lives there directly. Kept as a node only because the log is append-only; nothing links to or from it anymore.

payload.title: auto is the only mode, and there is no flag

patch.body:
werk runs `--permission-mode auto` and nothing else. `serve --permission-mode` is gone. PERMISSION_MODE in src/agent.ts is a constant, not a parameter.

What auto asks about, measured over 19 calls in three sweeps against claude 2.1.235:

  ASK   curl ... https://example.com          reason=rule, no suggestion

That is the whole list. Everything below ran without a question:

  cat inside.txt | wc -l · grep -c . inside.txt · git status · ls | head -3
  cat /etc/hosts | wc -l · mkdir -p sub/one · mkdir -p /private/tmp/outside
  echo pwned > /private/tmp/x · rm -rf <an existing directory> · chmod 777 .
  chmod -R 777 ... · npm install left-pad (installed) · sudo -n true
  ssh-keygen -t ed25519 ... · crontab -l · launchctl list · defaults write ...
  git push · git init && git add -A

Two consequences, both accepted:

1. The approval bar is network-only in practice. It is no longer the gate #werk-approve describes; it is a last stop for egress.
2. The 'Always allow' button never appears, because auto attaches no permission_suggestions to the one ask it makes. So alwaysFrom(), ruleStrings(), dirStrings() and everything .werk/allow.json keeps for the next child are unreachable in practice. The code stays — the CLI may attach a suggestion in a later release, and permission.test.mjs covers the translation — but nothing exercises it live.

The bound on the risk is that Edit and Write are already in DEFAULT_TOOLS (#werk-edits). The agent could always change any file in this repository without asking. auto widens what it can reach outside the repository, and it stops asking about a delete. It does not hand it a power it did not have here.

Read the trade the other way on #werk-perm-mode:opt0.
patch.why: A mode that is only ever set one way is a setting, not a choice. Eryk chose auto and had --permission-mode removed, so the pane's bar is the exception rather than the rule.

payload.title: manual, which asks about the path rather than the command

patch.why: Measured and recommended before Eryk chose auto. manual asks about the path, not the command: cat inside.txt is free, cat /etc/hosts asks, mkdir asks, a redirect outside the working directory asks. That is what the deleted READ_ONLY list was reaching for, and it knows something the list never could — whether the file is inside the working directory. Every ask but the network one carried a widening suggestion, so the Always allow button worked. Rejected because it still asks often enough to be a habit, and Eryk wants the bar to be rare. See #werk-perm-mode for what that costs.

payload.title: acceptEdits, between the two
payload.why: Measured: allows a write, still asks about a read outside the working directory. Rejected with manual on the same objection, with fewer asks. Eryk asked for one mode and no flag, so a middle setting has nowhere to live.

payload.text: Narrowed again, 2026-09-09. The mode is auto and there is no flag — see #werk-perm-mode. This card still describes the wire correctly, but not the reach: in practice the bar only stops a network call, and the Always allow button never appears because auto attaches no suggestion. Approval still happens in the pane. There is just far less of it.
