```json
        "destination": "localSettings"
      },
      {"type": "addDirectories", "directories": ["/tmp"], "destination": "session"},
      {"type": "setMode", "mode": "acceptEdits", "destination": "session"}
    ]
  }
}
```

The answer goes back on stdin, on the same pipe the turn already uses:

```json
{
  "type": "control_response",
  "response": {
    "subtype": "success",
    "request_id": "...",
    "response": {
      "behavior": "allow",
      "updatedInput": {...},
      "updatedPermissions": [<a suggestion>]
    }
  }
}
```

Deny is `{"behavior": "deny", "message": "...", "interrupt": false}`.

Three results measured before shipping:

1. In --permission-mode auto the CLI asked nothing for 'ls /tmp | head -3', 'grep -c . /etc/hosts' and 'cat /etc/hosts | wc -l'. No READ_ONLY list was involved.
2. It did ask for 'curl -s https://example.com | head -3', for Write, and for 'mkdir -p /tmp/werk-probe-dir'.
3. Answering allow with the CLI's own addRules suggestion at destination:session stopped the second identical mkdir from asking. So 'Always allow' needs no patternFor heuristic — the button carries the rule the CLI itself proposes.

What this cost: the werk read commands (node src/cli.ts show|stale|events|inbox) lost their explicit READ_ONLY entries. The CLI classifies 'node ...' as script execution, so those ask unless --allowedTools keeps a Bash(node src/cli.ts:*) rule. That one rule is kept; the list is dropped.

Three parts and no dependencies.

1. .werk/log.jsonl — the agent appends one event per decision, in the same turn.
2. src/fold.ts — folds the log into {nodes, edges} and derives stale and needsReview.
3. web/ — one view = one node, live over server-sent events.

Node 25 runs the TypeScript directly. There is no build step.
Seeded by importing decision-map-data.json: 154 nodes, 191 edges, 345 events.

#pr-log names the same append-only-log idea for the future standalone engine. werk's own log.jsonl is a separate, working implementation of it, not a consumer of pr-log's — pausing the engine does not pause the tool you are using to plan it.

payload.title: # triggers card search in the chat textarea, like / triggers commands
payload.why: Both now match a word starting with / or # anywhere in the text, not only at line start. A backtick right before the trigger character turns off the match, so inline code like `#id` or `/cmd` stays plain text.

payload.title: Several conversations at once, in tabs
payload.why: One turn blocks the pane. A second topic has to wait for the first to finish.
payload.body:
The problem: a turn takes minutes. Eryk has a second topic ready and no place to put it.

Two wins, not one:
1. Throughput. Start topic B while topic A runs.
2. Tokens. A forked conversation carries only what its branch needs, and shares a cached prefix with its parent.

Five sub-decisions, each its own card: how a conversation starts (#werk-mc-fork), what binds it (#werk-mc-split), the gesture that opens one (#werk-mc-open), the tab strip (#werk-mc-tabs), and what happens to an old tab (#werk-mc-park).

The one Eryk did not name, and the one that decides whether this works at all: two live conversations both write to the map. See #werk-mc-shared.

payload.text: #werk-multichat reopens the scope of this card. 'Never resets' stays true. 'One' does not: the pane would hold several conversations, one visible at a time. Nothing decided yet.

payload.title: Fork the session, do not start it empty
payload.why: Claude Code supports --fork-session. A fork keeps the shared prefix, so the cache still hits.
payload.body:
Measured, not guessed: `claude --help` lists

    --fork-session   When resuming, create a new session ID (only works with --resume or --continue)

So `claude --resume <parent-id> --fork-session` gives a child that starts with the parent's full history and its own id. The parent keeps running. This is exactly the operation the feature needs, and werk already stores a session id per conversation (SESSION_PATH in src/agent.ts).

What a fork costs. Prompt caching is keyed on the token prefix, not on the session id. So while the parent's cache block is warm, the fork's first turn reads it at cache-read price. After the TTL expires, the fork pays full input price once to rewrite it. A fresh context pays less on turn 1 and then pays again to re-read every file the parent already read.

What a fork does NOT get: anything the parent says after the split. The two histories diverge and never rejoin. That is the point of #werk-mc-shared.

Prototype question, and the reason this is who:prototype: does a fork of a 100k-token conversation actually hit the cache, or does the CLI rewrite the prefix and bill it as new input? One run with two `--print` calls answers it. About 20 minutes.

An empty context is still the right start for a topic with no relation to the parent. Make it the second button, not the default. See #werk-mc-fork:opt0.

payload.title: A fresh, empty context for every new conversation
payload.why_not: Cheapest on turn one and worst by turn five. The new conversation re-reads the same repository files, the same card bodies, and the same CLAUDE.md the parent already holds. It also loses the thing that makes the split worth doing: the shared understanding built up so far. Keep it as an explicit second button for an unrelated topic.

payload.title: A conversation has a home card, not a subtree boundary
payload.why: Focus is a label, not a fence. A conversation crosses subtrees whether you allow it or not.
payload.body:
Eryk's two options were 'arbitrary split' and 'per-subtree focus'. Neither, exactly. Take the third:

A conversation records the card that was open when it started. That id is its name, its tab label, and the seed context sent on its first turn. It is not a fence. The conversation may navigate anywhere, and the pane keeps sending the open card on every turn, as it does today.

Why not a real subtree fence: this very conversation opened at #root and is now writing under #werk-chat. A fence would have blocked it or forced a switch. The map's tree is where a card sits; it is not where a thought stays.

What the home card buys, with no fence:
- The tab reads '#werk-mc-fork' instead of 'Chat 3'.
- Two tabs on the same home card are visibly a mistake.
- The fold can compute what changed under that card since the fork point. See #werk-mc-shared.

payload.title: Per-subtree focus: a conversation is bound to one subtree
payload.why_not: The map cannot enforce it and Eryk would fight it. A conversation that starts at #werk-chat and needs to check #vi-prop is normal, not an error. A fence turns that into a tab switch or a refusal. The one real benefit of a fence — scoped context, fewer tokens — is already bought by the fork point, without the cost.

payload.title: The map is the only shared state between forks
payload.why: Two forks never see each other's messages. They both write the same log. That is a conflict unless the map is treated as the channel.
payload.body:
Nobody named this and it decides whether the feature works.

Two facts collide:
1. A fork's history freezes at the split. Tab A never hears a word tab B says.
2. Both tabs run `node src/cli.ts add|status|link` against the same .werk/log.jsonl.

So tab B can decide #x while tab A still believes #x is open, and tab A will happily contradict it. Worse, tab A's stale copy of a card body is exactly the failure CLAUDE.md already warns about with #pr-now and #tk-verbs — but now it happens live, between two agents, not across weeks.

Three ways out, in order of preference:

1. **Re-seed on focus.** When a tab becomes visible, or before its next turn, werk sends a diff: 'these cards changed since your fork point: ...'. The fold already has the sequence numbers to compute this. Cheap, no locking, and it makes the map the channel — which is the tool's whole thesis. #vi-overwrite says the map is overwritten, not appended; this is the same idea applied to a conversation's memory of it.
2. **Write lock on the log.** Only the focused tab may run a write command. Simple, but a background turn that reached a decision then cannot record it, and CLAUDE.md's 'in the same turn' rule breaks.
3. **Nothing.** Let them collide. The log is append-only so no write is lost, but the fold takes the last event and the loser never knows. Not acceptable for a tool whose product is the record.

Option 1 is the recommendation. It needs a prototype to size: how large is the diff after ten minutes of a parallel tab, and does it confuse the model more than it helps.

payload.title: A tab strip of card-id chips above the composer
payload.why: Tabs are the only shape that fits. The map already carries the titles, so the chips can be short.
payload.body:
Eryk ruled out a vertical list (too much space) and an auto-collapsing sidebar (disturbing). Agreed, both. See #werk-mc-tabs:opt0.

The shape that fits werk specifically: the tab label is a card-id chip, not a title. '#werk-mc-fork', '#vi-prop', '#root'. Short, monospace, and it already looks like a #card-id link, which the pane renders everywhere else (#werk-reflink). Four or five fit on one row at pane width. A title would fit one.

Each chip carries state, because the reason for the feature is that a background turn is running:
- a pulsing dot: that tab's turn is running
- a solid dot: that tab finished while you were away, unread
- nothing: idle and read

Two shapes worth considering before this is decided:
1. **Chips, always visible.** What is described above.
2. **No strip at all.** The chat pane header shows only the active conversation, and Cmd+K opens a switcher listing every conversation. Zero pixels when you have one conversation, which is most of the time. But a running background turn becomes invisible, and that is the state you most need to see.

Shape 1, unless the strip proves noisy at one conversation. It can hide itself when the count is one.

payload.title: A vertical conversation list, or an auto-collapsing sidebar
payload.why_not: Eryk rejected both. A vertical list costs width the pane does not have, next to a map that needs the rest of the screen. An auto-collapsing sidebar moves under the cursor, so every switch is a hover-and-wait. A horizontal strip costs one row of height and never moves.

payload.title: Shift+click forks. A plain click still navigates.
payload.why: Navigating the map is the common act. It must stay free.
payload.body:
Eryk's two options:
1. Shift+click a card link: navigate AND open a new tab.
2. Plain click: open a new tab by default.

Option 2 is wrong, and the reason is in this session. Eryk navigates constantly while one turn runs — that is what the '[the map is now at #id]' line exists for. Under option 2 every one of those clicks would have spawned a fork. He would end the hour with thirty tabs and no way to say 'stay here, keep talking'.

Option 1 is right, with one change: Shift+click should NOT also move the main view. It forks in the background and leaves you where you are. Otherwise the gesture does two things and you can never do just one.

So three gestures, learnable:
- click            -> the map goes there. The conversation follows, as today.
- Shift+click      -> a background fork rooted at that card. The map does not move.
- Shift+click again on the same card -> switches to that tab. It does not fork twice.

There is a second entry point that costs nothing: a '+' at the end of the tab strip forks at whatever card is open now. Same operation, no card link needed.

payload.title: A plain click on a card link opens a new tab by default
payload.why_not: It taxes the gesture Eryk uses most. He clicks through the map continuously while a turn runs, and every one of those clicks would fork. It also removes the ability to say 'stay in this conversation, I am just looking' — which is the normal case, not the exception.

payload.title: Park an idle tab. Nothing is ever closed.
payload.why: A Claude Code session lives on disk. Closing a tab should hide it, not end it.
payload.body:
Eryk is right that this is the crux. A tab strip with fifteen chips is worse than no tabs.

The rule, in three parts:

1. **A cap on visible chips.** Five. The sixth fork parks the least-recently-touched idle tab. A tab with a running turn is never parked.
2. **Parked is not closed.** The strip ends with a '...' menu listing every parked conversation: home card, last message time, unread dot. Clicking one un-parks it and parks whatever is now least recent. The session id is on disk, so un-parking is a `--resume`, not a restart.
3. **No explicit close button, at first.** There is nothing to close. If a conversation is done it goes idle and drifts into the menu on its own. Add an explicit 'forget' later only if the menu gets long enough to be useless.

Who: me. Every part of this is reversible and none of it is visible in the record. The cap of five is a number to try, not a decision to defend.

The one thing that is not mine to pick: whether a parked conversation's child process is killed. Killing it frees memory and costs a resume on wake. Keeping it alive costs nothing but memory. Start by killing it — #werk-resume already proves a resume is transparent.

payload.title: Cross-tab memory is pulled from the session logs, not pushed into context

patch.body:
Eryk decided the direction. A fork that does not know what its sibling said is not a bug to fix. It is the normal state, and the fix is a search, not a broadcast.

Two channels, both pull, neither push:

1. **State — the map.** Tab A's context can say #x is open while tab B decided it. That is harmless, because no agent answers from its context: it runs `node src/cli.ts show <id>` before it writes. The map on disk is always current. This is already how every turn works today, so it needs no new mechanism at all.

2. **What was said — the session log.** `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl`, one file per session, complete, including turns compaction dropped. Eryk's global CLAUDE.md already carries the `prior-conversations` skill for exactly this, and it already handles the hard part: it groups worktrees by git origin and strips tool noise.

    SCRIPT=~/.claude/skills/prior-conversations/scripts/convo-search.py
    python3 "$SCRIPT" search "keyword" "another"
    python3 "$SCRIPT" show <session-id> --grep "keyword" --context 3

werk can do better than that skill, and should. The skill guesses which session to read from keywords. werk *knows*: it writes the session id for every conversation itself (SESSION_PATH in src/agent.ts). So it can hand the agent an exact list of sibling conversations and their home cards, and skip the search-and-hope step. See #werk-mc-recall.

What this rejects: feeding a tab a 'here is what changed since your fork' diff on focus. See #werk-mc-shared:opt0.
patch.why: Eryk: a stale sibling is fine. When one conversation needs another, it searches the session log on disk instead of being fed a diff.

payload.title: Push a 'what changed since your fork' diff into a tab when it gets focus
payload.why_not: It pays on every switch for something that is needed on a few of them. It also fights the tool's own model: the map on disk is the current state, so an agent that reads a card before writing it is never wrong, whatever its context believes. A diff would only be re-telling the agent something it can look up. Pull beats push here because the need is rare and the lookup is exact.

payload.title: Two CLI verbs let a tab read its siblings: convos and recall
payload.why: werk already stores every conversation's session id. It can point straight at the file the prior-conversations skill would have to search for.
payload.body:
Logic in a program, not in a markdown skill — CLAUDE.md rule 1. The prompt gets two lines; the program does the work.

    node src/cli.ts convos
      #werk-mc-fork   session 8f21ac3e   12 turns   last 4m ago   running
      #vi-prop        session b0d94417   31 turns   last 26m ago  parked

    node src/cli.ts recall <card-id|session> --grep "cache" --context 3

`recall` resolves the home card to a session id, builds the path
`~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl`, and prints the matching exchange with the noise stripped. werk knows the cwd and it wrote the session id, so there is no search step and no wrong-worktree failure mode.

Two sources to read, and this is the prototype question:

1. **The Claude Code jsonl.** Complete. Has tool calls, thinking, and everything compaction dropped. Noisy.
2. **werk's own chat.jsonl.** Already the shape the pane shows, already tagged with the card each message was sent under (see the `card` field on ChatMessage in src/agent.ts). Cleaner, but it drops what the sibling *did*, only what it said.

Guess: `recall` reads chat.jsonl by default and takes `--tools` to fall back to the raw jsonl. Worth 30 minutes to check that chat.jsonl alone answers the questions Eryk actually asks a sibling about.

Reuse, do not rewrite: `~/.claude/skills/prior-conversations/scripts/convo-search.py` already parses this format and strips system-reminder and tool-result noise. Shell out to it with an exact `show <session-id>` before writing a second parser.

patch.body:
Logic in a program, not in a markdown skill — CLAUDE.md rule 1. The prompt gets two lines; the program does the work.

    node src/cli.ts convos
      #werk-mc-fork   session 8f21ac3e   12 turns   last 4m ago   running
      #vi-prop        session b0d94417   31 turns   last 26m ago  parked

    node src/cli.ts recall <card-id|session> --grep "cache" --context 3

`recall` resolves the home card to a session id, builds the path
`~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl`, and prints the matching exchange with the noise stripped. werk knows the cwd and it wrote the session id, so there is no search step and no wrong-worktree failure mode.

## Which file recall reads

Two candidates, and the difference is smaller than it first looks.

**werk's own chat.jsonl already keeps tool calls and their results.** Measured on this session's file: 28 tool entries, 27 results. It is not a text-only log. So the choice is not 'said' against 'did'. It is how much detail survives, and it loses detail in exactly two places, both in src/agent.ts:

1. `label()` (src/agent.ts:705) flattens a tool call to one line. A Bash call keeps its whole command — which is nearly everything werk's own agent runs, so a sibling's every `node src/cli.ts add ...` is there in full, flags and body text included. A non-Bash call keeps the name and one field. `Edit src/agent.ts` tells you the file was edited. It does not tell you what changed.
2. A tool result is cut to 4000 characters (src/agent.ts:549). On this session: 3 of 28 results hit that cap, so 11 percent are truncated.

**The raw Claude Code jsonl** loses nothing, and costs the noise the `prior-conversations` script exists to strip.

So the lean is chat.jsonl by default, with `--raw` to fall back. The one question a sibling will ask that chat.jsonl cannot answer is 'what did that edit actually change', and for a conversation whose work is the map rather than the code, that is rare.

Prototype, about 30 minutes: run `recall` over an existing werk session both ways, ask the same three questions of each, and count how often the flattened Edit label loses the answer.

Reuse, do not rewrite: `~/.claude/skills/prior-conversations/scripts/convo-search.py` already parses the raw format and strips system-reminder and tool-result noise. Shell out to its `show <session-id>` for the `--raw` path before writing a second parser.

Built. src/convos.ts and two verbs in src/cli.ts.

    node src/cli.ts convos
    #root                813bff8f    4 turns  just now   We build and fix software...  now at #werk-mc-shared

    node src/cli.ts recall <#card|session|name> [--grep "term" ...] [--context 2] [--tail 20]
                                                [--tools] [--thinking] [--max-chars 2000] [--raw]

## What it does

`convos` lists every conversation with its home card, session id, turn count, and last activity. `recall` resolves a reference — a conversation name, a session id or prefix, or a card id — to one transcript and prints it. An ambiguous card id is an error, not a guess: two conversations on one card is a mistake worth seeing.

`--grep` takes case-insensitive regexes and may repeat. A message must match all of them. `--context` prints messages either side of a hit.

## The two sources, both wired

Default is werk's own chat.jsonl. Tool calls and results are in it but hidden unless you pass `--tools`, because they are most of the file.

`--raw` shells out to `~/.claude/skills/prior-conversations/scripts/convo-search.py show <session-id> --include-tools`. No second parser. That script already strips system-reminder noise and finds the file from a session prefix. If it is not installed, `--raw` fails with the transcript's own path so the work is not blocked.

## The prototype question, answered by building both

There was no need to choose. chat.jsonl is the default because it is clean and already card-tagged; `--raw` is one flag away when a flattened `Edit` label hides the answer.

## Forward layout

`listConvos` reads `.werk/conversations/<name>/{session,chat.jsonl}`, and also lists today's single conversation — `.werk/session` plus `.werk/chat.jsonl` — under the name `main`. So this works before #werk-multichat exists and keeps working after, with no migration.

## The prompt side

SYSTEM in src/agent.ts now tells the agent these verbs exist and, more importantly, tells it never to answer 'I have no access to the other conversation'. That is a launch flag, so a running child keeps the old prompt until it restarts.

payload.title: A permission ask names its tab, and a background ask still stops you
payload.why: There is one ask bar and one Asks instance. A second child would block on a question nobody can see.
payload.body:
This is the gap that breaks the feature, not a polish item.

Today: server.ts:144 makes one `Asks`, hands it to one `Agent`, and app.js:448 renders one bar. An ask carries a tool name and a label. It does not carry a conversation, because there has only ever been one.

With two children, a background tab's `can_use_tool` request arrives, the bar shows it with no hint of where it came from, and the child sits blocked. If the bar showed only the active tab's asks, the background child would block silently and forever — the exact failure the feature is meant to prevent, since the point of a background tab is that it runs while you look away.

So two decisions, and the second is the real one:

1. **Every ask carries its conversation.** Not optional. The bar prefixes the card-id chip: '#vi-prop · Bash wants to run'. Mechanical.
2. **What a background ask does to you.** Three settings:
   - **Show it in the shared bar, do not switch.** Every tab's asks queue in one bar, each labelled. You answer without leaving what you are doing. The blocked tab's chip pulses.
   - **Badge only.** The chip marks 'waiting'; the bar stays yours alone. You must switch to answer. Quieter, and it is how a background turn should behave — but a tab you forget stays blocked, and you have no idea what it wanted.
   - **Pull focus.** The tab that asks takes the pane. Never: it destroys the thing being protected.

Recommendation: the shared labelled queue. A permission question is the one interruption that is always worth showing, because nothing moves until it is answered, and answering it takes one keypress — app.js:504 already binds Enter to allow and Escape to deny.

The unresolved part of that recommendation: with two asks queued from two tabs, Enter is now ambiguous. Either the shortcut applies to the top of the queue only, or it is disabled while more than one ask is open. Lean to the first, and make the top one visibly the target.

payload.title: Switching tab moves the map to that conversation's card
payload.why: The pane and the map must agree on the subject, or the '[the map is now at #id]' line becomes a lie.
payload.body:
Nobody named this and every tab switch hits it.

A conversation tracks two cards: the one it started at (`home`) and the one it last spoke about (`at`). `node src/cli.ts convos` already prints both. When you click tab B, does the main view jump to B's `at`?

**Yes, it should.** The chat pane's whole contract is that the open card is the subject — src/agent.ts:674 prepends '[the map is now at #id]' to every turn. If tab B is a conversation about #vi-prop and the map is showing #werk-mc-park, then B's next turn tells the agent the subject is #werk-mc-park, and the conversation silently changes topic. Not a display problem: a correctness problem in the prompt.

The cost is that the map moves under you when you switch. That is the right cost. You switched conversations; the subject changed; the map should say so.

Two consequences worth naming:

1. **Switching back restores the other tab's card.** Each conversation owns its position. Navigating the map inside a tab updates only that tab's `at`.
2. **Shift+click must not move the map** — already decided on #werk-mc-open. It forks in the background, so the new tab gets a `home` and an `at` without stealing your view. The two rules agree: the map follows the *focused* conversation, and a background fork is not focused.

payload.title: Switching tab leaves the map where it is
payload.why_not: It splits the subject in two. The pane prepends the open card to every turn (src/agent.ts:674), so a tab resumed under someone else's card would be told the wrong subject and would follow it. The saving — the map does not move — is worth less than a conversation that stays about what it is about.

payload.title: The map marks a card that has a live conversation on it
payload.why: The map is the primary view. A tab strip only tells you about conversations while you are looking at the strip.
payload.body:
The tab strip lives in the chat pane. The map is the bigger surface and the one Eryk reads. So the map should carry the same state the chips carry.

A card with a conversation homed on it gets a small mark, using the same three states as the chip on #werk-mc-tabs: running, finished-unread, idle. Clicking the mark switches to that tab instead of navigating.

What this buys, and why it is not decoration: it answers 'what is running right now' from the view you are already in, and it makes a duplicate visible — two conversations homed on one card show as one mark with a count, which is the mistake #werk-mc-split says is worth seeing.

Where the mark goes is open: on the card header in the detail view, on the child rows in the 'below' list, or both. Both, probably, since a running conversation two levels down is the one you would otherwise miss.

Who: me. It is presentation, it is reversible, and it leaves no trace in the record.

payload.text: Keyboard, folded in here rather than given its own card. Cmd+1 to Cmd+5 select a chip by position; Cmd+[ and Cmd+] step through them. Position beats stepping as the primary, because the strip is capped at five (#werk-mc-park) and a fixed position is learnable. app.js already owns a global keydown handler for the ask bar (app.js:501), so this is one more branch, not new machinery.

patch.body:
The problem: a turn takes minutes. Eryk has a second topic ready and no place to put it.

Two wins, not one:
1. Throughput. Start topic B while topic A runs.
2. Tokens. A forked conversation carries only what its branch needs, and shares a cached prefix with its parent.

## The sub-decisions

Mechanics:
- #werk-mc-fork — fork the session, do not start it empty
- #werk-mc-split — a conversation has a home card, not a subtree boundary
- #werk-mc-shared — cross-tab memory is pulled, not pushed (decided; #werk-mc-recall is built)

Interface:
- #werk-mc-open — Shift+click forks, a plain click still navigates
- #werk-mc-tabs — a strip of card-id chips above the composer
- #werk-mc-park — park an idle tab, close nothing
- #werk-mc-follow — switching tab moves the map to that conversation's card
- #werk-mc-asks — a permission ask names its tab, and a background ask still stops you
- #werk-mc-live — the map marks a card that has a live conversation on it

Build #werk-mc-asks first, whatever else changes. One `Asks` and one bar (server.ts:144, app.js:448) means a second child can block on a question nobody can see. Everything else on this list degrades gracefully; that one does not.

payload.title: Badge the chip only. A background ask waits until you switch to that tab.
payload.why_not: Quieter, and it keeps a background turn genuinely background — but a tab you forget stays blocked with no sign of what it wanted. A permission question is the one interruption where nothing moves until it is answered, so hiding it costs more than showing it.

payload.title: The tab that asks pulls the pane to itself
payload.why_not: It destroys the thing the feature protects. You start a background task so it can run while you look away; a question that yanks you out of the conversation you are in is worse than the wait it replaces.

payload.title: One shared ask queue. Every ask names its tab. Nothing steals focus.

patch.body:
Eryk decided this. It is also the gap that would break the feature, not a polish item.

Today: server.ts:144 makes one `Asks`, hands it to one `Agent`, and app.js:448 renders one bar. An ask carries a tool name and a label, not a conversation, because there has only ever been one.

## What is decided

1. **Every ask carries its conversation.** The bar prefixes the card-id chip: '#vi-prop · Bash wants to run'.
2. **One shared queue, whatever tab asked.** You answer without leaving the conversation you are in. The blocked tab's chip pulses until you do.
3. **No focus stealing.** See #werk-mc-asks:opt1.

Rejected: badging the chip and making you switch to answer (#werk-mc-asks:opt0). A forgotten tab would stay blocked with no sign of what it wanted.

## The one part still open

app.js:504 binds Enter to allow and Escape to deny. With two asks queued from two tabs, that is ambiguous. Either the shortcut applies to the head of the queue only, or it is disabled while more than one ask is open.

Lean to the head of the queue, with the head visibly the target — a border, not just first position. Disabling the shortcut punishes the common case (one ask) for the rare one.

payload.title: Cmd+1 to Cmd+5 select a tab by position
payload.why: The strip caps at five, so a fixed position is learnable. Stepping is not.
payload.body:
Eryk decided this.

Cmd+1 through Cmd+5 select the chip in that position. Position, not recency: a chip that moves would make the shortcut unlearnable, so the strip must keep a stable order (insertion order, not last-touched).

That constrains #werk-mc-park. Parking the least-recently-touched tab reorders the strip. It must remove a chip and close the gap, never reshuffle the survivors.

Cmd+[ and Cmd+] step to the previous and next chip. Kept as a secondary, not the primary — see #werk-mc-keys:opt0.

app.js already owns a global keydown handler for the ask bar (app.js:501), so this is one more branch, not new machinery.

payload.title: Cmd+[ and Cmd+] stepping only, with no positional shortcut
payload.why_not: Stepping needs you to know where you are and count. With a cap of five, a fixed position is one keypress from anywhere and needs no counting. Stepping stays as a secondary binding; it just is not the primary.

payload.title: The conversation owns the card. The map follows the focused tab.

patch.body:
Eryk decided this, and his framing is better than the one this card started with. The difference is the direction of the arrow.

Today the map owns the position and the scope chip above the composer reflects it: map -> chip. With tabs it inverts. The conversation owns its card; focusing a tab sets both the chip and the main view: tab -> (chip, map).

Why it is not cosmetic. src/agent.ts:674 prepends '[the map is now at #id]' to every turn. A tab resumed while the map still shows the previous tab's card would be told the wrong subject, and it would follow it. The conversation would change topic without either of you deciding to.

## What follows from the inversion

1. **Each conversation keeps its own position.** Navigating the map inside a tab updates only that tab's card. Switching away and back restores it.
2. **A background fork does not move the map.** Already decided on #werk-mc-open: Shift+click forks and leaves you where you are. The two rules agree, because the map follows the *focused* conversation and a background fork is not focused.
3. **A draft belongs to its tab.** Text typed in the composer and not sent must survive a switch, because it was written under that tab's card. Otherwise the inversion is half done: the scope moves with the tab but what you were saying about it does not.

Point 3 is the only thing not visible in the screenshot, and the only part Eryk did not name. It is small and it is who:me.
patch.why: Eryk: the scope shown above the composer must be the tab's card, not the previous tab's. So the map must move.

payload.text: Constraint from #werk-mc-keys, now decided: Cmd+1..5 selects by position, so the strip order must be stable. Parking a tab may remove its chip and close the gap. It must never reshuffle the survivors, so the strip is in insertion order, not last-touched order.

#werk-mc-follow is decided: the conversation owns the card and the map follows the focused tab. That settles what a marker click does here — it focuses that tab, and the map then moves to that tab's card as a consequence. It is not a second navigation rule.

payload.title: Shift+click forks in the background and leaves the map where it is
payload.why_not: It was the earlier recommendation and Eryk reversed it, correctly. It makes one gesture move the view and the other not, which is two rules to learn. Since a focused tab moves the map to its own card (#werk-mc-follow), and the new tab's card is the one you just clicked, focusing the fork lands you exactly where the click pointed. Nothing is lost: the conversation you left keeps running its turn while you are away, which is the whole point of the feature.

payload.title: Shift+click forks and goes there. A plain click still navigates.

patch.body:
Eryk decided this, and reversed the earlier recommendation of a background fork. See #werk-mc-open:opt1.

## The three gestures

    click              the map goes there. This conversation follows, as today.
    Shift+click        a fork rooted at that card, focused. The map goes there too.
    Shift+click again  on a card that already has a tab: switches to it. It does not fork twice.

Both gestures move the view to the card you clicked. That is one rule, not two. The difference between them is only whether a new conversation starts there.

Nothing is added by the fork moving the view: it follows from #werk-mc-follow. Focusing a tab moves the map to that tab's card, and the fork's card is the one under the cursor. So this card does not introduce a navigation rule; it just says the fork is focused rather than backgrounded.

## Why the throughput is not lost

Leaving a conversation does not pause it. The turn you started in tab A keeps running while you are in tab B. That is the feature. What you give up by focusing the fork is the ability to *read* A while B starts, and that is worth one keypress — Cmd+1, see #werk-mc-keys.

## Second entry point

A '+' at the end of the tab strip forks at whatever card is open. Same operation, no card link needed, and the map does not move because you are already there.

Rejected: a plain click opening a tab by default (#werk-mc-open:opt0). It taxes the gesture Eryk uses most.
patch.why: Both gestures land on the card you clicked. The only difference is whether a new conversation starts there.

## What follows from the inversion

1. **Each conversation keeps its own position.** Navigating the map inside a tab updates only that tab's card. Switching away and back restores it.
2. **A fork is focused, so a fork moves the map.** This card is why. #werk-mc-open depends on it and states the gesture. An earlier draft of this card claimed the opposite — that a background fork leaves the map alone — and Eryk reversed it: one rule for both gestures beats two.
3. **A draft belongs to its tab.** Text typed in the composer and not sent must survive a switch, because it was written under that tab's card. Otherwise the inversion is half done: the scope moves with the tab but what you were saying about it does not.

Point 3 is the only part Eryk did not name. It is small and it is who:me.

Eryk decided this. It is also the gap that would break the feature, not a polish item.

Today: server.ts:144 makes one `Asks`, hands it to one `Agent`, and app.js:448 renders one bar. An ask carries a tool name and a label, not a conversation, because there has only ever been one.

## What is decided

1. **Every ask carries its conversation.** The bar prefixes the card-id chip: '#vi-prop · Bash wants to run'.
2. **One shared queue, whatever tab asked.** You answer without leaving the conversation you are in. The blocked tab's chip pulses until you do.
3. **No focus stealing.** See #werk-mc-asks:opt1.
4. **Enter and Escape act on the head of the queue.** app.js:504 binds them today and two queued asks would make them ambiguous. The head is the target, and it is visibly the target — a border, not just first position. Disabling the shortcut while more than one ask is open was the alternative; it punishes the common case of one ask for the rare case of two.

Rejected: badging the chip and making you switch to answer (#werk-mc-asks:opt0). A forgotten tab would stay blocked with no sign of what it wanted.

Confirmed. `--fork-session` hits the cache in full, and the parent is untouched.

## Method

`cd /tmp/werk-fork-proto` (scratch, outside this repo). Three `claude --print --output-format json` calls, same model:

1. A baseline turn carrying ~70k tokens of filler, no history.
2. A plain `--resume <session>` turn: a two-word reply, no new content.
3. A `--resume <session> --fork-session` turn: same, but forked.

## Result

    call        cache_creation_input_tokens   cache_read_input_tokens
    baseline    70118                         0
    control     61                            70118
    fork        61                            70179

The fork's `cache_read_input_tokens` (70179) equals the full prefix at the moment of the fork — the baseline plus the control turn, both already written to cache. It pays cache-read price for all of it and only writes 61 new tokens, the same number the plain control turn wrote for its own new content. A fresh, empty context would have paid full input price for that turn's own text and nothing else — cheaper in isolation, but it would then re-read every file and every card body the parent conversation already holds, on its own turns.

## What actually happens on disk

    ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/f35a3cc8-....jsonl   parent: baseline, control. Stops there.
    ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/29559e9c-....jsonl   fork: baseline, control, then its own FORK turn.

The fork is a full copy of the parent's history up to the fork point, under its own session id, as its own file. The parent file gains no fork turn — confirmed by reading both files after the run. So `resolveConvo` in src/convos.ts, which already keys off a session id, needs no change for this: a fork is just another session id with its own `chat.jsonl`.

## What this settles

- Werk's fork button should call `claude --resume <parent-session> --fork-session`, not start empty by default. #werk-mc-fork:opt0 stays the explicit second choice.
- The fold point for #werk-mc-shared's 'what changed since' question is exactly this: the last event each side saw as of the fork's parent-session read, which the log's `seq` numbers already carry.
- No further prototype needed here. The remaining unknown was fidelity of the cache hit under `--fork-session` specifically (as opposed to a bare new session), and it hit in full.

payload.title: A tab strip of card-id chips, in the bottom control cluster

patch.body:
Reversed from the first draft, which put the strip 'above the composer'. Checked against web/index.html: the DOM order inside .chat is chat-log, asks, chat-composer, chat-head — and .chat uses flex-direction:column (web/style.css:21), so chat-head renders last, at the very bottom of the pane. That is where the model selector and the context pie already live (web/index.html:51-60), in the 'CONVERSATION' bar the screenshot on #werk-mc-follow shows.

Eryk's reasoning: those two controls are already conversation-scoped, and they sit at the bottom because that is where the user's eye and hand are while typing, not at the top of a pane that may be scrolled through a long log. A tab strip is the same kind of control — conversation-scoped, needed at the moment you are about to type — so it joins that cluster instead of sitting above the composer, mid-scroll.

## Placement

A new row inside chat-head, above the existing title/state/context/model row, or the two merge into one row if width allows. Either way it is part of the bottom cluster, not a separate strip floating above the textarea.

## What stays true from the first draft

- Card-id chips, not titles — #werk-mc-tabs still holds. Four or five fit one row.
- Each chip carries the running / finished-unread / idle state.
- The strip caps at five with the rest in a menu — #werk-mc-park.
- Cmd+1..5 by position, Cmd+[ / Cmd+] to step — #werk-mc-keys.

What changes is only where on screen, not the chip design or the cap.
patch.why: Eryk: the model selector and context pie already sit at the bottom because they are focused to the conversation, and so is the composer. Tabs belong with them, not at the top of the pane.

payload.title: An explicit close button, with a history of closed conversations
payload.why_not: More surface for no more value than parking already gives. A parked conversation's session lives on disk regardless (Claude Code, not werk, owns that), so 'closed' and 'parked' would end up meaning the same thing — the session is still resumable either way. A second concept and a history view to browse it would be built to distinguish two states that behave identically. Park already is the history: the '...' menu lists every parked conversation, sorted by last activity.

payload.title: A per-tab marker for running, waiting, and dead — the last two also surface a prompt

patch.body:
Eryk decided this. Three states, not one, and two of them do more than mark.

1. **Running.** A pulsing dot on the tab chip and, per #werk-mc-live's original point, on the card elsewhere in the tree that the conversation is homed on. Passive: confirms the turn is still going.
2. **Waiting for input.** The conversation has a queued permission ask. Already decided on #werk-mc-asks: it does not wait for you to notice the dot. It appears in the shared ask queue immediately, labelled with its tab, with no focus steal. The dot on the chip is a secondary cue for a glance, not the primary channel.
3. **Dead.** The child process exited. #werk-fullerr and #werk-crashmsg already decided what the message says and when a retry is safe, for the one conversation that used to be the only one. Neither one asks *where* that message goes when the dying conversation is not the one in focus. Decided here: a background death is not something you find by chance. It surfaces the same way an ask does — a visible line in the pane, naming the tab, not buried behind a dot you'd have to notice on your own.

So the marker itself is three-state (running / waiting / dead), and 'waiting' and 'dead' are not marker-only: they each already push or now push a message into a surface you're looking at, whichever tab you're on. Only 'running' stays a pure ambient signal.
patch.why: A dot alone answers 'is it still going'. A permission ask and a dead child are both things you must act on, not just notice.

payload.title: A silent dot only, for both a queued ask and a dead child
payload.why_not: It makes two things you must act on discoverable only by chance. A permission ask blocks its conversation until answered; a dead child needs a decision on whether to retry. Both are already surfaced this way once, on the pane you're actually looking at, for the single-conversation case (#werk-mc-asks, #werk-fullerr, #werk-crashmsg). Downgrading them to a passive dot for a background tab would make the feature worse at exactly the moment it matters most — while you're not looking.

payload.text: Backend and frontend for the multichat subtree are built and wired into this running server: ConvoManager (multiple Agent instances, one per conversation, each with its own .werk/conversations/<name>/{session,chat.jsonl}), fork via --resume <parent-session> --fork-session (confirmed working end-to-end against a scratch server), a shared Asks queue tagged per conversation, and a tab strip in the chat pane (fork with Shift+click a card or the + button, Cmd+1..5 to switch, park at 5 with a parked menu, per-tab drafts and map position, a dead-conversation notice bar). patch.body:
Eryk is right that this is the crux. A tab strip with fifteen chips is worse than no tabs.

The rule, in three parts:

1. **A cap on visible chips.** Five. The sixth fork parks the least-recently-touched idle tab. A tab with a running turn is never parked.
2. **Parked is not closed.** The strip ends with a '...' menu. Corrected live: it lists *every* conversation, not only the parked ones — visible chips included, marked apart from parked ones, with the active one marked too. The number on the button is the total count, not just what is parked, so nothing is only reachable by scrolling the strip. Clicking a visible one switches to it; clicking a parked one un-parks it and parks whatever is now least recent. The session id is on disk, so un-parking is a `--resume`, not a restart.
3. **No explicit close button, at first.** There is nothing to close. If a conversation is done it goes idle and drifts into the menu on its own. Add an explicit 'forget' later only if the menu gets long enough to be useless.

Who: me. Every part of this is reversible and none of it is visible in the record. The cap of five is a number to try, not a decision to defend.

The one thing that is not mine to pick: whether a parked conversation's child process is killed. Killing it frees memory and costs a resume on wake. Keeping it alive costs nothing but memory. Start by killing it — #werk-resume already proves a resume is transparent.

payload.text: Bug found and fixed: Agent.stop() didn't mark its own kill as deliberate, so parking a tab (or a server shutdown killing every live conversation) made the exit handler treat it as a crash — printing "The agent stopped" plus whatever old, unrelated text had piled up in that child's stderr tail over its whole life. That's what the #werk-mc-tabs screenshot was: a parked/killed child's stale startup warning (about .claude/settings.json permissions needing the trust dialog accepted) surfacing at exit time, looking like a real error. Added a stopping flag, set only when there's a live child to kill, checked before the crash-reporting branch in the exit handler. Verified against a scratch server: park while idle and park mid-turn both now stay silent, busy correctly resets to false either way.

Confirmed end to end after a real server restart (the serve() HMR guard from #werk-hmr does not cover this code): the model received the composed answer text as the tool result, not a denial.

Follow-up: the log painted a picked answer as an error. The CLI reports every AskUserQuestion answer as a tool_result with is_error: true, because the wire behavior is still deny (see above) — but a picked answer is not a failure, so the chat log must not paint it red like one. Fix: agent.ts now has a private answeredAsks Set<string> keyed by the call's tool_use_id. permission() adds to it whenever the pane sent a message (an answer, not a bare decline). The 'user' event handler that builds the log entry checks and clears that set, and only sets error: true when is_error is true AND the id isn't in answeredAsks. Same as the earlier round: this sits inside server.ts's HMR-guarded module graph (see #werk-hmr), so it needs a real restart to take effect — not yet verified live.
