Active tab corners, 4th attempt: inverse corner. The fillet is the part of a 6x6 box OUTSIDE a circle centred at the far corner, not the quarter-disc inside it. Earlier tries filled the disc (bulge) or stacked two discs (S). Each piece is 7px wide so its last column paints over the tab's own side border, which must not show above the arc's tangent point.

Two corrections to the corner pieces: top:-1px (absolute top is measured from the padding box, so top:0 sat 1px below the seam line) and z-index 3 on the active chip and its pieces, so the fillet paints over the neighbour chip's rounded corner.

Seam line gaps fixed: .tab-strip now paints the line as a 1px background gradient across its full width. A border-top would shift the chips down 1px and the active chip could no longer cover the line. The three gaps were the 16px left padding, the 2px gaps between chips, and the gap before .tab-actions.

Iterated live once more on the built chip strip: the gap between chips is 4px (#tab-chips in web/style.css), up from the original 2px — Eryk asked for it one pixel at a time, confirmed against a screenshot each step. The seam-line background on .tab-strip already covers this gap and the two other breaks (16px left padding, the gap before .tab-actions), so widening it needed no other change — see the comment above .tab-strip.

payload.title: dev-pipeline-research-semantic-diff.md: topic-level diff, beyond word/line
payload.finding: No shipped product or paper diffs a short document at topic level. arXivEdits (arXiv 2210.15067) does sentence+span alignment plus a trained edit-intention classifier — too heavy for one brief. Lightest buildable path: reuse the LLM that proposes the edit as the classifier. It tags each new-body sentence against the old body as elaborated / new, and lists unmatched old sentences as removed. Verify its quoted old-sentence match against the real text in code before rendering, so a wrong LLM tag cannot silently produce a wrong diff. Render: word-level diff only inside elaborated pairs; plain add/remove markers for new/removed sentences.

payload.title: A system diagram is a third view over the same graph, not a new format
payload.why: Both diagram types Eryk named already exist in the data model. A dependency diagram is depends_on edges over nodes of kind component. A data flow diagram is the status transition graph. Neither needs a drawing tool, a new file, or a new edge type.
payload.body:
The two diagrams are orthogonal and both reduce to what the log already holds.

**Dependency view.** Add --kind component. A component node carries no decision, only a name and a boundary. depends_on between components is the same edge as depends_on between decisions — see #vi-edges. The UI subsystem connecting to the agent subsystem at several entries is four component nodes and five edges.

**Data flow view.** Not structure. A loop: ideate -> prototype -> decide. werk already stores that loop as open -> proto -> decided, per card, with every transition timestamped in the log. So the data flow diagram of the planning subsystem is not drawn, it is counted. See #vi-flow.

The interesting part is that a component node and a decision node sit in one graph. "This card is true only because that component exists" is a depends_on edge that crosses the two kinds. Delete the component, the decisions that needed it go stale. That is a thing no diagram tool does.

payload.title: Derive the component graph from the code, by reading imports under src/
payload.why_not: It maps files, not intent. src/cli.ts imports src/fold.ts, which is true and says nothing. A subsystem boundary is a judgement — 'the agent subsystem' is not a directory. An import graph also cannot hold a depends_on edge to a decision card, so staleness stops at the code.

payload.title: The data flow diagram of the planning loop is counted from the log, not drawn
payload.why: Every status change is one event in log.jsonl with a timestamp. The loop open -> proto -> decided is therefore measurable: how many cards sit at each step, how long each step takes, and which edges of the loop are never used.
payload.body:
Draw the loop once as three or four boxes. Then fill it from the log:

- the count of cards now at each step
- the median time a card spends at the step before it moves
- the traffic on each arrow, including the backward ones — reopen is an arrow from decided to open, and it is the arrow that tells you the plan was wrong

A hand-drawn flow diagram goes stale the day it is drawn. This one cannot, because it is a fold over the log, the same as the map — see #werk.

Open: whether ideate and prototype are two steps or one. The log has open and proto. Eryk named ideate -> prototype -> decide, which is three.

payload.title: Zoom levels come from the refines tree. There is no second axis
payload.why: Eryk's zoom levels — one point for the whole system down to a single component — are exactly a refines tree over component nodes. C4 (context, container, component, code) names the same four levels. So the existing tree view gives zoom for free, and the level a node sits at is its depth.
payload.body:
The consequence is that the number of levels is not fixed at four. A project picks its own depth, the same way #vi-levels decides who creates the levels for decisions.

One thing does not come free: a diagram at level N must show an edge whose real endpoints are at level N+2. Two leaf components talk to each other, so their parents must be drawn as talking. That is edge rollup, the same operation as the status rollup bar already in the tree.

payload.text: System diagram as a third view -> #vi-sysdiag, with #vi-flow and #vi-sysdiag-zoom under it. All three proto.

payload.title: Show a background agent still running after the turn ends
payload.why: Claude Code keeps a persistent marker while a background agent runs and announces it when it starts. Werk's pane does not carry that signal, so a background agent finishes invisibly.

payload.title: The product diagram is a second graph. The map is not a picture of the product

patch.body:
Two graphs over the same project, answering two different questions.

| | map | product diagram |
|---|---|---|
| node | a claim | a part of the built thing |
| question | why is it like this | what is there now |
| shape | history, append-only | current state, overwritten |
| goes stale | by propagation | the moment code lands |

The map already answers why. Nothing renders what. The set of decided cards implies a system — UI, agent, log, fold, CLI, server — and today that system exists only in the reader's head.

Corrected from the earlier version of this card, which claimed the product diagram was just a new node kind inside the map. It is not. Adding --kind component to log.jsonl would put parts and claims in one node set, and then the rollup, the staleness closure, and the drained count would all count parts as if they were unsettled decisions.

The edge that does connect them runs one way only: a component points back at the cards that decided it. See #vi-sysdiag-derive for whether that edge is authored or derived.
patch.why: The map's nodes are claims. A product diagram's nodes are parts of the thing being built. One decision can create four components; one component can be the sum of ten decisions. There is no one-to-one mapping, so no view of the map is a product diagram.

payload.title: Is the product diagram authored, or folded out of the decided cards
payload.why: This is the whole cost question. Authored means a second thing to keep current by hand, which is the failure mode of every architecture diagram. Derived means an agent reads the decided set each time, which is slow, non-deterministic, and can contradict the code.
payload.body:
Three candidates, cheapest first.

1. **Folded from the decided cards.** An agent reads the decided set and emits components and edges. Nothing to maintain. But it describes what was decided, not what was built, and those differ.
2. **Folded from the code.** Real, always current, and blind to intent — it maps files, not subsystems. See #vi-sysdiag:opt0.
3. **Authored, with an edge back to the deciding cards.** Exact, and it rots unless something forces the update.

The rule from #vi-images points at 1 or 2: the diagram is a view, so it is regenerated, never stored. The gap between 1 and 2 is the gap between plan and build, and a diagram that showed both — decided but not built, built but not decided — would be worth more than either alone.

payload.title: werk is the one project where the product's data flow and the card status loop coincide. Do not generalize from it

patch.body:
The trap: testing the product-diagram prototype on werk itself will make a derived diagram look correct for the wrong reason. The card statuses will supply the data flow, and it will read as if the fold worked.

Test it on a second project before believing it.

The coincidence does buy one real thing, separate from the product diagram. The card status loop is measurable, because every transition is a timestamped event in the log — see #werk:

- the count of cards now at each status
- the median time a card holds a status before it moves
- the traffic on each arrow, including reopen, which runs backward from decided to open and is the arrow that says the plan was wrong

That is telemetry on the map, not a diagram of the product.
patch.why: werk's product is the planning loop. So its data flow — ideate, prototype, decide — is the same loop as open, proto, decided in log.jsonl. For any other project the two are unrelated: a payments system's data flow is not its planning statuses. This coincidence is what made the first version of #vi-sysdiag wrong.

payload.title: Zoom levels are a refines tree over components, separate from the map's refines tree

patch.body:
Depth is the level. The count of levels is therefore not fixed at four; a project picks its own, the way #vi-levels decides who creates the levels for decisions.

One thing does not come free. A diagram at level N must draw an edge whose real endpoints are at level N+2: two leaf components talk, so their parents must be drawn as talking. That is edge rollup — the same operation as the status rollup bar in the map's tree, over a different graph.
patch.why: Eryk's levels — one point for the whole system down to a single component — are a refines tree, and C4 (context, container, component, code) names the same four. But it is a tree over parts, not over claims, so it is a second tree in a second graph. See #vi-sysdiag.

payload.text: Corrected: the product diagram is a second graph, not a view of the map -> #vi-sysdiag. Open question is authored vs folded -> #vi-sysdiag-derive. #vi-flow now records the self-reference trap.

payload.title: The diagram is folded from the cards by an agent, cached as text, and dirty-marked by edges

patch.body:
Three claims, in order.

**1. The fold needs judgement.** No projection of card fields yields a component. #vi-graph3d decides a view; #werk-hmr decides a dev loop; #vi-edges decides a data shape. One is a part of the product, one is a part of the build, one is a part of the schema. Only a reader can tell which, and at which level.

**2. So the diagram text is a cached artifact, not a view.** It is a peer of the card text, stored, diffed, and edited in place. The picture drawn from it stays disposable — #vi-images.

**3. So it is kept current incrementally, never regenerated.** A card changes, the elements that card decided are marked, and the agent revisits only those. Full regeneration is wrong for the same reason a full re-derivation of the map is wrong: non-deterministic output makes every diff unreadable, and a rephrasing is indistinguishable from a real change.

The mechanism for step 3 is #vi-sysdiag-backedge. It is the same architecture as staleness in the map: the edge is recorded when the element is written, the marking is mechanical, and the judgement happens only at a marked node.
patch.why: Cards describe different parts of the system at different grain, so reading them into components needs interpretation, not a data transformation. But an agent read is slow and non-deterministic, so it cannot run on every view. The resolution is the split #vi-images already made: the diagram text is cached, the render is not.

payload.title: Fold the cards into the diagram as a pure data transformation, no agent
payload.why_not: A card carries no field that says which part of the product it touches, or at which level. #vi-graph3d, #werk-hmr and #vi-edges are all decided cards about three different layers — a view, the build loop, the schema. Any rule that sorts them is the interpretation it was meant to avoid.

payload.title: Regenerate the whole diagram from the whole decided set, every turn
payload.why_not: Agent output is not stable across runs. The same card set yields a differently worded, differently grouped diagram each time, so every render is a large diff and a rephrasing cannot be told from a real change. It also pays the full read cost to answer a one-card question.

payload.title: A diagram element records the cards that decided it, at the moment it is written
payload.why: This is the only edge that connects the two graphs, and it is the thing that makes synchronisation mechanical. Without it, finding which part of the diagram a changed card affects means asking a model to scan the whole diagram — the same single-hop check that recovers 6% to 11%, per #vi-prop.
payload.body:
The edge runs one way: element -> cards. The map never points at the diagram, so log.jsonl keeps no knowledge of it.

What it buys, per card change:

1. A card is edited, reopened, or added. Its id is already in the log.
2. Every element holding that id is marked dirty. Mechanical, no model.
3. The agent revisits the dirty elements only, and rewrites them.

Step 2 is the reverse closure from #vi-prop, over a second edge set. Step 3 is the only place judgement runs, and it runs on a small input.

The discipline cost is the same one #vi-prop already imposes, and it has the same failure mode: write the element without its card ids and the edge cannot be recovered later.

payload.title: What is an element — one diagram file, or one record per node and edge
payload.why: Dirty-marking is only as fine as the thing that carries the card ids. One file per diagram means any card change dirties the whole diagram, and the agent rewrites all of it — which is #vi-sysdiag-derive:opt2 with extra steps.
payload.body:
Two shapes.

**One text file per diagram.** Simple, readable, editable by hand. But the card ids sit in one header, so the grain of the mark is the whole file.

**One record per component and per edge, each with its card ids.** The mark lands on three nodes out of forty, and the agent rewrites three. Layout then has to be computed rather than written, and a human can no longer edit the diagram directly.

This needs a build, not an argument: take the current decided set of werk, fold it once by hand, then change one card and count how much of the diagram actually had to move.

payload.text: Decided: agent fold, cached text, incremental. Mechanism -> #vi-sysdiag-backedge. Open -> #vi-sysdiag-grain.

payload.title: Store the diagram as one record per node and edge, each carrying its card ids
payload.why_not: It buys a fine-grained dirty mark, and pays for it by removing the judgement that matters. A marked set of three nodes tells the agent what changed and forbids it from asking whether the grouping still holds. Layout also has to be computed instead of written, and a human can no longer edit the diagram by hand.

payload.title: One diagram file. Redraw it whole each turn, with the old drawing in context

patch.body:
Eryk's framing, which holds: with no resource limit you would redraw from scratch every time. The old drawing is then not a saving, it is an input — it is what makes the new drawing continuous with the reader's mental model.

So the grain question was posed wrong. It is not "which storage shape is cheaper". It is "is the scope of the redraw mechanical or judged". Judged. One file, rewritten whole, with the previous file in the prompt.

What this costs: the redraw can silently restructure. The reader cannot tell a moved box from a rethought boundary. That has to be declared — see #vi-sysdiag-declare.

Where it stops holding: this works because a forty-node diagram and its card set fit in one read. Nothing needs recovering, so #vi-prop's 6% to 11% does not apply. Past that size the marked-set mechanism comes back — see #vi-sysdiag-backedge.
patch.why: The scope of a redraw is a judgement, not a lookup. Given the changed card and the whole current diagram, the agent can see whether this is a renamed box or a wrong grouping, and choose a minimal edit or a rethink. A fine-grained dirty mark hands it the answer to that question before it asks it.

payload.title: A redraw declares whether it was a local edit or a restructure
payload.why: A whole-file redraw can move anything. Without a statement of which it did, the reader must diff the picture to find out, and a restructure looks the same as a rename. This is the one real cost of #vi-sysdiag-grain, and it is not paid by storage shape.
payload.body:
Two outcomes, named on the redraw:

- **local** — the same components and the same grouping, with text or one edge changed. The reader can trust their mental model.
- **restructure** — a boundary moved, a component split, or a group re-formed. The reader has to look again, and the redraw says why.

A restructure is the interesting event. It means a single card changed something that the previous reading of the whole card set had wrong. That is worth surfacing in the map, not hiding in a picture.

payload.title: The card ids on the diagram are a hint now. They become the mechanism when the diagram outgrows one read

patch.body:
Corrected. The earlier version made this the synchronisation mechanism. #vi-sysdiag-grain moved the scope decision to the agent's judgement instead, so the ids no longer drive the redraw.

They still earn their place for two reasons that are not synchronisation:

1. They answer "why is this box here" — the element points at the cards that decided it, which is the only edge between the two graphs.
2. They are the fallback. Past the size where one read covers the diagram and the card set, the reverse closure from #vi-prop is the only way to bound the redraw. The ids must already be there by then, for the reason #vi-prop gives: an edge not written at creation cannot be recovered.

So write them now, and do not depend on them yet.
patch.why: #vi-prop's 6% to 11% is about recovering edges that were never written. Nothing is being recovered here: the changed card and the whole diagram are both in the agent's context, so the affected elements are read, not inferred. The argument for a mechanical mark returns only when the diagram stops fitting.

patch.body:
Three claims, in order.

**1. The fold needs judgement.** No projection of card fields yields a component. #vi-graph3d decides a view; #werk-hmr decides a dev loop; #vi-edges decides a data shape. One is a part of the product, one is a part of the build, one is a part of the schema. Only a reader can tell which, and at which level.

**2. So the diagram text is a cached artifact, not a view.** It is a peer of the card text, stored, diffed, and edited in place. The picture drawn from it stays disposable — #vi-images.

**3. So the cached text is the base for the next redraw, not a thing patched in place.** The diagram is rewritten whole each turn with the previous version in context, and the agent decides whether that comes out as a local edit or a restructure — #vi-sysdiag-grain. This is not #vi-sysdiag-derive:opt2: opt2 regenerates from the card set alone, with no previous drawing, so it has nothing to be continuous with.

Amended: the first version of claim 3 said the redraw was bounded mechanically by a marked set. #vi-sysdiag-grain replaced that with judgement. The card ids stay on the diagram for a different reason — #vi-sysdiag-backedge.

payload.text: Decided: one file, whole redraw, old drawing as input. #vi-sysdiag-backedge downgraded to a hint. New cost -> #vi-sysdiag-declare.

payload.title: Mermaid flowchart plus a card-id mapping block, in one file that werk renders itself
payload.why: #vi-images rejected Mermaid because a tracker may not render it. That objection is about the publish target, not the local view: werk renders its own picture, so the format only has to satisfy werk. Mermaid is hand-editable, diffs line by line, and needs no layout code.
payload.body:
One file, two sections.

```
flowchart TD
  ui[UI] --> agent[Agent]
  agent --> log[(log.jsonl)]

%% cards
%% ui: vi-onview, vi-graph3d
%% agent: werk, vi-compl
```

The flowchart is what gets drawn. The mapping block holds the element-to-card ids from #vi-sysdiag-backedge, in comments, so one file stays the unit — as #vi-sysdiag-grain requires.

What this buys for a prototype: no layout code and no renderer to write. Mermaid from a CDN draws it, the same way 3d-force-graph is already loaded for #vi-graph3d.

Reversible. The fold produces text; swapping the text format later costs one redraw, not a migration. The mapping block is the part that must survive a format change, so it stays separate from the flowchart syntax.

payload.title: A bespoke node and edge text format, rendered by werk's own layout code
payload.why_not: It holds card ids per record more cleanly than a comment block, and costs a layout engine before the first picture exists. The question the prototype asks is whether an agent can fold cards into components at all. A renderer is not on that path.

payload.title: Prototype: fold werk's own decided set into one dependency diagram, then change one card
payload.why: Three decided cards rest on an untested assumption — that an agent can read a set of decision cards and name the components of the product. #vi-sysdiag-derive, #vi-sysdiag-grain and #vi-sysdiag-declare are all wrong if it cannot.
payload.body:
Scope, in order. Nothing outside this list.

1. Fold the decided cards of the werk subtree into one Mermaid file, by hand, per #vi-sysdiag-format. Level 1 and level 2 only, per #vi-sysdiag-zoom.
2. Load Mermaid from a CDN and draw it in a tab beside the tree and the 3D graph.
3. Change one card. Redraw with the old file in context. Record whether the result is local or a restructure, per #vi-sysdiag-declare.

Not in scope: the data flow diagram, because #vi-flow says werk is the one project where it cannot be trusted. Not in scope: any layout code, per #vi-sysdiag-format:opt0. Not in scope: automating the fold — step 1 is done by hand, to find out what the fold needs before a command wraps it.

What it can show is false:

- the card set does not name components, only views and schema and build steps
- the same card set folds two different ways on two reads, so there is no stable diagram to be continuous with
- every one-card change reads as a restructure, which would mean the drawing carries no reusable structure

payload.text: Format decided -> #vi-sysdiag-format (Mermaid, one file, CDN render). Prototype scoped -> #vi-sysdiag-proto.

payload.title: The components come from the cards. The edges between them do not
payload.why: Step 1 of #vi-sysdiag-proto produced 24 elements from 66 cards without trouble. Every edge in the drawing came from knowing the code, not from reading a card. Almost no card says 'A calls B' — a card says what a part is and why it exists.
payload.body:
The trap this rules out: a card's depends_on edge is not a component's depends_on edge.

#werk-shots depends_on #werk-pane. That means "the screenshot decision needed the pane decision to be settled first". It does not mean the screenshot code calls the pane. The two graphs read the same word and mean different things — which is exactly #vi-sysdiag's point, now measured.

So the fold has two inputs, not one:

- **nodes** — from the decided cards. Judgement, per #vi-sysdiag-derive.
- **edges** — from the code. Imports, calls, HTTP routes, file reads.

#vi-sysdiag:opt0 was rejected for deriving the whole diagram from imports. That still holds for the node set: imports name files, not subsystems. It was wrong about the edge set. An import graph is the only honest source for an arrow.

Consequence: the drawing shows a plan-versus-build gap for free. A component the cards decided, with no code edge touching it, is not built yet.

payload.title: A card is structural, behavioural, or method. Only a structural card makes an element
payload.why: The fold of 66 cards into 24 elements sorted them into three classes before anything could be drawn. Without that sort, the method cards fold into the picture and put the map's own rules inside the product.
payload.body:
The three classes, with examples from the fold:

1. **Structural** — names a part. #werk-multichat is the tab strip. #vi-graph3d is the 3d view. #werk-perm-native is the permission gate. These make elements.
2. **Behavioural** — constrains a part that already exists. #werk-cmdenter, #werk-forloop, #werk-loopbody, #werk-approve-habits are all findings and fixes on the permission gate. They attach to an element and add no box.
3. **Method** — about how the map is kept, not about the product. #drained, #al-two, #vi-prop, #werk-contract. These fold to nothing.

Class 3 is the one that matters. werk is a tool for keeping maps, so its method cards look structural — #vi-prop is a rule for the map, and the map is also the product. Any project has some of these; werk has the most possible. #vi-flow warned about exactly this kind of self-reference.

The sort is judgement, and no card field carries the class. A first pass by an agent got it right by reading the title and the why.

payload.title: Nodes are folded from the cards by an agent. Edges come from the code. The text is cached

patch.body:
Four claims.

**1. The node fold needs judgement.** No projection of card fields yields a component. #vi-graph3d decides a view; #werk-hmr decides a dev loop; #vi-edges decides a data shape. Only a reader can tell which is a part of the product, and at which level. The sort that makes this possible is #vi-sysdiag-classes.

**2. The edges do not come from the cards at all.** They come from the code. #vi-sysdiag-edges measured this: the node fold worked, and every arrow in the first drawing was supplied from outside the card set.

**3. So the diagram text is a cached artifact, not a view.** It is a peer of the card text — stored, diffed, edited in place. The picture drawn from it stays disposable, per #vi-images.

**4. So the cached text is the base for the next redraw.** The diagram is rewritten whole with the previous version in context, and the agent decides whether that lands as a local edit or a restructure — #vi-sysdiag-grain. This is not #vi-sysdiag-derive:opt2, which regenerates from the card set alone and so has nothing to be continuous with.

Re-derived after step 1 of #vi-sysdiag-proto. Claim 2 is new and was the assumption this card got wrong: it read as if cards were the only input.
patch.why: Cards name the parts of the product but not the arrows between them, so the fold reads two sources — see #vi-sysdiag-edges. Reading cards into parts needs interpretation, not a data transformation. An agent read is slow and non-deterministic, so it cannot run on every view; the resolution is #vi-images' split, where the diagram text is cached and the render is not.

payload.text: Step 1 done. .werk/diagram.mmd holds 24 elements from 66 cards. Two findings -> #vi-sysdiag-classes and #vi-sysdiag-edges. #vi-sysdiag-derive reopened and re-derived on the second one. Steps 2 and 3 not started.

payload.title: An element with no code edge means three different things. Only one of them is 'not built'
payload.why: I claimed the plan-versus-build gap falls out for free. It does not. An arrow arrives at a file, and a file is not an element, so the test gives false positives before the element-to-code mapping exists.
payload.body:
Three causes of a box with no arrow, from the 24 elements in .werk/diagram.mmd:

1. **Decided, not built.** #werk-write is proto: the map is read-only and the CLI writes it. No write path exists in web/. This is the case worth seeing.
2. **Built, but the boundary is not a code boundary.** The permission gate is one element in the cards. In code it is src/permission.ts, a hook config, allow.json, and a classifier inside agent.ts. Any arrow lands on one of those files, not on the element.
3. **Built, but too small to have an edge.** The one-server lock is a few lines inside server.ts. No import distinguishes it from anything else in that file.

Cases 2 and 3 are the majority, so the naive test reports mostly noise. Making it work needs a third mapping block: element to files and symbols, written the same way and at the same time as the card ids — see #vi-sysdiag-codemap.

payload.title: A third mapping block: element to files and symbols
payload.why: The element-to-card block answers 'why is this box here'. Nothing answers 'where is this box'. Both the code edges of #vi-sysdiag-edges and the not-built test of #vi-sysdiag-notbuilt need the second answer, and neither can compute it.
payload.body:
Same shape as the card block in .werk/diagram.mmd, same file, per #vi-sysdiag-grain:

```
%% code
%% gate:    src/permission.ts, src/agent.ts:classify, .werk/allow.json
%% lock:    src/server.ts:acquireLock
%% cliwrite: (none)
```

`(none)` is a value, not a gap. It is what makes case 1 of #vi-sysdiag-notbuilt readable: an element that claims no code is decided and unbuilt, and an element that claims code nobody imports is dead.

This is the only part of the diagram a compiler could check. A path that no longer exists is a hard error, unlike a card id, which can only be dangling.

payload.title: Prototype 2: draw the code graph under the same element names, and read the disagreement
payload.why: Eryk's question — how would a card-folded diagram differ from a code-mapped one. The difference is the artifact, not either drawing. Neither diagram alone says anything the reader could not get from reading the cards or the code.
payload.body:
Two drawings, one set of element names. Three classes of disagreement, and each one is a different problem:

1. **Decided, no code.** A plan not yet built, or abandoned without a card saying so.
2. **Code, no card.** A part of the product nobody decided in the map. Candidates in this repo today: src/convos.ts, src/convo-manager.ts, src/commands.ts, web/md.js. This is the valuable class — it is undocumented judgement, and it is invisible in the map by construction.
3. **Boundary disagreement.** The cards call the permission gate one thing; the code splits it across four files, and one of those files also holds the agent runner. Either the card boundary is wrong or the code is.

Order: this comes after step 2 of #vi-sysdiag-proto, because there is nothing to compare until one drawing renders. It needs #vi-sysdiag-codemap first.

What would make it not worth building: if class 2 turns out to be everything. If most of the code has no card, the map is not a record of this product and the overlay measures that instead.

payload.title: The diagram helps decide the shape to build. It does not check the code
payload.why: Eryk: the code that exists is a prototype. It works because it does what was decided. Its shape is an accident, not a plan. So the code cannot be the thing the diagram is measured against.
payload.body:
The diagram looks forward, not back.

It shows the shape we want. The code shows the shape we have. When the two differ, the code is wrong more often than the diagram, because nobody chose the code's shape.

Three things follow.

1. The diagram is drawn from the cards. Cards hold decisions. See #vi-sysdiag-derive.
2. A part of the diagram with no code is normal. It means we decided it and have not built it.
3. A part of the code with no card is normal too. It is prototype scaffolding. It is not a hidden decision.

This lowers the value of #vi-sysdiag-overlay and #vi-sysdiag-codemap. Both compare the diagram to the code. That comparison is useful when the code is built on purpose. It is not useful yet.

patch.body:
First, a trap to avoid. A depends_on edge between two cards is not an arrow between two parts.

#werk-shots depends_on #werk-pane. That means the screenshot decision needed the pane decision first. It does not mean the screenshot code calls the pane. Same word, two graphs, two meanings.

Second, what the empty arrows mean. We decided what the parts are. We never decided how they talk. The diagram makes that visible for the first time. An empty arrow is a question to answer, not data to fetch — see #vi-sysdiag-ask.

So the arrows come from the cards, once the cards exist. Reading them out of the prototype code would hide the gap instead of showing it.
patch.why: Step 1 of #vi-sysdiag-proto made 24 parts from 66 cards with no trouble. Not one card said how two parts talk. I drew the arrows from the code. That was the wrong source: the code is a prototype, per #vi-sysdiag-purpose. The arrows are missing because they were never decided.

payload.body:
The tool draws the parts. Then it asks about the blank arrows.

"The chat pane and the agent runner are both parts. How do they talk?" That is a question with an answer, and the answer is a decision. So it becomes a card.

This is the first case where the diagram writes to the map, not the other way round. It fits #vi-compl: the tool does not choose the answer, it finds the missing question.

It also gives the diagram a way to be incomplete on purpose. A blank arrow is a real state, drawn as a dashed line with a mark. A tool that cannot draw "we have not decided this" will guess instead.

patch.body:
Decided: the marker lives in the tab's own chat pane, not on the tab chip. A permanent line pinned to the bottom of that pane, present only while a background agent is running there, gone once it finishes.

The card's live indicator (#werk-mc-live) counts a background agent as 'running' too. A tab whose main turn already finished but that still has a background agent going must not read as idle.

A per-tab marker for running, waiting, and dead — the last two also surface a prompt

Eryk decided this. Three states, not one, and two of them do more than mark.

1. **Running.** A pulsing dot on the tab chip and, per #werk-mc-live's original point, on the card elsewhere in the tree that the conversation is homed on. Passive: confirms the turn is still going. Per #werk-mc-bgagents: a background agent counts as running too — a tab whose main turn finished but that still has a background agent going must not read as idle.
2. **Waiting for input.** The conversation has a queued permission ask. Per #werk-mc-asks: the tab's own dot blinks yellow, and the '...' button blinks yellow too if the waiting tab is hidden behind it. No shared queue, no line in another tab's pane.
3. **Dead.** The child process exited. #werk-fullerr and #werk-crashmsg already decided what the message says and when a retry is safe, for the one conversation that used to be the only one. Neither one asks *where* that message goes when the dying conversation is not the one in focus. Decided here: a background death is not something you find by chance. It surfaces the same way an ask does — a visible line in the pane, naming the tab, not buried behind a dot you'd have to notice on your own.

So the marker itself is three-state (running / waiting / dead). 'Waiting' now signals through the dot and the '...' button, per #werk-mc-asks. 'Dead' still pushes a line into whatever pane you're looking at — that mechanism did not change with the ask redesign, but it now reads as inconsistent with 'waiting' and needs a look: should a dead child also just blink the dot red, instead of interrupting the pane?

payload.text: Correction from Eryk: 'style' means positioning, level of detail, and texture — not a recolor of one shared layout. Redoing Style B as a genuinely different treatment: a radial tree (http at the center, rings by hop distance) instead of Style A's top-down grid; titles + short tags instead of full sentences; hand-drawn wobble strokes, gradient fills, and a grained background instead of flat orthogonal lines. Style A (dark, orthogonal, full detail) stays as the other pole of the contrast.

Style B rebuilt as a radial tree: http+sse at the center, everything else on rings by hop-distance, angle allocated by subtree weight (like a sunburst). Detail level dropped to a title + 2-3 word tag (no sentences, no per-edge text — a color legend replaces the labels). Texture: gradient-filled circular/pill nodes, hand-drawn wobble strokes (seeded jitter, not straight beziers), open chevron arrowheads, a faint grain filter over the background. The two cross-links that don't fit the tree (cli->log, gate->approvebar) are dashed. Style A is untouched — still the dense top-down grid with full sentences and flat orthogonal lines. Re-verified live via Playwright: renders correctly in the running server, no console errors, no restart needed since diagram-b.svg is swapped in as a static file.

Fixed Style A per Eryk: 'one-server lock' and 'claude code child' were overlapping (a coordinate bug from the last edit), row-to-row gaps were as little as 26px so edge labels sat on top of node borders, and the runner->chatlog line cut straight through the claude-code-child box. Reworked the vertical rhythm to a consistent ~110px gap between every row, gave lock/child clear separation, added a 'side' route so runner->chatlog dodges around child instead of through it, staggered the two labels leaving agent runner so they no longer collide, and widened the text-wrap safety margin (a description was clipping past its box edge on chat.jsonl). Re-verified live: no overlaps, no clipped text, no console errors.

Text alignment bug from Eryk's screenshot: the node <text> elements had no text-anchor, so it defaulted to 'start' — every title/description was left-aligned starting AT the node's horizontal center instead of being centered on it, worst on 'http + sse' where the wide bar's text ran off past the visible edge. Added text-anchor="middle" to both node text branches (rect and cylinder) in the Style A generator. Re-verified live, no console errors.

Four more Style A fixes from Eryk's screenshots:
1. Vertical text centering: box height was a fixed constant (64/60/80) regardless of how many lines a description wrapped to, so a 4-line box (refines tree) crammed its title near the top with no bottom padding while a 1-line box had lots. Rewrote to compute each box's height from its own wrapped line count with consistent top/bottom padding, then leveled every box within a shared row up to that row's tallest member (else siblings' bottoms wouldn't align and their outgoing arrows would zigzag).
2. Browser vs map view / chat pane spacing: group boxes were hand-placed rectangles that happened to sit close to their nested boxes. Rewrote as auto-fit rects computed from member node positions plus fixed padding constants (GROUP_PAD_TOP/SIDE/BOTTOM, NEST_PAD for nesting) — the gap is now a real constant, not leftover space.
3. Boxes too close to area labels: same auto-fit change, with GROUP_PAD_TOP=40 giving consistent clearance below every label.
4. Store shapes: the cylinder was one hand-rolled arc path fighting itself into a pinched hourglass. Rebuilt as a plain rect body + two side lines + a bottom arc + a full ellipse lid layered on top — a real cylinder/tube shape now.
Re-verified live, no console errors.

Added a legend above the diagram, shown only for Style A (Style B already draws its own inside the SVG; Mermaid has no color coding). Seven color swatches match the edge categories exactly (browser reads, state, agent, permission, write, external, dev), plus a line-style key: solid = direct call, dashed = a check, not the main flow. Hit one bug: toggling it with the hidden attribute did nothing at first — .diagram-legend{display:flex} in the stylesheet has the same specificity as the browser's [hidden]{display:none} and comes later, so it won. Fixed with an explicit .diagram-legend[hidden]{display:none} override. Verified live: legend shows only on Style A, hides correctly on the other two, no console errors.

payload.title: Nodes are folded from the cards by an agent. Edges come from the cards, once decided. The text is cached

patch.body:
Four claims.

**1. The node fold needs judgement.** No projection of card fields yields a component. #vi-graph3d decides a view; #werk-hmr decides a dev loop; #vi-edges decides a data shape. Only a reader can tell which is a part of the product, and at which level. The sort that makes this possible is #vi-sysdiag-classes.

**2. Edges come from the cards, once a card decides them — not from the code.** #vi-sysdiag-edges tried reading arrows from the prototype code. That was wrong: the code's shape is an accident, not a decision, per #vi-sysdiag-purpose. Reading it in would hide the gap where a decision is still missing. A missing arrow is a question to answer, per #vi-sysdiag-ask, not data to fetch.

**3. So the diagram text is a cached artifact, not a view.** It is a peer of the card text — stored, diffed, edited in place. The picture drawn from it stays disposable, per #vi-images.

**4. So the cached text is the base for the next redraw.** The diagram is rewritten whole with the previous version in context, and the agent decides whether that lands as a local edit or a restructure — #vi-sysdiag-grain. This is not #vi-sysdiag-derive:opt2, which regenerates from the card set alone and so has nothing to be continuous with.

Corrected twice. First re-derived after step 1 of #vi-sysdiag-proto, when claim 2 said edges come from the code. #vi-sysdiag-edges then measured that this was wrong too: the code is prototype scaffolding, not a decision, so it cannot supply the arrows either.

payload.title: Agent rewrites the card directly; Eryk spots the change by re-reading it
payload.why_not: Rejected. This breaks in three ways: the agent may also touch a subcard or an adjacent card, so a rewrite in one place is not the whole change. A large rewrite is hard to scan for what actually moved. A small, nuanced rewrite is just as hard to catch, since nothing marks it as changed at all.

payload.text: Both readings are one mechanism: the agent proactively builds N prototypes on its own (not on request) whenever the requirement is unclear enough that competent implementations could diverge. The divergence between them IS the ambiguity signal, and the prototypes ARE the alternatives to ask about.

Resolved: 'ambiguous build vs. detecting a fork mid-implementation' is not a real choice for this card. The card's mechanism is sampling — build N versions independently, no cross-talk, compare after. Divergence is found empirically by diffing finished artifacts, not by one agent noticing its own fork mid-build. Fork detection is a weaker alternative: it relies on a single agent consciously flagging its own arbitrary choice, which it often will not do. So there is no separate trigger step — N is always sampled, and divergence is the detector, not a prediction made before building.

Worked example: task 'add pagination to /orders'. 3 independent runs of the same prompt diverge into offset/limit (A) vs. cursor-on-id (B) vs. cursor-on-created_at (C). Extracting each run's answer to 'pagination style' and 'sort key' finds two forks. Two targeted questions resolve both — no broad question, no guessing what to ask.

Trigger clarified: this method is for when the contrast CANNOT yet be named through discussion. If you and the agent can already name 2-3 real candidates by talking, that's the existing option/alternative_to mechanism (see CLAUDE.md) — build those named options directly, no blind sampling needed. Sampling is the fallback for when nobody can name the fork in advance: N independent, blind, no-cross-talk builds of the SAME prompt, and the disagreement between finished results is what names the fork. The agent never proposes pre-named options under this mechanism — it proposes running the blind sample itself.
