payload.text:
Round 2, after Eryk found real remaining problems in the actual render, not just the two spots I'd checked. Traced every one to a specific bug, not vague 'needs more tuning':

1. declutter() grouped labels by *exact* rounded y (or x) match. Two labels from different bands, 4px apart, don't round to the same key, so they were never compared against each other — yet their plates plainly overlapped (graph3d->state at y=383.5, composer->live at y=379.25, x-ranges overlapping). Replaced the whole function with declutterAll(): phase 1 clusters by y-*proximity* (union-find, tolerance 6px) and packs x within a cluster; phase 2 sweeps clusters apart in y, one pass, no iteration. An iterative pairwise-force-push version was tried first and made things worse at 40 iterations than at 6 - it doesn't reliably converge with several mutually-adjacent labels. The two-phase version does, because neither phase iterates.

2. Found the *same* endpoint-exclusion bug three more times while building the guards for phase 1/2 - the exact class of bug already caught once in placeLabels' band-snap check and in rule 7. Every new box-collision guard I wrote first excluded an edge's own to/from box, which is right for pickLabelSegment's *initial* candidate search but wrong for every *safety* check - a pushed label can land on its own edge's box exactly as easily as on a stranger's. Now fixed everywhere: safety checks use every box, no exceptions.

3. First fix reduced the label-vs-box count but revealed a label pushed 116px sideways to dodge a neighbor could end up nowhere near its own line (cli->log's label landed at x=565 while its line only runs x=280-418). Added MAX_PUSH (220px cap on how far phase 1 will move a label from its own natural position) with partial-credit behavior: push as close to the ideal spot as the cap allows, don't just give up at zero movement if the ideal is out of reach.

4. Rule 8 added to check.ts: label-vs-label overlap, the defect rule 7 (label-vs-box) never covered. This is what caught the remaining 2 cases precisely instead of more screenshot-hunting.

Down to 2 warnings, both explained, neither hidden:
- rule 7, dev->state overlaps state: the dev/fold/state/child/gate corner already flagged as the busiest corner in the diagram.
- rule 8, graph3d->state overlaps composer->live: composer's label needs to move right to clear graph3d's, but approval bar and tab strip flank the entire range it would need to cross within MAX_PUSH of its own line - genuinely not enough room without either edge routing changes or shrinking that section, not a declutter bug.

Card margin (rule 6) and forced-straight-entry (rule 3/route-libavoid) were unaffected by this round - already working from the first pass, confirmed unchanged.

payload.title: Tiling systems / recognizable picture languages: the formal name for a 2D language defined by allowed tiles
payload.finding: Giammarresi and Restivo, 1992, then the Handbook of Formal Languages survey. A local picture language is defined by listing the authorized 2x2 tiles over the alphabet plus a boundary symbol. REC, the recognizable picture languages, is what you get by projecting a local one. This is the exact formalism for rules 1.1 to 1.7: a finite set of legal local neighbourhoods, and a picture is in the language iff every window is legal. Also characterised by existential monadic second-order logic (Giammarresi, Restivo, Seibert, Thomas 1996), so the grammar has a logic form as well as a tile form.

payload.title: Wang tiles and Wave Function Collapse: the same constraints, run generatively instead of as a check
payload.finding: Wang tiles, Hao Wang 1961: square tiles with coloured edges, legal iff touching edges match. Model synthesis (Paul Merrell) and then Wave Function Collapse (Maxim Gumin) solve exactly that constraint set to generate a grid, by AC-3 style propagation plus lowest-entropy cell choice. Shipped in Townscaper, Bad North, Caves of Qud. The relevant warning for a diagram: WFC is strong on local adjacency and weak on global objectives - it can satisfy every local rule and still produce a globally poor arrangement. A diagram needs global properties (this edge connects these two specific cards), so the solver form is the wrong half; the checker form is the right half.

payload.title: The Kandinsky model: boxes on a coarse grid, edges routed on a finer grid
payload.finding: The standard graph-drawing model for exactly this shape. Each vertex is a box centred on a coarse grid point; each edge is an alternating horizontal/vertical run routed on a finer grid. Node size is derived from the largest number of edges attaching to one side. Extends Tamassia's orthogonal model past degree 4, and is the basis for UML and business-process layout tools. Sobering result: minimising total bends in this model is NP-complete (Bläsius, Krug, Rutter, Wagner) - an earlier min-cost-flow formulation was found incorrect by Eiglsperger, who gave a 2-approximation. Relevant because it says: do not try to make the program optimise the grid. Let the agent place, and check.

payload.title: svgbob, ditaa, a2s: working implementations of text grid in, styled SVG out
payload.finding: Existence proof for step 3 of the idea. svgbob (Rust, Apache-2.0) reads ASCII art and emits SVG, inferring corners, junctions and arrowheads from a character's neighbours rather than requiring them to be named. It has a scale directive that converts character cells to SVG units, plus font-size/family and colour directives. ditaa (Java) came first; a2s is a Go reimplementation, written because ditaa was verbose, rasterised, and needed a JVM per run. What none of them have: a formal grammar that rejects an invalid drawing. They are lenient parsers, not checkers.

payload.title: CSS grid-template-areas: the mainstream DSL that is already ASCII-art placement with a validity rule
payload.finding: Called the ascii-art method in its own docs. One quoted string per row, whitespace-separated name tokens, . for an empty cell. Two rules worth copying exactly: every row must have the same token count or the whole declaration is invalid, and a named area must form a rectangle - an L-shape makes the browser discard the entire template rather than guess. Precedent for fully-constrained-or-do-not-render. Critically, the tracks themselves are sized independently of the grid (auto, fr, fixed): the ascii art fixes topology, not pixels.

payload.title: Grid resolver: the agent draws the diagram on a topological grid, a tile grammar checks it, a program renders it
payload.why: #vi-sysdiag-intent only lets the agent control which cards sit in which row. Edges, labels and spacing are left to the resolver, and six rounds of fixes on #vi-sysdiag-render-polish show the agent cannot see what it produced without rendering and screenshotting. A grid the agent writes cell by cell is legible to its own author before anything is rendered.
payload.body:
Eryks design, three parts: reuse Mermaid syntax for relations, card content and ids; add a grid DSL for placement, constrained by formal adjacency rules; render the checked grid with a deterministic program and parametrised components.

This is the same Substance/Style split as #penrose - Mermaid says what exists, the grid says where it goes - applied to a medium the author can read back.

**The reason this is worth building, stated plainly.** Not control. Legibility. Every defect this session was found by Eryk looking at a picture, never by me reading the input. An intent file cannot be proofread. A grid can: it is a low-fidelity rendering of itself. That closes the loop #vi-sysdiag-lint only half closed - the checker catches what it has a rule for, the grid shows everything else.

**Prior art, none of it invented here.** #tiling-systems is the formal name for rules 1.1 to 1.7. #wang-wfc is the same constraint structure solved generatively. #kandinsky is exactly boxes-on-coarse-grid, edges-on-fine-grid, and warns that optimising it is NP-complete. #svgbob is a working text-grid-to-SVG renderer. #css-grid-areas is the DSL, already shipped, with the rectangle rule and the same-token-count rule worth copying verbatim.

**Three decisions that have to be made before any code.** See the notes on this card.

payload.text:
Decision 1, and it is the one that kills the idea if we get it wrong: **the grid must be topological, not metric.**

Cell (3,5) must mean "column 3, row 5", never "x=300, y=500". Column widths and row heights get computed from what lands in them, exactly like CSS auto tracks - see #css-grid-areas, where the ascii art fixes topology and the track list sizes it separately.

If cells are uniform we have rebuilt #vi-sysdiag-d2 and it fails the same way: D2 grid was rejected because a column forces one width on every member, which produced the empty regions Eryk rejected in the first place. That failure is already on the map with its evidence. A uniform-cell grid walks straight back into it.

Consequence worth naming: a card occupying 7x3 cells does not mean the card is 7 units wide. It means the card spans 7 columns, and those columns are as wide as their contents need. The min-width and min-height rules in 1.1 are then about *how many columns a card claims*, which is a routing budget - how many edge lanes can pass beside it - not a size.

Decision 2: **how much does the agent write, and how much does the program infer?**

The 7 block types in the sketch can be cut to 4. #svgbob already infers corners, junctions and arrowheads from a cell's neighbours rather than making the author name them. Same trick applies:

Authored: `.` empty, `<card-id>` a cell of that card, `<edge-id>` a cell of that edge's path, `@<edge-id>` a cell of that edge's label.
Inferred: straight vs corner vs junction (from which neighbours share the edge id), arrowhead position and direction (the path cell adjacent to a card cell), label box extent (contiguous run of @ cells).

That drops rules 1.3, 1.6 and most of 1.5 from things the agent must get right to things the checker derives. What the grammar still has to enforce, and these are the rules that carry the weight:

1. A card's cells form a filled rectangle (#css-grid-areas rejects the whole template otherwise - copy that).
2. An edge's cells form a connected path, no branches except at a declared junction.
3. Exactly two of an edge's path cells touch a card cell, and they must be its two declared endpoints in the Mermaid half.
4. A label's cells form a rectangle, contiguous, touching at least one cell of its own edge.
5. Every row has the same cell count.

Five rules, four tokens. That is a much smaller thing to build and to author than seven block types.

Decision 3, the real risk: **authoring cost.**

werk's current diagram is 21 cards and 24 edges. On a grid that is maybe 24 columns by 18 rows - call it 430 cells, 2 to 4k tokens to write out, and a rewrite on every change because a grid has no diff-friendly unit smaller than a row.

That is the thing most likely to make this fail, and it is not a coding problem, so writing the renderer first would tell us nothing about it.

Three mitigations, in order of how much they would help:
- The grid only needs enough columns for card spans plus edge lanes. A fan-in of 9 edges genuinely needs 9 lanes, but that is a real constraint the agent should be confronting, not a cost of the format.
- #kandinsky says minimising bends on this model is NP-complete, so there is no solver worth reaching for anyway. Authoring is the plan, not a fallback.
- #wang-wfc is the tempting escape - let a solver fill the grid - and it is the wrong one: WFC satisfies local rules while ignoring global objectives, and "edge E1 connects card A to card B" is exactly a global objective.

payload.title: Step 1 is not code: hand-author one grid for six cards and see if it reads
payload.why: Authoring cost is the risk most likely to kill #vi-sysdiag-grid, and it is the only part a renderer cannot tell us about. Writing the checker and renderer first would prove the mechanism works while leaving the actual question untouched.
payload.body:
Four steps, cheapest first, each one able to stop the line.

**1. Hand-author, no code. ~30 minutes.**
Take a six-card subset of the real diagram: the four MAP VIEW cards, `state`, and `fold`. That is enough to contain a 4-into-1 fan-in, at least two corners, and four labels - every hard case this session hit, at a size that fits on a screen.
Write the grid by hand in the proposed four-token vocabulary. No parser, no renderer.
What it answers: can the thing be authored at all, does it read back, and how many tokens per card does it really cost. Extrapolate to 21 cards and decide whether to continue.
What would show it false: it takes more than a couple of attempts to get a legal grid by hand, or the result is unreadable as text, or the six-card grid is already so wide that 21 cards will not fit a sane canvas.

**2. The checker. ~150 lines.**
The five rules from the note on #vi-sysdiag-grid. Nothing else. Run it against the step 1 grid, including deliberately broken variants, and confirm it catches each.

**3. The renderer. ~200 lines.**
Grid to geometry to SVG. Reuses `metrics.ts` and most of `render.ts` unchanged - measurement, wrapping and the colour classes all still apply. The new part is only: column widths from contents, row heights from contents, then cells to shapes.

**4. Full diagram, side by side with the libavoid output.**
Only now is a comparison meaningful, and only now do we know whether to keep #vi-sysdiag-resolve at all.

Not in scope for any step: a solver that fills the grid, junction blocks, diagonal edges, more than one label per edge.

payload.title: An explicit close parks a tab. It does not end the session.
payload.why: A reused free tab keeps the old card's name once you clear context to start something unrelated. A finished conversation should not have to wait for the five-tab cap to push it out.

patch.body:
Close is a manual trigger for the same parked state #werk-mc-park already defines, not a
new state. Clicking a tab's close control:

1. Removes the chip from the visible strip immediately, regardless of the five-tab cap or
   recency — a user close always wins over the LRU rule.
2. Puts the conversation in the '...' menu, marked parked, exactly like an automatic
   eviction. The session id stays on disk, so opening it again from the menu is a
   `--resume`, not a restart.
3. Does not kill the underlying Claude Code process. See #werk-mc-reap for when a parked
   session's process actually dies.

This replaces the earlier "no explicit close button, at first" line in #werk-mc-park.

payload.title: A 30-minute idle sweep kills a parked session; reopening it resumes
payload.why: Parking and closing both keep a live process. Left alone that accumulates. A sweep job answers the kill-timing question #werk-mc-park left open.

patch.body:
A background job checks every parked conversation. A running turn is never parked, so this
never touches a live turn.

1. A parked conversation untouched for 30 minutes has its Claude Code process killed. The
   number 30 is a start, not a defended value.
2. The conversation list keeps the Claude Code session id for every entry, swept or not.
3. Opening a swept conversation from the '...' menu resumes it with `--resume` — the same
   path #werk-resume already proves is transparent. The user sees no difference between a
   parked-but-alive tab and a parked-and-swept one, other than resume taking slightly
   longer.

This replaces the "start by killing it [on park]" suggestion in #werk-mc-park: a parked
session stays alive until it has actually been idle, not from the moment it is parked.

Eryk is right that this is the crux. A tab strip with fifteen chips is worse than no tabs.

The rule, in three parts:

1. **A cap on visible chips.** Five. The sixth fork parks the least-recently-touched idle tab. A tab with a running turn is never parked.
2. **Parked is not closed.** The strip ends with a '...' menu. Corrected live: it lists *every* conversation, not only the parked ones — visible chips included, marked apart from parked ones, with the active one marked too. The number on the button is the total count, not just what is parked, so nothing is only reachable by scrolling the strip. Clicking a visible one switches to it; clicking a parked one un-parks it and parks whatever is now least recent. The session id is on disk, so un-parking is a `--resume`, not a restart.
3. **An explicit close, added now.** A tab's close control parks it immediately, ahead of the five-tab cap — see #werk-mc-close. It does not end the session; see #werk-mc-reap for when a parked session's process actually dies.

Who: me. Every part of this is reversible and none of it is visible in the record. The cap of five is a number to try, not a decision to defend.

The kill-timing question is decided — see #werk-mc-reap. A parked session is not killed the moment it is parked; it survives until it has been idle 30 minutes.

payload.title: Close also kills the underlying session
payload.why_not: Adds complexity this decision is meant to cut: detecting whether the chat is mid-turn, and asking the user to confirm a kill. Parking without killing needs none of that.

payload.text:
Step 1 done, by hand, before any code: .werk/diagram-grid.wgrid. Four cards (map view, chat pane, state, live + sse), two groups, three labelled edges. 10 columns x 7 rows = 70 cells, 7 lines of grid.

**Authoring cost, measured not guessed.** One pass, no retries. Roughly 17 cells per card including its share of lanes and labels. Extrapolating to the real 21-card diagram: about 360 cells, which is the low end of the 430 estimated on #vi-sysdiag-grid. The grid section itself is 7 lines here and would be perhaps 25 there - shorter than the current .werk/diagram-a.intent, not longer. The cost estimate that looked like the main risk now looks like the smaller half of the file.

**It reads.** That was the thing that could not be answered by building anything. Looking at the seven lines you can see two cards top, two bottom, three lanes running between them, and where each label sits, without rendering. That is the property no version of #vi-sysdiag-intent has ever had.

**Two format decisions that only surfaced by writing it.**

1. An edge needs no id of its own. Mermaid does not name edges, and does not have to: `<from>_<to>` is already unique and already written in the content section. `mv_st` is self-documenting in a way `e1` is not. One less thing to declare and keep consistent.

2. A label cell must never also be a path cell - the label sits BESIDE the line, in its own reserved cells, never on top of it. I tried it the other way first (label plate on the line, matching what the current renderer draws) and it breaks rule 2: a label spanning three columns across a vertical lane leaves two dead-end stubs, so the path is no longer a clean path.

Decision 2 is worth more than it looks. Every label defect fought on #vi-sysdiag-render-polish - plate over a box, plate over another plate, plate detached from its own line after being pushed - becomes **structurally impossible**, because the grid reserved the space before anything was measured. Not "checked for and repaired". Impossible to express.

payload.title: Never kill a parked session
payload.why_not: After hours or days of the program running, every past conversation is still a live Claude Code process. Memory use only grows and never comes back down.

patch.body:
Close is a manual trigger for the same parked state #werk-mc-park already defines, not a
new state. Clicking a tab's close control:

1. Removes the chip from the visible strip immediately, regardless of the five-tab cap or
   recency — a user close always wins over the LRU rule.
2. Puts the conversation in the '...' menu, marked parked, exactly like an automatic
   eviction. The session id stays on disk, so opening it again from the menu is a
   `--resume`, not a restart.
3. Does not kill the underlying Claude Code process. See #werk-mc-reap for when a parked
   session's process actually dies.

This replaces the earlier "no explicit close button, at first" line in #werk-mc-park.

## The close control on a chip

The '×' sits in the same corner as the running/waiting/dead dot, not beside it, so a chip
never changes width when the control appears. It stays hidden until the chip is hovered,
then it draws over the dot. The dot itself is still there underneath — moving the mouse
away shows it again.

patch.why: bubble() returns a tool call's existing DOM node without restoring tab.toolGroup when a later, non-tool message already closed it. addChat then calls updateSummary(null), throwing on every hydrateTab replay that contains this ordering — reproduced switching into #werk-multichat's own tab, and again switching into a 4th hydrated tab whose tool bubble id had first been created as a non-tool message, so .closest('.tool-group') found nothing to reopen. Fixed in two parts: bubble() reopens the group from the node's own DOM when it can; updateSummary(group) itself now no-ops on a null group, so a case the reopen can't cover no longer aborts the whole Promise.all hydration batch.

payload.text:
Steps 2-4 built (src/gridsys/, five files, nothing in src/sysdiag touched). Verified independently, not taken on report: build runs 0 errors, and I rasterised and read the output rather than trusting the checker.

**The core question is answered yes.** Content-derived tracks came out genuinely uneven, no degenerate zeros:

colW [32.7, 58.7, 83.4, 50.6, 113.3, 67.3, 41.3, 67.3, 54.8, 54.8]
rowH [33, 33, 26, 26, 26, 33, 33]

Column 4 is 113.3 because it holds the single-cell label "sends what you type" and nothing else. Columns 8 and 9 are 54.8 each because they split a two-cell label. Columns 1, 5 and 7 sit near 67 because a 26px lane baseline got topped up by their share of a three-column card span. Rows 0 and 1 are 33 each: 33 + 14 gap + 33 = 80, exactly the measured card height. Canvas 828x406.

That is the #vi-sysdiag-d2 trap avoided by construction. A D2 grid column forces one width on every member. Here a column is as wide as its own contents demand and a card spanning three of them contributes to all three. Same authoring model, opposite sizing rule, and the sizing rule was the thing that killed D2.

**All five checker rules fire when violated**, each refusing to write the SVG: L-shaped card, cut path, branched path, path ending short of its card, label detached from its edge, short row, unknown id. Verified by deliberately breaking the input, not by reading the code.

**One correction to my own rule 2.** A degree test alone does not catch a cut path - two disjoint straight runs each have exactly two ends and pass the count. Connectivity needs its own flood fill. That is a real hole in the grammar as I specified it on #vi-sysdiag-grid, now closed in the implementation.

payload.title: Five things the grid format cannot express yet, found by building it once
payload.why: The prototype rendered cleanly on the first attempt, so the remaining questions are not about whether the mechanism works. They are about what the DSL leaves the author unable to say, or unable to see. Each needs a decision before the format is worth extending to the full 21-card diagram.
payload.body:
Ordered by how much they threaten the design, not by how hard they are.

**1. A lane is not centred in the card it leaves, and the author cannot see that.**
`mv` spans columns 0 to 2 and its lane is column 1, but equal distribution across a span does not cancel column 1s 26px lane baseline, so the lane sits about 25px left of the card centre. Every line in the render leaves its card visibly off-centre.
This is the one that matters, because the entire argument for this design is that the grid is legible to its own author before rendering. Here it is not: the information is present (lane at column 1 of a 0-2 span is left of middle) but it takes counting to see, and the consequence is invisible.
Cheapest fix, and it keeps the property: a checker rule. "Edge X attaches to card Y off-centre" as a warning. The author still cannot see it, but no longer has to.

**2. Group frames are metric and the grid reserves no space for them.**
A frame needs a header strip above its top card. BROWSER is in row 0, so its frame computed to y = -4 and the whole drawing had to be shifted afterwards to compensate. Worse, the SERVER PROCESS top border currently crosses row 4s lane cells, and its header text misses the vertical line by luck.
A group is a first-class thing in the content section but has no cells of its own. Either it gets them (a `browser` token that fills its frame cells, so the author sees and controls the header strip), or rows gain a declared type. Undecided.

**3. A wide label sits further from its own line than a narrow one.**
A label is centred in its own cell box, so the two-cell `@lv_cp` puts its text about 55px from the line it belongs to, while the one-cell `@cp_lv` reads tight against it. More cells means further away, which is backwards from what an author intends by spending more cells.
Fix is small: a label box should hug the side of its box nearest its own lane, not centre in it.

**4. An empty column collapses to zero width.**
There is no token meaning "a gap of at least N here". The only way to buy horizontal air is to put something in the column. On a four-card diagram this never bites; on 21 cards it will.

**5. The derived edge id is ambiguous.**
`<from>_<to>` collides with any node id containing an underscore, and `a_b -> c` and `a -> b_c` both produce `a_b_c`. The implementation resolves a bare token as a card first, then an edge, which is a guess, not a rule.
Better: make the grid token `mv->st` rather than `mv_st`. Unambiguous, and it reads as what it is. Costs two characters per cell.

payload.text:
The Grid tab showed the old hand-drawn SVG, not the grid render. Cause: the route change was correct on disk but the running server did not have it - #werk-hmrs guard means a route edit inside serve() only applies on a restart, and every diagram style added this session has cost one.

Fixed so it is the last one. /api/diagram-svg now resolves ?style=X to .werk/diagram-X.svg by convention instead of a hand-maintained table of names. Adding a rendering pipeline from here costs a file and a button, with no edit to server.ts and therefore no restart.

Three legacy names are kept mapped explicitly (d2, resolver, libavoid) rather than renaming their files, because another conversation may be reading them.

The style parameter becomes a filename, so it is stripped to [A-Za-z0-9-] first. Checked: "../../etc/passwd" resolves to diagram-etcpasswd.svg and "a/../b" to diagram-ab.svg - both harmless names inside .werk, neither able to escape it.

Investigated on request, not fixed. Point 3 above understates this - it reads as a minor asymmetry ("wide label sits further than narrow") but the measured gaps are 104 to 117px for EVERY label in the four-card prototype, regardless of label length. Traced with a debug script reading resolveGrid()s actual output, not inferred from the screenshot.

Mechanism, in full: a labels cells sit BESIDE its lane, never straddling it (by rule 4 - a label cell must never also be a path cell, which is what removes plate-on-line overlap). render.ts centres the label text in its own box (resolve.ts:83-85). Nothing anywhere relates that boxs position to the lanes position - they are two independent centre-of-my-own-cells computations that happen to be topologically adjacent, with no arithmetic step tying the geometry together.

The gap size is close to constant (104-117px) because it is really `label block width / 2 roughly`, not a function of the specific text: a label block has to be wide enough to hold the whole label (up to MAX_LABEL_W=130 plus padding), and when a ~110-150px block sits flush against one side of a ~30-60px lane, its centre lands about half the blocks own width away, by geometry alone.

A second, smaller effect compounds this for mv_st specifically: its label spans columns 2-3, and column 2 is ALSO part of card mvs own 3-column span. satisfy() processes shortest-span-first, so the label demand splits columns 2/3 evenly first (~50.7 each), then mvs wider card demand tops up column 2 again alongside columns 0 and 1 (+32.7 each) because column 2 does double duty. Column 3, untouched by any other demand, stays at 50.6 - nearly half of column 2s 83.4. The solver has no notion that a column shared between a card and a label should be treated differently for either purpose.

This is why the router pipeline (src/sysdiag/resolve.ts) never had this problem: there, a label is placed at the midpoint of an actual segment of the line itself, so the labels formula and the lines formula are the SAME formula - proximity is guaranteed by construction, not by convention. Separate label cells fixed label-on-box and label-on-label overlap outright (confirmed: no plate needed, nothing overlaps in the four-card render). It traded that defect for this one, and this one needs its own fix, not inherited from the router pipeline.

payload.title: Put the label cell inside the lane's own column, between two path-cell segments
payload.why_not: Tested directly: mv_st / @mv_st / mv_st in column 1, run through the real checker. Fails R2 - a label cell is a different token from a path cell, so it does not extend the path through it, it cuts the path into two disconnected pieces (isolated cells at (2,1) and (4,1)). Making this legal would mean redefining R2 so an edge's own label cells count as pass-through for connectivity - which requires the line to run behind or around the label visually, i.e. exactly the line-under-label overlap that needing an opaque plate was built to hide. R4 (a label cell must never also be a path cell) exists specifically so that overlap can never happen. This option does not add a feature to the grid design, it undoes the reason labels got their own cells.

payload.title: Analyze images through a subagent, not a direct Read
payload.why: A direct Read of a PNG puts its base64 bytes in the main context for the rest of the session. One diagram-iteration session hit 920,805 cached tokens this way, almost all from 57 image reads. A subagent reads the image and returns text; the base64 data is discarded with it.

payload.text: Instruction added to CLAUDE.md: 'Analyze images through a subagent'.

payload.title: A label cell can sit inline in its own edge's lane, not only beside it
payload.why: The checker now allows a same-edge label rectangle to bridge a cut path when it touches every disconnected piece, instead of only allowing a label to touch a fully-connected path from the side. resolve.ts then walks each side of the cut as its own segment and clips it to the label's box; render.ts draws two <path> elements with the arrowhead only on the segment reaching 'to'. Verified against 'mv_st / @mv_st / mv_st': 0 checker errors, line breaks cleanly around the label with no stroke through the text.

payload.title: Keep the grammar as-is: a label may only sit beside its lane, never inside it
payload.why_not: This was the original call, made when a label cell first cut a path's connectivity check into two isolated pieces. Eryk overrode it and asked for the grammar to support the inline case directly, since it draws a straight lane without needing a side column for the label.

patch.why: The checker allows a same-edge label rectangle to bridge a cut path when it touches every disconnected piece, instead of only allowing a label to touch a fully-connected path from the side. resolve.ts draws the line straight through, card border to card border, passing through the label's own centre; render.ts paints a plate in the canvas's own background colour over the label's box, after the line and before the text, so the label reads as a gap in the line without the line's geometry actually breaking. Verified against 'mv_st / @mv_st / mv_st': 0 checker errors, line reads as cleanly gapped with no stroke visible through the text.

payload.text: Changed the render approach after the first pass: instead of two line segments clipped to the label's box edges, the line is now drawn straight through and a background-colour plate masks it under the label. Simpler, and it is what was asked for — the label sits visually above the line.

Applied to the real prototype: .werk/diagram-grid.wgrid's mv_st lane now uses the inline label, .werk/diagram-grid.svg rebuilt, 0 errors. Verified by sampling pixel colour along the line's x through the label's y-range in a headless-Chrome render (not a subagent's visual read, which gave two contradictory answers on this one) — background colour for the full height of the plate, line colour above and below. The app serves both files live off disk.

Applied to all three edges now (mv_st, cp_lv, lv_cp) — every label in the diagram sits inline in its own lane. Verified all three with the same pixel-sampling method: line colour above and below each label's row, background colour through it. Diagram narrowed from 778 to 606px wide since the old beside-label columns collapsed to zero, which is the format working as designed (#vi-sysdiag-grid-gaps item 4 is exactly this collapse, on the record already).

payload.title: Built the full 21-card diagram — 2 real rendering bugs found and fixed, 1 new gap found
payload.why:
Translated .werk/diagram.mmd (21 cards, 22 edges) into .werk/diagram-grid-full.wgrid/.svg, wired to the app as 'Grid (full)'. Findings, in order of consequence:

1. FIXED — check.ts wrongly flagged a valid 1-cell path (two cards stacked with exactly one gap row between them) as 'isolated', because its degree math only recognises OTHER path cells as neighbours. A cell touching both from and to directly has degree 0 and was rejected outright. Never triggered before because every edge in the 4-card prototype happened to span 3+ cells.

2. FIXED, more serious — the same 1-cell case broke resolve.ts's rendering even where the checker allowed it: clipping the single point to the 'to' card overwrote the earlier clip to the 'from' card at the same array index, collapsing the line to one point. 20 of this diagram's 22 edges rendered as invisible before the fix (confirmed by grep on the SVG's path d= attributes, not by eye). A subagent's visual QA pass on the broken render reported 'no floating ends found' — flatly wrong, caught only by checking the SVG source directly. Fixed the same way bridgedPathPoints already handled its own 1-cell arms: duplicate the point, clip each copy to a different card.

3. NOT FIXED, new gap — a group's frame is the bounding box of its members (#vi-sysdiag-grid-gaps item 2 already flagged this is metric, not reserved space). payload.body:
Three rules.

1. **Default is fit.** `scale = min(1, availW/w, availH/h)`, floor 0.15. The readout says `fit 42%`, so the number is never a mystery.
2. **100% is the maximum.** #vi-sysdiag-metrics sizes every glyph exactly at the authored size. Past 100% there is nothing more to see, only softer text.
3. **The svg element is resized, not transformed.** Setting `width`/`height` on the `<svg>` re-rasterises through the viewBox, so text stays sharp. A CSS `transform: scale()` would scale the finished raster instead.

Controls: `−  fit 42%  +` in the toolbar, where the readout toggles fit to 100% and back. Ctrl/Cmd + wheel zooms; a plain wheel still scrolls the pane.

Also fixed here, because the same panel owns it: the diagram and graph panels were sized `calc(100vh - 74px)`, which guessed a one-line header and ignored main's own padding. The panel ran 38px past the window, so the debug button and the #vi-sysdiag-link overlay fell off the bottom of the screen. Both panels are flex children of a measured column now, with no number to get wrong.

payload.title: The card ids on the diagram are a live two-way link, not a footnote
payload.why: #vi-sysdiag-backedge wrote the ids for one reason: 'why is this box here'. Written in a file, that question is answered by grepping. Written into the drawn SVG, it is answered by clicking — and the reverse direction, 'what did this card draw', comes free from the same data.
payload.body:
The mechanism is one attribute per element. `render.ts` emits every node as `<g class="wd-node" data-node="..." data-cards="a,b">` and every edge the same way, so the browser needs no second copy of the mapping.

Both directions:

- **Map to diagram.** A card's hero has two icon buttons now, not one labelled `⌖ locate`: `⌖` for the 3D graph, `▦` for the diagram. `▦` switches view and puts a 3.2px white stroke on every element whose `data-cards` names this card, then scrolls the first into the middle of the pane.
- **Diagram to map.** Clicking an element opens an overlay in the bottom-left of the pane, listing the map cards that decided it as links. Clicking one goes back to the map, on that card.

Two things needed changing to carry the ids at all:

1. The `.wgrid` content section now takes a trailing `@id,id` on a node line and on an edge line. Same place #vi-sysdiag-intent-edgecard put it, now in the grid format.
2. An edge carries a **list**, not the single card #vi-sysdiag-intent-edgecard accepted as a loss. That loss was cheap when the id was a citation; it is not cheap when the id is the link, because the second deciding card then has no way back to the drawing.

An edge also gets an invisible 11px-wide copy of its own path, under the real 1.6px line. A line that thin is not a pointer target.

payload.title: Resolve the link in the browser by matching card text to element titles
payload.why_not: This is exactly the inference #vi-prop measured at 6% to 11%. The ids are already written; guessing them back is strictly worse than reading them.

payload.title: A card created after a reopen is marked stale by it. Seven of the nine red marks on the map are this
payload.why: deriveStaleness compares rederivedAt (0 for a card that never needed one) against the reopen's seq. A card added at seq 2600 therefore inherits a reopen from seq 1339 — an invalidation it was written with already in hand, and could not have been written against.
payload.body:
The line, in `src/fold.ts:206`:

```ts
if ((rederivedAt.get(dependent) ?? 0) < seq) target.add(dependent)
```

`?? 0` means "never rederived", which the rule then reads as "not yet re-checked". For a card that existed before the reopen that is right. For a card that did not exist, there is nothing to re-check.

**Measured, 2026-09-14.** Eight cards are stale only because they were born after a reopen they descend from:

| card | reopen it inherits |
|---|---|
| #vi-sysdiag-link, #vi-sysdiag-zoomui, #vi-sysdiag-grid-edgeid, #vi-sysdiag-grid-mincell | #vi-sysdiag-edges |
| #werk-mc-desc, #werk-mc-askqa | #werk-mc-tabs |
| #werk-mc-reload-storm | #werk-dev |
| #tk-gates-readback | #lp-rubric |

Nine cards are stale in total. Seven of them are in that table. The mark that is supposed to mean "this was true and may now be wrong" mostly means "this is new".

**The preview, one line.** Seed `rederivedAt` from `node.added` instead of from nothing:

```ts
const rederivedAt = new Map(addedAt)   // then node.rederived overwrites, as now
```

That makes creation count as a first derivation, which is what it is — the author had the corrected upstream card in front of them.

**Why this is yours and not mine.** It changes what the red mark means across the whole map, and the counter-case is real: a new card can cite a stale ancestor without having read the correction, exactly the failure #vi-prop says a model cannot detect. The question is whether creation-time is evidence of a read. Not a question code can answer.

payload.title: Leave it. Rederive each new card by hand once it is written
payload.why_not: That is the behaviour now, and it produced seven false red marks out of nine. A mark that is usually wrong stops being read at all, which costs the two real ones.

payload.title: Prevent it: seed rederivedAt from node.added, so a new card is never born stale

patch.why_not: Eryk, 2026-09-14: creation-time is not proof the author read the correction. A new card can cite a stale ancestor without having taken the correction in, which is exactly the failure #vi-prop says a model cannot detect. Suppressing the mark would hide that case to tidy up seven noisy ones. Explain the mark instead of removing it.

payload.title: Leave it exactly as it is. The reader learns to ignore a new card's red mark
payload.why_not: That is what produced the question 'why is this card stale?' with no answer on the card. The mark names no origin, no path and no date, so tracing it costs a log query every time.

payload.title: A card born after a reopen keeps the mark. The card explains it instead

patch.body:
**Decided 2026-09-14, by Eryk: do not prevent it. Explain it.**

The rule in `src/fold.ts` is unchanged. What changed is that a flagged card now carries its own reason.

`deriveStaleness` returns a third value, `flagWhy: Map<id, FlagTrace[]>`. One entry per reopen the card inherits:

| field | what it answers |
|---|---|
| `origin`, `reason`, `at` | which reopen, what kind, when |
| `why` | the text typed at reopen time |
| `via` | the depends_on hops from this card to the origin, shortest path, origin last |
| `bornAfter` | the card was created after the reopen it inherits |

Two places render it. The map gets a **Why this card is stale** section above *Why a dependency is flagged* — that older section only ever covered a card's own direct depends_on targets, so a card four hops downstream showed nothing at all. `werk show` prints the same lines.

`bornAfter` changes the wording, and that is the whole point:

- **born after** — "written with the correction already in hand. The mark is inherited, not a sign this card is wrong."
- **predates it** — "its content really was written against the old decision. Re-read it before clearing."

**Measured before the change, 2026-09-14.** Eight cards were stale or paused only because they were born after a reopen they descend from: #vi-sysdiag-link, #vi-sysdiag-zoomui, #vi-sysdiag-grid-edgeid, #vi-sysdiag-grid-mincell (from #vi-sysdiag-edges), #werk-mc-desc, #werk-mc-askqa (from #werk-mc-tabs), #werk-mc-reload-storm (from #werk-dev), #tk-gates-readback (from #lp-rubric). Nine cards were stale in total.

**Why the count is not the argument.** Seven noisy marks out of nine is a good reason to look. It is not a reason to suppress, because the one case suppression would hide is the dangerous one: a new card that cites a stale ancestor without its author having read the correction. #vi-prop says that read cannot be inferred. So the mark stays and the reader gets the facts to judge it.
patch.why: deriveStaleness compares rederivedAt (0 for a card that never needed one) against the reopen's seq, so a card added at seq 2600 inherits a reopen from seq 1339. Seven of the nine marks on the map were that case. The mark is correct to keep — creation-time is no proof the author read the correction — but nothing on the card said which reopen reached it, or how far away it was.

payload.title: Resolved: child->diagram drawn, via a junction and reordering runner's south fan

payload.text: Drawn for real in .werk/diagram-grid-full-minimal.wgrid. Two things did it: #vi-sysdiag-grid-junction's crossing (child->diagram + gate->approvebar share one cell, each blind to the other), and reordering runner's south fan so child sits next to the lane instead of on the far side of chatlog/lock — the actual blocker was never gate_approvebar alone, it was that child was positioned behind a cluster of uncrossable 1-hop bridge edges (runner->child, child->gate, child->cli), and junctions can't cross those (no pass-through cell). Moving child, not routing around it, is what worked. 0 build errors; verified programmatically that the resolved path actually starts at diagram and ends at child, and that all 22 prior cards/edges are still present. First attempt (a background agent trying to solve this by reasoning alone) failed by exhausting its output budget without acting — did it by hand instead, using the exact routing constraints already mapped out in conversation.

child->diagram is drawn for real now — see #vi-sysdiag-grid-lanewall. Required moving child in runner's south fan, not just adding a junction; the junction alone wasn't enough because child was boxed in by uncrossable short edges, not just gate_approvebar. 0 errors, verified programmatically.

payload.title: A junction renders as a hop: the horizontal edge arcs over the vertical one
payload.why: Two lines drawn flat across each other read as a corner or a branch — exactly what R6 swears a junction is not. The crossing at (12,5) in diagram-grid-full-minimal.wgrid was indistinguishable from a turn. A 5px semicircle over the other line is the convention every wiring diagram has used since lines first had to cross on paper, and it needs no new authoring: the junction token already says where the crossing is.

payload.title: Break the under-line instead: a gap in the vertical line where the horizontal one passes
payload.why_not: A gap reads as a cut path, and a cut path is a real thing in this format — a bridged inline label (#vi-sysdiag-grid-inline-label) already draws one on purpose. Two different meanings for the same picture. The gap also has to be painted as a background-colour plate over the other edge, which makes the crossing depend on paint order between two independent edges; the arc does not.

payload.title: Let the author declare which of the two edges hops, in the junction token
payload.why_not: There is no judgement in the choice, so it is arithmetic, not intent — #vi-sysdiag-render's whole split. Worse, an author picking per crossing makes the rule vary across one picture, so a reader has to re-read which line is on top each time. A fixed rule (the horizontal one hops) is learned once and holds everywhere. R6 already guarantees exactly one horizontal and one vertical edge per junction, so the rule always resolves.

payload.text:
Built and verified. resolve.ts gains `attachHops`: it reads check.ts's junction list, asks which of the two edges owns the cells east and west of the crossing, and hands that edge the junction cell's centre as a hop point. The point is already a vertex of that edge's path (walkPath emits one point per cell), so nothing about the route changes.

render.ts's `edgePath` replaces that one vertex with three commands: stop 5px short, `A5,5` across, carry on. The arc always bows north for a horizontal hop, whichever way the line travels — the sweep flag flips with the direction. R6 guarantees a junction's two path neighbours are the crossing edge's own cells, never a card border, so a full cell of straight line sits on each side of the arc and it can never eat a turn or reach a card.

Verified on .werk/diagram-grid-full-minimal.svg, by reading the two path strings back, not by eye:
  gate->approvebar  ... L1145.21,837 L1145.21,770 L1145.21,703 ...   (straight through)
  child->diagram    ... L1150.21,770 A5,5 0 0 0 1140.21,770 ...      (arc centred on 1145.21,770)
0 errors, same 2 pre-existing U-turn warnings, canvas unchanged at 2726x1303.

The vertical branch of edgePath (bow east) is written but never taken, since attachHops only ever hops the horizontal edge. It stays because the arithmetic belongs with the drawing, not with the rule that picks the edge.

Eryk: the hopping line must always be higher on the z axis. SVG has no z-index, so that is a paint-order guarantee, and the author's edge order cannot be trusted to provide it.

resolve.ts now sorts edges before returning them. `paintOrder` is a topological sort over one relation only — a hopping edge lands after every edge it hops — seeded in document order, so an edge that hops nothing keeps the place the author gave it. ResolvedGrid.edges is a PAINT order now, and render.ts says so at the loop.

A cycle (A hops B at one crossing, B hops A at another) has no paint order that works. Those edges keep document order and the build emits a warning, because the alternative is one crossing silently drawn the wrong way round.

Proved it reorders, not just that it runs: moved `child -->|...| diagram` to be the FIRST edge in the content section of a copy of the file. It still paints at index 22 of 23, after gate->approvebar at 17. In the real file the two were already in that order by luck of authoring, so the picture there is unchanged — the sort is what makes it a guarantee instead of luck.

Checked: no instruction anywhere tells the agent to reconsider the diagram after a map update. CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md only cover keeping the card map current, not the diagram file. This decision (redraw whole, each turn) and #vi-sysdiag-declare (say local vs. restructure) are designed but not wired into any trigger yet — that wiring depends on #vi-sysdiag-derive and #vi-sysdiag-proto landing first.

payload.title: Two subagents: sysdiag-scout judges whether the diagram should change, sysdiag-updater edits the .wgrid and rebuilds until the tile grammar passes
payload.why: Splits the judgement from the mechanics. sysdiag-scout does the slow, non-deterministic read #vi-sysdiag-derive already named as the reason a fold can't run on every view; sysdiag-updater only ever runs a deterministic edit-then-check.ts loop, so it can retry safely without re-deciding anything scout already settled.

payload.text: Corrected: the two subagent prompts (.claude/agents/sysdiag-scout.md, sysdiag-updater.md) cited werk's own card ids (#vi-sysdiag-grain, #vi-sysdiag-derive, #vi-sysdiag-declare) and used werk's actual architecture (tree/state/foldfn nodes) as the worked example. Since these ship as part of the product and must run against any project's own map, not just this repo's, every reference is now expanded inline in plain prose and the example uses a fictitious auth/billing system instead. CLAUDE.md's own instruction section is unchanged — it is this repo's dev instructions, not shipped agent content, so citing this repo's cards there is correct.

Gated sysdiag-scout on current status, not on 'did something change': only a card whose status is currently decided may justify diagram content. A reopen sets status back to open immediately, so the moment a decided card reopens, scout must find every content line citing it and either drop just that citation (if another decided card still justifies the line) or remove the line outright. A stale-but-still-decided card keeps its standing — staleness flags a card for review, it does not itself revoke decided status; only an actual reopen does. Fixed CLAUDE.md's trigger condition too: it previously excluded status flips as a trigger, which was backwards — a status change (becoming decided, or a decided card reopening) is exactly the case that matters.

Built the missing half: rederiveOrder in src/fold.ts topologically sorts stale ∪ paused so a card's flagged depends_on targets print before it. 'werk stale' now prints that order instead of scan order, so fixing top-to-bottom never redoes work against a still-wrong dependency.

payload.title: The frontend needs a component stack
payload.why: web/app.js is 2422 lines of hand-rolled rendering. Six criteria decide the replacement, and they do not all point the same way.

payload.title: Progressive loading is an API shape decision, not a framework feature
payload.why: /api/graph sends all 418 nodes (503 KB) on load AND refetches all of it on every log append. No framework fixes that.
payload.body:
Measured on the live server, 2026-09-17:

    payload           503,456 bytes
    nodes / edges     418 / 671
    card bodies       142,751 bytes = 28% of the payload

Two separate problems hide behind 'the map is too big to load at once', and only one of them is about the frontend.

1. **The whole fold ships on every change.** web/app.js line ~1713: `stream.addEventListener('changed', load)`, and `load()` does `fetch('/api/graph')` — the entire 503 KB. Every turn that appends one event refetches all 418 nodes. That is not a rendering cost, it is a transport cost, and it is paid whichever framework renders the result.

2. **Every card body ships whether or not it is read.** #vi-onview already decided one view = one card. So the 28% of the payload that is card bodies is, by werk's own design, one card's worth of needed text and 235 cards' worth of waste.

What actually fixes it, independent of the framework choice:

- `/api/card/<id>` — one card, its body, and its immediate neighbours' titles. What #vi-onview needs to render a view.
- `/api/graph?shape=1` — ids, kinds, statuses and edges only, no bodies. What the tree, the rollups and the 3D graph need.
- The `changed` SSE event carries the changed ids, so the client patches instead of refetching.

Do this first. A component framework on top of a 503-KB-per-keystroke API is a faster renderer for the same stall.

payload.title: Stay vanilla. Add web components or Lit for structure
payload.why_not: Keeps the no-build-step property, but has no answer for criterion 2: there is no per-component state-preserving HMR for hand-rolled DOM code. It also does not fix the real complaint — 2422 lines in one file is an organisation problem a class-per-file refactor only relabels.

payload.title: Astro with islands, React or Svelte inside
payload.why_not: Best-in-class answer to criterion 4 and the wrong shape for werk. Astro is page-oriented: a navigation is a document swap. werk's chat pane holds a live SSE stream, per-tab transcripts and a streaming turn (#werk-multichat) that must survive every card navigation. That is the one thing an MPA model makes hardest. Islands HMR also tends to remount the island, losing criterion 2 exactly where state matters most.

payload.title: SolidJS with Vite
payload.why_not: Wins criterion 3 on raw rendering: fine-grained reactivity updates one card without diffing a tree, which is the best fit for a 418-node map. Loses on criteria 2 and 6. Solid's HMR historically remounts a component rather than preserving its signals, and its share of agent training data is a fraction of React's — the two criteria Eryk ranked hardest.

payload.title: Svelte 5 with runes, plus Vite
payload.why_not: The strongest runner-up. Compiles away, so the static 28% of the payload ships near-zero JS — criterion 4 without adopting an islands framework. Two risks decided against it: svelte-hmr preserves state less reliably than React Fast Refresh for the case that matters (a component holding a live stream), and runes landed recently enough that agents still write Svelte 4 store idioms, which cuts directly against criterion 6.

patch.body:
Eryk decided this. A new implementation is built on this stack from scratch — this card is not a migration plan, and nothing here asks anyone to port web/app.js.

## The stack

    runtime      Bun, bun --hot            already decided, #werk-hmr
    client       React + Vite              Vite as the CLIENT dev server, middleware mode
    hydration    islands as a pattern      multiple small roots, NOT Astro, NOT RSC

Vite runs as middleware inside werk's own Bun server. It is not the server runtime. That distinction is the whole reason this does not contradict #werk-hmr, which rejected **vite-node as the process host** after it crashed werk outright (#werk-hmr:src2). One process: Bun serves the API and the SSE stream and hot-reloads its own modules; Vite transforms and hot-reloads the client.

## Why, against the six criteria

1. **Component architecture** — React. No argument needed; every candidate satisfied this.
2. **Per-component HMR preserving state** — the discriminator. React Fast Refresh preserves hook state per component and is the most proven implementation of exactly this requirement. Every rejected option lost or weakened this: Lit has no equivalent (#werk-stack:opt0), Solid remounts (#werk-stack:opt2), svelte-hmr is less reliable for the case that matters (#werk-stack:opt3), and an Astro island tends to remount (#werk-stack:opt1). werk's chat pane holds a live SSE stream and an in-flight turn; a remount on save is the failure this criterion exists to prevent.
3. **Progressive loading** — not solved by the framework. See #werk-stack-api. The API is card-scoped from day one; React's role is only that Suspense boundaries make a card-at-a-time fetch natural to express.
4. **Partial hydration for static content** — islands as a pattern, not a platform. The server already holds the fold, so it server-renders card HTML that never hydrates. React roots mount only where state actually lives:

        hydrated            the chat pane, the tab strip (#werk-mc-tabs), the ask bar,
                            the map controls, the 3D graph view
        never hydrated      the card body, rendered Markdown, the evidence and
                            depends-on lists, breadcrumbs, rollup bars

   This is what buys criterion 4 without adopting the MPA model that fights the chat pane.
5. **Backend** — Bun, unchanged. Out of scope here; #werk-hmr owns it.
6. **Agent proficiency** — React by a wide margin. Eryk ranked this alongside criterion 2, and it is the reason the Svelte 5 runner-up lost: runes are recent enough that agents still reach for Svelte 4 store idioms.

## Explicitly not chosen

RSC. It answers criteria 3 and 4 natively, and it needs Waku, Parcel-RSC or equivalent on a custom Bun server — bleeding edge in exactly the layer that must not break. Hand-rolled islands get most of the benefit with none of that risk. Revisit only if the manual-roots approach proves insufficient, and record it as a reopen with a reason.

The three other candidates are #werk-stack:opt0 through :opt3, each with its own why_not.
patch.why: Eryk decided. Criterion 2 (state-preserving per-component HMR) and criterion 6 (agent proficiency) both point at React, and neither runner-up wins them back.

patch.body:
This is a constraint on the new implementation, not a bug report against the old one. The measurement below is evidence for the constraint; the current build is where it was taken, and that build is not being ported (see #werk-stack).

Measured on the running server, 2026-09-17:

    payload           503,456 bytes
    nodes / edges     418 / 671
    card bodies       142,751 bytes = 28% of the payload

Two problems hide behind 'the map is too big to load at once', and only one is about rendering.

1. **The whole fold ships on every change.** The current client subscribes `changed` to a full `/api/graph` refetch, so a turn that appends one event re-downloads all 418 nodes. That is transport, not rendering. No component framework makes it cheaper.

2. **Every card body ships whether or not it is read.** #vi-onview decided one view = one card. So the 28% that is bodies is one card's worth of needed text and 235 cards' worth of waste.

## What the new implementation builds instead

    GET /api/card/<id>        one card: body, why, status, and its immediate
                              neighbours' titles and ids. Exactly what #vi-onview
                              needs to render one view.
    GET /api/graph?shape=1    ids, kinds, statuses, edges, rollups. No bodies.
                              What the tree, the rollup bars and the 3D graph need.
    SSE changed               carries the ids that changed, so the client patches
                              its cache instead of refetching the fold.

The shape query is what keeps the 3D graph and the rollups working — they genuinely need every node, and they never need a single body. Splitting on that line, rather than paginating, is what makes 'render one card at a time' fall out for free.

React's part in this is small and worth stating so nobody over-credits the framework: a Suspense boundary per card view makes the card-scoped fetch natural to express, and nothing more. The saving is in the API.
patch.why: 418 nodes ship on load and on every append in the current build. A from-scratch implementation should never inherit that shape.

patch.body:
The idea still holds: capture how you decide, not what to build, so alignment does not reset every work item. But nothing built so far has hit the same trade-off twice — #werk-stack's six criteria, the tab placement calls, the permission-mode choice were each one-off. Building a profile mechanism now would be process for a problem that has not shown up yet.

Skip, not reject: the difference from #decisionmd (still supported_by, still worth reading if this reopens) is that this is not a dead end, it is deferred until the trigger condition actually occurs — the same class of trade-off coming up a second time.
patch.why: Eryk: skipped, deliberately. Decisions have not repeated enough yet to earn a standing-preference mechanism. Reopen this if that changes.

payload.title: What sampling costs to build
payload.body:
Five parts. The runner is easy; the divergence detector is the whole problem.

1. **Fan-out runner** — N headless agents from one brief, each in a throwaway git worktree. Reuses `Agent` (src/agent.ts already spawns `claude` per conversation) and `ConvoManager`. New: concurrency cap, per-sample worktree create/delete, and an auto-allow permission policy, because a headless sample cannot stop at the permission bar. About one day.

2. **A no-questions prompt contract** — the sample agent may not ask. It must pick, and record every pick. Half a day.

3. **Divergence detection** — the hard part. A plain diff of N trees is noise: naming, order, formatting. So do not diff the code. Each sample returns a **decision manifest**: the requirement choices it made, one line each. werk clusters the manifests; a field where the samples disagree is a fork. This is #al-diff-cli's pattern one level up — the agent supplies the structure, code verifies the claim against the artifact. About one day.

4. **Fork to options** — each cluster becomes an option card, the samples become its evidence (screenshot + .patch per #al-ephem), and the question names only the fork. #al-two's rules apply: two or more, diverse, short rationale, explicit "I do not care". About one day.

5. **Budget control** — N=3, a wall-clock cap, kill on overrun. A sample run costs real tokens and minutes, so the cap is not optional.

First real run: about three to four days. A crude version in one afternoon, if the samples are plans and not code — see the options below.

payload.title: Sample full implementations in N worktrees
payload.body: What #al-sample says now. Highest fidelity: the divergence is real, running, and screenshotable. Costs the most — N worktrees, N builds, minutes per run, and the manifest must be verified against real code.

payload.title: Sample the plan, not the code
payload.body: Each of N agents writes only the brief it would build. No worktree, no build, no screenshot. Ambiguity in a requirement shows up in the plan text, which is where the fork lives anyway. Cheap: one afternoon, seconds per run. Loses the running prototype that #al-two wants attached to each option.

payload.title: Sample only what you cannot read
payload.body:
Plan-or-code is not a setting. It is a per-item call, made at the moment the fork is found. Two tests, both must pass before any sampling run:

1. **The fork lives in an artifact you have to look at.** Layout, wording, timing, feel. If two sentences of prose make the fork clear — as they did for this card's own plan-vs-code options — the samples show nothing you cannot read. Write the options and ask (#al-two).
2. **The agent cannot predict the pick.** If the manifests would agree, there is no fork and the run is pure cost.

When both pass, the substrate is the cheapest artifact where the fork becomes visible: plan text, then running code, then a screenshot. Climb only as far as needed.

ops.old: First real run: about three to four days. A crude version in one afternoon, if the samples are plans and not code — see the options below.
ops.new: First real run: about three to four days. A crude version in one afternoon, if the samples are plans and not code. Which one applies is decided per item, not once — see #al-sample-when. The two options below are kept as record: they were weighed as a global choice and rejected as one.

payload.title: Accept/discard as a button, not a typed word
payload.body:
Adds `✓ accept` / `✕ discard` buttons to the blue pending panel (`pendingHTML` in web/app.js), wired to two new routes, `POST /api/change/accept` and `POST /api/change/discard` (src/server.ts). Each route re-checks the node still has a pending proposal, then appends the same `change.accepted`/`change.discarded` event the CLI already writes — no new event type, no new rule. The log-file watcher already redraws every open map on any append, so no separate broadcast is needed.

Replaces the note on #al-diff-cli that said "no button here yet, on purpose." That was a placeholder, not a rejected design — nothing argued against a button, the CLI path just came first.

payload.title: Fork inherits the parent's context reading
payload.body:
Two bugs, both from the same root cause: a forked tab's Agent object exists before its child process ever starts, and contextUsed stays its constructor default (0) until the first real turn reports usage.

1. **Pie showed 0% right after a fork**, even though the forked session already carries the parent's full history — #werk-mc-fork confirmed the cache hit is real, so the tokens are real too. Fixed: ConvoManager.fork() now passes the parent's current context() into the child Agent's constructor (initialContext), so the pie reads the inherited size immediately, before any turn runs.

2. **Clear context did nothing before the first message.** clearContext() cleared the session file and the transcript, but never touched forkFrom — the in-memory pointer a pre-first-message fork uses instead of a session file. So the next send still forked the parent. Fixed: clearContext() now also sets forkFrom = null, so clearing before the first message produces a genuinely empty conversation.

patch.body:
An icon button (`✓`, primary blue) sits in the locate-btns row, top-right of a pending card, next to the ⌖ and ▦ icons. payload.title: Wayfinder is the same pipeline as a prompt file. The graph is what it cannot hold
payload.why: Closest prior art. Same thesis — plan as a map of decisions, worked one at a time. It lacks the two things that need a program: computed staleness and recorded contrast.
payload.body:
`/wayfinder` is a Markdown skill (`~/.agents/skills/wayfinder/SKILL.md`). It charts a big, foggy effort as one **map** issue on the repo tracker, with **decision tickets** as child issues, and resolves them one per session until the way to the destination is clear.

## The same

| wayfinder | werk |
|---|---|
| Plan, don't do — tickets resolve decisions, not build slices | intent + options is the MVP — see #mvp |
| Map is an index; detail lives in the ticket | map is an index; detail lives in the card |
| Native blocking edges; the frontier is the unblocked set | `depends_on` edges; `stale` is the derived frontier |
| Ticket types: research / prototype / grilling / task, each HITL or AFK | `--who you`/`me`/`prototype` decides the same thing |
| Fog of war — do not chart what you cannot see | `open` and `proto` cards; the map is deliberately partial |
| Prototype to raise fidelity of the discussion | #al-ephem, #al-two |
| Refer by name, never by bare id | the card title is the handle |

## The difference

1. **Propagation.** Wayfinder's blocking is a *scheduling* edge: what is takeable next. It is not a truth edge. Closing a ticket never marks a downstream decision suspect — the skill only says "if the decision invalidates other parts of the map, update or delete those tickets," which is an instruction to a model, and #vi-prop measured that at 6–11% recall. werk's `depends_on` is a truth edge and `reopen` walks the closure. This is the whole reason the logic is in a program — see #pr-logic.
2. **Contrast.** Wayfinder records only the answer, in a resolution comment. The rejected alternative is gone. werk records it as an `option` node with `--why_not` and an `alternative_to` edge, and `unchallenged` counts what was never weighed — see #ro-unchal.
3. **Shared gaze.** Wayfinder's map is text the agent reads. werk's map is open next to the chat, and the agent is told which card Eryk is looking at every turn — see #werk-card-blind, #visual.
4. **Gates.** A skill cannot refuse. werk's contract check lives in the CLI and blocks `decided` — see #werk-contract.
5. **Grain.** A wayfinder ticket is sized to one 100K-token session. A werk card is one decision with one why.
6. **Method of alignment.** Wayfinder's default type is `grilling` — conversation, asking. #align holds that asking is the weak instrument and showing variants is the strong one.

## What wayfinder has and werk does not

A named **Destination** per effort, and an **Out of scope** section. werk's map has a root statement but no per-effort destination node, and no place to record work consciously ruled out. See #pr-wf-dest.

payload.title: No per-effort destination, and nowhere to record out-of-scope
payload.why: Wayfinder names a Destination for each effort and keeps an Out of scope section. werk's map has a root statement and no equivalent for either.
payload.body:
Two gaps that #pr-wayfinder surfaced.

1. **Destination.** #root is one permanent statement for the whole tool. A wayfinder map names, per effort, what reaching the end looks like — a spec, a decision, a migration — and every session orients to it before picking work. werk has no node that says "this branch of the map is finished when X." `drained` (#drained) is the closest, and it is a count, not an intent.
2. **Out of scope.** There is no way to say "we ruled this out of this effort." A rejected *option* has `--why_not` and `alternative_to`. A rejected *area* has nothing — it either stays `open` forever and inflates the count, or it is deleted and the reason is lost.

Open question for Eryk: is a destination a new `kind`, or the `why` on the card the subtree hangs from? And is out-of-scope a fourth status, or a `--why_not` on a `card`?

patch.body:
## What the destination actually is

A real named goal, written as one or two lines on the map body. Its *type* is constrained: "the spec, decision, or change this effort is finding its way to." So usually the planning artifact — "a spec for a tool doing X, ready to hand off" — not "the tool doing X". Not always: the skill allows "a change made in place like a data-structure migration", and an effort can carry execution into the map through its Notes.

But naming the goal is not what the destination is *for*. It does two jobs:

1. **A stopping rule.** The map is done when nothing is left to decide. Then the map closes and is thrown away.
2. **A scope boundary.** "Fog only ever gathers toward the destination." Out of scope exists only because a finish line exists.

## Why #root cannot do that job

#root is a thesis. Every card refines it, and it is never reached — you cannot be finished with "we build and fix software with agents in one repeating pipeline." A wayfinder map is an **effort**: disposable, with a finish line. werk's tree is a permanent belief structure. They are different objects that both sit at the top.

So *destination as named goal* is redundant here. #root already does it.

## The plan/build split does not transfer

Correct — werk plans by prototyping and then builds, in loops. Wayfinder's split is real for wayfinder because it is a one-shot planning campaign that ends in a handoff. werk has no handoff. So the finish line, if werk gets one, is **per subtree or per loop**, not per map.

## What is left of the gap

Two things, both narrower than the card started:

1. **A finish line per subtree.** #drained is the closest: settled and unchallenged is zero. It counts; it does not judge. Nothing on the map says "#align is finished when we can sample ambiguity on a real brief." Open: is that a field on the subtree root, or is it what `why` should already be doing?
2. **Out of scope.** Still a real hole and independent of the first. A rejected *option* has `--why_not` and `alternative_to`. A rejected *area* has nothing — it stays `open` forever and inflates the count, or it is deleted and the reason is lost. Open: a fourth status, or `--why_not` on a `card`?
patch.why: Wayfinder's Destination is a named goal whose job is a stopping rule and a scope boundary. #root is a thesis that is never reached. The gap is not the goal — it is the finish line, and out-of-scope.

payload.title: Isolation matches what a sample mutates, not one policy for every sample
payload.why: A git worktree is git's own isolation for a sample that edits tracked files. Most code-rung samples don't — they read the repo and write one derived artifact to a path of their own choosing. Two of those never collide if each gets its own output path.

payload.title: Always run every code-rung sample in its own git worktree
payload.why_not: Unneeded git overhead when a sample only produces a derived artifact and never edits a tracked file — a private scratch output directory is parallel-safe by construction and needs no git operation at all.

patch.body:
Two tiers, picked per sample by what it does — the same per-item call #al-sample-when already
asks the builder to make, extended from substrate to isolation:

1. Output-only. The fork is about what gets produced (a rendered SVG, a manifest), and the
   sample never edits a tracked file. Each sample gets a private scratch output directory
   (os.tmpdir()/werk-sample-<runId>-<i>/), runs against the real checkout read-only, and the
   build command is pointed at that path. No git operation at all. Parallel-safe by
   construction: distinct paths cannot collide, so there is nothing for two samples to step on.

2. Source-mutating. The fork is about how tracked files change. Edit/Write calls would land
   on shared paths, so this tier needs #al-ephem's worktree: cheap because it shares the git
   object store, and `git diff` produces the .patch for free.

The signal: does resolving this fork require touching source, or only producing an artifact
from source as it stands. "How should the diagram look" -> output-only. "How should
resolve.ts compute it" -> worktree. Rejected: al-sample-build-isolation:opt0 (worktree for
every code-rung sample) — unneeded git overhead when a scratch directory already gives
parallel safety for free.

Six parts. The runner is easy; the divergence detector is the whole problem.

1. **Fan-out runner** — N headless agents from one brief. Reuses `Agent` (src/agent.ts already spawns `claude` per conversation) and `ConvoManager`. New: concurrency cap, an auto-allow permission policy (a headless sample cannot stop at the permission bar), and per-sample isolation — see #al-sample-build-isolation for which samples need a worktree and which need only a scratch output path. About one day.

2. **A no-questions prompt contract** — the sample agent may not ask. It must pick, and record every pick. Half a day.

3. **Divergence detection** — the hard part. A plain diff of N trees is noise: naming, order, formatting. So do not diff the code. Each sample returns a **decision manifest**: the requirement choices it made, one line each. werk clusters the manifests; a field where the samples disagree is a fork. This is #al-diff-cli's pattern one level up — the agent supplies the structure, code verifies the claim against the artifact. About one day.

4. **Fork to options** — each cluster becomes an option card, the samples become its evidence (screenshot + .patch per #al-ephem), and the question names only the fork. #al-two's rules apply: two or more, diverse, short rationale. "I do not care" is offered live when the fork is actually asked about — never written as a graph option, or a card could be marked decided on indifference, which names nothing. About one day.

5. **Budget control** — N=3, a wall-clock cap, kill on overrun. A sample run costs real tokens and minutes, so the cap is not optional.

6. **The artifact builder is not optional.** #al-sample-when picks the substrate per item, so the ladder has to reach its top rung when a fork needs it: a build, a Playwright screenshot, the .patch kept per #al-ephem. Plan-only sampling is the cheap subset of the same runner — same fan-out, same manifest, no filesystem isolation at all. It is not a second design, and it does not let parts 1 and 5 be skipped.

First real run: about three to four days. A crude version in one afternoon, if the samples are plans and not code. Which one applies is decided per item, not once — see #al-sample-when. The two options below are kept as record: they were weighed as a global choice and rejected as one.

real group extent, bottom edge 25.0px short. Column widths 0-4 in this diagram are
[204, 212, 141, 195, 214] against opt0's assumed average of 175.3 — not close to uniform.
A 146.6px shortfall on a group whose members span 1023px means the shape-grid outline would
NOT contain the real "diagram" card (214px wide, the group's own widest member) — the exact
containment failure #vi-sysdiag-grid-groupshape exists to prevent.

opt1 (proportional mapping via real per-column lookup, not a fraction of total extent): exact
match on all four edges, by construction — it looks up colX/colW directly instead of
assuming any distribution.

Also checked "proc" (SERVER PROCESS), a group spanning nearly the full grid width: opt0
still drifted 25.8px on the row axis, confirming the column-axis result was not a fluke of
one group's shape.

Decision: opt1. opt0 is not a simplification with acceptable rounding error — it can produce
a shape cell that a checker would need to hard-fail against, in exactly the pipeline whose
whole point is that fitting is a checked fact, not a coincidence.

/tmp/werk-proto-groupshape/ (script + rendered SVG overlay) — ephemeral, deleted after this
note, per #al-ephem.

patch.why_not: Prototyped against the real full-minimal diagram: a fixed scale factor assumes every column/row is the same size. Real columns range 141-214px wide here — the assumption is off by up to 147px on a real group's edge, enough to clip the group's own widest member. See :ex0.

Decided: opt1 — map shape-grid coordinates to pixels by looking up each column/row's real
resolved bound (colX/colW/rowY/rowH from resolve.ts), not by a fixed integer scale factor.
