Confirmed by the code, not by argument. `EdgeType` in `src/types.ts` carries exactly these four and nothing else:

refines — the level edge. Children get reviewed.
depends_on — propagates staleness through the reverse closure.
supported_by — evidence. Flags for review, never auto-invalidates.
alternative_to — a rejected option, kept, restored when the decision reopens.

The grammar stayed small enough to maintain during live conversation, across hundreds of decisions in this map. That is the constraint, not expressiveness.

Two graphs over the same project, answering two different questions.

| | map | product diagram |
|---|---|---|
| node | a claim | a part of the built thing |
| question | why is it like this | what is there now |
| shape | history, append-only | current state, overwritten |
| goes stale | by propagation | the moment code lands |

The map already answers why. Nothing renders what. The set of decided cards implies a system — UI, agent, log, fold, CLI, server — and today that system exists only in the reader's head.

Corrected from the earlier version of this card, which claimed the product diagram was just a new node kind inside the map. It is not. Adding --kind component to log.jsonl would put parts and claims in one node set, and then the rollup, the staleness closure, and the drained count would all count parts as if they were unsettled decisions.

The edge that does connect them runs one way only: a component points back at the cards that decided it. See #vi-sysdiag-derive for whether that edge is authored or derived.

Built, not just planned: `.werk/diagram-grid-full-minimal.wgrid` and `src/gridsys/` are a real second graph, kept current by the sysdiag-scout and sysdiag-updater agents rather than by hand.

payload.title: The agent needs a test harness it can run itself
payload.why: The agent builds werk but cannot see the result. Two feedback channels are missing: assertions over the pure code, and a real browser it can open, screenshot and inspect.
payload.body:
Eryk asked for both in one go, and they are one problem with two halves.

1. Unit tests, with high but reasonable coverage, so a change to fold.ts or permission.ts fails loudly instead of silently.
2. Visual tests: the agent starts werk, drives a browser, takes a screenshot, reads the DOM, and gets feedback on what it just built.

Today the whole repository has one test file: src/permission.test.mjs, 121 lines, run by `npm test` as a plain node script with hand-rolled check(). 7061 lines of source, one test file, no runner, no coverage, no browser.

Four choices sit below. Each is separate and each can be decided on its own.

payload.title: One test runner, or one per side
payload.why: The runtime is Bun and the client will be Vite. Each brings its own runner. Running both is a real option, not a failure.
payload.body:
`bun test` is already in the runtime decided at #werk-hmr. Jest-compatible `expect`, watch mode, `--coverage` built in, zero dependencies added. It replaces the hand-rolled `check()` in src/permission.test.mjs directly.

Vitest reads the same vite.config the client app uses, so a component test resolves JSX, aliases and CSS exactly like the running app does. #werk-stack-framework puts Vite in the stack whether or not it is used for tests.

The fork is whether the client tests are worth a second runner and a second command.

payload.title: What 'high but reasonable' coverage means here
payload.why: A single repo-wide percentage sends tests to the places that are cheapest to cover, not the places that break.
payload.body:
The source splits cleanly in two.

**Pure.** src/fold.ts (391), src/permission.ts (234), src/types.ts (164), src/log.ts (56). Input in, value out. A line here is cheap to cover and a bug here is invisible: fold.ts derives stale and needsReview, and a wrong derivation looks like a correct map.

**I/O.** src/agent.ts (894), src/server.ts (535), src/cli.ts (886), src/convos.ts (246). These hold a live claude child process, an SSE stream and the append-only log. Lines here are covered only by faking the thing that makes them hard.

A percentage over the whole repository counts both the same. The fork is whether to accept that, or to gate the two halves by different rules.

payload.title: How the agent drives a real browser
payload.why: Eryk asked for it directly: load the tool in a browser, screenshot, inspect, and get feedback on what was just built.
payload.body:
The loop the agent needs: start werk, open a page, click or navigate, capture what came out, and read it.

Three ways to hold the browser:

- a library called from a test file, so a visual run is one command and the artifacts land in a directory
- a browser-automation MCP server, so the agent steers tool call by tool call and can improvise
- the client runner's own browser mode, tied to #werk-stack-framework's Vite

These are not exclusive in principle. Picking two means two ways to write the same test.

payload.title: What makes a visual test pass
payload.why: A screenshot does not assert anything by itself. Something has to decide, and #img-subagent forbids the cheapest answer.
payload.body:
#img-subagent already decided the agent must never Read a PNG in the main conversation. One session reached 920,805 cached input tokens from 57 direct image Reads. So 'the agent looks at the screenshot' is not free here, and is not the default.

Two candidate verdict sources:

- a stored pixel baseline, compared automatically, failing on any diff over a threshold
- deterministic assertions over the DOM and the accessibility tree, with the screenshot kept only as evidence a vision subagent reads on demand

The first is a hard gate that a tool under heavy layout churn will fail constantly for correct reasons. The second never fails on a look, only on a structure.

payload.title: A browser-automation MCP server, steered tool call by tool call
payload.why_not: Its screenshots return into the main conversation, one per tool call. That is the exact pattern #img-subagent banned after a session reached 920,805 cached input tokens from 57 image Reads. An MCP browser makes that the normal path, not the mistake.

payload.title: A stored pixel baseline, compared automatically on every run
payload.why_not: The client does not exist yet (#werk-stack-framework). A baseline over a UI being built from scratch is rebaselined on nearly every commit, so the gate teaches the agent to accept a diff rather than read it. It also answers a question Eryk did not ask: he said 'screenshot and inspect... get feedback', which is a judged look, not an automatic gate.

patch.body:
Decided without asking, because the constraints already settle it. Reversible — say so and it flips.

**A visual test passes on structure, never on pixels.** The assertions run over the DOM and the accessibility tree: the card title is present, the detail pane holds the body, the stale mark is on the right node, the chat pane shows N messages. These fail for a reason a human can read in one line.

**The screenshot is evidence, not a verdict.** Every run writes a PNG to a directory. Nothing compares it. When the agent wants to know how the thing looks, it spawns a subagent that reads the PNG and reports in text — #img-subagent, which this card depends on. The image never enters the main conversation.

So a red test always names a broken structure. A look that is wrong but structurally correct is found by asking, not by failing.

#werk-test-visual-judge:opt0 is the pixel-baseline branch and why it lost.
patch.why: Not a real fork. The sampler refused to sample it: every sample lands on the same branch, for two reasons already on the map.

payload.title: Vitest browser mode, through the client's own Vite config
payload.why_not: Its unit is a mounted component, not a running werk. It cannot boot the Bun server, hold the SSE stream open, or drive a live claude child — and that loop is what Eryk asked to see in a browser. It would also drag a second runner in as a side effect rather than as a decision (#werk-test-runner).

payload.title: Both: Vitest browser mode for components, Playwright for flows
payload.why_not: Two ways to write the same browser test. The agent then has to pick the level correctly on every new test, and picking wrong is silent. Rejected for now, not forever: if component-level browser tests turn out to be needed, this is the card to reopen.

patch.body:
**Playwright, called as a library from a test file.** Not an MCP server, not the client runner's browser mode.

A visual test boots werk the way a person does — the Bun server from #werk-hmr, the real routes, the real SSE stream — then opens Chromium, navigates, clicks, asserts, and writes a PNG to a directory. One command runs the whole file.

This is the only option that covers the loop Eryk named. The other two mount a component or steer a browser from outside, and neither can hold a live claude child through a turn.

It costs the repository its first heavy dependency: a browser binary. That is the trade, taken knowingly — werk had zero dependencies until this card.

What a run asserts, and what happens to the PNG, is #werk-test-visual-judge.

Rejected: #werk-test-visual:opt0 (browser MCP), #werk-test-visual:opt1 (Vitest browser mode), #werk-test-visual:opt2 (both).
patch.why: Eryk chose it. Only Playwright-as-a-library exercises the thing he asked to see: werk running for real, with its server, its stream and its child process.

payload.title: One repo-wide coverage percentage, around 70%
payload.why_not: It prices a line in fold.ts and a line in agent.ts the same. The cheap lines are in the pure modules, so an agent under a single number covers those and leaves the child-process paths bare — the opposite of what the number was meant to buy.

payload.title: Report coverage, gate nothing
payload.why_not: Nothing then stops coverage drifting down as the tool grows, and Eryk asked for high coverage, not for a report.

patch.body:
**Two gates, not one.**

**Pure modules — a coverage number.** src/fold.ts, src/permission.ts, src/log.ts, src/types.ts. Threshold 90% of lines. A bug here does not throw: fold.ts derives stale and needsReview, so a wrong fold renders a wrong map that looks entirely correct. These lines are cheap to cover and expensive to get wrong. That is exactly where a hard number belongs.

**I/O modules — a named behaviour list, no percentage.** src/agent.ts, src/server.ts, src/cli.ts, src/convos.ts. These hold a live claude child, an SSE stream and the append-only log. Covering a line here means faking the thing that makes the line hard, and a percentage would reward the fake. Instead each module carries a written list of behaviours that must have a test, and the list is the gate.

The behaviour lists are not written yet. They go on their own cards under this one, one per module.

Rejected: #werk-test-scope:opt0 (one repo-wide percentage), #werk-test-scope:opt1 (report only).
patch.why: Eryk chose the split rule. 'High while reasonable' means high where a line is cheap and a bug is invisible, and named behaviours where a line is expensive and a bug is loud.

payload.title: bun test only, with Playwright called as a bare library
payload.why_not: It saves one dependency and costs the trace viewer, which is the main way anyone reads why a browser test failed. Launch, teardown and retry would be hand-written per file, and an agent writing the fiftieth test file gets that wrong quietly.

payload.title: Three runners: bun test, Vitest, @playwright/test
payload.why_not: Three configs for a 7000-line tool. Vitest earns its place only if a Vite-specific transform makes a component behave differently under Bun's transpiler than in the app. That has not happened yet — the React client does not exist yet (#werk-stack-framework). Reopen this if it does.

patch.body:
**`bun test` for everything in-process. `@playwright/test` for everything in a browser.**

`bun test` is already in the runtime from #werk-hmr. Jest-style `expect`, watch mode, and `--coverage` built in — that last one is what enforces the 90% gate on the pure modules in #werk-test-scope. It adds no runner dependency. It also replaces the hand-rolled `check()` in src/permission.test.mjs, which is the only test the repository has today.

React component tests run under `bun test` with happy-dom. Vitest stays out until a Vite-specific transform makes a component behave differently under Bun's transpiler than in the running app — see #werk-test-runner:opt1.

`@playwright/test` runs the browser flows from #werk-test-visual. It is worth the second runner for the trace viewer, fixtures, retries and parallel workers. A bare library call inside `bun test` would mean hand-writing launch and teardown in every file.

Two scripts:

    bun test        # src/ and components
    bun run e2e     # playwright test

Rejected: #werk-test-runner:opt0 (bun test only), #werk-test-runner:opt1 (three runners).
patch.why: Eryk chose the two-runner split. Each runner drives a different thing, so there is never a question which one a new test belongs to.

patch.body:
Eryk asked for both halves in one go, and they are one problem: the agent builds werk and cannot see the result.

Today the whole repository has one test file — src/permission.test.mjs, 121 lines, a hand-rolled `check()` run by `npm test` as a plain node script — against 7061 lines of source. No runner, no coverage, no browser.

Four cards below settle it. All four are decided.

    runner      bun test + @playwright/test              #werk-test-runner
    coverage    number for pure, behaviours for I/O      #werk-test-scope
    browser     Playwright as a library, real server     #werk-test-visual
    verdict     structure asserts, the PNG is evidence   #werk-test-visual-judge

Two commands:

    bun test        # src/ and React components, --coverage gates the pure modules
    bun run e2e     # playwright test, boots the real werk server

This card is the requirement, not a choice. No alternative was weighed against having tests.

payload.title: The named-behaviour list for each I/O module is not written yet
payload.why: #werk-test-scope made the list the gate for agent.ts, server.ts, cli.ts and convos.ts. A gate with no list is not a gate.
payload.body:
One list per module. Each entry names a behaviour that must have a test, in words a person can check against the code.

The four modules: src/agent.ts (894), src/server.ts (535), src/cli.ts (886), src/convos.ts (246).

#al-sample-when's rule applies. Which behaviours matter is a plan-tier question where independent samples would disagree, so it is worth sampling rather than guessing — but only now that #werk-test-scope has settled the rule they serve.

payload.title: Ambiguous convo ref attribution
payload.why: Found by sampling #al-sample-build against #werk-test-behaviours: the samples disagreed here.

payload.title: List the 'ambiguous conversation reference fails' behaviour only under convos.ts (resolveConvo/findQuote), not under cli.ts
payload.body:
cli.ts only parses flags and calls the logic; the actual check lives in convos.ts

Sample(s): 0, 1

payload.title: List 'recall/quote fail on ambiguous reference' as a cli.ts behaviour, separate from the convos.ts resolveConvo item
payload.body:
the command-level failure (recall/quote silently acting on the wrong conversation) is a distinct user-facing effect worth its own entry

Sample(s): 2

payload.title: Model switch during turn
payload.why: Found by sampling #al-sample-build against #werk-test-behaviours: the samples disagreed here.

payload.title: setModel/clearContext throw an error and refuse to run while a turn is in flight
payload.body:
killing a live turn on a config change would silently lose the user's in-progress message

Sample(s): 1

payload.title: setModel/clearContext do kill the child, but the resulting exit is suppressed from the 'agent stopped' crash message
payload.body:
otherwise every deliberate model switch would look like a crash to the user

Sample(s): 2

payload.title: Always rule mechanism
payload.why: Found by sampling #al-sample-build against #werk-test-behaviours: the samples disagreed here.

payload.title: an 'always' permission choice is re-sent as --allowedTools/--add-dir flags on the next launch of the child process
payload.body:
otherwise the same click has to be answered again every restart

Sample(s): 1

payload.title: an 'always' decision is written to allow.json and merged directly into the live in-memory allow list
payload.body:
otherwise the same click would have to be repeated on every restart of that tool call

Sample(s): 2

patch.why_not: src/convos.ts:114-126 is the only place resolveConvo lives. cli.ts calls it and prints the result; it holds no ambiguity logic of its own to test separately. A behaviour listed under cli.ts here would test convos.ts through an extra layer for no reason.

patch.body:
Decided from the code, not from taste — see #werk-test-behaviours-model-switch-during-turn and #werk-test-behaviours-always-rule-mechanism for the same kind of call.

The ambiguous-reference behaviour belongs on the convos.ts list only: 'a ref matching more than one conversation by session-id prefix or by card id is reported ambiguous, never auto-picked' and 'findQuote reports ambiguous rather than picking the first hit when a needle appears in more than one message'.

It is not a separate cli.ts behaviour. cli.ts's recall/quote commands hold no ambiguity logic — they call resolveConvo/findQuote and print whatever comes back.

Rejected: #werk-test-behaviours-ambiguous-convo-ref-attribution:opt1 (a separate cli.ts item).
patch.why: Read directly from source, not a taste call. src/convos.ts:114-126 (resolveConvo) and :212-219 (findQuote) are the only code that decides ambiguous — a name match wins outright, a session-id prefix or card id match of more than one conversation returns {ambiguous: [...]} instead of picking one. cli.ts has no branch of its own on this; it only prints whichever result convos.ts returns.

patch.why_not: src/agent.ts:326-329 and :354-356: setModel and clearContext both start with 'if (this.busy) throw new Error(...)' and return before touching this.proc. Neither kills the child while busy — the throw happens first. This option does not match the code.

patch.body:
Decided from the code. setModel/clearContext throw and refuse to run while a turn is in flight (this.busy). Only when idle does setModel kill and relaunch the child (agent.ts:330-333), and that kill is expected — this.switching is set first, so the pane shows 'Switched to <model>' instead of a crash message.

Behaviour for the agent.ts list: 'setModel/clearContext throw instead of running while a turn is in flight, so a mid-turn config change can never kill the child holding it.'

Rejected: #werk-test-behaviours-model-switch-during-turn:opt1 (kill-but-suppress) — does not match the code.
patch.why: Read directly from source. src/agent.ts:326-334 (setModel) and :354-363 (clearContext) both open with 'if (this.busy) throw new Error(...)', before any code that could touch this.proc. A busy turn is never killed by either call.

patch.why_not: True but half the mechanism. It names only the on-disk persist-and-relaunch path (permission.ts:156-162 allow.json, agent.ts:287-289 read on construction, :463-466 sent as --add-dir/--allowedTools at spawn). It leaves out that the click also updates the running process's this.allow/this.dirs immediately, without waiting for a relaunch.

True but half the mechanism. It names only the immediate in-memory merge (agent.ts:783-784: 'for (const rule of rules) if (!this.allow.includes(rule)) this.allow.push(rule)'). It leaves out that addAlways (permission.ts:156) also writes allow.json, which is what makes the rule survive past this process — agent.ts:287 reads it back on the next launch.

patch.body:
src/agent.ts:775-785, on an 'always' click: the update is pushed into the pane's session-scope list (line 779), `addAlways` writes rules and dirs into allow.json (permission.ts:156-162), and in the same breath `this.allow`/`this.dirs` are updated in memory (agent.ts:783-784) — so the click applies without waiting for a restart. agent.ts:287-289 reads allow.json back into `this.allow`/`this.dirs` when a new child is constructed, and :463-466 sends them as `--add-dir`/`--allowedTools` at spawn. Both halves are one mechanism, not a choice between them.

Behaviour for the agent.ts list: 'an "always" choice is written to allow.json and merged into the live allow/dirs list in the same step, so it holds for the current process and for every relaunch after it.'

Neither sampled option stands alone: #werk-test-behaviours-always-rule-mechanism:opt0 (relaunch only) and :opt1 (in-memory only) are each half of this card's body.
patch.why: Read directly from source. Not a real fork — the two sampled options each named one true half of a single mechanism, not two rival claims.

payload.title: agent.ts behaviour list
payload.body:
Nine behaviours. The three samples agreed almost word for word on all but two points, both resolved from source: #werk-test-behaviours-model-switch-during-turn, #werk-test-behaviours-always-rule-mechanism.

1. On restart, the child resumes the session id stored on disk instead of starting a blank conversation.
2. A crashed child is replayed with its in-flight turn exactly once, then gives up — never loops, never silently drops the message.
3. An auth/login/credential failure is never auto-retried; it surfaces instead of hammering a broken login.
4. "No conversation found with session ID" clears the stored session and starts fresh, instead of bricking that conversation forever.
5. setModel/clearContext throw instead of running while a turn is in flight, so a mid-turn config change can never kill the child holding it (#werk-test-behaviours-model-switch-during-turn).
6. When setModel does restart an idle child, this.switching suppresses the crash message — a deliberate switch never reads as "the agent stopped".
7. Denying a permission ask returns interrupt:false with a message, not a killed turn — one denied tool call does not abort the whole turn.
8. Context-used is read from one assistant message's own usage, never the turn's summed modelUsage — a multi-tool-call turn must not overstate how full the context is.
9. An "always" choice is written to allow.json and merged into the live allow/dirs list in the same step, so it holds for the current process and every relaunch after it (#werk-test-behaviours-always-rule-mechanism).

payload.title: server.ts behaviour list
payload.body:
Eight behaviours. All three samples converged on the same set, near word for word.

1. Two server processes can never run against the same .werk directory at once.
2. Image upload rejects any content-type outside png/jpeg/gif/webp, and any body over 20 MB.
3. /api/image only ever serves a file resolved by basename() under ATTACHMENTS — a crafted name cannot read a file outside it.
4. Static file serving stays confined under WEB after path normalization — the same traversal risk, on the whole fallback route.
5. Every pushed SSE event (chat, delta, status, context, background) carries the correct convo name, so one tab's turn never renders in another tab.
6. /api/chat rejects a request with neither text nor images — an empty send fails loudly instead of spawning an empty turn.
7. /api/model rejects any model/advisor value outside the fixed allow-list, before it ever reaches the child's spawn args.
8. The diagram route's ?style= query param is stripped to [a-zA-Z0-9-] before it becomes part of a filename.

payload.title: cli.ts behaviour list
payload.body:
Eight behaviours. cli.ts has the widest surface of the four modules, so the list covers the checks that keep the map's decision record honest, and skips low-risk commands that only print or replay the log (events, stale, inbox, import).

1. add refuses an id that already exists, instead of silently clobbering it.
2. add --status decided is rejected outright — every decided card must pass through the status command's own checks.
3. status <id> decided enforces who is set, a depends_on edge (or --no-basis), and — when who is you — an alternative_to option or --unchallenged; it fails with the exact fixing command otherwise.
4. link/unlink fail if either endpoint id does not already exist as a node.
5. reopen --reason postponed marks the reverse-dependency closure paused; any other reason marks it stale — never both, never the wrong one.
6. quote only records an excerpt when the text is an exact, single match in the transcript; zero or more than one match fails.
7. prototype refuses fewer than two options — #al-two exists precisely to stop a built option with nothing to compare it against.
8. sample and prototype clamp n and timeout to their hard caps regardless of what flag value is passed.

payload.title: convos.ts behaviour list
payload.body:
Six behaviours. Includes the ambiguous-reference item settled at #werk-test-behaviours-ambiguous-convo-ref-attribution — it lives here, not on the cli.ts list.

1. A ref matching more than one conversation, by session-id prefix or by card id, is reported ambiguous, never auto-picked (#werk-test-behaviours-ambiguous-convo-ref-attribution).
2. findQuote reports ambiguous rather than picking the first hit, when a needle matches more than one message.
3. findQuote only searches you/agent messages, never tool/result — a transcript's own echo of the search text must not count as a sighting.
4. recall --grep keeps only messages matching every given term, not just one.
5. recall without --tools/--thinking hides tool/result/thinking messages by default.
6. listConvos still lists the legacy single-conversation layout (main, .werk/session and .werk/chat.jsonl) alongside every directory under conversations/ — dropping it would make recall blind to everything said before multichat existed.

patch.why: Content drawn from source (agent.ts/server.ts/cli.ts/convos.ts) and cross-checked against three independent sample runs of #werk-test-behaviours's brief, which agreed almost word for word on this list. This is the gate #werk-test-scope set for I/O modules — a list, not a percentage.

Content drawn from source (agent.ts/server.ts/cli.ts/convos.ts) and cross-checked against three independent sample runs of #werk-test-behaviours's brief, which agreed almost word for word on this list. This is the gate #werk-test-scope set for I/O modules — a list, not a percentage.

Content drawn from source (agent.ts/server.ts/cli.ts/convos.ts) and cross-checked against three independent sample runs of #werk-test-behaviours's brief, which agreed almost word for word on this list. This is the gate #werk-test-scope set for I/O modules — a list, not a percentage.

Content drawn from source (agent.ts/server.ts/cli.ts/convos.ts) and cross-checked against three independent sample runs of #werk-test-behaviours's brief, which agreed almost word for word on this list. This is the gate #werk-test-scope set for I/O modules — a list, not a percentage.

patch.body:
Four lists, one per I/O module named in #werk-test-scope.

    agent.ts     9 behaviours   #werk-test-behaviours-agent
    server.ts    8 behaviours   #werk-test-behaviours-server
    cli.ts       8 behaviours   #werk-test-behaviours-cli
    convos.ts    6 behaviours   #werk-test-behaviours-convos

Built by sampling: three independent tries at the same brief, per #al-sample-when. All three agreed almost word for word on every module's list. Three genuine forks came out of clustering, all resolved by reading the actual code rather than by asking — a mechanism question is not a taste call:

    #werk-test-behaviours-ambiguous-convo-ref-attribution   convos.ts owns it, cli.ts is a thin wrapper
    #werk-test-behaviours-model-switch-during-turn          setModel/clearContext throw, never kill mid-turn
    #werk-test-behaviours-always-rule-mechanism              both halves are true at once, not a choice
patch.why: All four module lists are decided below. The three sampled forks were resolved by reading source, not by asking Eryk — see each fork card's why.

payload.title: The scout/updater exchange runs in the background; Eryk sees only the verdict
payload.why: The pipeline itself works, per Eryk, but running sysdiag-scout and sysdiag-updater inline printed their full exchange into the main chat. Eryk wants the two subagents to talk to each other in the background, and the main chat to show one line only: product diagram updated, or no need to update the product diagram at this point.

payload.title: Pure code gets a coverage number. I/O code gets a sampled behaviour list.

patch.body:
A rule for any module in any project on this platform, not only werk's four files today.

**1. Classify the module by one question.** Does a wrong line throw, hang, or crash — or does it quietly produce a result that looks correct? A quiet wrong answer is pure. A loud failure is I/O.

**2. Pure code gets a number.** A pure module is a plain function of its input, cheap to call from a test, and a bug in it never announces itself. Set a high line-coverage threshold. Testing it is cheap and missing a bug in it is expensive, so a hard number belongs here.

**3. I/O code gets a named list, never a percentage.** An I/O module holds something live — a child process, a socket, an open file, a network call. Covering a line here means faking the live thing, and a percentage rewards the fake, not the real risk. Write one list per module instead: named behaviours, no number.

**4. Find the behaviours by sampling, not by guessing.** Run several independent readings of the module against one brief: name what breaks the tool if this is wrong. Where the readings agree, that is the list. Where they disagree, the disagreement is a fact question about the code, not a taste question — read the source and settle it. Do not ask a person to guess at what code already does.

**5. Write each behaviour as a responsibility, not as a location.** 'A crash never loses the in-flight message' survives a rewrite. 'agent.ts line 326 throws' does not. A list built this way stays true when the file under it changes, as long as the module's job stays the same. Only a changed responsibility needs the list re-run — not a renamed file or a moved line.

Rejected: #werk-test-scope:opt0 (one repo-wide percentage — prices a cheap pure line and an expensive I/O line the same). #werk-test-scope:opt1 (report only, gate nothing).

Applied to werk today, as evidence: #werk-test-scope:src0.
patch.why: Generalized from werk's own split, so any project on this platform classifies its own modules the same way — werk is the first project built here, not the only one #product plans for. #werk-test-scope:src0 holds werk's own numbers as evidence, not as the rule.

payload.title: Applied to werk today: fold/permission/log/types at 90%, agent/server/cli/convos as behaviour lists
payload.body:
Werk's own split, produced by running #werk-test-scope's method against werk's current code.

**Pure — 90% line threshold.** src/fold.ts, src/permission.ts, src/log.ts, src/types.ts. fold.ts derives stale and needsReview; a wrong fold renders a wrong map that looks entirely correct, so a bug here is invisible without a hard number.

**I/O — a named behaviour list, no percentage.** src/agent.ts, src/server.ts, src/cli.ts, src/convos.ts. Each holds something live: a claude child process, an SSE stream, the append-only log on disk. The four lists are #werk-test-behaviours-agent, #werk-test-behaviours-server, #werk-test-behaviours-cli, #werk-test-behaviours-convos.

This card is evidence, not the rule. When werk's client is rebuilt at #werk-stack, or any of these four files is split or renamed, re-run #werk-test-scope's method against the new code — do not hand-edit this card to chase the refactor.

payload.title: Sample one brief for the list. Settle each fork against source, not taste.

patch.body:
The recipe for #werk-test-scope's step 4, reusable on any project's I/O modules.

**1. Write one brief for every target module together.** Ask for named behaviours that would break the tool if wrong, one sentence each, small enough to read in one sitting. One shared brief costs one sampling run instead of one per module.

**2. Run a handful of independent samples against it.** `werk sample-options <target-id> "<brief>"` — each sample reads the real code and writes its own list; none may ask a question.

**3. Convergence is the list.** Where the samples agree almost word for word, that agreement is the behaviour, with no further check needed. Most of a real module's list settles this way.

**4. A fork is a fact question or a design question — tell them apart before you touch it.** A fact question asks what the code already does. Settle it by reading the source and citing the exact lines, never by asking a person to guess at running code. A design question asks what the code should do, and nothing decides that but a person with real contrast in front of them, per #al-two.

**5. Write the resolved list back onto one card per module,** each item at the responsibility level per #werk-test-scope's step 5, with any resolved fork kept as its own card so the reasoning survives even after the behaviour sounds obvious in hindsight.

Applied to werk today, as evidence: #werk-test-behaviours:src0.
patch.why: The procedure behind #werk-test-scope's step 4, generalized so any project on this platform can run it against its own I/O modules — werk is the first project here, not the only one. #werk-test-behaviours:src0 holds werk's concrete run: the brief, the three forks, and how each was settled.

payload.title: Applied to werk today: one brief across four files, three forks, all settled from source
payload.body:
Werk's own run of #werk-test-behaviours's procedure.

One brief covered all four modules at once. Three independent samples via `werk sample-options`. All three agreed almost word for word on every module's list — no fork needed for most of it.

Clustering surfaced three real forks, all fact questions about existing code, each settled by reading source rather than asking:

    #werk-test-behaviours-ambiguous-convo-ref-attribution   convos.ts owns it, cli.ts is a thin wrapper
    #werk-test-behaviours-model-switch-during-turn          setModel/clearContext throw, never kill mid-turn
    #werk-test-behaviours-always-rule-mechanism              both halves are true at once, not a choice

Four resulting lists: #werk-test-behaviours-agent (9), #werk-test-behaviours-server (8), #werk-test-behaviours-cli (8), #werk-test-behaviours-convos (6).

This card is evidence, not the recipe. When werk's own modules are rewritten or split differently, re-run #werk-test-behaviours's procedure against the new code — do not hand-edit the four lists to chase the refactor.

payload.title: test-scope: a subagent that runs #werk-test-scope's rule on demand
payload.why: The rule and the recipe existed only as cards a human or agent had to remember to apply by hand. A subagent plus an AGENTS.md trigger makes the build step apply them automatically, on any project, not just when someone happens to reread #werk-test-scope.
payload.body:
.claude/agents/test-scope.md — read-only, classifies a module as pure or I/O per #werk-test-scope step 1, and for I/O runs #werk-test-behaviours' sampling procedure (`node src/cli.ts sample`, plan tier only). It never writes to the map and never invents a coverage number for pure code — a missing threshold policy is reported, not guessed.

AGENTS.md, new section 'Before deciding what to test, classify the module first': tells the main agent to spawn `test-scope` proactively whenever the build step reaches a module with no test policy yet, and to write the result onto the map itself — a threshold card, a behaviour-list card, or a design-question fork card per #al-two.

Same shape as the existing sysdiag-scout/sysdiag-updater split: the subagent decides and reports, the main agent is the only one that writes.

payload.title: werk v0
sample's JSON output was missing each sample's manifest
payload.why: Found by running #werk-test-subagent for real against src/convo-manager.ts. #werk-test-behaviours step 3 says to read where samples converge from the sample command's own JSON output — src/cli.ts:655 (before the fix) only ever emitted {id, error, outputDir} per sample, never the manifest text. Convergence was structurally unreadable; only disagreements (forks) were ever visible.
payload.body:
Fixed in src/cli.ts's sample case: each entry in samples now also carries manifest, the same raw decision-manifest text findForks already had. No behaviour changed for findForks or for the existing sampler subagent, which never read this field — this only adds data that was being computed and then thrown away.

This is why #werk-test-subagent's first real run had to fall back to reading source directly to build convo-manager.ts's behaviour list instead of reading convergence off the command's own output, per its own report.

payload.title: The 90% threshold covers any pure code in werk, not just the four named files
payload.why: The subagent's first real run flagged this as unresolved: src/convo-manager.ts:20-30 (dirFor, nameForCard) are pure by #werk-test-scope's own test, but named nowhere in #werk-test-scope:src0's file list, so it correctly refused to apply 90% without asking.
payload.body:
#werk-test-scope:src0 names fold.ts/permission.ts/log.ts/types.ts because those were the pure modules that existed when the card was written, not because the threshold was meant to stop there. The decision was about a category — pure code — not an enumerated file list. A new pure function anywhere in werk falls under the same 90% line, automatically, the moment it exists.

dirFor and nameForCard in src/convo-manager.ts are pure by the test in #werk-test-scope step 1 (a name collision is quiet-wrong, never throws) and are covered by the 90% threshold as of this card.

This closes the one gap #werk-test-subagent's first real run reported rather than guessed at.

payload.title: convo-manager.ts (ConvoManager) behaviour list
payload.body:
Nine behaviours for the ConvoManager class (src/convo-manager.ts:32-114). The two free functions above it, dirFor and nameForCard, are pure — see #werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope.

Produced by #werk-test-subagent's first real run: three samples via `node src/cli.ts sample`, three forks from clustering, resolved by reading source.

1. main() creates the main agent on first reference unconditionally — no disk check, never throws.
2. ensure(name) for any other name only succeeds if a directory record already exists on disk; otherwise it throws 'no conversation named "<name>"'.
3. A live agent already held in memory is always reused — ensure()/main() never spawn a second Agent for a name that already has one.
4. Every agent this manager ever creates, including main, is announced to every onSpawn listener at creation time, and a listener that unsubscribes stops receiving calls.
5. fork() requires the parent conversation to already have sent a message — it throws if the parent has no sessionId yet, so an empty conversation cannot be forked.
6. A forked conversation's name is checked for uniqueness only against currently-live agent names, not against conversations that exist on disk but have no live Agent — a collision with an un-ensure'd disk-only conversation is not guarded against.
7. Every agent this manager creates shares one Asks queue, so a permission prompt from any conversation surfaces in the same place.
8. Parking a conversation stops its child process but leaves its directory and session file intact, so the next message to that name resumes the same conversation.
9. stopAll() stops every live agent's child process — none is left running after it returns.

One design-question fork could not resolve from source and goes to Eryk: #werk-test-behaviours-convo-manager-onspawn-granularity.

payload.title: One onSpawn bullet, or split out the main-agent case?
payload.why: test-scope's sampling run found both halves true from source — onSpawn fires for every agent including main, and unsubscribe stops it — but whether that is one behaviour-list entry or two is a documentation choice, not a fact the code settles.
payload.body:
Item 4 on #werk-test-behaviours-convo-manager's list currently reads as one bullet: 'every agent this manager ever creates, including main, is announced to every onSpawn listener at creation time, and a listener that unsubscribes stops receiving calls.'

Two ways to write it instead:

A. Keep it as one bullet — the whole onSpawn contract as a single registry guarantee.
B. Split it — a dedicated bullet just for 'fires for main too,' because main is the one agent easy to forget to test, and burying that case inside a general line risks it getting skipped.

payload.title: Keep one bullet for the whole onSpawn contract
payload.why_not: Not yet rejected — open choice.

payload.title: Split into two bullets, one just for the main-agent case
payload.why_not: Not yet rejected — open choice.

patch.why_not: Eryk picked one bullet. Splitting would break the pattern of the other eight items on the list, each one guarantee, for a case that isn't proven to need special emphasis.

patch.body:
Decided: keep item 4 as one bullet. 'Every agent this manager ever creates, including main, is announced to every onSpawn listener at creation time, and a listener that unsubscribes stops receiving calls.' No change to #werk-test-behaviours-convo-manager's list.

Rejected: #werk-test-behaviours-convo-manager-onspawn-granularity:opt1 (a dedicated main-only bullet).
patch.why: Eryk chose one bullet, matching the style of the list's other eight items.

payload.title: werk v0 ships the inner build loop: plan in, code out
payload.why: Planning is scoped enough to build werk from scratch. The next thing to prove is that the plan can be executed by the loop, not by hand.

patch.body:
Eryk, 2026-09-20: planning is scoped enough to build werk from scratch. The next thing to prove is the other half — that the plan gets executed by the loop, not by hand.

Scope cut, from him: the **inner** loop only. Build and test. Validate, grade, and iterate stay in #loop's other children, still paused.

So v0's promise is one sentence: point the loop at a card, and get back a branch that implements that card and everything decided under it, with its own tests passing.

#werk-test gives the loop its eyes — `bun test` and `bun run e2e`. That is the only piece already settled. Six more are not:

    unit     what one pass of the loop is given        #werk-loop-unit
    state    'decided' is not 'built'                  #werk-loop-state
    brief    what text the child agent actually gets   #werk-loop-brief
    done     the inner-loop stop condition             #werk-loop-done
    land     where the code goes, how Eryk reads it    #werk-loop-land
    gap      what happens when the plan runs out       #werk-loop-gap

Machinery already exists and is not in question: src/prototype.ts runs a headless `claude -p` in a throwaway worktree and captures the diff; the log takes new event kinds; web/diff.js renders a patch. The loop is not new plumbing. It is the six decisions above.

payload.title: What one pass of the loop is given
payload.why: The map is a decision tree, not a task list. #werk alone is 91 cards. Nothing today says where one build task starts and stops.

payload.title: 'decided' is not 'built'
payload.why: A card goes decided the moment the argument settles, long before code exists. The loop cannot tell the two apart, so it cannot tell what is left to do.

payload.title: What text the child agent actually gets
payload.why: A card body alone assumes its ancestors. The whole subtree degrades the context. #lp-stateless makes this the loop's main lever.

payload.title: The inner-loop stop condition for v0
payload.why: A loop needs a stop condition. Validate is out of scope, so v0's is the test harness and a retry cap — not a rubric.

payload.title: Where the code goes, and how Eryk reads it back
payload.why: 'Check out the results' is a requirement on the output shape: a branch, a commit per unit, a diff per card.

payload.title: What happens when the plan runs out mid-build
payload.why: The plan is detailed, not complete. An agent that stops to ask kills autonomy; an agent that guesses silently loses the decision.

patch.body:
`decided` answers 'is the argument settled'. It does not answer 'does the code exist'. Today #werk has 85 decided cards and roughly one of them is implemented per file in src/ — the map cannot tell you which.

The loop needs the difference to pick its next unit at all, and Eryk needs it to see progress on the map instead of in a terminal.

My reading: do not add a field. Derive it, the way #fold already derives stale and needsReview — new log events (build.started, build.passed, build.failed) carry the card id and the commit, and fold turns them into a per-card built flag plus the commit that did it. That keeps the log the only writer and makes the map show build progress for free.

The counter-reading worth a line: git is already the record. Ask git whether the card's files changed since the card was decided, and keep no build events at all. Cheaper, but it needs card-to-file mapping, which only #vi-sysdiag-codemap has started.

Eryk cut validate out of v0, so the stop condition is not a rubric. It is the harness from #werk-test plus a cap.

Pass for one unit:

    bun test        # with #werk-test-scope's coverage gate on the pure modules
    bun run e2e     # playwright against the real server
    tsc --noEmit

Fail: feed the failing output back as the next pass's input, per #lp-stateless — fresh agent, same brief, plus the last failure. Cap the retries. On the cap, stop the whole run and leave the branch where it is; do not skip to the next unit with a broken tree underneath it.

Two things this deliberately does NOT do, both deferred to #loop's other children: no graded judgement (#lp-two), no held-out check set (#lp-split). v0 can be reward-hacked by the agent writing weak tests. That is a known, accepted hole for v0 — name it here so it is not rediscovered as a surprise.

'Be able to check out the results' is a requirement on the output shape, not a nicety.

My reading: one branch per run, one commit per unit, the card id in the commit message. Eryk runs `git checkout` once and reads the history as the plan in build order. src/prototype.ts already does the hard part — a throwaway worktree per #al-ephem, diffed and removed — but it throws the worktree away and keeps a .patch. The loop wants the opposite: keep the branch.

In the map: the card shows its commit, and web/diff.js renders that commit's diff in the card. Reading the build then happens where the decision is, not in a terminal.

Open inside this: does a failed run leave its branch behind, or delete it? Leaving it is how you debug the loop; deleting it is how you avoid twenty dead branches after a week.

The plan is detailed. It is not complete. Every unit will hit something the cards do not settle — a name, a file split, an error case.

Three ways this can go, and only the third keeps both properties Eryk asked for:

1. The agent stops and asks. Kills autonomy. Out.
2. The agent picks and says nothing. Keeps autonomy, loses the decision — the map now lies about what was decided, and the next pass cannot see the pick.
3. The agent picks, and the pick becomes a card: who:prototype, status open, parented under the unit it came from, with the reading it chose in the body.

3 is already werk's own convention — `--who prototype` exists in `werk add` for exactly this. It also turns the build into a source of planning work instead of a consumer of it: after a run, `werk find` shows Eryk what the loop had to invent.

#al-sample is the related mechanism one layer up, at plan time. This is its build-time counterpart: plan-time sampling asks a human, build-time picking tells a human afterwards.

Open: does a pick that contradicts an existing decided card behave differently — stop the run rather than file a card?

#lp-stateless says one fresh agent per pass, and the repository is the memory. That makes the brief the loop's main lever: it is the only thing the pass knows that git does not already show it.

Too little and the agent re-invents decisions that are already on the map. Too much and the context degrades, which is the exact failure #lp-stateless was written to avoid.

My reading of what one brief holds:

1. The unit card — title, why, body, verbatim.
2. Its ancestor chain up to the root, title and body. The card assumes them.
3. Every decided descendant. That is the 'all levels of detail' part of Eryk's ask.
4. The **rejected** options — `alternative_to` cards — as 'do not do this, here is why'. The map is the only place the rejections exist. Without them the agent rediscovers and re-picks them.
5. The last failure, on a retry pass, and nothing else from the previous pass.

Item 4 is the one a generic coding agent cannot have and werk can. It is the reason the map is worth building the loop on instead of a markdown spec.

payload.title: Decided leaves only. Interior cards are containers.
Every decided card, deepest first. Interior cards build too.
One rung per pass, recursive. Parent's shape, then each child.

patch.body:
Sampled: NO SAMPLE. The sampler ruled the fork clear in prose, and killed two of my four readings against the sibling cards.

**Two readings are already dead, by cards I wrote an hour ago.**

'Units are not cards, a first pass emits a task list' contradicts #werk-loop-land ('the card id in the commit message'), #werk-loop-state (build events 'carry the card id'), and #werk-loop-gap (a new card 'parented under the unit it came from'). All three name a card as the unit.

'The whole pointed subtree is one unit' contradicts #werk-loop-land's 'a commit per unit' and a history you 'read as the plan in build order'. That needs many units per run.

**What is actually open** is narrower: the selection rule inside the pointed subtree. Three options, #werk-loop-unit:opt0 / :opt1 / :opt2.

**Two measurements from the #werk subtree that shape the choice.**

Leaf size is not uniform. Decided-leaf bodies run 0 to 2973 characters, median 778. Six decided leaves have an empty body. #werk-find is an empty leaf; #werk-hmr is a 2973-character who:you leaf. 'Leaf' does not mean 'one buildable unit'.

Depth is not uniform. The #werk subtree by depth: {0:1, 1:12, 2:9, 3:17, 4:30, 5:17, 6:4, 7:1}. A leaf sits anywhere from depth 1 to depth 7.

**One unresolved conflict, to settle with whichever option wins.** #werk-loop-brief item 3 puts 'every decided descendant' in the brief. :opt2 (one rung per pass) then repeats work: a child's pass rebuilds what its parent's pass already committed with the same descendant text in hand. Either the brief drops item 3 for interior passes, or :opt2 loses.

**A fifth question the options do not raise.** 39 of 64 leaves under #werk are who:me — a reversible call the agent made and reported, not a decision Eryk took. Whether a who:me leaf is a unit at all, or just brief text for its parent, is open.

58 of the 91 cards under #werk are decided leaves. Each is one pass. An interior card is never built directly — it only supplies brief text to the leaves under it.

For: the leaf is the rung where the map stopped subdividing, which is the map's own signal that nothing smaller was worth recording. No pass ever repeats another's work, so #werk-loop-brief item 3 stays as written.

Against: pass size swings hard. An empty-bodied leaf like #werk-find and a 2973-character leaf like #werk-hmr are the same unit. And a leaf at depth 1 with no children is a whole feature; a leaf at depth 7 is one line of a function.

85 passes under #werk: 58 decided leaves plus 27 decided interior cards, deepest first. An interior card's pass runs after its children and builds whatever the children did not — the glue, the shape, the thing that makes the parts one feature.

For: matches how the map was actually written. A parent card often holds a real decision, not just a heading — #werk-test-scope is 5 numbered rules with its children under it. Under :opt0 that text is only ever context, never a thing anyone builds.

Against: 85 passes for one subtree. And the boundary is vague — after the children commit, what is left for the parent is decided by the agent, not by the map.

Build the pointed card's shape first, then recurse: each decided child gets its own pass, which recurses again. The tree is walked top-down, not bottom-up.

For: the top pass can lay out files and interfaces before any detail exists, so the children fill in a frame instead of negotiating one. Even pass size by rung, not by luck of depth.

Against: this is the option that collides with #werk-loop-brief item 3. If the parent pass already got every decided descendant in its brief, it will build them, and the child passes then rewrite their own parent's work. Fixing that means the brief holds only one rung down for interior passes — which throws away the 'all levels of detail' property Eryk asked for.

payload.title: One pass per decided card, deepest first

patch.body:
Eryk, 2026-09-20: **every decided card is a pass, deepest first.** 85 passes under #werk — 58 decided leaves plus 27 decided interior cards. An interior card's pass runs after all its children have committed, and builds what they did not: the glue, the shape, the thing that makes the parts one feature.

**who:me leaves are passes too**, same as any other. Status is what counts, not who set it. No special case in the selection code.

Why this one. A parent card in this map often holds a real decision, not a heading — #werk-test-scope is five numbered rules with fourteen cards under it. Under 'leaves only' that text is only ever context and nobody builds it.

Rejected: #werk-loop-unit:opt0 (leaves only — interior decisions never get built, and pass size still swings from an empty leaf to a 2973-character one anyway). #werk-loop-unit:opt2 (one rung per pass — collides with #werk-loop-brief item 3; fixing it costs the all-levels-of-detail property).

**Two readings never reached the options**, killed by sibling cards: 'a first pass emits a task list, units are not cards' contradicts #werk-loop-land, #werk-loop-state and #werk-loop-gap, which all key on a card id; 'the whole pointed subtree is one unit' contradicts #werk-loop-land's commit per unit.

**What deepest-first now forces on #werk-loop-brief.** An interior pass sees descendants that are *already built and committed*. Its brief must say so, or it rebuilds them. Item 3 stands, but it needs a second half: for an interior card, every decided descendant plus the commit each one landed as.

**Known cost, accepted.** 85 passes for one subtree is a lot of passes. Pass size is still uneven: bodies run 0 to 2973 characters, median 778, and depth runs 1 to 7. Nothing in this option evens that out.

#lp-stateless says one fresh agent per pass, and the repository is the memory. That makes the brief the loop's main lever: it is the only thing the pass knows that git does not already show it.

Too little and the agent re-invents decisions that are already on the map. Too much and the context degrades, which is the exact failure #lp-stateless was written to avoid.

My reading of what one brief holds:

1. The unit card — title, why, body, verbatim.
2. Its ancestor chain up to the root, title and body. The card assumes them.
3. Every decided descendant. That is the 'all levels of detail' part of Eryk's ask.
4. The **rejected** options — `alternative_to` cards — as 'do not do this, here is why'. The map is the only place the rejections exist. Without them the agent rediscovers and re-picks them.
5. The last failure, on a retry pass, and nothing else from the previous pass.

Item 4 is the one a generic coding agent cannot have and werk can. It is the reason the map is worth building the loop on instead of a markdown spec.

**Item 3 needs a second half, forced by #werk-loop-unit.** Deepest-first means an interior card's pass runs *after* its descendants are built and committed. Their text alone would make it rebuild them. So for an interior pass item 3 reads: every decided descendant, each with the commit it landed as. The pass is then told plainly — these are done, build only what joins them.

Still open here: whether item 2 (the whole ancestor chain) is affordable at depth 7, and whether item 3 is affordable for a card with 60 descendants like #werk-chat.

Eryk, 2026-09-20: planning is scoped enough to build werk from scratch. The next thing to prove is the other half — that the plan gets executed by the loop, not by hand.

Scope cut, from him: the **inner** loop only. Build and test. Validate, grade, and iterate stay in #loop's other children, still paused.

So v0's promise is one sentence: point the loop at a card, and get back a branch that implements that card and everything decided under it, with its own tests passing.

#werk-test gives the loop its eyes — `bun test` and `bun run e2e`. Six more decisions sit under this card:

    unit     decided  every decided card is a pass, deepest first   #werk-loop-unit
    brief    open     what text the child agent actually gets       #werk-loop-brief
    gap      open     what happens when the plan runs out           #werk-loop-gap
    state    open     'decided' is not 'built'                      #werk-loop-state
    land     open     where the code goes, how Eryk reads it        #werk-loop-land
    done     open     the inner-loop stop condition                 #werk-loop-done

Machinery already exists and is not in question: src/prototype.ts runs a headless `claude -p` in a throwaway worktree and captures the diff; the log takes new event kinds; web/diff.js renders a patch. The loop is not new plumbing. It is the six decisions above.

One number to keep in view: #werk-loop-unit makes #werk itself 85 passes.

payload.title: A card is not a unit of work

patch.body:
**Superseded the same day it was decided.** Eryk, 2026-09-20, reading the result: 'the map is a decision log but it doesn't necessarily define work to be done — or at least card != unit of work.' A ticket step goes between the map and the builder: #werk-loop-ticket.

Earlier that hour this card decided the opposite — every decided card is a pass, deepest first, 85 passes for #werk. The three options weighed (#werk-loop-unit:opt0 leaves only, :opt1 every decided card, :opt2 one rung per pass) differ only in *which* cards are units. None of them questioned that a card is a unit. The fork was mis-framed, so picking the best option in it could not help.

**The evidence was already on this card and I read it as a cost instead of a refutation.** Decided-leaf bodies run 0 to 2973 characters, median 778, six of them empty. Depth runs 1 to 7. I wrote 'nothing in this option evens that out' and accepted it. Unequal size is what decisions look like. Tasks are not supposed to look like that, and the fact that no option could make them look otherwise was the signal.

**The second refutation, from #al-sample's own vocabulary.** A buildable unit is a tracer bullet — a narrow but complete path through schema, API, UI and tests, verifiable on its own, sized to one fresh context. A vertical slice like that cuts across cards in different subtrees. The refines tree is a *decision* hierarchy; slicing by it gives horizontal layers, which is the shape the slice rule exists to forbid.

**What the sampler got wrong, and why.** It killed the reading 'units are not cards, a first pass emits a task list' by citing #werk-loop-land, #werk-loop-state and #werk-loop-gap — three sibling cards I had written forty minutes earlier, all of which key on a card id. It was reasoning correctly from the map. The map was wrong, because I had put my own unexamined assumption into three cards before anything tested it. A fresh assumption written into siblings reads exactly like an established constraint. Those three cards are now stale and must be re-derived against #werk-loop-ticket.

Kept as evidence, not as live options: #werk-loop-unit:opt0, :opt1, :opt2.
patch.why: The map is a decision log. A decision is not a task. Every option weighed here assumed it was, and all of them were wrong.

payload.title: A ticket step sits between the map and the builder
payload.why: Eryk, 2026-09-20: the map is a decision log, not a definition of work. Something must turn decided cards into tracer-bullet tickets before any build agent is handed anything.

patch.body:
Eryk, 2026-09-20: 'there must be a ticket definition step before we hand over anything to the agent to actually build (not prototype). A skill like /to-tickets may be handy.'

Wide mechanical refactors are the stated exception and get expand–contract instead of a slice.

Three of those properties are things a card does not have and cannot be given. Complete through every layer: a slice crosses subtrees, because the map groups by decision, not by layer. Sized to one context: card bodies here run 0 to 2973 characters. Demoable alone: most cards are a constraint on a thing, not the thing.

**The blocking edges are the part the map genuinely does hold.** `depends_on` already means 'this rests on that', and #tk-verbs already has linkDependsOn mapped to Linear's blocking relation and GitHub's blocked_by. 2. Who writes it — a skill Eryk runs and approves (/to-tickets quizzes the user at step 4), or an agent the loop runs unattended? Step 4 is a human gate, which is a G2 in #stages terms.
3. Which cards does one ticket cite, and does the citation go back on those cards so the map shows what got built?

    unit     open   a card is not a unit of work (settled -)  #werk-loop-unit
    brief    open   what text the build agent actually gets   #werk-loop-brief

    land     open   where the code goes, how Eryk reads it    #werk-loop-land

patch.body:
Eryk, 2026-09-20: planning is scoped enough to build werk from scratch. The next thing to prove is the other half — that the plan gets executed by the loop, not by hand.

Scope cut, from him: the **inner** loop only. Build and test. Validate, grade, and iterate stay in #loop's other children, still paused.

**The shape, in his words, 2026-09-20.** Six steps:

    1  plan       decisions go on the map                        (this, today)
    2  select     the user picks a subtree and triggers          #werk-loop-ticket
                  ticket planning. Some subtrees are not
                  buildable or are too small — the user judges
    3  plan work  the planner reads the whole subtree, with      #werk-loop-planner
                  access to the whole map, and writes tickets
    4  fan out    one agent per ticket, one worktree each,       #werk-loop-fanout
                  as many at once as independence allows
    5  hand back  each marks its work done and shares a diff.    #werk-loop-land
                  Local, not a real PR, if possible
    6  merge      a coordinator merges the finished, tested      #werk-loop-merge
                  tickets and resolves conflicts

Step 2 is the answer to a question I got wrong earlier today. #werk-loop-unit tried to derive the unit of work from the card tree. A person picks the subtree, and the planner cuts it. Neither job belongs to the shape of the refines tree.

#werk-test gives steps 4 and 6 their eyes — `bun test` and `bun run e2e`.

Ten decisions sit under this card. Four of them — brief, gap, state, land — were written before step 2 existed and are stale.

Machinery already exists and is not in question: src/prototype.ts already runs headless `claude -p` agents in throwaway worktrees in parallel and captures each diff — that is step 4 and half of step 5. The log takes new event kinds. web/diff.js renders a patch.

**The hard part is step 6, and it is last.** Every other step has a working precedent in this repo. Nothing here has merged N independently-green worktrees before.

Eryk: 'the planner gets entire subtree and defines what to build; it has access to the entire map so it can track cross-subtree references, the product diagram and everything.'

Two inputs, and they are different in kind. The **subtree** is read in full and verbatim — it is the brief. The **rest of the map** is a reference the planner consults, not text it is handed.

**Why that split is forced.** The map is 234 cards. #werk alone is 91, and #werk-chat is 60. A subtree at the size a person would actually select is already a large read. The whole map on top of it is not one context, and #lp-stateless says a degraded context is the failure mode to design against.

**What the planner consults instead of reading everything.** This is what #vi-sysdiag-grid-minimal was built for and it lands here earlier than expected. The minimal grid is the whole running system as one compressed picture, with card ids on the elements — so the planner sees the system shape at a glance and follows an id only where it needs the argument. #vi-sysdiag-codemap's element-to-files-and-symbols mapping is the other half: it tells the planner which files a ticket will touch, which is what #werk-loop-fanout needs to schedule anything safely.

Open:

1. Does the planner read the subtree's **rejected options** too? #werk-loop-brief argued this is the map's one advantage over a markdown spec. It matters more here than at build time — the planner is the one that could re-propose a rejected shape.
2. Does the planner see the **open and proto** cards in the subtree, or only the decided ones? An open card inside a selected subtree is a hole in the plan. It should probably block ticket planning and say so, rather than be silently skipped.
3. Is the ticket set written back to the map, or kept beside it? #werk-loop-ticket question 1.

Eryk: 'tickets are handed over to multiple agents — as many as possible considering how much different tickets are independent, and they work in their own worktrees all at once.'

**Mostly already built.** src/prototype.ts runs N headless `claude -p` agents concurrently, each in a `git worktree add --detach` off HEAD, captures each one's staged diff as a patch, and removes the worktree in a `finally` per #al-ephem. Swap 'option of a fork' for 'ticket' and change the cleanup to keep the branch, and step 4 exists.

**The real problem is what 'independent' means, and the tickets answer the wrong half of it.** /to-tickets gives each ticket its blocking edges — which ticket must finish before another can *start*. That is logical order. It says nothing about two unblocked tickets both editing src/server.ts. Those run at the same time, both go green alone, and collide at #werk-loop-merge.

So the scheduler needs a second input the ticket format does not carry: an estimate of which files each ticket touches. #vi-sysdiag-codemap is the map-side source for it. /to-tickets' own wide-refactor rule — expand–contract, batches sized by blast radius — is the same problem seen from the ticket-writing side, which suggests the estimate belongs to #werk-loop-planner, not to the scheduler.

Open:

1. File overlap: does it block two tickets from running together, or is the collision left for the coordinator to resolve?
2. Do the worktrees branch off HEAD, or off the previous ticket's merge? Off HEAD is simple and maximises parallelism; off the merge is sequential and has no conflicts at all.
3. What is the cap? 'As many as possible' against a real machine and a real rate limit is a number, and it is not 85.

Eryk: 'there must be a coordinator agent/overseer, that is able to merge the PRs for finished and internally tested tickets, resolves conflicts if needed.'

**This is the step with no precedent in this repo, and it is last.** Steps 1 to 5 all have working code or a close cousin. Nothing here has merged N independently-green worktrees.

**The fact that makes it hard, stated plainly.** Each ticket is green in its own worktree, off the same base. Green alone does not imply green merged. Two tickets can both pass with no textual conflict and still break each other — one renames what the other calls, one changes a shape the other constructs. A clean `git merge` is not evidence.

So the coordinator's real job is not conflict resolution. It is: merge one, re-run #werk-loop-done's checks on the merged tree, and only then take the next. Conflict resolution is the visible part; re-testing after every merge is the part that decides whether the loop works.

**When a merge goes red, something has to give, and nothing says what.** Candidates: reopen the last-merged ticket and rebuild it on the new base; hand the coordinator the fix itself; stop the run and leave the branch for Eryk. These are different products.

**This is also where the hole in #werk-loop-done closes cheaply.** v0 accepted having no held-out checks (#lp-split) because the builder writes its own tests. The coordinator is a different agent, running after the merge, on a tree no single builder controls. A held-out set run exactly there costs one more test command and removes most of the reward-hacking exposure the v0 scope cut accepted.

**Relation to #lp-overseer.** That card's overseer watches the event log and cancels a stalled agent. This one merges. Same process or two is open — the log-watching is shared, the merge authority is not.

      bun run e2e                   playwright, real server (#werk-test-visual)

patch.body:
A rubric is the loop's stop condition. There are two, and the loop picks by what happens to the output: `prototype` when the artifact is thrown away after it answers a question, `production` when the code is merged.

**Both are built into werk.** Not files in the repo being judged, not drafted per project, not derived per work item. Two constants the tool ships with. #lp-rubric:opt3 holds the per-project-file version — deferred, not rejected; it is what these become once a second project exists.

Each rubric has three sections, and the split is not cosmetic. **checks** are deterministic — a command, an exit code, no model (#lp-two). **judgements** are graded by an agent, because no exit code answers them. **held-out** is not shown to the builder and runs once at the end (#lp-split).

## production

    checks                          deterministic, exit code decides
      bun test
      bun test --coverage           90% lines on fold.ts, log.ts,
                                    permission.ts, types.ts (#werk-test-scope:src0)
      bun run e2e                   playwright, real server (#werk-test-visual)
      tsc --noEmit

    judgements                      an agent grades each 1-5, 3 to pass
      every acceptance criterion has a test that fails without the change
      each I/O module touched still meets its named behaviour list
      no new exported function in src/ without a doc comment naming its card
      no code path rewrites or deletes a line of .werk/log.jsonl
      card text is never mutated outside the CLI (#werk-write)

    held-out                        the coordinator runs this after the merge.
                                    Builders never see this file.
      boot the server on a copy of log.jsonl, open a card, post a note,
        assert it lands in the log and re-renders
      run add -> link -> status decided -> reopen -> rederive in sequence,
        assert the derived stale set matches a hand-computed one
      the pure-module coverage number, measured against tests written by
        the held-out author, not by the builder

Three of the five judgements are project rules no generic linter knows. That is what a rubric is for. The two coverage-shaped lines are checks, not judgements, because a number decides them.

The held-out block tests **composition** — server plus log plus fold plus browser in one path — not isolated features. #lp-split gives the reason: a builder optimises whatever it can see, and features it can see in isolation are the cheapest thing to fake.

## prototype

    checks
      the artifact exists at the declared path
      its entry point exits 0, if it has one

    judgements
      the artifact answers the question the fork asked, and nothing more
      where the brief was silent, the reading it chose is stated in one line
      nothing was written outside the worktree or scratch dir (#al-ephem)

    not checked, on purpose
      coverage, lint, doc comments, naming, dead code, commit hygiene

The 'not checked' block is what makes a prototype rubric worth writing. Without it a builder applies production habits to a throwaway and the prototype stops being cheap.

**The cost of hardcoding, stated so it is not a surprise.** The production checks name `bun`, `tsc` and playwright, and the judgements name `.werk/log.jsonl` and the werk CLI. Pointing the loop at any second project requires editing werk's source. That is the moment #lp-rubric:opt3 stops being deferred.

Rejected: #lp-rubric:opt0 (derived per work item, approved at a gate — a per-run gate is the recurring human input the rubric exists to remove). #lp-rubric:opt1 (project baseline plus per-item additions — same cost, and the per-item part is where a builder would negotiate its own bar).

One pass over one ticket ends in one of three states: the checks pass, the checks fail and a retry remains, or the cap is reached.

The checks are #lp-rubric's `production` block, not a new list:

    bun test
    bun test --coverage      90% on fold.ts, log.ts, permission.ts, types.ts
    bun run e2e
    tsc --noEmit

On a fail, the next pass is a fresh agent with the same brief plus the last failure, per #lp-stateless. Nothing else carries over.

On the cap, stop the run and leave the branch where it is. Do not move to the next ticket with a broken tree underneath it — a second ticket built on a red base makes the failure harder to attribute, not easier.

**What a builder pass does not run.** The `judgements` block and the `held-out` block of the same rubric. Judgements need a grader agent, which is #lp-two, still open. Held-out is withheld from the builder by definition and belongs to #werk-loop-merge, which runs after the merge on a tree no single builder controls.

So the builder's bar is exit codes only. The graded and held-out bars exist and are placed; they are just not this pass's job.

Open: the retry number.
