payload.text: The held-out block now exists: #lp-rubric's production rubric ships one, built into the tool. This card is where it runs — after the merge, by a different agent, on a tree no single builder controls. The earlier note on #werk-loop-done that v0 accepts no held-out set is superseded; the set is defined, and placing it here costs one test command.

#lp-rubric is decided, and its production rubric carries a held-out block that is withheld from builders and run by the coordinator after the merge. The stale mark here dates from 2026-09-01 and predates that. Re-derive this card against the new text before working it.

payload.title: The production rubric
payload.why: Merged code has to clear a bar that a throwaway does not. These are the lines of that bar.

payload.title: The prototype rubric
payload.why: A throwaway artifact is judged on whether it answered the question. Everything a production bar checks makes it slower without making it more useful.

patch.body:
The bar for code that gets merged. Three sections; the split between them is what makes the rubric usable, not cosmetic.

## checks — deterministic, an exit code decides

    bun test
    bun test --coverage      90% lines on fold.ts, log.ts, permission.ts,
                             types.ts (#werk-test-scope:src0)
    bun run e2e              playwright against a real server (#werk-test-visual)
    tsc --noEmit

Both coverage-shaped lines sit here, not in judgements, because a number decides them. #werk-test-scope forbids a percentage on an I/O module, which is why only the four pure modules are named.

## judgements — an agent grades each 1-5, 3 to pass

    every acceptance criterion has a test that fails without the change
    each I/O module touched still meets its named behaviour list
    no new exported function in src/ without a doc comment naming its card
    no code path rewrites or deletes a line of .werk/log.jsonl
    card text is never mutated outside the CLI (#werk-write)

Three of these five are project rules that no generic linter knows. That is the whole reason a judgement layer exists. 'Meets its named behaviour list' is a judgement and not a check precisely because #werk-test-scope rule 3 refuses to give an I/O module a number.

## held-out — run once after the merge. Builders never see this section.

    boot the server on a copy of log.jsonl, open a card, post a note,
      assert it lands in the log and re-renders
    run add -> link -> status decided -> reopen -> rederive in sequence,
      assert the derived stale set matches a hand-computed one
    the pure-module coverage number, measured against tests written by
      the held-out author, not by the builder

Every line here is a **composition** — server plus log plus fold plus browser in one path — never an isolated feature. #lp-split gives the reason: a builder optimises whatever it can see, and an isolated feature is the cheapest thing to fake. #werk-loop-merge is where this section runs, because the coordinator is a different agent working on a tree no single builder controls.

Reading the three sections together: a builder pass clears **checks** only. **judgements** need a grader agent (#lp-two). **held-out** is withheld by definition.

The bar for an artifact that gets thrown away after it answers a question.

## checks

    the artifact exists at the declared path
    its entry point exits 0, if it has one

## judgements

    the artifact answers the question the fork asked, and nothing more
    where the brief was silent, the reading it chose is stated in one line
    nothing was written outside the worktree or scratch dir (#al-ephem)

Judgement 2 is the no-questions contract already in src/prototype.ts made checkable: a headless build cannot stop at a question, so it picks and says so. A prototype that silently picked is worth less than one that picked and named the pick.

## not checked, on purpose

    coverage, lint, doc comments, naming, dead code, commit hygiene

This section is what makes a prototype rubric worth writing at all. Without it a builder carries production habits into a throwaway, and the prototype stops being cheap — which removes the only reason to build one instead of arguing about it.

There is no held-out section. Held-out exists to stop a builder gaming a bar it can see (#lp-split). Nothing is merged here and nothing accumulates, so there is no bar worth gaming.

A rubric is the loop's stop condition. There are two, and the loop picks by what happens to the output: #lp-rubric-proto when the artifact is thrown away after it answers a question, #lp-rubric-prod when the code is merged.

**Both are built into werk.** Not files in the repo being judged, not drafted per project, not derived per work item. Two constants the tool ships with.

Each has three sections, and the split is what makes a rubric usable:

    checks        deterministic — a command, an exit code, no model (#lp-two)
    judgements    an agent grades each, because no exit code answers them
    held-out      withheld from the builder, run once at the end (#lp-split)

The production rubric has all three. The prototype rubric has no held-out section — held-out exists to stop a builder gaming a bar it can see, and a throwaway accumulates nothing worth gaming.

**Written once, not per work item.** That is the property the rejected options give up. A rubric re-derived per run needs approval per run, and the recurring human input is exactly what the rubric exists to remove.

**The cost of hardcoding, stated so it is not a surprise.** #lp-rubric-prod's checks name `bun`, `tsc` and playwright; its judgements name `.werk/log.jsonl` and the werk CLI. Pointing the loop at a second project means editing werk's source. That is the moment #lp-rubric:opt3 stops being deferred.

Deferred: #lp-rubric:opt3 (a prototype.md and production.md file in each project, drafted from the repo and corrected once). Not rejected — it is what the hardcoded pair becomes once a second project exists.

Rejected: #lp-rubric:opt0 (derived per work item, approved at a gate). #lp-rubric:opt1 (project baseline plus per-item additions — the per-item part is where a builder would negotiate its own bar).

The loop sees only the visible checks. A held-out set runs every merge, inside the coordinator's loop, not once at the end. The agent that writes the tests must not be the agent that writes the code. Watch composition, not isolated features.

This is the most serious problem found in the whole research pass.

payload.title: Reopen the last-merged ticket and rebuild it on the new base
Hand the coordinator the fix itself
Stop the run and leave the branch

patch.body:
A coordinator merges the finished, internally tested tickets and resolves the conflicts.

**The fact that makes it hard.** Each ticket is green in its own worktree, off the same base. Green alone does not imply green merged. Two tickets can both pass with no textual conflict and still break each other — one renames what the other calls, one changes a shape the other constructs. A clean `git merge` is not evidence.

So the coordinator's real job is not conflict resolution. It is: merge one, re-run #werk-loop-done's checks on the merged tree, and only then take the next. Conflict resolution is the visible part; re-testing after every merge is the part that decides whether the loop works.

**When a merge goes red, the merge stands.** The run does not stop, and the ticket is not rebuilt in place. A follow-up ticket is filed for the regression. That follow-up ticket carries one instruction beyond a normal fix: add a check that would have caught this, so the same regression cannot recur unseen. This trades a temporary regression on the merged tree for uninterrupted progress. #werk-loop-merge:opt0 (reopen the last-merged ticket and rebuild it on the new base) and #werk-loop-merge:opt1 (hand the coordinator the fix itself) both stop the run to fix in place instead; #werk-loop-merge:opt2 (stop the run and leave the branch) stops it outright. All three were rejected: none is worth the progress they cost.

**The held-out check belongs here.** #werk-loop-done accepts having no held-out set (#lp-split) because the builder writes its own tests. The coordinator is a different agent, running after the merge, on a tree no single builder controls. A held-out set run exactly there costs one more test command and removes most of that exposure.

**Relation to #lp-overseer.** That overseer watches the event log and cancels a stalled agent. This one merges. Same process or two is open — the log-watching is shared, the merge authority is not.

No precedent exists in this repo. Every other step of #werk-loop has working code or a close cousin; nothing here has merged N independently-green worktrees.

payload.title: A new card is a proposal too, not a direct append
payload.why: Cards nobody decided are fuzzy, unbelievable, and indistinguishable from decided ones once they are in the log.

payload.title: A card can be removed, not only rewritten
payload.why: A map with a few wrong cards is not a broken map. Cleaning up one card must not mean rewriting it into something else.

patch.body:
Creation follows the same staged path as an edit (#al-diff-cli). `add` keeps its name, gains no bypass flag, and always stages. It prints "proposed", not "added".

The pending card enters the log at once, in a pending state, and shows as a ghost node in the refines tree under its proposed parent — grey or dashed, distinct from the blue tint that marks a pending edit on a real card. Two different facts, two different marks: "this card does not exist yet" against "this card has a pending change".

Accept is one card at a time, with the same ✓ button as #al-diff-cli-btn. No batch accept.

An edge proposed with a card is part of that card: it accepts or discards with it, never on its own. A `link` naming a still-pending node produces a pending edge.

Accepting a child auto-accepts the pending refines ancestors above it, up to the first real one, so a click cannot orphan a card. Discarding a card discards its pending descendants.

This narrows #werk-contract, which decided that the contract check fires only at the decided transition and that "card creation and proto stay free". Creation is no longer free. The contract check and the accept gate are different gates on different facts.

payload.title: A pending panel outside the tree holds the turn's proposed cards
payload.why_not: A second place to check the same fact. The refines tree already nests a proposed card under its proposed parent for free, including a chain of them.

patch.body:
Removal is reversible and additive. `werk remove <id>` appends a `node.removed` event; `fold.ts` hides the node and its edges. Nothing leaves the log. `werk restore <id>` brings it back, and `werk removed` lists what is out.

A removed card is gone from the tree, not struck through in place. Struck-through text keeps the noise it was meant to clear.

The control sits in the card view, next to ⌖ and ▦, for the same reason accept has a button (#al-diff-cli-btn): cleanup happens while reading the map, and the judgement is already made by the time the card is on screen. The CLI verb exists too, because the agent needs a way to propose a removal.

An agent never removes a card directly. It proposes the removal and the card shows it pending, like any other change.

Children: `remove` takes the refines subtree with it. `--reparent` keeps the children and attaches them to the grandparent instead, for a bad parent over good children.

payload.title: A removed card stays in the tree, struck through
payload.why_not: The point of removing a card is that it stops taking space and attention. A struck-through line keeps both.

payload.title: Rewrite a wrong card into a right one instead of removing it
payload.why_not: A card that should not exist has no right version. Rewriting it hides a deletion inside an edit, and the log then reads as if the idea evolved.

payload.title: Only kind:card stages; source, option and excerpt append directly
payload.why_not: Fewer clicks, but an option node carries an agent-written --why_not, which is invented content of the same class the gate exists to catch.

payload.title: A repeated add overwrites the pending card in place
payload.why_not: One accept instead of a discard plus a new propose, but the card can change between two looks at it. The ✓ would then commit something never read.

patch.body:
The first fix (this card, first version) only told the main agent not to print the exchange. It did not say how to launch the subagents, so the agent skipped the Task tool and did sysdiag-scout's job itself, inline, in the main turn — reading the .wgrid file, grepping it, and writing the full analysis as its own chat reply. A one-line instruction to stay quiet cannot work if the agent never delegates in the first place.

Fix: AGENTS.md now names the tool call directly — Task, subagent_type: sysdiag-scout / sysdiag-updater, run_in_background: true — and forbids the main agent from reading or reasoning about the diagram itself. The visible reply is exactly one line: product diagram updated, or no need to update the product diagram at this point.

ops.new: Built on 2026-09-22. `node.proposed` is its own event type, not a flag on `node.added`: the two facts read differently in the log, and fold.ts keeps one branch per meaning. A ghost sits in `nodes` with `proposed: true` and outside every derivation — live edges, rollup, staleness, unchallenged. Its own edges wait in `ghostEdges` and go live by themselves once both ends are real, so accepting a card needs no second event for its edges.

Frozen means the words. `edit --body`, `edit --why` and `retitle` refuse on a ghost; `link`, `status` and `edit --who` do not. A held edge still feeds the decided-contract check, so a card can be proposed already decided, with its basis and its options, and commit as one unit.

`accept` refuses unless it is run with `--actor you`. The allow list in .werk/allow.json passes every `node src/cli.ts` call, so that check is a speed bump, not a wall — a deny rule for one verb has nowhere to live yet. The ✓ in the map is the real path.

ops.old: Children: `remove` takes the refines subtree with it. `--reparent` keeps the children and attaches them to the grandparent instead, for a bad parent over good children.
ops.new: Children: `remove` takes the refines subtree with it. `--reparent` keeps the children and attaches them to the grandparent instead, for a bad parent over good children.

Two events, `node.removed` and `node.restored`. fold.ts applies them after the event loop and drops the node with every edge touching it, so nothing downstream learns a new concept: a removed card makes nothing stale, counts in no rollup, and cites nothing.

Removal takes the options and the excerpts of what it removes, not only the refines subtree. An option node sits nowhere in the tree, so one left behind is an orphan no view can reach and no later cleanup can find. A source two cards cite stays while either of them stays.
`--reparent` is a CLI flag with no button. The ✕ asks once, naming how many cards go with it, and that is the whole confirmation: nothing leaves the log, so the cost of a wrong click is one restore.

payload.title: An op list that leaves a block unnamed is refused, not applied
payload.why: applyOps rebuilds the body from the ops alone, so a block named in no op disappears on accept, with nothing in the diff to show it.
payload.body:
Every block of the current body must appear as the `old` of an `elaborated` or `removed` op. Keeping a block unchanged is `{"tag":"elaborated","old":X,"new":X}`. Dropping it on purpose is `{"tag":"removed","old":X}`, which the diff strikes through and the reader sees.

`propose` fails otherwise, and prints the blocks that were at risk. A deletion nobody can see and a deletion in the diff must not be the same call.

This is the same rule as the one al-diff-cli already applies to a quoted `old`: a claim the body does not support is never trusted silently. That rule checked the quotes that were given. This one checks the blocks that were not.

patch.body:
Agreed 2026-09-01.

Eight steps: intent, options, prototype, plan, build, validate, ship, measure. Step 8 opens the next step 1. Compressed view: plan, build, validate (see #stages). Everything below refines this one statement.
Plan, build, validate (see #stages).

patch.why:
Plan (intent, options, prototype, plan), build (build, ship), validate (measure). The parenthesized groups are the three stages from #stages.

Plus one more state: blocked. The loop enters it after three failures on the same check, and posts the check, the error, and the three attempts to the issue.

Validate's only granular step named here is measure — worth checking whether validate needs a step distinct from measure, or the two are the same thing.
You approve at G1, the end of plan, G2, the end of build, and G3, the end of validate.

patch.body:
```
PLAN:      intent -> options -> prototype -> [G1] -> plan
BUILD:     build -> ship -> [G2]
VALIDATE:  measure -> [G3] -> back to intent

G1  prototype is right
G2  pull request is correct
G3  production measurement holds up
```

G1 sits after #st-six's prototype step, before plan is finalized. G2 sits at the build/validate boundary — this is the same PR approval the old G3 named, moved one slot earlier now that a gate exists after measurement too. G3 is new: #stages previously said gates stop at the PR, 'nowhere else' — that no longer holds.

```
PLAN:      intent -> options -> prototype -> [G1] -> plan
BUILD:     build -> ship -> [G2]
VALIDATE:  measure -> [G3] -> back to intent

G1  prototype is right
G2  pull request is correct
G3  production measurement holds up
```

G1 sits after the prototype step, before plan is finalized. G2 sits at the build/validate boundary: the pull request approval. G3 sits after production measurement, at the end of validate, closing the loop back to intent.

payload.title: A card's words describe its own subject, not the session that wrote it
payload.why: A card is read later, cold, by someone who needs to act on its subject. Session facts (who said what, what came before, what stage the conversation was at) are stale on arrival and carry no decision weight.

payload.body:
No planning-process narration in a title, why, or body: no "Eryk said", no "the next thing to prove", no comparison to where the conversation stands.

This includes a card's own edit history. "X is new", "Y used to say/name Z", "that no longer holds/applies" still narrate the session, even when the subject is the card itself. State the current fact plainly.

A reversal is still fair game to record — a superseded card can say what replaced it and why the earlier reading was wrong — but as a fact about the subject, not a play-by-play of the conversation that produced it. Attribution lives in eryk.napierala   console      Sep 22 01:45  and in the log, not in prose.

payload.title: A risk tier decides which gates wait for a human
payload.why: Kiro turned one small bug fix into 4 user stories and 16 acceptance criteria. Overhead scales badly downward.

ops.old: fix → the loop only, no gates. change → brief, loop, ship. feature → all six stages.
ops.new:
A tier never removes a stage. Plan, build, and validate always run, and every gate still emits its transition, so the log stays uniform for #tk-gates. The tier decides which of G1, G2, G3 waits for a human and which auto-passes.

```
fix       G1 auto   G2 auto   G3 auto
change    G1 auto   G2 human  G3 auto
feature   G1 human  G2 human  G3 human
```

G1 is the prototype, G2 the pull request, G3 the production measurement, per #st-gates.

ops.old: Where the boundaries sit is not knowable by talking. It needs real work items.
ops.new: Where the boundaries sit — which change is a fix and which is a change — is not knowable by talking. It needs real work items. That is a separate question from what a tier removes, which the gate table above settles.

ops.old: This also matches the tiered merge pattern reported across 2026: auto-merge for low risk, human-only for critical paths.
ops.new: This also matches the tiered merge pattern reported across 2026: auto-merge for low risk, human-only for critical paths. That pattern varies the approval, not the work, which is why the tier here does the same.
Open: who sets the tier, and when. The candidates are Eryk at intent, the agent at intent from the diff it plans, or a re-rating at G2 when the real diff exists. Nothing here picks one yet.

payload.title: A tier skips whole stages: fix runs build only
payload.why: The cheapest reading of the Kiro overhead problem — if plan is the cost, delete plan.
payload.body:
fix runs build alone. change runs build and validate. feature runs all three. No gate auto-passes, because the skipped stages have no gate to pass.

Rejected: a skipped stage emits no gate transition. #tk-gates publishes G1, G2, G3 outward as the record of the run, and #st-merge keys merge to G3. Under this option a fix produces a log with holes in it, and merge has no G3 to key on. Varying the approval keeps one shape of run and still removes the overhead.

payload.title: Eryk sets the tier, at intent
payload.why: The tier decides whether G1 waits, and G1 ends plan. The rating has to exist before planning finishes, so intent is the only place left for it.
payload.body:
One rating, set once, at intent. No stage runs before it exists.

A rule good enough to hand to the agent is not writable yet. Judgment about what counts as a fix improves with runs, and there are not enough runs yet to draw a rule from.

What happens when the rating turns out wrong is #st-tier-escalate.

payload.title: The agent rates from the diff it plans
payload.why: It removes a step from Eryk at the one moment he is least informed — before any code exists.
payload.body:
The agent reads the intent, drafts the change it expects, and picks the tier from the size and blast radius of that draft.

Rejected. The agent has to judge risk from a diff it only predicts, before it has written anything. That is harder than the problem it solves. A wrong low rating auto-passes G3, so the cost of being wrong lands in production.

payload.title: Escalation is a discard and restart, not a mid-run tier bump
payload.why: A change that needs more and more fine-tuning is not a fix. The signal is felt during the review, not measured.
payload.body:
Eryk raises the tier by discarding the changes and restarting the run in planning mode at the higher tier. A tier is never re-rated inside a live run.

This keeps the gate sequence clean. No gate that already passed has to be reconsidered, and no log entry is rewritten. A restart is a new run with a new rating.

The trigger is Eryk's own judgment while reviewing: repeated rounds of fine-tuning on the same change. There is no counter and no threshold.

Distinct from #st-safe, which catches a bad change after production, with a pause and a revert. This one fires before merge, on work that is not wrong yet, only under-planned.

payload.title: The agent detects that it should escalate
payload.why: Eryk has to be watching for it. An agent that noticed on its own would catch it without him.
payload.body:
The agent counts revision rounds, or watches the diff grow past what the tier assumed, and raises the tier itself.

Rejected for now. The threshold is not known. More runs are needed before a rule can be written that beats a person noticing. Re-rating inside a live run also reopens gates that already passed.

payload.title: Where Eryk sets the tier, in practice
payload.why: #st-tier-who names the actor and the moment. It does not name the control. Nothing at intent has a place to put a rating yet.
payload.body:

payload.title: The tier is spoken in prose, and the agent echoes it back
payload.why: A select or a pair of buttons puts a form in front of every topic. The rating is already implicit in how the request is phrased.
payload.body:
The tier arrives inside the first sentences of a topic, in ordinary words: keep it simple, just build it. No field, no buttons, no menu. Escalation arrives the same way, as a course correction said mid-conversation.

The agent replies with one line naming the tier it heard and what that costs: running this as a fix, no gate will wait for you. One line, not a screen.

The echo is what keeps #st-tier-who true. The agent is the one parsing the sentence, so without the echo the agent is the one choosing. With it, a wrong reading costs one word to correct, before any stage runs.

payload.title: A tier control at intent: a field, or three buttons
payload.why: It is unambiguous. There is nothing to parse and nothing to echo back.
payload.body:
The map, or the issue, carries a tier control. Eryk picks fix, change or feature before the run starts.

Rejected. It puts a form in front of every topic, including the ones where the whole point is to skip the overhead.

payload.title: A spoken tier becomes a log event, scoped to the run
payload.why: A sentence in a chat is not readable at G3. Compaction drops it, and two gates can read the same sentence differently.
payload.body:
The agent appends an event to .werk/log.jsonl the moment it hears the tier. The gates read the event, never the conversation.

This needs a new member in the EventType union at src/types.ts:74, which is closed. Escalation appends a second event that supersedes the first, so the history of course changes stays readable, as with everything else in the log.

The scope is one run, not one session. #st-tier-escalate makes a restart a new run, so one session holds several runs at several tiers. Nothing in the code carries a run today — see #st-run-id.

payload.title: The agent re-reads the conversation at each gate
payload.why: No new event type, no new state. The sentence is already in the transcript.
payload.body:
At G1, G2 and G3 the agent looks back at what was said and judges the tier again.

Rejected. Compaction drops the sentence, so a long run loses its own tier. Two gates can also read the same words differently, which makes the tier unstable inside one run.

payload.title: Silence means feature: every gate waits
payload.why: The failure is not symmetric. A forgotten keep-it-simple costs one extra approval. A wrongly assumed fix auto-passes G3 into production.
payload.body:
No tier spoken, no tier event, all three gates wait for a human.

Speed is opted into with a sentence. It is never fallen into by forgetting to say one.

payload.title: Silence means change: G2 waits, G1 and G3 auto-pass
payload.why: The middle tier as the resting state. Most work is a change, so the default matches the common case and saves two approvals a run.
payload.body:
The pull request is always reviewed. Prototypes and production measurements pass on their own unless a tier is spoken.

Rejected. G3 auto-passing on a run nobody rated is the exposure. The saving is two approvals per unrated run, which is worth less than the risk it buys.

payload.title: Nothing in the code carries a run
payload.why: #st-tier-event scopes the tier to a run. src/types.ts has no run type, and .werk/session holds one bare session id.
payload.body:
Open. A run-scoped tier needs a run identity to hang on, and nothing creates one. A session is not it: #st-tier-escalate makes a restart a new run inside the same session.

Open too: what starts a run and what ends it. Intent starts it, and G3 or a discard ends it, is the obvious reading. Nothing has picked it.

payload.title: A run is one pass at one issue
payload.why: #st-six already posts to the issue when the loop blocks. The anchor exists, so nothing new has to be invented.
payload.body:
The tier is recorded against the issue, and every gate reads it from there. The issue is the work unit the pipeline runs on, start to finish.

A restart under #st-tier-escalate is a second pass at the same issue, at a higher tier. So an issue carries a sequence of tiers, not one. The latest wins, and the earlier ones stay readable.

Open: what a discarded pass leaves behind on the issue, besides its tier.

payload.title: Invent a run entity in the code
payload.why: A run has a clean boundary: it starts at intent and ends at G3 or a discard. An issue is an external thing the pipeline does not own.
payload.body:
A new type in src/types.ts, with a run id created at intent and closed at G3.

Rejected. It duplicates what the issue already is. #st-six posts to the issue when the loop blocks, so the issue is already the thing the pipeline reports against.

payload.title: A tier changes who waits, never what is recorded
payload.why: Skipping an approval and skipping the record are different things. Only the first is the overhead worth removing.
payload.body:
A fix auto-passes G1, G2 and G3. It still writes its decisions to the map. One pass can produce several cards.

The map is the durable half. A gate is a pause for a human. A card is the reason the work took the shape it did. Removing the pause does not remove the reason.

Open: who accepts the cards a no-gate pass proposes — see #st-tier-ghosts.

payload.title: A fix writes nothing to the map
payload.why: If nobody waits at a gate, nobody reads the cards either. Writing them is overhead with no reader.
payload.body:
The lowest tier runs and merges without touching the map.

Rejected. The record is what makes the next decision cheaper. A fix that silently changes behaviour leaves the map describing a system that no longer exists.

payload.body:

Candidates: the agent accepts its own cards at the fix tier; the ghosts wait in a batch cleared when Eryk chooses; or a fix writes cards already accepted, and Eryk reopens the wrong ones.

payload.title: What makes the map update impossible to skip
payload.why: #st-tier-record says a pass must never change code and leave the map untouched. Nothing enforces that, and a rule the agent is asked to follow will drift.
payload.body:
Two candidates are live.

The pipeline creates the obligation. The CLI command that starts a build appends it to the log, before any code is written. The agent then places it: the title, the why, the parent in the refines tree, the depends_on. The CLI cannot choose the parent, because knowing what a decision refines is judgment. The obligation is data, not an instruction, so it does not drift, and an unsatisfied one is visible in the map.

Or the absence is detected afterwards. A hook, or a check at G2. A gate still runs its checks at the fix tier — the tier decides who waits, not whether a check runs — so an auto-passed gate can still refuse.

One obligation means at least one card for the pass, not exactly one. A pass that weighs three decisions writes three.

Ruled out: relying on the end-of-pass report in #st-fix-cards. It needs a person to notice an absence, and people forget.

payload.title: A check is one command and its exit code
payload.why: Without one test for the layer, every borderline line gets argued twice — once when it is written, once when it fails.
payload.body:
The test for this layer: one command decides the line, the same way on every run, with no model reading the output. A threshold counts. A coverage percentage is a check, because a number passes or fails it.

Three rules follow.

1. A check names its command, not the property it wants. `tsc --noEmit`, not "the types are right".
2. A check whose output a person has to read is a judgement with a command attached. It belongs in the other layer.
3. The builder runs the checks itself, on every pass. Nothing grades them, so nothing negotiates with them.

The check commands for werk are in #lp-rubric-prod. This card holds the test that put them there.

payload.title: AGENTS.md is the rubric
payload.body:
AGENTS.md is the closest thing in the repo to a written bar, so the grader reads its rules as the judgement lines.

For: one file, already version-controlled with the code, already the place a project rule gets written down.

Against: AGENTS.md holds rules for how an agent edits the map — proposal flow, depends_on at creation time, who accepts a card, which subagent to call. Those govern a session, not merged code. Where it does touch code it points at cards instead of stating the bar: its test section defers to #werk-test-scope for the rule and refuses to name a coverage number. So a grader pointed at AGENTS.md would score the wrong thing, and every instruction added later for the agent would silently become a merge bar.

Rejected. #lp-rubric:opt3 is this idea done on purpose: a file whose only job is the bar.

payload.title: A check calls a pnpm script, not a tool
payload.why: A hardcoded tool name binds the rubric to one toolchain. A script name survives a change of test runner.
payload.body:
Every check line is `pnpm <script>`: `pnpm test`, `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`. The script lives in package.json, beside the code it judges. The rubric holds the name, the repo holds the command.

Two things this buys.

1. A change of tool is a one-line edit in package.json. No rubric line moves.
2. The same line means the right thing in another project, because every project answers `pnpm test`.

What it costs: a check is only as strong as the script behind it. A `lint` script with no config passes.

The repo today has `test` and `test:live` in package.json. `lint` and `typecheck` do not exist yet, and `engines` names bun. The check section of #lp-rubric-prod is still in the tool-call form this card replaces, so it needs the same edit.

Rejected: #lp-checks-scripts:opt0, one tool call per check line.

payload.title: Name the tool in each check line

For: nothing is hidden. The line says exactly what runs, and no package.json edit can quietly turn it into something weaker.

Against: the rubric now knows the toolchain. A move off bun, or off tsc, edits werk instead of the repo. The same line also stops meaning anything in a second project — the cost #lp-rubric names as the moment #lp-rubric:opt3 stops being deferred.

Rejected.

payload.title: The run-level exit condition
payload.why: "All tickets ready for agents are built, and the review check passes" is the right shape for a run-level exit, but three of its words do not resolve to anything an agent can evaluate.

payload.text:
A run ends when every ticket in the set is built and the review check passes. That is the right shape — a run-level exit, counted across tickets. Nothing on the map states one today.

#werk-loop-done is not it. It settles one pass over one ticket: checks pass, checks fail with a retry left, or the cap is reached. On the cap it says stop the run. So the run has a written abort path and no written success path.

#lp-rubric is not it either. A rubric grades an artifact. This counts work items. Two different objects, and the loop needs both.

**Three words an agent cannot evaluate as written.**

    ready          Ready means every blocker is built. #werk-loop-ticket
                   derives blockers from depends_on edges, so this part is
                   computable. But a ticket whose blocker hit the retry cap
                   is never ready — and 'every ready ticket is built' is then
                   true with half the set unbuilt. An agent exits and calls
                   it a success. The condition must count the whole set, not
                   the ready part of it.

    built          #werk-loop separates step 3, green in its own worktree,
                   from step 5, merged. A ticket green in a worktree that
                   never merged is not built. The exit must name which.

    review check   #lp-rubric has three named sections: checks, judgements,
                   held-out. 'Review check' matches none of them. Held-out
                   runs once after the merge, per #werk-loop-merge, so it is
                   the only one that can be a run-level bar. Judgements need
                   a grader agent, which is #lp-two, still open.

**Not ambiguous: the ticket set is frozen at the start of a run.** #werk-loop-gap has a builder file what it had to invent as an open card, so `werk find` shows Eryk after the run. #werk-loop-ticket derives tickets from decided cards, and those new cards are open. They cannot enter the run that made them. A person triggers the next run — that is the human gate #werk-loop-ticket calls a G2.

Open: does 'built' mean merged, and is 'review check' the held-out section run once on the merged tree?

payload.title: A check calls a make target, not a tool

patch.body:
Every check line is `make <target>`: `make test`, `make lint`, `make typecheck`. The target lives in the project's Makefile, beside the code it judges. The rubric holds the name, the project holds the command.

Two things this buys.

1. A change of tool is a one-line edit in the project's Makefile. No rubric line moves.
2. The same line means the right thing in every project, because each one answers `make test` with its own command: `pnpm test` behind the target in a Node project, `xcodebuild test` behind it in an iOS project, `./gradlew test` behind it in an Android project.

What it costs: a check is only as strong as the target behind it. A `lint` target with no config passes.

A project with no such target yet is a project that gets one. A missing `lint` or `typecheck` target is work to do, not a reason to call a tool directly. The check section of #lp-rubric-prod is still in the tool-call form this card replaces, so it needs the same edit.

Rejected: #lp-checks-scripts:opt0, one tool call per check line.
Rejected: #lp-checks-scripts:opt1, a pnpm script in place of the target — works only for a Node project.
patch.why: A hardcoded tool name binds the rubric to one toolchain. A make target survives a change of test runner, and works the same way in a web, backend, or mobile project.

payload.title: A check calls a pnpm script
payload.why_not:
Every check line is `pnpm <script>`, the script defined in package.json.

For: no extra file. A Node project already has a package.json, so the script has a natural home.

Against: `pnpm` and `package.json` name a Node toolchain. A mobile project has no package.json — an iOS project builds with Xcode, an Android project with Gradle. The line stops meaning anything there, the same cost #lp-checks-scripts names for a hardcoded tool name. A make target sits one layer above pnpm and above Xcode or Gradle alike, so it does not carry this cost.

Rejected.

patch.body:
Every rubric line belongs to one of two layers.

**Check.** One command decides the line, the same way on every run. Its exit code is the whole verdict. The rules for this layer are in #lp-checks.

**Judgement.** An agent reads the diff against one decided card. It returns a score and the gap between the diff and the card. The rules for this layer are in #lp-prod-judge.

**The dividing line.** If pass or fail needs someone to weigh the output, the line is a judgement. If a command can decide it, the line is a check, even when it looks like a quality question. Example: "no new public function without a doc comment" is a lint rule, so it is a check.

The split does not need #lp-split. Which checks the builder sees is a separate question from which layer a line is in.
patch.why: A check and a judgement fail in different ways and are fixed in different ways. Mixed in one list, each line gets argued as both.

payload.title: A held-out line is Given/When/Then steps, not test code
payload.why: The steps are written before the UI exists, so they can name only what the user sees and does.
payload.body:
Each held-out line is plain text in Given/When/Then form (the Gherkin syntax). No Cucumber runtime: the steps are input for #lp-heldout-binder, which writes the real tests.

```
Given the map is open with 50 cards
When a card is added from the command line
And the user searches for its title
Then the new card is in the results
```

A step names a user action or a thing the user sees. It names no selector, file, or function. The same steps stay valid if the implementation changes.

Most held-out lines are end-to-end, but that is not what makes them held out. A line is held out because the builder does not write it and cannot read it.

payload.title: The held-out author writes Playwright tests directly, with role and text locators
payload.why_not: The author works before the UI exists, so it guesses the roles and labels. The tests also tie the set to one tech stack.

payload.title: A step author writes the steps from the brief, in parallel with the builder
payload.why: The steps need only the brief and the decided cards, not the code. So they can be written while the code is.
payload.body:
The step author is a separate agent. It starts when the builder starts, from the same brief. It never reads the builder's code.

The steps are stored outside the builder's worktree. The builder cannot read them. The coordinator runs them at merge time (#werk-loop-merge).

payload.title: A binder agent turns steps into tests, and never makes a test pass
payload.why: The binder reads the code. If it may change a test until it passes, it fits the test to the code, and the held-out set checks nothing.
payload.body:
The binder reads the merged code, finds the elements each step names, and writes the tests for the project's stack.

Two rules.

1. The binder cannot change step text. It only maps each step to UI actions and assertions.
2. The binder does not make a test pass. When a step fails, it records the failure and stops. It fixes only its own errors, for example a typo in a locator.

"Element not found" can be a binder error or a missing feature. The binder reports which one it thinks it is, and the coordinator reads that report.

Example of what rule 2 stops: search does not update live. A binder that may make tests pass adds a page reload before the search. The test passes and the feature is still wrong.

Accepted risk: a binder writes a wrong test, and a correct feature fails. This is fixed when it happens, not prevented.

payload.title: On a held-out fail, the builder gets the text of the failed step
payload.why: The builder needs a reason to fix the code. The step text gives one in user terms and contains no test code.
payload.body:
The next builder pass gets the failed step, word for word, with the brief (#lp-stateless). It does not get the test code or the other steps.

Accepted risk: each failure shows the builder one step. After many failures, the builder has seen most of the set. This is watched and fixed if it happens.

payload.title: The builder gets the failing test code
payload.why_not: The test is no longer held out. The builder can fit the fix to that one test.

payload.title: The builder gets a written description of what the user saw and what the user expected
payload.why_not: Some agent must write it for each failure, and its detail varies. The step text is already in user terms.

payload.title: The held-out set belongs to validate, and validate runs beside build
payload.why: Validate is everything the builder cannot see. The held-out set is the first part of it, and it has to run at each merge to catch a break where it starts.
payload.body:
Validate is defined by who can see it, not by when it runs. Build holds what the builder sees and runs: its own tests, the checks, the judgements. Validate holds what the builder never sees: the held-out set (#lp-prod-heldout) now, and measurement against production later.

So validate starts with build, not after it. The step author (#lp-heldout-author) starts when the builder starts. The coordinator runs the held-out set at each merge (#werk-loop-merge). On a fail, the builder gets the failed step (#lp-heldout-feedback) while build is still running.

The gates keep their order: G2 still closes build and G3 still closes validate. What changes is that the two stages overlap, and G2 needs every held-out step green on the merged tree.

payload.title: Build: a builder loop per ticket and a merge loop per run

patch.body:
Build turns a decided subtree into merged, checked code. It runs on two levels.

**Per ticket: the builder loop.** One ticket, one worktree.

1. Implement. A fresh builder agent gets the brief, the decided cards, and the last failure, if there is one (#lp-stateless).
2. Check. The checks run: one command each, exit code only (#lp-checks).
3. Grade. A grader agent reads the diff against each decided card (#lp-prod-judge).

A fail at step 2 or 3 starts a new pass at step 1. There is no separate fix step: a fix is a new implement pass with the failure in its input. A retry cap stops the loop (#werk-loop-done).

**Per run: the merge loop.** The coordinator takes the finished tickets one at a time (#werk-loop-merge).

1. Merge one ticket into the run's tree.
2. Run the checks again on the merged tree. Green alone does not mean green merged.
3. Run the held-out set. This step belongs to validate, not build (#st-validate-heldout).

A red result at step 2 or 3 files a follow-up ticket, and the merge stands. Build ends when every ticket is merged and every held-out step passes (#st-g2-heldout).

**Words.** The per-ticket step is "check", not "validate". Validate is the stage that holds what the builder cannot see.

One fresh agent per pass. Give it the brief, the decision, the rubric, and the last failure. It does one unit of work and exits. The repository is the memory.

This changes the engine's shape: no agent lives longer than one pass.

## Prototype

**Question:** does a loop of fresh agents, with the repository as the only memory, reach green checks as reliably as one long session, and at what cost?

**Design.** One new file, `src/loop.ts`, about 150 lines. It uses the headless `claude -p` runner and the worktree code from `src/prototype.ts`.

1. Input: a ticket brief, a list of check commands (for werk: `bun test`, `tsc --noEmit`), and a cap (default 5).
2. Make one worktree off `HEAD`.
3. Pass n: start a fresh `claude -p` in the worktree. The prompt holds the brief, the decided cards in its depends_on closure, and the last failure: the failed command and the end of its output, cut to about 4,000 characters.
4. When the agent exits, the loop commits the worktree as "pass n". The next agent reads the history with `git log` and `git diff`, and gets nothing else.
5. The loop runs the checks. The loop's own run is the verdict, even if the agent ran the checks itself.
6. All green: stop. Red: save the failure and go to step 3. At the cap: stop and keep the branch.
7. Write one line per pass to `.werk/runs/<id>.jsonl`: check results, time, and cost from `--output-format json`.

No grader step. Checks only, the same as the v0 scope in #werk-loop-done.

**Comparison.** The same ticket goes to one long `claude -p` session, told to work until the checks pass. Compare pass or fail, cost, time, and the diff. In the diff, look for faked tests.

**Work.**

1. Export the runner helpers from `src/prototype.ts`.
2. Write `src/loop.ts` and a command `werk loop <brief> --check "..." --cap 5`.
3. Pick 2 or 3 real tickets from the map.
4. Run both approaches on each ticket: about 6 to 30 agent runs.

**Limit.** Context loss shows only on long tasks. Small tickets test the mechanics, not the claim. At least one ticket must be large enough to fill a long session's context.
patch.why: Long contexts degrade. The file system and git do not.

patch.body:
Two inputs, different in kind. The **subtree** is read in full and verbatim — it is the brief. The **rest of the map** is a reference the planner consults, not text it is handed.

**Why the split is forced.** The map is 234 cards. #werk alone is 91, and #werk-chat is 60. A subtree at the size a person would select is already a large read. The whole map on top of it is not one context, and #lp-stateless names a degraded context as the failure mode to design against.

**What the planner consults instead of reading everything.** #vi-sysdiag-grid-minimal is the whole running system as one compressed picture, with card ids on the elements — the planner sees the system shape at a glance and follows an id only where it needs the argument. #vi-sysdiag-codemap's element-to-files-and-symbols mapping is the other half: it says which files a ticket will touch, which is what #werk-loop-fanout needs to schedule anything safely.

Open:

1. Does the planner read the subtree's **rejected options** too? It matters more here than at build time — the planner is the one that could re-propose a rejected shape.
2. Does the planner see the **open and proto** cards in the subtree, or only the decided ones? An open card inside a selected subtree is a hole in the plan. It should probably block ticket planning and say so, rather than be silently skipped.
3. Is the ticket set written back to the map, or kept beside it? #werk-loop-ticket question 1.

## Prototype

**Question:** can one agent turn a decided subtree into tickets that cover every decision, fit one context each, and block each other in the same order as depends_on?

**Design.** One new file, `src/plan.ts`, and a command `werk plan <subtree-id>`. The prototype takes a position on each open question above.

1. Input: the subtree, in full and word for word — every card body, the rejected options, and the sources. (Open question 1: yes.)
2. Reference, consulted and not handed over: an index of all card ids and titles, the `werk show` command, the system diagram, and the code map.
3. An open or proto card in the subtree stops the run. The planner names the card and writes no tickets. (Open question 2.)
4. The planner is a headless `claude -p`. It writes one file per ticket to `.werk/tickets/<run>/NN.md`, with: the title and the tracer-bullet slice, `cites` (the card ids it builds), `blocked_by` (other ticket ids), `files` (what it expects to touch), and the check commands.
5. Tickets stay beside the map, not on it. (Open question 3, for the prototype only.)
6. A person reads the tickets before any build starts. This is the human gate from #werk-loop-ticket. The tickets show on a board (#werk-board).

**Checks on the output.** Each one is a command, per #lp-checks:

- every decided card in the subtree is cited by at least one ticket
- the `blocked_by` graph has no cycle and agrees with the depends_on edges between the cited cards
- each ticket brief is under a size limit

**What it feeds.** The tickets are the input for the #lp-stateless prototype. Tickets fit one context each by design, so that comparison runs a whole subtree: one long session builds every ticket, against one fresh pass per ticket.

payload.title: A ticket board is a fourth view, beside the map, the graph, and the diagram
payload.why: Tickets are units of build work, not decisions. A person reads them as a set of columns to move through, not as a tree.
payload.body:
A small board in the style of Trello. One column per ticket state, one card per ticket. It shows the tickets that #werk-loop-planner writes, and a person reads them there before any build starts (the gate in #werk-loop-ticket).

Each ticket card shows its title, the map cards it cites, and what blocks it. A click on a cited id opens that card on the map.

Open:

1. The columns. Which ticket states exist is not decided yet.
2. Read-only, or can a person edit, reorder, or reject a ticket on the board?

payload.title: The builder loop: one ticket, fresh passes until the checks and the grader pass
payload.why: A fix is a new implement pass with the failure in its input, so the loop has three steps, not four.
payload.body:
One ticket, one worktree.

1. Implement. A fresh builder agent gets the brief, the decided cards, and the last failure, if there is one (#lp-stateless).
2. Check. The checks run: one command each, exit code only (#lp-checks).
3. Grade. A grader agent reads the diff against each decided card (#lp-prod-judge).

A fail at step 2 or 3 starts a new pass at step 1. There is no separate fix step. A retry cap stops the loop (#werk-loop-done).

payload.title: The merge loop: merge one ticket, check the merged tree, run the held-out set
payload.why: Each ticket is green alone. Only a run over the merged tree shows whether they are green together.
payload.body:
The coordinator takes the finished tickets one at a time (#werk-loop-merge).

1. Merge one ticket into the run's tree.
2. Run the checks again on the merged tree. Green alone does not mean green merged.
3. Run the held-out set. This step belongs to validate, not build (#st-validate-heldout).

A red result at step 2 or 3 files a follow-up ticket, and the merge stands. Build ends when every ticket is merged and every held-out step passes (#st-g2-heldout).

patch.body:
Build turns a decided subtree into merged, checked code. It runs on two levels.

- **Per ticket:** #st-build-ticket. A builder loop in one worktree: implement, check, grade, and a fresh pass on a fail.
- **Per run:** #st-build-run. A merge loop over the finished tickets: merge one, check the merged tree, run the held-out set.

**Words.** The per-ticket step is "check", not "validate". Validate is the stage that holds what the builder cannot see.

payload.title: Plan, build, and validate repeat in small slices
payload.why: What gets built changes what gets decided next. A plan made before any build runs is a plan made without that information.
payload.body:
A project does not decide everything, then plan everything, then build. A person decides part of the map, plans part of it, and builds part of it, and each part can start before the others end.

So a ticket can be built while other cards are still open, and new tickets can join the board during a run.

payload.title: Decide every card, then plan every ticket, then build
payload.why_not: It is waterfall: nothing that the build teaches can change a decision, because every decision is already made.

payload.title: The board follows the whole run, with one column per ticket state
payload.why: The board is where a person watches the build, not only where they approve the plan.
payload.body:
Columns: blocked, ready, building, merging, merged. A ticket moves right as the loop moves it.

A red result after a merge is a new follow-up ticket in ready, not a column. The merge stands (#werk-loop-merge).

A red held-out step is a state of the run, not of one ticket (#st-g2-heldout). It shows in the board header.

payload.title: The board shows the tickets at the gate only, as a list sorted by blocked_by
payload.why_not: Before build, every ticket is in the same state, so the board cannot show the build as it runs.

payload.title: A person reorders, deletes, and triggers the build of one ticket at a time
payload.why: Build order is a person's choice while the process is iterative (#st-iterative), and a manual trigger keeps that choice in their hands.
payload.body:
Three direct actions on the board:

1. Reorder tickets in ready.
2. Delete a ticket.
3. Trigger the build of one ticket.

No ticket starts to build by itself. For the prototype, every build starts with a trigger. If each new ticket turns out to need a build anyway, the trigger goes and builds start by themselves.

A ticket is not edited on the board. A person asks an agent to change it, and the agent runs the planner's checks again (#werk-loop-planner).

payload.title: Read-only board; approve or reject the whole ticket set with a note
payload.why_not: One gate for the whole set makes the plan a single step before the build. It gives no control over which ticket is built, or when.

payload.title: Edit a ticket's text directly on the board
payload.why_not: A direct edit can break the planner's checks. An agent that edits and then checks again keeps them true.

patch.body:
A small board in the style of Trello. One column per ticket state, one card per ticket. It shows the tickets that #werk-loop-planner writes, and it follows them through the run.

Each ticket card shows its title, the map cards it cites, and what blocks it. A click on a cited id opens that card on the map.

The columns are in #werk-board-columns. What a person can do on the board is in #werk-board-control.

Two inputs, different in kind. The **subtree** is read in full and verbatim — it is the brief. The **rest of the map** is a reference the planner consults, not text it is handed.

**Why the split is forced.** The map is 234 cards. #werk alone is 91, and #werk-chat is 60. A subtree at the size a person would select is already a large read. The whole map on top of it is not one context, and #lp-stateless names a degraded context as the failure mode to design against.

**What the planner consults instead of reading everything.** #vi-sysdiag-grid-minimal is the whole running system as one compressed picture, with card ids on the elements — the planner sees the system shape at a glance and follows an id only where it needs the argument. #vi-sysdiag-codemap's element-to-files-and-symbols mapping is the other half: it says which files a ticket will touch, which is what #werk-loop-fanout needs to schedule anything safely.

Open:

1. Does the planner read the subtree's **rejected options** too? It matters more here than at build time — the planner is the one that could re-propose a rejected shape.
2. Does the planner see the **open and proto** cards in the subtree, or only the decided ones? An open card inside a selected subtree is a hole in the plan. It should probably block ticket planning and say so, rather than be silently skipped.
3. Is the ticket set written back to the map, or kept beside it? #werk-loop-ticket question 1.

## Prototype

**Question:** can one agent turn a decided subtree into tickets that cover every decision, fit one context each, and block each other in the same order as depends_on?

**Design.** One new file, `src/plan.ts`, and a command `werk plan <subtree-id>`. The prototype takes a position on each open question above.

1. Input: the subtree, in full and word for word — every card body, the rejected options, and the sources. (Open question 1: yes.)
2. Reference, consulted and not handed over: an index of all card ids and titles, the `werk show` command, the system diagram, and the code map.
3. An open or proto card in the subtree stops the run. The planner names the card and writes no tickets. (Open question 2.)
4. The planner is a headless `claude -p`. It writes one file per ticket to `.werk/tickets/<run>/NN.md`, with: the title and the tracer-bullet slice, `cites` (the card ids it builds), `blocked_by` (other ticket ids), `files` (what it expects to touch), and the check commands.
5. Tickets stay beside the map, not on it. (Open question 3, for the prototype only.)
6. The tickets show on the board (#werk-board). A person triggers the build of each ticket there (#werk-board-control). That trigger is the human gate from #werk-loop-ticket.

**Checks on the output.** Each one is a command, per #lp-checks:

- every decided card in the subtree is cited by at least one ticket
- the `blocked_by` graph has no cycle and agrees with the depends_on edges between the cited cards
- each ticket brief is under a size limit

**What it feeds.** The tickets are the input for the #lp-stateless prototype. Tickets fit one context each by design, so that comparison runs a whole subtree: one long session builds every ticket, against one fresh pass per ticket.

payload.title: Nothing bounds the number of follow-up tickets in one run
payload.why: A red merge files a follow-up ticket, and each follow-up gets a fresh retry cap. So a run whose held-out set stays red never ends.
payload.body:
#st-build-run ends build when every ticket is merged and every held-out step passes (#st-g2-heldout). A red step at a merge files a follow-up ticket, and the merge stands.

#werk-loop-done caps the passes on one ticket. A follow-up is a new ticket, so it starts with a new cap. Nothing counts follow-ups across the run.

The failure: a held-out step that no builder can make green. Each merge files one more follow-up. The run never reaches G2 and never stops.

The run needs one more stop state beside success and the per-ticket cap: a limit on follow-ups, and what happens at that limit.

Open: the limit — a count per run, or a count per held-out step — and whether the limit stops the run or opens G2 with the red step named.

payload.title: A run has no limit on follow-up tickets, for now

patch.body:
#st-build-run ends build when every ticket is merged and every held-out step passes (#st-g2-heldout). A red step at a merge files a follow-up ticket, and the merge stands. #werk-loop-done caps the passes on one ticket. A follow-up is a new ticket, with a new cap.

**No limit on follow-ups in v0.** Nothing counts follow-up tickets across a run.

**The cost, stated.** A held-out step that no builder can make green gives a run that never reaches G2 and never stops. Each merge files one more follow-up. The run is unbounded in time and in tokens.

**Why accept that cost.** It is not known that current models fall into repeated bug-fix-bug-fix cycles. A limit picked before the first real run is a number with no data behind it. The first runs show whether the cycle happens, and how long a run that does converge takes.

**When to revisit.** A run that files follow-ups for the same held-out step more than once. That is the evidence the limit needs.
patch.why: No run has shown a bug-fix-bug-fix loop yet. A limit set now is a guess about behaviour nobody has observed.

payload.title: A limit on follow-up tickets per run, or per held-out step
payload.why: Bounds the run, but the number would be set before any run shows how often follow-ups repeat.

patch.body:
A coordinator merges the finished, internally tested tickets through a merge queue, one at a time.

**The fact that makes it hard.** Each ticket is green in its own worktree, off the same base. Green alone does not imply green merged. Two tickets can both pass with no textual conflict and still break each other — one renames what the other calls, one changes a shape the other constructs. A clean `git merge` is not evidence.

**The queue.** For the ticket at the head of the queue, the coordinator:

1. Makes a temporary tree: the run's current tree plus the ticket's branch. Conflict resolution happens here.
2. Runs #werk-loop-done's checks on that temporary tree.
3. Green: the temporary tree becomes the run's tree, and the ticket is merged. Red: nothing merges. The ticket goes back to building, with the failure in its next pass's input (#lp-stateless).

The run's tree is never red, so a later ticket's checks always start from green, and a red result always belongs to the ticket under test. Only the failed ticket goes back; the rest of the queue goes on.

This is the standard merge-queue pattern. The prototype runs one ticket at a time. Testing several queued tickets together as a speculative stack is a later speed-up.

**Rejected.** #werk-loop-merge:opt3 (merge first and let the merge stand, with a follow-up ticket for the break) leaves the run's tree red until the follow-up is built, and every check in between runs on a red base. #werk-loop-merge:opt1 (hand the coordinator the fix itself) makes the coordinator a second builder. #werk-loop-merge:opt2 (stop the run and leave the branch) stops all progress for one ticket's failure.

**Relation to #lp-overseer.** That overseer watches the event log and cancels a stalled agent. This one merges. Same process or two is open — the log-watching is shared, the merge authority is not.

No precedent exists in this repo. Every other step of #werk-loop has working code or a close cousin; nothing here has merged N independently-green worktrees.

payload.title: Merge first; the merge stands, and a follow-up ticket fixes the break
payload.why_not: The run's tree stays red until the follow-up is built, and every later check runs on a red base, so a new break looks like the old one.

**When to revisit.** A run that files follow-ups for the same held-out step more than once. That is the evidence the limit needs.

patch.body:
Eryk decided this, and reversed the earlier recommendation of a background fork. See #werk-mc-open:opt1.

## The three gestures

    click              the map goes there. This conversation follows, as today.
    Shift+click        a fork rooted at that card, focused. The map goes there too.
    Shift+click again  on a card that already has a tab: switches to it. It does not fork twice.

Both gestures move the view to the card you clicked. That is one rule, not two. The difference between them is only whether a new conversation starts there.

Nothing is added by the fork moving the view: it follows from #werk-mc-follow. Focusing a tab moves the map to that tab's card, and the fork's card is the one under the cursor. So this card does not introduce a navigation rule; it just says the fork is focused rather than backgrounded.

## Why the throughput is not lost

Leaving a conversation does not pause it. The turn you started in tab A keeps running while you are in tab B. That is the feature. What you give up by focusing the fork is the ability to *read* A while B starts, and that is worth one keypress — Cmd+1, see #werk-mc-keys.

## Second entry point

A '+' at the end of the tab strip forks at whatever card is open. Same operation, no card link needed, and the map does not move because you are already there.

patch.body:
The goal: no agent stays stuck, whatever the cause. The overseer watches every running agent session and acts on three signs:

1. A permission prompt that nobody answers. The agent waits and does nothing else.
2. An unintentional loop. The agent repeats the same tool call, or the same failing check, and makes no progress.
3. A tool call with no timeout. A command that never returns holds the session forever.

It is the real safety control for auto-merge.
patch.why: A second process reads the event log in real time.

ops.old: Six parts. The runner is easy; the divergence detector is the whole problem.
ops.new: Six parts. The runner is easy; the divergence detector is the whole problem.

ops.old: 1. **Fan-out runner** — N headless agents from one brief. Reuses `Agent` (src/agent.ts already spawns `claude` per conversation) and `ConvoManager`. New: concurrency cap, an auto-allow permission policy (a headless sample cannot stop at the permission bar), and per-sample isolation — see #al-sample-build-isolation for which samples need a worktree and which need only a scratch output path. About one day.
ops.new: 1. **Fan-out runner** — N headless agents from one brief. Each sample is a one-shot `claude --print` process, not an `Agent` or a `ConvoManager` conversation: a sample has no chat pane, no resumed session, and no permission bar to stop at, so the conversation machinery adds nothing. Tools are pre-allowed with `--allowedTools` — read-only for a plan sample, write tools only for a sample with its own scratch path. The concurrency cap is N itself. Per-sample isolation — see #al-sample-build-isolation for which samples need a worktree and which need only a scratch output path. About one day.

ops.old: 2. **A no-questions prompt contract** — the sample agent may not ask. It must pick, and record every pick. Half a day.
ops.new: 2. **A no-questions prompt contract** — the sample agent may not ask. It must pick, and record every pick. Half a day.

ops.old: 3. **Divergence detection** — the hard part. A plain diff of N trees is noise: naming, order, formatting. So do not diff the code. Each sample returns a **decision manifest**: the requirement choices it made, one line each. werk clusters the manifests; a field where the samples disagree is a fork. This is #al-diff-cli's pattern one level up — the agent supplies the structure, code verifies the claim against the artifact. About one day.

"I do not care" is offered live when the fork is actually asked about — never written as a graph option, or a card could be marked decided on indifference, which names nothing. About one day.

payload.title: The overseer is a deterministic process, not an agent
payload.why: Most liveness questions have an answer without a model. A process that is itself an agent can stall like the agents it watches.
payload.body:
The overseer is plain code. It reads the event log and answers "is this still alive?" and "is this still moving?" without a model.

It spawns an agent only for a question that needs judgement, such as whether a permission ask makes sense (#lp-overseer-asks). That agent is a short classification call. The overseer waits for it with a timeout, like any other tool call.

Nothing watches the overseer. It has no model inside it, so it has no way to stall in the way an agent does.

payload.title: An AI overseer, with a deterministic watchdog that records its heartbeats and steps live, so it can resume where it stopped
payload.why_not: It needs two processes where one does the job. The deterministic layer has to exist anyway, and it already answers most of the questions.

payload.title: The overseer answers a permission ask itself
payload.why: The loop runs without a person. An ask that waits for one stops the agent until someone looks.
payload.body:
The overseer answers every permission ask, and the agent does not wait for a person.

1. The overseer sends the ask to a classification agent (#lp-overseer-det): the tool, its input, and the ticket the agent is building.
2. The ask makes sense for that ticket: the overseer allows it.
3. Something looks wrong: the overseer denies it, with a comment that says why. The agent reads the comment and continues without that call.

Every answer goes into the event log, with the comment. A person reads the answers later. They do not approve each one as it comes.

payload.title: Send a permission ask to a person, and cancel only a loop or a hung tool
payload.why_not: A person in the path stops the loop at each ask, and the loop exists so that it does not need a person.

payload.title: No new event for a set time means the agent is stuck
payload.why: The named signs cover known causes. A stuck agent can also have a cause nobody named: an API retry storm, a rate limit, a model that stops answering.
payload.body:
The overseer treats an agent as stuck when its session writes no new event for a set time, whatever the cause.

This rule does not replace the named signs in #lp-overseer. It catches what they miss.

The time limit is not set yet. A tool call that is still running is not silence: #lp-overseer-inflight decides about it.

payload.title: The overseer tells a working tool call from a frozen one
payload.why: A test that waits on a promise that never resolves, or an I/O call to a resource it cannot reach, looks the same as a long build from outside. Only the process shows the difference.
payload.body:
Two sources show a tool call that is still running:

1. The tool-call stream. A call that has started and has no result yet is in flight. The overseer knows the tool, its input, and its start time.
2. The operating system. A shell call is a process tree. For each process the overseer reads the CPU time, the state, the output written, and the open files and network connections.

Together they tell working from frozen:

| CPU time | Output | Open connections | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| grows | any | any | working |
| flat | grows | any | working |
| flat | flat | one, to a host that does not answer | frozen on I/O |
| flat | flat | none | frozen on a wait that never ends, such as a promise that never resolves |

A frozen call is cancelled. The agent gets the cancel as the call's result, with the evidence, and continues.

A test runner with a per-test timeout catches most frozen tests first. The overseer catches what the runner does not: a hang outside any test, a runner with no timeout, or a command that is not a test.

Open: how long "flat" must last before the overseer calls it frozen.

payload.title: What counts as progress
payload.why: The loop sign in #lp-overseer is 'repeats and makes no progress'. Without a definition of progress, the overseer cannot tell a loop from slow, real work.
payload.body:
The overseer needs a signal it can compute without a model (#lp-overseer-det). Candidates:

1. The diff changes. The working tree differs from the last check point.
2. A check result changes. A failing check passes, or fails with a different message.
3. The agent touches a file it has not touched before.

Each one has a false reading:

- An edit that is made and then undone changes the diff twice and ends where it started.
- A check that fails with a new message each time can be a loop that moves nothing forward.
- Reading many files is normal at the start of a ticket.

Open: which signal, or which combination, and over what window.

payload.title: An overseer keeps an agent from getting stuck
No new event for 60 seconds means the agent is stuck
payload.why: The named signs cover known causes. A stuck agent can also have a cause nobody named: an API retry storm, a rate limit, a model that stops answering.
payload.body:
The overseer treats an agent as stuck when its session writes no new event for 60 seconds, whatever the cause.

60 seconds is the starting value. The first runs show whether it cancels real work too often or waits too long.

This rule does not replace the named signs in #lp-overseer. It catches what they miss.

A tool call that is still running is not silence: #lp-overseer-inflight decides about it.

payload.title: The overseer tells a working tool call from a frozen one
payload.why: A test that waits on a promise that never resolves, or an I/O call to a resource it cannot reach, looks the same as a long build from outside. Only the process shows the difference.
payload.body:
Two sources show a tool call that is still running:

1. The tool-call stream. A call that has started and has no result yet is in flight. The overseer knows the tool, its input, and its start time.
2. The operating system. A shell call is a process tree. For each process the overseer reads the CPU time, the state, the output written, and the open files and network connections.

Together they tell working from frozen:

| CPU time | Output | Open connections | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| grows | any | any | working |
| flat | grows | any | working |
| flat | flat | one, to a host that does not answer | frozen on I/O |
| flat | flat | none | frozen on a wait that never ends, such as a promise that never resolves |

"Flat" means no change for 60 seconds, the same starting value as #lp-overseer-silence. The first runs show whether it needs to change.

A frozen call is cancelled. The agent gets the cancel as the call's result, with the evidence, and continues.

A test runner with a per-test timeout catches most frozen tests first. The overseer catches what the runner does not: a hang outside any test, a runner with no timeout, or a command that is not a test.

payload.title: Cancel any tool call after a fixed wall-clock time
payload.why_not: A long build or a full test run that is still working gets cancelled the same as a frozen one. Wall-clock time alone cannot tell them apart.

payload.title: A fingerprint of the diff and the check results; a fingerprint seen before is not progress
payload.why_not: It is brittle in the direction that hides loops: any small change to a file or to the order of tool calls gives a new fingerprint, so a loop that changes one character each pass reads as progress.

payload.title: A classifier agent decides every 5 minutes whether the agent is looping
payload.why: Progress has no fingerprint a program can compute: a loop that changes one character each pass looks new to any hash. Whether work moves forward is a judgement.
payload.body:
Every 5 minutes, the overseer starts a classifier agent for each running agent (#lp-overseer-det). The classifier has one task: say whether the agent is looping.

1. **Input.** The ticket's brief, and the tool calls since the classifier's last verdict. Not the whole log: it grows without limit, and old passes add noise.
2. **Output.** "looping" or "not looping", with a reason in one or two sentences.
3. **The wait.** The overseer waits for the verdict with a timeout, like any other tool call. No verdict counts as "not looping". The 60-second rules still apply to the agent (#lp-overseer-silence, #lp-overseer-inflight).
4. **On "looping".** The overseer cancels the agent and starts a fresh pass. The classifier's reason goes into the new pass's brief, so the next pass knows what did not work (#lp-stateless).

A loop can run for up to 5 minutes before a verdict. That is acceptable for a repeat. A hard stall is caught at 60 seconds by the other rules.

The cost is one model call per running agent every 5 minutes.
