payload.title: Trend reports across work items: the loop's effort per ticket

patch.body:
Rot means that each change makes the next change harder, slower, or riskier. No single merge breaks anything. The cost adds up. With auto-merge, no human sees it add up.

The quality of one change is the job of the per-change gates. A trend report watches the whole run and the runs after it. It is a report, not a gate: it does not block a merge.

**The main metric: the loop's effort per ticket.** For each ticket, record:

- the number of builder passes until the checks and the grader pass
- the tokens spent
- the wall time
- the number of grader fails

This is the outcome that the code metrics only predict. When the codebase rots, the same size of ticket needs more passes. The metric applies to every project the loop builds, not only to one.

**Secondary metrics, in the same report:**

- the check runtime, and the number of flaky tests. A slow or flaky check makes each pass cost more.
- drift between the project's agent docs and its code. No exit code decides this, so a judgement reads it.

Open: how the report normalizes for ticket size, and what change in the trend makes the report raise an alert.
patch.why: A per-change gate judges one diff. Rot is a cost that grows over many diffs, so only a measure across work items can show it.

payload.title: Per-change ratchets and budgets on code metrics
payload.why_not: These are per-change quality checks, so they belong to the per-change gates. They do not measure the cost across work items, which is what rot is.

payload.title: Per-change ratchets and budgets on code metrics
payload.body:
Each change is measured two times with the same commands: on the main branch just before the merge, and just after it. The check fails on the difference, not on the final value.

| Metric | Limit per change |
| --- | --- |
| escape hatches: `any`, lint and type suppressions, skipped tests | +0 (a ratchet: the count never goes up) |
| assertion count, coverage of the changed lines | must not go down |
| duplicated blocks | a small budget |
| dependency count | +0, unless the ticket names the dependency |
| complexity, file size | a budget, for example +20 points |

Example: the project has 120 lint warnings. A change adds one. A pass-or-fail check with a limit of 200 passes. This check fails, because the count went from 120 to 121.

The check catches a small loss of quality in one change, before it merges.
payload.why_not: It judges one change at a time. Rot is a cost that grows across many changes, and a budget still lets it grow: 50 changes at +19 each all pass. The quality of one change is a separate question from the trend.

payload.title: A quality review of each diff, separate from the grader
payload.why: The grader asks only whether the diff does what the decided cards say. Nothing then catches a problem that no card names: duplication, weak tests, escape hatches, a new dependency.
payload.body:
A reviewer agent reads the diff after the grader passes. It asks whether the change is good code. It does not ask whether the change is the right change. That is the grader's job (#lp-prod-judge). The two steps stay separate, so each one has one source of lines.

**The rubric is fixed and built into the tool**, the same for every project (#lp-rubric). It has five areas:

1. Design: module boundaries, coupling, error handling, fit with the code around it.
2. Maintainability: duplication, complexity, dead code, escape hatches such as type or lint suppressions and skipped tests.
3. Tests: assertions that fail without the change, edge cases, failure paths. Also any test that the change made weaker.
4. Security and dependencies: input validation, secret handling, each new dependency and the reason for it.
5. Performance: extra work, expensive queries, unbounded loops on the input.

**Only the diff.** A finding must point at the diff or at code that the diff directly affects. The reviewer does not review the whole repository.

**Output.** Each finding has a severity (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW), a file and a line, the impact, and a fix.

- CRITICAL or HIGH fails the pass. The findings go into the next builder pass, the same as a grader gap (#lp-stateless).
- MEDIUM and LOW do not block. The loop records them. Their count per ticket goes into the trend report (#lp-trend).

Open: one agent for all five areas, or one agent per area with a fresh context each. One agent per area anchors less, but it costs about five times as much.

payload.why: The grader asks only whether the diff does what the decided cards say. Nothing then catches a problem that no card names: duplication, weak tests, escape hatches, a new dependency.
payload.body:
Reviewer agents read the diff after the grader passes. They ask whether the change is good code. They do not ask whether the change is the right change. That is the grader's job (#lp-prod-judge). The two steps stay separate, so each one has one source of lines.

The review is part of the production rubric only. Prototype code does not get it (#lp-rubric-proto).

**The rubric is fixed and built into the tool**, the same for every project (#lp-rubric). It has five areas:

1. Design: module boundaries, coupling, error handling, fit with the code around it.
2. Maintainability: duplication, complexity, dead code, escape hatches such as type or lint suppressions and skipped tests.
3. Tests: assertions that fail without the change, edge cases, failure paths. Also any test that the change made weaker.
4. Security and dependencies: input validation, secret handling, each new dependency and the reason for it.
5. Performance: extra work, expensive queries, unbounded loops on the input.

**One agent per area.** Each reviewer gets a fresh context and one area. Five agents run at the same time. A reviewer with one area does not anchor on the findings of another area. The cost is about five times that of one agent.

**Only the diff.** A finding must point at the diff or at code that the diff directly affects. A reviewer does not review the whole repository.

- MEDIUM and LOW do not block. The loop records them. Their count per ticket goes into the trend report (#lp-trend).

**The loop.** A failed review starts a new builder pass, and that pass runs the checks, the grader, and all five reviewers again (#st-build-ticket). The loop ends when no CRITICAL or HIGH finding remains, or when the retry cap stops it. A fresh reviewer can find a new HIGH issue on each pass. The cap is what stops a loop that does not converge.

payload.why: A large ticket needs more passes than a small one. Without a size measure, a run of large tickets looks like rot.

Against: it comes from the build. Rot makes diffs larger, so the effort per line hides the rot it is meant to show.

payload.body:
For: nothing to build. Over many tickets, the size differences average out.

Against: it assumes a stable mix of ticket sizes. A run of large tickets still reads as rot. It needs many tickets before it shows anything.

payload.body:

Against: it costs a full loop run each time. The task must stay valid as the project grows.

payload.title: Ticket size is the number of user stories in the ticket

patch.body:
The report divides the effort per ticket (#lp-trend-primary) by the number of user stories in the ticket. A user story has the form: As an <actor>, I want <feature>, so that <benefit>.

**The size comes from the plan, not from the build.** A rotting codebase makes the builder write larger diffs. A size taken from the diff grows with the rot, so the effort per unit of size looks stable. The stories are written before the build starts. The builder cannot change them.

**Consistent, not exact.** One story can be small or large, so the count is a rough size. The trend only needs the count to be measured the same way on every ticket. Over many tickets, the differences between stories average out.

**A ticket with no user story counts as 1.** A refactor or an internal fix has no actor and no benefit for a user. Without this rule, the report divides by zero.

Required: each ticket carries its user stories. The plan stage writes them.

Each ticket has a field: a numbered list of user stories, in the form

payload.title: The /to-spec skill: a spec template with a numbered list of user stories
payload.body:
The spec template that `#st-ticket-stories` takes its user-story form from. Copied verbatim from `~/.agents/skills/to-spec/SKILL.md`.

````markdown
---
name: to-spec
description: Turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the project issue tracker — no interview, just synthesis of what you've already discussed.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

This skill takes the current conversation context and codebase understanding and produces a spec. Do NOT interview the user — just synthesize what you already know.

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not.

## Process

1. Explore the repo to understand the current state of the codebase, if you haven't already. Use the project's domain glossary vocabulary throughout the spec, and respect any ADRs in the area you're touching.

2. Sketch out the seams at which you're going to test the feature. Existing seams should be preferred to new ones. Use the highest seam possible. If new seams are needed, propose them at the highest point you can. The fewer seams across the codebase, the better - the ideal number is one.

Check with the user that these seams match their expectations.

3. Write the spec using the template below, then publish it to the project issue tracker. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label - no need for additional triage.

<spec-template>

## Problem Statement

The problem that the user is facing, from the user's perspective.

## Solution

The solution to the problem, from the user's perspective.

## User Stories

A LONG, numbered list of user stories. Each user story should be in the format of:

1. As an <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>

<user-story-example>
1. As a mobile bank customer, I want to see balance on my accounts, so that I can make better informed decisions about my spending
</user-story-example>

This list of user stories should be extremely extensive and cover all aspects of the feature.

## Implementation Decisions

A list of implementation decisions that were made. This can include:

- The modules that will be built/modified
- The interfaces of those modules that will be modified
- Technical clarifications from the developer
- Architectural decisions
- Schema changes
- API contracts
- Specific interactions

Do NOT include specific file paths or code snippets. They may end up being outdated very quickly.

Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it within the relevant decision and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts — not a working demo, just the important bits.

## Testing Decisions

A list of testing decisions that were made. Include:

- A description of what makes a good test (only test external behavior, not implementation details)
- Which modules will be tested
- Prior art for the tests (i.e. similar types of tests in the codebase)

## Out of Scope

A description of the things that are out of scope for this spec.

## Further Notes

Any further notes about the feature.

</spec-template>
````
payload.finding: A spec has a Problem Statement, a Solution, a long numbered list of user stories in the form 'As an <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>', Implementation Decisions, Testing Decisions, Out of Scope, and Further Notes.

payload.title: Plan ends with one spec per subtree, then tickets from the spec
payload.why: A subtree holds many decisions, not one statement of the work. A spec puts the problem, the user stories, and the test seams in one agreed place. The tickets then split one whole.
payload.body:
The plan stage ends in two steps:

1. **Spec.** `/to-spec` runs over one decided subtree. It writes one spec: the problem, the solution, a numbered list of user stories, the implementation and testing decisions, and what is out of scope (#to-spec).
2. **Tickets.** `/to-tickets` runs over that spec. It writes one or more tickets (#st-ticket). Each ticket is a tracer-bullet slice with its blocking edges (#to-tickets).

One subtree gives one spec. One spec gives one or more tickets.

Both skills check with a person before they publish: `/to-spec` confirms the test seams, and `/to-tickets` confirms the breakdown. These checks are part of the plan stage.

payload.why_not: The tickets then split a set of separate decisions. Nothing states the problem, the user stories, or the test seams once, for all the tickets.

````markdown
---
name: to-tickets
description: Break a plan, spec, or the current conversation into a set of tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its blocking edges, published to the configured tracker — edges as text in one file per ticket locally, or native blocking links on a real tracker.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# To Tickets

Break a plan, spec, or conversation into a set of **tickets** — tracer-bullet vertical slices, each declaring the tickets that **block** it.

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not.

## Process

### 1. Gather context

Work from whatever is already in the conversation context. If the user passes a reference (a spec path, an issue number or URL) as an argument, fetch it and read its full body and comments.

### 2. Explore the codebase (optional)

If you have not already explored the codebase, do so to understand the current state of the code. Ticket titles and descriptions should use the project's domain glossary vocabulary, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

Look for opportunities to prefactor the code to make the implementation easier. "Make the change easy, then make the easy change."

### 3. Draft vertical slices

Break the work into **tracer bullet** tickets.

<vertical-slice-rules>

- Each slice cuts a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests) — vertical, NOT a horizontal slice of one layer
- A completed slice is demoable or verifiable on its own
- Each slice is sized to fit in a single fresh context window
- Any prefactoring should be done first

</vertical-slice-rules>

Give each ticket its **blocking edges** — the other tickets that must complete before it can start. A ticket with no blockers can start immediately.

**Wide refactors are the exception to vertical slicing.** A **wide refactor** is one mechanical change — rename a column, retype a shared symbol — whose **blast radius** fans across the whole codebase, so a single edit breaks thousands of call sites at once and no vertical slice can land green. Don't force it into a tracer bullet; sequence it as **expand–contract**. First expand: add the new form beside the old so nothing breaks. Then migrate the call sites over in batches sized by blast radius (per package, per directory), each batch its own ticket blocked by the expand, keeping CI green batch to batch because the old form still exists. Finally contract: delete the old form once no caller remains, in a ticket blocked by every migrate batch. When even the batches can't stay green alone, keep the sequence but let them share an integration branch that all block a final integrate-and-verify ticket — green is promised only there.

### 4. Quiz the user

Present the proposed breakdown as a numbered list. For each ticket, show:

- **Title**: short descriptive name
- **Blocked by**: which other tickets (if any) must complete first
- **What it delivers**: the end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work

Ask the user:

- Does the granularity feel right? (too coarse / too fine)
- Are the blocking edges correct — does each ticket only depend on tickets that genuinely gate it?
- Should any tickets be merged or split further?

Iterate until the user approves the breakdown.

### 5. Publish the tickets to the configured tracker

Publish the approved tickets. **How** depends on the tracker `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` configured — the tickets are the same either way, only the shape of the blocking edges changes:

- **Local files** → write one file per ticket under `.scratch/<feature-slug>/issues/<NN>-<slug>.md`, numbered from `01` in dependency order (blockers first). Each file's "Blocked by" lists the numbers/titles it depends on. Use the per-ticket file template below — one ticket per file, never a single combined file.
- **A real issue tracker (GitHub, Linear, …)** → publish one issue per ticket in dependency order (blockers first) so each ticket's blocking edges can reference real identifiers. Use the platform's native blocking / sub-issue relationship where it has one; otherwise set each ticket's "Blocked by" to the blocking issues. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label unless instructed otherwise — the tickets are agent-grabbable by construction.

Work the **frontier**: any ticket whose blockers are all done. For a purely linear chain that means top to bottom.

Do NOT close or modify any parent issue.

<local-ticket-template>

# <NN> — <Ticket title>

**What to build:** the end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work, from the user's perspective — not a layer-by-layer implementation list.

**Blocked by:** the numbers/titles of the tickets that gate this one, or "None — can start immediately".

**Status:** ready-for-agent

- [ ] Acceptance criterion 1
- [ ] Acceptance criterion 2

</local-ticket-template>

<issue-template>

## Parent

A reference to the parent issue on the tracker (if the source was an existing issue, otherwise omit this section).

## What to build

The end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work, from the user's perspective — not layer-by-layer implementation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Criterion 1
- [ ] Criterion 2

## Blocked by

- A reference to each blocking ticket, or "None — can start immediately".

</issue-template>

In either form, avoid specific file paths or code snippets — they go stale fast. Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts — not a working demo, just the important bits.
````

1. As an <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>

<user-story-example>
1. As a mobile bank customer, I want to see balance on my accounts, so that I can make better informed decisions about my spending
</user-story-example>

This list of user stories should be extremely extensive and cover all aspects of the feature.

## Implementation Decisions

A list of implementation decisions that were made. This can include:

- The modules that will be built/modified
- The interfaces of those modules that will be modified
- Technical clarifications from the developer
- Architectural decisions
- Schema changes
- API contracts
- Specific interactions

Do NOT include specific file paths or code snippets. They may end up being outdated very quickly.

Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it within the relevant decision and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts, not a working demo, just the important bits.

## Testing Decisions

A list of testing decisions that were made. Include:

- A description of what makes a good test (only test external behavior, not implementation details)
- Which modules will be tested
- Prior art for the tests (i.e. similar types of tests in the codebase)

## Out of Scope

A description of the things that are out of scope for this spec.

## Further Notes

Any further notes about the feature.

</spec-template>
````

payload.title: Tracer-bullet tickets, each with its blocking edges and acceptance criteria
payload.body:
The skill that #st-spec uses for this step, from Matt Pocock's skills repository. Copied verbatim at commit `d81f3a1`.

````markdown
---
name: to-tickets
description: Break a plan, spec, or the current conversation into a set of tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its blocking edges, published to the configured tracker (edges as text in one file per ticket locally, or native blocking links on a real tracker).
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# To Tickets

Break a plan, spec, or conversation into a set of **tickets**: tracer-bullet vertical slices, each declaring the tickets that **block** it.

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

## Process

### 1. Gather context

Work from whatever is already in the conversation context. If the user passes a reference (a spec path, an issue number or URL) as an argument, fetch it and read its full body and comments.

### 2. Explore the codebase (optional)

If you have not already explored the codebase, do so to understand the current state of the code. Ticket titles and descriptions should use the project's domain glossary vocabulary, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

Look for opportunities to prefactor the code to make the implementation easier. "Make the change easy, then make the easy change."

### 3. Draft vertical slices

Break the work into **tracer bullet** tickets.

<vertical-slice-rules>

- Each slice cuts a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests): vertical, NOT a horizontal slice of one layer
- A completed slice is demoable or verifiable on its own
- Each slice is sized to fit in a single fresh context window
- Any prefactoring should be done first

</vertical-slice-rules>

Give each ticket its **blocking edges**: the other tickets that must complete before it can start. A ticket with no blockers can start immediately.

**Wide refactors are the exception to vertical slicing.** A **wide refactor** is one mechanical change (rename a column, retype a shared symbol) whose **blast radius** fans across the whole codebase, so a single edit breaks thousands of call sites at once and no vertical slice can land green. Don't force it into a tracer bullet; sequence it as **expand–contract**. First expand: add the new form beside the old so nothing breaks. Then migrate the call sites over in batches sized by blast radius (per package, per directory), each batch its own ticket blocked by the expand, keeping CI green batch to batch because the old form still exists. Finally contract: delete the old form once no caller remains, in a ticket blocked by every migrate batch. When even the batches can't stay green alone, keep the sequence but let them share an integration branch that all block a final integrate-and-verify ticket; green is promised only there.

### 4. Quiz the user

Present the proposed breakdown as a numbered list. For each ticket, show:

- **Title**: short descriptive name
- **Blocked by**: which other tickets (if any) must complete first
- **What it delivers**: the end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work

Ask the user:

- Does the granularity feel right? (too coarse / too fine)
- Are the blocking edges correct: does each ticket only depend on tickets that genuinely gate it?
- Should any tickets be merged or split further?

Iterate until the user approves the breakdown.

### 5. Publish the tickets to the configured tracker

Publish the approved tickets. **How** depends on the tracker `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` configured; the tickets are the same either way, only the shape of the blocking edges changes:

- **Local files** → write one file per ticket under `.scratch/<feature-slug>/issues/<NN>-<slug>.md`, numbered from `01` in dependency order (blockers first). Each file's "Blocked by" lists the numbers/titles it depends on. Use the per-ticket file template below: one ticket per file, never a single combined file.
- **A real issue tracker (GitHub, Linear, …)** → publish one issue per ticket in dependency order (blockers first) so each ticket's blocking edges can reference real identifiers. Use the platform's native blocking / sub-issue relationship where it has one; otherwise set each ticket's "Blocked by" to the blocking issues. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label unless instructed otherwise; the tickets are agent-grabbable by construction.

Work the **frontier**: any ticket whose blockers are all done. For a purely linear chain that means top to bottom.

Do NOT close or modify any parent issue.

<local-ticket-template>

# <NN>: <Ticket title>

**What to build:** the end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work, from the user's perspective, not a layer-by-layer implementation list.

**Blocked by:** the numbers/titles of the tickets that gate this one, or "None (can start immediately)".

**Status:** ready-for-agent

- [ ] Acceptance criterion 1
- [ ] Acceptance criterion 2

</local-ticket-template>

<issue-template>

## Parent

A reference to the parent issue on the tracker (if the source was an existing issue, otherwise omit this section).

## What to build

The end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work, from the user's perspective, not layer-by-layer implementation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Criterion 1
- [ ] Criterion 2

## Blocked by

- A reference to each blocking ticket, or "None (can start immediately)".

</issue-template>

In either form, avoid specific file paths or code snippets: they go stale fast. Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts, not a working demo, just the important bits.
````
payload.finding: Each ticket is a vertical slice that fits one fresh context, with blocking edges, a 'What to build' from the user's side, and acceptance criteria. No file paths. Wide refactors use expand-contract.

patch.body:
The plan stage ends in two steps:

1. **Spec.** `/to-spec` runs over one decided subtree. It writes one spec: the problem, the solution, a numbered list of user stories, the implementation and testing decisions, and what is out of scope (#to-spec).
2. **Tickets.** `/to-tickets` runs over that spec. It writes one or more tickets (#st-ticket). Each ticket is a tracer-bullet slice with its blocking edges (#to-tickets).

One subtree gives one spec. One spec gives one or more tickets.

**An agent answers the skills' questions, not a person.** Both skills stop to ask: `/to-spec` asks whether the test seams are right, and `/to-tickets` asks about the granularity, the blocking edges, and the splits. The pipeline builds without a person, so an agent answers each question. It answers from the decided cards of the subtree and the map around it.

**An answer that no card gives becomes a card.** When the decided cards do not settle a question, the agent's answer is a new decision. It goes on the map under the subtree, so a person can see it and reopen it. It is never only in the spec.

ops.old: A ticket is the unit of build work. It is a tracer bullet: a narrow but complete path through every layer the change touches. It can be shown working on its own, and it fits one fresh context.

payload.title: A ticket lists the spec stories it delivers

patch.body:
The spec holds the user stories, as a numbered list (#st-spec). A ticket does not copy them. It has a field `stories` that lists the numbers of the stories it delivers.

**Written in the plan.** The agent that writes the tickets assigns the stories to them. Every story in the spec is delivered by at least one ticket. One story can need more than one ticket.

**Frozen at the build.** When the build of the ticket starts, the builder cannot change its stories or the spec. A change to either one is a change to the plan.

**A ticket can deliver no story.** A prefactor, a refactor, or an internal fix has no actor and no benefit for a user. Its list is empty. It does not get an invented story.

Two cards read the list: #lp-trend-size counts it, and the builder gets the listed stories in its brief as the definition of done from the user's side.
patch.why: A ticket needs a size that is fixed before the build, and a statement of done from the user's side. The spec's user stories give both, so each ticket points at the stories it delivers.

payload.title: Ticket size is the number of spec stories the ticket delivers

patch.body:
The report divides the effort per ticket (#lp-trend-primary) by the number of spec stories that the ticket delivers (#st-ticket-stories).

**The size comes from the plan, not from the build.** A rotting codebase makes the builder write larger diffs. A size taken from the diff grows with the rot, so the effort per unit of size looks stable. The stories are fixed before the build starts.

**Consistent, not exact.** One story can be small or large, so the count is a rough size. The trend only needs the count to be measured the same way on every ticket. Over many tickets, the differences between stories average out.

**A ticket with no user story counts as 1.** A prefactor, a refactor, or an internal fix has an empty list. Without this rule, the report divides by zero.

payload.text: Built: src/loop.ts and 'werk loop' (fresh and long modes). Two smoke tests are green, including the red-then-green path. The comparison on real tickets has not run, so the claim is not tested yet.

payload.title: What change in the trend raises an alert
payload.why: A report that nobody reads catches nothing. With auto-merge, the report must say when the trend needs a person.
payload.body:
The report shows the effort per story across tickets (#lp-trend-primary, #lp-trend-size). This card decides when the report raises an alert, and to whom.

Open: the rule, for example a rise over a rolling window compared with an earlier window, and how many tickets the window holds.

patch.body:
Rot means that each change makes the next change harder, slower, or riskier. No single merge breaks anything. The cost adds up over many merges. With auto-merge, no human sees it add up.

A trend report watches the cost across work items and across runs. It is a report, not a gate: it does not block a merge. The quality of one change is the job of the per-change gates (#lp-prod-review).

- #lp-trend-primary: the loop's effort per ticket.
- #lp-trend-secondary: signals that predict a rise in effort.
- #lp-trend-size: ticket size is the number of user stories.
- #lp-trend-alert: what change in the trend raises an alert.

- #lp-trend-secondary: signals that predict a rise in effort.
- #lp-trend-size: ticket size is the number of spec stories the ticket delivers.

payload.title: An alert on a 20% rise over 10 tickets, information only
payload.why: A report that nobody reads catches nothing. With auto-merge, the report must say when the trend needs a person, without stopping the build.
payload.body:
**The rule.** For each metric in #lp-trend-primary and #lp-trend-secondary, compare two windows of tickets:

- the base: the first 10 tickets of the project
- the current window: the last 10 tickets

The report raises an alert when a metric in the current window is 20% or more above the base. The effort metrics are measured per story (#lp-trend-size). The first 10 tickets cannot raise an alert, because they are the base.

**The numbers are a first guess.** 10 tickets and 20% are the same for every metric. They change when real data shows which metrics are noisy.

**An alert is information only.** It does not block a merge and it does not stop the build. The person sees it, and the loop continues.

patch.why: One ticket is built alone in its own worktree. A run merges many tickets into one tree. The two need different loops with different stop conditions.

payload.title: The build pipeline is tested at its command line, with a scripted fake agent
payload.why: The build goes wrong in the process spawns, the pipes, and the git calls. Only a seam above all of them sees those.
payload.body:
Tests run the build commands against a temporary git repository. A fake agent binary on the PATH replays a scripted stream of events and edits files the way a real agent does. The grader, the reviewers, and the classifiers are fake agents too.

Every time limit is a parameter, so a test sets the 60-second and 5-minute limits to milliseconds.

A test checks what a person sees: the exit code, the branch and its commits, the merged tree, the event log, and the records. It does not check internal function calls.

One seam covers the builder loop, the merge loop, the overseer, and the trend report.

payload.title: Three seams: an injected agent runner, the overseer as a pure function, the trend report as a pure function
payload.why_not: Three seams where one covers all. A seam below the command line does not see the process spawns, the pipes, or the git calls.

payload.title: On silence, the overseer cancels the session and a fresh pass starts
payload.why: A stall from a rate limit or a retry storm goes away on a new session. One silent pass is no evidence that the ticket cannot be built.
payload.body:
When a builder session is silent past the limit, the overseer cancels it. The builder loop starts a fresh pass. The brief says that the last pass was cancelled for silence.

A silent grader or reviewer is cancelled and counts as a failed step, with silence as the reason.

The fresh pass counts against the ticket's retry cap, so a stall that repeats on every pass still stops.

payload.title: Cancel the session and stop the ticket
payload.why_not: A stall from a rate limit or a retry storm goes away on a new session. Stopping the ticket loses work that a fresh pass would finish.

payload.title: A run builds one ticket at a time, for now
payload.why: Whether two unblocked tickets may build at the same time depends on their file overlap, and that is not decided. A serial build is correct with any answer.
payload.body:
A run starts a ticket only when every ticket that blocks it is merged. It builds one ticket at a time. The merge queue is one at a time anyway (#st-build-run).

The cost: a run takes as long as the sum of its tickets.

When to revisit: when #werk-loop-fanout decides how file overlap is handled.

payload.title: Build every unblocked ticket at the same time, one worktree each
payload.why_not: Two unblocked tickets can edit the same file and collide at the merge. How to handle that overlap is not decided.

payload.title: Claude Code's own permission engine decides what is safe; werk only asks about the rest

patch.body:
werk does not classify tool calls. Claude Code's permission engine does, in auto mode (#werk-perm-mode). werk only sees the calls that the engine cannot resolve, and puts each one in front of a person in the pane.

How it works:

1. The child runs with `--permission-prompt-tool stdio`. A call that the engine cannot resolve becomes a `can_use_tool` control request on the child's stdout, on the same pipe the turn already uses.
2. The pane shows the question. The child stays blocked until werk answers.
3. werk writes one `control_response` on stdin, with the same request id: allow, or deny with a message.
4. Always allow sends back the permission updates that the CLI itself attached to the question. werk never writes a rule of its own.
5. werk stores those updates in `.werk/allow.json` and gives them to the next child as `--allowedTools` and `--add-dir`. werk stores the rules but never interprets them.
6. Every answered question is appended to `.werk/asks.jsonl` (#werk-approve-log).

What werk keeps: the open questions, the ask log, and the stored Always-allow rules. It keeps no shell parser, no list of read-only commands, and no rule matcher.

Measured before the switch, in auto mode: `ls /tmp | head -3`, `grep -c . /etc/hosts` and `cat /etc/hosts | wc -l` ran without a question. `curl -s https://example.com | head -3`, Write, and `mkdir -p /tmp/werk-probe-dir` asked. Allowing the mkdir with the CLI's own suggestion at session scope stopped the second identical mkdir from asking.
patch.why: Deciding which tool call is safe is the job of Claude Code's auto mode. A second classifier inside werk has to copy that job, and every gap in the copy is a wrong question or a missed one.

payload.title: werk classifies every call itself, with a hand-written shell splitter, a read-only list and a prefix matcher
payload.why: werk owns the decision and can make it as strict as it wants, independent of the CLI's mode.
payload.body:
A PreToolUse hook ran on every tool call and asked werk what to do. werk answered from its own rules:

1. Split the Bash line on the operators that start a new command (`;`, `&&`, `||`, `|`, newline). Refuse any line with a backtick or `$(`, because a substitution can hide any command.
2. Allow the line if every part is on a hand-kept READ_ONLY list, or if every part matches the same prefix rule, such as `Bash(node src/cli.ts:*)`. Matching only the first part would let `node src/cli.ts add x; rm -rf /` through.
3. Otherwise ask in the pane. Always allow built a prefix rule from the call with a heuristic.

Why it lost:

1. It was a partial shell parser, and each gap showed up as a wrong question: a redirect to `/dev/null`, `cd` and `sleep`, a `\\` line continuation, a `for` loop. Each one needed a patch and a test.
2. It asked about read-only commands it did not know.
3. It let any script run without a question, because `Bash(node:*)`, `Bash(python3:*)` and `Bash(bun:*)` were allowed, and a script can do anything.
4. The hook ran on every call, so werk repeated the filtering that the CLI had already done.
payload.why_not: Too much work to copy Claude Code's auto mode reliably. Every gap in the copy needed its own patch, and the copy still asked about safe reads and let any script through.

patch.body:
A PreToolUse hook ran on every tool call and asked werk what to do. werk answered from its own rules:

1. Split the Bash line on the operators that start a new command (`;`, `&&`, `||`, `|`, newline). Refuse any line with a backtick or `$(`, because a substitution can hide any command.
2. Allow the line if every part is on a hand-kept READ_ONLY list, or if every part matches the same prefix rule, such as `Bash(node src/cli.ts:*)`. Matching only the first part would let `node src/cli.ts add x; rm -rf /` through.
3. Otherwise ask in the pane. Always allow built a prefix rule from the call with a heuristic.

Why it lost:

1. It was a partial shell parser, and each gap showed up as a wrong question: a redirect to `/dev/null`, `cd` and `sleep`, a `\` line continuation, a `for` loop. Each one needed a patch and a test.
2. It asked about read-only commands it did not know.
3. It let any script run without a question, because `Bash(node:*)`, `Bash(python3:*)` and `Bash(bun:*)` were allowed, and a script can do anything.
4. The hook ran on every call, so werk repeated the filtering that the CLI had already done.

payload.title: Approval happens in the pane

patch.why: The CLI already writes a can_use_tool control request on the pipe the turn uses, when it is started with --permission-prompt-tool stdio. Answering it on stdin needs no extra process. This is the mechanism that shipped — see #werk-perm-native.

patch.why_not: An MCP server is one more process between the CLI and the pane. --permission-prompt-tool stdio gives the same question on the pipe werk already reads.
It still needs a hook process and a route back to the pane. The control request removes both, and it fires in auto mode.
A restart loses the turn in progress. The control request holds the turn open while the question waits.

patch.body:
A tool call that needs approval is answered in the chat pane, and the turn waits for the answer. A refused or unanswered call must never widen a permission.

The path:

1. Claude Code's own permission engine decides first (#werk-perm-native). A call it can resolve never reaches werk.
2. A call it cannot resolve arrives as a question. The server pushes it to the pane over the existing SSE channel. The child stays blocked.
3. You click Allow once, Always allow, or Deny. Cmd+Enter allows, Escape denies.
4. The answer goes back to the child, and the tool runs or does not.

Always allow applies the widening suggestions the CLI attached to the question, at session scope. werk keeps them in `.werk/allow.json`, so the next child starts with them as `--allowedTools` and `--add-dir`.

Two lists decide without a click: `--allow` from the command line and `.werk/allow.json`. werk gives both to the CLI to interpret.

payload.title: The agent rewrites a file with Edit or Write, not through a shell

patch.body:
SYSTEM in `src/agent.ts` tells the agent: "Do not rewrite a file by piping it through python or sed. Use Edit or Write instead."

Edit and Write are in DEFAULT_TOOLS, so they never ask. They also show the change as a diff, and a shell script does not.
patch.why: A shell rewrite such as python3 -c "...open(path, 'w')..." asks for approval, because it runs a script that writes a file. Edit and Write are already allowed, so the same change needs no click.

patch.body:
What a person must check, about two minutes:

1. Start the server. Ask the pane for a call that stops for approval, for example a network fetch.
2. Click Allow once. The call must run in the same turn.
3. Ask again, click Deny. The reply must say it was denied, with no retry.
4. Ask again, click Always allow, if the bar shows it. Check that `.werk/allow.json` gains the rule and that the next identical call does not ask. The bar shows Always allow only when the CLI attached a suggestion, so a network fetch can have no such button (#werk-perm-mode).
5. Repeat steps 2 and 3 once with Cmd+Enter and once with Escape.
patch.why: The pane's click path has not been run by a person: the buttons, their handlers, and the two keystrokes.

payload.title: Every answered approval question goes to .werk/asks.jsonl

patch.body:
One JSON line per answered question, appended and never rewritten: `at`, `tool`, `label`, `input`, `reason`, `decision` (allow, always, or deny), and `widened` (the rules an Always allow added).

Only calls that reached the pane are recorded. A call the CLI allowed by itself asked nobody, so it says nothing about what to widen.

The writer is `appendAsk()` in `src/permission.ts`.
patch.why: To find which calls keep asking, and which rules are worth adding to the defaults, there must be a record of each question and its answer.

payload.title: werk allows a read-only call itself, from a hand-kept READ_ONLY list
payload.why: A bar that pops up for grep teaches you to click Allow without reading it. Then a real question gets waved through too.
payload.body:
READ_ONLY was a fixed list of calls that cannot change anything: Read, Grep, Glob, the werk read commands (show, stale, events, inbox), and about 20 shell commands (grep, rg, cat, head, tail, wc, ls, file, which, diff, date, pwd, echo, and git status/log/diff/show/branch/blame/remote).

Left out on purpose: any write, delete, install or network call. sed was out, because `sed -i` writes. find was out, because `find -exec` runs anything. sort and uniq were out, because both take an output file.

werk split the Bash line into commands and allowed it only if every command was on the list. `cat README.md | head -20` was free. `grep x; rm -rf /` asked, because rm is not on the list. A line with `$(` or a backtick always asked. A redirect such as `echo pwned > /etc/hosts` split off `/etc/hosts`, which matched nothing, so it asked too.
payload.why_not: Claude Code's auto mode already runs read-only calls without a question, and its classifier needs no list to keep in sync. A hand-kept list asked about every safe read it did not name. See #werk-perm-native.

payload.title: The approval bar shows the call, the CLI's reason, and only the buttons that can act
payload.why: A question in the pane must be read before it is answered. The bar shows what will run and why it stopped, and it does not offer a choice the CLI did not give.
payload.body:
The bar sits above the composer, in the tab that owns the question (#werk-mc-asks).

1. The header names the tool: "**Bash** wants to run. The turn is waiting."
2. The call is shown as a code block, so the whole command can be read before a click.
3. A line under it gives the CLI's reason: "Claude Code could not decide: `<reason>`". The value is shown as-is. werk does not know every value the CLI can send, and prose written for one would read as fact.
4. The buttons are Allow once, Always allow, and Deny. Always allow appears only when the CLI attached a widening suggestion, and the button shows that rule inline, for example "Always allow `Bash(mkdir:*)`". Without a suggestion, the bar has two buttons. A button there would have to invent a rule (#werk-perm-native).
5. One click disables every button in the bar. A second click cannot answer twice, and the wait does not read as broken.
6. Several open questions stack in the bar. Cmd+Enter and Escape answer the first one (#werk-cmdenter).

An AskUserQuestion call uses the same bar with a different body: the question and its options, with Decline and Submit answer (#werk-mc-askqa).

payload.title: Each sample is a one-shot claude --print process
payload.why: A sample has no chat pane, no resumed session, and no permission bar to stop at, so the conversation machinery adds nothing.
payload.body:
The runner starts N headless agents from one brief. Each sample is a one-shot `claude --print` process, not an `Agent` or a `ConvoManager` conversation.

Tools are pre-allowed with `--allowedTools`: read-only tools for a plan sample, write tools only for a sample with its own scratch path. The concurrency cap is N itself.

payload.why: A fork is only useful as a question with real options attached. The samples already are those options.

payload.body:

patch.body:
Six parts, each its own card below: the runner (#al-sample-runner), the no-questions contract (#al-sample-noask), divergence detection (#al-sample-diverge), fork to options (#al-sample-fork-options), the budget clamp (#al-sample-budget), and the artifact builder (#al-sample-artifact).

First real run: about three to four days. A crude version in one afternoon, if the samples are plans and not code. Which one applies is decided per fork, not once — see #al-sample-when. The two options below were weighed as a global choice and rejected as one.

Two tiers, picked per sample by what it does. This is the same per-item call #al-sample-when makes for the substrate, applied to isolation.

1. **Output-only.** The fork is about what gets produced (a rendered SVG, a manifest), and the sample never edits a tracked file. Each sample gets a private scratch output directory (`os.tmpdir()/werk-sample-<runId>-<i>/`), runs against the real checkout read-only, and the build command writes to that path. No git operation at all. Distinct paths cannot collide, so the samples can run in parallel.

Most code-rung samples are output-only: they read the repo and write one derived artifact.

patch.why_not: A worktree adds git overhead to a sample that edits no tracked file. A scratch output directory already makes those samples safe to run in parallel.

The next user message removes every button in that tab, so only the latest offer is clickable.

The Next: format comes from the user's global instructions. A message in another wording gets no button, and nothing else changes. Code: nextPhrase() in web/app.js.

The pane shows the agent's question as a form. Each question lists its options as lettered choices with their descriptions. A free-text field takes an answer that is not listed. Submit answer sends the picks back. Decline refuses the question.

The answer reaches the model as plain text, one line per question: For "<question>": <picked labels>. The model reads it as the reply to its question, not as a failed tool call.

Two constraints shape this:
1. A generic call description keys on file, path, pattern or URL. A question has none of them, so without a form the pane falls back to a truncated JSON dump.
2. The permission channel has no field for an answer. A tool call is never edited on approval, so a command is not changed silently. The answer travels as the reason of a refusal. The log must not show that refusal as a failure, because a picked answer is a normal reply.

payload.title: A written rule is enforced by a check when a record moves to a new state
payload.why: A rule that exists only as prose is not enforced. Over time the records stop following their own rules.
payload.body:
A pipeline has rules about its records. Example: a ticket may only move to Done if it has a linked pull request. If this rule is only prose in a skill file, an agent can forget it. Nobody notices, and the records drift.

The rule becomes a small program, a check. The check runs at the moment a record changes state. In the example, it runs when the ticket moves to Done. It does not run when the ticket is created, because a new ticket has no pull request yet.

**Example.** An agent runs `tracker status T-12 done`.
1. The check looks for a linked pull request on T-12.
2. It finds none, so the move fails.
3. The check prints the next command: `tracker link T-12 <pr-url>`.
4. The agent runs that command, then repeats the move. It passes.

**Escape hatch.** Some tickets have no pull request, for example a research ticket. Such a ticket moves to Done with `--no-pr "research only"`. The reason is written to the record. A check never skips a rule silently.

**Three parts, always:**
- The check runs at the state change, not at creation.
- Every failure prints the exact command that fixes it. The agent corrects itself and needs no human.
- Every rule has an escape hatch that leaves a written reason.

This is #pr-logic applied to the records: a rule is code, not a sentence in a prompt.

payload.title: Keep the rule as prose in the skill file and trust the agent to follow it
payload.why: Why not: an agent forgets a sentence in a prompt, and nobody sees the miss. The records drift and the first sign is a wrong state, found late.

patch.body:
This card applies #pr-gate to the werk map. It states what the MVP check includes.

**Where it runs.** Inside cli.ts, not in a Claude Code hook. A hook works only in this harness, and #product says the harness is temporary.

**When it runs.** Only at the move to decided. Creating a card and setting proto stay free. `add --status decided` is refused, so decided is reachable only through `status <id> decided`.

**What it checks.** Three facts. Each has an escape hatch that is written to the log:
- `who` is set.
- A depends_on edge exists, or `--no-basis` states that none applies.
- An alternative_to option node exists, or `--unchallenged` states that none was weighed.

**What a failure prints.** The exact next command for each missing fact. The agent corrects itself without a human.

**Why it replaces a guess.** Before this, fold.ts guessed `unchallenged` from the data: decided, who:you, no linked option. That guess cannot tell "no option was weighed" from "weighed but never written down". The check asks the question at decide time, so the answer is a record and not an inference.

**Also in the MVP.** `edit` accepts `--who`, `--no-basis`, and `--unchallenged`. A card can then fix a missing fact without being created again.

**Not in the MVP.** Checks on any other state change, and checks on the text of a card.
