- Pipeline tests: #st-build-seam.

Reduced: the risk tier, in #werk-loop-tier.

Out of v0: trend reports (#lp-trend).

payload.title: v0 runs every build at the feature tier
payload.why: One fixed tier needs no tier event, no spoken tier, and no escalation. Every gate waits for a person, which is the safe default (#st-tier-default).
payload.body:
v0 does not build #st-tier's mechanism. Every run is a feature run, so every gate waits for a person.

Not in v0: #st-tier-say, #st-tier-event, #st-tier-escalate and the cards under it.

payload.title: The full tier: spoken, recorded, and escalated
payload.why_not: A tier changes only who waits (#st-tier-record). In v0 a person watches every run anyway, so the mechanism buys nothing yet.

payload.title: Plan without a spec: tickets straight from the subtree
payload.why_not: The spec is where the user stories and the test seams are agreed. Tickets without it have no stories (#st-ticket-stories) and no common whole to split.

payload.title: Builder runs checks only, no grader and no review
payload.why_not: Checks see exit codes only. The grader and the review are what compare the diff with the cited cards.

payload.title: Merge queue without the held-out set
payload.why_not: The held-out set is the only bar the builder cannot see. Without it, the builder can game every check it runs.

payload.title: Overseer reacts to silence only
payload.why_not: Silence misses a loop that keeps producing events, and an ask that waits for nobody. The loop runs with no person in the middle.

payload.title: Trend reports in v0
payload.why_not: The first 10 tickets are the base, so no alert can fire in a v0 run.

payload.title: No pipeline tests: test with real agent runs only
payload.why_not: The overseer's 60-second and 5-minute limits cannot be tested in a usable time without a fake agent and parameterised limits.

patch.body:
What v0 contains. Each item is a concept elsewhere on the map; this card only says it is in v0. A depends_on edge to each item records the inclusion.

- The chat pane beside the map: #werk-chat.
- The CLI as the only write path, with remove and find: #werk-write.
- Extracted excerpts: #werk-excerpt.
- Card rendering: #werk-reflink, #werk-codeblock.
- The wording rule for card text: #werk-wording.
- Reopen reasons in the staleness view: #reopen-reason-gap.
- New cards as proposals: #werk-propose-new.
- The contract check at decided: #werk-contract.
- The dev loop and the Bun runtime: #werk-dev, #werk-hmr.
- The test harness: #werk-test.
- The ticket board: #werk-board.
- Multichat: #werk-mc-scope.
- The inner build loop: #werk-loop.

The log, the fold, and the web view are the three parts. Bun runs the TypeScript directly (#werk-hmr). There is no build step.

#pr-log names the same append-only-log idea for the future standalone engine. werk's own log.jsonl is a separate, working implementation of it, not a consumer of pr-log's.

payload.title: Ticket state is its own append-only log, .werk/board.jsonl, beside the decision log
payload.why: A ticket is a unit of build work, not a decision (#st-ticket). Putting its moves in log.jsonl would mix build churn into the record of what was decided.
payload.body:
One event per line, the same {seq, at, actor, type, payload} shape as log.jsonl. src/board.ts folds it with a pure function, so the server, the CLI, and the build loop all read the board the same way.

Events: ticket.planned, ticket.moved, ticket.reordered, ticket.archived, ticket.restored, ticket.build.started, ticket.pass, ticket.build.ended, ticket.heldout.

A ticket id is <plan run>/<NN>. The ticket's text stays in .werk/tickets/<plan run>/<NN>.md; the board log holds only where the ticket is and what happened to it.

The person's moves are rules in code: manualMove() allows ready to building (only with no open blocker) and building to ready; canArchive() allows only ready and blocked.

payload.title: Ticket events in .werk/log.jsonl, folded with the cards
payload.why_not: Build churn (passes, moves, live flags) would fill the decision record, and every ticket move would refetch and refold the whole map.

patch.body:
v0 does not build the way a tier is chosen. Every run is a feature run: every gate waits for a person.

The tier event is still written at the start of each run, as #st-tier-default requires, so a run always has a first event.

Not in v0: #st-tier-say, #st-tier-escalate and the cards under it.
patch.why: A fixed tier needs no spoken tier and no escalation. Every gate waits for a person, which is the safe default (#st-tier-default).

payload.title: Every decision carries kill criteria: what must become true to revisit it
payload.why: The author sets the revisit trigger when the decision is made. A later challenge only checks that trigger, so a challenge has a low social cost. A machine-checkable trigger lets a background agent watch the decision, like an SLO alert on a decision.
payload.body:
The agent asks one question at every decision: what must become true to change this decision? The ask is mandatory. A metric in the answer is not.

Answers, from best to weakest:
1. A metric to track. Example: median eSIM install time > 4 min over 7 days, PostHog query X. If the metric does not exist yet, building it becomes part of the decision.
2. A manual test by the author: "I test this myself and see if it works."
3. "No metric, because ..." with a reason.
4. "Revisit at any time." This is a valid answer. It is recorded as such.

A criterion points to a rejected alternative (an :optN node). When it fires, the fallback is already on the map.

Parts, each its own card:
- When and how the agent asks: #kill-ask.
- The shape of a criterion, and the no-metric reasons: #kill-shape.
- What checks a criterion, and when: #kill-trigger.
- What happens when a criterion fires: #kill-fire.

The history of fired and unfired criteria is data about decision quality. It feeds #measure.

Related ideas, not yet cards: supersede instead of overturn, scoped exceptions, soft and hard links, assumptions as separate nodes.

payload.title: The agent asks for kill criteria at decided, with drafted suggestions
payload.why: The question must be cheap to answer, or the author skips it. Drafted suggestions make the good answer the easy answer.
payload.body:
The agent drafts 1 to 3 criteria from the hypothesis and the rejected options. The author picks one, edits one, or writes "revisit at any time".

Example questions:
- What would invalidate the hypothesis that made you choose this over the alternatives?
- What makes this helpful? If that is not true in reality, we should consider killing it.

Unclear hypothesis: if the author cannot say why this beat the alternatives, the agent pushes back one time. Then it accepts the answer.

Open: does the answer gate `werk status decided` the way #werk-contract gates who and depends_on? "Revisit at any time" would pass the gate. Only a missing answer fails.

payload.title: A criterion has a source, metric, threshold, and window, or a stated reason for none
payload.why: Without all four parts an agent cannot check the criterion. Without a stated reason, a missing metric hides an unclear hypothesis.
payload.body:
Machine-checkable form: data source, metric, threshold, time window, minimum sample size. The agent drafts the query. The author confirms it.

No-metric reasons and their revisit mechanism:

| Reason | Meaning | Revisit |
|---|---|---|
| Unclear hypothesis | Cannot say why this beat the alternatives | Agent pushes back once |
| Not worth measuring | Cheap and reversible (copy, spacing) | Not tracked |
| Slow or noisy | Real effect outside the feedback window (trust, retention) | Proxy metric and a review date |
| Taste or values | A commitment, not a hypothesis | Link to a written principle |
| Constraint | Regulatory or contractual | Event trigger on the source |
| Manual test | The author checks it by use | Review date, or the next use |

The warning sign is a decision with no stated reason, not a decision with no metric.

payload.title: Three trigger types: metric on a schedule, event, and review date
payload.why: A metric needs a scheduled check. Some criteria fire on a change, not a number. A review date catches every criterion that has neither.
payload.body:
- Metric: a scheduled agent runs the query.
- Event: a new decision touches the same entity, a launch in a new market, a change to a cited source (#werk-dispute flow).
- Time: the review date passes. This is the fallback.

A failed check is loud. A query that errors or returns no rows marks the decision "unmonitored". It never reads as "criterion not met".

Noise control: time windows and minimum sample sizes. One bad day does not fire a criterion.

payload.title: A fired criterion proposes a supersession. It never changes the decision
payload.why: The author keeps the judgement. The agent brings the evidence and the fallback option.
payload.body:
When a criterion fires, the agent proposes a new card that supersedes the decision. The proposal carries the evidence and the rejected alternatives the criterion points to.

- The old decision stays on the map, marked superseded, not rejected.
- A one-way-door decision (irreversible, wide blast radius) is never reverted automatically.
- The fired criterion maps to a reopen reason on #reopen-reason-gap.

payload.title: Three trigger types: metric on a schedule, event, and review date
payload.why: A metric needs a scheduled check. Some criteria fire on a change, not a number. A review date catches every criterion that has neither.
payload.body:
- Metric: a scheduled agent runs the query.
- Event: a new decision touches the same entity, a launch in a new market, or a cited source is disputed (`werk dispute`).
- Time: the review date passes. This is the fallback.

A failed check is loud. A query that errors or returns no rows marks the decision "unmonitored". It never reads as "criterion not met".

Noise control: time windows and minimum sample sizes. One bad day does not fire a criterion.

payload.title: The spec and ticket writers return their own decisions as data; the program proposes the cards
payload.why: An agent that runs werk add itself can write a card nobody can trace to the plan step. Data the program reads can be checked first.
payload.body: Each writer writes every answer that no card gives to a JSON file beside the spec: id, title, why, body. The program reads the file and runs werk add for each entry, under the planned subtree, with who me. A card it cannot add is reported with the reason. The writers' own tools are Read, Grep, Glob and Write.

payload.title: A failed set check does not hold back the tickets that pass their own checks
payload.why: One bad ticket, or one uncited card, should not keep every good ticket off the board.
payload.body: A ticket that passes its own checks (size, sections, no file paths, make-target checks) goes on the board. A failed set check (every card cited, every story delivered, blocked_by agrees with depends_on) is reported, and werk plan exits 1. A ticket check that is not make <target> fails (#lp-checks-scripts).

payload.title: A builder pass: checks stop at the first red, then the grader, then the review
payload.why: The cheap verdict runs first. A grader or reviewer that breaks must not let a pass through.
payload.body:
1. The checks run in order and stop at the first red one.
2. The grader runs only on green checks. It scores the cited decided cards; a card it leaves out scores 0.
3. The five reviewers run only on a passing grade. An unknown severity counts as MEDIUM and does not block.
4. A broken or silent grader or reviewer fails the pass as a failed step, with the reason in the next brief.

A silenced builder pass still commits its edits, skips the checks, and counts against the cap. A ticket whose build ends red stays in building. Each werk build writes one card obligation (#st-build-card); an unsatisfied obligation does not block the build.

payload.title: werk run drives one run: a temporary merge worktree, a guarded branch move, and a stop when a build stays red
payload.why: The merge loop has to be safe to resume and must never overwrite a run tree that moved under it.
payload.body:
- The verb is werk run <plan run>. Starting it is the person's trigger for the whole run. Running it again resumes.
- The merge queue merges the ticket's branch in a detached worktree and runs the ticket's own checks there.
- The run branch werk-run/<run> moves by update-ref with its old value, so a tree that changed in between is never overwritten.
- After a red merge, the next build starts from the ticket's old branch when that branch sits on top of the run tree.
- A ticket's retry cap counts passes across all its builds, so it also bounds the trips between the builder and the merge queue.
- A build that stays red stops the run as stuck.
- Every run writes the feature tier event to the board log first (#werk-loop-tier).
- G2 belongs to the run tree's tip: a later merge opens it again. werk gate <run> approve needs --actor you.

payload.title: One step author per ticket with no tools, and a binder whose report is void if it writes outside its directory
payload.why: The held-out set only works if the builder cannot see it and the binder cannot make a feature look present.
payload.body:
- One step author per ticket. It runs with no tools; the program stores its answer under .werk/heldout/<run>/. A follow-up ticket gets no step author.
- The binder binds every step of the run in a temporary worktree. If it changes a file outside .werk-heldout/, its whole report is void.
- A binder error files no follow-up. The set runs once more at the end of the run; an error that stays ends the run as heldout and waits for a person.
- One held-out run files one follow-up for all newly failed steps. A step that an open follow-up already carries files no second one.
- The red badge stays on the merged ticket after its follow-up goes green.

Known gap: the builder's Read tool can reach .werk/heldout/ by an absolute path. The steps are out of the builder's worktree, not out of its reach.

payload.title: The overseer runs inside the headless runner; no verdict means deny or not looping
payload.why: A timer beside the session it watches needs no second process. A classifier that does not answer must not widen a permission.
payload.body:
- The silence watchdog is a timer inside runHeadless, not a separate process.
- In-flight check: only the CPU time of the agent's child processes is read, with ps. A frozen call with no process of its own cancels the session, the same as silence. Output bytes, open files and connections are not read yet.
- Asks: only builder sessions send asks to the classifier. No verdict means deny.
- Progress: the classifier is skipped when there is no new tool call since its last verdict. No verdict means not looping.
- Every overseer act is a werk_overseer line in the session log and in the live log.

payload.title: Multichat details: the reap sweep, the switcher fallback, and where the live dot sits
payload.why: Small readings the multichat cards leave open, recorded so a later change can see them.
payload.body:
- The reap sweep checks every min(limit, 60 s). Any agent activity restarts a parked tab's clock. The sweep skips a parked tab with an open ask or a background agent. A chat send un-parks on the server.
- A switcher row with no Claude Code title shows the conversation's first prompt, up to 80 characters. Headless sessions write no title records, so this fallback is the normal case. Titles are read again each time the menu opens.
- main has no home card, so the live dot sits on its current card. A pending ask does not count as running for the map dot.
- The background line sits directly under the chat log, above the dead bar.
- A position saved in the browser wins over the server's. A load with no hash moves the map to the active tab's card.
- The last visible chip has no close control.
- /api/ask/open keys the Always-allow lists by conversation.

payload.title: The 90% gate reads an explicit list of pure files, and pure code moves into its own file to join it
payload.why: Bun's coverage threshold is global. A per-file gate needs a list, and a file can only be gated whole.
payload.body:
src/test/coverage-gate.ts reads lcov and fails any file in its PURE list under 90% lines. A pure file no test loads has no lcov record and counts as 0%.

Pure halves of I/O modules move out so the gate can hold them: convo-names.ts, loop-prompt.ts, plan-tickets.ts. Some pure helpers still sit inside I/O files and are not gated: cli.ts slug, humanize and budgetN; commands.ts frontmatterField; convos.ts ago; agent.ts label and describe.

patch.body:
Nine behaviours for the ConvoManager class (src/convo-manager.ts:32-114). The two free functions above it, dirFor and nameForCard, are pure — see #werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope.

Produced by #werk-test-subagent's first real run: three samples via `node src/cli.ts sample`, three forks from clustering, resolved by reading source.

1. main() creates the main agent on first reference unconditionally — no disk check, never throws.
2. ensure(name) for any other name only succeeds if a directory record already exists on disk; otherwise it throws 'no conversation named "<name>"'.
3. A live agent already held in memory is always reused — ensure()/main() never spawn a second Agent for a name that already has one.
4. Every agent this manager ever creates, including main, is announced to every onSpawn listener at creation time, and a listener that unsubscribes stops receiving calls.
5. fork() requires the parent conversation to already have sent a message — it throws if the parent has no sessionId yet, so an empty conversation cannot be forked.
6. A forked conversation's name is checked for uniqueness only against currently-live agent names, not against conversations that exist on disk but have no live Agent — a collision with an un-ensure'd disk-only conversation is not guarded against.
7. Every agent this manager creates shares one Asks queue, so a permission prompt from any conversation surfaces in the same place.
8. Parking a conversation keeps its child process. A sweep kills a parked child left untouched past #werk-mc-reap's limit, and leaves its directory and session file intact, so the next message to that name resumes the same conversation.
9. stopAll() stops every live agent's child process — none is left running after it returns.

One design-question fork could not resolve from source and goes to Eryk: #werk-test-behaviours-convo-manager-onspawn-granularity.

payload.title: When the process probe itself fails, is the call frozen or unknown?
payload.why: psProbe returns an empty sample when ps cannot run. runHeadless reads an empty sample as a frozen call with no process of its own, and cancels the session.
payload.body:
Today a failed ps call cancels a session that may be working. The other reading lets the 60-second silence rule and the wall-clock cap decide, because the probe has no evidence either way.

Recommendation: unknown (:opt1). A broken probe should not stop work the overseer cannot see; silence still catches a real stall.

payload.title: Frozen: cancel the session, as the code does today
payload.why_not: A transient ps failure kills a pass that may be working, and charges the ticket a pass for it.

payload.title: Unknown: ignore the sample and let silence or the cap decide
payload.why_not: A call that is really frozen and still writes heartbeat events is caught only by the wall-clock cap, later.

payload.title: When the run branch moved during the merge checks, is that a red merge or a retry?
payload.why: The merge moves werk-run/<run> by compare-and-swap. When the swap fails, run.ts treats it as a red merge: the ticket goes back to building, uses a pass, and its builder is told a check failed.
payload.body:
In a serial run only something outside the run can move the branch. The ticket's code passed its checks; the failure says nothing about it.

Recommendation: retry (:opt1). Merge again on the moved branch, run the checks there, and charge no pass.

payload.title: A red merge: back to building, one pass charged, as the code does today
payload.why_not: The builder is told a check failed when none did, and spends a pass on code that was green.

payload.title: A retry: merge again on the moved branch, and charge no pass
payload.why_not: An outside process that keeps moving the branch makes the merge retry without end, unless a retry limit is added.

payload.title: prototype.ts runHeadless behaviour list
payload.why: The gate #werk-test-scope sets for an I/O module: a named list of behaviours, not a percentage. Read from source; the module's pure helpers fall under the 90% line instead (#werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope).
payload.body:
1. Every stream line reaches the session log and onEvent as it arrives; the final result sets the answer, the cost and the turns.
2. No event for the silence limit cancels the session as silent; a steady stream never does.
3. The abort signal ends the session as stopped; the wall-clock cap ends it as an error.
4. A non-zero exit is an error.
5. A running call whose process tree uses CPU is not silence; a call whose CPU stays flat has only its own processes killed, and the session goes on.
6. A frozen call with no process of its own cancels the session.
7. With asks on, the prompt goes in on stdin, every ask gets an allow or a deny, and the answer is logged.
8. A failed log write never changes the result.

payload.title: build.ts behaviour list
payload.why: The gate #werk-test-scope sets for an I/O module: a named list of behaviours, not a percentage. Read from source; the module's pure helpers fall under the 90% line instead (#werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope).
payload.body:
1. A ticket that cannot build — blocked, archived, in the wrong column, or with no ticket file — is refused before any event or agent call.
2. The card obligation is in the log before any code is written.
3. Each pass is a fresh agent that gets the last failure; a cancelled pass still has its work committed.
4. The checks stop at the first red one; the grader and the review run only after green checks, and the first failing gate ends the pass.
5. The cap stops the loop and the ticket stays in building; when the last pass went silent too, the build ends as silence.
6. The abort signal ends the build as stopped.
7. The worktree is always removed, on success, stop and error alike; the branch is kept.
8. A sent-back ticket resumes from its earlier work only when that work sits on the run tree; otherwise it starts fresh from the run tree.
9. Green moves the ticket to merging and never merges it.

payload.title: run.ts behaviour list
payload.why: The gate #werk-test-scope sets for an I/O module: a named list of behaviours, not a percentage. Read from source; the module's pure helpers fall under the 90% line instead (#werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope).
payload.body:
1. One ticket builds at a time; a ticket whose blockers are all merged moves to ready, with a reason.
2. A red merge merges nothing and sends the ticket back to building with the failure.
3. A build that stays red stops the run as stuck.
4. A run with no tickets is an error before any agent call.
5. A restarted run continues from the board and does not open G2 twice.
6. A red held-out step files one follow-up and the merge stands; a step an open follow-up already carries files no second one.
7. G2 waits for a person; a passed tip ends the run as done; a later merge opens G2 again for the new tip.
8. A held-out set still red at the end runs once more, then ends the run as heldout with no gate.
9. The step author runs beside the builder, and only for a ticket that is not a follow-up.

payload.title: merge.ts behaviour list
payload.why: The gate #werk-test-scope sets for an I/O module: a named list of behaviours, not a percentage. Read from source; the module's pure helpers fall under the 90% line instead (#werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope).
payload.body:
1. The merge and its checks happen in a temporary tree; the person's checkout never changes.
2. A red check or a merge conflict leaves the run branch where it was.
3. The run branch moves by compare-and-swap, so a tree that moved during the checks is never overwritten.
4. The temporary tree is always removed.

payload.title: heldout.ts behaviour list
payload.why: The gate #werk-test-scope sets for an I/O module: a named list of behaviours, not a percentage. Read from source; the module's pure helpers fall under the 90% line instead (#werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope).
payload.body:
1. The step author has no tools, and its steps are stored outside every tree.
2. An author answer with no scenario writes no file and reports an error.
3. The binder's tests never reach the run tree; a copy is kept for a person.
4. A binder that changes a file outside its test directory voids its whole report.
5. A failed binder session or an unreadable answer marks every step a binder error, never a pass.
6. A follow-up ticket holds only the failed steps, word for word, and goes to ready.

payload.title: overseer.ts behaviour list
payload.why: The gate #werk-test-scope sets for an I/O module: a named list of behaviours, not a percentage. Read from source; the module's pure helpers fall under the 90% line instead (#werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope).
payload.body:
1. An ask with no readable verdict is denied, with a comment.
2. A progress check with no verdict counts as not looping.
3. The classifiers run with no tools and under a timeout.
4. The process probe sums the CPU time of every descendant process.

payload.title: plan.ts behaviour list
payload.why: The gate #werk-test-scope sets for an I/O module: a named list of behaviours, not a percentage. Read from source; the module's pure helpers fall under the 90% line instead (#werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope).
payload.body:
1. An open or proto card in the subtree stops the run before any agent call.
2. The spec comes first, then the tickets; a spec with no user story stops the run, and an agent error at either step stops it too.
3. Each decision the writers return becomes a proposed card through the CLI; an unreadable decisions file is reported, not ignored.
4. Only tickets that pass their own checks go on the board.

payload.title: grade.ts behaviour list
payload.why: The gate #werk-test-scope sets for an I/O module: a named list of behaviours, not a percentage. Read from source; the module's pure helpers fall under the 90% line instead (#werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope).
payload.body:
1. A low score, a cited card left out, or an answer with no JSON fails the pass, and the gaps go to the next brief.
2. A silent or broken grader is a failed step.
3. A ticket that cites no card passes the gate without an agent call.
4. The diff is cut at the size limit, with a pointer to the full diff.

payload.title: review.ts behaviour list
payload.why: The gate #werk-test-scope sets for an I/O module: a named list of behaviours, not a percentage. Read from source; the module's pure helpers fall under the 90% line instead (#werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope).
payload.body:
1. Five reviewers, one per area, run after the grader passes.
2. A CRITICAL or HIGH finding fails the pass; MEDIUM and LOW are only recorded.
3. A broken reviewer fails the pass as a step only when no finding already blocks it, and its error is recorded.

payload.title: Board details: where archive and stop live, the retry badge, and the run strip
payload.why: Small readings the board cards leave open, recorded so a later change can see them.
payload.body:
- Archive is a button in the drawer header, not on the board card. Stop has no button: it is only the drag from building to ready (#werk-board-control).
- The retry badge shows when a ticket has more than one pass.
- The live preview shows one summarised line per stream event, overseer lines included, not raw JSON.
- When a build child exits while its ticket is still live, the server ends the build: error for an exit code, stopped for a signal.
- A line above the columns shows G2 per run, waiting or passed, with the werk gate command. The board has no approve button, because the board does no editing.
- werk ticket import makes ids the way werk plan does, <run>/<NN>, and adds nothing on a second run.

payload.title: Board details: where archive and stop live, the run strip, and the live preview
payload.why: Small readings the board cards leave open, recorded so a later change can see them.
payload.body:
- Archive is a button in the drawer header, not on the board card. Stop has no button: it is only the drag from building to ready (#werk-board-control).
- The live preview shows one summarised line per stream event, overseer lines included, not raw JSON.
- When a build child exits while its ticket is still live, the server ends the build: error for an exit code, stopped for a signal.
- A line above the columns shows G2 per run, waiting or passed, with the werk gate command. The board has no approve button, because the board does no editing.

payload.title: board-routes.ts behaviour list
payload.why: The gate #werk-test-scope sets for an I/O module: a named list of behaviours, not a percentage. Read from source; the module's pure helpers fall under the 90% line instead (#werk-test-scope-src0-pure-scope).
payload.body:
1. GET /api/board returns each column, each ticket's text, and each run's gate state.
2. A reorder must name exactly the ready column, or it is refused with 409.
3. Archive accepts only a ready or blocked ticket; an unknown id is 404.
4. A trigger starts exactly one build, and refuses a ticket with an open blocker or one already building.
5. A stop kills the build's whole process group, also after a server restart, and returns the ticket to ready.
6. A build that dies or fails to spawn without ending its session gets an error end, so the ticket stops showing as live; a build refused before it starts moves back to ready with the reason.
7. The log tail pushes only new whole lines: it holds back a half-written line, starts again from zero after truncation, and never loses or doubles a line at the backfill seam.
8. A malformed POST body gets a 4xx JSON error, never a hung request; an unknown route is 404.
9. A change to board.jsonl or the tickets folder pushes one debounced board event.

payload.body:
Kill criteria are recorded while the card is open, before the decision.

The gate: `werk status <id> decided` fails when the card has no recorded kill answer. This extends #werk-contract. Like its other checks, it reads the log, not the prose.

The failure message is the prompt. It names the command that fixes it, and it carries 1 to 3 drafted criteria built from the card's hypothesis and its rejected options. Example questions:
- What would invalidate the hypothesis that made you choose this over the alternatives?
- What makes this helpful? If that is not true in reality, we should consider killing it.

An answer is any one of the forms in #kill-shape: a metric, a manual test, "no metric, because ...", or "revisit at any time". Only a missing answer fails. Your own test is better than "revisit at any time". A metric is better than both. If the metric does not exist yet, building it joins the decision.

Unclear hypothesis: if the author cannot say why this beat the alternatives, the agent pushes back one time. Then it accepts the answer.

criterion.text: I use the pipeline to build werk itself and one other app (for example the iOS music player). If I find the result disappointing for any reason, I revisit this decision.

patch.body:
A card records a decision. It does not define a unit of build work. A ticket from #st-ticket is the unit of build work. A ticket cites the decided cards it builds.

Two facts show that a card cannot be a unit of work:

1. **Decisions have unequal size.** Under #werk, decided-leaf bodies run from 0 to 2973 characters, with a median of 778. Six of them are empty. Depth runs from 1 to 7. A leaf at depth 1 can be a whole feature. A leaf at depth 7 can be one line of a function. No rule that picks cards from the tree (#werk-loop-unit:opt0, :opt1, :opt2) makes the passes even. The unequal size is normal for decisions. It is wrong for tasks.
2. **A buildable unit is a vertical slice.** A tracer bullet is a narrow, complete path through schema, API, UI and tests. It can be verified on its own and fits one fresh context. Such a slice crosses cards in different subtrees. The refines tree is a decision hierarchy. A cut along that tree gives horizontal layers, and the slice rule forbids that shape.

Cards that key build state on a card id (#werk-loop-land, #werk-loop-state, #werk-loop-gap) must key it on a ticket instead.

Rejected: all three options treat a card as the unit. They differ only in which cards count. See #werk-loop-unit:opt0, :opt1, :opt2.

payload.body:
A ticket that fails its own checks (size, sections, no file paths, make-target checks) does not go on the board. It gets no ticket.planned event.

Every other ticket goes on the board. A failed set check (every card cited, every story delivered, blocked_by agrees with depends_on and has no cycle) is reported, and werk plan exits 1.

payload.title: Six checks on one ticket, each read from the ticket file alone
payload.why: A check that needs only the file can run as soon as the planner writes it, and its failure names exactly one ticket.
payload.body:
Each check reads one ticket file and nothing else.

| Check | Passes when |
| --- | --- |
| title | The file has a `title:` line. A file with no title is not parsed, so no other check runs on it. |
| size | The file is 4000 characters or fewer. |
| what to build | The `## What to build` section is not empty. |
| acceptance | The `## Acceptance criteria` section has at least one bullet. |
| no file paths | The file has no `files:` line. |
| make targets | Every bullet under `## Checks` is `make <target>` (#lp-checks-scripts). |

An empty `## Checks` section passes. The ticket then uses the rubric's default checks.

`stories:` and `cites:` can be empty and still pass. A prefactor delivers no story (#st-ticket-stories). Whether the cards and stories are covered is a question about the whole set (#st-ticket-set-checks).

payload.title: Three checks on the whole ticket set: cards cited, stories delivered, blocked_by
payload.why: Coverage and order are properties of the set. No single ticket can pass or fail them alone.
payload.body:
The set checks read every parsed ticket of one plan run, the decided cards of the planned subtree, the depends_on edges between those cards, and the spec's story numbers.

**1. Cards cited.** Every decided card in the planned subtree is in the `cites:` of at least one ticket. A failure lists the cards no ticket cites.

**2. Stories delivered.** Every story number in the spec is in the `stories:` of at least one ticket (#st-ticket-stories). No ticket lists a number that is not in the spec. A failure lists the missing or unknown numbers.

**3. blocked_by.** Three conditions:
- Every number in `blocked_by` is a ticket in the set.
- The `blocked_by` graph has no cycle.
- It agrees with depends_on. For each depends_on edge A → B between two subtree cards, every ticket that cites A either also cites B, or is blocked_by every ticket that cites B. An edge to a card that no ticket cites is left to check 1.

A failure of check 3 names tickets: the ticket that misses a blocker, the ticket it must wait for, or the tickets in a cycle. Checks 1 and 2 name cards and stories, not tickets.

A ticket that fails its own checks (#st-ticket-own-checks) is not in the set these checks read.

patch.body:
A ticket is the unit of build work. It is a tracer bullet: a narrow but complete path through every layer the change touches. It can be shown working on its own, and it fits one fresh context.

A ticket is not a card. A card groups by decision, so a slice usually crosses several cards, and most cards are a constraint on a thing, not the thing.

Fields:

- title
- what to build: the end-to-end behaviour the ticket makes work, from the user's side
- acceptance criteria
- stories: the numbers of the spec's user stories it delivers (#st-ticket-stories)
- cites: the decided cards it builds
- blocked_by: other tickets
- checks: the commands that decide it

A ticket names no file paths. They go out of date before the build reaches the ticket.

blocked_by comes from the depends_on edges between the cited cards. It is derived, not guessed.

Two groups of checks decide whether a ticket set is valid (#lp-checks):

1. Checks on one ticket (#st-ticket-own-checks).
2. Checks on the whole set (#st-ticket-set-checks).

#st-ticket-partial says what a failure of each group does to the board.

An agent writes the tickets from the spec (#st-spec). A person decides which ticket gets built, and when (#vi-board).

A ticket that fails its own checks (#st-ticket-own-checks) does not go on the board. It gets no ticket.planned event.

Every other ticket goes on the board. A failed set check (#st-ticket-set-checks) is reported, and werk plan exits 1.

A failed set check that names a ticket puts that ticket in blocked, with the failed check as its blocking reason. A blocked ticket cannot move to building (#werk-board-control). Only the blocked_by check names tickets. The cards-cited and stories checks name no ticket, so they block none. An agent clears the reason when it fixes the tickets and the set check passes again.

**2. Stories delivered.** Every story number in the spec is in the `stories:` of at least one ticket (#st-ticket-stories). No ticket lists a number that is not in the spec. A failure lists the missing or unknown numbers.

**3. blocked_by.** Three conditions:
- Every number in `blocked_by` is a ticket in the set. A blocker that failed its own checks is not in the set, so it fails this condition.
- The `blocked_by` graph has no cycle.
- It agrees with depends_on. For each depends_on edge A → B between two subtree cards, every ticket that cites A either also cites B, or is blocked_by every ticket that cites B. An edge to a card that no ticket cites is left to check 1.

A failure of check 3 names tickets: the ticket that misses a blocker, the ticket it must wait for, or the tickets in a cycle. Checks 1 and 2 name cards and stories, not tickets.

A criterion card adds to its metric only what is special to that criterion.

patch.body:
One fresh agent per pass. Give it the brief, the decision, the rubric, and the last failure. It does one unit of work and exits. The repository is the memory.

This changes the engine's shape: no agent lives longer than one pass.

**How a pass works** (`werk loop`, `src/loop.ts`):

1. The loop makes one worktree from a snapshot of the working tree.
2. Pass n starts a fresh `claude -p` in the worktree. The prompt holds the brief, the decided cards in its depends_on closure, and the last failure: the failed command and the end of its output, cut to about 4,000 characters.
3. When the agent exits, the loop commits the worktree as "pass n". The next agent reads the history with `git log` and `git diff`, and gets nothing else.
4. The loop runs the checks. The loop's own run is the verdict, even if the agent ran the checks itself.
5. All green: stop. Red: save the failure and go to step 2. At the cap: stop and keep the branch.
6. The loop writes one line per pass to `.werk/runs/<id>.jsonl`: check results, time, and cost.

**Evidence.** The research sources (#ralph, #tdp) support fresh passes. Two smoke runs went green in one and two passes. The planned comparison against one long session on real tickets did not run.

**One mode only.** The loop has no long-session mode. The long session (#lp-stateless:long) is the fallback of the kill criterion. It is built again only when that criterion fires.

payload.title: Build state lives on tickets, not on cards

patch.body:
`decided` answers 'is the argument settled'. It does not answer 'does the code exist'. The build state answers the second question, and it lives on tickets.

A ticket (#st-ticket) is the unit of build work, and a card is not (#werk-loop-unit). The board (#vi-board) shows each ticket in its column: blocked, ready, building, merging, done (#werk-board-columns). The loop picks its next unit from the board, not from the map.

A card has no 'built' flag, and the map shows no build progress. To see what is built, a person reads the board.
patch.why: A card goes decided when the argument settles, long before code exists. A ticket is the unit of build work, so the ticket carries the build state.

payload.title: Tickets hold the state, and the map derives a built mark per card
payload.why_not: A card is built when every ticket that cites it is merged. That needs new fold logic, and the board already shows the progress.

criterion.text: A person asks the map which decided cards have no code yet, and the board cannot answer it.

patch.body:
One agent per ticket, one throwaway worktree each, as many at once as the tickets are independent.

**Independence comes from the tickets alone.** The run scheduler reads each ticket's blocked_by edges (#st-ticket). A ticket whose blockers are all merged can start. The scheduler reads no other input. No agent judges overlap, and the ticket format has no field for the files a ticket touches.

**File overlap does not block.** Two unblocked tickets may edit the same file. Both build green alone. At the merge queue (#st-build-run), the second one fails `git merge`. That is a red merge: the ticket goes back to the builder loop with the conflict output as its last failure, the same as a red check (#st-build-run-mechanics).

**Mostly already built.** src/prototype.ts runs N headless `claude -p` agents concurrently, each in its own worktree, and removes the worktree in a `finally` per #al-ephem. Swap 'option of a fork' for 'ticket' and keep the branch, and this step exists.

Open:

1. Does a run build in parallel now, or does #st-build-serial stay until later?
2. What is the cap? 'As many as possible' against a real machine and a real rate limit is a number.
patch.why: Ticket blocking edges give the order. Two tickets with no blocking path between them may build at the same time. A file they both edit is a merge conflict, and the merge queue handles it.

payload.title: A run builds up to 3 unblocked tickets at once, each off the run branch tip
payload.why: Ticket blocking edges give the order. Two tickets with no blocking path between them may build at the same time. A file they both edit is a merge conflict, and the merge queue handles it.
payload.body:
A ticket can start when every ticket in its blocked_by list is merged. The run builds up to 3 such tickets at the same time, each in its own worktree.

**Independence comes from the tickets alone.** The run scheduler reads each ticket's blocked_by edges (#st-ticket). It reads no other input. No agent judges overlap, and the ticket format has no field for the files a ticket touches.

**File overlap does not block.** Two unblocked tickets may edit the same file. Both build green alone. At the merge queue (#st-build-run), the second one fails `git merge`. That is a red merge: the ticket goes back to the builder loop with the conflict output as its last failure, the same as a red check.

**The base.** Each worktree branches off the run branch tip at the moment its build starts. A ticket that starts after an earlier merge has that merge in its tree.

**The cap.** 3 is a first guess. It changes when a real machine or a real rate limit shows a better number. The merge queue still takes one ticket at a time.

payload.title: One ticket at a time
payload.why_not: A run takes as long as the sum of its tickets. Merge conflicts are already handled as a red merge, so serial builds buy nothing.

payload.title: Block two tickets that touch the same file
payload.why_not: It needs an estimate of the files each ticket touches, and the ticket format does not carry one. A conflict costs one more builder pass.

payload.title: Every worktree branches off HEAD
payload.why_not: A ticket that starts after a merge would not see it, and would conflict with it more often.

criterion.text: Merge conflicts send more than 1 ticket in 4 back to the builder over a run.
Builds hit the rate limit, or the machine cannot keep up with 3 builds. Then change the cap.

patch.body:
werk builds #st-build-parallel from parts it already has.

src/prototype.ts runs N headless `claude -p` agents at the same time, each in its own worktree, and removes the worktree in a `finally` per #al-ephem. The run scheduler in src/run.ts uses the same pattern for tickets: up to 3 builds at the same time, each worktree off the run branch tip, and the branch kept for the merge queue.
patch.why: The rule is in #st-build-parallel. This card is how werk builds it.

criterion.text: Revisit when #st-build-parallel changes.

payload.title: werk run drives one run: a temporary merge worktree, a guarded branch move, and a stop when a build stays red
payload.why: The merge loop has to be safe to resume and must never overwrite a run tree that moved under it.
payload.body:
- The verb is werk run <plan run>. Starting it is the person's trigger for the whole run. Running it again resumes.
- The merge queue merges the ticket's branch in a detached worktree and runs the ticket's own checks there.
- The run branch werk-run/<run> moves by update-ref with its old value, so a tree that changed in between is never overwritten.
- After a red merge, the next build starts from the ticket's old branch when that branch sits on top of the run tree.
- A ticket's retry cap counts passes across all its builds, so it also bounds the trips between the builder and the merge queue.
- A build that stays red stops the run as stuck.
- Every run writes the feature tier event to the board log first (#werk-loop-tier).
- G2 belongs to the run tree's tip: a later merge opens it again. werk gate <run> approve needs --actor you.

criterion.text: Revisit when #st-build-parallel or #st-build-run changes.

payload.title: One werk instance runs in a repo, so a moved run branch needs no handling
payload.why: Inside one werk run, nothing else moves werk-run/<run>: the merge queue takes one ticket at a time, and each builder writes only its own branch.
payload.body:
werk assumes one werk instance in a repo. Nothing enforces it: werk run takes no lock.

The merge moves werk-run/<run> by compare-and-swap (#st-build-run-mechanics). Under the assumption, the swap fails only when a person or a second werk instance moves the branch during the merge checks. The code treats that the same as a red merge: the ticket goes back to building and uses a pass. No code handles the case on its own.

payload.title: A retry: merge again on the moved branch, and charge no pass
payload.why_not: It handles a case that the one-instance assumption excludes.

payload.title: A lock: werk run refuses to start while another werk run holds the repo
payload.why_not: It prevents a case that the one-instance assumption excludes.

criterion.text: A run reports a failed update-ref on werk-run/<run>, or a person wants two werk instances in one repo.

payload.title: An alert blocks the merge until a person looks
payload.why_not: 10 tickets and 20% are a first guess. A noisy metric would stop the build for nothing, and with auto-merge the run must keep going.

ops.old: The state machine, the tracker adapter, the rubric runner, and the loop controller go into a small TypeScript CLI. Skills become three-line wrappers that call it.
ops.new: The state machine of the records, the checks on each state change, the tracker adapter, the rubric runner, and the loop controller go into a small TypeScript CLI. A skill file becomes a thin wrapper. It names the command to run and holds no rule of its own.

## The boundary

A step goes in the program if the same input must always give the same result. Examples: a state change, a staleness walk, a contract check, a retry cap, a time limit, a merge.

A step goes in a prompt if it needs judgement. Examples: writing a spec, grading against a rubric, reviewing a diff, classifying a stuck agent.

The program calls the prompt and parses the answer. The prompt returns an answer. The program decides what happens next.

## A prompt holds no control flow

A prompt is text that the program builds and sends. The sentence "if the checks fail, retry three times" is a loop. A loop is code, so it goes in the program, not in the prompt.

## Why

An agent follows a rule in prose most of the time. A product needs the rule followed every time (#pr-gate). A prompt file also runs only inside one agent harness, so a pipeline made of skills cannot become a standalone product (#product).

## Scope

This card says where the logic lives. It does not say when the standalone engine is built. That timing is #pr-now. The engine's adapters are #pr-iface.

payload.title: The pipeline is a set of skill files. The agent reads each step and runs it.
payload.why_not: An agent follows a prose rule most of the time, not every time. A skill file also runs only inside one agent harness.

criterion.text: Follows from #product: a skill file runs only inside one agent harness. Revisit only if #product is dropped.

ops.old: The state machine of the records, the checks on each state change, the tracker adapter, the rubric runner, and the loop controller go into a small TypeScript CLI. A skill file becomes a thin wrapper. It names the command to run and holds no rule of its own.
ops.new:
A pipeline has steps and rules. "Run the checks." "If they fail, try again up to five times." "A ticket moves to Done only with a linked pull request." Each rule lives in one of two places: in a skill file that an agent reads, or in a program that runs it.

This card puts the rules in a program, a small TypeScript CLI. The state machine of the records, the checks on each state change, the tracker adapter, the rubric runner, and the loop controller live there. A skill file is a thin wrapper. It names the command to run and holds no rule of its own.

## The two places

| | Skill files (#pr-logic:opt0) | A program (this card) |
|---|---|---|
| Where a rule lives | Markdown text the agent reads | Code in the CLI |
| Who runs a loop | The agent reads "retry five times" and does it | The program counts to five |
| What the agent does | Every step | Only the steps that need judgement |
| An agent forgets a rule | Nothing stops it | The program refuses the action |
| Cost of a change | Edit a sentence | Edit code and its tests |
| Runs outside one agent harness | No | Yes |

ops.new: A step goes in a prompt if it needs judgement. Examples: writing a spec, grading against a rubric, reviewing a diff, classifying a stuck agent.

ops.old: The program calls the prompt and parses the answer. The prompt returns an answer. The program decides what happens next.

ops.old: ## A prompt holds no control flow
ops.new: ## A prompt holds no control flow

ops.old: A prompt is text that the program builds and sends. The sentence "if the checks fail, retry three times" is a loop. A loop is code, so it goes in the program, not in the prompt.
ops.new: A prompt is text that the program builds and sends. The sentence "if the checks fail, retry three times" is a loop. A loop is code, so it goes in the program, not in the prompt.

ops.old: ## Why
ops.new: ## Why

ops.old: An agent follows a rule in prose most of the time. A product needs the rule followed every time (#pr-gate). A prompt file also runs only inside one agent harness, so a pipeline made of skills cannot become a standalone product (#product).
ops.new: An agent follows a rule in prose most of the time. A product needs the rule followed every time (#pr-gate). A prompt file also runs only inside one agent harness, so a pipeline made of skills cannot become a standalone product (#product).

## Examples

Example project, werk: `werk status <id> decided` refuses a card that has no `depends_on` edge or no kill criterion, and prints the command that fixes it. As prose in `AGENTS.md`, the same rule was skipped twice: #ro-unchal and #vi-backend.

Example project, werk: `werk build` runs the checks, caps the passes, and enforces the silence limit in code. The builder agent writes code, the grader grades, and the reviewers review. None of them decides whether another pass runs.

payload.title: The plan scope is the subtree plus every card it links, one hop out
payload.why: A scope card often lists the cards it includes instead of holding them. With the subtree alone, the planner sees those cards as an id and a title, and fills the gaps itself.
payload.body:
The plan stage reads two sets of cards in full: the subtree, and every card a subtree card links. Both sets are the scope.

A link is one of two things:
1. A depends_on edge from a subtree card.
2. A #card-id reference in a subtree card's title, why, or body.

Only one hop. A linked card's own links are not followed. They stay in the map index, by id and title.

The scope rules apply to linked cards the same as to subtree cards:
- An open or proto linked card stops the run before any agent call.
- Every linked card must be cited by at least one ticket.

The prompt keeps the two sets apart: the subtree first, then the linked cards under their own heading.

payload.title: The subtree only. Other cards by id and title
payload.why_not: A scope card that lists its cards by id gives the planner only titles. The planner then invents the content.

payload.title: The whole depends_on closure
payload.why_not: From a top-level scope card it reaches hundreds of cards, including open and paused ones far from the work. The open ones block the run.

payload.title: Linked cards in full, as context only: not gated, not cited
payload.why_not: A linked card is often the work itself. As context only, no check makes sure that a ticket covers it.

criterion.text: A plan run must cite a linked card that the planned work does not change, only to pass the coverage check. Or a planner prompt grows past one context window because of linked cards.

payload.title: A fork keeps the parent's model and links back to the fork point
payload.why: A fork is a continuation. A different model and a chat with no origin both make it look like a new conversation.
payload.body:
## Model

A fork starts on its parent's model and advisor, not on the default. `ConvoManager.fork()` copies `modelSetting()` to the new agent before its first start.

## Notice

The fork's chat opens with one system line: "Continued from <parent>." It carries `forkOf: {convo, at, session}`.

- `at` is the time of the parent's last `you` or `agent` message at the moment of the fork.
- The pane renders a "Go to the last message before the fork" button. A click switches to the parent tab, scrolls to that message, and outlines it for a short time.
- Each message node carries `data-at`, so the button finds its target.
- If the message is older than the 200-line history window, the button only switches tabs.

## Restart

`session` and the notice's `card` let a fork that never sent a message survive a server restart. `describeConvo` reads them back as `home` and `forkFrom`, so the first send still forks the parent.

The model is not on disk for any conversation. After a server restart, a rebuilt fork falls back to the default model, the same as every other tab.

criterion.text: I fork a tab on a non-default model, check the model selector, and click the notice's link

payload.title: Four facts gate decided, each with a written escape hatch

ops.old:
Three facts must hold before a card is decided:
- `who` is set.
- A depends_on edge exists, or `--no-basis` states that none applies.
- An alternative_to option node exists, or `--unchallenged` states that none was weighed.
ops.new:
Four facts must hold before a card is decided:
- `who` is set.
- A depends_on edge exists, or `--no-basis` states that none applies.
- An alternative_to option node exists, or `--unchallenged` states that none was weighed.
- A kill criterion is on record (#kill-ask). `werk kill` records one. A criterion of the form no-metric or revisit states that no metric applies (#kill-shape).

ops.old: `edit` accepts `--who`, `--no-basis`, and `--unchallenged`. A card fixes a missing fact without being created again.
ops.new: `edit` accepts `--who`, `--no-basis`, and `--unchallenged`, and `werk kill` adds a criterion. A card fixes a missing fact without being created again.

ops.old: One ticket, one worktree.
ops.new: One ticket, one worktree.

ops.old:
1. Implement. A fresh builder agent does one unit of work toward the ticket (#st-build-implement).
2. Check. The checks run: one command each, exit code only (#lp-checks).
3. Grade. A grader agent reads the diff against each decided card (#lp-prod-judge).
4. Review. Five reviewer agents, one per quality area, read the diff (#lp-prod-review).

1. Implement. A fresh builder agent does one unit of work toward the ticket (#st-build-implement).
2. Check. The checks run: one command each, exit code only (#lp-checks).
3. Grade. A grader agent reads the diff against each decided card (#lp-prod-judge).
4. Review. Five reviewer agents, one per quality area, read the diff (#lp-prod-review).

ops.old: A fail at step 2, 3, or 4 starts a new pass at step 1. There is no separate fix step. A retry cap stops the loop (#werk-loop-done).
ops.new: A fail at step 2, 3, or 4 starts a new pass at step 1. There is no separate fix step. A retry cap stops the loop (`werk build --cap`, default 5; #st-build-run-mechanics).

ops.old: #st-build-ticket-order gives the order inside one pass.
ops.new: #st-build-ticket-order gives the order inside one pass.

ops.old: #st-build-run ends build when every ticket is merged and every held-out step passes (#st-g2-heldout). Red checks in the merge queue send the ticket back to the builder, and the ticket's retry cap (#werk-loop-done) bounds that. A red held-out step after a merge files a follow-up ticket, and the merge stands. A follow-up is a new ticket, with a new cap.
ops.new: #st-build-run ends build when every ticket is merged and every held-out step passes (#st-g2-heldout). Red checks in the merge queue send the ticket back to the builder, and the ticket's retry cap (#st-build-run-mechanics) bounds that. A red held-out step after a merge files a follow-up ticket, and the merge stands. A follow-up is a new ticket, with a new cap.

ops.old: **No limit on follow-ups in v0.** Nothing counts follow-up tickets across a run.
ops.new: **No limit on follow-ups in v0.** Nothing counts follow-up tickets across a run.

ops.old: **The cost, stated.** A held-out step that no builder can make green gives a run that never reaches G2 and never stops. Each merge files one more follow-up. The run is unbounded in time and in tokens.
ops.new: **The cost, stated.** A held-out step that no builder can make green gives a run that never reaches G2 and never stops. Each merge files one more follow-up. The run is unbounded in time and in tokens.

ops.old: **Why accept that cost.** It is not known that current models fall into repeated bug-fix-bug-fix cycles. A limit picked before the first real run is a number with no data behind it. The first runs show whether the cycle happens, and how long a run that does converge takes.
ops.new: **Why accept that cost.** It is not known that current models fall into repeated bug-fix-bug-fix cycles. A limit picked before the first real run is a number with no data behind it. The first runs show whether the cycle happens, and how long a run that does converge takes.

ops.old: **When to revisit.** A run that files follow-ups for the same held-out step more than once. That is the evidence the limit needs.

ops.old:
1. main() creates the main agent on first reference unconditionally — no disk check, never throws.
2. ensure(name) for any other name only succeeds if a directory record already exists on disk; otherwise it throws 'no conversation named "<name>"'.
3. A live agent already held in memory is always reused — ensure()/main() never spawn a second Agent for a name that already has one.
4. Every agent this manager ever creates, including main, is announced to every onSpawn listener at creation time, and a listener that unsubscribes stops receiving calls.
5. fork() requires the parent conversation to already have sent a message — it throws if the parent has no sessionId yet, so an empty conversation cannot be forked.
6. A forked conversation's name is checked for uniqueness only against currently-live agent names, not against conversations that exist on disk but have no live Agent — a collision with an un-ensure'd disk-only conversation is not guarded against.
7. Every agent this manager creates shares one Asks queue, so a permission prompt from any conversation surfaces in the same place.
8. Parking a conversation keeps its child process. A sweep kills a parked child left untouched past #werk-mc-reap's limit, and leaves its directory and session file intact, so the next message to that name resumes the same conversation.
9. stopAll() stops every live agent's child process — none is left running after it returns.

ops.old: ## The difference
ops.new: ## The difference

ops.old:
1. **Propagation.** Wayfinder's blocking is a *scheduling* edge: what is takeable next. It is not a truth edge. Closing a ticket never marks a downstream decision suspect — the skill only says "if the decision invalidates other parts of the map, update or delete those tickets," which is an instruction to a model, and #vi-prop measured that at 6–11% recall. werk's `depends_on` is a truth edge and `reopen` walks the closure. This is the whole reason the logic is in a program — see #pr-logic.
2. **Contrast.** Wayfinder records only the answer, in a resolution comment. The rejected alternative is gone. werk records it as an `option` node with `--why_not` and an `alternative_to` edge, and `unchallenged` counts what was never weighed — see #ro-unchal.
3. **Shared gaze.** Wayfinder's map is text the agent reads. werk's map is open next to the chat, and the agent is told which card Eryk is looking at every turn — see #werk-card-blind, #visual.
4. **Gates.** A skill cannot refuse. werk's contract check lives in the CLI and blocks `decided` — see #werk-contract.
5. **Grain.** A wayfinder ticket is sized to one 100K-token session. A werk card is one decision with one why.
6. **Method of alignment.** Wayfinder's default type is `grilling` — conversation, asking. #align holds that asking is the weak instrument and showing variants is the strong one.

ops.old:

payload.title: Each build starts from a board trigger on one ticket; werk run does not build by itself
payload.why_not: The run then needs one click per ticket, and the merge queue and the 3-at-once rule have no single owner.

payload.title: Two separate entry points: the board trigger merges its own ticket, and werk run is a batch path
payload.why_not: Two paths reach the same merge, and a person keeps them in step by hand.

payload.title: The grader judges only the cited cards
payload.why_not: A builder can break a card it read through the closure, and the grader would not see it.

payload.title: Every decided card needs an option or --unchallenged
payload.why_not: The agent decides many cards itself. It would fill them with --unchallenged waivers that carry no information.

payload.title: Command-line behaviour list
payload.why: Drawn from the source of the agent, the server, the command line and the conversation store, and cross-checked against three independent sample runs of the #werk-test-behaviours brief, which agreed almost word for word. This is the gate #werk-test-scope sets for I/O modules: a list, not a percentage.

ops.old: Eight behaviours. cli.ts has the widest surface of the four modules, so the list covers the checks that keep the map's decision record honest, and skips low-risk commands that only print or replay the log (events, stale, inbox, import).

ops.old:
1. add refuses an id that already exists, instead of silently clobbering it.
2. add --status decided is rejected outright — every decided card must pass through the status command's own checks.
3. status <id> decided enforces four facts: who is set; a depends_on edge (or --no-basis); when who is you, an alternative_to option (or --unchallenged); and a kill criterion on record (#kill-ask). It fails with the exact fixing command otherwise.
4. link/unlink fail if either endpoint id does not already exist as a node.
5. reopen --reason postponed marks the reverse-dependency closure paused; any other reason marks it stale — never both, never the wrong one.
6. quote only records an excerpt when the text is an exact, single match in the transcript; zero or more than one match fails.
7. prototype refuses fewer than two options — #al-two exists precisely to stop a built option with nothing to compare it against.
8. sample and prototype clamp n and timeout to their hard caps regardless of what flag value is passed.

7. prototype refuses fewer than two options — #al-two exists precisely to stop a built option with nothing to compare it against.
8. sample and prototype clamp n and timeout to their hard caps regardless of what flag value is passed.

A card stays at the level of the decision. It names behaviour, concepts, and the commands and flags a person types. It does not name source files, functions, classes, constants, line numbers, or internal endpoints. Those change with every refactor, and the card would go stale while its decision still holds. The code points to the card, not the other way round.

ops.old: The pie reads modelUsage from the CLI's own 'result' event — inputTokens + outputTokens + cacheReadInputTokens + cacheCreationInputTokens over contextWindow, both reported by the model itself, so the fill and the limit are never a guess baked into this file. It turns var(--proto) blue under 33%, var(--open) yellow from 33%, var(--stale) red from 66%, drawn with a conic-gradient on a 16px button — no canvas, no chart library.
ops.new:
The pie shows the context in use over the context window. The model reports both, so neither is a guess.

- The numerator is the usage of the latest assistant message: input tokens + output tokens + cache-read tokens + cache-creation tokens. One assistant message is one API call, so its usage is the size of the conversation at that call.
- The denominator is the context window size from the turn's final result. Only the window size is read from there. The final result sums the usage of every call of the turn, so a turn with ten tool calls reports ten times the real size.

The pie is blue (the proto colour) under 33%, yellow (the open colour) from 33%, and red (the stale colour) from 66%. It is a CSS conic gradient on a 16px button, with no canvas and no chart library.

payload.why: Screenshots from the libavoid render showed four separate, recurring defects, not one-off glitches: a line grazing a card with no clearance, adjacent labels with no gap reading as one string, an edge entering a card sideways when it should always enter straight, and a long label pushing its neighbors out of position. ops.old: Four rules, each mechanical, each independent of the others:
ops.new: Four rules, each mechanical, each independent of the others:

ops.old:
1. **Card margin.** Every line and label plate keeps a minimum clearance from every box it does not connect to.
2. **Label separation.** Two label plates that land near each other keep a minimum gap — currently 6px (LABEL_GAP), effectively invisible; raising it is the fix.
3. **Forced straight entry.** An edge assigned to a boxs top pin always makes its final approach vertical, arriving from above. Same for bottom (from below), left (from the right side... from further left), right (from further right). Never a sideways nudge into a top/bottom pin, never an up/down nudge into a side pin.
4. **Label wrapping.** A label wider than some cap wraps to multiple lines inside its plate, instead of one long plate that shoves its neighbors aside when decluttered.

payload.why:
gate_approvebar entered "approval bar" from the top with an up-then-down reversal (the routed edge climbed to a routing row above all the cards, then had to come back down into the card). Two fixes follow: that edge enters from the left, and a U-turn is a general rule, not avoided at every price.

The specific case: gate_approvebar's corridor climb stops at approvebar's own row and steps sideways into its left border, instead of overshooting to a row above everything and coming back down. The top routing row is not needed and is gone from the diagram.

The rule is a WARNING, not a grammar error. ops.old:
1. main() creates the main agent on first reference unconditionally — no disk check, never throws.
2. ensure(name) for any other name only succeeds if a directory record already exists on disk; otherwise it throws 'no conversation named "<name>"'.
3. A live agent already held in memory is always reused — ensure()/main() never spawn a second Agent for a name that already has one.
4. Every agent this manager ever creates, including main, is announced to every onSpawn listener at creation time, and a listener that unsubscribes stops receiving calls.
5. fork() requires the parent conversation to already have sent a message — it throws if the parent has no sessionId yet, so an empty conversation cannot be forked.
6. A forked conversation's name is checked for uniqueness only against currently-live agent names, not against conversations that exist on disk but have no live Agent — a collision with an un-ensure'd disk-only conversation is not guarded against.
7. Every agent this manager creates shares one Asks queue, so a permission prompt from any conversation surfaces in the same place.
8. Parking a conversation keeps its child process. A sweep kills a parked child left untouched past #werk-mc-reap's limit, and leaves its directory and session file intact, so the next message to that name resumes the same conversation.

payload.why: The edge into "approval bar" made an up-then-down reversal. That edge now enters from the left, and a U-turn in general is a build warning, not an error.

ops.new: ## The problem
The edge into "approval bar" entered from the top. It climbed to a routing row above all the cards, then came back down into the card: an up-then-down reversal.
## The fix for that edge
The corridor climb for gate_approvebar now stops at the card's own row and steps sideways into its left border. The routing row above everything is not needed and is gone from the diagram.
## The general rule

- A U-turn is a **warning**, not a grammar error. The build still succeeds.
- A U-turn is an edge whose path reverses direction on one axis, with only a perpendicular run between the two halves.
- The build prints each one as a "warning: ..." line.
- A U-turn is not avoided at every price. Sometimes it is the cheapest route.
## The result

- gate_approvebar: no warning any more.
- cli_log: the warning stays, correctly. Its corridor must dip below the whole diagram and come back up to reach cli from underneath. That is still cheaper than any other route found so far.

payload.title: A U-turn in an edge is a build warning, not an error
payload.why: An edge that reverses direction on one axis between two runs makes a U-shape that is hard to read. The build warns about each one. It does not fail, because a U-turn is sometimes the cheapest route.

ops.new: ## The rule
A U-turn in an edge is a **warning**, not a grammar error. The diagram build still succeeds and prints a "warning: ..." line for each one.
## What a U-turn is
An edge whose path reverses direction on one axis, with only a perpendicular run between the two halves. Here the edge from A leaves upward, runs sideways, and comes back down into B:
The same edge without the U-turn enters B from the side:
## Why a warning and not an error

A U-turn is not avoided at every price. Sometimes it is the cheapest route: a corridor may have to dip below the whole diagram and come back up to reach a card from underneath. The warning shows the author each case, and the author decides if the route is acceptable.

payload.title: The builder never sees the held-out steps, and the binder cannot fake a pass
The builder never sees the held-out steps

patch.body:
The binder cannot fake a pass.

- One step author per ticket. It runs with no tools; the program stores its answer under .werk/heldout/<run>/. A follow-up ticket gets no step author.
- The binder binds every step of the run in a temporary worktree. If it changes a file outside .werk-heldout/, its whole report is void.
- A binder error files no follow-up. The set runs once more at the end of the run; an error that stays ends the run as heldout and waits for a person.
- One held-out run files one follow-up for all newly failed steps. A step that an open follow-up already carries files no second one.
- The red badge stays on the merged ticket after its follow-up goes green.

Known gap: the builder's Read tool can reach .werk/heldout/ by an absolute path. The steps are out of the builder's worktree, not out of its reach.

patch.body:
No planning-process narration in a title, why, or body: no "Eryk said", no "the next thing to prove", no comparison to where the conversation stands.

This includes a card's own edit history. "X is new", "Y used to say/name Z", "that no longer holds/applies" still narrate the session, even when the subject is the card itself. State the current fact plainly. The same holds for where the text came from: "moved here from #x", "split out of #y", "merged from #z". The log records the move; the card states the fact.

A reversal is still fair game to record — a superseded card can say what replaced it and why the earlier reading was wrong — but as a fact about the subject, not a play-by-play of the conversation that produced it. Attribution lives in the "who" field and in the log, not in prose.

A card stays at the level of the decision. It names behaviour, concepts, and the commands and flags a person types. It does not name source files, functions, classes, constants, line numbers, or internal endpoints. Those change with every refactor, and the card would go stale while its decision still holds. The code points to the card, not the other way round.

The map records decisions that hold for any module, not results for one module. Applying a rule to one module — its behaviour list, its coverage threshold, its test plan — produces an artifact, not a decision. That artifact lives next to the code it describes, in the module's own tests. A card for one module is fair only when that module raises a real design fork the general rule cannot settle.

A read-only `test-scope` subagent classifies a module as pure or I/O per #werk-test-scope step 1. For an I/O module it runs #werk-test-behaviours' sampling procedure (`werk sample`, plan tier only). It never writes to the map and never invents a coverage number for pure code — a missing threshold policy is reported, not guessed.

The project instructions tell the main agent to spawn `test-scope` proactively whenever the build step reaches a module with no test policy yet. The main agent writes the result into the module's own tests, not onto the map: a behaviour list becomes the named test cases, a threshold becomes the coverage setting. The map gets a card only for a real design-question fork `test-scope` could not settle, per #al-two and #werk-wording.

Same shape as the sysdiag-scout/sysdiag-updater split: the subagent decides and reports, the main agent is the only one that writes.

The pane reads the last line of each finished agent message. A line that matches Next: say "<phrase>" or Next: reply "<phrase>" (straight or curly quotes, optional bold) adds a button under the message. The button label is <phrase>. Text after the closing quote, such as "and I do steps 1-4", is ignored.

A click posts <phrase> to /api/chat as a normal user message, with the open card as context. It does not touch the composer, so a draft and its pending images stay.

The next user message removes every button in that tab, so only the latest offer is clickable.

The Next: format comes from the user's global instructions. A message in another wording gets no button, and nothing else changes. Code: nextPhrase() in web/app.js.

An unclicked button also blinks the tab chip yellow, and the '...' button when the tab is not the current one (#werk-mc-asks). The offer ends on a click or on the next message. Code: tab.offer in addChat().
