patch.body:
The test: take the full diagram, cut every card to one cell, and leave all path and label cells as they are. 20 of 22 edges then failed the rule that an edge must touch its card.

Two causes:

1. **Too many edges on one card.** A one-cell card has four neighbour cells. state touches 5 and live touches 6, so neither can be one cell in any layout. runner takes 2 edges in and sends 3 out.
2. **Row gaps depend on card height.** foldfn has one edge in and one edge out, on opposite sides. It broke too. Its two-row height let its top row touch the edge above and its bottom row touch the edge below. After the cut, the paths no longer span the one-row gap.

Why the 4-card proof (#vi-sysdiag-grid-singlecell) worked: its author wrote it one cell per card from the start, row gaps included. Cutting an existing multi-cell layout is not the same as writing one from scratch. The from-scratch result is #vi-sysdiag-grid-minimal.
patch.why: Cutting the full 21-card diagram to one cell per card breaks it. A one-cell card has four neighbour cells, and some cards need more.

patch.body:
A card takes one cell. It widens only when edges force it: several edges arrive at, or leave from, the same side in the same direction.

How we know:

1. **Small proof.** A 4-card grid written at one cell per card builds with 0 errors.
2. **A cut does not work.** Cutting the full 21-card diagram to one cell per card, with every path left as it was, broke 20 of 22 edges. A one-cell card has four neighbour cells. state touches 5 and live touches 6, so neither can be one cell in any layout. A card like foldfn broke too, because its two-row height let the paths above and below reach it. The 4-card proof worked because its author wrote it one cell per card from the start, row gaps included.
3. **From scratch works.** The full diagram rewritten at one cell per card is 12x22 cells, down from 39x23. It builds with 0 errors and reads the same. Two long detour edges had caused most of the old width. Each detour now has its own column, so it does not run through columns that other cards need.

Only state, live, runner, and child are wider than one cell. Each has a counted reason: N edges arrive at, or M edges leave, the same side. Every other card fits in one cell, including cards with real edges such as gate and cli.
patch.why: A one-cell card is the smallest grid, and it works at full scale. A card widens only when it needs it. Writing the diagram from scratch at one cell per card gave 12x22 cells, down from 39x23, with 0 build errors.

payload.title: A single edge that leaves a card off its middle is a build warning
payload.why: Gap 1: a lane can sit about 25px off the centre of the card it leaves, and the grid text does not show it. The build now measures each card face that carries exactly one edge and warns when the line is more than 3px off the middle. The warning names the fix: an odd number of cells on that face, or the edge in the middle cell. A face with several edges is a fan and is off-centre by design, so it is not reported.

payload.title: Change the track solver so a lane always lands on the card's middle
payload.why_not: It moves lanes the author placed, so the grid text stops matching the picture. The warning keeps the grid as the source of truth.

payload.title: A spacer token keeps an empty column or row at least one lane wide
payload.why: Gap 4: a column of empty cells collapses to zero width, so the author had no way to buy air between two cards. The tilde token means empty, but its column and row keep at least one lane's width. An empty-cell token still collapses.

payload.title: Give every column a minimum width
payload.why_not: It adds air everywhere, also where the author wants cards tight. A token puts the air only where the author asks.

payload.title: Where a label sits inside a label box wider than one cell
payload.why: Gap 3: a label is centred in its own cell box, so a two-cell label sits about 55px from its line and a one-cell label sits tight against it. More cells puts the text further away, which is the reverse of what the author means. Not changed in the build yet.

payload.text: Gap 1 is built as a build warning: a card that is wider than one cell, with one edge on a face, warns when the edge is off the card's middle. Gap 4 is built as a spacer cell, written ~, that keeps its column and row at least one lane wide. Gap 2: the build now names every card that a group frame holds without being a member. On the full diagram, proc holds 10 and store holds 7. The fix is a new card layout, so the shape grid in #vi-sysdiag-grid-groupshape still waits for it.

payload.title: Keep the label centred in its box
payload.why_not: More cells then put the text further from its line, which is the reverse of what the author means by giving a label more cells.

payload.title: Allow a label only one cell

payload.title: The grid format gets one fix per gap the first build found, each on its own card
payload.why: The first build rendered cleanly, so the open questions were about what the format cannot say or show. Each gap has a separate fix with its own alternative, so each is its own decision: off-centre lanes are a build warning, group shape comes from a shape grid, wide labels hug their lane, a spacer token buys empty width, and an edge token is from->to. Later builds found more gaps; they hang here too.

payload.title: What the author writes: the grid's tokens
payload.why: A grid cell holds one token, and the token set is the whole authoring language. Each token is its own decision: a card cell, a path cell named from->to, a label cell beside or inside its lane, a spacer that keeps empty width, and a junction where two edges cross on purpose. Group shape is written in a second, coarser grid in the same file.

payload.title: What the build does with a grid: refuse, warn, or place
payload.why: The build refuses a grid that breaks a tile rule. It warns, but still renders, when the result is legal and hard to read: a U-turn, or a single edge off a card's middle. It places each label against its own lane. Every rule of this kind is its own decision under this card.

payload.title: A single edge that leaves a card off its middle is a build warning
payload.why: A lane can sit far from the middle of the card it leaves, and the grid text does not show it. The build measures each card face that carries exactly one edge, and warns when the line is more than 3px off the middle. The warning names the fix: an odd number of cells on that face, or the edge in the middle cell. A face with several edges is a fan. A fan is off-centre by design, so the build does not report it.

payload.title: Change the track solver so a lane always lands on the card's middle
payload.why_not: It moves lanes the author placed, so the grid text stops matching the picture. A warning keeps the grid as the source of truth.

payload.title: A spacer token keeps an empty column or row at least one lane wide
payload.why: An empty cell collapses: a column of empty cells has zero width. The tilde token is also empty, but its column and row keep at least one lane's width. This is the only way an author adds space between two cards.

payload.title: Give every column a minimum width
payload.why_not: It adds space everywhere, also where the author wants cards tight. A token adds space only where the author asks.

payload.title: A label sits against the side of its box nearest its own lane
payload.why: A label box can span more than one cell, to make room for long text. The text sits against the side of the box nearest its lane, so more cells never put it further from its line. It hugs on the axis that points to the lane and stays centred on the other axis. When the lane is equally near on both sides, the text stays centred. The gap to the box edge is a small fixed inset.

payload.title: Centre the label in its box
payload.why_not: More cells then put the text further from its line, which is the reverse of what the author means by giving a label more cells.

payload.title: Allow a label only one cell
payload.why_not: It removes the only way to make room for a long label.

payload.why: A path cell names its edge as from->to. The older form from_to collides with any card id that contains an underscore: a_b -> c and a -> b_c both give a_b_c. No card id can contain '->', so the new token is never ambiguous.

payload.title: A separate shape grid defines each group's shape, and the diagram's cards must fit inside it
payload.why: A group frame drawn as the bounding box of its cards has two defects. It reserves no cells for its own header strip, and its rectangle can cover a card that is not a member of the group. A shape grid uses the card-grid syntax at a coarser resolution, so the author declares each group's shape as its own checked artifact. Each card must then fit inside its group's declared cells. The checker enforces that rule, so layout does not decide it by chance. One group nests in another when its cells sit inside the other group's cells.

criterion.text: Build the full diagram. If most columns need a spacer only to look normal, the default is wrong: give every column a minimum width.
Build the full diagram. If off-middle warnings stay in the output because the cell fix costs more than the defect, the warning is noise: centre lanes in the track solver.

- A rederive counts only if the card was stale at that moment. The answer comes from a fold of the log up to the rederive, so it matches what werk stale said then.

The section is a gauge, so the value and the criterion are read in one look:

- One bar for all cleared marks in the window. It has three parts: unchanged with the card born after the reopen, unchanged for another reason, and text changed. The two unchanged parts together are the share.

- A legend under the bar gives the count of each part. At the right, the sample: how many cleared in the window, and the minimum. It turns amber when the sample is below the minimum.

patch.body:
The agent decides the level of every card it writes: the parent, and whether to promote or demote it with werk move. It does not ask first.

Eryk refines the tree afterwards. He asks for a reposition in chat, and the agent runs the move.

One rule for the agent: do not build a chain of single-child cards. A parent with one child is a sign that the two are one decision. Merge the child into the parent, or put it beside the parent, unless it is a separate decision that will get siblings soon.

Measured on the map: 42 of 110 parents have exactly one child card. Four of those start a chain of three or more, for example #ro-unchal, #ro-live and #ro-optparent.
patch.why: The agent's placement is usually right. A correction costs one request, so placing by hand would be work for no gain.

payload.title: Reroute the edge whose lane blocks the new edge
payload.why_not: It moves an edge that was already correct, and the next new edge can hit the same wall. A junction lets the author cross a lane without changing any other edge.

payload.title: A junction cell lets two edges cross at one cell that the author names
payload.why: A lane can block a new edge along its whole length, even when both ends of the new edge have a free face. A junction token names two edges in one cell. Each edge reads the cell as its own path cell, as if the other edge were not there. The two edges must pass straight through on different axes, one vertical and one horizontal. A junction is never a turn, and the build never infers one.

A label cell can sit in its own edge's lane, between two parts of the path, as well as beside the lane. The checker accepts the label when it touches every part of the cut path. The line is drawn straight through from card to card, and a plate in the background colour sits under the text. The label then reads as a gap in the line, but the line itself is not cut.

payload.title: A label beside its lane sits against the side of its box nearest the lane
payload.why: A label box can span more than one cell, to make room for long text. When the label sits beside its lane, the text sits against the side of the box nearest the lane, so more cells never put it further from its line. It hugs on the axis that points to the lane and stays centred on the other axis. The gap to the box edge is a small fixed inset. A label inline in its lane is not covered here: the line passes through the centre of that box, so the text stays centred (see #vi-sysdiag-grid-inline-label).

ops.old: Ordered by how much they threaten the design, not by how hard they are.

**1. A lane is not centred in the card it leaves, and the author cannot see that.**
`mv` spans columns 0 to 2 and its lane is column 1, but equal distribution across a span does not cancel column 1s 26px lane baseline, so the lane sits about 25px left of the card centre. Every line in the render leaves its card visibly off-centre.
This is the one that matters, because the entire argument for this design is that the grid is legible to its own author before rendering. Here it is not: the information is present (lane at column 1 of a 0-2 span is left of middle) but it takes counting to see, and the consequence is invisible.
Cheapest fix, and it keeps the property: a checker rule. "Edge X attaches to card Y off-centre" as a warning. The author still cannot see it, but no longer has to.

**2. Group frames are metric and the grid reserves no space for them.**
A frame needs a header strip above its top card. BROWSER is in row 0, so its frame computed to y = -4 and the whole drawing had to be shifted afterwards to compensate. Worse, the SERVER PROCESS top border currently crosses row 4s lane cells, and its header text misses the vertical line by luck.
A group is a first-class thing in the content section but has no cells of its own. Either it gets them (a `browser` token that fills its frame cells, so the author sees and controls the header strip), or rows gain a declared type. Undecided.

**3. A wide label sits further from its own line than a narrow one.**
A label is centred in its own cell box, so the two-cell `@lv_cp` puts its text about 55px from the line it belongs to, while the one-cell `@cp_lv` reads tight against it. More cells means further away, which is backwards from what an author intends by spending more cells.
Fix is small: a label box should hug the side of its box nearest its own lane, not centre in it.

**4. An empty column collapses to zero width.**
There is no token meaning "a gap of at least N here". The only way to buy horizontal air is to put something in the column. On a four-card diagram this never bites; on 21 cards it will.

**5. The derived edge id is ambiguous.**
`<from>_<to>` collides with any node id containing an underscore, and `a_b -> c` and `a -> b_c` both produce `a_b_c`. The implementation resolves a bare token as a card first, then an edge, which is a guess, not a rule.
Better: make the grid token `mv->st` rather than `mv_st`. Unambiguous, and it reads as what it is. Costs two characters per cell.

ops.new:
Three kinds of rule, one card each:

- **Refuse.** A grid that breaks a tile rule does not build. The tile rules are on #vi-sysdiag-grid.
- **Warn.** A legal grid that is hard to read still builds, with one warning per case: #vi-sysdiag-grid-uturn, #vi-sysdiag-grid-offcentre.
- **Place.** Where the build puts label text and the line under it: #vi-sysdiag-grid-labelhug, #vi-sysdiag-grid-inline-label.

payload.title: Give no mark when the depends_on link is newer than the reopen
payload.why_not: A new link can rest on a stale ancestor whose correction its author never read. The link time does not prove that read, the same as the creation time does not.

payload.detail: 2026-10-10: 89% of 145 cleared stale marks in 30 days left the text unchanged. Born-after marks: 19 of 126 led to a text change (15%). Other marks: 4 of 38 (11%). Born-after marks are not the noise source; all marks are cleared mostly unchanged.

payload.text: Kill criterion fired on 2026-10-10 (89% unchanged, threshold 80%). Split: born-after marks changed text in 19 of 126 clears, other marks in 4 of 38. So exempting born-after cards (vi-prop-bornstale:opt-newlink) would hide most of the marks that did lead to an edit. A text change after a clear also does not prove the mark caused it: on 2026-10-10 several grid cards were rewritten for a reframe and then cleared.

Third cause for the 89%, from Eryk: the reader cannot see why a card depends on the stale one, so the reader clears the mark. A depends_on link stores no reason, and the stale trace shows only the hop ids. This also explains why distance does not change the rate: a 1-hop link has no visible reason either.

payload.title: A depends_on link carries one sentence that says why
payload.why: A reader who clears a stale mark cannot see why the card depends on the reopened one, so the reader clears it unread. A reason on each link lets the reader judge if the reopen reaches this card.
payload.body:
- A new depends_on link needs a reason: `werk link <from> <to> --type depends_on --why "..."`. Without `--why` the command fails.
- The reason is one sentence about what the card takes from its dependency, not about the dependency itself.
- The stale trace shows the reason next to each hop, so a reader sees the whole chain of reasons from the card to the reopen.
- An old link has no reason. The trace says "no reason recorded" for that hop, and the reader can add one with `werk link` again.
- A reason can change later without a new link.

payload.title: Ask for a reason when the mark is cleared, not when the link is made
payload.why_not: It measures the problem but does not fix it: the reader still sees no reason at the moment of the decision. It can be added later, on top of a reason on the link.

payload.title: Make the reason optional on a new link
payload.why_not: An optional field stays empty under time pressure, and an empty reason is the problem this card fixes. #vi-prop says the link is recorded at creation or never; the same holds for its reason.

payload.text: Built on 2026-10-10. A depends_on link fails without --why; linking again sets the reason; show and the map print the reason per hop. Backfill: 533 links, 528 kept with a reason (48 low confidence), 5 removed. Review list: .werk/linkwhy-review.md

payload.title: Re-check a link's reason after every change to either linked card
payload.why_not: Not needed yet. A reason written at link time may still go wrong later. Try this when a sweep finds links that make no sense although they have a reason.

criterion.text: Run the next sweep of all depends_on links. If it finds links that make no sense although they have a reason, reconsider the approach: the reason may be written at the wrong moment, or a link may need a re-check after any change to either card.

payload.title: A depends_on link never points to an ancestor or a descendant
payload.why: The refines tree already says that a card is part of its parent. A depends_on link to an ancestor or a descendant repeats that, and it hides the links that matter: the ones that cross subtrees. werk link refuses such a link, and a move between subtrees re-checks the card's links.
payload.body: Today 201 of 528 depends_on links point to an ancestor, 183 of them to the direct parent, and 1 points to a descendant. For 113 cards, the parent link is the only basis for the decided contract. Staleness follows only depends_on, so this rule needs an answer first: what does a reopen reach when ancestor links are gone (see #vi-prop-nolineage-reach).

payload.why: The rule narrows which links need the reason that #vi-prop-linkwhy requires.

payload.title: A reopen marks every card in the refines subtree below it
payload.why: Without ancestor links, the refines tree must carry a reopen down, or a parent's reopen reaches no child. A refines hop needs no reason: being part of the parent is the reason.
It changes which cards the staleness propagation of #vi-prop marks.

payload.title: A reopen no longer reaches the cards below it
payload.why_not: A parent's reopen then leaves its children unmarked, although they are part of it. The 183 parent links mark children stale today.

payload.title: Keep the existing ancestor links, refuse only new ones
payload.why_not: Old cards are marked through ancestor links and new cards are not, so two cards in the same place behave differently.

payload.title: A reopen marks every card in the refines subtree below it
payload.why: A card is part of its parent, so a parent's reopen can make any card below it wrong. The refines tree carries the reopen down. A refines hop needs no reason: being part of the parent is the reason.

payload.title: A reopen does not reach the cards below it
payload.why_not: A parent's reopen then leaves its children unmarked, although they are part of it.

payload.title: Keep the existing ancestor links, refuse only new ones
payload.why_not: Old cards are marked through ancestor links and new cards are not, so two cards in the same place behave differently.

payload.title: Cards relate through typed links, and a change travels along them
payload.why: The rules for how one card relates to another are the map's model, not a property of the visual medium. They hold the same in the tree, the graph, the board, and the CLI.
payload.body: Covers: the link types, what each one means, which links are allowed, and how a reopen reaches other cards.

ops.new:
Four link types, and nothing else. Each child card below defines one part of this picture.

```
                        ┌──────────┐
                        │   root   │
                        └────▲─────┘
                  refines    │    refines
              ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
         ┌────┴────┐                   ┌────┴────┐
         │    A    │                   │    B    │
         └────▲────┘                   └────▲────┘

| depends_on | card → card in another subtree | A1 uses something B1 decided. Carries one sentence why. |
| supported_by | card → source or excerpt | B1's evidence. |
| alternative_to | option → card | A rejected option of A1, kept for a reopen. |

patch.body:
Inspected on 2026-09-01 from the process table and Conductor's application-support directory.

**How it runs Claude Code.** Conductor starts its own pinned claude binary as a child process, through a sidecar runtime. The child's stdin, stdout and stderr are unix sockets to the sidecar, not a terminal. One user turn is one JSON line written to stdin, in stream-json format. Conductor never pastes text and never simulates keystrokes. Because the sidecar owns that stdin, no other program can write into a Conductor session.

**How it stores events.** Each session has one outbox file. The file holds a version, the session id, a next-sequence counter and a list of pending events. Each pending event wraps the raw stream-json payload with a session id, a turn id and a user-message id. The queue drains into a SQLite database.

**What it confirms for werk.** The outbox is an append-only event log with a sequence number, and the database is a projection of it. werk's log and fold have the same shape, so a production app reached the same design independently. Conductor also drains the queue, which works like a snapshot. werk has no snapshot yet (see #pr-log-snapshot).

1. **The link is gone.** The card no longer depends on the path that carries the reopen. The mark drops by itself. No rederive is needed.
2. **The card changed.** Its title, why, or body was edited after the reopen.
3. **A reason is given.** `werk rederive <id> --why "..."` says why the card holds unchanged.

A card created after the reopen has no exemption (#vi-prop-bornstale). Its reason can say that it was written with the correction in hand.

payload.title: A stale mark clears only with one of three facts on record
payload.why: To clear a stale card, remove the link that carries the reopen, edit the card, or give a reason why it holds unchanged. werk rederive refuses any other clear, so no mark is cleared unread.
payload.body:
## The three facts

1. **The link is gone.** The card no longer depends on the path that carries the reopen. The mark drops by itself, because staleness follows the links that exist now. No rederive is needed.
2. **The card changed.** Its title, why, or body was edited after the reopen. Then `werk rederive <id>` clears it.
3. **A reason is given.** `werk rederive <id> --why "..."` says why the card holds unchanged. The log keeps the reason with the clear.

## Enforcement

`werk rederive` checks facts 2 and 3 against the log. With neither, it fails and prints the commands that fix it, in the form #werk-contract-fix sets. The check lives in the CLI, not in a hook (#werk-contract-where), so it applies to the agent, a script, and a human.

The agent chooses the fact before it runs rederive. `werk show` lists the three choices under the trace (#vi-prop-trace).

## Related

- A card created after the reopen has no exemption (#vi-prop-bornstale). Its reason can say that it was written with the correction in hand.
- A clear with a reason and no edit is the "unchanged" case that #vi-prop-metric counts. The reason lets a reader judge each one.
- #vi-prop-linkwhy:opt0 asked for a reason at clear time instead of on the link. This card asks for both.

A born-after card gets no exemption, because #vi-prop-bornstale keeps its mark.

patch.body:
- **say** — verbatim excerpts from this conversation, attributed, so “how did we arrive here” is answerable without re-reading anything.
- **ev** — a pointer to a source node, whose finding carries the numbers.
- **alt** — the options that were rejected, kept, never deleted.

Three versions failed before this one. V1 had titles only. V2 hid the proof in a side panel that leaf cards never opened. V3 copied source text into every card.

Where it renders: the card body, the why line, the finding line, the notes thread, your own messages in the pane, and the agent's replies. Not the card summary in a grid tile, because that tile is a button and a link inside a button is invalid.

Only an id the map knows becomes a link. A dead reference stays plain text, so a link always lands somewhere. A click needs no handler, because the link is the route the map already uses for a card.

A reference has two forms:
- With the #, any known id links: #align, #al-diff.
- Without the #, an id links only if it has a hyphen or a colon: al-diff, pr-iface:opt0. That shape never occurs in prose. A bare single word like align or loop is an ordinary English word as often as an id, so it needs the #.

A code span links when it holds nothing but a card id: `al-diff` or `#al-diff`. A command in a code span stays code, because the whole span must be only the id.

What it leaves alone:
- A code span with more than an id in it. `node src/cli.ts show #rollup` is a command, not a reference.
- A fenced block.
- A heading. `# rollup` needs a space, an id does not have one.
- A URL fragment. The character before the # must not be a word character or a slash.

Bold and italic markers inside a code span stay literal text.

Every add, edit, retitle, and propose passes the card's title, why, and body through a check against the wording rules in #werk-wording.

Open: what does the check, and when it runs.

A phrase check can catch code names and fixed narration phrases. It cannot judge narration in general. A model can judge it, but its verdict is not deterministic.

payload.why: Cheap and covers every session, but it is prose again. #pr-gate rejects this for any rule the map depends on.

payload.title: A deterministic phrase check in the CLI on add, edit, retitle, and propose
payload.why: Fails loudly and the same way each time. It catches file names, function names, and fixed narration phrases. It misses narration in other words.

payload.title: A reviewer subagent reads each proposed card against the rules
payload.why: Judges meaning, so it catches narration in any words. It costs a model call per card, and its verdict can vary.

payload.title: The agent prompt states the card wording rules

patch.body:
The prompt that every werk session and subagent loads states the wording rules of #werk-wording: a card describes its own subject, not the session that wrote it, and it stays at the level of the decision.

No program checks the text. The human read before accept stays the last gate.

This is not a state-transition rule. Wording applies to every add, edit, and retitle, not to one move between states.
patch.why: Card text drifts back to session narration and code names when the agent that writes it does not see the rules. Putting the rules in the prompt every session loads costs nothing per card.

patch.why_not: Catches only code names and fixed phrases. Narration in other words passes, and the phrase list needs upkeep.
A model call per card, and its verdict can vary. More cost than the problem justifies before a sweep shows the prompt is not enough.

criterion.text: Periodic review sweep: count the cards that break the #werk-wording rules among cards written after this decision, against cards written before it. No drop in the rate means the prompt is not enough.

payload.why: the wording rules the prompt states

payload.text: AGENTS.md now carries the five wording rules of #werk-wording, with a wrong/correct example, in the section 'Write a card about its subject, at the level of the decision'.

patch.body:
## Rule

When a decision comes from real contrast, add the rejected alternative as its own option node. Do it in the same turn as the decision.

```
node src/cli.ts add <id>:opt0 --kind option --title "..." --why_not "..."
node src/cli.ts link <id>:opt0 <id> --type alternative_to
```

Real contrast means a named alternative and a reason it was rejected.

## Why

- `unchallenged` cannot tell "no option was weighed" from "an option was weighed and never written down".
- The same discipline holds for `depends_on`: record it when the card is created, or it cannot be reconstructed.

## Evidence

Two cards were corrected after the fact, and both were indistinguishable from a decision made with no contrast:

- #ro-unchal:opt0 — count every decided card. Rejected as too much noise.
- #vi-backend:opt0 — the tracker owns state. Rejected for losing ordered event history.
patch.why: A rejected option is written down as its own node when it is weighed. Written later, the card looks like a decision made with no contrast.

payload.why: The rule names the alternative_to link and the depends_on link. #vi-edges defines both.

payload.body:
## Rule

Write each `depends_on` link in the same step that creates the card, with its reason:

```
node src/cli.ts link <from> <to> --type depends_on --why "what <from> takes from <to>"
```

Link types are defined in #vi-edges. How a mark moves along the links is #vi-prop.

## Why

- A card is true only because another card is true. Only the author knows this at creation.
- Read later, the cards do not show which one a card needed. A single-hop model check recovers 6% to 11% of an invalidation chain.
- Without the link, a reopen of the target marks nothing, and the map shows a card that looks current but is not.

## Consequence

A card created after a reopen can arrive already marked. See #vi-prop-bornstale for whether that mark stays.

patch.body:
This card applies #pr-gate to the werk map. A card moves to decided only after a program check passes. Each decision about the check is its own card:
- Where the check lives: #werk-contract-where.
- When it fires: #werk-contract-when.
- What it checks: #werk-contract-facts. Four facts; the fourth is a kill criterion, from #kill-ask.
- What a failure prints: #werk-contract-fix.
- Where "unchallenged" comes from: #werk-contract-guess.

Two other state changes have their own checks. An amend runs these facts again (#map-frozen). A review of a stale card has its own check (#rederive-reason). The text of a card is not checked.

payload.title: A hook warns after a turn that settled something the map does not record
payload.why_not: The hook runs after the turn and only warns. It does not stop a card from becoming decided, so a missing fact stays missing. It cannot tell drift from a deliberate pause. It also repeats the check outside the CLI, so two places hold one rule.

payload.title: A hook warns after a turn that settled something the map does not record
payload.why_not: The hook runs after the turn and only warns. It does not stop a card from becoming decided, so a missing fact stays missing. It also cannot know why nothing was logged: the agent may have forgotten, or the user may have chosen to wait. It warns in both cases, so many warnings are wrong and people learn to ignore them. It also repeats the check outside the CLI, so two places hold one rule.

payload.title: A decided card is frozen. A change to it is an amend: a reopen and a decide in one step
payload.why: Other cards depend on a decided card because of what it says. If its text could change without a reopen, those cards would not learn about the change. With this rule, an edit works the same way as an invalidation: both mark the next hop.
payload.body:
Frozen: the title, the why, the body, the depends_on links, and the parent. Free: options, sources, kill criterion state, and comments.

A change to a frozen field is a proposal (#al-diff-cli). Your ✓ amends the card: it reopens and decides it in one step, so the map never shows it open. The amend runs the decide facts again (#werk-contract-facts) and marks the next hop (#vi-prop).

A card that fails a decide fact, such as a missing kill criterion, cannot be amended until the fact is fixed.

payload.why: An amend is accepted the way #al-diff-cli stages and accepts an edit.
An amend runs the decide facts that #werk-contract-facts lists.
An amend is a change, so it marks the next hop as #vi-prop sets.

payload.title: An edit stays in place and flags each link reason for review
payload.why_not: A second mark next to stale, with its own clear. One mechanism for every change is simpler to read and to check.

payload.title: An edit to a decided card marks nothing
payload.why_not: The cards that depend on it do not learn about the change, so their link reasons can describe text that is no longer on the card.

payload.title: Paused and rejected are separate reopen reasons

patch.why: A reopened card has two possible reasons. Paused means the content is still true and the work waits. Rejected means the content is wrong. Each reason puts a different mark on the cards that depend on it: paused is grey and keeps the status colour, stale is red.

payload.text: Reworded the title and why. The table row 'the mark it fans out' still uses old wording.

patch.body:
The distinction that survives #pr-wf-scope. Out of scope is not a third state — but *not now* and *wrong* are two, and `reopen` already separates them.

| | `--reason postponed` | `--reason rejected` / `invalidated` |
|---|---|---|
| the content | still true | now wrong |
| the mark on dependent cards | `paused` — grey, keeps the status colour | `stale` — red |
| which cards get the mark | every card downstream, at any distance. A paused card is never reviewed, so the mark cannot move hop by hop | the next hop only (#vi-prop) |
| a conflict | if a postponement and an invalidation reach one card, **stale wins**. A real invalidation is never allowed to look calm | |
| return | expected. `rederive` clears it when work resumes | only by deciding the opposite, which is a new decision |

## The test

**Would you build it unchanged if you had the time?** Postponed: yes. Rejected: no, it would come back different.

#pr-logic is the postponed case and it is exactly right — "logic in a program, Markdown holds prompts" is still the answer. Only the engine build is deferred, and the mark reached four hops down to #vi-oos-render.

## Neither one is a status

A werk status describes the **decision**, not the build. #tracker is `decided` with nine decided cards under it and nothing published yet. That is not a contradiction, and it is not postponed either, because no reopen fired. Same reason the mark is drawn on top of the status colour instead of replacing it, and the reason #pr-wf-scope refused a fourth `Status`.

patch.body:
Removal is reversible and additive. `werk remove <id>` takes a card out of the map. Nothing leaves the log. `werk restore <id>` brings it back, and `werk removed` lists what is out.

A removed card is gone from the tree, not struck through in place. Struck-through text keeps the noise it was meant to clear.

The control sits in the card view, next to ⌖ and ▦, for the same reason accept has a button (#al-diff-cli-btn): cleanup happens while reading the map, and the judgement is already made by the time the card is on screen. The CLI verb exists too, because the agent needs a way to propose a removal.

An agent never removes a card directly. It proposes the removal and the card shows it pending, like any other change.

Children: `remove` takes the refines subtree with it. `--reparent` keeps the children and attaches them to the grandparent instead, for a bad parent over good children.

A removed card is out of every view and every edge touching it is out too. It makes nothing stale, counts in no rollup, and cites nothing. Restoring it returns the card and its edges as they were.

Removal takes the options and the excerpts of what it removes, not only the refines subtree. An option node sits nowhere in the tree, so one left behind is an orphan no view can reach and no later cleanup can find. A source two cards cite stays while either of them stays.

`--reparent` is a CLI flag with no button. The ✕ asks once, naming how many cards go with it, and that is the whole confirmation: nothing leaves the log, so the cost of a wrong click is one restore.

payload.title: The CLI is the agent's interface to the map, and each verb belongs to the card that defines its operation
payload.why: The agent has a shell and no other way to touch the map. One list of verbs, with each verb pointing at the card that defines it, lets a card describe an operation without naming a command.

patch.body:
The map draws the fold of the log (#pr-log). No view edits a drawn card in place. Every change is a new event in the log, and every view redraws from it.

A control in a view, such as accept (#al-diff-cli-btn) or remove (#vi-remove-btn), appends an event. It does not write to the card it sits on.
patch.why: The map is a view of the log. A second way to change it would be a second store to keep in step with the first.

payload.why: The map is read-only because it is the fold of the log that this card defines.
Removal is one more log event, and the map changes only when the log changes, so the removed card can come back.

payload.title: Show one verdict line in the chat
payload.why_not: The line carries no action for the user. When the chat agent relays a background result, the full subagent report and a question come with it.

payload.title: The chat agent starts the subagents at the end of its turn
payload.why_not: The update then depends on the chat agent remembering a rule, and the completion notice resumes the chat session, which prints the report.

payload.text: The one-line verdict is replaced by no chat output at all — see #vi-sysdiag-silent.

payload.title: The diagram follows the map with no trace in the chat and no question to the user
payload.why: The user assumes the product diagram matches the map, after a short delay. A diagram update is never a topic of conversation: the chat shows no verdict line, no subagent report, no file path, and no question.
payload.body:
A change to a decided card starts the scout and updater as a background job. The trigger is the change in the map, not the chat agent at the end of its turn, so no completion notice comes back into a chat session.

The updater never hands a choice to the user. A leftover it finds inside the diagram file, such as a comment that quotes an old label, it fixes in the same run. Anything else it drops.

A run that cannot reach 0 errors leaves the previous diagram in place and shows a mark on the diagram view. It does not post in the chat.

See #vi-sysdiag-agents for what the two subagents do.

payload.why: It changes where the two subagents defined there are started, and what they may report.

patch.body:
## Two endings

1. **Confirm.** The reviewer confirms each outgoing depends_on reason. The mark stops at this card.
2. **Amend.** The card changes through a proposal. Its direct dependents and direct children go stale.

A removed link also drops the mark, because the mark follows the links that exist now. A link made after the change has nothing to review.

## Enforcement

A confirm fails while the card's basis is open or stale, or while one of its link reasons is not confirmed. The failure prints the commands that fix it. The check lives in the CLI, not in a hook, so it applies to the agent, a script, and a human.

The agent may confirm any card. It amends a `who:you` card only through a proposal that you accept.
patch.why: A confirm says the card holds unchanged, and it records that each outgoing link reason was checked. An amend changes the card, which marks the next hop. A confirm that skips a link is refused, so no mark is cleared unread.

payload.title: werk link and werk unlink add or remove one typed link between two cards
payload.why: Linking is the only way to write an edge, so every rule about which links are allowed is checked here, at the moment the link is made.
payload.body:
```
werk link <from> <to> --type refines|depends_on|supported_by|alternative_to [--why "..."]
werk unlink <from> <to> --type <t>
```

- A depends_on link needs `--why`: what <from> takes from <to> (#vi-prop-linkwhy). Without it, the command fails.
- Linking an existing depends_on pair again replaces its reason.
- A depends_on link to an ancestor or a descendant of <from> fails, and the message says why (#vi-prop-nolineage).
- A link on a ghost card is held until the card is accepted (#werk-propose-new).
- `werk unlink` removes one link from the map. The log keeps it.

payload.why: The command refuses an ancestor or descendant target because #vi-prop-nolineage forbids such a link.
The required --why, and its replacement on a second link, carry the reason that #vi-prop-linkwhy requires.
A link on a ghost is held because #werk-propose-new holds every edge of a ghost until acceptance.

The refines tree already says that a card is part of its parent, so such a link repeats it and hides the links that cross subtrees. Linking refuses such a link, and a move removes any link it turns into one.

patch.body:
The scout and updater run in the background and talk only to each other.

The trigger is a change to a decided card in the map, not the chat agent at the end of its turn. When the chat agent starts the subagents itself, the result of a finished background task comes back into the chat session, and the chat agent relays the full updater report — file paths, a change list, and a Next: question. An instruction to stay quiet does not stop that, so the trigger moves out of the chat.

The updater never hands a choice to the user. A leftover it finds inside the diagram file, such as a comment that quotes an old label, it fixes in the same run. It drops anything else.

A run that cannot reach 0 errors keeps the previous diagram and shows a mark on the diagram view, not in the chat.

See #vi-sysdiag-agents for what the two subagents do.
patch.why: A diagram update is not a topic of conversation. The chat shows one line at most: product diagram updated, or no need to update the product diagram at this point. It never shows the subagent exchange, a file path, a process log, or a question to the user.

payload.title: The chat agent starts the subagents at the end of its turn
payload.why_not: The update depends on the chat agent remembering a rule, and the finished background task resumes the chat session, which then prints the full report.

payload.title: Two subagents: a scout judges the diagram, an updater edits it

patch.body: The scout does the slow, non-deterministic read that #vi-sysdiag-derive gives as the reason a fold cannot run on every view. The updater only runs a deterministic edit-then-check loop. It can retry safely without re-deciding anything the scout settled.
patch.why: The scout decides whether the diagram changes. The updater applies the change and rebuilds until the tile grammar passes.

Cards name the parts of the product but not the arrows between them, so the fold reads two sources. Reading cards into parts needs interpretation, not a data transformation. An agent read is slow and non-deterministic, so it cannot run on every view. The diagram text is cached and the render is not.

payload.title: An agent folds cards into nodes. Cards give the edges. The text is cached
The diagram text is stored. The picture drawn from it is not
payload.why: The agent read is slow, so its result is stored and the picture is redrawn from it on every view.
payload.body: The diagram text is a peer of the card text: stored, diffed, edited in place. It is also the base for the next redraw. See #vi-sysdiag-grain. The split of stored text and disposable picture is #vi-images.

payload.why: The cache exists because the agent fold in #vi-sysdiag-derive is too slow to run on every view.
It follows the split of text stored and image never stored.

payload.title: An agent folds cards into diagram nodes. Edges come from decided cards

patch.body:
The node fold needs judgement. No projection of card fields yields a component. #vi-graph3d decides a view; #werk-hmr decides a dev loop; #vi-edges decides a data shape. Only a reader can tell which is a part of the product, and at which level. The sort that makes this possible is #vi-sysdiag-classes.

The rest of the design sits on its own cards:

- Edges are not folded. They come from decided cards, never from the code: see #vi-sysdiag-edges.
- The fold's output is stored text, and the picture is redrawn from it: see #vi-sysdiag-cache.
- Each redraw starts from the stored text and the agent judges its scope: see #vi-sysdiag-grain. Regenerating from the card set alone is rejected, because it has nothing to be continuous with.

payload.title: Card ids on diagram elements link to cards and bound a redraw at scale

patch.body:
The ids do not drive the redraw. The agent judges its scope, see #vi-sysdiag-grain. They earn their place for two other reasons:

1. They answer "why is this box here". The element points at the cards that decided it, which is the only edge between the two graphs.
2. They are the fallback. Past the size where one read covers the diagram and the card set, the reverse closure from #vi-prop is the only way to bound the redraw. The ids must exist by then, for the reason #vi-prop gives: an edge not written at creation cannot be recovered.

#vi-prop's 6% to 11% is about recovering edges that were never written. Nothing is recovered while the changed card and the whole diagram sit in the agent's context: the affected elements are read, not inferred. The argument for a mechanical mark returns only when the diagram stops fitting.

The limit is on the diagram text and the card set, not on the picture. It applies the same to the Mermaid render and to #vi-sysdiag-svg.

Write the ids at creation. The redraw does not depend on them while one read covers the diagram.
patch.why: The ids say which cards decided an element. When the diagram outgrows one read, they also bound the redraw.

payload.finding: The node served a one-shot state fetch and the chat pane's live stream. The diagram already grouped its consumers into a map view and a chat pane, which matches the state and live boundary. The node became 'state' and 'live'.

payload.title: A run starts when the set of decided cards changes, not on a list of event types
payload.why: Only a decided card may justify diagram content, so the question is what changed among decided cards. Comparing the decided set before and after answers it directly, including an accepted ghost and a removed card.
payload.body:
The job folds the log at the last checked position and at the end, and compares the decided, live cards in each. A change is one of: a card became decided, a card stopped being decided (reopened, set open, or removed), a decided card was retitled, its why or body changed, or one of its depends_on or refines edges was added or removed.

Notes, open and proto cards, ghosts, options and sources change nothing. Each change becomes one line in the scout's brief, in the scout's own operation words.

payload.title: Start a run on a fixed list of log event types
payload.why_not: The list must repeat the fold's rules: a status event on a ghost, an accept that makes a ghost real, a remove that takes a subtree. Every new event type would need a new rule here.

payload.why: It defines what counts as the map change that #vi-sysdiag-quiet says starts the job.

payload.title: A burst of map changes gives one run, and only one run happens at a time
payload.why: One chat turn writes several events in a few seconds. A run per event would start the scout many times for one decision and let two updaters edit the same file.
payload.body: The job waits 5 seconds after the last log change, then runs. A change that arrives during a run queues exactly one more run after it, which covers every change since the last checked position.

payload.why: It sets when the background job that #vi-sysdiag-quiet describes starts and how runs queue.

payload.title: A first start takes the diagram as it stands; it does not replay the log
payload.why: The diagram was kept by hand before the job existed. Replaying thousands of events would start a run with nothing new to say and a large token cost.
payload.body: The job stores the last checked log position next to the log. With no stored position, the current end of the log is the baseline. The position survives a restart of werk serve, so changes made while it was down are checked on the next start.

payload.title: Replay the whole log on the first start
payload.why_not: Every decided card would reach the scout at once. The brief is too large to judge well, and the diagram already reflects most of it.

payload.why: The stored position is the 'before' side of the decided-set comparison that #vi-sysdiag-sync-trigger defines.

payload.title: The job runs the diagram build itself and keeps the result only on 0 errors
payload.why: The updater's report is model output. A claim of 0 errors is not proof, and a half-edited file must never stay on disk.
payload.body: Before the updater runs, the job copies the diagram source and the drawing. After the updater, it runs the build and reads the error count. On anything but 0 errors, on an updater failure, or on a crash, it puts both copies back.

payload.why: It checks the tile-grammar build that #vi-sysdiag-agents gives the updater as its finish line.

payload.title: A failed run keeps the last good diagram, shows a mark on the diagram view, and retries on the next map change
payload.why: A failure is information about the diagram, so it belongs where the diagram is, not in a chat. Retrying on a timer would spend tokens in a loop on a failure that needs a different input.
payload.body: A failed run does not move the checked position, so the next map change retries the same changes together with the new ones. The Diagram view shows a red mark with the reason on hover until a run passes. A change that touches no decided card does not clear the mark. While a run is going, the view shows that it is updating, and it reloads the drawing when a run updates it.

payload.title: Retry a failed run on a timer
payload.why_not: A failure that comes from the input repeats on every retry and spends tokens each time.

payload.why: A build that fails the check in #vi-sysdiag-sync-verify is the main failure this card handles.

payload.title: The scout may only read; only the updater may edit, and only the diagram build may run
payload.why: The job runs unattended with no one to answer a permission prompt, so each agent gets exactly the tools its job needs and nothing that can change the map.
payload.body: The scout gets file reading and search, and the one command that shows a card. The updater gets the same reading tools, file edits, and the diagram build command. Neither can run the map's write commands. Both run headless with no saved session, so they never appear in the conversation list.

payload.why: It gives each of the two subagents that #vi-sysdiag-agents defines its tool set.

payload.title: The diagram follows the decided cards in a background job inside werk serve; no chat shows it

patch.body:
werk serve runs the scout and the updater as one background job. The trigger is a change in the map, not the chat agent at the end of its turn. When a chat agent starts the subagents itself, the result of the finished background task comes back into its chat session, and the agent relays the full updater report. An instruction to stay quiet does not stop that, so the job lives outside every chat.

The updater never hands a choice to the user. A leftover it finds inside the diagram file, such as a comment that quotes an old label, it fixes in the same run. It drops anything else.

The design decisions are the cards below: what starts a run (#vi-sysdiag-sync-trigger), how runs batch and queue (#vi-sysdiag-sync-batch), where a first start begins (#vi-sysdiag-sync-baseline), how a result is checked (#vi-sysdiag-sync-verify), what a failure does (#vi-sysdiag-sync-fail), and which tools each agent gets (#vi-sysdiag-sync-tools). See #vi-sysdiag-agents for what the two subagents do.
patch.why: A diagram update is not a topic of conversation. No chat shows the subagent exchange, a file path, a process log, or a question to the user. The user can assume the diagram matches the decided cards after a short delay.

payload.title: werk status <id> decided runs the four-fact check and fails with the fixing command
payload.why: Deciding is the one state change the contract gates, so the command that makes it is where each missing fact is reported and fixed.
payload.body:
```
werk status <id> decided
```

The command moves a card to decided only if the four facts hold (#werk-contract-facts). It checks the log, not the card text.

- A missing fact makes the command fail. The message names the command that fixes it, with the card id filled in (#werk-contract-fix).
- `who`, the basis flag and the unchallenged flag are set with `werk edit` (#werk-cli-edit).
- A kill criterion is recorded with `werk kill` (#kill). One call adds one criterion.
- On a ghost, the check runs against the held edges, so the card commits as one unit (#werk-propose-new).
- `werk rederive <id> --status decided` runs the same check (#rederive-reason).
- The command never changes the text of a card (#map-frozen).

payload.title: werk edit sets who, --no-basis and --unchallenged on a card without recreating it
payload.why: A card that fails the decide check needs one missing fact recorded. Edit is the one command that records it, so the fix never costs a new card.
payload.body:
```
werk edit <id> [--who you|me|prototype] [--no-basis] [--unchallenged]
```

- `--who` sets who decides the card.
- `--no-basis` records that the card needs no depends_on target and no decided parent (#werk-contract-facts).
- `--unchallenged` records that no option was weighed against a `you` card (#werk-contract-guess).
- Each flag is a record on the card. None is a default.
- The flags apply to an open card. The text of a decided card is frozen: a change to it is a proposal, not an edit (#map-frozen, #al-diff-cli).
- The text of a ghost is frozen too. Discard it and propose it again (#werk-propose-new).

payload.why: The command reports and records the four facts that #werk-contract-facts lists.
The command reports and records the four facts that #werk-contract-facts lists.
The failure message of the command is the fix message that #werk-contract-fix defines.
Edit refuses the frozen fields because #map-frozen makes a change to them a proposal.
Edit refuses a ghost because #werk-propose-new freezes it.
The check on a ghost runs against held edges because #werk-propose-new holds them.
The decide command points at edit for the flags that record a missing fact.

Four facts must hold before a card is decided:
- `who` is set.
- A basis exists: a depends_on target or a refines parent that is decided and not stale, or `--no-basis` states that none applies. While the basis is open or stale, the card waits (#map-wait). A decided parent is a basis for its child, so a child never needs a depends_on link to its parent.
- When `who` is you, an alternative_to option node exists, or `--unchallenged` states that none was weighed. A `me` or `prototype` card needs neither.
- A kill criterion is on record (#kill-ask). `werk kill` records one. A criterion of the form no-metric or revisit states that no metric applies (#kill-shape).

payload.title: A decided card is structural, behavioural, or method. Only a structural card makes a diagram node

patch.body:
Each decided card does one of three things to the product diagram:

1. **Structural** — names a running part and makes a node. #werk-multichat is the tab strip. #vi-graph3d is the 3D view. #werk-perm-native is the ask queue.
2. **Behavioural** — constrains a part that is already drawn. It adds a citation to that node, not a box. #werk-mc-tabs and #werk-perm-mode are cited on the nodes the structural cards above make.
3. **Method** — about how the map is kept, not about the product. It makes nothing. #drained, #al-two, #vi-prop.

One card can be both method and structural: when werk builds a map rule as a running check, the check is a part of the product. #werk-contract is a rule for the map and also a check the command line runs before a card becomes decided, so it is cited on the command-line node. This is the self-reference #vi-flow warns about, and werk has more of it than any other project will.

The sort is judgement. No card field carries the class. The scout applies it on every run, see #vi-sysdiag-agents.
patch.why: The diagram's nodes are running parts, and most decided cards are not about a running part. Without the sort, method cards fold into the picture and put the map's own rules inside the product.

payload.why: The fold of cards into nodes needs the sort this card defines, to know which cards make a node at all.
The scout applies the three classes this card defines to decide whether a changed card adds a node, a citation, or nothing.

payload.title: Structural: #werk-multichat, #vi-graph3d and #werk-perm-native each make diagram nodes
payload.why: Worked cases of the structural class: each card names a part a user can see or a process that runs.
payload.finding:
#vi-graph3d makes one node, the 3D graph view, and one edge from it to the state it loads. One card, one part: the plainest case.

#werk-multichat makes or co-justifies three nodes: the tab strip, the conversation manager that runs one agent per conversation, and the per-conversation transcript store. It is the case for one decision creating several parts, which is why the map and the diagram cannot be one graph (#vi-sysdiag).

#werk-perm-native makes the ask queue: the part that holds tool calls Claude Code's own permission engine could not decide. It also co-justifies the store of always-allow rules. The card reads like a policy, but the policy is carried out by a running part, so it is structural.

payload.title: Behavioural: #werk-mc-tabs and #werk-perm-mode add a citation to a node, not a box
payload.why: Worked cases of the behavioural class: each card constrains a part that a structural card already drew.
payload.finding:
#werk-mc-tabs decides where the tab strip sits and how it looks: card-id chips in the bottom control cluster. The tab strip node exists because of #werk-multichat. #werk-mc-tabs only adds its id to that node's citation list.

#werk-perm-mode decides that auto is the only permission mode and that no flag sets it. It changes how the ask queue behaves, not whether it exists, so it is a second citation on the ask queue node beside #werk-perm-native.

Both show the test: delete the card, and the diagram keeps the same boxes and edges. Only a citation goes.

payload.title: Method: #drained, #al-two and #vi-prop are rules for keeping the map and make nothing
payload.why: Worked cases of the method class: each card is a rule about how decisions are recorded, not about the product.
payload.finding:
#drained defines when a topic is finished: settled and unchallenged is zero. #al-two says a decision is never shown with one option. #vi-prop says a change marks only the next hop of dependents. None names a part, and none appears in the diagram.

They are the trap the class exists for. werk is a tool for keeping maps, so a rule for the map reads as if it described the product. #vi-prop in particular sounds like a component — a staleness propagator — and an early hand fold of the cards did map it onto the fold function. In any other project these cards would be obviously about process.

payload.title: Method and structural at once: #werk-contract is a map rule that also runs as a check
payload.why: The worked case of a card in two classes: a map rule that werk builds as a running check.
payload.finding:
#werk-contract says a card cannot become decided until a program check passes: who, depends_on, rejected options, kill criteria. As a rule, it is about keeping the map — method. But the command line runs that check before every status change, so the check is a part of the product, and the diagram cites the card on the command-line node.

It shows the class is not a property of the card's topic. It depends on whether the decision is carried out by a running part. This overlap happens in werk because the product is the planning loop (#vi-flow); a payments project would have no such card.

payload.title: Flow counts the depends_on edges that cross from one subtree to another
payload.why: A depends_on edge between two subtrees couples them: a reopen in one marks cards in the other. The count shows which subtrees are tangled and which stand alone.
payload.body:
A cross-tree dependency is one depends_on edge whose two ends sit in different subtree rows (#vi-flowtab-subtrees). An edge inside one subtree does not count. A refines edge never counts.

At the top of the tab: the total number of cross-tree edges in the current scope.

In the subtree table: one column `in / out` per row.

- out — edges from a card in this subtree to a card outside it.
- in — edges from a card outside this subtree to a card in it.

An edge that leaves the current scope counts as out or in for its row, but not in the total, because the other end has no row.

Edges of a proposed card are held, so they do not count until the card is accepted (#werk-propose-new).

payload.why: The rows that define a subtree boundary, and the table that gets the in / out column, come from #vi-flowtab-subtrees.
Held edges of a proposed card are left out of the count, as #werk-propose-new defines.

In the subtree table (#vi-flowtab-subtrees): one `in / out` column per row, for both row settings.

- out — edges from a card in this subtree to a card outside it.
- in — edges from a card outside this subtree to a card in it.

Here an edge that leaves the scope counts too, because the row boundary is the subtree, not the scope.

patch.body:
A cross-tree dependency is one depends_on edge between two cards in different subtrees. A refines edge never counts. Edges of a proposed card are held, so they do not count until the card is accepted (#werk-propose-new).

payload.title: werk stale lists every marked card, in the order to fix them, with the reason for each mark
payload.why: A mark that nobody reads does nothing. One command shows what needs a person, without opening each card, and puts a card's basis before the card.
payload.body:
```
werk stale [<id>] [--kind stale|paused|waiting|review]
```

- Without `<id>`, the list covers the whole map. With `<id>`, it covers that card and its refines subtree.
- `--kind` keeps one kind of mark. Without it, all four kinds print.
- One line per card: the kind, the id, the title. Under it, one line with the origin of the mark, the reason of the change, and its date (#vi-prop-trace). A waiting card names the basis it waits for (#map-wait).
- Order: fix order. A card prints after the card it depends on, because a card cannot be confirmed while its basis is stale (#rederive-reason).
- `review` lists the cards that cite a disputed source (#vi-srcnode).
- The command reads the log and writes nothing. It exits 0 when the list is empty, and then prints that nothing is marked.

A person clears a mark on the card itself, with `werk rederive` (#rederive-reason).

payload.title: In a flow table, the card name opens the card on the map, and the rest of the row goes one level deeper
payload.why: A row carries two actions: read the card, or look inside it. One click target for each keeps both one click away.
payload.body:
In every flow table, the subtree table and the card list:

- A click on the id or the title switches to the map view and opens that card.
- A click anywhere else on the row makes that card the scope of the Flow tab. Every section then shows its subtree (#vi-flowtab-subtrees).

The two targets look different under the pointer. The row gets a background on hover. The id and the title get their own highlight and an underline, and the row background goes away while the pointer is on them. The user then sees which action the click starts.

In a narrow pane only the id is shown (#vi-flowtab-narrow). The id alone is then the link.

payload.why: The row click narrows the scope to the subtree rows and stats that #vi-flowtab-subtrees defines.
The card list rows that get the two click targets are the list #vi-flowtab-list defines.
The link sits on the id and title cell, which #vi-flowtab-narrow shrinks to the id alone.

payload.title: The whole row opens the card on the map
payload.why_not: Then a row has no way to go deeper, and the table cannot be used to walk down the tree.

payload.title: Each view has its own address, so Back and Forward move between places in that view
payload.why: With the view kept outside the address, Back in Flow jumps to the previous map card. The Back button then means nothing in any view but the map, and a reload or a shared link can open the wrong view.
payload.body:
Addresses:

- `/map/<id>` — the map with that card open. `/map` opens the home card.
- `/flow` and `/flow/<id>` — Flow, scoped to the whole map or to that card's subtree.
- `/graph`, `/diagram`, `/board` — the other views.

Back and Forward move through these addresses. A switch between views adds one entry. In Flow, a row click that goes one level deeper adds one entry, so Back goes up one level (#vi-flowtab-click).

Filters, sort order, and the Subtrees row setting stay out of the address. They are display settings, not places.

A `#id` link in a card or in the chat opens `/map/<id>` from any view. An old address `/#id` opens `/map/<id>`.

The server answers every view address with the app.

The open-card line in the chat (#werk-card-blind) names the card in the current address: the map card, or the Flow scope. A view with no card in its address keeps the last card named.

payload.why: The /flow address and its scope come from the Flow tab that #vi-flowtab defines.
The set of views that get an address includes the board that #vi-board adds.
Back in Flow undoes the go-deeper row click that #vi-flowtab-click defines.
The chat's open-card line, defined in #werk-card-blind, now reads its card from the address.

payload.title: Hash routes: #/map/<id>, #/flow/<id>
payload.why_not: They work with no server change, but the whole place is one fragment after the hash. A path such as /flow/<id> is an address a person reads, types, and shares as it is.

payload.title: Keep the view in browser storage and push a history entry on each view switch
payload.why_not: Back would work, but the address still does not name the view. A reload or a shared link opens whatever view the browser last stored.

criterion.text: I use Back and Forward in each view. If a step lands somewhere I did not expect, the address scheme is wrong.
