`werk edit` sets who, `--no-basis` and `--unchallenged` on a card without recreating it
`werk stale` lists every marked card, in the order to fix them, with the reason for each mark
Breadcrumbs stay one line high; hover shows the whole path
payload.why: A path that wraps makes the header grow with tree depth and moves every view below it. A fixed height keeps the layout still at any depth.
payload.body:
The breadcrumbs above the views are one line high at every depth.

- The last two segments always show. A third shows when the left pane is at least 700px wide. The pane width counts, not the window width, because the chat pane takes space beside it.
- A `…` stands in for the hidden ancestors.
- Each segment is cut with an ellipsis. No segment wraps to a second line.
- Hover over the breadcrumbs opens the full path as an overlay above the header. The overlay wraps. It does not push the layout. Each segment in it opens its card.
- A path of two segments or fewer has no overlay, because nothing is hidden.

payload.title: Wrap the breadcrumbs onto more lines
payload.why_not: The header grows with depth and shifts the map, the graph, and the other views down on every navigation.

criterion.text: Open a card five levels deep. If the header height changes, or the hover path hides a segment, the decision fails.

payload.title: Breadcrumbs show the path from the root to the open card
payload.why: A card sits deep in a tree of refinements. The path tells you where you are and gives one click to any level above.
payload.body:
Breadcrumbs are the list of cards from the root down to the card open on the map. Each card refines the one before it.

- Every segment above the open card is a button. A click opens that card on the map.
- The last segment is the open card. It is bold and does not click.
- Segments are separated by `›`.
- The path changes when the open card changes, by click, by a `#id` link, or by the address (#vi-routes).
- Where they sit is #vi-crumbs-place. How much of the path shows is #vi-crumbs-line.

payload.title: A Back control that returns to the previous card
payload.why_not: Back steps through history, not through the tree. It cannot jump to a chosen ancestor and it does not show where the card sits.

payload.title: Breadcrumbs sit in the sticky header, above the counts and the view tabs
payload.why: The path is needed in every view and at every scroll position. The header is the one place that stays on screen and is shared by all views.
payload.body:
The breadcrumbs are the first row of the header on the left pane. Below them are the whole-map counts and the Map, Graph, Diagram and Board tabs. The header sticks to the top, so the path stays visible while a card scrolls.

The path is that of the card open on the map (#vi-crumbs). A view with no card in its address keeps the last card named (#vi-routes).

payload.why: The path follows the card named in the address, which #vi-routes defines.

payload.title: Breadcrumbs inside the card, above its title
payload.why_not: The path scrolls away with the card and is absent from the graph, diagram and board views.

criterion.text: Scroll a long card and switch to the Graph tab. If the path is not on screen in both, the decision fails.

payload.title: Breadcrumbs stay one line high; hover shows the whole path
payload.why: A path that wraps makes the header grow with tree depth and moves every view below it. A fixed height keeps the layout still at any depth.
payload.body:
The breadcrumbs are one line high at every depth.

- The last two segments always show. A third shows when the left pane is at least 700px wide. The pane width counts, not the window width, because the chat pane takes space beside it.
- A `…` stands in for the hidden ancestors.
- Each segment is cut with an ellipsis. No segment wraps to a second line.
- Hover over the breadcrumbs opens the full path as an overlay above the header. The overlay wraps and does not push the layout. Each segment in it opens its card.
- A path of two segments or fewer has no overlay, because nothing is hidden.

payload.why: The overlay opens over the header row that #vi-crumbs-place fixes.

payload.title: Wrap the breadcrumbs onto more lines
payload.why_not: The header grows with depth and shifts the map, the graph, and the other views down on every navigation.

criterion.text: Open a card five levels deep. If the header height changes, or the hover path hides a segment, the decision fails.

payload.title: The screen is a map pane on the left and a chat pane on the right
payload.why: The map redraws while the reply streams in, so both stay in view side by side. Each pane keeps its own controls, so neither moves when the other changes.
payload.body:
Two panes sit side by side.

**Left pane: the map.** A sticky header over a scrolling body.
1. Breadcrumbs, one row (#vi-crumbs-place).
2. A row with the whole-map counts, the view tabs, a jump-to-card search box, and a live marker.
3. The body is the view the tab picks. The views and their addresses are in #vi-routes.

**Right pane: chat.** The transcript, then the composer with the open-card chip, then the conversation tab strip at the bottom (#werk-mc-tabs). The pane itself is #werk-pane.

The width of the left pane, not the window, decides how views adapt. Rules for a narrow pane live on the cards of each view.

payload.why: The right pane is the chat pane that #werk-pane defines.
The view tabs in the left header are the views that #vi-routes gives addresses.
The tab strip at the bottom of the right pane is the one #werk-mc-tabs defines.
The header row it fills belongs to the left pane that #vi-layout defines.

payload.title: Chat as a drawer or overlay that opens over the map
payload.why_not: The drawer hides the part of the map that the reply is changing, so the person cannot read the reply and watch the map redraw at the same time.

criterion.text: Send a message that edits a card. If the redraw is out of view while the reply streams, the decision fails.

patch.body:
v0 starts in a new, empty repository. Nothing is ported from the prototype code.

- The spec is the decided cards that #werk depends on, not the prototype code.
- The prototype code is a reference. A builder may read it to see how a decided behaviour looks. It does not copy it.
- The stack is #werk-stack: React + Vite for the client, inside the Bun server from #werk-hmr. Vite transforms the client, so v0 has a client build step.

Why not extend the prototype: it works well as a product, but its code is messy. A clean build tests whether the decided cards are enough to rebuild the behaviour.

Kill criterion: the from-scratch v0 is reopened for reconsideration if its result is too far from the prototype's behaviour. The prototype's behaviour is good, so it sets the bar. Then the alternative is to extend the prototype code (see the option on this card).

criterion.text: I build v0 from scratch and compare it with the prototype. If v0's behaviour is too far from the prototype's, I reconsider and extend the prototype instead.

payload.title: A backtick span in a card title renders as code wherever the title is a heading or a row
payload.why: Card titles name commands, and a command in plain text reads as a word. Code styling marks it as something a person types.
payload.body: A title may contain a span between backticks. The map shows the span in code style in the tree, the card header, the cards below, the basis list and the breadcrumbs. The backtick characters are not shown. The diff of a pending title stays plain text so the change is readable. Search results, the browser tab title and confirmation prompts show the title as plain text.

criterion.text: I open a card whose title has a backtick span and see code style in each listed place

payload.title: A card reads in three layers: the title, the why, and the body
payload.why: The title tells a reader what the card is about. The why gives most of the understanding, so a reader can stop there. The body holds the details for the reader who needs to act.
payload.body:
**Title**

- A plain sentence with a subject and a verb. More words are fine when they make it easier to read.
- One idea. A second clause moves down to the why.
- High level: no mechanism, no tool or subagent names, no "now".
- Name the members of a small set, not a slogan: "Four link types: refines, depends_on, supported_by, alternative_to".

**Why**

- Two or three short sentences. A reader who stops here understands about 80% of the card.
- It gives the reason in plain causal steps, not as an aphorism.
- No card references and no commands. Those go in the body.

**Body**

- Short paragraphs and bullet lists. One item or one option per bullet.
- References to other cards, examples, and ASCII diagrams go here.
- A general overview. It does not repeat the titles of subcards, because the tree shows them.
- Every paragraph helps a reader decide or act. A paragraph that does not is cut.
- A rejected alternative is an option node, not prose.

**Every layer**

- No coined phrases. "Fans out a calm mark" becomes "puts a grey mark on the cards that depend on it".
- When a layer is too long, its content moves down one level: title, then why, then body, then a subcard.

Example:

```
WRONG  title: Four facts gate decided, each with a written escape hatch
       why:   A silent default hides a missing fact. An escape hatch turns the gap into a record.

RIGHT  title: A card needs four facts before it is decided
       why:   A missing fact must not hide behind a default. A fact can be waived, but the waiver is written down.
```

See #werk-wording for what a card must not contain: session narration, edit history, and code names.

payload.why: the content rules every layer follows: no session narration, no edit history, no code names

payload.title: Short, compressed titles and a dense why, even if a reader must decode them
payload.why_not: Compressed coined phrases read as cryptic. A cold reader cannot tell what the card decides without opening the body.

criterion.text: Cards written under this rule still get reword requests for cryptic titles or a long why

payload.title: `werk add` proposes a card, an option or a source as a ghost
payload.why: Every new node enters the map through one command, so the ghost rule holds for every kind.
payload.body:
```
werk add <id> --title "..." [--why "..."] [--body "..."] [--parent <id>]
         [--kind card|option|source] [--status open|proto] [--who you|me|prototype]
         [--why_not "..."]              for --kind option
         [--url ...] [--finding ...]    for --kind source
```

- The command prints "proposed". No flag skips the ghost (#werk-propose-new).
- `--status decided` is refused. A card reaches decided only through `werk status` (#werk-contract-when).
- A second `werk add` with the same id fails. `werk edit --body`, `werk edit --why` and `werk retitle` refuse on a ghost. `werk link`, `werk status` and `werk edit --who` work on a ghost.
- A rejected option takes two commands: `werk add <id>:opt0 --kind option --title "..." --why_not "..."`, then `werk link <id>:opt0 <id> --type alternative_to` (#ro-live, #ro-optparent).

payload.why: The command stages every kind as a ghost and refuses a word change on one, as this card requires.
The refusal of --status decided comes from the rule that decided is reached only through the decide check.
The option form of the command records the rejected alternative that this card requires.
The option recipe links by alternative_to only, because this card forbids a refines link from an option.

criterion.text: I propose a card, an option and a source with the command, and see if each one shows as a ghost and refuses a word change.

payload.title: `werk propose`, `werk accept` and `werk discard` stage, commit and drop a change
payload.why: A staged change needs one command to stage it, one to commit it and one to drop it. The ✓ in the map runs the same accept.
payload.body:
```
werk propose <id> [--title "..."] [--why "..."] [--ops '[{"tag": ...}]']
werk accept <id> --actor you
werk discard <id>
```

- `--ops` is a JSON list. A tag is `elaborated` {old, new}, `new` {new}, or `removed` {old}.
- Every block of the current body must be the `old` of an op. Keep a block unchanged with an `elaborated` op whose old and new are equal. Otherwise the command fails and prints the blocks at risk (#al-diff-cli-cover).
- An `old` that does not quote a real block is shown as removed plus new, never trusted (#al-diff-cli).
- `werk accept` fails without `--actor you`. The ✓ in the map appends the same event (#al-diff-cli-btn). Accepting a ghost also accepts its ghost refines parents, options and sources (#werk-propose-new).
- `werk discard` on a ghost also drops its ghost children.

payload.why: The three commands write the proposed, accepted and discarded events that this card defines.
The command refuses an op list that leaves a block unnamed, as this card requires.
The ✓ in the map and the accept command append the same event.
Accept and discard of a ghost carry its ghost parents, options and children, as this card defines.

criterion.text: I stage a change with the command, then accept it in the map, and see if the diff matches the ops and no block is lost.

payload.title: `werk reopen` takes a reason, and `werk rederive` clears the mark on one card
payload.why: The reason decides which mark a reopen puts on the dependent cards, so it is typed at the reopen, not inferred later.
payload.body:
```
werk reopen <id> [--reason postponed|invalidated|rejected] [--why "..."]
werk rederive <id> [--status decided]
```

- `--reason` defaults to `invalidated`. `postponed` marks the dependent cards paused. `invalidated` and `rejected` mark them stale (#pr-wf-paused).
- `--why` is the text that the stale trace shows.
- `werk rederive` clears the mark on one card (#vi-prop). With `--status decided` it runs the same check as `werk status <id> decided`.

payload.why: The three reason values and the mark each one puts on dependent cards come from this card.
The rederive command clears one card's mark, which is the review step this card defines.

criterion.text: I reopen a card with each reason, and see if the dependent cards get the mark that the reason card names.

payload.title: `werk show` prints one card with its rollup, its links and the trace of each mark
payload.why: The agent has no map view. One command gives it what the card view gives a person.
payload.body:
```
werk show [<id>]
```

- The rollup prints as one line for the card, and again on each incoming refines link, so a branch can be ranked before it is opened (#rollup).
- A flagged depends_on row carries the reopen reason, date and text, or a pointer to the card further upstream (#werk-depwhy).
- Each stale or paused mark prints its trace (#vi-prop-trace).

payload.why: The command prints the rollup that this card defines, on the card and on each child.
The command prints the reopen reason under a flagged depends_on row, as this card defines.
The command prints the trace of each mark that this card defines.

criterion.text: I run the command on a stale card, and see if I can tell why it is marked without opening the map.

payload.title: `werk convos`, `werk recall` and `werk quote` read and cite another conversation
payload.why: werk stores the session id of every conversation, so the commands go straight to the right transcript instead of a search.
payload.body:
```
werk convos
werk recall <#card|session|name> [--grep "term" ...] [--context 2] [--tail 20]
            [--tools] [--thinking] [--max-chars 2000] [--raw]
werk quote <card-id> <#card|session|name> --text "..."
```

- `werk convos` prints one line per conversation: name, home card, session id, turn count and last activity.
- `werk recall` takes a conversation name, a session id or prefix, or a card id. A card id with two conversations fails as ambiguous.
- `--grep` takes a case-insensitive pattern and repeats. A message must match every pattern. `--context` adds the messages on each side of a hit.
- Tool calls and thinking stay hidden without `--tools` or `--thinking`. `--raw` reads the Claude Code transcript instead of werk's own.
- `werk quote` fails when the text is not an exact match, or matches more than one message (#werk-excerpt).

payload.why: The list and the read commands carry out the cross-conversation lookup that this card defines.
The quote command extracts the verbatim excerpt that this card requires, and fails on an inexact match.

criterion.text: I ask the agent about another conversation, and see if it finds and quotes the right message with these commands.

payload.title: `werk say` writes a note on a card's thread, and `werk inbox` reads the notes
payload.why: The agent answers on the card that the person reads, not only in the chat.
payload.body:
```
werk say <id> "..."
werk inbox [--since <seq>] [-n 20]
```

- `werk say` appends one note to the card's thread. The map shows it on the card.
- `werk inbox` prints the notes typed in the map. `--since` starts after one log position. `-n` caps the count.

payload.why: The two commands read and write the card thread through which the agent answers, as this card defines.

criterion.text: I type a note on a card, and see if the agent reads it and answers on the same card.

payload.title: `werk sample`, `werk sample-options` and `werk prototype` run samples and prototype builds
payload.why: Parallel runs, caps and isolation live in code, so the agent makes one call per run and never nests subagents.
payload.body:
```
werk sample --brief-file <path> [--n 3] [--tier plan|output] [--timeout 300]
werk sample-options <target-id> "<brief>" [--n 3] [--timeout 300]
werk prototype --fork <question-id> | --fork-file <path> [--tier output|worktree] [--timeout 600]
```

- `werk sample` writes nothing to the map. It prints the forks as JSON. A read-only subagent uses this command.
- `werk sample-options` writes each fork to the map: one open card per fork under the target, one option per sampled choice.
- `--n` caps at 5. `--timeout` caps at 900 seconds. The caps are in code.
- `werk sample` rejects the worktree tier. That tier belongs to `werk prototype` (#al-sample-build-isolation).
- `werk prototype` builds one artifact per option, in parallel, and proposes each result as a source on its option (#al-sample-proto-agent).

payload.why: The sample commands run the parallel, capped sampling that this card defines.
The prototype command builds one artifact per option in parallel, as this card defines.
The tier flags and the refusal of the worktree tier for sampling follow the isolation rule of this card.

criterion.text: I run a sample and a prototype on one fork, and see if each run stays inside its tier and its caps.

payload.title: `werk plan`, `werk loop`, `werk build`, `werk run`, `werk gate` and `werk ticket` start the build stages
payload.why: Each build stage is one command that a person or an agent starts, so a stage runs the same way from the terminal and from the board.
payload.body:
```
werk plan <subtree-id> [--timeout 600] [--run <id>] [--silence 60]
werk loop "<brief>" --check "..." [--card <id> ...] [--cap 5] [--timeout 600]
werk build <ticket-id> [--cap 5] [--timeout 600] [--silence 60] [--check-timeout 300]
werk run <plan-run> [the flags of werk build]
werk gate <plan-run> [approve --actor you]
werk ticket list | move <id> blocked|ready --reason "..." | archive <id> | restore <id> | import <plan-run>
```

- `werk plan` turns a decided subtree into a spec and tickets (#st-spec). It exits 1 when a set check fails.
- `werk loop` builds one brief in a throwaway worktree, one fresh agent per pass (#lp-stateless).
- `werk build` runs the builder loop on one ticket (#st-build-ticket). `--cap` is the retry cap, 5 by default.
- `werk run` runs the merge loop over one plan run (#st-build-run-mechanics). Running it again resumes.
- `werk gate <plan-run> approve` passes G2 and needs `--actor you` (#st-gates).
- `werk ticket` moves, archives, restores and imports tickets on the board (#werk-board-control). A move needs `--reason`. An import makes ids as `werk plan` does, and adds nothing on a second run.

payload.why: The plan command writes the spec and tickets that this card defines.
The loop command runs the stateless passes that this card defines.
The build command runs the builder loop and its retry cap from this card.
The run command drives the merge loop and resumes it, as this card defines.
The gate command passes G2, which only a person may do under this card.
The ticket commands make the agent's board moves that this card allows.

criterion.text: I plan, build and run one small subtree with these commands, and see if each stage starts from one command and stops where its card says.

payload.title: `werk serve` starts the map and the chat pane, one server per .werk directory
payload.why: The server holds the conversation, the tool allowlist and the lock, so its flags set those and nothing else.
payload.body:
```
werk serve [--port 4000] [--allow "Read,Edit,Bash"] [--new]
```

- Without `--new`, the server resumes the stored conversation. `--new` starts a fresh one (#werk-resume).
- `--allow` narrows the tools of the pane's agent (#werk-edits).
- No flag sets the permission mode. The mode is always auto (#werk-perm-mode).
- A second `werk serve` on the same .werk directory refuses to start. Set WERK_LOG to run a second instance on purpose (#werk-onelock).
- Start the server in a shell where `claude` is logged in (#werk-authenv).

payload.why: The default resume and the --new flag come from the resume rule of this card.
The --allow flag narrows the default allowlist that this card defines.
The command has no permission-mode flag because this card fixes the mode to auto.
The command takes the one-server lock that this card requires.
The command must start in a logged-in shell, because the agent takes its credentials from that shell.

criterion.text: I start the server twice on one directory and once with --new, and see if the lock and the fresh start behave as written.

ops.old: A pipeline has steps and rules. "Run the checks." "If they fail, try again up to five times." "A ticket moves to Done only with a linked pull request." Each rule lives in one of two places: in a skill file that an agent reads, or in a program that runs it.
ops.new: A pipeline has steps and rules. "Run the checks." "If they fail, try again up to five times." "A ticket moves to Done only with a linked pull request." Each rule lives in one of two places: in a skill file that an agent reads, or in a program that runs it.

ops.old: This card puts the rules in a program, a small TypeScript CLI. The state machine of the records, the checks on each state change, the tracker adapter, the rubric runner, and the loop controller live there. A skill file is a thin wrapper. It names the command to run and holds no rule of its own.
ops.new: This card puts the rules in a program, a small TypeScript CLI. The state machine of the records, the checks on each state change, the tracker adapter, the rubric runner, and the loop controller live there. A skill file is a thin wrapper. It names the command to run and holds no rule of its own.

ops.old: ## The two places
ops.new: ## The two places

ops.old:
| | Skill files (#pr-logic:opt0) | A program (this card) |
|---|---|---|
| Where a rule lives | Markdown text the agent reads | Code in the CLI |
| Who runs a loop | The agent reads "retry five times" and does it | The program counts to five |
| What the agent does | Every step | Only the steps that need judgement |
| An agent forgets a rule | Nothing stops it | The program refuses the action |
| Cost of a change | Edit a sentence | Edit code and its tests |
| Runs outside one agent harness | No | Yes |
ops.new:
| | Skill files (#pr-logic:opt0) | A program (this card) |
|---|---|---|
| Where a rule lives | Markdown text the agent reads | Code in the CLI |
| Who runs a loop | The agent reads "retry five times" and does it | The program counts to five |
| What the agent does | Every step | Only the steps that need judgement |
| An agent forgets a rule | Nothing stops it | The program refuses the action |
| Cost of a change | Edit a sentence | Edit code and its tests |
| Runs outside one agent harness | No | Yes |

ops.old: ## The boundary
ops.new: ## The boundary

ops.old: A step goes in the program if the same input must always give the same result. Examples: a state change, a staleness walk, a contract check, a retry cap, a time limit, a merge.
ops.new: A step goes in the program if the same input must always give the same result. Examples: a state change, a staleness walk, a contract check, a retry cap, a time limit, a merge.

ops.old: A step goes in a prompt if it needs judgement. Examples: writing a spec, grading against a rubric, reviewing a diff, classifying a stuck agent.
ops.new: A step goes in a prompt if it needs judgement. Examples: writing a spec, grading against a rubric, reviewing a diff, classifying a stuck agent.

ops.old: The program calls the prompt and parses the answer. The prompt returns an answer. The program decides what happens next.
ops.new: The program calls the prompt and parses the answer. The prompt returns an answer. The program decides what happens next.

ops.old: ## A prompt holds no control flow
ops.new: ## A prompt holds no control flow

ops.old: A prompt is text that the program builds and sends. The sentence "if the checks fail, retry three times" is a loop. A loop is code, so it goes in the program, not in the prompt.
ops.new: A prompt is text that the program builds and sends. The sentence "if the checks fail, retry three times" is a loop. A loop is code, so it goes in the program, not in the prompt.

ops.old: ## Why
ops.new: ## Why

ops.old: An agent follows a rule in prose most of the time. A product needs the rule followed every time (#pr-gate). A prompt file also runs only inside one agent harness, so a pipeline made of skills cannot become a standalone product (#product).
ops.new: An agent follows a rule in prose most of the time. A product needs the rule followed every time (#pr-gate). A prompt file also runs only inside one agent harness, so a pipeline made of skills cannot become a standalone product (#product).

ops.old: ## Examples
ops.new: ## Examples

ops.old: Example project, werk: `werk status <id> decided` refuses a card that has no `depends_on` edge or no kill criterion, and prints the command that fixes it. As prose in `AGENTS.md`, the same rule was skipped twice: #ro-unchal and #vi-backend.
ops.new: Example project, werk: the decide check (#werk-contract) refuses a card that has no `depends_on` edge or no kill criterion, and prints the command that fixes it. As prose in `AGENTS.md`, the same rule was skipped twice: #ro-unchal and #vi-backend.

ops.old: Example project, werk: `werk build` runs the checks, caps the passes, and enforces the silence limit in code. The builder agent writes code, the grader grades, and the reviewers review. None of them decides whether another pass runs.
ops.new: Example project, werk: the builder loop (#st-build-ticket) runs the checks, caps the passes, and enforces the silence limit in code. The builder agent writes code, the grader grades, and the reviewers review. None of them decides whether another pass runs.

ops.old: ## Scope
ops.new: ## Scope

ops.old: This card says where the logic lives. It does not say when the standalone engine is built. That timing is #pr-now. The engine's adapters are #pr-iface.
ops.new: This card says where the logic lives. It does not say when the standalone engine is built. That timing is #pr-now. The engine's adapters are #pr-iface.

ops.old: One fresh agent per pass. Give it the brief, the decision, the rubric, and the last failure. It does one unit of work and exits. The repository is the memory.
ops.new: One fresh agent per pass. Give it the brief, the decision, the rubric, and the last failure. It does one unit of work and exits. The repository is the memory.

ops.old: This changes the engine's shape: no agent lives longer than one pass.
ops.new: This changes the engine's shape: no agent lives longer than one pass.

ops.old: **How a pass works** (`werk loop`, `src/loop.ts`):
ops.new: **How a pass works:**

ops.old:
1. The loop makes one worktree from a snapshot of the working tree.
2. Pass n starts a fresh `claude -p` in the worktree. The prompt holds the brief, the decided cards in its depends_on closure, and the last failure: the failed command and the end of its output, cut to about 4,000 characters.
3. When the agent exits, the loop commits the worktree as "pass n". The next agent reads the history with `git log` and `git diff`, and gets nothing else.
4. The loop runs the checks. The loop's own run is the verdict, even if the agent ran the checks itself.
5. All green: stop. Red: save the failure and go to step 2. At the cap: stop and keep the branch.
6. The loop writes one line per pass to `.werk/runs/<id>.jsonl`: check results, time, and cost.
ops.new:
1. The loop makes one worktree from a snapshot of the working tree.
2. Pass n starts a fresh `claude -p` in the worktree. The prompt holds the brief, the decided cards in its depends_on closure, and the last failure: the failed command and the end of its output, cut to about 4,000 characters.
3. When the agent exits, the loop commits the worktree as "pass n". The next agent reads the history with `git log` and `git diff`, and gets nothing else.
4. The loop runs the checks. The loop's own run is the verdict, even if the agent ran the checks itself.
5. All green: stop. Red: save the failure and go to step 2. At the cap: stop and keep the branch.
6. The loop writes one line per pass to `.werk/runs/<id>.jsonl`: check results, time, and cost.

ops.old: **Evidence.** The research sources (#ralph, #tdp) support fresh passes. Two smoke runs went green in one and two passes. The planned comparison against one long session on real tickets did not run.
ops.new: **Evidence.** The research sources (#ralph, #tdp) support fresh passes. Two smoke runs went green in one and two passes. The planned comparison against one long session on real tickets did not run.

ops.old: **One mode only.** The loop has no long-session mode. The long session (#lp-stateless:long) is the fallback of the kill criterion. It is built again only when that criterion fires.
ops.new: **One mode only.** The loop has no long-session mode. The long session (#lp-stateless:long) is the fallback of the kill criterion. It is built again only when that criterion fires.

ops.old: The agent decides the level of every card it writes: the parent, and whether to promote or demote it with werk move. It does not ask first.
ops.new: The agent decides the level of every card it writes: the parent, and whether to promote or demote it. It does not ask first.

ops.old: The person refines the tree afterwards. They ask for a reposition in chat, and the agent runs the move.

ops.new: ## The difference

ops.old:
1. **Propagation.** Wayfinder's blocking is a *scheduling* edge: what is takeable next. It is not a truth edge. Closing a ticket never marks a downstream decision suspect — the skill only says "if the decision invalidates other parts of the map, update or delete those tickets," which is an instruction to a model, and #vi-prop measured that at 6–11% recall. werk's `depends_on` is a truth edge and `reopen` walks the closure. This is the whole reason the logic is in a program — see #pr-logic.
2. **Contrast.** Wayfinder records only the answer, in a resolution comment. The rejected alternative is gone. werk records it as an `option` node with `--why_not` and an `alternative_to` edge, and `unchallenged` counts what was never weighed — see #ro-unchal.
3. **Shared gaze.** Wayfinder's map is text the agent reads. werk's map is open next to the chat, and the agent is told which card the user is looking at every turn — see #werk-card-blind, #visual.
4. **Gates.** A skill cannot refuse. werk's contract check lives in the CLI and blocks `decided` — see #werk-contract.
5. **Grain.** A wayfinder ticket is sized to one 100K-token session. A werk card is one decision with one why.
6. **Method of alignment.** Wayfinder's default type is `grilling` — conversation, asking. #align holds that asking is the weak instrument and showing variants is the strong one.

payload.title: The merge loop drives one run: a temporary merge worktree, a guarded branch move, and a stop when a build stays red

ops.old:

- A ticket's retry cap counts passes across all its builds, so it also bounds the trips between the builder and the merge queue.

patch.body:
**Scope.** Both places count the open card and everything below it. On the root card that is the whole map. A card with no children shows no counts.

**Dot.** A filled circle in a status color: amber for open, blue for proto, green for decided. Every card in the subtree has exactly one status, so the three dot numbers add up to the total.

**Ring.** A hollow circle that marks a flag, not a status: purple for unchallenged, red for stale, grey for paused. A flag cuts across status, so a ring number is not part of the sum. The unchallenged number is a bare count. Its hover title gives the ratio to the decided cards.

**Order.** The total, then the dots (open, proto, decided), then the rings (unchallenged, stale, paused). A zero is left out.

**Two forms.**
1. The header strip is the short form: bare numbers, no words. Each number has a hover title that names it, such as '10 open'. The total's title names the scope.
2. The line on the card is the long form: the same dots, rings, colors and order, each number followed by its word, under a segmented bar in the status colors.
patch.why: One scheme for counts means a reader learns it once. The header strip is the short form of the line on the card.

patch.body:
**Scope.** Both places count the open card and everything below it. On the root card that is the whole map. A card with no children shows no counts.

**Dot.** A filled circle in a status color: amber for open, blue for proto, green for decided. Every card in the subtree has exactly one status, so the three dot numbers add up to the total.

**Ring.** A hollow circle that marks a flag, not a status: purple for unchallenged, red for stale, grey for paused. A flag cuts across status, so a ring number is not part of the sum.

**Order.** The total, then the dots (open, proto, decided), then the rings (unchallenged, stale, paused). A zero is left out.

**Two forms.** The header strip is the short form, see #vi-counts-header. The line on the card is the long form, see #vi-counts-card.

payload.title: Evidence: single-child parents, measured on the map as of log event 5067
payload.why: The rule against single-child chains rests on a count of the map. A reader who sees the map change can compare against this snapshot.
payload.body:
**Point of measurement.** The map as folded at log event 5067, recorded on 2026-10-09 at 23:44 UTC. Fold the log up to that event to reproduce the counts. Cards added or moved after it are not in them.

**Result at that point.** 42 of 110 parents had exactly one child card. Four of those started a chain of three or more single-child cards.

**Cards named as examples.** #ro-unchal, #ro-live and #ro-optparent. These were the examples when the figures were recorded. Their parents then were the cards they refine today: #rollup, #map-card and #relations. Compare each card's present parent and child count with that. A change means the example no longer shows the pattern.

**What a change means for the rule.** If the share of single-child parents falls well below 42 of 110, or the named chains are merged, the rule has worked and the evidence is spent. If it holds or grows, the agent is not following the rule.

The agent decides the level of every card it writes: the parent, and whether to promote or demote it. It does not ask first.

The person refines the tree afterwards. They ask for a reposition in chat, and the agent runs the move.

payload.title: A failed process probe leaves a running call unknown, not frozen

patch.body:
When the process probe cannot read the process table, the overseer treats the sample as unknown. The sample does not count toward the flat CPU time of #lp-overseer-inflight, and it cancels nothing.

The probe tells a failed read apart from a read that found no process. Only a read that ran can report that a call has no process of its own.

**What still stops a real stall.** While a tool call runs, the silence rule of #lp-overseer-silence does not fire. So during a probe failure, the only stop is the wall-clock cap on the pass (#al-sample-budget). A stalled pass runs to that cap, not to the 60-second mark.

**The cost, stated.** A real stall during a probe failure costs up to one full cap of time and tokens. Cancelling instead costs a pass that may be working, and charges the ticket a retry for a fault in werk's own probe.

The overseer records each failed probe as an event. A pass that ends at the cap then shows that the probe was blind.
patch.why: A probe that cannot read the process table gives no evidence about the call. Reading its empty answer as a frozen call with no process cancels a pass that may be working.

payload.title: Unknown: ignore the sample and let the wall-clock cap decide

payload.why: During a probe failure, the wall-clock cap on the pass is the only stop for a real stall.

criterion.text: A pass ends at the wall-clock cap, and every probe sample in its last 60 seconds failed.

payload.title: The Flow tab shows the share of process probe samples that failed
payload.why: It is the measure for the metric kill criterion of #lp-overseer-psfail. When the probe fails often, more passes run blind to the wall-clock cap. The number comes from the pass event streams, not from a hand count.
payload.body:
- Each pass records how many probe samples it took and how many of them failed. The probe samples only while a tool call runs.
- The share is the failed samples over all samples, summed over the passes in the window.
- The threshold, window, and minimum sample come from the metric kill criterion of #lp-overseer-psfail.
- The gauge shows when the Flow scope contains #lp-overseer-psfail. Probe samples belong to passes, not to cards, so every scope that shows the gauge counts every pass.
- Colour follows the state: red fires, green holds, grey not enough data.

payload.why: The gauge is a section of the Flow tab that #vi-flowtab defines.

payload.title: Record every probe sample as its own event
payload.why_not: One line every few seconds for each running call floods the pass event stream that the board reads. Two counts per pass answer the same question.

criterion.text: A view over counts that already exist. It is cheap to change.

criterion.source: the probe counts each pass records in its event stream
criterion.metric: share of process probe samples that failed

payload.title: Each stage records its cost in dollars and wall time, at the finest grain it can attribute
payload.why: Tokens alone mislead: a cache read costs about a tenth of a fresh input token. Dollars add up across stages and across models. Token counts do not.
payload.body:
- **Unit.** Dollars, with input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens as the breakdown. Wall time beside it.
- **Plan, card refinement: per card.** Each conversation has a home card (#werk-mc-split), and each turn names the card that is open on the map. So each turn's cost goes to one card. A turn with no card goes to its day.
- **Plan, spec and tickets: per spec** (#st-spec).
- **Build: per ticket**, the effort that #lp-trend-primary records. The merge loop's cost is per run (#st-build-run).
- **Size.** Each cost is also shown per unit of size: per decided card in plan, per spec story in build (#lp-trend-size).
- **Shape.** A distribution: median, 90th percentile, maximum. Not a mean, because one runaway ticket hides in a mean.
- **Threshold.** None at first. The first 10 tickets and the first 30 days of card refinement set the base.

payload.why: Per-card plan cost uses the home card and the per-turn open card of each conversation.
Build cost per ticket is the effort that this card already records.
Build cost per unit of size uses spec stories as the size.
Spec-and-ticket cost is attributed per spec, the unit this card defines.

payload.title: Plan cost as one daily total across all chats
payload.why_not: Each conversation already has a home card and a per-turn open card, so per-card cost costs no more to collect. A daily total cannot show which cards were expensive.

payload.title: Raw token counts as the unit of cost
payload.why_not: Cache reads, cache writes, input and output tokens have different prices, and different models have different prices. A token sum compares unlike things.

payload.title: Each failed pass records which gate failed it, and the cause
payload.why: A pass count says how often the loop failed, not what to fix. A fail from a spec gap needs a plan fix, and a fail from a flaky check needs a check fix. Neither is a builder mistake.
payload.body:
**Gate.** Each fail names its gate:
- a check, by name: type check, lint, unit test, and so on (#lp-checks)
- the grader, with the card the diff failed against (#lp-prod-judge)
- a review area, with the finding's severity (#lp-prod-review)
- the merge loop, for a conflict with another ticket (#st-build-run)

**Cause.** Each fail gets one cause: builder error, spec gap, flaky check, or false finding. A false finding is one that passes on the next pass with no change to the code it names. The next builder or a classifier sets the cause.

**Derived numbers.**
- first-pass success rate
- passes per ticket, split by cause
- cap-hit rate: the share of tickets that reach the retry cap (#st-build-ticket)

**Starting thresholds.** These are guesses until data exists.
- A cap-hit rate above 10% of tickets points at ticket size or spec quality, not at the builder.
- One finding type that fails three tickets in a row becomes a check or a rubric line (#ms-rubric).
- A false-finding share above 20% for one reviewer or the grader means its prompt needs a fix.

payload.why: It classifies the fails of the builder loop and uses its retry cap for the cap-hit rate.
A check fail is named by the check, one command each, as this card defines.
A grader fail names the card the diff failed against, which is how this grader judges.
A review fail carries the area and severity that this review assigns.
A conflict fail comes from the merge loop that this card defines.

payload.title: The number of passes per ticket counts the builder's mistakes
payload.why_not: A fail can come from the spec, a flaky check, or a false finding. Counting every fail as a builder mistake points the fix at the wrong stage.

payload.title: Quality outcomes sit beside cost: escapes, human interventions, and rework
payload.why: Cost alone rewards a pipeline that builds the wrong thing cheaply. A cheaper variant is better only if it lets no more defects through and takes no more of the person's time.
payload.body:
**Escapes.** A defect that passed the builder loop and was found later. Record where it was found: the merge loop, the held-out set (#st-build-run), the person at review, or after merge. Each escape is a missing check or rubric line, so it is the most important number here.

**Human interventions.** Each time a person must act: answer a question, reject at a gate, fix code by hand, restart a stuck loop. Record the count and the time, per ticket and per card. The person's time is scarcer than tokens.

**Rework.**
- A decided card reopened after a ticket was built from it. The reopen count comes from #vi-flow-telemetry.
- Code from a ticket that is changed or reverted within 14 days of its merge.

**Plan quality.** Plan has no exit code. Its signal is what build finds missing: spec-gap fails (#ms-fail), the assumptions the builder records where the spec was silent, and the rework above.

**Starting thresholds.** These are guesses until data exists.
- An escape that a check could have caught adds that check. No window and no threshold.
- Interventions per ticket must go down over time. A rise raises an alert by the rule of #lp-trend-alert.

payload.why: Escapes found by the merge loop and the held-out set come from the steps that this card defines.
The reopen count for rework comes from the status-loop telemetry that this card defines.
A rise in interventions per ticket uses the alert rule that this card defines.
Plan quality reads the spec-gap fails that this card classifies.

payload.title: Judge the pipeline by cost and pass counts only
payload.why_not: A variant that skips a reviewer is cheaper and passes sooner, and it lets more defects through. Cost without an outcome measure ranks it higher.

payload.title: Compare pipeline variants on a fixed replay set of tickets
payload.why: Tickets from two periods differ in size, area, and difficulty, so a cost difference between them says little about the pipeline. The same tickets run through both variants isolate the pipeline.
payload.body:
- **The set.** 10 to 20 finished tickets, each with its spec and its starting commit. Choose them across sizes and areas of the code.
- **A run.** A variant, for example one model per stage (#st-six:opt0), builds every ticket in the set. Compare cost (#ms-cost), fails by cause (#ms-fail), and escapes against the held-out set (#ms-outcome).
- **Repeats.** Build each ticket at least 3 times per variant. One agent run varies a lot from one try to the next.
- **Two roles.** Production data shows the trend over time (#lp-trend). The replay set is the experiment that compares variants.

payload.why: A replay run compares the cost that this card defines.
A replay run compares fails by the causes that this card defines.
A replay run compares escapes, the outcome that this card defines.

payload.title: Compare a variant against the production history of the current pipeline
payload.why_not: The two periods build different tickets, so a difference in cost or escapes can come from the tickets and not from the pipeline.

payload.title: Named steps in sequence, grouped into plan, build, validate

patch.why: The named steps run in sequence. Each one sits inside one of the three stages from #stages.

payload.title: Named steps in sequence, grouped by stage

payload.why_not: Today's models do not reliably plan, build and validate from one instruction. Without stages there is no point where a human approves, and no checkable output between the steps. The rejection depends on current model capability, so it holds only until a more capable model class makes the unstaged run reliable.

criterion.text: A new model generation arrives (Opus 6 or GPT 7 class). Give it one high-level instruction on a real decision and see whether it plans, builds and validates with checkable output. If it does, revisit the stages.

payload.title: The pipeline measures its own quality: escapes, interventions, and follow-ups
payload.why: A software factory promises working software from a decided plan. How often it delivers that is a product measure in its own right, on a separate axis from cost.
payload.body:
**Escapes.** A defect that passed the builder loop and was found later. Record where it was found: the merge loop, the held-out set (#st-build-run), the person at review, or after merge. Each escape is a missing check or rubric line.

**Interventions.** Each time the pipeline needs a person to continue:
- a question that stops an agent until the person answers
- a rejection at a gate
- a forced restart of a stuck loop

Record the count and the time each one waits, per ticket and per card.

**Follow-ups.** A request from the person after a finished build. Each one gets one of two classes:
- **Plan miss.** The build did what the plan said, and the plan was wrong or silent. Example: A must be something else. Rebuild.
- **Build miss.** The plan was right, and the build got it wrong. Example: B has a logical bug. This is also an escape.

The plan-miss count is the main signal of plan quality, because plan has no exit code. An early signal comes before the person sees the build: each assumption the builder records where the spec was silent. A rise in builder assumptions predicts plan misses. The spec-gap fails of #ms-fail are a third source.

**Rework.**
- A decided card reopened after a ticket was built from it. The reopen count comes from #vi-flow-telemetry.
- Code from a ticket that is changed or reverted within 14 days of its merge.

**Starting thresholds.** These are guesses until data exists.
- An escape that a check could have caught adds that check. No window and no threshold.
- Interventions and follow-ups per ticket must go down over time. A rise raises an alert by the rule of #lp-trend-alert.

payload.why: Escapes found by the merge loop and the held-out set come from the steps that this card defines.
The reopen count for rework comes from the status-loop telemetry that this card defines.
A rise in interventions or follow-ups per ticket uses the alert rule that this card defines.
Plan quality also reads the spec-gap fails that this card classifies.
A replay run compares escapes, the outcome that this card defines.

payload.title: The pipeline measures its own quality in four categories
payload.why: A software factory promises working software from a decided plan. How often it delivers that is a product measure in its own right, on a separate axis from cost.
payload.body:
1. **Escapes:** defects that the builder loop let through (#ms-outcome-escape).
2. **Interventions:** each time the pipeline needs a person to continue (#ms-outcome-interv).
3. **Follow-ups:** requests from the person after a finished build (#ms-outcome-followup).
4. **Rework:** decided work that is undone later (#ms-outcome-rework).

payload.title: Escapes: defects that passed the builder loop, by where they were found
payload.why: Each escape is a missing check or rubric line. The place where it was found shows which gate should have caught it.
payload.body:
An escape is a defect in a ticket that passed the builder loop (#st-build-ticket).

Record for each escape:
- where it was found: the merge loop, the held-out set (#st-build-run), the person at review, or after merge
- whether a check could have caught it

**Numbers.** Escapes per ticket, split by where they were found.

**Starting threshold.** An escape that a check could have caught adds that check. No window and no threshold.

payload.why: An escape is a defect that passed the builder loop that this card defines.
The merge loop and the held-out set are two of the places where an escape is found.

payload.title: Interventions: each stop where the pipeline waits for a person
payload.why: An autonomous pipeline that often waits for a person is not autonomous. The count and the wait time show where it still needs one.
payload.body:
Three kinds:
- a question that stops an agent until the person answers
- a rejection at a gate
- a forced restart of a stuck loop

Record the kind, the card or ticket, and the time from the stop to the answer.

**Numbers.** Interventions per ticket and per card, by kind. The total wait time.

**Starting threshold.** Interventions per ticket must go down over time. A rise raises an alert by the rule of #lp-trend-alert.

payload.why: A rise in interventions per ticket uses the alert rule that this card defines.

payload.title: Follow-ups: requests after a finished build, as plan misses or build misses
payload.why: Plan has no exit code. A request after a finished build is the clearest sign of what the plan or the build got wrong.
payload.body:
Each follow-up gets one of two classes:
- **Plan miss.** The build did what the plan said, and the plan was wrong or silent. Example: A must be something else. Rebuild.
- **Build miss.** The plan was right, and the build got it wrong. Example: B has a logical bug. A build miss is also an escape (#ms-outcome-escape).

**Early signals of plan misses.** These come before the person sees the build:
- each assumption the builder records where the spec was silent
- the spec-gap fails of #ms-fail

**Numbers.** Plan misses and build misses per ticket. Builder assumptions per ticket.

**Starting threshold.** Follow-ups per ticket must go down over time. A rise raises an alert by the rule of #lp-trend-alert.

payload.why: A build miss also counts as an escape, as that card defines.
The spec-gap fails that this card classifies are an early signal of plan misses.
A rise in follow-ups per ticket uses the alert rule that this card defines.

payload.title: Rework: decided cards reopened and merged code changed soon after a build
payload.why: Work that is undone soon after it is done cost twice. Rework shows it even when no one filed a follow-up.
payload.body:
Two kinds:
- a decided card reopened after a ticket was built from it. The reopen count comes from #vi-flow-telemetry.
- code from a ticket that is changed or reverted within 14 days of its merge

**Numbers.** Rework events per ticket, by kind. The 14 days are a first guess.

A replay run compares escapes against the held-out set, as that card defines them.

Two kinds:
- a decided card reopened after a ticket was built from it. The reopen count comes from #vi-flow-telemetry.
- code from a ticket that is changed or reverted within 14 days of its merge

**Numbers.** Rework events per ticket, by kind. The 14 days are a first guess.

payload.title: The pipeline measures what it gets wrong and where it needs a person
A rerun of the red check sets the flaky cause. The next builder pass sets the other causes
payload.why: The next pass already reads the failure and the code to fix it, so it knows the cause with no extra session. Only flakiness needs no judgement: the same check on the same commit either passes again or does not.
payload.body:
- **Flaky check.** A red check runs once more on the same commit. Green on the rerun gives the cause flaky check. The pass stays red: the rerun classifies, it does not change the verdict.
- **Builder error, spec gap, false finding, conflict.** The next pass names one cause of the last failure, with one sentence of reason, at the end of its work. Conflict applies only to a fail from the merge loop.
- **No next pass.** A fail at the retry cap has no next pass, so its cause stays unknown.

The cause is stored on the pass that named it, and the report attributes it to the pass before.

payload.why: The next pass is a fresh agent with the failure in its brief, which is what lets it name the cause.

payload.title: A separate classifier agent reads each failure and names its cause
payload.why_not: It costs one more session per fail, and it sees less than the next builder pass, which reads the failure and the code in order to fix it.

payload.title: Past plan cost is rebuilt from the agent transcripts that past sessions left on disk
payload.why: Plan ran for a month before cost recording existed. The transcripts already hold every response's token counts, model and time, so the base for plan cost need not wait 30 more days.
payload.body:
- **Source.** Each past session left a transcript. Each model response in it carries input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens, the model, and a timestamp. A response split into several blocks repeats its counts: count each response once. A subagent's transcript counts toward the turn that started it.
- **Dollars.** Tokens times the price for that model and token kind. A cache write is priced by its lifetime (5 minutes or 1 hour). The price table carries the date it is valid from.
- **Wall time.** From the person's message to the last response of that turn.
- **Chat-pane turns.** Each goes to the card that was open in that turn (see #werk-mc-split). These sessions hold about 30% of all past tokens.
- **Size.** The per-card denominator is the decided cards in the log, by day (see #lp-trend-size for build).
- **Not plan cost.** The background runs that keep the product diagram in step.
- **Window.** History starts on 2026-09-09. No earlier session left a transcript for this project.
- **Open.** Terminal sessions hold the other 70% of tokens. They have no open card. They mix map writes with work on the code.

payload.why: Per-card attribution of a chat-pane turn uses the card open in that turn.

payload.title: Past plan cost is rebuilt from the agent transcripts that past sessions left on disk
payload.why: Plan ran for a month before cost recording existed. The transcripts already hold every response's token counts, model and time, so the base for plan cost need not wait 30 more days.
payload.body:
- **Source.** Each past session left a transcript. Each model response in it carries input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens, the model, and a timestamp. A response split into several blocks repeats its counts: count each response once. A subagent's transcript counts toward the turn that started it.
- **Dollars.** Tokens times the price for that model and token kind. A cache write is priced by its lifetime (5 minutes or 1 hour). The price table carries the date it is valid from.
- **Wall time.** From the person's message to the last response of that turn.
- **Chat-pane turns.** Each goes to the card that was open in that turn (see #werk-mc-split). These sessions hold about 30% of all past tokens.
- **Terminal turns.** These hold the other 70% and have no open card. A terminal turn is plan cost when it wrote to the map. Its cost is split in equal parts over the cards it wrote. A turn that only changes code is not plan cost.
- **Mixed turns.** A turn that writes to the map and also changes code counts as plan in proportion to its responses: a response that wrote to the map is plan, a response that changed code is not, and the other responses follow that ratio.
- **Size.** The per-card denominator is the decided cards in the log, by day.
- **Not plan cost.** The background runs that keep the product diagram in step.
- **Window.** History starts on 2026-09-09. No earlier session left a transcript for this project.

payload.why: Per-card attribution of a chat-pane turn uses the card open in that turn.

payload.title: Count only chat-pane turns
payload.why_not: Chat-pane sessions hold about 30% of past tokens. Most map writes happened in terminal sessions, so the base would undercount plan cost by more than half.

payload.title: Every terminal turn goes to its day
payload.why_not: Terminal sessions also build the tool itself. Code work would count as plan cost and inflate the base.

payload.title: `werk fails` reports the builder loop's failed passes by gate and cause

payload.title: One append-only pipeline log holds every step's start, end, and cost; agent transcripts are files beside it
payload.why: The metrics and the debugging trace come from the same facts: when each step started and ended, what it cost, and how it ended. One event log with one fold serves both, in the same shape as the decision log and the board log.
payload.body:
**The pipeline log.** One append-only file for the whole project, one event per line, in the shape of the decision log (#pr-log).
- A step started, and a step ended, for every step of every stage: a plan turn, spec, tickets, each builder pass, each check, the grader, each reviewer, a merge, the held-out set.
- An ended event carries the wall time, the cost and token breakdown (#ms-cost), the result, and for a red step its gate and cause (#ms-fail).
- Every metric is a pure fold over this log. No metric is stored as a summary that can disagree with the events.

**Beside it, as files.** Each agent session's full transcript, and each check's full output. An event names its file. These are large, so no fold reads them.

**What git keeps.** The pipeline log is small and is committed, like the decision log, so the measures outlive a worktree. The transcripts and check outputs are not committed.

**What stays where it is.** The board log keeps only where a ticket is and what happened to it (#vi-board-state). It does not hold step events.

patch.body:
- **Source.** Each past session left a transcript. Each model response in it carries input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens, the model, and a timestamp. A response split into several blocks repeats its counts: count each response once. A subagent's transcript counts toward the turn that started it.
- **Dollars.** Tokens times the price for that model and token kind. A cache write is priced by its lifetime (5 minutes or 1 hour). Fast mode costs twice the standard rate. The price table carries the date it is valid from. A session on a subscription did not pay these prices, so the result is an API-equivalent cost, not a bill. A response from a model with no price counts as zero and is reported.
- **Wall time.** From the person's message to the last response of that turn. A gap of more than 15 minutes between two responses is idle: a background task woke the turn again. Idle time is not wall time.
- **Chat-pane turns.** Each goes to the card that was open in that turn (see #werk-mc-split). A session is a chat-pane session when the conversation store names it, or when its prompts name an open card. The store names only the current session of each conversation. Chat-pane turns hold about 88% of past cost.
- **Terminal turns.** A terminal turn is plan cost when it wrote to the map. Its cost is split in equal parts over the cards it wrote. A turn that only changes code is not plan cost. Terminal turns that wrote to the map hold about 7% of past cost. The other 5% is not plan cost.
- **Mixed turns.** A terminal turn that writes to the map and also changes code counts as plan in proportion to its responses: a response that wrote to the map is plan, a response that changed code is not, and the other responses follow that ratio.
- **Size.** The per-card denominator is the cards that first became decided on each day.
- **Not plan cost.** The background runs that keep the product diagram in step. They write no card, so the terminal rule already leaves them out.
- **Window.** History starts on 2026-09-09. No earlier session left a transcript for this project.

patch.why_not: Terminal turns that wrote to the map hold about 7% of past plan cost. Leaving them out drops the whole cost of the cards built from a terminal, not only a share of it.

payload.title: One word, postponed, for the reason and for the mark it leaves
payload.why: A reopen with the reason postponed and the mark it leaves on cards are one state: the work waits, and the content still holds. Two words for one state make the reader look for a difference that does not exist.

ops.old: `ReopenReason` is `'postponed' | 'invalidated' | 'rejected'` (`src/types.ts:12`). The mark it fans out is called `paused` everywhere else. A reopen gives the reason postponed and the map answers `PAUSED`.
One word per meaning. Rename the mark.
## Scope

| file | occurrences of `paused` |
|---|---|
| `src/fold.ts` | 26 — the `paused` set, `deriveStaleness`'s return, the `Rollup` counters |
| `web/app.js` | 36 — `G.paused`, `classOf`'s `is-paused`, `.ring.paused`, the hover titles |
| `src/cli.ts` | 14 — the reopen output and the printed trace |
| `src/types.ts` | 11 — `Rollup.paused`, `openPaused`, `protoPaused`, `decidedPaused` |
| `web/style.css` | 9 |

Mechanical. No behaviour changes. `stale` keeps its name: `invalidated` and `rejected` both produce it, so no single reason word fits it, and `stale` is the honest description of the state rather than the act.
## The one argument for keeping two words

It was deliberate, not drift — see the comment at `src/fold.ts:217`. *Postponed* names the **act**, and only the origin was postponed. *Paused* names the **state** of a dependent four hops away that nobody touched. After the rename, #vi-oos-render will read "postponed", which is not something anyone did to it.
Accepted anyway: the trace already says where the mark came from and how far away it is — #vi-prop-bornstale built exactly that. The word does not have to carry it.

ops.new: The reason on a reopen, the mark on the card that was reopened, and the mark on every card downstream of it all read **postponed**, wherever the map or its output names the state.
Stale keeps its own word. Two reasons produce it, invalidated and rejected, so no single reason word fits it. Stale names the state, not the act.
## Why one word is enough

Postponed names an act, and only the origin was postponed. A card four hops downstream had nothing done to it. The word does not have to carry that: the trace on each marked card shows where the mark came from and how far away it is (see #vi-prop-bornstale).

payload.title: A separate overseer process that tails the event log of every session
payload.why_not: Only the process that starts a session holds its input pipe, so a separate process cannot answer a permission ask without a new channel to the session. It also needs its own way to find live sessions and its own start, stop and recovery, and nothing watches it. It gains two things: it sees sessions that werk did not start, and it outlives a runner that crashes. The build passes are the only sessions it must watch, and the runner starts each of them.

payload.title: Which sessions does the overseer watch: only the build passes, or every agent session of the project?
payload.why: #lp-overseer says the overseer watches every running agent session. The overseer today sees only the headless build passes that werk starts. The chat-pane sessions and terminal sessions have no overseer.
payload.body:
The answer sets where the overseer runs.

| Option | Sessions it sees | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build passes only | the headless passes werk starts | nothing new: a timer inside the runner |
| Every session, through a hook | build passes, chat pane, terminal sessions | a hook in each session that reports events and receives asks; each session carries its own watcher |
| Every session, through a separate process | the same | a process that finds live sessions, tails their transcripts, and has its own start, stop and recovery; a permission ask needs a new channel into the session |

A paused edge from #lp-overseer limits the third option: no standalone engine is built until the first two stages give validated results.

Recommendation: build passes only (:opt0). No real build has used the overseer yet. A hook is the next step if a stuck chat-pane or terminal session shows the need.

payload.why: A watcher outside the runner must still answer permission asks, which needs a channel into the session that #lp-overseer-asks requires.

The chat-pane sessions and the terminal sessions have no overseer. A person watches them.

In #lp-overseer, "every running agent session" means every build pass.

**When to revisit.** A chat-pane or terminal session stays stuck, and nobody sees it for a long time. A hook inside each session (:opt1) is then the next step.

payload.title: Chat-pane wait: how long an agent's question waits for the person
payload.why: A chat-pane agent that ends a turn with a question to the person stops until the person answers. The person leads that conversation, so the wait measures how long work sits idle on the person, not how often an autonomous pass needs one.
payload.body:
A wait starts when a chat-pane turn ends with a question to the person: a choice to make, or a fact to give. A turn that only reports starts no wait. The wait ends with the next message from the person in the same conversation.

Record the conversation, the card the map was at, the start, and the end.

**Numbers.** The median wait per conversation and the total wait per day. A wait that is still open shows its age.

A chat-pane wait is not an intervention per ticket, and it raises no alert by the rule of #lp-trend-alert.

payload.why: A wait belongs to one conversation, and the conversations are the tabs that #werk-multichat defines.

payload.title: Which chat-pane turn ends with a hanging question?
payload.why: The chat-pane wait starts only at a turn that leaves a question for the person. The rule that picks those turns decides what the wait measures and what it misses.
payload.body:
| Option | Counts | Misses or costs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Text rule plus structured asks (:opt0) | a structured ask with no answer, or a last paragraph that ends in a question mark | an ask written without a question mark |
| Structured asks only (:opt1) | a structured question, a permission ask, a suggested next-action button with no click | every question in free text |
| A classifier (:opt2) | the turns a short model call reads as waiting on the person | a model call per turn, and a judgement that can be wrong |
| Every turn end (:opt3) | every gap between a finished turn and the next message | nothing, but it counts a gap after a turn that asked nothing |

Two smaller rules go with the choice:

- **The end of a wait.** The next message from the person in the same conversation ends it, whether or not it answers the question. Only a classifier can tell an answer from a new topic.
- **Short waits.** Every wait is recorded. The median absorbs short ones, so no minimum length applies.

Recommendation: :opt0. It costs no model call, and the chat pane already ends a turn that needs the person with a question.

payload.title: Text rule plus structured asks: a structured ask with no answer, or a last paragraph that ends in a question mark
Structured asks only
A classifier reads the last message of each turn
Every turn end counts as a wait
A hanging question is a pending structured question or an unclicked next-action button
payload.why: The pane already knows both without reading prose: a structured question sits in the tab's ask bar, and a next-action button is an offer with no click. Both blink the tab chip, so the wait is the time the tab blinks.
payload.body:
A chat-pane turn ends with a hanging question when it leaves one of these:

1. A structured question in the tab's ask bar, with no answer yet (#werk-mc-asks).
2. A next-action button with no click (#werk-mc-nextbtn).

The wait ends when the question is answered, the button is clicked, or the person sends the next message in that conversation. These are the same events that stop the tab chip from blinking (#werk-mc-asks-offer).

A question written in free text, in any other form, starts no wait. Every wait is recorded, with no minimum length.

payload.why: A pending structured question is the ask that #werk-mc-asks keeps on its tab until it is answered.
An unclicked next-action button is the offer that #werk-mc-nextbtn renders from the last line of a message.
The wait starts and ends with the same events that start and stop the tab blink of #werk-mc-asks-offer.

payload.title: A text rule: a last paragraph that ends in a question mark

payload.title: A classifier reads the last message of each turn

payload.title: Measure the pipeline's cost, failures and escapes, to choose how to change the pipeline

patch.body:
The pipeline records three things for each ticket it builds:

1. **Cost:** dollars and wall time per stage (#ms-cost).
2. **Failures:** which gate failed each pass, and the cause (#ms-fail).
3. **Outcome:** defects that escaped the loop, and each point where it stalled and needed a person (#ms-outcome).

All three come from one pipeline log (#ms-store). A change to the pipeline is judged on a fixed replay set of tickets, by these measures (#ms-replay).
patch.why: A product measure says whether one feature works. It does not say which stage, gate or model to change. Only measures of the pipeline itself can compare two pipeline designs.

payload.title: Flow shows the pipeline measures as panels, one question per panel
payload.why: A measure helps only when a person can act on it. A chart framed as a question says what to look for, and a drill-down says where to look next.
payload.body:
Flow shows the measures of #ms-self beside the status-loop stats.

- **One question per panel.** The question is the title, for example: is effort per story going up? Which stage costs the most? Why do passes fail? Where does the pipeline wait for a person? Did a variant beat the current pipeline on the replay set?
- **Transform first.** A panel shows a fold over the logs, not raw events: per unit of size, a distribution (median, 90th percentile, maximum), a window, or a ratio. The fold, not the chart, holds the arithmetic.
- **Drill-down.** A mark opens the items behind it: the tickets, cards, and transcripts.
- **Reference band.** Each panel compares against its own history: #vi-flow-ms-ref.
- **Live.** A panel redraws when the pipeline log or the decision log gets an event.

Open: the visual form of the panels.

payload.body:
- **The band.** The median to the 90th percentile of the base window, drawn behind the data. The base window and the alert rule are those of #lp-trend-alert. The band is labelled as learned, with its sample size.
- **Too few items.** Below the base window size, the panel draws the data with no band and says how many items are missing.
- **Promotion.** A person can turn a line on a panel into a fixed threshold. The threshold is stored as a metric kill criterion on the card it guards (#kill). The panel then draws the threshold instead of the band.
- **No automatic action.** A band or a threshold only marks a point. It does not block, stop, or change the pipeline.

payload.title: The tool computes statistical control limits and alerts on them by itself
payload.why_not: An alert that acts on its own was rejected for the trend report (#lp-trend-alert:block). Limits from a few dozen agent runs are noise, and the person must see the data before a line becomes a rule.

patch.body:
**Gate.** Each fail names its gate:
- a check, by name: type check, lint, unit test, and so on (#lp-checks)
- the grader, with the card the diff failed against (#lp-prod-judge)
- a review area, with the finding's severity (#lp-prod-review)
- the merge loop, for a conflict with another ticket (#st-build-run)

**Cause.** Each fail gets one cause. A mechanical check and a judgement have different causes, so each kind has its own set.

- **A check:**
  - *code breaks the check*: the diff adds a type error, breaks a lint rule, or fails a test
  - *test is wrong*: the test asserts old behaviour, and the diff is right
  - *check infrastructure*: the tool crashed, timed out, or lacked a dependency, and the code did not run
  - *flaky*: the check passes on a rerun with no change to the code
- **The grader or a review:**
  - *diff misses the spec*: the spec was clear, and the diff does not do it
  - *spec gap*: the spec does not say what the diff should do
  - *false finding*: the finding passes on the next pass with no change to the code it names
- **The merge loop:** a conflict with another ticket.

The next builder or a classifier sets the cause.

**Derived numbers.**
- first-pass success rate
- passes per ticket, split by cause
- cap-hit rate: the share of tickets that reach the retry cap (#st-build-ticket)

**Starting thresholds.** These are guesses until data exists.
- A cap-hit rate above 10% of tickets points at ticket size or spec quality, not at the builder.
- One finding type that fails three tickets in a row becomes a check or a rubric line (#ms-rubric).
- A false-finding share above 20% for one reviewer or the grader means its prompt needs a fix.
- Any share of check-infrastructure or flaky fails is a fix to the check, not to the builder.

The cause names are those of #ms-fail.

- **Flaky.** A red check runs once more on the same commit. Green on the rerun gives the cause flaky. The pass stays red: the rerun classifies, it does not change the verdict.
- **Check infrastructure.** The check reports a crash, a timeout, or a missing tool before the code ran. The check run sets this cause itself, with no judgement.
- **Every other cause.** The next pass names one cause of the last failure, with one sentence of reason, at the end of its work. Conflict applies only to a fail from the merge loop.
- **No next pass.** A fail at the retry cap has no next pass, so its cause stays unknown.

The cause is stored on the pass that named it, and the report attributes it to the pass before.

payload.title: Read an image directly; use a subagent only for long image loops or a short text fact

patch.body:
**Default: read the image directly.** One image costs less than 5k tokens.

**Use a subagent in two cases:**
1. A render-and-check loop that will read more than about 10 images in one session. The images then add up, and the subagent keeps them out of the main context.
2. The agent needs only a short text fact from the image.

**Tell the subagent what to check.** A text report loses visual detail: overlaps, spacing, colors. A subagent with no checklist reports only what it finds notable.
patch.why: A Read of a PNG or JPG gives the model a native image block, not encoded text. On the current model families one image costs at most 4,784 tokens, because larger images are scaled down first. A direct Read is cheap. A large context comes from text and tool output, not from a few images.

ops.new: **An answer that no card gives becomes a card.** When the decided cards do not settle a question, the agent's answer is a new decision. It goes on the map under the subtree, so a person can see it and reopen it. It is never only in the spec.
