payload.title: The fold is a runtime operation: every read replays the log from the first event

patch.body:
The map is not stored anywhere. Each read folds the whole log at runtime, from the first event to the last.

The fold time grows with the log, because the log only grows. The kill criterion watches that time. When it fires, the fallback is a stored snapshot (#pr-log-snapshot:opt0).

The fold time of every fold is recorded, so the criterion has data to check. Recording it is part of this decision. Flow shows it as a panel: #vi-flow-ms-fold.
patch.why: A full replay keeps the log the only state. A full fold of about 7,400 events takes 13–20 ms (measured 2026-10-15), so a snapshot would buy nothing yet.

payload.title: Start the fold from a stored snapshot of the map
payload.why_not: A snapshot is a second copy of the map state that must agree with the log, and it must be rebuilt when the fold logic changes. At 13–20 ms per full fold, that cost buys nothing.

criterion.source: the fold time recorded on every fold of the decision log
criterion.metric: median fold time of a full fold

payload.title: Panel: is the fold still fast enough to run on every read?
payload.why: The fold runs on every read, and its time grows with the log. The panel shows how close the fold time is to the limit that reopens #pr-log-snapshot.
payload.body:
- **Marks.** One dot per fold, at its time in ms, against the log size in events at that fold. A line for the median of the current window.
- **Reference band.** The band comes from the panel's own history (#vi-flow-ms-ref). A horizontal line marks the kill threshold on #pr-log-snapshot.
- **Outlier.** A dot above the band is coloured. The line turns the stale colour when the window median crosses the threshold.
- **Drill-down.** A dot opens the read that ran the fold: the view or the command, and the log size.

payload.why: The panel plots the fold time that #pr-log-snapshot records, against the threshold of its kill criterion.

patch.body:
- **Marks.** One dot per full fold, at its time in ms, against the log size in events at that fold. A line for the median of the window.
- **Threshold.** The kill criterion on #pr-log-snapshot sets the threshold, so the panel draws it as a line instead of a learned band (#vi-flow-ms-ref). The window and the minimum sample come from the same criterion.
- **Outlier.** A dot above the threshold is coloured. The median line turns the stale colour when it crosses the threshold.
- **Drill-down.** A dot names the read that ran the fold: the view or the command, the log size, and the time.

payload.why: A panel with a set threshold draws it instead of a learned band, as this card rules.

payload.text: The open, proto and decided tiles on Flow now filter the Cards list. The Cards section also has open, proto and decided pills before the stale pill. Clicking an active tile clears the filter.

payload.title: Flow lists every map card flat, with filters for status and for marks

patch.body:
The tree hides a card under its parent. A flat list shows all cards at once, and a filter answers one question: what needs me now.

One row per card: id, title, status, and its marks.

Fixed filters, in two groups. Status filters show cards by their own status: open, proto, decided. Mark filters show cards by a mark:

1. Stale — a card it depends on was reopened as wrong (#vi-prop).
2. Paused — a card it depends on was postponed (#pr-wf-paused).
3. Proposed — a new card or an edit waits for approval (#werk-propose-new).

The filters are pills above the list. The status tiles at the top of Flow, and the stale, paused, and proposed tiles, set the same filter. A click on the active tile clears it.

A click on a row opens the card on the map.

Sorting: the headers of card, status, and last move sort the list. A click sorts in the natural order of that column: id up, status in the order open, proto, decided, and last move with the newest first. A second click reverses it. A card with no move yet sorts last in both directions. The list opens sorted by last move, newest first. The sort works together with the filters and the search.

payload.text: Build review: built. Reads the pipeline log, prints every number the card lists, has --json, and has unit tests. Gaps: 3 of 4 threshold signals (no infra/flaky signal); no CLI-level test.

Causes differ: 'code breaks the check' and 'diff misses the spec' are one builder-error cause; 'test is wrong' and 'check infrastructure' do not exist. Passes are counted per build (loop run), not per ticket, and not split by cause. Thresholds: cap-hit needs >=10 builds, false-finding needs >=5 fails (not on card); repeat-fail counts builds and any gate key; infra/flaky signal missing.

Build review: built except one rule. Flaky rerun, next-pass cause with one sentence, attribution to the pass before, unknown at the cap: all built and tested. Missing: a check run does not set 'check infrastructure' on a crash, timeout or missing tool; it records a plain red.

patch.body:
A wait starts when a chat-pane turn leaves a hanging question for the person, and ends when the person answers it or moves on. #ms-outcome-interv-chat-q defines both ends.

Record the conversation, the card the map was at, the start, and the end.

**Numbers.** The median wait per conversation and the total wait per day. A wait that is still open shows its age.

**Where it shows.** A section of the Flow tab, over the last 30 days: the median wait, the wait today, the open waits and the oldest one, a total for each of the last 7 days, and one row per conversation. It follows the Flow scope by the card the person had open; the whole map also counts waits with no card.

**Where the data comes from.** Button waits come from the chat history of each conversation. A resolved question wait comes from the ask history, which records when a structured question went up and which conversation asked it. An open question wait comes from the live ask queue, because the ask history gets a line only when the ask resolves. Asks resolved before the history held those two facts have no wait.

A chat-pane wait is not an intervention per ticket, and it raises no alert by the rule of #lp-trend-alert.

criterion.text: After 30 days of use, check whether the waits section ever led to a change, such as answering sooner or asking fewer questions. If it never did, remove the section.

patch.body:
The cause names are those of #ms-fail.

- **Flaky.** A red check runs once more on the same commit. Green on the rerun gives the cause flaky. The pass stays red: the rerun classifies, it does not change the verdict.
- **Check infrastructure.** The check reports a crash, a timeout, or a missing tool before the code ran. The check run sets this cause itself, with no judgement, and the check is not run again. A stop by the person is not a check infrastructure fail.
- **Every other cause.** The next pass names one cause of the last failure, with one sentence of reason, at the end of its work. Conflict applies only to a fail from the merge loop.
- **No next pass.** A fail at the retry cap has no next pass, so its cause stays unknown.

The cause is stored on the pass that named it, and the report attributes it to the pass before. A cause the check run set comes before a cause the next pass names.

criterion.text: After 20 builds, read the fails by cause. If the next pass names a cause that contradicts the failure it was given in more than a few cases, switch to a separate classifier.

Over the next 20 sync runs, read the scout verdicts. If the diagram gains a box for a behavioural or method card, or misses a structural one, more than twice, merge the two agents or change the scout prompt.

patch.body:
**Gate.** Each fail names its gate: a check by name, such as type check, lint or unit test (#lp-checks); the grader, with the card the diff failed against (#lp-prod-judge); a review area, with the finding's severity (#lp-prod-review); or the merge loop, for a conflict with another ticket (#st-build-run). A gate that judged nothing — a stalled or looping pass, a broken step — is named too, and has no cause.

**Cause.** Each fail gets one cause:

- *builder error*: an earlier pass got the code wrong, and the spec was clear. The gate says whether it broke a check or missed the spec, so one cause covers both.
- *test is wrong*: the test asserts old behaviour, and the diff is right. Only a check or a merge fail can have it.
- *spec gap*: the spec does not say what the diff should do.
- *false finding*: the finding passes on the next pass with no change to the code it names.
- *check infrastructure*: the check crashed, timed out, or lacked its tool, and the code did not run.
- *flaky*: the check passes on a rerun with no change to the code.
- *conflict*: the ticket clashes with work merged after it was built. Only a merge fail can have it.

#ms-fail-cause says who sets each cause.

**Derived numbers.** The first-pass success rate, the cap-hit rate (the share of builds that reach the retry cap, #st-build-ticket), the passes per build as median, 90th percentile and maximum, and the fails by cause and by gate. A build is one run of the builder loop over one ticket. A ticket that the merge loop sends back builds twice, and each build counts on its own.

**Starting thresholds.** These are guesses until data exists. Each needs a minimum sample, so that one bad build does not fire it.

- A cap-hit rate above 10%, over at least 10 builds, points at ticket size or spec quality, not at the builder.
- One gate key that fails three builds in a row becomes a check or a rubric line (#ms-rubric).
- A false-finding share above 20% for one reviewer or the grader, over at least 5 of its fails, means its prompt needs a fix.
- Any flaky or check-infrastructure fail is a fix to that check, not to the builder.

criterion.text: After 20 builds, read the fail report. If a threshold never fires, or fires on builds that needed no change, adjust that threshold. If most fails land in builder error with no pattern by gate, the cause set is too coarse.

patch.body:
Two outcomes, named on the redraw:

- **local** — the same components and the same grouping, with text or one edge changed. The reader can trust their mental model.
- **restructure** — a boundary moved, a component split, or a group re-formed. The reader has to look again, and the redraw says why.

A restructure is the interesting event. It means a single card changed something that the previous reading of the whole card set had wrong. That is worth surfacing in the map, not hiding in a picture.

The agent that redraws names the outcome and its reason in a fixed line that a program reads. The background job keeps it with the last run. The diagram view shows the last outcome beside its status, and a restructure is shown with its reason. A restructure also adds a note to each card whose change caused it, so it reaches the map.

payload.title: Show the outcome in the diagram view only
payload.why_not: A restructure says the earlier reading of the card set was wrong. A person who reads only the map never sees it.

criterion.text: After 10 restructure notes, check whether each one named a real boundary change. If most were renames or single edges, the agents misjudge the outcome, and the note becomes noise.

payload.text: Rejected. The diagram is a grid file that werk lays out and renders itself; Mermaid is not used. #vi-sysdiag-grid-mvp decides what the author writes, and #vi-sysdiag-intent-edgecard puts each element's card ids inline on its own line, so no separate mapping block exists. One file stays the unit, as #vi-sysdiag-grain requires.
Rejected. A connection's card ids sit inline on the edge line (#vi-sysdiag-intent-edgecard), not in a separate edges block.

Postponed. Zoom levels need a collapse state per group and an edge rollup from leaf components to their parent groups. That is a large addition to the layout and the renderer. The diagram fits on one screen today, so nested frames are enough. Revisit when one screen no longer shows the whole diagram clearly.
Postponed. Measure and analyse work on a released product, and no product is released yet. Revisit when the first release goes to users.

payload.body:
The stripes are the same diagonal hatch as the rollup bar and the 3D view (#vi-graph3d-paused). They apply to the postponed card itself and to every card downstream of it, in the list of child cards and on the card's own page. The left border stays grey.

In a parent's rollup bar, a postponed card keeps the width of its real status and is hatched grey. The postponed card itself counts there, not only the cards downstream of it, so a postponed leaf with no dependents still shows in its parents' bars.

payload.title: A postponed card shows a grey postponed tag and grey diagonal stripes, and a striped slice in its parents' bars

patch.body:
- **The tag.** In the row of tags at the top of the card page, after the status tag. Grey, the same colour as the mark on downstream cards. Never the red of a stale card: a postponement is not an invalidation. On hover it explains itself: postponed, not wrong, the work waits.
- **The stripes.** Grey diagonal stripes over the card, in the list of child cards and on the card's own page. They are the same hatch as the 3D view (#vi-graph3d-paused), faint enough to read the text through. The left border keeps the colour of the card's status, so a postponed card still shows whether it is open, proto or decided.
- **The parent's bar.** A postponed card keeps the width of its real status in a parent's rollup bar and is hatched grey. The postponed card itself counts there, so a postponed leaf with no dependents still shows in its parents' bars.
- **What it marks.** See #pr-wf-postponed for which cards carry the mark and when it goes.
patch.why: The status tag still reads open on a postponed card, and a thin border is easy to miss in a grid of cards. The tag says that the work waits and the content still holds. The stripes say it at a glance and leave the border free for the status colour.

payload.text: What the experiment settled, against its three false-conditions. (1) Cards do not name components: refuted. 66 decided cards folded into 24 parts. Recorded as #vi-sysdiag-classes (only structural cards make nodes) and #vi-sysdiag-edges (cards name parts, not arrows). (2) Two reads fold two ways: never tested. (3) Every one-card change is a restructure: never tested as step 3. The background redraws now run, but the last run records only 'updated', not local or restructure, so #vi-sysdiag-declare is not observable yet. Side finding: Mermaid auto-layout did not read at this size, which led to #vi-sysdiag-render and the rejection of #vi-sysdiag-format. Open gaps: #vi-sysdiag-derive stale since 2026-09-11; this card stale from the format rejection.

payload.title: Does one decided set fold into the same parts on two cold reads?
payload.why: A redraw always starts from the old drawing, so the fold's own stability is never seen. If two cold reads of one card set give different parts, the diagram's structure comes from whichever read came first, not from the cards.
payload.body:
Two agents with no prior diagram fold the same decided set. Compare their parts and their groupings.

Stable: the two part sets differ only by names and by the level a part sits at. Unstable: a boundary sits in a different place, or one read merges what the other splits.

If unstable, the first read needs review as a decision of its own, because every later redraw inherits it.

payload.why: Both reads use this sort to choose which cards make a node.

payload.title: Is a one-card change usually a local redraw?
payload.why: If most one-card changes come out as a restructure, the drawing carries no reusable structure, and keeping the old drawing as input buys nothing.
payload.body:
The evidence is the stream of real redraws, one per change to a decided card. Count the declared outcomes over the runs.

Holds: most runs are local, and each restructure names a card that changed a boundary. Fails: restructures are common, or their reasons do not point at the card that changed.

The count needs each run to keep its declared outcome, which #vi-sysdiag-declare requires.

payload.title: The diagram shows the decided shape of the product. It does not map to code
payload.why: The diagram answers what we decided to build, not what exists. Mapping elements to code would tie the drawing to a prototype whose shape nobody chose, and would add a mapping to keep in step with every refactor.
payload.body:
This is a scope choice, not a finding. A part with no code is a decided part not built yet, and the diagram does not mark it. Whether a part is built is read from the code and the map, not from the drawing.

It follows #vi-sysdiag-purpose to its end: the diagram is drawn from the cards and is never compared to the code. A drawing of the code, and any block that links elements to files, is outside the diagram's scope.

payload.title: Map each element to files and symbols, so the diagram can show what is built
payload.why_not: A box with no code arrow means three different things and most are noise. The mapping must follow a prototype whose shape nobody chose, so the diagram would inherit the code's accidents.

payload.why: It takes the rule that the diagram looks forward and is drawn from cards, and applies it to every code mapping.

criterion.text: A scope choice about what the diagram is for. Revisit if the code is built on purpose and the plan-versus-build gap becomes a question the map must answer.

payload.title: Map each diagram element to files and symbols, so the diagram shows what is built
payload.why_not: The diagram shows the shape we decided, not the shape that exists. A box with no code arrow has three meanings and most are noise. The mapping must follow a prototype whose shape nobody chose, so the diagram would inherit the code's accidents.

payload.title: The map and the product diagram differ in node, question, shape and staleness
payload.why: A reader who takes the diagram for a view of the map expects history and claims, and finds current parts. The four differences say which graph answers which question.
payload.body:
| | map | product diagram |
|---|---|---|
| node | a claim | a part of the built thing |
| question | why is it like this | what is there now |
| shape | history, append-only | current state, overwritten |
| goes stale | by propagation | when the product changes |

The map already answers why. Nothing else renders what. The set of decided cards implies a system, and that system lives only in the reader's head until the diagram draws it.

payload.title: Parts are not a node kind in the map
payload.why: A part inside the map would be counted as an unsettled decision, and every count that reads the map would be wrong.
payload.body:
Adding a component kind to the log puts parts and claims in one node set. The rollup, the staleness closure and the drained count then treat a part as a claim that is settled or not. A part is neither.

So the parts live in their own graph. The only edge across runs from a part to the cards that decided it, see #vi-sysdiag-backedge.

payload.title: Parts are not a node kind in the map
payload.why: A part inside the map would be counted as an unsettled decision, and every count that reads the map would be wrong.
payload.body:
Adding a component kind to the log puts parts and claims in one node set. The rollup, the staleness closure and the drained count then treat a part as a claim that is settled or not. A part is neither.

So the parts live in their own graph. The only edge between the two graphs runs from a part to the cards that decided it, see #vi-sysdiag-backedge.

criterion.text: Splitting a card into subcards changes no decision. Merge them back into the parent if the split does not help reading.
Splitting a card into subcards changes no decision. Merge them back into the parent if the split does not help reading.

patch.body:
Two graphs cover the same project and answer two different questions. The map holds claims and answers why the product is like this. The product diagram holds the parts of the built thing and answers what there is. The four differences are on #vi-sysdiag-compare.

One decision can create four components, and one component can be the sum of ten decisions. There is no one-to-one mapping, so no view of the map is a product diagram.

Parts cannot join the map as a node kind (#vi-sysdiag-nokind). The one edge between the two graphs runs from a part to the cards that decided it (#vi-sysdiag-backedge). Whether that edge is authored or derived is decided in #vi-sysdiag-derive.

payload.title: The product diagram is a separate graph of the product's parts, not a view of the map
Product diagram parts are not a node kind in the map
Draw each diagram as a hand-positioned static SVG
payload.why_not: A built prototype read well, but only because the agent chose the lanes and the order. The hand arithmetic for label plates and box borders was where the spacing errors came from, and it repeats on every redraw. A program does that arithmetic exactly (see #vi-sysdiag-render).

payload.title: One diagram file: a content section says what exists, a grid section says where it goes
payload.why: The fold writes judgement, and judgement is stored as text that can be read, diffed and edited in place. Two sections keep the two judgements apart: what the product has, and where each part is drawn.
payload.body:
The content section names each part with its title and description, each connection with its label, the groups, and the colour classes, in a small Mermaid-like syntax. Each part line and each connection line ends with the ids of the cards that decided it, so the link back to the map sits on the line it explains (#vi-sysdiag-backedge). A connection can carry several ids, because several decisions can feed one drawn connection.

The grid section places what the content names (#vi-sysdiag-grid). The content never names a cell, and the grid never names a title.

The file is the stored form. The picture is drawn from it on every build and never edited by hand, per #vi-images. The file is also the base of the next redraw (#vi-sysdiag-grain).

payload.why: It stores the diagram as text and redraws the picture, the split this card sets.
Each line carries the card ids that this card requires on every diagram element.

payload.title: A Mermaid flowchart with the card ids in a separate comment block
payload.why_not: werk draws its own picture, so Mermaid syntax buys nothing at render time. A separate block puts one fact in two places: the element on one line, the cards that decided it on another, and the two drift.

payload.title: The agent places every part on a grid. A checker refuses a broken grid, and a program sizes and draws it

patch.body:
The agent writes every cell: each part, each path cell of a connection, each label and each crossing (#vi-sysdiag-grid-mvp). No program chooses a position.

A checker refuses a grid that breaks a tile rule. A part is a filled rectangle. A connection is one unbranched path whose two ends touch its two parts. A label sits in its own path and splits it. A crossing is two straight runs on different axes. All rows have the same length. A legal grid that reads badly still builds, with a warning (#vi-sysdiag-grid-gaps).

A program then sizes each column and row from the measured text (#vi-sysdiag-metrics), turns path cells into lines, and draws the picture. Sizing is arithmetic and needs no judgement.

This is the split of #penrose: the content says what exists, the grid says where it goes. The tile rules have prior art in #tiling-systems, #kandinsky and #css-grid-areas.
patch.why: Every layout defect in the earlier attempts was found by looking at the picture, never by reading the input. A grid that the agent writes cell by cell is a coarse drawing of itself, so its author can read it back before anything is rendered.

payload.why: The grid places the parts and connections that the content section of this card names.

payload.title: Mermaid draws the diagram with its own auto-layout
payload.why_not: Once connections carried labels and parts carried descriptions, the layout left large empty regions and crossing lines. Auto-layout takes the placement away from the author, and placement is the judgement that makes the diagram readable.

payload.title: The agent draws a static SVG by hand, positions and sizes included
payload.why_not: The drawing read well because the agent chose the lanes and the order. The hand arithmetic for box and label sizes was where the spacing errors came from, and it repeats on every redraw.

payload.title: An intent file of groups and rows, with a one-pass resolver that places the connections
payload.why_not: The agent controls only which part sits in which row. Connections, labels and spacing come from the resolver, and the agent cannot see what it produced without rendering and looking at the picture.

payload.title: D2 grid layout with TALA routing
payload.why_not: A D2 grid gives order but not proportion: every member of a column has one width, and no part can span columns. The workaround is invisible spacers, which is hand-tuning under another name.

payload.title: An object-avoiding router (libavoid) on top of the resolver
payload.why_not: It removed lines drawn through boxes, but its paths bend more and hug corners, so labels landed on box text. Each fix needed another finishing rule, and the agent still could not read the result back.

payload.why: The link reads the card ids that each content line carries, as this card defines them.

patch.body:
Every drawn part and connection carries the ids of the cards that decided it, so the browser needs no second copy of the mapping.

From the map to the diagram: a card has a button that opens the diagram, highlights every element that names the card, and scrolls the first one into view. From the diagram to the map: clicking an element lists the cards that decided it, and each one links back to that card in the map.

A connection carries a list of ids, not one. With one id, a second deciding card would have no way back to the drawing. A thin line gets a wider invisible copy under it, so it is a usable click target.
patch.why: The ids answer 'why is this box here'. In a file that answer needs a search. In the drawing it needs one click, and the reverse question, 'what did this card draw', comes from the same data.

payload.why: One connection can stand for several features because each connection line names every card that decided one of them.

patch.body: Grouping several features under one connection is normal, as long as the connection names every card that decided one of them (#vi-sysdiag-file). It follows from #vi-sysdiag-purpose: the diagram shows the shape we want, not an audit of the code.
patch.why: Several features can share one drawn connection between two parts, even where the code has separate channels for them. A connection marks a boundary between concepts, not a route in the code.

payload.title: Spacing rules in a skill file, with the agent doing the arithmetic
payload.why_not: Logic goes in a program, not in markdown. The agent's arithmetic was the source of the spacing errors, and a written rule does not make it exact.

payload.title: A constrained auto-layout engine, such as ELK or dagre with lane constraints
payload.why_not: A solver still chooses the positions, and a constraint can only forbid a bad layout, not express the one the author wants. The author cannot read the result back before it is drawn.

patch.body:
The node fold needs judgement. No projection of card fields yields a component. #vi-graph3d decides a view, #werk-hmr decides a dev loop, and #vi-edges decides a data shape. Only a reader can tell which is a part of the product, and at which level, using the sort in #vi-sysdiag-classes.

Connections are not folded from the code. They come from decided cards (#vi-sysdiag-edges). Each redraw starts from the stored file, and the agent judges its scope (#vi-sysdiag-grain). Regenerating from the card set alone has nothing to be continuous with.

The ids do not drive the redraw. The agent judges its scope (#vi-sysdiag-grain).

They answer why a box is there, as the only edge between the two graphs (#vi-sysdiag-link). They are also the fallback at scale. Past the size where one read covers the diagram and the card set, the reverse closure from #vi-prop is the only way to bound a redraw, and the ids must already exist, because an edge not written at creation cannot be recovered.

#vi-prop's 6% to 11% is about recovering edges that were never written. While the changed card and the whole diagram sit in one context, nothing is recovered: the affected elements are read, not inferred.

The diagram looks forward, not back. It shows the shape we want. The code shows the shape we have. When the two differ, the code is wrong more often than the diagram, because nobody chose the code's shape.

So the diagram is drawn from the cards, which hold decisions (#vi-sysdiag-derive). A part of the diagram with no code is normal: it is decided and not built yet. A part of the code with no card is normal too: it is prototype scaffolding, not a hidden decision.

A depends_on edge between two cards is not an arrow between two parts. #werk-shots depends_on #werk-pane means the screenshot decision needed the pane decision first. It does not mean the screenshot code calls the pane. Same word, two graphs, two meanings.

An empty arrow is a question to answer, not data to fetch (#vi-sysdiag-ask). The arrows come from the cards once the cards exist. Reading them out of the prototype code would hide the gap instead of showing it.
patch.why: The decided cards name the parts of the product readily. No card says how two parts talk. The code is the wrong source for the arrows, because it is a prototype (#vi-sysdiag-purpose). The arrows are missing because nobody decided them.

patch.body:
The tool draws the parts. Then it asks about the blank arrows.

"The chat pane and the agent runner are both parts. How do they talk?" That is a question with an answer, and the answer is a decision. So it becomes a card.

This is the first case where the diagram writes to the map, not the other way round. It fits #vi-compl: the tool does not choose the answer, it finds the missing question.

It also gives the diagram a way to be incomplete on purpose. A blank arrow is a real state, drawn as a dashed line with a mark. A tool that cannot draw "we have not decided this" will guess instead.
patch.why: If the tool treats a missing arrow as missing data, it fills the arrow in from the code and the gap disappears. If it treats the arrow as an open question, it coaches judgement, which is the job #visual gives it.

patch.body:
The view opens fitted to the pane, and the readout shows the fit percentage. 100% is the maximum, because text is sized exactly at 100% (#vi-sysdiag-metrics) and past it there is only softer text.

Zoom resizes the drawing instead of scaling a finished raster, so text stays sharp. The toolbar holds zoom out, the readout, and zoom in. The readout toggles between fit and 100%. A modifier key with the wheel zooms, and a plain wheel scrolls.
patch.why: The full diagram is far larger than a pane. At 1:1 the view opened on its top-left corner, the one part nobody needs first. The shape of the whole system is the first read.

patch.body:
A part's id fills the cells of that part (#vi-sysdiag-grid-mincell). A path cell names its connection by its two parts (#vi-sysdiag-grid-edgeid). A label cell names the connection it labels, and sits beside or inside that connection's lane (#vi-sysdiag-grid-inline-label). A spacer keeps an empty column or row open (#vi-sysdiag-grid-spacer). A junction lets two connections cross (#vi-sysdiag-grid-junction). An empty cell collapses.

Group frames come from their members. A declared group shape is #vi-sysdiag-grid-groupshape.
patch.why: A grid cell holds one token, and the token set is the whole authoring language. Anything a program can compute is not a token.

Two lines drawn flat across each other read as a corner or a branch, which a junction never is. A small semicircle over the other line is the convention wiring diagrams use. It needs no new authoring: the junction token already says where the crossing is.

criterion.text: Two cold reads of one decided set fold into different part boundaries; see #vi-sysdiag-foldstable.
Most one-card changes come out as a restructure; see #vi-sysdiag-localrate.

payload.title: Text widths come from a table measured once in the browser, for the one font the diagram uses

patch.body:
A headless browser measures every printable character at each size and weight the diagram uses, once. The table is checked in, and the build reads it, so the build needs no browser.

The table is right only for one font. The diagram names the system font, so the widths hold on the kind of machine the table was made on, and can be wrong on another. Today every reader views the diagram inside werk on that kind of machine. Embedding one font in the picture removes the machine from the answer, and is the fallback when that stops being true.
patch.why: Every column and row size comes from the width of the text in it. A guess per character was wrong before anyone typed it. A table measured by a real browser makes the sizes exact wherever the diagram's font is the font the table was measured with.

payload.title: Embed one font in every picture and measure from that font's own tables
payload.why_not: It makes text exact on every machine and in every viewer, but adds 30 to 80 kB to each picture and needs new code. No reader today views the diagram on a different machine or outside werk.

criterion.text: Text overflows its box on a second kind of machine, or in a viewer other than werk.

payload.title: A label sits inline in its own lane and splits the path

patch.why: A label cell sits in its own connection's lane, between two parts of the path. The checker accepts the label only when it touches every part of the cut path. The line is drawn straight through from part to part, and a plate in the background colour sits under the text, so the label reads as a gap in the line while the line itself is not cut.

patch.body: The tile rules that make the build refuse a grid are on #vi-sysdiag-grid.
patch.why: The build refuses a grid that breaks a tile rule. It warns, but still renders, when the grid is legal and hard to read, because the cheapest legal route is sometimes the hard-to-read one. It places each label inside its own lane. Every warning and every placement rule is its own decision under this card.

payload.title: A label beside its lane as well as inline, with its text against the side nearest the lane
payload.why_not: A label beside the lane can drift from its line as its box grows, and needs its own rule for where the text sits in a wider box. A label inside the lane cannot drift, so the build needs no placement rule for it.

payload.title: Make every hard-to-read case an error
payload.why_not: Some hard-to-read routes are the cheapest legal route, such as a detour under the whole diagram. An error would force the author to redraw a correct grid, and the updater would fail a run that should pass.

patch.body:
The build refuses a grid that breaks a tile rule, and those rules are on #vi-sysdiag-grid.

It warns, and still draws the picture, when a legal grid reads badly: a connection that doubles back on itself (#vi-sysdiag-grid-uturn), or a single connection that leaves a part away from the middle of its side (#vi-sysdiag-grid-offcentre).

It places every label inside its own connection's lane, where the label cannot drift from its line (#vi-sysdiag-grid-inline-label).
patch.why: A grid can be legal and still hard to read. Refusing it would fail a correct grid whose cheapest route is awkward. Accepting it in silence would hide the problem from its author. So the build has three answers, not two.

payload.text: Postponed. Group frames still come from the bounding box of their members. On the current product diagram some frames look broken, but the diagram stays readable, so the shape grid can wait. The 7 subcards hold the design for when it is built.

payload.title: An agent folds the decided cards into the diagram's parts
Each redraw rewrites the whole file, with the old drawing in context
The Flow tab shows the share of one-card diagram redraws that stayed local
payload.why: It is the measure for #vi-sysdiag-localrate. The diagram view shows only the last redraw. A share over every run, read from the log, replaces a hand count.
payload.body:
Each finished run of the diagram job writes one ended event to the pipeline log (#ms-store). The event holds the result (updated, unchanged or failed), the declared outcome and its reason (#vi-sysdiag-declare), the decided cards whose change started the run, the wall time and the cost.

The gauge counts only updated runs that exactly one card started. A run that batched several cards cannot say what one card does, and an unchanged or failed run made no redraw. Beside the share, the gauge shows the count of batched, unchanged and failed runs, so a small sample is visible.

Under the gauge, a list shows each restructure in the window, with its reason and the card that started it. A click on the card opens it on the map. A person reads this list for the second half of the test: does each reason point at the card that moved a boundary.

The threshold, window and minimum sample come from #vi-sysdiag-localrate. If that card names no threshold, the gauge shows the share in grey with no state. With a threshold, colour follows the state: red fires, green holds, grey not enough data.

The gauge shows when the Flow scope contains #vi-sysdiag-localrate. Runs belong to the diagram, not to a subtree, so every scope that shows the gauge counts every run.

payload.why: The gauge measures the hypothesis this card states, with its holds and fails test and its threshold.
It counts the local and restructure outcomes that this card makes each redraw declare.
Each run writes its event to the pipeline log that this card defines, and the share is a fold over it.
The gauge is a section of the Flow tab that this card defines.
Batching can start one run from several cards, so the gauge separates one-card runs from batched runs.

payload.title: Keep only the last run, as the diagram view does
payload.why_not: A share needs every run. One overwritten record cannot be counted.

payload.title: Count every updated run, batched or not
payload.why_not: A batched run that restructures cannot be traced to one card. The hypothesis is about one-card changes.

payload.title: A panel among the pipeline measures
payload.why_not: Those panels measure the build pipeline of #ms-self against a band learned from history. This is one hypothesis with a holds-or-fails test, which is the gauge shape of #vi-prop-metric.

criterion.text: After 20 one-card runs, compare the gauge counts and the restructure list with the run events in the pipeline log, and check that the list lets a person judge each reason without opening the diagram.

payload.text: The gauge on #vi-flow-localrate reads its threshold, window and minimum sample from this card. This card does not name them yet. Until it does, the gauge shows the share in grey.

payload.why: v0 includes the alignment practices that #align defines: sampling for ambiguity, two options at least, ephemeral prototypes, diffs, and the decision profile.

payload.title: v0 includes the tracker export
payload.why_not: Not core. The map is the record and the board shows the tickets, so a one-way publish to Linear or GitHub Issues adds nothing v0 needs.

payload.title: v0 includes the validate stage
payload.why_not: Validate measures production. v0 has no production until it is built and in use, so the stage comes after v0.

payload.title: v0 includes pipeline self-measurement
payload.why_not: The build loop that builds v0 already records its own cost and failures. A separate measurement layer duplicates it.

patch.body:
What v0 contains. Each item is a concept elsewhere on the map; this card only says it is in v0. A depends_on edge to each item records the inclusion.

- The chat pane beside the map: #werk-chat.
- The CLI as the only write path, with remove and find: #werk-write.
- Extracted excerpts: #werk-excerpt.
- Card rendering: #werk-reflink, #werk-codeblock.
- The wording rule for card text: #werk-wording.
- Reopen reasons in the staleness view: #reopen-reason-gap.
- New cards as proposals: #werk-propose-new.
- The contract check at decided: #werk-contract.
- The dev loop and the Bun runtime: #werk-dev, #werk-hmr.
- The test harness: #werk-test.
- The ticket board: #werk-board.
- Multichat: #werk-mc-scope.
- The inner build loop: #werk-loop.
- Alignment before building: #align.

The core of v0 is three views: the map, the board, and the chat. The product diagram, the 3D graph, and the Flow view are outside v0. So are the tracker export, the validate stage, and pipeline self-measurement.

v0 is a new project in its own repository, built from scratch on #werk-stack (#werk-base). The log, the fold, and the web view are the three parts. Bun runs the server TypeScript directly (#werk-hmr). Vite transforms the client.

#pr-log names the same append-only-log idea for the future standalone engine. werk's own log.jsonl is a separate, working implementation of it, not a consumer of pr-log's.

payload.title: The record of a work item's progress outlives its branch

patch.body:
The record holds milestones only: a work item entered the build loop, a rubric passed, it is blocked, it is done. A machine log of every cycle stays in the agent's own session.

The record is stored outside the branch's own working tree. Deleting a branch or a worktree without merging it must not lose the progress of its work items, because no other copy exists to rebuild it from.
patch.why: A branch's commits, test runs, and tool calls already live in git and in the coding agent's own session. werk owns none of that. werk keeps only the map and the progress of each work item, and that record must survive the branch being deleted.

payload.why: The record is the append-only event log that #pr-log defines, so it can be stored apart from any branch.

payload.title: v0 is tested at two seams: the command line and the browser
payload.why: The command line is the only write path and the build's own seam, and the browser is the only place the three views exist, so no lower seam is needed for behaviour.
payload.body:
werk v0 is tested at two seams, each the highest one for its half of the product. Both put one scripted fake agent first on the PATH, so no test reaches a real agent.

The command line, run against a temporary project and a temporary git repository, covers every write to the map — the events of each verb, the ghost and accept rules, the contract check, reopen reasons and marks, excerpts and notes — and the whole build pipeline (see #st-build-seam). Because the map is written only through the command line (#werk-write), the seam that #st-build-seam sets for the build also covers the map.

The browser, through a real server on a copy of a fixture project, covers the map, card rendering, the chat pane, multichat, and the board (#werk-test).

Pure code also gets unit tests under the coverage gate of #werk-test. That gate measures coverage; it is not a third seam for behaviour.

payload.title: The from-scratch v0 is compared with the prototype by running the same user paths on both
payload.why: The kill criterion of #werk-base says 'too far from the prototype's behaviour' but names no measure. A shared set of user paths makes the distance a count.
payload.body: The kill criterion of #werk-base is measured by running the prototype's browser test paths against v0. The prototype's own browser tests are the reference paths, because they already pass on the prototype. A path that passes on the prototype and fails on v0 is one measured gap. The count of such gaps is the distance from the prototype's behaviour. A gap is first a missing or unclear card, not a reason to copy prototype code.

payload.title: In dev, Vite runs inside the werk server, and a client change it cannot apply in place reloads the page
payload.why: #werk-dev was decided for a client with no build step. With a Vite client (#werk-stack), the server must transform the client itself, and the reload rule must still keep the draft.
payload.body: In dev, the werk server runs Vite inside its own process to transform the React client, so there is one process and one port, and the server's lock and hot-reload guard (#werk-hmr) still cover everything. A client change that Vite applies in place needs no reload. A change it cannot apply in place sends the reload event on the live channel that #werk-dev decides, and the composer draft survives it in session storage, as #werk-dev requires. Each tab's draft is kept by tab (#werk-mc-follow).

patch.body: In dev, the werk server runs Vite inside its own process to transform the React client. There is one process and one port, so the lock and the hot-reload guard cover the client too (#werk-hmr). Vite applies a client change in place when it can. A change it cannot apply in place reloads the page by the rule in #werk-dev, with the composer draft kept per tab (#werk-mc-follow).
patch.why: A Vite client must be transformed by the server in dev, and a reload must not lose the composer draft.

payload.why: takes the reload event and the draft-keeping rule
takes the single-process lock and hot-reload guard
takes the Vite client that the server must transform
takes the per-tab ownership of the draft
takes the kill criterion whose measure this card defines

payload.title: v0 is killed if it fails the prototype's user paths
payload.why: A kill criterion with no measure cannot be applied. Running the same user paths on both makes the distance a count.
payload.body: v0 as a whole is reopened for reconsideration when it is too far from the prototype's behaviour. The measure is a run of the prototype's browser test paths against v0. These paths are the reference because they already pass on the prototype. A path that passes on the prototype and fails on v0 is one gap. The count of gaps is the distance. A gap is first a missing or unclear card, not a reason to copy prototype code. #werk-base sets the from-scratch choice that this criterion can overturn.

payload.why: takes the from-scratch choice that a failed comparison reopens

criterion.text: Run the prototype's browser test paths against v0. Each path that passes on the prototype and fails on v0 is one gap. Reopen v0 when the gap count is too high. A gap is first a missing or unclear card, not a reason to copy prototype code.

payload.title: A ticket that extends a card another ticket built also cites it, and is blocked by that earlier ticket
payload.why: depends_on edges alone leave a ticket with no blocker when it builds on a card with no outgoing edge, so the ticket could start before the code it extends exists.
payload.body: A ticket cites every card it builds, including a card that an earlier ticket first built and this ticket extends. The first ticket that cites a card introduces it. blocked_by then follows two rules: a ticket is blocked by the ticket that introduces each card its own cited cards depend_on, and a ticket is blocked by the ticket that introduces a card it cites and extends. No other order is added.

criterion.text: Run the prototype's browser test paths against v0. Each path that passes on the prototype and fails on v0 is one gap. Reopen v0 when the gap count is too high. A gap is first a missing or unclear card, not a reason to copy prototype code.

patch.body:
v0 starts in a new, empty repository. Nothing is ported from the prototype code.

- The spec is the decided cards that #werk depends on, not the prototype code.
- The prototype code is a reference. A builder may read it to see how a decided behaviour looks. It does not copy it.
- The stack is #werk-stack: React + Vite for the client, inside the Bun server from #werk-hmr. Vite transforms the client, so v0 has a client build step.

Why not extend the prototype: it works well as a product, but its code is messy. A clean build tests whether the decided cards are enough to rebuild the behaviour.

The kill criterion for this choice is recorded on #werk. The prototype's behaviour sets the bar. The fallback is to extend the prototype code (see the option on this card).

payload.text: First plan run on #werk: the spec writer was cancelled at 60 s of silence while it did real work. In the next run the longest gap between events was 86 s (spec writer) and 88 s (ticket writer). Each gap is the model generating one large file write. The headless runner does not ask for partial-message events, so token output during a tool call is invisible to the overseer.

payload.title: A ticket that extends a card another ticket built also cites it, and is blocked by that earlier ticket
payload.why: depends_on edges alone leave a ticket with no blocker when it builds on a card with no outgoing edge, so the ticket could start before the code it extends exists.
payload.body: A ticket cites every card it builds, including a card that an earlier ticket first built and this ticket extends. The first ticket that cites a card introduces it. blocked_by then follows two rules: a ticket is blocked by the ticket that introduces each card its own cited cards depend_on, and a ticket is blocked by the ticket that introduces a card it cites and extends. No other order is added.

payload.why: adds a blocked_by rule that the set check on blocked_by must accept

criterion.text: A ticket set written under this rule still lets a ticket start before the ticket that introduces a card it extends has merged.

patch.body:
The set checks read the tickets of one plan run that passed their own checks (#st-ticket-own-checks), the decided cards of the planned subtree, the depends_on edges between those cards, and the spec's story numbers. A ticket that fails its own checks is not on the board, so its cites and stories do not count.

**1. Cards cited.** Every decided card in the planned subtree is in the `cites:` of at least one ticket. A failure lists the cards no ticket cites.

**2. Stories delivered.** Every story number in the spec is in the `stories:` of at least one ticket (#st-ticket-stories). No ticket lists a number that is not in the spec. A failure lists the missing or unknown numbers.

**3. blocked_by.** Every number in `blocked_by` is a ticket in the set; a blocker that failed its own checks is not in the set, so it fails this condition. The `blocked_by` graph has no cycle. And it agrees with depends_on: for each depends_on edge A → B between two subtree cards, every ticket that cites A either also cites B, or reaches every ticket that cites B along `blocked_by`, directly or through other blockers. A ticket cannot start before its blockers are done, and they cannot start before theirs, so a blocker of a blocker already holds the ticket back. An edge to a card that no ticket cites is left to check 1.

A failure of check 3 names only the tickets that must not start: the ticket that misses a blocker, the ticket that names a blocker not in the set, and the tickets on a cycle. The ticket it should wait for is not named. That ticket is not wrong, and blocking it holds back every ticket after it, the first ticket of the run included. Checks 1 and 2 name cards and stories, not tickets.

payload.title: A ticket must list every ticket it waits for directly in blocked_by
payload.why_not: A blocker of a blocker already holds the ticket back. The direct-only reading fails a correct ticket set and forces each ticket to repeat its blockers' blockers.

payload.title: A blocked_by failure also names the ticket that should be waited for
payload.why_not: That ticket is not wrong. Blocking it holds back every ticket after it; on the first plan of #werk it put ticket 01, which has no blockers, in blocked, so no ticket could start.

patch.body:
The set checks read the tickets of one plan run that passed their own checks (#st-ticket-own-checks), the decided cards of the planned subtree, the depends_on edges between those cards, and the spec's story numbers. A ticket that fails its own checks is not on the board, so its cites and stories do not count.

**1. Cards cited.** Every decided card in the planned subtree is in the `cites:` of at least one ticket. A failure lists the cards no ticket cites.

**2. Stories delivered.** Every story number in the spec is in the `stories:` of at least one ticket (#st-ticket-stories). No ticket lists a number that is not in the spec. A failure lists the missing or unknown numbers.

**3. blocked_by.** Every number in `blocked_by` is a ticket in the set; a blocker that failed its own checks is not in the set, so it fails this condition. The `blocked_by` graph has no cycle. And it agrees with depends_on: for each depends_on edge A → B between two subtree cards, every ticket that cites A either also cites B, or reaches the ticket that introduces B along `blocked_by`, directly or through other blockers. The ticket that introduces a card is the first ticket, by number, that cites it (#st-ticket-cite-extends). A ticket cannot start before its blockers are done, and they cannot start before theirs, so a blocker of a blocker already holds the ticket back. An edge to a card that no ticket cites is left to check 1.

A failure of check 3 names only the tickets that must not start: the ticket that misses a blocker, the ticket that names a blocker not in the set, and the tickets on a cycle. The ticket it should wait for is not named. That ticket is not wrong, and blocking it holds back every ticket after it, the first ticket of the run included. Checks 1 and 2 name cards and stories, not tickets.

payload.title: A ticket that cites A waits for every ticket that cites B
payload.why_not: A ticket that extends B also cites it (#st-ticket-cite-extends), so a widely used card is cited by many tickets. Waiting for all of them orders tickets that share no code, and it contradicts the rule that a ticket waits for the ticket that introduces the card.

payload.title: Every token the model writes counts as an event for the silence limit
payload.why: A model can write one large file in a single tool call for longer than the silence limit. The finished message arrives only at the end, so without the tokens the overseer cancels a model that is still working.
payload.body:
The overseer asks the agent for its partial-message stream, one event per piece of generated text. Each piece resets the silence limit in #lp-overseer-silence, so silence means that the model produces nothing at all.

The partial messages only keep the limit armed. They do not go into the session's event log and do not reach any other reader. The log already holds each finished message, and a token stream would bury the events that a reader follows.

On the first plan of a large subtree, the longest gap between finished messages was 86 seconds for the spec writer and 88 seconds for the ticket writer. Each gap was one long file write.

payload.why: The token stream is read where the overseer runs, inside the runner of each agent session.

payload.title: Raise the silence limit to cover the longest file write
payload.why_not: The gap grows with the size of the file the model writes, so no fixed number covers it, and a longer limit waits longer on a real stall.

payload.title: Write the partial messages to the event log too
payload.why_not: One session writes thousands of token events. They bury the finished messages and the overseer acts that a reader follows, and add nothing the finished messages do not hold.

criterion.metric: silence cancels per 100 agent sessions

patch.body:
A ticket can start when every ticket in its blocked_by list is merged and no failed set check holds it (#st-ticket-partial). The run builds up to 3 such tickets at the same time, each in its own worktree.

**Independence comes from the tickets alone.** For the order, the run scheduler reads each ticket's blocked_by edges (#st-ticket). It reads no other input. No agent judges overlap, and the ticket format has no field for the files a ticket touches. A set-check hold is not an order: it says the ticket set is wrong, and it lifts only when an agent fixes the tickets and the set check passes again.

**File overlap does not block.** Two unblocked tickets may edit the same file. Both build green alone. At the merge queue (#st-build-run), the second one fails `git merge`. That is a red merge: the ticket goes back to the builder loop with the conflict output as its last failure, the same as a red check.

**The base.** Each worktree branches off the run branch tip at the moment its build starts. A ticket that starts after an earlier merge has that merge in its tree.

**The cap.** 3 is a first guess. It changes when a real machine or a real rate limit shows a better number. The merge queue still takes one ticket at a time.

payload.why: A ticket that a failed set check holds does not start, even when every blocker is merged.
Takes the command-line seam that the build pipeline is tested at.
The map is written only through the command line, so the command-line seam covers every map write.
Takes the browser seam and the coverage gate for pure code.

criterion.text: A bug reaches use that a test at neither seam can catch, only a test below them.
I edit a client file in dev: the page updates in place, or reloads and keeps the composer draft of each tab. If the draft is lost or the server restarts, this is wrong.

payload.why: Takes the Vite client that the server must transform in dev.
v0 is built on the component stack that #werk-stack and its children decide, Vite in dev included.

payload.title: In v0, alignment before building is the accept gate and the plan's proposed decisions
payload.why: No card names what v0 builds for alignment, and both mechanisms already put every agent answer in front of the person before code.
payload.body: v0 builds no separate alignment feature. Alignment before building is delivered by two mechanisms that are already in v0: every card, option, source and excerpt an agent adds waits for the person's accept (see #werk-propose-new), and every answer that the spec or ticket writer gives and no card gives comes back as a proposed card before the build (see #st-spec). Every build gate also waits for the person (see #werk-loop-tier).

payload.title: The held-out set is built and gated on the run's tree before the merge loop runs it at each merge
payload.why: The merge loop depends on the held-out set, so the held-out set has to work on its own first.
payload.body: The held-out set is built as its own slice before the merge loop: the step author, the binder, the run on the run's tree, the feedback to the builder, and the G2 refusal while a step is red (see #lp-prod-heldout, #st-g2-heldout). The merge loop then adds the run after each merge and the follow-up ticket on a red step (see #st-build-run).

payload.title: Each plan writes a new run with its own spec and a full ticket set
payload.why_not: A second or interrupted plan over the same subtree puts a duplicate ticket set on the board, and the person has to find it and archive it.

payload.title: A plan over a subtree extends that subtree's spec and open tickets, and a run is not an entity
payload.why: A second or interrupted plan over the same subtree otherwise puts a second, full ticket set on the board beside the first.
payload.body:
A plan over a subtree first looks for the spec and the tickets that an earlier plan wrote for the same subtree. When they exist, the plan extends them. It updates the one spec of the subtree (#st-spec) and changes the open tickets in place, under their own ids. It does not write a second set.

Open means ready or blocked. A ticket in building, merging or done stays as it is, because only the merge loop moves it (#werk-board-control). The new and changed tickets cover only the scope that those tickets do not already cover.

Planning produces a spec and tickets, and nothing else. There is no run entity that owns them (the same rejection as #st-run-issue).

A plan over a parent or a child of an earlier plan's subtree is an overlap. This card does not settle the overlap case.

payload.why: It changes tickets in place, so it relies on the ticket fields and ids that #st-ticket defines.
It leaves building, merging and done tickets alone because #werk-board-control lets only the merge loop move them.
It drops the run entity for the reason #st-run-issue already gives against inventing one.

criterion.text: I run a second plan over a subtree that already has tickets, and check that the board holds one ticket set for it, not two.

payload.title: Tickets merge straight onto the main line, with no integration branch
payload.why: With no run entity, nothing owns a separate branch, and one line to merge onto is the simplest start.
payload.body:
Each ticket that passes its checks merges onto the main line. The merge queue still makes a temporary tree of the main line plus the ticket and runs the checks there first (#st-build-run). The held-out set runs on the main line after each merge.

G2 belongs to the tip of the main line for the tickets of one subtree: it opens when every ticket of that subtree is merged and every held-out step is green, and a later merge opens it again (#st-g2-heldout).

payload.title: One integration branch per planned subtree, keyed by its root card id
payload.why_not: It needs an owner for the branch, which brings back the run entity under another name, and it adds a second merge onto the main line.

payload.why: It keeps the merge queue of #st-build-run and changes only the line that the queue merges onto.
It keeps the G2 condition of #st-g2-heldout and scopes it to one subtree's tickets on the main line.

payload.title: A plan archives an open ticket that the subtree's current spec no longer needs
payload.why: A ticket no spec asks for must not stay buildable, and the archive is reversible, so the person loses nothing.
payload.body: When a plan extends a subtree's tickets and an open ticket delivers nothing in the new spec, the plan archives it. The archive records that the plan did it and why. A restore puts the ticket back, the same as a person's archive (#werk-board-control).

payload.title: The plan moves the ticket to blocked with the reason 'not in the current spec', and the person archives it
payload.why_not: The person must clear each stale ticket by hand after every re-plan, and the archive is reversible anyway.

payload.why: It uses the reversible archive of #werk-board-control and adds the plan as a second actor that may archive.

criterion.text: I run a second plan over a planned subtree and check the result on the board.
I run a second plan over a planned subtree and check the result on the board.

patch.body:
Four direct actions on the board:

1. Reorder tickets within ready.
2. Archive a ticket. Only a ready or blocked ticket shows this action; a ticket already building, merging, or done does not. Archiving asks for confirmation first, and the confirmation says the ticket is never deleted for good — an agent can restore it, the same reversible pattern #werk-remove already uses for a map card.
3. Trigger the build of a ready ticket inside an active run. Either press the trigger icon, or drag the ticket into building.
4. Stop the build of a building ticket, returning it to ready. Drag the ticket back into ready.

These are the only manual column-to-column moves. Every other move is not a person's call:

- Ready and blocked: an agent moves the ticket, and always either states the blocking reason or resolves it.
- Building, merging, and done: the merge loop moves the ticket (#st-build-run). A red check in merging sends it back to building automatically, never by a manual drag.

A plan is the one actor besides a person that archives: it archives an open ticket that the subtree's current spec no longer needs, with that reason, and a restore puts it back (#st-plan-archive).

Nothing builds before a person starts the run. Starting the merge loop on a plan run is the person's trigger for the whole run (#st-build-run). Inside an active run, the board trigger starts one ready ticket early. That ticket builds, then goes through the same merge queue: building, merging, done. Up to 3 tickets build at once (#st-build-parallel).

A ticket is not edited on the board. A person asks an agent to change it, and the agent runs the ticket-set checks again (#st-ticket).

```
werk plan <subtree-id> [--timeout 600] [--silence 60]
werk loop "<brief>" --check "..." [--card <id> ...] [--cap 5] [--timeout 600]
werk build <ticket-id> [--cap 5] [--timeout 600] [--silence 60] [--check-timeout 300]
werk run <plan-run> [the flags of werk build]
werk gate <plan-run> [approve --actor you]
werk ticket list | move <id> blocked|ready --reason "..." | archive <id> | restore <id> | import <plan-run>
```

- `werk plan` turns a decided subtree into a spec and tickets (#st-spec). The spec is `.werk/specs/<subtree-id>.md` and each ticket id is `<subtree-id>/NN`. A second `werk plan` over the same subtree updates that spec, rewrites its open tickets under their ids, adds tickets after the highest number, and archives the open tickets the spec no longer needs (#st-plan-extend). It exits 1 when a set check fails.
- `werk loop` builds one brief in a throwaway worktree, one fresh agent per pass (#lp-stateless).
- `werk build` runs the builder loop on one ticket (#st-build-ticket). `--cap` is the retry cap, 5 by default.
- `werk run` runs the merge loop over one plan run (#st-build-run-mechanics). Running it again resumes.
- `werk gate <plan-run> approve` passes G2 and needs `--actor you` (#st-gates).
- `werk ticket` moves, archives, restores and imports tickets on the board (#werk-board-control). A move needs `--reason`. An import makes ids as `werk plan` does, and adds nothing on a second run.

payload.why: The plan command extends an earlier plan of the same subtree as #st-plan-extend decides.

payload.title: Tickets merge straight onto the main line, with no integration branch
payload.why: With no run entity, nothing owns a separate branch, and one line to merge onto is the simplest start.
payload.body:
Each build starts from the tip of the main line, never from a snapshot of a working tree. Each ticket that passes its checks merges onto the main line. The merge queue still makes a temporary tree of the main line plus the ticket and runs the checks there first (#st-build-run). The held-out set runs on the main line after each merge.

The main line may be checked out somewhere. Then the merge moves that checkout with a fast-forward, so its files follow the branch. A checkout whose local changes block the fast-forward stops the merge, and nothing moves.

G2 belongs to the tip of the main line for the tickets of one subtree. It opens when every ticket of that subtree is merged and every held-out step is green, and a later merge opens it again (#st-g2-heldout).

payload.title: One integration branch per planned subtree, keyed by its root card id
payload.why_not: It needs an owner for the branch, which brings back the run entity under another name, and it adds a second merge onto the main line.

payload.why: It keeps the merge queue of #st-build-run and changes only the line that the queue merges onto.
It keeps the G2 condition of #st-g2-heldout and scopes it to one subtree's tickets on the main line.

criterion.text: I run a second plan over a planned subtree and check the result on the board.

payload.title: v0 is built on the main branch of this repository, and the prototype is a sibling branch deleted once v0 matches the map
payload.why: The main branch holds an empty tree, so it is the new, empty repository that v0 starts in, and the prototype never becomes its base.
payload.body:
v0's main line is the main branch, which starts empty. Every ticket of #werk builds from its tip and merges onto it (#st-plan-main).

The prototype lives on its own branch beside the main branch. It may be committed, but it is never merged into the main branch and never a build's base. It is deleted when the v0 that werk built on the main branch matches what the decided cards say.

payload.title: Build v0 on the prototype branch, from a snapshot of its working tree
payload.why_not: The prototype code would become v0's base, which #werk-base rules out: v0 starts empty and only reads the prototype.

payload.why: It names which branch is the main line that #st-plan-main merges every ticket onto.

criterion.text: I check that no build of a #werk ticket starts from or merges onto the prototype branch.

payload.title: A hot reload keeps the server and swaps in the new request handler
payload.why: The guard on the global object must keep every long-lived thing, but an agent that edits a route handler also needs to see the edit without a restart.
payload.body: The guard keeps the listening server, its port, the open live-channel connections and the long-lived children on the global object. Each hot reload evaluates the start-up again. The guard then puts the request handler of the new evaluation in place of the old one and logs that it reuses the live server. It never listens a second time and never starts a second child. So an edit to a route handler is live after the reload, and only an edit to the start-up code itself needs a restart. See #werk-hmr for the guard and the runtime.

payload.title: Keep the first request handler for the life of the process
payload.why_not: An edit to a route handler would not go live until a restart, and a restart kills the live chat session that the guard exists to keep. Swapping the handler costs nothing: the server, the clients and the children stay.

payload.title: The unit test run cleans the environment of every process a test starts
payload.why: Bun's own process spawn, executable lookup and shell read the environment the test process started with, not the edited one, so a fake agent put first on PATH in the test setup is not enough on its own.
payload.body: Before the first test, the run removes every werk variable that the shell passed in, so no test can write to a real project's log. It puts the fake agent first on PATH. It then makes the runtime's process spawn, executable lookup and shell default to that cleaned environment. A test that starts an agent with no explicit environment still gets the fake. Every process that a test harness starts gets the same cleaned environment, and the browser test server refuses to start when the fake agent is not first on its PATH.

payload.why: cleans the environment of the bun test runner that #werk-test-runner chooses, whose spawn defaults are the gap

payload.title: Only edit PATH in the test setup
payload.why_not: The runtime's own spawn ignores the edit: a test that started an agent with no explicit environment reached the real agent.

payload.title: Component tests share one DOM for the whole unit run
payload.why: Server tests and React component tests run in one process, and they need different globals.
payload.body: One happy-dom window is registered before any test file loads, so React finds a DOM when it first loads. The runtime's own network, stream and timer globals are put back after the registration, so a server test in the same run uses the real fetch, not the DOM's. Each component test unmounts what it rendered.

payload.title: Register a DOM per component test file and remove it after the file
payload.why_not: React checks for a DOM once, when it loads, and its scheduler still runs after a file ends. A DOM removed between files broke the next file's component tests.

payload.title: v0 grows in its own directory beside the prototype, with its own packages and checks
payload.why: v0 needs a clean project with nothing from the prototype, and the build runs inside the prototype's repository.
payload.body: v0 has its own package list, lockfile, compiler and test configuration in one top-level directory. Nothing in it imports from the prototype. Every check runs inside that directory and installs its packages first when they are missing. Moving v0 to its own repository is a copy of that one directory. See #werk-base for why v0 is a new project.

payload.title: Delete the prototype code from the build branch and build v0 at the top level
payload.why_not: It removes the reference that builders read to see how a decided behaviour looks, and a merge of the branch would delete the prototype from the main line.

patch.body:
- Starting the merge loop on a planned subtree is the person's trigger for its tickets. Starting it again resumes.
- The merge queue merges the ticket's branch in a detached worktree and runs the ticket's own checks there.
- The main line moves only from the value it had when the merge started, so a main line that changed in between is never overwritten (#st-plan-main). A checkout of the main line moves with it by a fast-forward. A checkout whose local changes block that fast-forward stops the loop, and nothing moves.
- After a red merge, the next build starts from the ticket's old branch when that branch sits on top of the main line.
- A ticket's retry cap counts passes across all its builds, so it also bounds the trips between the builder and the merge queue.
- A build that stays red stops the loop as stuck.
- Every start of the loop writes the feature tier event to the board log first (#werk-loop-tier).
- G2 belongs to the main line's tip: a later merge opens it again. Only a person passes it (#st-gates).

payload.why: It moves the main line that #st-plan-main makes the merge target, instead of a branch of its own.

payload.title: The fold sets aside an event that breaks a map rule, and a write refuses it
payload.why: One bad line in a committed log must not hide the whole map, and a new event must not add a bad line.
payload.body: A write checks its events against the folded map, in order, and appends all of them or none. An event that breaks a rule (an unknown card, a second parent, a link from an option other than alternative_to, a cycle) is refused with the rule it breaks. The fold applies the same check: an event that fails it is not applied, the fold lists it as a problem with its place in the log, and the events after it still fold. The log is never rewritten to remove the bad line.

payload.title: Fail the whole fold on the first event that breaks a rule
payload.why_not: A log is committed and merged, so one bad line can arrive from a merge. A failed fold shows no map at all, and the reader cannot see or fix the card the line is about.

payload.why: the link rules that a write and the fold check, such as an option's single alternative_to link

payload.title: The address of a card page is the path /card/ followed by the card id
payload.why: The address bar must name the open card, so a view can be shared and comes back after a reload.
payload.body: The root page is the bare address. A card page is /card/ and the card id, URL-encoded, so an id with a colon such as an option or a source id works. Opening a card in the page adds a history entry, so Back returns to the card before it. A card that is not in the map, or is removed, gets a page that says so.

criterion.text: A committed log with one bad line still shows every other card, and the problem names the line.

payload.title: The root page lists the cards that refine nothing, and a source only when no card cites it
payload.why: A source that a card is supported_by is evidence for that card. On the root page it would read as a top-level decision.
payload.body: The root page uses the same shape as every other page. Its sub-cards are the cards that refine no other card. An option never appears there: it lives under Options on the card it is an alternative to. A source that some card is supported_by appears only under that card's evidence. A source that no card cites stays on the root page, so it is never out of reach.

payload.why: which links place a node in the tree (refines) and which make a source evidence (supported_by)

payload.title: Adding a card under a parent is one event
payload.why: One change is one event. The place of a new card is part of what was added, not a second change.
payload.body: The added event names the parent, and the fold makes the refines link from it at the same place in the log. A later link to a parent is its own event. See #pr-log for the log and #vi-edges for what refines means.

payload.why: takes refines as the link that places a card in the tree

payload.title: Add the card and its refines link as two events
payload.why_not: One command would then write two events, and a reader of the log sees two changes where the person made one.

payload.title: The location hash names the open card
payload.why: The page is one document. A hash change opens a card without a request to the server, and the address still names the card.
payload.body: The address of a card is the page address with the card id as its hash. No hash is the root page. Opening a card, Back, a reload and a shared address all read the hash. See #vi-onview for why the address names the card.

payload.title: A path per card, such as /card/<id>
payload.why_not: Every card path must then fall back to the page on the server, and the server must know the client's routes.

payload.title: A log change pushes changed, and each view fetches the fold again
payload.why: Every view reads the fold through the one read path. The push only says that the log grew.
payload.body: The server watches the log. When it grows, the server sends changed on the live channel to every open page. The page then fetches the map again and draws the new fold. The push carries no events and no state, so there is one read path. See #werk-write and #pr-log.

payload.title: Send the new events or the new fold on the live channel
payload.why_not: The page would then have a second read path next to the map fetch, and the two can disagree.

payload.title: The chat agent child belongs to the live server, so a reload reuses it
payload.why: A child started from module scope is orphaned by a hot reload. Held on the state that survives the reload, the next turn after an edit reaches the same child.
payload.body: The server holds one chat agent child for the project, under a fixed name, in the same state that keeps the port and the live channel's clients across a reload (#werk-hmr). The first chat turn starts the child in the project directory, with the stream-json flags of #werk-chat-stdin. Every later turn, before or after a reload, writes to the same child. A turn never starts a second child while the first one runs. The child's output goes to every open live channel as agent events. Stopping the server stops the child.

payload.why: The child is a claude child that reads turns as stream-json lines on stdin, as this card decides.

payload.title: A hot reload names the server modules it picked up
payload.why: Without a name in the output, a person cannot tell that an edit reached the running server, or which edit did.
payload.body: When a reload reuses the live server, the output prints two lines. The first names every server module whose file was saved after the previous load. Tests and client files are left out, because the server does not import them. The second says the live server is reused on its port and process, and does not listen a second time (#werk-hmr).
