File save times decide the list, because the runtime does not tell the server which file changed.

payload.why: The report prints when a reload keeps the server and swaps in the new handler, the reuse that this card decides.
The child stays because a reload keeps the server state and only swaps the handler, as this card decides.

payload.title: The werk server answers only the local machine and its own pages
payload.why: A chat turn starts an agent with the user's credentials and tools. A page on another site, or another host on the network, must not be able to start one or read its replies.
payload.body: The server listens on the loopback interface only, so another host on the network cannot connect. It refuses any request whose Host header is not the loopback name and port it serves; this stops a DNS rebinding page that reaches the port under its own origin. A chat turn needs a JSON content type, which a cross-origin page cannot send without a CORS preflight, and the server never grants one. A chat turn with an Origin header from any other origin is refused. A request with no Origin, as from a local script or the CLI, is accepted.

payload.why: the client pages that may send a chat turn are the ones the in-process Vite server serves on the same origin

payload.title: A per-boot random token that the client must send
payload.why_not: It is needed only when werk must answer another host or a foreign page. Neither is a use case, and the loopback bind, Host check and preflight rule close both without a secret to pass to the client.

payload.title: Deciding a postponed card again resumes its work
payload.why: A postponed card is open, and its content still holds. Deciding it again is the moment its work resumes, so that decide clears every paused mark the postponement put downstream.
payload.body: A resume needs no event of its own. The decide that closes the postponement is the resume, and it clears only the paused marks that this card caused. A paused mark from a different postponed card stays until that card is decided again. A stale mark is not touched: only a review clears it (#vi-prop). A decide of a paused card itself does not clear its paused mark, because the work it waits for has not resumed.

payload.why: takes the rule that only a review clears a stale mark

payload.title: A postponement pauses the links that existed when it happened
payload.why: The paused mark goes every distance, over refines children and depends_on dependents. A card linked after the postponement was written against the current text, the same as for a stale mark.
payload.body: The closure is walked once, at the postponement, over the links in the map at that moment. A card that links to a paused card later carries no paused mark from it (#vi-prop-bornstale). It waits on its basis instead (#map-wait). The walk follows the same two link types a change follows (#vi-edges), but goes on past the first hop (#pr-wf-paused).

payload.why: takes the rule that a change marks only the links that existed when it happened
takes the two link types that carry a change: refines and depends_on
takes the two reopen reasons and the paused mark at any distance
takes the rule that every view draws from the one log

payload.title: The log watcher belongs to the live server, so a reload keeps one watcher
payload.why: A watcher started on each evaluation would push every log change once per reload so far, and a watcher lost on reload would stop the live map.
payload.body: The server starts one watcher on the project's log when it first boots. It holds that watcher in the same state that keeps the port, the live channel's clients and the chat agent child across a reload (#werk-hmr-swap). A reload never starts a second watcher. After a reload, a change to the log still reaches every open live channel as one push. Stopping the server closes the watcher.

payload.why: The watcher stays because a reload keeps the server state and swaps only the handler, as this card decides.

payload.title: A mark's trace names the reopen reason, and a paused trace names the path
payload.why: The reader decides what to do with a marked card from its trace. The reopen reason says whether the content is still true, and a paused mark far from its origin needs the cards between to be followed back.
payload.body: A mark from a reopen carries its reason, postponed or rejected (#pr-wf-paused). A mark from an amend carries no reason: the content changed, so the mark is stale. A stale trace stays one hop long. A paused mark can sit any distance away (#pr-wf-paused-reach), so its trace also names each card the postponement passed through, nearest to the changed card first, and the link type of the last hop. The staleness listing and the card page print the same trace.

payload.why: takes the two reopen reasons and which mark each one puts
takes the paused mark at any distance, which makes a path necessary

payload.title: A refused decide lists every missing fact, each with its own fixing command
payload.why: An agent that sees one fact at a time needs one failed decide per fact. With the full list, it fixes the card in one pass.
payload.body: The refusal names each missing fact in a fixed order: who, basis, options, kill criterion. Each fact has one line that says why it is missing, and one command that supplies it, with the card id filled in (#werk-contract-fix). The waiver of a fact is named in its reason line, not given as a second command, so each fact has exactly one command. When the basis is open or stale, the command decides that basis (#map-wait).

payload.why: It extends the fix message of #werk-contract-fix from one fact to the full list.
The list and its order are the four facts of #werk-contract-facts.

payload.title: Report only the first missing fact
payload.why_not: Each further fact costs one more failed decide, and the agent cannot see how far the card is from decided.

payload.title: An amend is any change to a decided card's frozen fields or contract facts
payload.why: A change that is not a text edit can also remove a fact from a decided card, for example the removal of its last option. Each such change must meet the check.
payload.body: The check runs again, on the card as the change would leave it, after a retitle, a text edit, a record of who or of a waiver, a new link from the card, and the removal of an option weighed against it. A card decided before a fact became required waits on that fact at its next amend (#map-frozen). The removal of a card that this card depends on is not an amend of this card, so the check does not refuse it. The text itself is not checked.

payload.why: An amend runs the decide facts again, as #map-frozen requires.
The facts that an amend must keep are the four of #werk-contract-facts.

payload.title: Check only text edits of a decided card
payload.why_not: The removal of the last option, or a change of who to you, would leave a decided card without a required fact, and no check would see it.

payload.title: A frozen change to a decided card needs every fact. A free change must not remove one
payload.why: A change that is not a text edit can remove a fact from a decided card, for example the removal of its last option. But a card decided before a fact became required must still be able to receive that fact, or no command can fix it.
payload.body: A change to a frozen field of a decided card (#map-frozen) runs the decide facts on the card as the change would leave it, and fails on any missing fact. So a card decided before a fact became required waits on that fact at its next frozen change. A free change, such as a record of who or of a waiver, a link to a source, or the removal of an option weighed against the card, fails only when it removes a fact that the card had. So each command that a refusal prints goes through. The removal of a card that this card depends on is not a change to this card, so the check does not refuse it. The text itself is not checked.

payload.why: The split into frozen and free changes is the one #map-frozen defines.
The facts that a change must keep are the four of #werk-contract-facts.
A printed fix must go through, as #werk-contract-fix requires, so a free change waits on no other fact.

payload.title: Every change to a decided card needs every fact
payload.why_not: On a card decided before the contract, each fix command is refused because another fact is still missing, so the card can never be fixed.

payload.title: Check only text edits of a decided card
payload.why_not: The removal of the last option, or a change of who to you, would leave a decided card without a required fact, and no check would see it.

payload.title: An excerpt points at one text-bearing line of the Claude Code session transcript
payload.why: A pointer is only worth keeping if a reader can open the same file later and land on the same characters.
payload.body: The transcript of a session is the file Claude Code writes for that session id, looked up in every project directory of the Claude configuration directory, so a session from another worktree is found too. A message is one line of that file from the user or the assistant that carries text; a line with only tool calls, tool results or meta content is never a match. The message index counts every line of the file from zero, so it stays valid whatever a reader filters out. The text of a message is its text blocks joined by a newline, and the span is the start and end character offset of the quote in that text. The speaker is the role on the line, user or assistant.

payload.title: A quote must occur exactly once in the whole transcript, not only in one message
payload.why: Two occurrences inside one message leave the span as much a guess as one occurrence in each of two messages.
payload.body: The quote fails in three distinct cases, and the failure names which one: no exact match, a match in more than one message (with the count of messages), and more than one match inside a single message. Each failure writes nothing to the log.

payload.title: A repeat inside one message takes its first occurrence
payload.why_not: The span would then point at a place the agent never chose, which is the guess #werk-excerpt forbids.

payload.title: A quote is one event that proposes the excerpt and holds its supported_by edge
payload.why: One command appends one event, and the excerpt with its edge accept or discard as one unit.
payload.body: The excerpt enters as a ghost with its own kind, distinct from a source: a source holds a finding that can be disputed, an excerpt holds a pointer into a transcript. The supported_by edge from the citing card is held until the excerpt is accepted (#werk-propose-new). The words of an excerpt never change: a retitle or a text edit refuses on an excerpt, before and after the accept, because the text is the transcript's, not the agent's. An excerpt is never added by hand; only the quote operation writes one.

payload.why: The excerpt enters as a ghost and its edge is held until the accept, as #werk-propose-new requires.
The quote changes the map only by appending to the log, as #werk-write requires.

payload.title: An excerpt is a source with transcript fields
payload.why_not: A disputed source puts every card it supports under review; an exact transcript pointer has no finding to dispute, and a hand-written source would pass as an extracted quote.

payload.title: A quote appends two events: the proposed excerpt, then its supported_by link
payload.why_not: A crash between the two leaves an excerpt that supports nothing, and every other map command appends exactly one event.

payload.title: A paused card is still a basis that holds
payload.why: Paused means the content is still true. A card that depends on a paused card can be decided on it, so a postponement never blocks work that only reads its content.
payload.body: The decide contract needs a basis that is decided and not marked (#map-wait). Only a stale mark or a review mark makes a basis fail. A paused mark does not: the content under it still holds, and only its build waits (#pr-wf-paused). A card whose basis is the postponed card itself still waits, because that card is open.

payload.why: a basis that is open or stale makes the card wait

payload.title: An accept carries the ghost's evidence; a discard leaves evidence in place
payload.why: An accept that left a ghost's sources behind would commit a card that points at evidence the map does not hold. A discard that dropped a shared source would delete evidence that another card still cites.
payload.body:
One accept makes real the ghost, its ghost refines parents up to the first real card, its ghost options, and the ghost sources and excerpts it is supported_by. An excerpt is evidence in the same way as a source: a card is supported_by it. A depends_on target stays a ghost, because it is a different card with its own words (see #werk-propose-new).

One discard drops the ghost, every ghost below it over refines, and the ghost options weighed against any of them, because an option has no meaning without its card. It leaves ghost sources and excerpts in place: one piece of evidence can support more than one card, and a card that is gone does not make the finding wrong.

payload.title: Contract facts still record on a ghost; only its words are frozen
payload.why: A ghost proposed already decided needs every contract fact before the decide, and a kill criterion is one of those facts.
payload.body: Frozen covers the title, the why, the body and the why-not reason. Who decides, a kill criterion, and the written reasons for no basis or no option are contract facts (see #werk-contract), each recorded on its own, so they still record on a ghost. Without them a ghost could never reach decided before the accept, and the one-unit proposal would be impossible. The facts show on the ghost, so the person reads them before the ✓ as well.

payload.why: the list of contract facts that stay recordable on a ghost

payload.title: An excerpt points at one text-bearing line of the Claude Code session transcript
payload.why: A pointer is only worth keeping if a reader can open the same file later and land on the same characters.
payload.body: The transcript of a session is the file Claude Code writes for that session id, looked up in every project directory of the Claude configuration directory, so a session from another worktree is found too. A message is one line of that file from the user or the assistant that carries text; a line with only tool calls, tool results or meta content is never a match. The message index counts every line of the file from zero, so it stays valid whatever a reader filters out. The text of a message is its text blocks joined by a newline, and the span is the start and end character offset of the quote in that text. A quote that covers the newline between two blocks is no match, because that newline is not in the file. The speaker is the role on the line, user or assistant.

payload.title: An excerpt is never disputed
payload.why: A dispute says a finding may be wrong. An excerpt holds no finding, only the words of one message, and the quote check already proved those words are in the transcript.
payload.body: A dispute applies to a source only, and it flags every card the source supports for review. An excerpt refuses a dispute and names the reason: its words are the transcript's. A card that cites a wrong excerpt is wrong in how it reads those words, and that is a change to the card, not to the excerpt.

payload.why: It takes from #werk-excerpt-event that an excerpt is its own kind with fixed words, distinct from a source.

payload.title: A held edge takes no mark from a change made while it was held
payload.why: A ghost is outside every staleness mark, and the person reads it against the current text at the accept. A mark from before the accept would ask for a review of something nobody had committed yet.
payload.body: A reopen, a retitle or an edit marks only the live edges of the changed card. A held edge waits on a ghost, so the change passes it by, even when the held edge is older than the change. When the accept makes the edge live, it arrives with no stale and no paused mark. The accept is the moment the edge enters the map, so it reads as a link made after the change (see #vi-prop-bornstale). If the edge's target is stale or postponed at the accept, the accepted card waits on it as its basis, and is not marked.

payload.why: a link newer than a change carries no mark from it; the accept is when the held edge becomes a link

payload.title: A reference is known when the map can open its card
payload.why: A link to a card the page cannot open lands on an empty page, so it is a dead reference in a new form.
payload.body: An id counts as known only when its card is in view: the card exists, and neither it nor a refines parent of it is removed. A removed card, or a card under a removed parent, is a dead reference and stays plain text. A restore makes its references link again, with no change to the text that names it. See #werk-reflink for the forms a reference takes, and #werk-remove for what removal does.

payload.why: that a removal takes the refines subtree out of view and a restore puts it back

payload.title: A sub-card tile shows the why line as plain words
payload.why: A tile is itself a link to its card. A rendered summary with a reference in it would put a link inside a link.
payload.body: Under its title, a sub-card tile shows the card's why line as one line of plain text. Every Markdown marker is dropped and the words stay, so a reference reads as #al-diff but is not a link, and a code span reads as its text. The card page itself renders the same why line in full, with its links. See #werk-reflink for why a tile holds no link.

payload.title: A log write in the moment a watch starts can go unseen, and the fetch on connect covers it
payload.why: The platform starts a directory watch on its own thread and gives no signal when the watch is live, so no watcher can promise to see a write that comes first.
payload.body: The server watches the directory that holds the log, so the write that creates the log is seen once the watch is live. A write that comes before the watch is live pushes no changed. That costs nothing: a page fetches the whole fold each time its live channel connects, so the page draws every event the log held at that moment (see #werk-write-changed). No polling of the log backs up the watch.

payload.why: the changed push and the fetch of the fold on each connect, which covers a write the watch missed

payload.title: Poll the log on a timer as well as watch it
payload.why_not: It adds a timer that runs for the whole life of the server, to cover a gap of a moment that the fetch on connect already covers.

payload.title: A page reads the chat thread back from the transcript when it connects
payload.why: A reload or a second tab showed an empty pane, though every finished block was already persisted.
payload.body: The transcript holds one finished block per line, in the order the blocks went out: the person's own messages, the agent's blocks, tool output, and the block that ends a turn with its duration and cost. A page reads the whole thread each time its live channel connects, so a reconnect after a server restart misses nothing. A block that still streams when the thread arrives stays until its finished form, with the same id, replaces it. A token is never in the transcript (see #werk-progress).

payload.title: A ticket file has four header lines and three sections, and a missing one fails the ticket
payload.why: A fixed shape lets a check read every field without a model, and a missing field is a plain failure, not a guess.
payload.body: A ticket starts with four header lines: title, stories, cites and blocked_by. Three sections follow: What to build, Acceptance criteria, and Checks. Stories, cites and blocked_by may be empty, and the Checks section may have no bullet. Each line and each heading must be there: a ticket without one fails its own check, and the failure names the missing field. Stories and blocked_by hold numbers, separated by commas. Cites holds card ids, with or without the hash sign.

payload.why: The stories line may be empty because #st-ticket-stories allows a ticket that delivers no story.

payload.title: A writer returns each new answer as a card record, and the plan proposes it as a ghost under the subtree root
payload.why: A person must see every answer that no card gives. A record with a title, a why and a body is enough to propose a card, and the program, not the writer, puts it on the map.
payload.body: The spec writer and the ticket writer each write a list of answers next to their output. Each answer has a short slug, a title, a why that names the question it settles, and a body. The plan proposes each answer as a ghost card that refines the root of the planned subtree, with the agent as the one who decides. The card id is the root id, a hyphen, and the slug. A writer never writes to the map itself. A record the plan cannot propose, for example an id that is already in the map, is reported, and the plan exits with an error.

payload.why: Each answer enters the map as a ghost, the way #werk-propose-new defines every new card.

payload.title: A ticket's own check accepts a blocker only when a depends_on edge or a shared cite explains it
payload.why: blocked_by is derived, not guessed. A blocker with no edge behind it is a guess, and that is a fault of the one ticket that lists it.
payload.body: The ticket that introduces a card is the first ticket, by number, that cites it. A blocker in a ticket's blocked_by is explained when it introduces a card that a cited card of the ticket depends on, or when it introduces, before this ticket, a card that this ticket also cites. A blocker that neither rule explains fails the ticket's own check, and the failure names the blocker. A required blocker that is missing is a different fault: the set check on blocked_by finds it.

payload.why: The shared-cite rule is the second blocked_by rule of #st-ticket-cite-extends.
A missing blocker is left to the set check on blocked_by that #st-ticket-set-checks defines.

payload.title: A rendered reference reads as #id, in both forms
payload.why: One look tells a reader which words are card links, whether the reference was written bare or inside a code span.
payload.body: A link to a card always shows the id with its # in front, in a monospace face. A bare al-diff and a code span that holds only al-diff render the same as #al-diff. A reference that does not link keeps the exact text it was written with.

payload.title: An excerpt's id is the citing card's id with :exN, the first free N
payload.why: The quote operation names the excerpt itself, so a quote needs no id from the agent, and the id says which card cites it.
payload.body: The first quote on a card gets :ex0, the next :ex1, in the same way a rejected option gets :optN. N is the first number with no node under that card. A discarded excerpt frees its id, so the next quote on that card can take it again. The excerpt's title is the quoted text, so the id carries no words of its own.

payload.why: It takes from #werk-excerpt-event that the quote operation itself creates the excerpt node, so the operation must also name it.

payload.title: A reference must not follow a word character, a slash, a #, a colon, a hyphen or an ampersand
payload.why: Without the wider guard, the tail of a longer token links: the x of ##x, the opt0 part after a colon, the end of a hyphenated word, and the name inside an HTML entity.
payload.body: The character before a reference decides whether it starts a reference. A word character or a slash means a URL fragment or a path (see #werk-reflink). A second # means a heading-like run or a doubled marker. A colon or a hyphen means the text is the inside of a longer id or word, which must link whole or not at all. An ampersand means the text is an escaped entity, which is never a card id. A removed card counts as unknown, so its id stays text.

payload.title: A later check of a plan run reads the map as it is at the check, not as it was at the plan
payload.why: A ticket set is valid against the decided cards that hold now. A card cited at the plan can be reopened, removed or gain a depends_on edge before the build, and a frozen verdict would still say ready.
payload.body: The plan run keeps the spec, the tickets and the root of the planned subtree. It does not keep a copy of the map. Each check of the run computes the scope again from the current map, then runs the checks on one ticket and the checks on the whole set (#st-ticket) against that scope, and writes the new verdict over the old one. So a check after the plan can fail where the plan passed, for example when a card is added to the subtree and no ticket cites it. The stories stay frozen (#st-ticket-stories): a re-check reads them, it never changes them.

payload.title: A fence names its language by its usual aliases, and an unknown language stays plain
payload.why: Card writers tag a fence the way they would in any Markdown file: sh as often as bash, tsx as often as ts. A guessed grammar would colour the wrong tokens.
payload.body: The highlighter knows four grammars (see #werk-codeblock). Each one answers to its common tags, in any case: json and jsonc; js, jsx and javascript; ts, tsx and typescript; bash, sh, shell and zsh. A fence with any other tag, or no tag, still renders boxed and scrolls sideways, but its code shows as plain escaped text. The tag shows in the corner of the box when there is one.

payload.why: the stories a re-check reads but never changes
a check is one command whose exit code is the verdict, so the same command must decide on every run against the current map

payload.title: Every test runs on a temporary project of its own, gone when the test ends
payload.why: A test that shares a project reads the cards another test wrote, and a directory left behind fills the disk. A fresh project per test gives each scenario exactly the map it names.
payload.body: The test harness gives a command-line test, a server test and a browser test the same thing: a fresh directory with a git repository and an empty map. The test writes its map with werk commands, reads each command's exit code and output, and, for a browser test, serves that map on a port of its own. The harness removes the directory and stops the server when the test's scope ends, also when the test fails. Every agent a werk command starts in a test is the scripted fake agent, never a real model. The map of a project is the fold of its own log (see #pr-log), so a fresh project is a fresh map.

payload.why: a fresh project is a fresh map because the map is the fold of that project's own log

payload.title: v0 is built in a new git repository whose main branch starts with zero files
payload.why: A repository of its own shares no files, history or map state with the prototype, so nothing of the prototype can become v0's base.
payload.body:
The main line of every #werk build is the main branch of a new git repository, separate from the prototype's repository (#st-plan-main). Its first commit holds no files. The spec and the first tickets set up the project from that empty tree: the package files, the build and test targets, and the folder layout.

The prototype stays in its own repository. A builder may read it as a reference (#werk-base), but no build starts from it and nothing merges into it.

payload.title: Build v0 on the main branch of the prototype's repository, with the prototype on a sibling branch
payload.why_not: The prototype's history, its map state and its files share one repository with v0, so a build can still start from or merge into the wrong tree.

payload.why: It names the repository whose main branch is the main line that #st-plan-main builds from and merges onto.

criterion.text: I check that the v0 repository's first commit has no files and that no #werk build starts from the prototype.

payload.text: Superseded by #werk-base-repo: v0 is built in a new repository, not on a branch of the prototype's repository. Remove this card when you accept that one.

payload.title: Up to 3 unblocked tickets build at once, and two tickets build at the same time only when they touch no module in common

patch.body:
A ticket can start when every ticket in its blocked_by list is merged and no failed set check holds it (#st-ticket-partial). The run builds up to 3 such tickets at the same time, each in its own worktree.

**Overlap blocks.** Each ticket names the modules it changes, by name and not by file path (#st-ticket). The scheduler starts a ticket next to the ones already building only when its modules and theirs share none. A ticket that shares a module waits until the other ticket has merged, then builds on top of it. The comparison is of the names alone: no agent judges overlap.

**A conflict can still happen.** A list of modules can miss one. Then the second ticket fails its merge, and the merge queue sends it back to the builder (#st-build-conflict).

**The base.** Each worktree branches off the main line's tip at the moment its build starts. A ticket that starts after an earlier merge has that merge in its tree.

**The cap.** 3 is a first guess. It changes when a real machine or a real rate limit shows a better number. The merge queue still takes one ticket at a time.
patch.why: Ticket blocking edges give the order, and the modules each ticket touches give the overlap. Two tickets that edit the same module and build at the same time conflict at the merge queue.

payload.title: File overlap does not block; the merge queue sends the second ticket back with the conflict
payload.why_not: Vertical slices all edit the same shared modules, so most parallel pairs conflict. In the first run of #werk, 7 of 16 failed passes were merge conflicts, and one ticket reached its cap through them.

patch.body:
A ticket is the unit of build work. It is a tracer bullet: a narrow but complete path through every layer the change touches. It can be shown working on its own, and it fits one fresh context.

A ticket is not a card. A card groups by decision, so a slice usually crosses several cards, and most cards are a constraint on a thing, not the thing.

Fields:

- title
- what to build: the end-to-end behaviour the ticket makes work, from the user's side
- acceptance criteria
- stories: the numbers of the spec's user stories it delivers (#st-ticket-stories)
- cites: the decided cards it builds
- blocked_by: other tickets
- touches: the modules it changes, by name, so that the scheduler can keep two tickets that share one apart (#st-build-parallel)
- checks: the commands that decide it

A ticket names no file paths. They go out of date before the build reaches the ticket. A module name is a concept, such as the fold or the command parser, not a path.

blocked_by comes from the depends_on edges between the cited cards. It is derived, not guessed.

Two groups of checks decide whether a ticket set is valid (#lp-checks):

1. Checks on one ticket (#st-ticket-own-checks).
2. Checks on the whole set (#st-ticket-set-checks).

#st-ticket-partial says what a failure of each group does to the board.

payload.title: werk's modules are single-purpose and small, so independent tickets touch different modules
payload.why: Two tickets build at the same time only when they share no module, so large shared modules turn independent tickets into a queue.
payload.body:
Each module does one thing and is named for that thing. A behaviour that more than one feature needs is a module of its own.

A shared list, such as the table of commands, the routes or the views, holds only the entries. Each entry's code lives in its own module, so a ticket that adds a command adds a module and one line, and does not edit another command's code.

A ticket names the modules it changes (#st-build-parallel). Small modules keep those names few and precise, so two tickets that do not depend on each other also share no module.

payload.title: A few large modules, one per layer
payload.why_not: Every vertical slice edits every layer, so every pair of tickets shares a module and no two tickets can build at the same time.

payload.why: Small modules matter because #st-build-parallel builds two tickets at once only when they share no module.

criterion.text: I look at how many ticket pairs of a #werk plan share a module, and how many merges conflict.

payload.title: A merge conflict rebuilds the ticket on the main line's tip and does not count against its retry cap
payload.why: A conflict means another ticket merged first, not that this ticket is wrong. Counting it lets other tickets' merges use up this ticket's passes.
payload.body:
When a ticket's merge fails because git cannot merge it, the next build of that ticket starts fresh from the main line's tip, not from the ticket's old branch. The builder gets the conflict output as its last failure. That pass does not count against the retry cap (#st-build-run-mechanics).

A red check on the merged tree is still the ticket's own failure and still counts.

A ticket whose merge conflicts three times in a row stops the merge loop as stuck, so a conflict that never resolves cannot run without end.

payload.title: A conflict counts against the cap like any red merge, and the next build starts from the old branch
payload.why_not: A ticket reaches its cap through other tickets' merges. In the first run of #werk, werk/07 did, and its cap stopped the whole run.

payload.why: It exempts a conflict from the retry cap and the old-branch restart that #st-build-run-mechanics sets for a red merge.

criterion.text: I check in the next run that no ticket reaches its cap through merge conflicts.

payload.title: A held-out step the binder could not run is not run, not red
payload.why: A binder that timed out or failed says nothing about the product. Showing it as red reports a break that nobody found.
payload.body:
After a merge, each held-out step ends green, red, or not run. A step is not run when the binder session failed, hit its time limit, or could not bind the step.

A not-run step files no follow-up ticket. On the board it shows as a grey badge on the done ticket, apart from the red badge of a step that ran and failed (#werk-board-columns). G2 still waits for it, because it is not green: the next held-out run after a later merge tries it again.

The binder's time limit grows with the number of steps it has to bind, so a large set does not time out where a small one would pass.

payload.title: A binder error or timeout counts as a red step
payload.why_not: In the first run of #werk, every one of the 8 merged tickets showed red because the binder hit its fixed 10-minute limit, so the red badge carried no information.

payload.why: It adds a grey not-run badge beside the red held-out badge that #werk-board-columns puts on a done ticket.
It tells a step that failed apart from a binder that could not run it, which #lp-heldout-binder reports.

criterion.text: I check in the next run that a red held-out badge always comes from a step that ran.

payload.title: A merge loop that stops moves each ticket it left in building or merging back to ready, with the stop reason
payload.why: A stopped loop builds nothing, so a ticket left in building looks like work in progress when none runs.
payload.body:
When the merge loop stops for any reason, such as stuck, a cap, a deadlock or a person's stop, every ticket it left in building or merging goes back to ready. The move carries the stop reason, which the drawer shows. Starting the loop again builds those tickets first.

So the building column shows only tickets that a live session is building (#werk-board-columns).

payload.title: Leave the tickets where the loop stopped them
payload.why_not: After the first run of #werk ended stuck, the board showed 2 tickets in building with no session running, and the board looked as if work went on.

payload.why: It keeps the building column to the tickets that #werk-board-columns says are being built.
It adds a step to the stop and the resume that #st-build-run-mechanics defines.

criterion.text: I stop a run and check that the building and merging columns are empty.

payload.title: Build and merge run in a target repository, while the map, the board and the ticket files stay with the map
payload.why: The product a pipeline builds can live in another repository than its map, and the board must still open every ticket it shows.
payload.body:
A build names its target repository. The worktrees, the checks, the merge and the held-out run all happen there, on its main line (#st-plan-main). The map, the board, the specs and the ticket files stay in the repository that holds the map, so the board reads every ticket from one place.

The target is given once for a subtree's tickets and recorded on the board. A later build, a resume, a gate pass and a trigger from the board use the recorded target. With no target, the target is the repository that holds the map.

payload.title: Start the pipeline from inside the target repository and point it at the map's log
payload.why_not: The specs and the tickets then live in the target's working tree, the board beside the map cannot open them, and the target's main line gets an untracked pipeline folder next to its code.

payload.why: The target repository's main line is the line that #st-plan-main builds from and merges onto.

criterion.text: I run a build with a target repository and check that the board opens its tickets and that only the target's main line moves.

patch.body:
```
werk plan <subtree-id> [--timeout 600] [--silence 60]
werk loop "<brief>" --check "..." [--card <id> ...] [--cap 5] [--timeout 600]
werk build <ticket-id> [--repo <path>] [--cap 5] [--timeout 600] [--silence 60] [--check-timeout 300]
werk run <subtree-id> [--repo <path>] [the flags of werk build]
werk gate <subtree-id> [approve --actor you]
werk ticket list | move <id> blocked|ready --reason "..." | archive <id> | restore <id> | import <subtree-id>
```

- `werk plan` turns a decided subtree into a spec and tickets (#st-spec). The spec is `.werk/specs/<subtree-id>.md` and each ticket id is `<subtree-id>/NN`. A second `werk plan` over the same subtree updates that spec, rewrites its open tickets under their ids, adds tickets after the highest number, and archives the open tickets the spec no longer needs (#st-plan-extend). It exits 1 when a set check fails.
- `werk loop` builds one brief in a throwaway worktree, one fresh agent per pass (#lp-stateless).
- `werk build` runs the builder loop on one ticket (#st-build-ticket). `--cap` is the retry cap, 5 by default.
- `werk run` runs the merge loop over one subtree's tickets (#st-build-run-mechanics). Running it again resumes.
- `--repo` names the target repository (#st-build-target). The first `--repo` for a subtree is recorded on the board; a later `werk build`, `werk run` or `werk gate` of that subtree, and a trigger from the board, use it. Without one, the target is the repository that holds the map.
- `werk gate <subtree-id> approve` passes G2 and needs `--actor you` (#st-gates).
- `werk ticket` moves, archives, restores and imports tickets on the board (#werk-board-control). A move needs `--reason`. An import makes ids as `werk plan` does, and adds nothing on a second run.

payload.why: The --repo flag of build, run and gate names the target repository that #st-build-target defines.

payload.title: Every project builds in a dedicated repository of its own, outside werk
payload.why: Werk is a product that builds other projects. Where werk itself is stored says nothing about where a project it builds lives, and this holds also when the project is werk.

payload.title: Every project builds in a dedicated repository of its own, outside werk
payload.why: Werk is a product that builds other projects. Where werk itself is stored says nothing about where a project it builds lives, and this holds also when the project is werk.
payload.body:
Each project names one git repository of its own as its target. The worktrees, the checks, the merge and the held-out run all happen there, on its main line (#st-plan-main). Werk keeps the project's map, board, specs and ticket files in its own store, never in the target repository, so the board reads every ticket from one place.

Where that store lives, and where werk's own code lives or is hosted, is internal to werk and changes nothing about a build. There is no default target: a project with no target repository cannot start a build. Werk built with werk follows the same rule. The werk under construction is a target project in its own repository, and the running werk treats it like any other project (#product).

payload.why: The target repository's main line is the line that #st-plan-main builds from and merges onto.
Werk is a standalone product, so its own code and storage are never the place a project is built.

payload.title: Start the pipeline from inside the target repository and point it at the map's log
payload.why_not: The specs and the tickets then live in the target's working tree, the board cannot open them from werk's store, and the target's main line gets an untracked pipeline folder next to its code.

payload.title: With no target named, build in the repository that holds the map
payload.why_not: It ties a project to where werk keeps its data. Werk built with werk would then merge into the running tool's own repository.

payload.why: The --repo flag of build, run and gate names the target repository that #st-build-target defines.

criterion.text: I build a project whose map lives in werk's store, and check that only the project's own repository's main line moves and that a project with no target refuses to build.

patch.body:
```
werk target [<path>]
werk plan <subtree-id> [--timeout 600] [--silence 60]
werk loop "<brief>" --check "..." [--card <id> ...] [--cap 5] [--timeout 600]
werk build <ticket-id> [--cap 5] [--timeout 600] [--silence 60] [--check-timeout 300]
werk run <subtree-id> [the flags of werk build]
werk gate <subtree-id> [approve --actor you]
werk ticket list | move <id> blocked|ready --reason "..." | archive <id> | restore <id> | import <subtree-id>
```

- `werk plan` turns a decided subtree into a spec and tickets (#st-spec). The spec and the tickets go to werk's store for the project, and each ticket id is `<subtree-id>/NN`. A second `werk plan` over the same subtree updates that spec, rewrites its open tickets under their ids, adds tickets after the highest number, and archives the open tickets the spec no longer needs (#st-plan-extend). It exits 1 when a set check fails.
- `werk loop` builds one brief in a throwaway worktree, one fresh agent per pass (#lp-stateless).
- `werk build` runs the builder loop on one ticket (#st-build-ticket). `--cap` is the retry cap, 5 by default.
- `werk run` runs the merge loop over one subtree's tickets (#st-build-run-mechanics). Running it again resumes.
- `werk build`, `werk run` and `werk gate`, and a trigger from the board, all use the project's target. With no target set, each exits 1 and names `werk target`.
- `werk gate <subtree-id> approve` passes G2 and needs `--actor you` (#st-gates).
- `werk ticket` moves, archives, restores and imports tickets on the board (#werk-board-control). A move needs `--reason`. An import makes ids as `werk plan` does, and adds nothing on a second run.

payload.title: `werk target`, `werk plan`, `werk loop`, `werk build`, `werk run`, `werk gate` and `werk ticket` start the build stages
A --repo flag on build, run and gate, recorded per subtree on its first use
payload.why_not: The target is one fact about the project. A flag per command lets two subtrees of one project build into two repositories, and a missing flag needs a default.

payload.why: The target command sets the one target repository per project that #st-build-target defines, and build, run and gate refuse to start without it.

A ticket is the unit of build work. It is a tracer bullet: a narrow but complete path through every layer the change touches. It can be shown working on its own, and it fits one fresh context.

A ticket is not a card. A card groups by decision, so a slice usually crosses several cards, and most cards are a constraint on a thing, not the thing.

A ticket holds a title, the end-to-end behaviour it makes work from the user's side, its acceptance criteria, the spec stories it delivers (#st-ticket-stories), the decided cards it cites, the tickets that block it, and the checks that decide it. The file format of these fields is fixed (#st-ticket-shape).

A ticket names no file paths. They go out of date before the build reaches the ticket.

blocked_by comes from the depends_on edges between the cited cards. It is derived, not guessed.

Two groups of checks decide whether a ticket set is valid (#lp-checks): the checks on one ticket (#st-ticket-own-checks) and the checks on the whole set (#st-ticket-set-checks).

#st-ticket-partial says what a failure of each group does to the board.

An agent writes the tickets from the spec (#st-spec). A person decides which ticket gets built, and when (#vi-board).

Each check reads one ticket file and nothing else. A ticket passes when it meets all seven:

- **title**: the file has a line `title: <text>` with non-empty text. A file with no title is not parsed, so no other check runs on it.
- **shape**: every header line and every section heading of the ticket format is present (#st-ticket-shape). A failure names each missing line or heading.
- **size**: the whole file, header and every section, is 4000 characters or fewer.
- **what-to-build**: the `## What to build` section has text. An empty section and a missing heading both fail.
- **acceptance**: the `## Acceptance criteria` section has at least one bullet, a plain `-` or a `- [ ]` checkbox.
- **no-file-paths**: the file names no file path, in the header or in the body. A path is a token with at least one `/` between two name characters that ends in a file extension (a dot and 1 to 5 letters or digits), for example `src/loop.ts` or `src/*.ts`. A `files:` line also fails. A URL, a bare file name such as `Makefile`, a slash command such as `/implement`, a card id, and a make target do not count. A failure lists each path with its line number.
- **make-targets**: every bullet under `## Checks` is `make <target>` (#lp-checks-scripts). An empty `## Checks` section passes, and the ticket then uses the rubric's default checks.

`stories:` and `cites:` can be empty and still pass. A prefactor delivers no story (#st-ticket-stories). Whether the cards and stories are covered is a question about the whole set (#st-ticket-set-checks).

payload.why: The shape check fails a ticket that lacks a header line or section heading of the format on #st-ticket-shape.

payload.title: Every ticket shares one fixed structure: four header lines, then three sections in a fixed order

patch.body: A ticket starts with four header lines, in this order: title, stories, cites and blocked_by. Three sections follow, in this order: What to build, Acceptance criteria, and Checks. Stories, cites and blocked_by may be empty, and the Checks section may have no bullet. Each line and each heading must be there: a ticket without one fails its own check, and the failure names the missing field. Stories and blocked_by hold numbers, separated by commas. Cites holds card ids, with or without the hash sign.

patch.body:
A ticket starts with five header lines, in this order: title, cites, blocked_by, stories and touches. Three sections follow, in this order: What to build, Acceptance criteria, and Checks. Cites, blocked_by and stories may be empty, and the Checks section may have no bullet. Each line and each heading must be there: a ticket without one fails its own check, and the failure names the missing field.

Cites holds card ids, with or without the hash sign. Blocked_by and stories hold numbers, separated by commas. Touches holds the names of the modules the ticket changes, as concept names and not file paths, because the scheduler compares them (#st-build-parallel).

```
title: A person can reopen a decided card from the map
cites: map-reopen, map-stale
blocked_by: 2
stories: 4, 7
touches: map view, decision log

## What to build

A person opens a decided card and presses reopen. The card goes back to open, and every card that depends on it shows a stale mark with the reason.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reopened card shows as open in the map.
- [ ] Each card that depends on it shows a stale mark that names the reopened card.

## Checks

- `make test`
- `make e2e`
```

patch.body:
The set checks read the tickets of one plan run that passed their own checks (#st-ticket-own-checks), the decided cards of the planned subtree, the depends_on edges between those cards, and the spec's story numbers. A ticket that fails its own checks is not on the board, so its cites and stories do not count.

**1. Cards cited.** Every decided card in the planned subtree is in the `cites:` of at least one ticket. A failure lists the cards no ticket cites.

**2. Stories delivered.** Every story number in the spec is in the `stories:` of at least one ticket (#st-ticket-stories). No ticket lists a number that is not in the spec. A failure lists the missing or unknown numbers.

**3. blocked_by.** Every number in `blocked_by` is a ticket in the set; a blocker that failed its own checks is not in the set, so it fails this condition. The `blocked_by` graph has no cycle. And it agrees with depends_on: for each depends_on edge A → B between two subtree cards, every ticket that cites A either also cites B, or reaches the ticket that introduces B along `blocked_by`, directly or through other blockers. The ticket that introduces a card is the first ticket, by number, that cites it (#st-ticket-cite-extends). A ticket cannot start before its blockers are done, and they cannot start before theirs, so a blocker of a blocker already holds the ticket back. An edge to a card that no ticket cites is left to check 1.

Check 3 catches a missing blocker, not an extra one. A blocker that no depends_on edge and no shared cite explains passes. It only makes the ticket wait longer, and it never lets a ticket start before the code it needs exists.

A failure of check 3 names only the tickets that must not start: the ticket that misses a blocker, the ticket that names a blocker not in the set, and the tickets on a cycle. The ticket it should wait for is not named. That ticket is not wrong, and blocking it holds back every ticket after it, the first ticket of the run included. Checks 1 and 2 name cards and stories, not tickets.

payload.title: A blocker that no depends_on edge or shared cite explains fails the check
payload.why_not: An extra blocker only makes a ticket wait longer. It never lets a ticket start before the code it needs exists, so its cost is speed, not a wrong build.

patch.body:
```
werk target [<path>]
werk plan <subtree-id> [--timeout 600] [--silence 60]
werk loop "<brief>" --check "..." [--card <id> ...] [--cap 5] [--timeout 600]
werk build <ticket-id> [--cap 5] [--timeout 600] [--silence 60] [--check-timeout 300]
werk run <subtree-id> [the flags of werk build]
werk gate <subtree-id> [approve --actor you]
werk ticket list | move <id> blocked|ready --reason "..." | archive <id> | restore <id> | import <subtree-id>
```

- `werk target <path>` sets the project's target repository (#st-build-target). Without a path it prints the current one. It refuses a path that is not a directory, has no main line, lies inside werk's own store, or holds that store.
- `werk plan` turns a decided subtree into a spec and tickets (#st-spec). The spec and the tickets go to werk's store for the project, and each ticket id is `<subtree-id>/NN`. A second `werk plan` over the same subtree updates that spec, rewrites its open tickets under their ids, adds tickets after the highest number, and archives the open tickets the spec no longer needs (#st-plan-extend). It exits 1 when a set check fails.
- `werk loop` builds one brief in a throwaway worktree, one fresh agent per pass (#lp-stateless).
- `werk build` runs the builder loop on one ticket (#st-build-ticket). `--cap` is the retry cap, 5 by default.
- `werk run` runs the merge loop over one subtree's tickets (#st-build-run-mechanics). Running it again resumes.
- `werk build`, `werk run` and `werk gate`, and a trigger from the board, all use the project's target. With no target set, each exits 1 and names `werk target`.
- `werk gate <subtree-id> approve` passes G2 and needs `--actor you` (#st-gates).
- `werk ticket` moves, archives, restores and imports tickets on the board (#werk-board-control). A move needs `--reason`. An import makes ids as `werk plan` does, and adds nothing on a second run.

payload.text: Reopened to question the premise of check 3. Open question: is blocked_by the delivery order that the planner decides, or is it derived from depends_on as a minimum? If the planner decides it, check 3 keeps only 'every blocker exists' and 'no cycle', and the matching rules on #st-ticket and #st-ticket-cite-extends change too.

The set checks read the tickets of one plan run that passed their own checks (#st-ticket-own-checks), the decided cards of the planned subtree, and the spec's story numbers. A ticket that fails its own checks is not on the board, so its cites and stories do not count.

**1. Cards cited.** Every decided card in the planned subtree is in the `cites:` of at least one ticket. A failure lists the cards no ticket cites.

**2. Stories delivered.** Every story number in the spec is in the `stories:` of at least one ticket (#st-ticket-stories). No ticket lists a number that is not in the spec. A failure lists the missing or unknown numbers.

**3. blocked_by.** Every number in `blocked_by` is a ticket in the set; a blocker that failed its own checks is not in the set, so it fails this condition. The `blocked_by` graph has no cycle.

The order itself belongs to the planner. `blocked_by` is the delivery order, and no check compares it with the depends_on edges between the cited cards. A decision edge and a build need often agree, but not always, and a check that forced one onto the other would make the pipeline larger for a rule it cannot apply exactly. A wrong order shows at the build, as a failed check or a merge conflict.

A failure of check 3 names only the tickets that must not start: the ticket that names a blocker not in the set, and the tickets on a cycle. Checks 1 and 2 name cards and stories, not tickets.

payload.title: blocked_by must agree with the depends_on edges between the cited cards
payload.why_not: A decision edge is not always a build need, and a build need often has no card edge. The check forces waits the build does not need and still misses real ones, while the planner's own order keeps the pipeline simple.

blocked_by is the delivery order, and the planner decides it. It is not derived from the depends_on edges between the cited cards (#st-ticket-set-checks).

payload.title: A change to a cited card blocks every open ticket that cites it
payload.why: A ticket is written against the cited cards as they were at the plan. If one of them changes before the build, the ticket can build the old decision, and nothing says so.
payload.body:
When a plan puts a ticket on the board, the board records the version of each card that the ticket cites. werk then watches the decision log. On each change it finds, by a reverse lookup from card to ticket, every ticket that cites the changed card. The process is a program, not a model, so the same log always gives the same marks.

A change counts when it can change what the ticket must build: a new title, why or body, a status change such as a reopen, a removal, a stale mark on the card (#vi-prop), or a depends_on edge added to or taken from the card. A comment and a change of view do not count.

Only an open ticket, ready or blocked, gets the mark. A ticket that is building, merging or done stays as it is.

A marked ticket goes to blocked. Its blocking reason names each changed card and the kind of change, the same way a failed set check blocks a ticket (#st-ticket-partial). The program cannot say if the ticket still makes sense. It says only that the ticket must be checked again. The mark clears when a plan over the subtree changes or keeps the ticket against the new versions (#st-plan-extend), and the board records those versions.

a mark blocks a ticket with a named reason, the way a failed set check does
a re-plan changes open tickets in place, which is how the mark clears
a stale mark on a cited card is one of the changes that counts

payload.why_not: Nothing runs the check at the moment of the change, so a ticket can start to build against a card that changed after the plan.

payload.title: A model reads the change and judges if the ticket still holds
payload.why_not: The verdict is not deterministic: the same change can mark a ticket on one run and not on the next.

payload.title: A record of how the person decides, built once the same kind of trade-off comes up twice

patch.body:
A decision profile records how the person decides, not what to build. Each entry is a preference that holds across work items, for example "fewer dependencies over a faster build" or "a new view gets its own tab". An agent checks the profile before it asks a question. When an entry answers the question, the agent applies it and names the entry, so alignment does not start again from nothing on each work item.

The profile is worth its cost only when a kind of trade-off comes back. Each decision on the map settles a different trade-off: the stack's six criteria (#werk-stack), where a tab goes, which permission mode an agent runs in. A profile made from them would hold entries that nothing reads a second time.

So no profile is built. The kill criterion names the trigger: the same kind of trade-off comes up a second time, and a standing preference would have answered it. The profile then starts from the portable DECISION.md format (#decisionmd).
patch.why: A standing preference lets an agent settle a repeated trade-off without asking the person again. A trade-off that comes up only once gives such a record nothing to answer.

payload.title: We do not build a record of how the person decides until the same kind of trade-off comes up twice
We do not build a record of how the person decides

patch.body:
v0 builds no separate alignment feature. Alignment before building is in v0 through these mechanisms:

- Every card, option, source and excerpt an agent adds waits for the person's accept (#werk-propose-new).
- Every answer that the spec or ticket writer gives and no card gives comes back as a proposed card before the build (#st-spec).
- Every build gate waits for the person (#werk-loop-tier).

The rest of #align is out of v0.

payload.title: During the plan, a writer returns each new answer as a card record, and the plan proposes it as a ghost under the subtree root

criterion.text: Read the answer cards that several plans propose. If most of them are nitpicks that add nothing to the map's decisions, rather than answers that matter to the product, proposing every answer as a card costs more than it gives.

payload.title: In v0, no gate passes on its own: every build is a feature build

patch.body:
A tier is the risk level of a change: fix, change or feature. It decides which gates pass on their own and which wait for a person (#st-tier). Feature is the tier where every gate waits.

In v0, nobody chooses a tier. Every build runs as a feature build, so every gate that v0 runs waits for a person.

Each run still records its tier, feature, as its first event (#st-tier-default). So every run has a first event, even with nothing chosen.

Not in v0: saying a tier for a build (#st-tier-say), and raising the tier during a build (#st-tier-escalate).
patch.why: Choosing a tier per build needs a way to say the tier and a way to raise it during the build. v0 builds neither, so it uses the tier where every gate waits for a person, which is the safe default (#st-tier-default).

payload.title: In v0, alignment before building is the accept gate, the plan's proposed answers and the build gates

patch.why: No card names what v0 builds for alignment, and these three mechanisms already put every agent answer in front of the person before code.

every answer a plan writer gives that no card gives comes back as a ghost before the build

criterion.text: Build with v0. If an agent builds the wrong thing because a reading of a requirement was never shown, and none of the three mechanisms caught it, v0 needs more of #align.

the G2 refusal while a step is red, which the slice gates on the run's tree

payload.title: Where the base cards conflict, v0 follows #werk-base-repo: a new repository, not a branch beside the prototype
payload.why: #werk-base-branch and #werk-base-repo are both decided and give two different main lines; #werk-base-repo names the sibling-branch approach as its rejected option.
payload.body: #werk-base-branch puts v0 on the main branch of the prototype's repository, with the prototype on a sibling branch. #werk-base-repo puts v0 in a new git repository whose first commit holds no files, and rejects the sibling-branch approach because a build can still start from or merge into the wrong tree. The two cannot both hold. v0 follows #werk-base-repo: every build starts from the main branch of the new repository, and nothing builds in or merges into the prototype's repository. #werk-base-branch is then superseded and needs a reopen or a removal.

payload.title: The plan card goes when the plan ends, like the building preview
payload.why_not: A failed plan then leaves nothing on the board, and its cause is visible only in a terminal. A card per plan run keeps the result and the log where the person watches the build.

payload.title: A planning column left of blocked
payload.why_not: The columns are ticket states (#werk-board-columns). A plan is not a ticket, so a column for it mixes two kinds of thing. Per-run state already sits above the columns.

payload.title: A plan shows as a card above the board columns, with its agent log, and as a marker on its subtree in the map
payload.why: A plan runs two agents for minutes and writes nothing to the board until the end, so a person cannot see that it runs, where it is, or why it failed.
payload.body:
Each plan gets one card in the line above the columns, beside the G2 run state (#vi-board-details). The card names the subtree, links to it on the map, and shows the step that runs now: spec writer, ticket writer, or checks. A running card pulses, by the same rule as a building ticket (#vi-board).

Clicking the card opens the drawer with the agent log of both writers, one summarised line per stream event, in the same form as the building preview. Spec writer lines come first, then ticket writer lines.

When the plan ends, the card stays and shows how it ended: the tickets it planned and archived, or the reason it stopped (an open card in the scope, an agent error with its step, or an invalid spec). The next plan of the same subtree replaces the card. The card displays the plan process only. It owns no spec and no ticket (#st-plan-extend).

While a plan runs, the subtree's root card on the map carries a marker. The marker links to the plan card on the board.

The board learns about a plan from two run events in the board log, plan started and plan ended with its result (#vi-board-state).

payload.why: The plan card folds from two new run events, plan started and plan ended, in the board log this card defines.
The plan card sits in the line above the columns and uses the drawer log form that this card sets.
One card per subtree, replaced by the next plan, follows from the subtree being the key of a plan and no run being an entity.
The plan gets no column because the columns are ticket states only.

criterion.text: Run a plan with the board open: the card appears at start, shows the current step and log lines live, and after the end shows the result. If the finished cards clutter the line, fall back to dropping them at the end.

payload.title: Each command-line verb lives in its own module and registers itself, so a new verb edits no shared list
payload.why: Which module a new verb changes decides whether two independent tickets can build at the same time.
payload.body: The command line finds its verbs by registration from their own modules. A ticket that adds a verb changes only the verb's module, not a central list of verbs. So two tickets that add different verbs touch no common module, and the scheduler can build them at the same time (see #werk-stack-modules, #st-build-parallel). The verb list that the command line prints comes from the registered verbs.

payload.title: The ticket checks run on their own from the command line, outside a plan
payload.why: The ticket format and its checks are built and shown working before the plan that calls them exists.
payload.body: A ticket-check operation reads a folder of ticket files and runs the checks on one ticket and the checks on the whole set (see #st-ticket-own-checks, #st-ticket-set-checks). It prints each failure with the ticket and the field. The plan calls the same checks. The operation also lets an agent that changes a ticket on a person's request run the set checks again (see #werk-board-control).

payload.title: The merge loop works with one build at a time first, and building up to three at once comes after it
payload.why: A red result in the first merge-loop slice must point at the merge loop, not at the parallel scheduler.
payload.body: The build is sequenced in two slices. The first slice makes the merge loop work end to end with one ticket building at a time, in the board's ready order. The second slice raises the limit to 3 and adds the rule that two tickets build at the same time only when their touches lines name no common module (see #st-build-parallel). This follows the same reason as #werk-heldout-before-merge: each part works on its own before the part that builds on it.

payload.title: A verb registers itself by being a module in the verbs folder
payload.why: A shared list of verbs would make every ticket that adds a verb edit the same file, and two tickets would conflict on it.
payload.body:
The command line finds its verbs by loading every module in one verbs folder. A module's default export is the verb: its name, a one-line summary, an optional usage line with its flags, and the function that runs it. No list of verbs exists in code, so a new verb is one new file and no other edit.

A module whose default export is not a verb, a name that is not lower-case words with hyphens, and two modules with one name each stop the command line with an error that names the file. A silent skip would hide the verb.

With no verb, the command line prints the verb list and exits 0. An unknown verb exits 1 and names the verb.

payload.title: The command-line test harness runs werk as a child process in a temporary git repository
payload.why: The command line seam checks what a person sees, so the test must run the real command line, not call its functions.
payload.body:
Each command-line test makes a temporary project directory that is the root of a git repository on main, with one empty commit. The harness runs werk in it as a child process and returns the exit code, stdout and stderr.

The harness isolates the repository from the git config of the person who runs the tests. It puts a fake claude first on PATH, which fails loudly until a test gives it a script, so no test reaches a real agent.

payload.title: The coverage gate judges each listed pure file on its own lines, and a file no test loads is 0%
payload.why: One total over every file prices an I/O line the same as a pure one, and a pure file that no test imports has no coverage record, so it would pass by absence.
payload.body:
The coverage run writes an lcov report. The gate reads it and judges only the files on an explicit list of pure files, each one against 90% of its lines. A listed file with no record in the report counts as 0% and fails. A listed file with no executable lines passes. A new pure file joins the list in the change that adds it.

The gate prints one line per listed file and exits 1 when any file is under the threshold.

payload.title: A plan is a persistent card below the board columns, colored by its state, linked from its tickets and from its subtree in the map

patch.body:
Each plan has one card in a row below the columns. The card stays: it is the board's record of the plan. The card names the subtree and links to it on the map. A second plan of the same subtree uses the same card (#st-plan-extend). The card displays the plan and its tickets. It owns no spec and no ticket.

The card has one color per state. Creating: the plan's agents run, and the card pulses and shows the step that runs now, spec writer, ticket writer, or checks. Building: the plan ended and at least one of its tickets is not done. Done: every ticket of the plan is done or archived. A plan that stops shows the stop color and the reason: an open card in the scope, an agent error with its step, or an invalid spec. Building and done follow from the ticket columns (#werk-board-columns).

Every ticket the plan created links to the plan card, from the ticket card and from the drawer sidebar.

Clicking the plan card opens the drawer with the agent log of both writers, one summarised line per stream event, in the same form as the building preview (#vi-board-details). Spec writer lines come first, then ticket writer lines. The drawer also lists the plan's tickets and how the last plan ended.

While a plan runs, the subtree's root card on the map carries a marker that links to the plan card on the board.

The board learns about a plan from two run events in the board log, plan started and plan ended with its result (#vi-board-state).
patch.why: A plan runs two agents for minutes and writes nothing to the board until the end, and afterwards nothing on the board ties its tickets together, so a person cannot see that a plan runs, why it failed, or how far its tickets are.

payload.why: tickets merge one by one onto the main line, so two tickets that each add a verb must not edit one shared file
the build seam checks the exit code and the output against a temporary git repository, with fake agents on PATH
The plan card's drawer log uses the one-line-per-event form of the building preview that this card sets.
a coverage percentage is a check: one command, and its exit code is the verdict
The building and done states of a plan follow its tickets' columns, and the plan gets no column because the columns are ticket states only.

payload.title: One plan card per plan run in the line above the columns, replaced by the next plan
payload.why_not: The line above the columns holds run state like G2, and a card replaced by the next plan loses the link from a ticket to the plan that made it. A persistent row below the columns keeps that link and the plan's progress.

payload.title: The client lives in its own folder beside the server code, and Vite builds it into a separate output folder
payload.why: The server is TypeScript that Bun runs directly. The client is code that Vite transforms. One folder per runtime keeps each tool on the files it owns.
payload.body: The client source sits in a folder of its own at the top of the repository, apart from the server source. Its entry is one HTML page and one React root component. Vite reads one config at the top of the repository. The config gives absolute paths, so the server can start Vite from any project directory. The client build step writes to an output folder that is not committed. The type check covers the client and the server in one run, with JSX compiled by the React automatic runtime. React is a runtime dependency. Vite and its React plugin are build tools, so they are development dependencies until the server ticket starts Vite in middleware mode.

payload.why: takes React + Vite, with Vite as a client transform inside the Bun server

payload.title: Each check installs the locked dependencies before it runs
payload.why: The merge queue runs the checks on a fresh tree with no installed dependencies, so a check that expects them fails on a tree that is correct.
payload.body: Every check target first installs the dependencies from the lock file, with no change to the lock. It installs again only when the package file or the lock file changes. A check therefore gives the same verdict on a fresh clone and on a working checkout.

payload.why: The merge loop runs the checks on a temporary tree, which starts with no installed dependencies.

payload.title: A writer proposes a card only for a decision about the product, never about the order of delivery
payload.why: The map records what the product is. The order in which tickets build leaves the finished product the same, so a card for it asks the person to accept noise.
payload.body: A delivery decision — which ticket comes first, how one feature splits into slices, what a ticket waits for — stays in the spec and in the tickets' blockers (see #st-spec). The writers return as data only an answer that changes what the finished subtree does or how it is built inside (see #st-spec-decisions). The test: the finished subtree is the same with the answer or without it, so it is a delivery decision and gets no card.

payload.title: Propose a card for every answer the writers give, delivery order included
payload.why_not: A delivery card leaves the finished product the same, so it adds a card to accept with nothing on the map to show for it.

payload.why: the same rule as one module's results going into its tests: one plan's delivery order goes into the spec, not onto the map

payload.title: A proposal carries its refines parent inside its own event
payload.why: An edge proposed with a card accepts and discards with it. One event for the card and its parent link means no log can hold the card without its link, or the link without its card.
payload.body: The proposal event names the parent. The fold derives the refines edge from it. The edge is held as a ghost edge while either end is a ghost, and goes live when both ends are real. No separate link event is written for the parent of a new card.

payload.title: An accept is one event, and the fold commits the ghost ancestors
payload.why: Accept is one card at a time. One accept event per click keeps the log equal to what the person did, and the fold derives the chain up to the first real card from the state before the event.
payload.body: The accept event names one card and records who asked. The fold walks the refines parents of that card while they are ghosts and makes each one real. A discard is also one event, and the fold drops the ghost and every ghost descendant. A discarded id is free again, so a new proposal with that id makes a fresh ghost. The fold also ignores a second proposal for an id it holds and any change to the words of a ghost, so a hand-written log line cannot unfreeze a ghost either.

payload.why: takes the rule that every change is one event at the end of the log

payload.title: Build v0 on the main branch of this repository, with the prototype on a sibling branch that is deleted once v0 matches the map
payload.body: The main branch holds an empty tree, and every ticket builds from its tip and merges onto it. The prototype lives on its own branch beside it. It is never merged into the main branch and never a build's base, and it is deleted when v0 matches what the decided cards say.
payload.why_not: The two lines share one repository, its history and its map state, so a build can still start from or merge into the prototype's tree. Only a separate repository makes that impossible.

payload.title: The dot sits inline before the title
payload.why_not: It takes a full slot in the row, so the title and badges get less width.

payload.title: The title wraps in full
payload.why_not: A long title makes a tall card, and the column shows fewer tickets.

payload.title: The columns shrink to fit the screen
payload.why_not: On a small screen each card gets too narrow to read.

payload.title: The live dot on a ticket card sits in its top-left corner
payload.why: An inline dot takes a whole slot in the card row and pushes the title and badges aside, on a card that is already narrow.
payload.body: The pulse of a building ticket with a live session (#vi-board) is a small dot pinned to the card's top-left corner. It takes no space in the row. Only the first line of the title moves a few pixels to the right, so the dot does not cover it.

payload.title: A ticket card shows at most two lines of its title, then an ellipsis
payload.why: A long ticket title makes one card many times taller than the others, so a column holds fewer tickets and becomes hard to scan.
payload.body: The card height is capped by its title: two lines at most, and a longer title ends in an ellipsis. Hovering the title shows it in full. The drawer header always shows the full title (#vi-board).

payload.title: A board column has a minimum width; a narrow screen scrolls the board sideways
payload.why: Five columns that shrink to fit a small screen leave each ticket card too narrow to read.
payload.body: Each of the five columns (#werk-board-columns) keeps a minimum width of 200 pixels and grows to share any extra width. When the screen is narrower than five minimum columns, the columns keep their width and the board gets a horizontal scrollbar.

criterion.text: Open the board while a ticket builds. If the corner dot is missed or covers the title, go back to the inline dot.
Read a column of real tickets. If two lines are not enough to tell tickets apart, show the full title.
Use the board on a laptop screen. If the sideways scroll hides columns that a person must watch together, let the columns shrink.

payload.title: The fake agent plays a JSON script of replies, chosen by role, turn, pass and prompt
payload.why: One binary plays every Claude Code child, so a reply must say which call it answers, and a test must read what each call got without reaching inside the fake.
payload.body:
A test writes a script: a list of replies. The first reply whose 'when' matches a turn answers it. 'when' can set role, turn (1-based, per process), pass (the nth call with this role in the test), and a prompt substring.

A reply is a list of steps. Each step has one kind: text, tool (with 'times' to repeat one call), write (a file edit plus a Write tool call), ask (a can_use_tool control_request; the fake waits for the control_response on stdin), sleep (no output for N ms), die (exit at once with a code, no result event), or event (one raw event). The fake then prints a result event, and exits with the reply's 'exit' code if set.

State lives in one folder per test: script.json, and calls/0001.json for each call (args, cwd, stdin, prompt, turns, role, pass, session id, resume, fork, permission answers, exit code). The pure half is src/test/fake-claude/script.ts and sits under the coverage gate.

payload.why: the seams card says one scripted fake stands in for every agent at both seams; this card gives that fake its script

payload.title: werk names the role of each agent child in WERK_AGENT_ROLE
payload.why: The real agent cannot tell a builder from a grader, so the fake needs a signal. Matching on prompt text breaks each time a prompt changes; an environment variable is stable and the real agent ignores it.
