payload.body: When werk starts a Claude Code child, it sets WERK_AGENT_ROLE to one of: chat, headless, builder, grader, reviewer, classifier, step-author, binder, spec-writer, ticket-writer. The fake reads it to choose a reply. Without it, the fake takes 'chat' for --input-format stream-json and 'headless' otherwise. The pass of a call is the count of calls with the same role in the test, so a build's pass N is the Nth builder call.

payload.why: the script chooses replies by role and pass; this card says where the role comes from

payload.title: The test command puts the fake claude first on PATH before Bun starts
payload.why: Bun reads PATH once at start-up: a preload that edits process.env.PATH does not change what Bun.spawn finds, so a test could still start the real agent.
payload.body: bun run test and bun run test:coverage prefix PATH with src/test/fake-claude/bin, which holds a fake claude with no script (it exits 127). A preload also prefixes process.env.PATH, for children that get process.env, and throws when the test process still finds a claude that is not a fake. So plain 'bun test' on a machine with the real agent installed stops with a message that names 'bun run test'. The command-line harness puts its own scripted fake first on each project's PATH.

payload.why: the harness card sets the test commands; this card changes bun test to bun run test so PATH is set before Bun starts

payload.title: A hot reload reuses the live server and swaps in the reloaded routes
payload.why: The guard alone keeps the old route handlers, so a route edit under bun --hot does nothing until a restart. Swapping one function keeps the live server and makes the edit live.
payload.body: startServer pins a promise of the live server on globalThis (Symbol.for('werk.liveServer')). A second evaluation awaits it, logs 'werk: hot reload, reusing the live server on port N (pid P)', and sets live.handle to the handler from the reloaded routes module. The HTTP server calls live.handle for each request. The lock, Vite, the listen, the live-channel clients and the long-lived children are created once, in the first start only. Long-lived children are a start-up parameter (children: string[][]); the agent of a later ticket goes there.

payload.title: Vite's full reload goes through the live channel, not Vite's own socket
payload.why: The page must stash the composer draft before it reloads. One reload path, the live channel, lets the page do that every time.
payload.body: werk wraps vite.environments.client.hot.send. A 'full-reload' payload is not sent to the Vite client; the server pushes 'reload' on /api/live instead. The page stashes the draft in sessionStorage (key werk.composer.draft) and calls location.reload(). Updates that apply in place (React Fast Refresh) still go through Vite's HMR socket, which shares the werk server's port.

payload.why: Vite runs in middleware mode inside the werk server, so the server sees its hot payloads

payload.title: The lock sits beside the log, and records the real port after the listen
payload.why: One log must have one server. WERK_LOG names the log file, so the lock follows the log, not the project directory.
payload.body: The lock is serve.lock in the folder of the log: <project>/.werk/serve.lock, or beside the file that WERK_LOG names. It is created with O_EXCL, holds {pid, port, at}, and is rewritten with the real port once the listen succeeds (port 0 picks a free port). A lock that does not parse, or whose pid is dead, is taken over. The wait, the poll interval, the listen retries and the retry pause are flags of werk serve: --lock-wait-ms 5000, --lock-poll-ms 250, --listen-retries 20, --listen-retry-ms 250.

payload.why: takes the 5 second lock wait and the 20 x 250 ms listen retry from it

payload.title: A test that edits werk's own code edits a copy of the app
payload.why: The hot reload and client reload tests must edit src/ and web/. An edit to the checkout would leave it dirty when a test fails.
payload.body: src/test/app-copy.ts copies src, web, vite.config.ts, package.json and tsconfig.json to a temporary folder. node_modules is a folder of links to each package of the checkout, except .vite, so each copy has its own Vite dependency cache: a shared cache for two app roots makes Vite optimize again and reload the page. The browser harness boots one werk serve per test from such a copy, on a copy of e2e/fixtures/project, with WERK_LOG removed from the environment.

payload.why: removes WERK_LOG so a test server never takes the lock of a real project

payload.title: A proposed excerpt carries its transcript pointer, and its body is the verbatim quote
payload.why: An excerpt enters as a ghost like every kind, but the agent must not write its words from memory. The pointer is found when the excerpt is proposed, so the person accepts a quote that the program already matched.
payload.body: Adding an excerpt names one session transcript and gives the exact quote as the body. The program finds the quote in the text of exactly one user or assistant message, and records the message line, the character span, the speaker and the session in the proposal event. No match, a match in two messages, or two matches in one message refuses, and nothing enters the log. Every other kind refuses a transcript. The supported_by link to the citing card is not part of this add: a link waits for the link operation.

payload.why: An excerpt still enters as a ghost and waits for the accept

patch.body:
- Archive is a button in the drawer header, not on the board card. Stop has no button: it is only the drag from building to ready (#werk-board-control).
- The live preview shows one summarised line per stream event, overseer lines included, not raw JSON.
- When a build child exits while its ticket is still live, the server ends the build: error for an exit code, stopped for a signal.
- A line above the columns shows G2 per run, waiting or passed, with the command that passes it. The board has no approve button, because the board does no editing.
- Importing ticket files makes ids the way planning does, <run>/<NN>, and adds nothing on a second run.
- While the drawer is open, each column shrinks to its cards and shows two at most; the rest scroll inside the column, so the drawer sits close under the board.
- The drawer header has two lines: the id, the running dot and the controls first, the title under them. A building ticket's time in the column shows only in the bar above the log, not in the header.
- The sidebar has a toggle in its top right corner that folds it to a narrow rail. The log has a toggle in its top right corner that hides the sidebar and doubles the log height. Both choices stay across redraws and page loads.
- Each log line shows its full time, top-aligned, in a column wide enough for it.

payload.title: The browser harness puts the shared stateless fake claude first on PATH
payload.why: One fake agent for every harness. A second copy in the browser harness would drift from the scripted fake that the command-line tests use.
payload.body: e2e/fixtures.ts puts src/test/fake-claude/bin first on the PATH of the werk serve it boots. That claude has no state folder, so it has no script and exits 127. No browser test can start the real agent. The browser harness does not write its own fake. A later browser test that needs agent replies installs a scripted fake with installFakeClaude from src/test/fake-claude/state.ts, under Bun.

payload.why: The harness boots the werk serve that #werk-dev defines, with the fake agent on its PATH.

payload.title: The claim that the person asked is the actor of the accept event
payload.why: A command-line accept must state that the person asked for it. The log already records who made each event, so the claim needs no second field.
payload.body: An accept from the command line names its actor. Only the person as actor commits the ghost. An agent actor, or no actor, refuses, and the refusal prints the accept with the person as actor. The accept event records the person as its actor, so the log shows who claimed the accept. The claim is a speed bump: an agent can still state it falsely.

payload.why: The actor of an event is a field the log keeps on every event, so the claim lives there.

payload.title: The place of a node is its link to its parent; the link operation adds only depends_on and supported_by
payload.why: A refines link and an option's alternative_to link put a node in the tree. A second way to set them would let a node sit in two places.
payload.body:
A node names its parent when it is proposed. The type of the link to the parent follows the kind: an option is alternative_to its parent, and every other kind refines its parent. An option must have a card as its parent, and it takes no other link.

The link operation adds only depends_on and supported_by. A supported_by link ends at a source or an excerpt. A link that names a ghost waits with the ghost, goes live by itself when both ends are real, and goes away when the ghost is discarded.

payload.why: a link that names a ghost waits, and accepts or discards with it

payload.title: The server folds the log per request and serves one card page at /api/view?id=, and the hash #<id> names the open card
payload.why: The page needs one call per view, and the address bar must name the card so a view survives a reload and can be shared.
payload.body: GET /api/view?id=<id> reads the log, folds it, and returns the page of that card: the card itself, its refines parent, its sub-cards (refines children, options excluded), say (supported_by excerpts), ev (supported_by sources and cards), alt (alternative_to options with whyNot), depends_on, and cited-by. No id returns the root page: card null, the top-level cards as sub-cards. An unknown id is a 404. The page reads the card id from location.hash (#<id>) and fetches again on hashchange and on a 'changed' event. The fold runs on each request, with no cache: the log is small, and a cache could show a stale card.

payload.why: the page is built from the fold of the append-only log
the page carries say, ev and alt

payload.title: The held-out run after a merge holds the steps of merged tickets only
payload.why: A step whose ticket is not on the main line describes behaviour nobody has merged yet, so its red result reports a break nobody made and files a follow-up that builds another ticket's work.
payload.body: The held-out set that runs after a merge holds the steps of the subtree's tickets that are merged onto the main line, and nothing else. A ticket's steps join the set in the merge that brings its code, so that merge's own run already includes them. Steps of a ticket that is still building or merging stay out, even when the step author has finished them. Steps of an archived ticket leave the set with the ticket, and a restore of the ticket brings them back (see #st-plan-archive). A red step therefore always points at code on the main line: either the ticket's own code or a later merge that broke it. When every ticket of the subtree is merged, the set is complete, so G2 still waits on every step of every live ticket.

payload.why: the run after each merge, and the follow-up on a red step, that this card limits to merged tickets
the reversible ticket archive that also takes the ticket's steps out of the set
steps are written per ticket from its brief, at build start, which is why a ticket's steps exist before its code is merged

payload.title: Run the whole set after each merge, and show a step of an unmerged ticket as not run instead of red
payload.why_not: The binder still binds and runs steps that cannot pass at every merge, and the grey badges carry no information about the main line.

payload.title: Keep the steps of an archived ticket in the set, because its behaviour may still be wanted
payload.why_not: A later plan that archives a ticket covers its scope with new tickets that carry their own steps. The old steps then fail against a main line that is built differently, and each fails as a follow-up ticket.

criterion.text: A break reaches G2 that a step left out of a merge's held-out run would have caught

payload.title: The printed card lists its proof in three sections: options, say and ev
payload.why: A reader of the printed card must see the rejected options and the evidence of the card without a second query, the same as on its page.
payload.body: The printed form of one card ends with up to three sections. Options lists each option that is an alternative to the card, with its why-not reason. Say lists each excerpt that supports the card, with its verbatim words. Ev lists each source that supports the card. A ghost in a section carries the proposed mark. An empty section is not printed.

payload.why: The sections read the alternative_to and supported_by link types.

payload.title: A removed card takes its links with it, and a restore brings each link back once both ends exist
payload.why: A remove is one more event, so a restore must give back the same map, links included, even when two linked cards were removed and restored in any order.
payload.body: A remove applies only to a real card; a ghost is discarded instead. The removed card leaves the map, and every link that touches it waits aside. A restore puts the card back, and each waiting link comes back once both of its ends are in the map again. A child that found a new parent while its old parent was removed keeps the new parent. The id of a removed card stays taken: a new add with that id refuses and points at the restore.

payload.title: The printed card lists its sub-cards below its detail
payload.why: The text view of one card has the same shape as its page: the detail on top, the sub-cards below it.
payload.body: Printing one card lists every card that refines it, after the detail and the proof. A ghost sub-card carries the proposed mark. A leaf prints no sub-card section. An option is not a sub-card, because its only link is alternative_to; it is listed under options.

payload.why: Done means the diff meets its ticket's criteria and breaks no decided card. Only an agent can read a card against a diff.

ops.old: The grader reads the ticket's depends_on closure. Each decided card in it becomes one judgement line: does the diff do what this card says?
ops.new: The grader scores two kinds of line. Each acceptance criterion of the ticket is one delivery line: does the diff meet this criterion? Each decided card in the ticket's depends_on closure, cited or not, is one contradiction line: does the diff do something this card forbids, or do it differently? A part of a card that the diff does not build yet passes its contradiction line, because another ticket builds it, and the plan's set checks make sure every decided card is cited by some ticket (#st-ticket-set-checks).

ops.old: There is no fixed list. The lines change with each ticket. The grader is the same for every project werk builds, because the project's context comes from its own cards.
ops.new: There is no fixed list. The lines change with each ticket. The grader is the same for every project werk builds, because the project's context comes from its own cards.

ops.old: For each card, the grader returns two things:
ops.new: For each line, the grader returns two things:

ops.old:
- a score, 1-5. A 3 passes.
- what is wrong: the gap between the diff and the card, with the file, line, or test that shows it.
ops.new:
- a score, 1-5. A 3 passes.
- what is wrong: the unmet criterion or the contradiction, with the file, line, or test that shows it.

ops.old: The second part is the output that matters. On a fail, the next builder pass gets it together with the brief (#lp-stateless). A score with no reason gives the builder nothing to fix.
ops.new: The second part is the output that matters. On a fail, the next builder pass gets it together with the brief (#lp-stateless). A score with no reason gives the builder nothing to fix.

ops.old: Rejected: #lp-prod-judge:opt1 (a fixed generic list — it does not know what was decided, so a diff can pass every line and still build the wrong thing). #lp-prod-judge:opt2 (a fixed core plus the card lines — two sources of lines. The cost of this choice: nothing catches a problem that no card names).
ops.new: Rejected: #lp-prod-judge:opt1 (a fixed generic list — it does not know what was decided, so a diff can pass every line and still build the wrong thing). #lp-prod-judge:opt2 (a fixed core plus the card lines — two sources of lines. The cost of this choice: nothing catches a problem that no card names).

payload.title: Every decided card in the closure is a delivery line: does the diff do what this card says?
payload.why_not: A ticket is one slice of a subtree, and its closure reaches the root card. The grader then fails a correct slice for work that later tickets build, and the builder can do nothing about the gap.

payload.title: Cited cards are delivery lines, and the other closure cards are contradiction lines
payload.why_not: Tickets cite broad cards such as a subtree's root, so a cited card still asks a slice for work it does not do. The ticket's acceptance criteria already state exactly the scope the ticket claims.

payload.why: a missing part of a card passes the grader only because the set checks make some ticket cite every decided card

payload.title: The fake agent keeps an ask open while the script goes on
payload.why: A test must script a permission ask, then a stall, repeated tool calls, or a death before anybody answers. A fake that blocks on the answer cannot play those steps.
payload.body: In the fake claude, an ask step prints the control_request and does not wait. The next steps play at once: a sleep, a tool call, a die. The turn waits for each open ask only before it prints the result event. With stream-json input, the answer comes from stdin. With no input channel, the ask is denied at the end of the turn. A die with an ask open exits with no tool result and no result event. Each sleep adds a 20 ms margin, so a reader never measures a silence shorter than the script asks for.

payload.title: An accept and a discard are each one event, and the fold walks the ghost tree
payload.why: One person action is one change, so it is one event in the log. The walk up to the first real card, and the walk down through the ghosts, are derived from the log and never written.
payload.body: An accept names one ghost. The fold commits that ghost and each ghost parent above it, up to the first real card. A discard names one ghost. The fold drops that ghost, every ghost below it, and every link that touches them, so the id is free for a new proposal. An accept or a discard that names a real card changes nothing. The words of a ghost stay frozen in the fold too: a retitle or a text edit on a ghost changes nothing, a status does.

payload.why: It takes the rule that every change is one event, and the fold derives the rest.

payload.title: A proposed option sits under its parent by alternative_to, every other kind by refines
payload.why: An option has one link only, alternative_to. A refines parent on an option would list it twice.
payload.body: A proposal names its parent. For an option the link to the parent is alternative_to. For a card, a source and an excerpt it is refines. The accept walk up and the discard walk down follow that parent link of each kind, so an option accepts and discards with the card it sits under.

payload.why: It takes the rule that an option has one link only, alternative_to.

payload.title: The accept command states the person's request with one switch, recorded on the accept event
payload.why: An accept from the command line must state that the person asked for it. A switch is the smallest statement, and the event keeps it so the log shows on what claim the card was committed.
payload.body: The accept command takes one id and a person-asked switch. Without the switch it refuses, and prints the full command with the switch. With it, the accept event carries the claim. The command accepts one id only: more than one id refuses.

payload.why: It takes the rule that an accept from the command line refuses without the person's request.
It takes the rule that the words of a ghost are frozen.
Edit refuses a ghost because #werk-propose-new freezes it.

payload.title: Edit also changes the title, the why and the body of an open card, and refuses on a ghost or a decided card
payload.why: A retitle of a real card needs a command, and the same command must refuse a change to the words of a ghost. One command for the words of an open card covers both.
payload.body: The edit command takes a new title, a new why and a new body. A new title is a retitle event. A new why or body is one text edit event. On a ghost it refuses and prints the correction: discard, then add again. On a decided card it refuses, because a change to a decided card is a proposal. With nothing to change it refuses.

payload.why: It refuses the words of a decided card, because this card makes that change a proposal.

payload.title: One press on a decided map card plans its subtree and then runs the merge loop, with no pause between
payload.why: A build over a whole subtree runs for hours, so it must start from the app, outlive the server, and need nobody between the plan and the run.
payload.body: A card in the map carries a Build button. The button works only when the plan's scope holds no open and no proto card (see #st-spec-linked). Otherwise it is grey and names the cards that block it. One press starts the plan and then the merge loop over the planned tickets, as one process that the server starts detached. The process has no time limit and outlives a restart of the server. A press on a subtree that already has a plan extends that plan and resumes its run (see #st-plan-extend). The press is the person's start of the whole run, so the plan's tickets build without a review between the plan and the run. The plan card on the board shows the progress and holds the stop, which ends the whole process (see #vi-board-plan).

payload.why: the scope check that enables the button is the plan's own scope: the subtree plus one hop of linked cards
a second press on a planned subtree extends that plan instead of writing a second ticket set
the plan card is where the press shows progress and where the person stops it
the merge loop that the press starts after the plan

payload.title: The press only plans; a second button on the plan card starts the run
payload.why_not: The person reads the tickets before they build, but an overnight build then needs the person awake after the plan ends to start the run.

criterion.text: An unattended build spends its passes on tickets that the person rejects on first reading after the run

payload.why: A verb in its own module follows the single-purpose, small module rule.
Two tickets build at the same time only if they share no module; self-registration keeps verb tickets disjoint.
The operation runs these checks on one ticket.
The operation runs these checks on the whole set.
An agent that changes a ticket on a person's request reruns the set checks.

criterion.text: Add two verbs in two tickets. If both need an edit to one shared module, or the printed verb list misses a registered verb, drop this decision.
Run the operation on a folder with one bad ticket and one bad set. If it does not name the ticket and the field, or the plan cannot call the same checks, drop this decision.

payload.title: The chat agent starts the plan and the run as a background command
payload.why_not: A background command of the chat agent runs under Claude Code's limit of two hours, and the limit kills the merge loop in the middle of a build over a whole subtree.

payload.title: The ticket-check operation exits non-zero when any ticket check fails
payload.why: No card says how the ticket-check operation reports its verdict; a check is one command and its exit code (#lp-checks), so the operation gives one.
payload.body: The ticket-check operation (#werk-ticket-check-verb) exits with a non-zero code when any check on one ticket or on the whole set fails, and with zero when every check passes. The printed failures, each with its ticket and field, are for the reader; the exit code is the verdict, the same as for every other check (#lp-checks). So a test, a make target, or an agent that changed a ticket can use the operation as a check without reading its output.

payload.title: The project setup puts the verb registration in place before any verb is built
payload.why: No card says when the registration exists; if a verb ticket adds it, every verb ticket before it touches the same shared module and they cannot build at the same time.
payload.body: The verb registration of #werk-verb-registry is part of the project setup from the empty tree (#werk-base-repo), before the first ticket that adds a map or build verb. Each later verb ticket then adds only its own module, so independent verb tickets touch no common module and the scheduler can build them at the same time (#st-build-parallel, #werk-stack-modules).

payload.title: The command line finds its verbs by loading every module in one verbs folder
payload.why: A folder listing is a list that no ticket edits: adding a verb adds a file, and two tickets that add different verbs touch no common file.
payload.body: At start, the command line imports every module in its verbs folder. Each module registers one verb when it loads. A test file in that folder is not loaded. The registry refuses two verbs with the same name, so two modules that claim one name fail at start and do not shadow each other. With no verb named, the command line runs help.

payload.title: The fake agent replays a script of ordered steps: an event to print, or a file to write
payload.why: One ordered list keeps an event and a file edit in the order a real agent makes them, so a test can check what was on disk when each event arrived.
payload.body: The harness gives each temporary project one script. The fake agent, first on the PATH under the real agent's name, reads it at launch. Each step is an event, printed as one JSON line, or an edit, a file written relative to the project. The script also sets the exit code. An edit outside the project fails. Each launch records its arguments, so a test can read what the agent was asked.

payload.why: takes the rule that the fake agent replays events and edits files the way a real agent does
takes the rule that a shared list holds only entries, here reduced to the folder listing

payload.title: Each check target installs the locked dependencies before it runs its tool
payload.why: The merge queue and each builder run the checks in a fresh tree with no installed dependencies, so a tool found higher up the search path runs without the project's types and fails.
payload.body: A check target first installs the project's dependencies from its lock file, and only then runs its tool. The install runs again only when the package list or the lock file changes. So a check gives the same verdict in a builder's worktree, in the merge queue's temporary tree, and in a checkout that already has the dependencies. A check never depends on the state that an earlier command left in the tree.

payload.why: the merge queue runs the checks in a temporary tree with no installed dependencies

payload.title: The proposed parent rides inside the node.proposed event, and the fold derives the refines edge
payload.why: Each map verb appends exactly one event. A separate edge event for the parent would make add two events, and a crash between them would leave a ghost with no parent.
payload.body: add --parent X writes parent: X into the node.proposed payload. The fold turns it into a refines edge from the card to X. The edge sits in ghostEdges while either end is a ghost, and moves to edges once both ends are real. An add with an unknown parent refuses and appends nothing.

payload.why: It takes the rule that every change is one event at the end of the log.

payload.title: The actor claim on the command line is --actor you
payload.why: The accept verb needs a stated claim that the person asked for it. One flag with one value is easy to read in a transcript and easy to check.
payload.body: Every event records actor: you or agent. The default is agent. accept refuses with exit 1 unless the call passes --actor you, and the accepted event records actor you. Any other value of --actor counts as agent.

payload.title: A note is one note.said event, and the fold keeps a thread per node
payload.why: The thread of a card must be readable from the log alone, by the same fold as the rest of the map.
payload.body: A note is the event note.said with payload { id, text }. The log gives it seq, at and actor. The fold collects the notes of each node into MapState.threads, in log order. A note on a ghost is allowed. A note never changes the node's title, why or body. The fold drops a note for an id the log does not hold.

payload.why: A note is one more append-only event in the decision log, read back through the fold.

payload.title: The excerpt proposal carries its pointer and the id of the card it supports; the fold derives the supported_by edge
payload.why: One quote appends one event, so the edge must ride inside the node.proposed event, the same way parent rides in it for refines.
payload.body: node.proposed gains two optional payload fields: excerpt = { session, msgIndex, span: [start, end], speaker: user|assistant } and supports = <citing card id>. The fold turns supports into an edge from the citing card to the excerpt with type supported_by. Like refines, the edge is a ghost edge until both ends are real. The title of the excerpt is the quote itself. Accepting the excerpt follows only refines edges up, never supported_by.

payload.why: It takes the rule that one quote is one event that holds both the excerpt and its supported_by edge.

payload.title: werk quote <card-id> <session-id> --text: the session is a Claude Code session id, found under every project of the Claude config dir
payload.why: werk v0 stores no conversations yet, so a card id or a conversation name cannot resolve to a session. The session id is the one handle that exists.
payload.body: The quote verb takes the citing card and a session id as positionals, and the quote as --text. It looks for <session-id>.jsonl in each directory under $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/projects, or ~/.claude/projects when that is unset. No file, or two files with that name, fails and writes nothing. Card ids and conversation names as the second argument wait for the conversation store (#werk-cli-recall).

payload.why: It takes the command form werk quote <card-id> <session> --text from the CLI card, narrowed to a session id.
It takes the lookup of a transcript in every project directory of the Claude config dir.

payload.title: werk say <id> --text writes a note; werk inbox [<id>] reads the threads
payload.why: An agent must read a whole thread and answer on the card with two plain commands.
payload.body: say takes one id and a required --text. It refuses an unknown id (exit 1) and a malformed call (exit 2), and then appends nothing. It takes no actor claim, so a note is from the agent. inbox prints every thread, grouped by card, in the order of each thread's first note. Each group starts with '#<id>  <title>', plus '(ghost)' for a ghost. Each note prints as '[seq] actor at: text'. inbox <id> prints one thread. show prints the same note lines under 'notes (n):'.

payload.why: say appends the note.said event, and inbox and show read the threads the fold builds from it.

payload.title: The fold keeps one edge list and splits it into live and held edges at the end
payload.why: An edge goes live by itself only if no event moves it. A split computed from node state needs no move.
payload.body: A link appends one edge.linked event. A proposed parent rides in node.proposed. The fold collects every edge in one list. After the last event, an edge with two real ends goes to edges, and every other edge goes to ghostEdges. An accept or a discard changes only nodes, so the edges follow without a second event. Show marks an edge in ghostEdges as held.

payload.title: An accept and a discard act on the same branch: the ghost chain plus each node's own ghost options and sources
payload.why: A ghost decided card with its options must commit as one unit, and a discard must not leave a ghost option pointing at nothing.
payload.body: Accept: the card, then each ghost up its refines chain to the first real card. Each node in that chain also brings its ghost options (alternative_to into it) and its ghost sources and excerpts (supported_by out of it). A depends_on target never comes. Discard: the ghost, every ghost refines descendant, and the own ghost options and sources of each. The discarded ids leave nodes, and every edge that names one of them drops, so the same id can be proposed again with a clean slate. Discard takes no actor claim: the agent corrects a ghost by discard, then a new propose. Discard refuses on a real card.

payload.title: Status is its own verb with the unchallenged statement, and who rides on edit, allowed on a ghost
payload.why: Frozen means the words. Status, who and links are not words, so they must reach a ghost through a path that the frozen check does not block.
payload.body: werk status <id> open|proto|decided [--unchallenged] appends node.status_set. --unchallenged is the author's statement at decide time (#werk-contract-guess) and refuses on any other status. werk edit <id> --who <w> appends node.edited with only who. On a ghost, edit refuses when it names --body or --why, and passes when it names only --who. Unchallenged is the set of real decided cards with who you, the statement, and no live alternative_to edge into them. The rollup of a real card counts the real cards in its live refines subtree. Both read only live edges and real nodes, so a ghost changes neither. Staleness waits for a reopen event, which this rebuild does not have yet.

payload.why: unchallenged is a stored statement made at decide time, never inferred from the data
only who:you cards count as unchallenged

payload.title: A transcript line marked isMeta, or whose type is not its role, is never a message to quote
payload.why: Claude Code writes command expansions and injected reminders as user lines with isMeta. Those words are the harness's, not the person's, so a quote from them would put words in the person's mouth.
payload.body: The transcript reader skips a line with isMeta: true, and a line whose top-level type differs from message.role. Text that occurs only in such lines gives no exact match.

payload.why: It narrows the pointer card's definition of a text-bearing user or assistant line.

payload.title: A real node cannot refine a ghost, and a refines link cannot close a loop
payload.why: An accept walks up the refines chain from the ghost. A real child under a ghost parent, or a loop, is a parent that no accept can reach.
payload.body: link refuses refines from a real node to a ghost, and refuses a refines link whose target already sits under its source. An own option or source counts only by kind: an option at the far end of alternative_to, a source or an excerpt at the far end of supported_by. A discard keeps an own ghost that a node outside the branch also holds.

payload.title: An excerpt has a thread like any node; a note on it never changes the quote
payload.why: The say verb and the quote verb merged on one fold. A note is a reply on a node, so it can question an excerpt without touching the transcript's words.
payload.body: say accepts an excerpt id, a ghost excerpt too. The note goes to state.threads, not to the excerpt's title or pointer. The fold keeps one edge list for refines and supported_by, and a separate threads map; notes never make edges.

payload.why: takes the note.said event and the rule that a note never edits the node's words

payload.title: The lock is .werk/server.lock beside the log, taken with an exclusive create
payload.why: An exclusive create (O_EXCL) makes two starts race safely: only one of them creates the file.
payload.body: The lock file sits in the directory of the log, so WERK_LOG moves the lock with the log. It holds {pid, port} as JSON. The port is null until the listen succeeds, then the file is rewritten with it. A holder whose pid is dead is a stale lock: the start removes it and tries again. A live holder: the start prints 'werk: waiting for pid N to let go of the lock', polls every 100 ms for 5 s, then refuses with the #werk-onelock message. The lock is removed on exit, SIGINT and SIGTERM, and only when it still holds this pid.

payload.why: takes the 5-second wait for a live holder

payload.title: A discard drops the notes of each ghost it drops
payload.why: A discarded id can be proposed again as a fresh ghost. Old notes on the new ghost would describe words that are gone.
payload.body: The fold deletes the thread of every node in the discarded branch, the same way it deletes the node and its edges. The note.said events stay in the log. A note said on the id after a new propose starts a new thread.

payload.why: takes the thread of a node, and that a ghost has one

payload.title: The server reads the log at GET /api/graph and pushes 'changed' at GET /api/events
payload.why: One read endpoint and one event channel keep the server a pure reader. The client refetches the whole fold on each change, so it holds no second copy of the map to keep in step.
payload.body: GET /api/graph returns the fold as JSON: nodes (every node, ghosts too, with proposed), edges, ghostEdges, and threads by id. GET /api/events is a server-sent event stream. It sends 'event: changed' after each change to the log file, seen by a watch on the log's directory with a 30 ms debounce. The client refetches /api/graph on each 'changed' and each time the stream opens, so a change made before the stream connects is not lost. The server is node:http under Bun, because Vite's middleware mode takes a Node request and response. The map draws only real nodes; a ghost waits for accept.

payload.why: mounts Vite in middleware mode inside the same server

payload.title: Each browser test boots its own werk server through an automatic Playwright fixture
payload.why: A test that runs add and accept changes its project, so a server shared by all tests would leak one test's cards into the next.
payload.body: e2e/harness.ts gives every test a 'werk' fixture with { url, dir, cli }. It copies e2e/fixture-project into a temporary git repository, puts the fake agent first on the PATH as claude, and starts 'werk serve --port 0' with a clean environment (no inherited WERK_LOG). The page may reach only the server's host; every other request is aborted. Local storage is cleared after the first load. After the test, one full-page screenshot is saved as evidence.png in the test's folder under test-results/. There is no webServer entry in playwright.config.ts. The e2e make target installs the Playwright chromium first; the install does nothing when it is cached.

payload.why: takes the browser seam: a real server on a copy of a fixture project, fake agent first on the PATH

payload.title: No hash opens the whole refines tree; a hash opens that card's page
payload.why: The map needs an entry page that shows every root. A card page shows only its own subtree, so the whole tree needs a page of its own.
payload.body: An empty hash draws the refines tree of every real card, as nested lists, roots in log order. '#<id>' (URI-encoded) draws the card page: breadcrumbs from 'The map' through the ancestors, the detail (title, why, body, why-not, kind, status, who), then the sub-cards as a nested tree. A ghost or an unknown id draws 'No card #<id> in the map.' The page holds text and links only: no input, no button, no contenteditable.

payload.why: the page holds no control that edits a drawn card

payload.title: show prints a node's own parent and supported_by edges as fields, every other edge as a link line
payload.why: The quote ticket printed supported-by as a field and this ticket prints every edge as a link line. One edge on two lines reads as two facts.
payload.body: On the node it leaves, a refines edge prints as 'parent: #x' and a supported_by edge prints as 'supported-by: #x, #y'. The link lines leave out these two, so each edge prints once. On the far end, both print as a link line, with '(held)' while either end is a ghost. So an excerpt shows 'link: supported_by <- #card (held)' until its card is accepted. The field lines carry no held mark: the ghost state of the node already says it.

payload.why: takes the supported_by edge from a card to its excerpt, which the quote verb proposes with the excerpt

payload.title: The lock is taken by a hard link of a fully written temporary file
payload.why: An exclusive create leaves an empty file for a moment, and a second start that reads it then sees no pid. A hard link puts the whole lock in place in one step, and the link still fails when the lock exists.
payload.body: takeLock writes {pid, port: null} to .werk/server.lock.<pid>, then links it to .werk/server.lock and removes the temporary file. EEXIST means another holder: a dead pid or an unreadable file is stale and is removed, a live pid makes the start wait up to 5 seconds, then refuse. Once the listen succeeds, a rename replaces the lock with the port in it, so a reader sees the old lock or the new one, never half of it. release removes the lock only while its pid is this process.

payload.why: takes the 5-second wait for a live holder before the start refuses

payload.title: werk ticket-check <folder> --root <card-id> --spec <file> prints one line per failure: ticket, check, field, message
payload.why: One fixed line form lets a person and an agent read a failure by ticket and field, and the exit code is the verdict (#lp-checks).
payload.body: The verb reads every .md file in the folder, the decided cards under --root from the map, and the story numbers of --spec. It prints one line per failure, in the form '<ticket file>: <check>: <field>: <message>'. A cards-cited or stories failure names no ticket, so its ticket part is 'ticket set'. A last line counts the tickets, the own-check failures, all failures, the decided cards and the stories. Exit 0 when nothing fails, 1 when a check fails, 2 for a malformed call: a missing flag, a missing folder or spec, a spec with no 'User stories' heading, or a root that is not in the map. The spec's stories are the numbered lines under its 'User stories' heading, up to the next heading of the same level or higher. The decided cards are the root and its refines descendants at any depth with status decided; a ghost does not count.

payload.title: A ticket's number is the leading digits of its file name
payload.why: blocked_by holds numbers, and the ticket format has no number field, so the set check needs one place that gives each ticket its number.
payload.body: The ticket files are named <NN>-<slug>.md, numbered from 01 (/to-tickets). The set check reads the number from the leading digits of the file name: 03-stale.md is ticket 3. A file with no leading digits has no number, so no blocked_by can name it, but it still counts for the cards-cited and stories checks.

payload.why: The ticket set part of each failure line follows the rule that only the blocked_by check names tickets.
The check names in each failure line are the eight own-check names.

payload.title: A guard file lets one start at a time remove a stale lock
payload.why: A read of the lock and its unlink are two steps. Two starts that both read a stale lock could each unlink it, and the second unlink could remove a fresh lock that a third start took in between. Then two servers share one log.
payload.body: Before it removes a stale .werk/server.lock, a start takes .werk/server.lock.reap with the same hard-link create. Under the guard it reads the lock again and removes it only if it is still stale. A start that finds the guard taken waits one poll and tries again. The guard holds its holder's pid, so a guard left by a dead start is removed.

payload.why: takes the hard-link create, which puts a whole file in place in one step or fails

payload.text: Correction after review: only a malformed call (a missing flag, an unknown flag, no folder operand) exits 2 with the usage line. A folder, spec file, User stories heading or root card that is not there exits 1 with no usage line, as the map verbs do, and the root error reads 'no node "<id>"'.

payload.title: The cards a plan must cite are read through live refines links only; a held link of a ghost adds none
payload.why: A ghost and the links it holds are not yet in the map, so a card reached only through them is not a decided card of the planned subtree, and a plan must not fail for not citing it.
payload.body: The cards-cited set check takes the root and every card that refines it, at any depth, through the live refines links of the fold, and keeps the decided cards. A link held by a ghost (a proposed card) is not live: neither the ghost nor a card under it counts. When the ghost is accepted, its links go live, and the next ticket-check run reads its decided cards.

payload.why: The subtree is read from the fold of the log, with its live and held links.

payload.title: The map tree is built from refines links only
payload.why: A depends_on or supported_by link that moved a card under another card would draw a part-of relation the log does not hold.
payload.body: The map view draws the fold as a tree. A card's parent in that tree is the target of its refines link, and nothing else. depends_on, supported_by and alternative_to links leave a card where its refines link puts it. A card with no refines link is a root. A ghost is not drawn until it is accepted.

payload.why: The tree is a read-only view of the fold; it takes the rule that every view draws from the log.

payload.title: The contract check runs once in the shared verb run, on the map as the change would leave it
payload.why: If each verb called the check, a new verb could skip it. One gate in the shared run means no change to a decided card skips the check.
payload.body: runMapVerb folds the log with the ruled event appended, and calls checkChange(before, after, event) from the pure module src/map/contract.ts. Only the card the event names is checked: the id of a status, edit, retitle, add or kill event, and the from end of a link. A move to decided, and a decide of a decided card, need every fact. On a decided card, a change to the title, why, body, a depends_on link or the parent is an amend and needs every fact. Any other change refuses only when it removes a fact the card had. A discard is not a change to the cards that point at the discarded node, so it is not checked.

payload.why: The amend rule: a change to a frozen field of a decided card runs the decide facts again.
The four facts that the gate checks.

payload.title: The basis fact holds when the card has a depends_on target or a parent, and every one of them is decided
payload.why: A card written against an open basis cannot be decided until that basis is (#map-wait). Every target is checked, because one open target is enough to make the card wait.
payload.body: The basis is the set of depends_on targets plus the refines parent, live or held. The fact is missing when the set is empty, or when one member is not decided. Empty: the command is werk link <id> <card-it-needs> --type depends_on, and the reason line names the waiver werk edit <id> --no-basis "<reason>". Not decided: the command is werk status <basis> decided. Staleness is not checked yet, because the map has no staleness.

payload.why: A card on an open basis waits until the basis is decided.
The definition of the basis fact.

payload.title: werk kill appends one kill.recorded event that holds one criterion in its form
payload.why: A kill criterion is a fact on the log. Without a verb that records it, no refused decide could print a command that fixes it.
payload.body: werk kill <id> --form metric|manual|no-metric|revisit. metric needs --source, --metric, --threshold and --window, and takes --min-sample N. manual and no-metric need --text. revisit takes nothing. A part of another form refuses, so nothing given is dropped. The event is kill.recorded with payload { id, criterion }. The fold appends the criterion to node.kills. It records on a ghost and on a decided card, because a criterion is a fact, not a word. Only a card takes one.

payload.why: The four forms and the parts of a metric.
The gate blocks decided until a kill answer is on record.

payload.title: The fix for a missing option is one shell line: an add of the option and its alternative_to link
payload.why: Each fact has one command (#werk-contract-all-missing). An option needs two events, a proposal and a link, so the command joins them with &&.
payload.body: werk add <id>:optN --kind option --title "<the option>" --why-not "<why it lost>" && werk link <id>:optN <id> --type alternative_to. N is the first free number. The reason line names the waiver: decide with --unchallenged. A held alternative_to edge from a ghost option counts, the same as a live one.

payload.why: A failed check prints the exact next command.
The --unchallenged statement is the waiver for the option fact.

payload.title: The no-basis waiver on edit takes a written reason, and records on a ghost too
payload.why: Every escape hatch leaves a written reason (#pr-gate). A bare flag would waive the basis with nothing to read.
payload.body: werk edit <id> --no-basis "<reason>" appends a node.edited event with noBasis. An empty reason refuses. Like who, it is a contract fact, not a word, so a ghost takes it.

payload.why: An escape hatch leaves a written reason.
edit is the command that records the basis waiver.

payload.title: A merge conflict is resolved on the ticket's own branch, and that ticket merges next
payload.why: A fresh build takes as long as the first one. The main line moves again in that time, so a ticket that touches a busy file conflicts again and again.
payload.body:
When git cannot merge a ticket, the next pass starts from the ticket's own branch with the main line's tip merged into it. The builder gets the conflicted files and the conflict output, resolves them, and runs the checks. This replaces the fresh rebuild that #st-build-conflict sets. The pass still does not count against the retry cap.

A ticket that comes back green from a conflict pass goes to the front of the merge queue, so no other merge can move the main line under it first.

Three conflicts in a row still mark the ticket stuck (#st-build-stuck-park says what stuck stops).

payload.title: Rebuild the ticket fresh from the main line's tip after each conflict
payload.why_not: The rebuild costs a full build, and every merge that lands during it can conflict with it again. A list that every ticket appends to conflicts on each try.

payload.why: The conflict pass is one more builder pass with the conflict as its failure, as #st-build-ticket defines a pass.
It keeps the temporary merge tree and the guarded branch move, and changes only where the next pass starts.

payload.title: The held-out set runs beside the merge queue, and the next merge does not wait for it
payload.why: The held-out set grows with every merged ticket. While the merge queue waits for it, the green branches behind it age and conflict.
payload.body:
After a merge, the held-out set starts on that merge's commit in the background. The merge queue takes the next ticket at once. A red step files a follow-up for the ticket whose merge it ran after, as #st-validate-heldout sets.

When a held-out run is still going and a newer merge lands, the older run is not stopped: each result belongs to its own commit. Only the result on the main line's final tip opens G2 (#st-g2-heldout).

payload.title: The merge queue waits for the held-out set after each merge
payload.why_not: Its time grows with the number of merged tickets, from about 3 to over 9 minutes in one run, and each minute is a window for the main line to move under a waiting branch.

payload.why: It keeps the held-out run at each merge and its follow-up on a red step, and changes only whether the merge queue waits.
G2 still reads the held-out result, so the run must know which result is on the final tip.

payload.title: A stuck ticket stops only itself and the tickets that need it
payload.why: One stuck ticket ends the whole run, so every independent ticket waits for a person until morning.
payload.body:
A ticket that hits its retry cap or its conflict limit moves to blocked with the stop reason. Every ticket that needs it, directly or through others, stays blocked behind it. The merge loop goes on with every other ticket.

The run ends only when nothing can build or merge. Then it reports each stuck ticket and what waits on it.

payload.title: The first stuck ticket ends the run
payload.why_not: It stops tickets that do not need the stuck one, and an overnight run then does nothing until a person looks.

payload.why: What may still build comes from the blocked_by edges that #st-build-parallel schedules on.
A parked ticket leaves building with its reason, as #st-build-stop-ready does for a stopped loop.
It names the conflict limit and relies on this card for what the limit stops.

criterion.metric: share of conflict passes whose next merge conflicts again
share of held-out runs that end with a step not run (binder error or timeout)
share of tickets built after a park in the same run that also go stuck

payload.title: A merge of the pure-file list keeps every entry from both sides
payload.why: Two builds each add their own pure modules to PURE_FILES. If a merge kept only one side, the coverage gate would stop judging the other side's pure modules, and nobody would notice.
payload.body: The contract check (src/map/contract.ts) and the ticket checks (src/ticket/*) both joined src/coverage/pure-files.ts at the same place, so git reported a conflict. The resolution keeps both sets of lines: each build's entries stay in the order that build wrote them, and the conflict is a union, not a choice. The coverage gate then judges all 20 pure files. A file leaves the list only when the file is deleted or stops being pure, never as a side effect of a merge.

payload.why: takes the explicit pure-file list that the 90% gate reads, which a merge must keep whole

payload.title: Two branches that each add pure files merge the coverage list as the union of both
payload.why: Each branch adds its own pure files in the change that writes them. A merge that keeps one side drops the other side's files from the gate, and they then pass unjudged.
payload.body: The pure-file list in src/coverage/pure-files.ts is a set, not an ordered record. When two branches each append files and git conflicts on the list, the resolution keeps every file from both sides. The order inside the list has no meaning. After the merge, the coverage gate must report every file of both branches.

payload.why: takes the explicit list of pure files that the gate judges, and the rule that a new pure file joins it in its own change

payload.title: Ticket state is the board log: .werk/board.jsonl, three event types
payload.why: The board needs a ticket state that the decision log does not hold, and a fold needs a fixed event shape to read.
payload.body: The board log sits beside the decision log, as board.jsonl in the same folder. It has three events. ticket.planned carries the ticket fields (number, title, cites, blockedBy, stories, touches, checks, brief) and puts a new ticket in ready; a second one for the same number replaces the fields and keeps the column and the retries. ticket.moved names the column, and a move to blocked carries the reason. ticket.retried counts one failed pass and does not move the ticket. A move or a retry of a ticket that was never planned changes nothing. A blocker that is not on the board counts as unmet.

payload.why: The board log is append-only and folded, the same as the decision log.

payload.title: The board lives at the hash #/board, and an open ticket at #/board/<number>
payload.why: A card id holds no slash, so a hash that starts with a slash never names a card, and a reload or a shared link keeps the open ticket.
payload.body: The client reads the location hash. #/board draws the board; #/board/3 draws the board with the drawer of ticket 3 open. Any other hash names a map card, as before. A nav at the top links the map and the board. A cited id in the drawer is a link to #<id>, so a click opens that card on the map.

payload.title: The ✓ posts to POST /api/accept/<id>, the server's one write route
payload.why: The browser cannot run the command line, and the accept must still go through the same rule and the log module.
payload.body: The server has one write route: POST /api/accept/<id>. It folds the log, runs the same accept rule as the accept verb with the actor 'you', and appends one node.accepted event through appendEvent. A refusal answers 409 with the rule's words and appends nothing. A GET answers 405. A request whose Origin header is not the server's own answers 403, so a page from another site cannot accept a card. The reply does not redraw the map: the log watcher pushes 'changed', and the page refetches the fold.

payload.why: It takes the accept rule: one card, its proposed ancestors and its own options and sources.

payload.title: When both sides of a merge add pure files at one place, the ticket's lines go first
payload.why: A union of two lists still needs one order. A fixed order makes each re-merge give the same file, so the next merge does not see a new difference.
payload.body: A second merge of main into werk/64 hit the same spot in src/coverage/pure-files.ts: this ticket added src/map/contract.ts and the main line added src/map/graph.ts. The resolution keeps both (werk-contract-pure-list-merge). The ticket branch's lines come first, then the main line's lines. The gate reads the list as a set, so the order has no effect on the verdict; it only keeps the merge result stable.

payload.why: takes the rule that a merge of the pure-file list is a union of both sides, and only adds the order of that union

payload.title: The contract check runs inside the one write path
payload.why: The ✓ route and the command line share appendRuled; a check outside it would let one view skip the contract.
payload.body: appendRuled folds the log, asks the rule for one event, runs checkChange on the map as the event would leave it, and appends only if both pass. A refusal returns refusalText joined by newlines as the error. The CLI and the map's ✓ route get the same check with no copy.

payload.why: Takes checkChange and refusalText, the check that every write must pass.

payload.title: An amend at the end of a review marks the next hop with the reason amended
payload.why: A review that changes the card is a change too, so its trace needs a reason. Neither reopen reason fits: the card was reviewed, not reopened.
payload.body: The rederive event holds the outcome, confirm or amend, and the sentence that says why. An amend clears the marks on the reviewed card that are older than it, and puts a stale mark on its direct dependents and direct children. Their trace reads: reason amended, cause the reviewed card, why the amend sentence. A confirm only clears.

payload.why: takes the two endings of a review, confirm and amend

payload.title: werk stale lists stale cards first, then paused cards, each group in basis order
payload.why: Only a stale card is reviewed, so it is the work to do now. A paused card waits for its origin to be decided again, so it goes last.
payload.body: In each group a card prints after the marked cards it stands on: its depends_on targets and its parent. Ties keep the log order of the oldest change. A card reached by both kinds is stale and prints every trace, the paused ones too, so the reader sees both reasons.

payload.why: takes the fix order: a basis prints before the card that depends on it

payload.title: A plan writes its feature tier as the first event of the run, on the board log, scoped to the subtree root
payload.why: The tier is run state, not a map change, and the board log already holds the run's other events. v0 has no issue, so the planned subtree root is the scope key.
payload.body: The plan appends tier.recorded with payload { tier: 'feature', root } to .werk/board.jsonl before it launches any writer and before it writes to the map. The payload type allows only 'feature', and the plan verb has no tier flag. The board fold ignores the event for the columns. A call that refuses before the run (a malformed call, a root that is not a decided real card) writes no tier event, because no run starts.

payload.why: It writes the feature tier as the first event, as the silence-means-feature card asks.

payload.title: A plan's writers write into one folder per subtree beside the log: spec.md, spec.answers.json, tickets/ and tickets.answers.json
payload.why: The plan must find each writer's output and its answers without parsing the agent's stream, and one folder per subtree lets a second plan extend the first.
payload.body: The folder is plans/<root>/ next to the decision log. The spec writer writes spec.md and spec.answers.json. The ticket writer writes one file per ticket in tickets/ and tickets.answers.json. An answers file is a JSON array of { slug, title, why, body }. A missing answers file is a reported failure, so no answer can be lost without a sign. Before each writer runs, the plan deletes its answers file, and before the ticket writer runs it empties tickets/, so stale output never counts; the open tickets stay readable on the board log, and the prompt lists them so the writer keeps a needed ticket under its own number. Each writer runs as claude -p with WERK_AGENT_ROLE set to spec-writer or ticket-writer. A slug is lower case letters, digits and hyphens.

payload.title: A plan archives an open ticket of its subtree whose number is in no ticket file of the new set
payload.why: The ticket writer keeps a needed ticket under its own number, so a number the writer no longer writes is a ticket the current spec does not need.
payload.body: A ticket on the board records the subtree root of the plan that wrote it. An open ticket (ready or blocked) of the same root with no file of that number in the new tickets folder gets ticket.archived with the reason 'the current spec of <root> no longer needs it'. An archived ticket leaves the five columns. A ticket whose new file fails its own checks is not archived; when it is open it moves to blocked with the reason that its new version fails its own checks, so an old version does not build. A ticket in building, merging or done is never changed by a plan.

payload.why: It uses the reversible archive and the open-ticket rule of the board controls.
It names each writer's role in WERK_AGENT_ROLE, as that card sets.

payload.title: The link rule, the highlighter and the renderer are three pure files under src/markdown
payload.why: The coverage gate judges only files under the pure-file list, and the web client has no unit seam. A pure module in src/ is tested by bun test, and the browser imports it as it is.
payload.body: src/markdown/reflink.ts holds the rule: refSegments(text, hrefOf) cuts a text into plain strings and links, and codeSpanRef(code, hrefOf) says if a code span is one id. src/markdown/highlight.ts colours json, js, ts and bash. src/markdown/render.ts is the Markdown renderer and returns an HTML string. The map knowledge comes in as one function, hrefOf(id), that returns the card route or undefined, so the rule never imports the client's route code.

payload.why: the highlighter colours the four languages that card names, and never reformats code

payload.title: A code span that holds only a single-word id links, the same as a hashed id
payload.why: The bare-word guard is for prose. A code span that holds nothing but an id is already marked on purpose, so it reads as a reference, not as English.
payload.body: Example: a code span holding only align links when align is a card. A code span with any other text, such as a command, stays code. A bare align in prose stays text.

payload.title: A ghost id links too
payload.why: The map draws a ghost and opens it at its own route, so a link to a ghost lands somewhere.
payload.body: hrefOf knows every node in the graph, ghosts included. A discarded card is gone from the graph, so its id stays text.

payload.title: The write path gives each rule the log as well as the fold
payload.why: A rule that reads the marks, such as rederive, needs the event order, and the write path reads the log one time only.
payload.body: appendRuled calls the rule with the folded state and the events it folded. A rule that needs only the state ignores the second argument. The stale marks are derived from the events, so rederive gets them without a second read of the log.

payload.why: rederive clears the marks that vi-prop derives from the event order

payload.title: The plan proposes each answer through the same checked append as every map verb
payload.why: Which write path does the plan use for its answers? A second path could skip the contract check that every other map write passes.
payload.body: The plan proposes each answer record through appendRuled, the one append that reads the log, folds it, asks the rule, and runs the contract check on the map as the event would leave it. The plan has no append of its own. A refusal from the rule or the check is reported for that record, and the plan exits with an error.

payload.why: Each answer is a node.proposed ghost, staged like every other new card.

payload.title: A restore undoes the whole removal, the moved children too
payload.why: A removal is one event, and its restore is its exact inverse. Then a remove followed by a restore leaves the map as it was, which is the promise that a removal is never final.
payload.body: A restore names the card that the removal named. It brings back every node the removal took: the refines subtree, and the options and sources that only the branch held. With the reparent option, the children that moved up to the grandparent go back under the restored card. A node that went out with another card is restored only through that card, so no card comes back under a parent that is still out. A branch removed earlier stays out when a card above it is removed and restored: each removal is undone on its own.

payload.why: It takes the rule that a removed card is one more event and can come back.

payload.title: Until a removal can be staged, only the person's call removes a card
payload.why: An agent never removes a card directly, but no staged path for a removal exists yet. The actor claim that accept already uses is the nearest check.
payload.body: The remove operation refuses unless the call states that the person asked for it, the same speed bump as accept (#werk-propose-new). A restore needs no claim: it only undoes a removal, and a second remove takes the card out again. A staged removal that the card shows as pending replaces this check when it exists.

payload.why: It uses the same actor claim that an accept from the command line needs.

payload.title: Find lists open and proto cards, and leaves out a postponed card too
payload.why: An agent looks for a card it can work on now. A card in proto is still work. A card reopened as postponed waits, the same as the cards it pauses.
payload.body: The find operation lists real cards, not options or sources, whose status is open or proto, in the refines subtree of one card, breadth first, the card itself included. With no card named, it reads each tree of the map. It leaves out a card with a paused or a stale mark (#pr-wf-paused), and a card whose last reopen was postponed with no status set since. A rejected card is open again and can be worked on, so find lists it. A removed card and a ghost are not in the map, so find never lists them.

payload.why: It takes the paused and stale marks, and that a postponed card waits.

payload.title: The map draws a mark as a pill next to the title, and the status as a stripe on the left
payload.why: Two separate places on the tile let the mark sit on top of the status colour without replacing it.
payload.body: The status colour is a 4px left stripe: open amber, proto blue, decided green. The mark is a pill after the title: stale red (#b3261e), paused grey (#757575). The graph API sends the marks by card id, with their traces, so the browser does not derive them.

payload.title: The card view names the mark it explains: 'Why this card is stale' or 'Why this card is paused'
payload.why: One word per meaning (#pr-wf-naming): a paused card is not stale, so its trace heading must not call it stale.
payload.body: Each trace names the changed card with its title, the reason, the event, the link the mark came along, the card it came through, and the why. The section ends with how the mark clears.

payload.why: takes the rule of one word per meaning
the tile shows only the current mark and status

payload.title: Each build gets its own branch werk-build/<run id> and a worktree folder under the temporary folder
payload.why: Two builds of one ticket must not share a branch, and a stopped build keeps its branch for a person to read.
payload.body: The run id is werk-<ticket>-<time in ms>. The branch is werk-build/<run id>. The worktree folder is under the temporary folder, outside the project, so it never shows in the main checkout. The loop removes the folder at the end of the build, green or stopped. The branch and its pass commits stay.

payload.why: The branch starts at the tip of the main line

payload.title: A build stopped at the cap stays in building, and its retry count is the failed passes that started another pass
payload.why: The ticket card names no column for a stopped build, and a retry is a new pass, not a failed one.
payload.body: Each red pass before the cap appends one ticket.retried event. The last red pass at the cap starts no pass, so it adds no retry: a build stopped at 5 passes shows 4 retries. The ticket stays in building. Only a person moves it back to ready (#werk-board-control).

payload.why: The building column and the retry count are what the board shows

payload.title: A builder pass runs with bypassPermissions, inside its own worktree
payload.why: No person answers a permission prompt in a headless pass, and the builder must run make and git to do its work.
payload.body: The headless runner starts claude -p with --output-format stream-json and --permission-mode bypassPermissions. The cost and the turn count come from the last result event of the stream. A session with no result event has an unknown cost, not zero.

payload.why: The overseer is the safety control for an agent that runs with no person

payload.title: The live channel carries each agent message whole, tagged with its conversation tab
payload.why: A view that reads the raw agent messages can grow (tool lines, approvals) without a change to the server.
payload.body: The server does not interpret the agent's stream. Each message that a conversation's agent writes goes out on the live channel as it arrives, with the tab it belongs to. The browser folds the text pieces of the messages into the reply that it shows. The person's own message is drawn by the browser when it is sent, and is not echoed back.

payload.why: The messages are the stream-json output of the per-conversation claude child that this card defines.

payload.title: The note route refuses a request that a browser page sends
payload.why: The note route writes in the agent's name and sets the person's clipboard. A web page must do neither.
payload.body: A browser names the page's origin on each write request. The note route refuses every request that carries an origin. So only a local process without a page, such as the agent's shell, reaches it. The note is the agent's: its actor is the agent.

payload.title: The pane's agent reads the card wording rules in its system prompt
payload.why: The pane's agent writes cards. It can follow only a rule that it reads.
payload.body: Each conversation's agent starts with a prompt added to its system prompt. The prompt states the wording rules (a card describes its subject and not the session, and names no file, function or line). It also says how the agent reads and writes a card's thread, and that each turn starts with the card the person looks at.

payload.why: The prompt states the wording rules that this card defines.

payload.title: The overseer answers every permission ask of a build pass with allow
payload.why: A build pass runs in its own git worktree on its own branch, and the checks and the grader judge the result. A deny would leave the agent stuck or make it work around the tool, which is the stuck state the overseer exists to end.
payload.body: When the agent's stream has a control_request of subtype can_use_tool, the overseer writes a control_response with behavior allow and the input unchanged to the agent's stdin. It records the act as 'answered' with the tool name in the run record. It does not judge the tool call itself.

payload.why: The fake agent emits a control_request and the test sees the answer and the agent going on, at the command line.

payload.title: The loop classifier reads the last 40 events, and a second looping answer cancels
payload.why: One looping answer can be a false positive on a slow but real fix. One warning gives the agent a chance to change its approach; a second yes shows the warning did not help.
payload.body: Every loop-every ms (5 minutes by default) the overseer starts a fresh classifier agent with role loop-classifier. Its prompt holds the last 40 stream events, each cut to 600 characters. An answer that starts with the word 'looping' is a yes; any other answer, or no answer, is a no. The first yes sends a warning as a user message; the next yes cancels the session, and the next pass hears why. Silence cancels only when no tool call is in flight: a tool_use opens a call, a tool_result with its id closes it.

payload.why: The silence limit and the loop interval are flags, so the fake classifier test sets them to milliseconds.

payload.title: A judge agent ends its reply with one JSON object, and an unreadable reply fails the pass
payload.why: The loop must read a score and a gap without a model. A judgement that did not run must not count as a pass.
payload.body: The grader and each reviewer end their reply with one JSON object. The grader object holds one entry per line: the line id, a score from 1 to 5, and the gap. A reviewer object holds a list of findings: severity, file, line, impact and fix. werk reads the object from the whole reply, the last fenced block, or the text from the first brace to the last brace. A reply with no readable object, a missing line, a score outside 1 to 5, or an unknown severity fails the pass with a problem that names it. The problem goes into the next prompt, the same as a gap. The run record keeps each graded line and every finding of the pass.

payload.why: takes the finding fields and the four severities from the review card
a problem with a reply goes into the next pass prompt like any failure

payload.title: The server answers its API only to a loopback name or its bound host, and only to its own page
payload.why: A chat turn runs an agent with a shell. A page on a rebound DNS name sends a matching Host and Origin, so a check of Origin against Host alone lets any site run code on the machine.
payload.body: Every API call, the live event channel included, must name this server in its Host: a loopback name or the bound host, on the bound port. A call with any other Host is refused. A call that passes then carries no Origin, as a command-line caller does, or the origin of that same allowed host. The map page passes both checks. A page from another site fails one of them, whatever DNS name it resolves.

payload.title: The test agent takes many turns only in the chat role; every other role takes one prompt and exits
payload.why: A chat child and a build agent both read stream-json on stdin, but a chat child lives across turns and a build agent ends after its reply. The test agent must act like each one.
payload.body: When the test agent reads stream-json, the role that werk names decides its life. In the chat role, each user message is one turn: the agent records it, replays the next scripted reply, and waits for the next message, and it ends when its input closes. In any other role, the agent waits for the first user message, replays one reply with its permission asks, and exits with the scripted code. A later user message in that role, such as a warning from the overseer, is not a new turn.

payload.why: takes the role name that werk passes to each agent it launches

payload.title: A judge agent runs with the read tools only and no prompt host
payload.why: The overseer allows every permission ask it gets. A judge must edit nothing, so no ask from a judge may reach the overseer.
payload.body: The grader and the five reviewers run as headless agents under the overseer, the same as a builder pass. A builder gets bypassPermissions and a prompt host, so the overseer answers each ask. A judge gets an allowed-tools list instead: Read, Grep, Glob, and the read verbs of git (diff, log, show). It gets no prompt host, so the agent itself denies every other tool, and the overseer never sees an ask from a judge. The overseer still watches the judge for silence and loops.

payload.why: The reviewers are judges too, and read only the diff.

payload.title: A card with no decider needs the option fact
payload.why: A card without who may be the person's to decide. If the option fact waits for who to be set, a bare card reports three facts, then a fourth after the fix.
payload.body: The options fact applies when who is you or when who is unset. A me or prototype card needs no option. So a card with only a title and a body reports who, basis, options and kill in one refusal, each with its own command (#werk-contract-all-missing). The reason line of the option says that the card has no decider, so it may be yours.

payload.why: It sets when the option fact of #werk-contract-facts applies to a card with no who.

payload.title: werk amend writes a reopen, the changes and a decide in one append, checked as one
payload.why: A decided card is frozen (#map-frozen), so its words and depends_on links change only by an amend. The log must show the amend as a reopen and a decide, and a refused amend must leave nothing.
payload.body: werk amend <id> --summary "..." [--title] [--why] [--body] [--unlink <target>] works only on a decided card. The rule returns a batch: node.reopened with the reason amended and the summary as its why, a retitle, a text edit, an edge.unlinked for the depends_on link, and node.status_set decided that keeps the unchallenged statement. appendRuled folds the whole batch, runs the four facts on the result, and appends every line in one write, or none. The amended reopen marks the next hop stale, like the amend of a review. edge.unlinked is the only way an edge leaves the map, and only an amend writes it.

payload.why: It is the command form of the amend that #map-frozen defines: a reopen and a decide in one step.
The batch goes through the one shared write path and its single contract check.

payload.title: Only a caller on the same machine can write through the server or start a chat turn
