payload.why: Host and Origin are headers that any caller on the network can forge. A chat turn runs an agent with a shell, so a write must be tied to where the connection comes from, not to what it claims.
payload.body: The server can bind to a public address so that another machine can read the map. A read stays open to such a caller. A write, the chat turn among them, is refused unless the connection comes from this machine. A bind to a public address therefore shares the picture and never the agent's shell or the log.

payload.why: It adds a peer check on top of the Host and Origin check, which alone a remote caller can forge.

payload.title: The held-out set of a subtree is a folder beside the log, with one steps file per ticket and the bound tests
payload.why: The author's answer, the binder's tests and the run results need one place outside every worktree, keyed by the subtree that a gate closes.
payload.body: The set of subtree <root> lives in heldout/<root>/ beside the decision log: steps-<ticket>.json holds the steps the program read from the author's answer, each with the id <ticket>.<n>, and tests/ holds the binder's tests, copied out of .werk-heldout/ after each bind. heldout/ holds a .gitignore of '*', so the set never enters a commit, and so never enters a worktree that branches off the main line. Each held-out run appends one heldout.ran event to the board log: the subtree, the commit it ran on, and green, red or not run per step id. The event holds no step text. The output of each test goes to heldout/<root>/runs/, for a person.

payload.why: the store under .werk/heldout/<run>/ and the program that stores the author's answer

payload.title: werk heldout <subtree> runs the held-out set on the main tip; werk gate <subtree> opens G2 only on a fresh, all-green run
payload.why: The run costs a binder agent, and the gate only reads, so the two stay separate verbs, and the gate can refuse a stale run.
payload.body: werk heldout <subtree-id> takes the steps of the subtree's done tickets, makes a temporary detached worktree at the main tip, copies the stored tests into .werk-heldout/, starts the binder there, voids its report when it changed a file outside .werk-heldout/, runs each bound command, and records the result. It exits 1 when a step is not green. werk gate <subtree-id> reads the last heldout.ran event of the subtree. It refuses, and exits 1, when there is none, when its commit is not the main tip, when the set has a step the run did not cover, when a step is red or not run, or when a live ticket of the subtree is not done. Otherwise it appends gate.opened for G2 and exits 0: G2 then waits for the person (approve is a later ticket).

payload.why: the G2 refusal while a held-out step is red on the merged tree
a not-run step is not green, so the gate waits for it

payload.title: Every builder of a subtree gets the red steps of the subtree's last held-out run, word for word, in its own prompt section
payload.why: Before the merge loop files follow-up tickets, the builders that run on top of the red main line are the ones that can fix it.
payload.body: At each pass, the builder loop reads the last heldout.ran event of the ticket's subtree. Each red step goes into the prompt under '## Held-out steps that fail on the main line', as the text the author wrote. A not-run step, the test code, the test output and the other steps never go in. The merge loop later narrows this to the follow-up ticket of the red step.

payload.why: the builder gets the failed step's text, not the test code

payload.title: A ticket restore is its own board event, and it puts the ticket back in the column it left
payload.why: The archive keeps the ticket's column and blocking reason, so a restore that only ends the archive undoes it exactly. A ticket.planned event would also work, but the log would then say 'planned' for a person's restore.
payload.body: werk ticket restore <number> appends ticket.restored with the ticket number to the board log. The fold ends the archive and keeps every other field, so the ticket is back in ready or in blocked with its old reason. A restore of a ticket that is not archived, or a number not on the board, refuses with exit 1 and appends nothing. The actor is the agent unless the call says --actor you, as in the map verbs. v0 builds only the restore subverb of werk ticket; list, move, archive and import wait for their own tickets.

payload.why: It is the restore that st-plan-archive names for a ticket the plan archived.
It is the reversible archive of the board controls, undone from the command line by an agent.

payload.title: A turn's first line starts with the open card's id and its title
payload.why: The agent must read the subject before the message, and a line that starts with the id is the same shape whether the card exists, is gone, or no card is open.
payload.body:
Every turn from the composer starts with one line, then a blank line, then the person's text, then one line per pasted image with the path of its saved file.

The line starts with the open card's id after a #, then the card's title in quotes. An id the map does not know still starts the line, and the line says the map has no such card. With no card open, the line says that the person looks at the whole map.

The agent's instructions say that 'this card' means the card on that line, unless the person names another id.

payload.title: The note route refuses every request that comes from a page
payload.why: The browser never calls the note route. A page that can call it could write to the log without the person, so the route enforces the rule instead of trusting it.
payload.body:
A request sent by a page carries its origin. The note route refuses any request with an origin, from this server's own page too. A request from a command line or a script carries none, and the route writes one note by the agent on the named card.

The note is written first. The clipboard copy comes after it, and a machine with no clipboard command still gets the note.

payload.why: Every turn names the card of its conversation, so the agent never follows the wrong subject.
A page writes to the log only through the person's own controls, and the note route is not one of them.

payload.title: A pure file's coverage counts only the lines its own test file hits
payload.why: render.test.ts loads reflink.ts, highlight.ts and escape.ts, so deleting reflink.test.ts left reflink.ts at 100% and the gate could not see the lost tests.
payload.body:
The coverage target runs each listed pure file's own test file, the file next to it named <name>.test.ts, alone with coverage on. The gate judges the pure file only on the lines that run hit. Lines that a caller's test hits do not count. A listed pure file with no own test file counts as 0%, and the gate names the missing test file.

The coverage target no longer runs the whole suite. make test runs it. The per-file runs write one combined lcov report, and the existing gate reads it unchanged.

payload.why: It keeps the per-file 90% gate and its lcov input, and narrows which test may hit a pure file's lines.

payload.title: Each message of a reply names the turn it belongs to
payload.why: A person can send a turn while a reply still runs. With no turn named, the rest of the running reply joins the new turn, and the running turn never ends.
payload.body: The browser names each turn when it sends it. The agent runs the turns of a conversation one after the other and ends each with one result, so the server keeps the turns that are sent and not yet ended in order. Each message of the agent belongs to the oldest of them, and its result moves on to the next. The live channel carries the turn with each message, and the pane adds the message to that turn. When the agent exits, each turn that it did not end gets the exit, so no turn waits forever. A message for a turn the pane did not send, such as after a reload, starts a new turn in the pane.

payload.title: The server answers its API only to a request that names it as the host
payload.why: The chat starts an agent that edits files and runs commands on the person's machine. A page that a DNS rebinding points at the server sends its own name as the host and a matching origin, so an origin check alone lets any website start the agent and read the reply.
payload.body: The server keeps a list of the host names that name it: the loopback names and the host it serves on, each with its port. A request to the API whose host is not on the list is refused, and so is a request from a page whose origin is not the host it was sent to. This holds for every API route, the live channel too, because the live channel carries the agent's transcript. A tool on the machine sends no origin. The note route is for such a tool alone and refuses any page. A person who opens the map through another name, such as a LAN address, is refused.

payload.title: A pure file's unit tests live in its own test file, and shared fixtures live in src/test
payload.why: With the own-test gate, fold.ts fell to 78.9% because its remove and restore tests sat in remove.test.ts, and parse.ts and failure.ts had no own test file at all.
payload.body: A test that calls only one pure file goes in that file's <name>.test.ts. A test that mixes files (fold with staleness, or with rules) stays in the test file of the verb it checks. A fixture two test files share moves to src/test, as removalTree moved to src/test/map-events.ts. Tests move; none is deleted, so the suite keeps every assertion.

payload.why: It takes the rule that only a file's own test file counts for its coverage, and says where tests must sit to meet it.

payload.title: The step author runs with no tools, beside pass 1, in the held-out store, and the build waits for it before it ends
payload.why: An author that can read the code writes steps that match the code, not the ticket. An author that runs after the build would leave the first held-out run with no steps.
payload.body: When the builder loop starts a ticket that has a subtree, it starts the step author at the same time, with the ticket brief and its stories only. The author runs in heldout/<root>/, not in the worktree, and gets no tool, so it cannot read the code or write a file. The program reads the steps from its reply and writes steps-<ticket>.json. A ticket that has a steps file gets no second author. A ticket with no subtree gets no author. The loop waits for the author after the last pass, so a build never ends with its steps still in flight.

payload.why: the author writes its steps into the store folder that card defines
the author starts when the builder starts, as validate runs beside build

payload.title: A red held-out run files one follow-up ticket per ticket whose steps went red, and no second one while it is open
payload.why: Grouping the red steps by the ticket they came from gives each follow-up the cites, touches and checks of the work it repairs, and an open follow-up already owns its steps, so a later merge must not file the same break again.
payload.body: After a merge, the merge loop groups the red steps of the held-out run by the ticket that each step id names. Each group whose steps no open follow-up covers yet becomes one new ticket in ready: the next free ticket number, the subtree of the run, the cites, touches and checks of the step's ticket, and a brief that quotes each red step word for word. A heldout.followup board event records the follow-up number, the done ticket whose merge the run followed, and the step ids it covers. A step stays covered while its follow-up is not done.

payload.why: a red step files a follow-up and the merge stands, as this card decides
the follow-up ticket appears in ready and the badge sits on the merged done ticket

payload.title: The held-out badge on a done ticket shows while its follow-up ticket is not done
payload.why: The badge marks a known break. When the follow-up that fixes it is merged, the break is gone from the main line, so a badge that stayed would show a break that is not there.
payload.body: The board fold gives each ticket the follow-up tickets filed after its merge. The card and the drawer metadata show one badge per follow-up that is not done yet, each a link to that follow-up ticket. A done follow-up drops its badge. The log keeps the heldout.followup event either way.

payload.why: the heldout.followup event that names the done ticket and its follow-up

payload.title: A builder session is a file pair per ticket in .werk/sessions, and the agent's pid decides if it runs
payload.why: The build runs in another process than the server, so the pulse and the live log need a place both can read. A board event per agent line would flood the append-only board log.
payload.body: Each builder pass writes .werk/sessions/<ticket>.json (the agent pid, the run, the pass, and live true or false) and .werk/sessions/<ticket>.jsonl (one line per stream event or overseer act, with its time). A new pass empties both. The runner sets live false the moment the agent exits. The server counts a session as running only while live is true and the pid is alive, so a session whose process was killed by hand stops pulsing too. The server watches the folder and pushes a session event on the event channel, so the map does not refetch on each agent line. The board shows the pulse and the preview only for a ticket in building; the files stay, and nothing shows them once the ticket leaves building.

payload.why: It writes overseer acts into the session log and keeps a time on each line, as the preview lines that card sets need.

payload.title: The scheduler compares touches names trimmed and in lower case
payload.why: A person or a planner writes the same module as 'Board' in one ticket and 'board ' in another. An exact compare would let the two build at the same time.
payload.body: Before the compare, each touches name loses its outer spaces and goes to lower case. Nothing else changes: no stemming, no synonyms, no agent. Two names match only when they are then the same string.

payload.title: A stop of the run starts no new build, and lets the running builds end
payload.why: With up to 3 builds at once, a stuck ticket or a cap stop can come while other builds still run. Killing them throws away paid passes.
payload.body: The first stop reason wins. After it, the scheduler starts nothing. Each running build ends; a green one still goes through the merge queue. When the main line could not move, nothing more merges, and a green build waits in merging so a restart merges it. The cap of parallel builds is the run verb flag --parallel, default 3.

payload.title: A pass that goes green moves its ticket from building to merging
payload.why: A pass with only MEDIUM and LOW findings is green, so the ticket must leave building. The builder loop is the one step that knows the pass is green.
payload.body: When the checks, the grader and the review all pass, the builder loop appends a ticket.moved event to merging at the end of the build. A ticket that stops at the retry cap stays in building. Each pass also appends one ticket.pass event with its number, whether it went green, and the reason the overseer cancelled its agent, or null. So the board log shows a silence cancel and the pass after it.

payload.why: takes the building and merging columns and the rule that the loop moves a ticket right

payload.title: A card added with no status is open
payload.why: A new card is in the map to be worked on. With no status, show prints none, find skips it, and the rollup does not count it as open.
payload.body: The add verb gives a card with no --status flag the status open. An option, a source and an excerpt get no default status, because the contract and the rollup read status only on cards.

payload.why: the add verb and its --status flag

payload.title: A card id may carry the hash sign on the command line
payload.why: Cards and tickets write ids as #id. An agent that copies #auth into a command must name the same card, not get no-node.
payload.body: Each positional operand, and the value of --parent, --unlink and --root, loses one leading #. Other flag values, such as a title, keep it.

payload.title: A stopped ticket waits in ready until a person triggers it
payload.why: A stop means the build went the wrong way. If the scheduler started the ticket again at once, the stop would undo nothing.
payload.body: A drag of a building ticket into ready appends a stopped event. The merge loop stops the builder of that ticket and keeps its branch. The ticket then waits in ready. The scheduler skips it when it picks ready tickets, so the run does not start it again. Only a trigger by a person starts it again in the same run: the trigger icon or a drag into building. A run whose open tickets are all stopped or blocked ends.

payload.why: the scheduler that picks ready tickets is the one that skips a stopped ticket

payload.title: The board page draws each control; the server rules on it, and a refusal shows as an alert
payload.why: One set of rules in the server keeps the page and the API in step. The page draws a control only where the rule can allow it.
payload.body: Every column takes a drop, and the server rules on it: a drop into merging or done comes back as the refusal text in an alert. Only ready and building tickets can be dragged. A drop on a ready ticket puts the dragged ticket just before it. The trigger icon shows only on a ready ticket whose plan run is active. Archive shows only on a ready or blocked ticket and opens a confirmation dialog that says the ticket is never deleted for good and an agent can restore it; a cancel posts nothing. The start button shows for each plan run that is not active.

payload.why: each control appends an event through the server and never moves a ticket in the page

payload.title: One board reply carries the live runs and the running builder sessions
payload.why: The start control and the trigger icon need to know which runs are active, and the pulse needs to know which builders run. Two replies could disagree about the same moment.
payload.body: The board read returns the fold of the board log with two filters on it. Its runs list holds only the runs whose process still runs, so a dead run shows its start control again. Its running list holds the tickets whose builder session runs now. The page draws the start control and the trigger icon from the first list, and the pulse and the live log from the second. A builder pass takes both the stop signal of a person's drag and the session recorder.

payload.why: the running list and the pulse come from the builder session files

patch.body:
Two sources show a tool call that is still running:

1. The tool-call stream. A call that has started and has no result yet is in flight. The overseer knows the tool, its input, and its start time.
2. The operating system. A shell call is a process tree. For each process the overseer reads the CPU time, the state, the output written, and the open files and network connections.

Together they tell working from frozen:

| CPU time | Output | Open connections | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| grows | any | any | working |
| flat | grows | any | working |
| flat | flat | one, to a host that does not answer | frozen on I/O |
| flat | flat | none | frozen on a wait that never ends, such as a promise that never resolves |

"Flat" means no change for 60 seconds, the same starting value as #lp-overseer-silence. The first runs show whether it needs to change.

A frozen call is cancelled. The agent gets the cancel as the call's result, with the evidence, and continues.

The watch covers every agent session that can run a tool, not only the builder: the grader, the reviewers, and the held-out binder (#lp-heldout-binder) too. The binder is the session that needs it most. It runs the whole held-out suite, often end-to-end browser tests, and that run prints nothing for minutes. Without the watch, the silence limit cancels it mid-run and every step comes back not run.

A test runner with a per-test timeout catches most frozen tests first. The overseer catches what the runner does not: a hang outside any test, a runner with no timeout, or a command that is not a test.

The binder reads the merged code, finds the elements each step names, and writes the tests for the project's stack.

Two rules.

1. The binder cannot change step text. It only maps each step to UI actions and assertions.
2. The binder does not make a test pass. When a step fails, it records the failure and stops. It fixes only its own errors, for example a typo in a locator.

"Element not found" can be a binder error or a missing feature. The binder reports which one it thinks it is, and the coordinator reads that report.

Example of what rule 2 stops: search does not update live. A binder that may make tests pass adds a page reload before the search. The test passes and the feature is still wrong.

Rule 2 is enforced after the session, not trusted: a binder that changed any file outside its own test directory has fitted the product to the test, and its whole report is void. Everything the binder and its test runner write inside that directory is its own, whatever the file names — screenshots, traces and result folders included. A path is compared as stored, never as a display form that quotes or escapes unusual characters, or the binder's own output reads as a change to the product and voids a correct report.

Accepted risk: a binder writes a wrong test, and a correct feature fails. This is fixed when it happens, not prevented.

payload.title: Only the page the server served may make a request that changes state or starts an agent
payload.why: A chat request starts an agent that edits files and runs shell commands without asking. Whoever can send that request can run code on the person's machine.
payload.body:
The server makes a random secret at each start and puts it into the page it serves. Every request that starts an agent turn, writes to the log, or moves a ticket must carry that secret, or the server refuses it. A web page from another site cannot read the served page, so it cannot learn the secret, whether it comes by a cross-site request or by DNS rebinding. Another machine on the network cannot learn it either.

The server also refuses a request whose Host is not a loopback name while it listens on loopback only. This closes DNS rebinding even before the secret is checked.

The secret never goes into a log, a transcript, or the environment of the agent the server starts, because that agent can read all three.

A read-only request needs no secret: it changes nothing and starts nothing. A test or a tool that makes a changing request reads the secret the same way the page does.

payload.title: Compare the Origin header with the Host header
payload.why_not: Both headers come from the sender. A DNS rebinding page sends a matching pair, and a request from another machine can send no Origin at all.

payload.title: Listen on loopback only and refuse a Host that is not a loopback name, with no secret
payload.why_not: It stops other sites and other machines, but not another program or another user on the same machine, which can still start an agent with write tools. It also forbids ever opening the map from another device.

payload.title: A secret per start, with no Host check
payload.why_not: The secret alone closes every known path, but a single mistake in where the secret is checked reopens all of them. The Host check costs one comparison and catches DNS rebinding on its own.

payload.why: One server per .werk directory means one secret per running map, so a page always talks to the server that served it.

payload.title: A builder that hits a decision no card makes proposes it, builds on the proposal, and the person rules after the fact
payload.why: A gap in the map looks like a failing ticket. The builder fixes one symptom per pass, the reviewer finds the next, and the cap parks the ticket and everything that needs it until a person wakes up.
payload.body:
The gap shows in two ways. The next pass names the cause of the last failure as a spec gap (#ms-fail-cause). Or the grader or the reviewers raise findings in the same area in two passes in a row, and no cited card answers the question behind them.

Then the next pass is a decision pass, not another fix. The builder states the question, picks an answer by a fixed guideline, and proposes it as a card: the question as its title, the answer and its reason, the options it weighed and why it rejected each, and what it depends on. The card is an ordinary proposal (#werk-propose-new), who decides is the person, and it is never accepted by an agent.

The guideline picks the answer that is easiest to undo and safest when wrong: deny by default, the least privilege that makes the ticket work, the smallest interface, no data deleted. When two answers are equally safe, the one that changes the fewest decided cards wins.

From that pass on, the ticket cites the proposal, and the grader and the reviewers judge the ticket against it as if it were decided. The ticket may merge on it, so the tickets that need it keep building.

The person rules on the proposal later. An accept leaves everything as it is. A discard, or an edit that changes the answer, files a follow-up ticket for every merged ticket that cited it, the same way a changed card blocks an open ticket (#st-ticket-watch). The run's end report lists every proposal the builders made, first.

A builder that still cannot reach green after its decision pass is parked as before (#st-build-stuck-park).

payload.title: Raise the retry cap
payload.why_not: The chase does not converge: each pass closes one hole and the reviewer finds the next. More passes cost more and end in the same park.

payload.title: Park the ticket at the first sign of a gap and ask the person
payload.why_not: It saves passes, but the ticket and everything that needs it still wait until the person reads the question.

payload.title: Propose the card and park only the ticket that raised it
payload.why_not: Nothing merges on an unaccepted decision, but the ticket and every ticket that needs it still wait until morning, which is the loss this card exists to remove.

payload.why: The spec-gap cause the next pass names is one of the two triggers.
The builder's decision enters the map only as a proposal that the person accepts or discards.
A discard or a changed answer reaches the merged tickets the same way a changed cited card reaches an open one.
A ticket still red after its decision pass falls back to the park.

payload.title: A request that changes state or starts an agent needs the synchronizer token, and the Host must be a loopback name
payload.why: A chat request starts an agent that edits files and runs shell commands without asking. Whoever can send that request can run code on the person's machine.
payload.body:
The server uses the synchronizer token pattern from the OWASP guidance on cross-site request forgery. It makes a random token at each start and puts it into the page it serves. Every request that starts an agent turn, writes to the log, or moves a ticket must carry the token, or the server refuses it. A page from another site cannot read the served page, so it cannot learn the token, by a cross-site request or by DNS rebinding. Another machine on the network cannot learn it either.

Host header validation closes DNS rebinding a second time: while the server listens on loopback only, it refuses a request whose Host is not a loopback name.

The token never goes into a log, a transcript, or the environment of the agent the server starts, because that agent can read all three.

A read-only request needs no token: it changes nothing and starts nothing. A test or a tool that makes a changing request reads the token the same way the page does.

payload.title: Compare the Origin header with the Host header
payload.why_not: Both headers come from the sender. A DNS rebinding page sends a matching pair, and a request from another machine can send no Origin at all.

payload.title: Listen on loopback only and validate the Host header, with no token
payload.why_not: It stops other sites and other machines, but not another program or another user on the same machine, which can still start an agent with write tools. It also forbids ever opening the map from another device.

payload.title: The synchronizer token alone, with no Host validation
payload.why_not: The token alone closes every known path, but a single route that forgets to check it reopens all of them. Host validation costs one comparison and catches DNS rebinding on its own.

payload.why: One server per .werk directory means one token per running map, so a page always talks to the server that served it.

criterion.metric: share of builder proposals from a decision pass that the person discards or changes

patch.body:
- **Marks.** One dot per finished ticket, in build order. Its value is the ticket's effort adjusted for the ticket's size (#lp-trend-size), so a run of large tickets does not read as a rise.
- **Lines.** The reference band over the base window, the alert line, and the median of the current window.
- **Outlier.** A dot above the band, and a stronger colour for a dot above twice the band's top. The alert line compares two window medians and often lies inside the band, so it does not mark a single dot.
- **Drill-down.** A dot opens its ticket, its passes, and their transcripts.

![Effort per ticket: dots per ticket, base band, alert line, current median](/api/image?name=vi-flow-ms-effort.png)

criterion.text: An edit to a route handler is saved, and the next request after the hot reload still runs the old handler.
A hot reload crashes the server, or leaves it unable to answer requests.

payload.text: Decided. Kill criteria 1 and 2 are manual tests; either one firing falls back to opt0. No depends_on: the only basis is the parent #werk-hmr, and the lineage rule forbids that edge, so --no-basis is on record.

payload.title: Tests never start the real agent or write to the real map
payload.why: A test that starts an agent must find the fake one, and a test must never write to a real project's log. Editing the search list for programs (PATH) in the test setup does not guarantee either, because Bun's process spawn, program lookup and shell read the environment the test process started with.
payload.body:
A unit test run isolates every test from the machine it runs on. Two things must not leak in. The first is the real agent: starting it costs money and time, and its answers change between runs. The second is the real project log: a test must never write to the map that a person is working in.

The run sets this up once, before the first test. It removes every variable that points at a real project, so a test has no way to reach the real log. It also puts the fake agent first in the program search list (the PATH variable), so a program lookup for the agent finds the fake before the real one.

Changing PATH inside the running test process is not enough. Bun's process spawn, its program lookup and its shell read the environment that the test process started with, not the environment as the setup edited it. A test that starts an agent without passing an environment of its own would still find the real agent. So the run also makes spawn, program lookup and the shell default to the cleaned environment. A process started by a test harness inherits the same cleaned environment.

The browser test server checks the same rule at start-up and refuses to start when the fake agent is not first in the search list. A leak then fails at once, not later as a surprise bill or a changed map.

payload.title: Only edit PATH in the test setup
payload.why_not: The edit changes the environment of the running test process. Bun's spawn, program lookup and shell still read the environment the process started with, so a test that starts an agent with no explicit environment can find the real agent. The leak is silent until a test costs money or changes a real log.

payload.why: cleans the environment of the bun test runner that #werk-test-runner chooses, whose spawn defaults are the gap

criterion.text: A test run starts the real agent, or writes to a real project's log, although the run cleaned the environment.

patch.body:
- **Marks.** One line per stage, cost in dollars per point. A point is one hour, six hours, a day or a week, depending on the period.
- **Legend.** On the right of the chart, one line per stage with its cost over the period. A click hides or shows that stage. A command-click shows only that stage, and a second command-click on it shows every stage but it. The legend is always open.
- **Period.** A selector sets how far back the chart looks: the last 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days, or all. A shorter period uses narrower points, so the same cost reads at a finer grain.
- **Outlier.** A line whose last point is above its own band is drawn heavier. The band is the median to the 90th percentile of the line's earlier points, once it has ten of them.
- **Drill-down.** A point opens the tickets or plan turns of that stage in that point's time span.

![Stage cost: one line per stage by week](/api/image?name=vi-flow-ms-stage-cost.png)

payload.text: Prototype built in the Flow tab: legend on the right with hide, solo and invert; period selector with finer grain for shorter periods.

payload.title: `werk ticket-check` prints one line per failure and exits 0, 1 or 2
payload.why: One fixed line form lets a person and an agent read a failure by ticket and field, and the exit code is the verdict (#lp-checks).
payload.body:
Form: `werk ticket-check <folder> --root <card-id> --spec <file>`

**Inputs.** The verb reads every `.md` file in the folder, the decided cards under `--root`, and the story numbers in the spec. The decided cards are the root and its `refines` descendants at any depth with status decided. A ghost does not count. The spec's stories are the numbered lines under its `User stories` heading, up to the next heading of the same level or higher.

**Output.** One line per failure:

```
<ticket file>: <check>: <field>: <message>
```

A cards-cited or stories failure names no ticket, so its ticket part is `ticket set`. A last line counts the tickets, the own-check failures, all failures, the decided cards and the stories.

**Exit code.**

```
0  nothing fails
1  a check fails
2  malformed call: missing flag, missing folder or spec,
   a spec with no `User stories` heading, or a root not in the map
```

payload.why: The form gives the operation that #werk-ticket-check-verb defines.
The check names in each failure line are the eight own-check names.
The ticket part of each failure line follows the rule that only the blocked_by check names tickets.

payload.title: The ticket checks run on their own as one operation with one verdict
payload.why: A planner, a person and an agent that edits a ticket all need to run the same checks without a plan, and read the result as one verdict plus the place of each failure.
payload.body:
One operation runs every ticket check on a folder of tickets: the own checks on each ticket (#st-ticket-own-checks) and the set checks on the whole set (#st-ticket-set-checks). It needs the folder, the decided cards the tickets may cite, and the spec whose stories they deliver.

Each failure names its ticket, the check and the field. A set failure that no ticket owns names the set. The reader finds the place to fix without reading the rest of the output.

The verdict is the exit code, as for every check (#lp-checks). A pass, a failed check and a malformed call are three different outcomes, so a call that could not run the checks never reads as a pass.

The operation has no tool of its own in this card. Which program carries it is decided elsewhere.

payload.why: The operation runs these checks on each ticket.
The operation runs these checks on the whole set. The target is stale now; the card was written with that in hand.
The verdict is the exit code of one command.
The form is the command line that carries this operation: its failure line, and its three exit codes.

criterion.text: An agent or a person runs the operation on a failing ticket set and cannot find the ticket and field to fix from the failure lines alone, or a call that could not run the checks exits 0.
A planner, a person or an agent runs the operation and cannot tell a pass from a call that could not run the checks, or cannot find the ticket and field of a failure.

payload.title: A ticket restore is its own board event, and it puts the ticket back in the column it left
payload.why: The archive keeps the ticket's column and blocking reason, so a restore that only ends the archive undoes it exactly. A planned event would also work, but the log would then say planned for a person's restore.
payload.body:
A restore is its own event on the board log, with the ticket number. The fold of the log ends the archive and keeps every other field, so the ticket is back in ready, or in blocked with its old reason.

A restore of a ticket that is not archived, or of a number not on the board, is refused and appends nothing. The event records who restored it, an agent or a person, as every map action does.

payload.title: `werk ticket restore <number>` puts one archived ticket back where it was
payload.why: One verb gives an agent and a person the restore that #st-ticket-restore defines, and a refusal leaves the board log unchanged.
payload.body:
Form: `werk ticket restore <number> [--actor you]`

**Effect.** It appends one restore event with the ticket number to the board log. The ticket returns to the column it left, with its old blocking reason.

**Refusal.** A ticket that is not archived, or a number not on the board, exits 1 and appends nothing.

**Actor.** The actor is the agent unless the call says `--actor you`, as in the map verbs.

**Scope.** `restore` is the only subverb of `werk ticket` that exists. Listing, moving, archiving and importing a ticket have no verb yet.

payload.why: The verb carries the restore that this card defines: its event, its refusals and its actor.

criterion.text: A restored ticket does not return to the column it left, or loses its blocking reason, or a refused restore appends to the board log.
An agent or a person runs the verb on an archived ticket and it does not return to its old column, or a refused call exits 0 or appends to the board log.

payload.title: A test gets the runtime globals its own code expects, and no test changes what another kind of test sees
payload.why: Server code and client component code run in one test process but expect different globals, so a setup made for one kind of test can break the other.
payload.body: A project can hold code that expects different runtime environments. Server code expects the runtime'"s

payload.title: A test gets the runtime globals its own code expects, and no test changes what another kind of test sees
payload.why: Server code and client component code run in one test process but expect different globals, so a setup made for one kind of test can break the other.
payload.body:
A project can hold code that expects different runtime environments. Server code expects the own network, stream and timer functions of the runtime. Client component code expects a browser-like environment. One test run may hold both kinds of test in one process.

Two rules keep them apart. A test sees the globals its own code expects. A setup that adds an environment for one kind of test puts back whatever it replaced for the other kind, and a test that builds something in that environment removes it when it ends.

How a project meets the rules depends on its stack. A card for the stack names the environment and when it is set up (see #werk-test-dom for werk). This card holds only the rule that every such choice must meet.

payload.title: Component tests share one DOM for the whole unit run
payload.why: Server tests and React component tests run in one process and need different globals, and React finds a DOM only if one exists when it first loads.
payload.body:
This is the way werk meets #werk-test-globals. One DOM window is registered before any test file loads, so React finds a DOM when it first loads. The network, stream and timer globals of the runtime are put back after the registration, so a server test in the same run uses the real network function, not the one of the DOM. Each component test unmounts what it rendered.

The test runner and the client framework that this rests on are chosen in #werk-test-runner.

payload.title: Register a DOM per component test file and remove it after the file
payload.why_not: React finds a DOM only when it first loads in the process. A DOM registered later, or removed and registered again for each file, is not the one React already holds, so only the first file would be safe. The shared DOM also costs one registration, not one per file.

payload.why: The single shared DOM is the way werk meets the rule that each test sees its own globals.
The DOM is registered for the bun test runner that #werk-test-runner chooses, with React from the same card.
The rule is about the globals of tests that share one process, as they do under the one in-process runner.

criterion.text: A component test fails because React found no DOM, or a server test in the same run uses the network function of the DOM, or one component test sees what another left rendered.

patch.body:
A stop is a place where the build cannot go on until a person acts. Chat-pane questions are not stops; they are measured on their own (#ms-outcome-interv-chat).

- **Kinds of stop.** A gate that waits for a person to pass it. A ticket blocked until a person unblocks it. A merge loop that stopped as stuck. A build that reached its retry cap. A session the overseer stopped for silence or looping. Each kind is read from the event the log already holds for it.
- **Length of a wait.** From the stop to the next event that moves the work on. The log does not say who acted, so the panel reports the length of the stop, not a person's response time.
- **Marks.** One dot per stop, one row per kind, at the length of the wait. The median of the current window per row. A stop still open counts up to now.
- **Outlier.** A dot above its row's band is coloured. A row with too few stops says how many more it needs.
- **Drill-down.** A dot opens the ticket, run or gate where the build stopped, with the reason the log holds.

payload.text: Reworded: stops of the build, not chat-pane waits. Kinds come from events the log already holds. Gate waits have no events yet.

payload.title: The client lives in its own folder beside the server code, and Vite builds it into a separate output folder
payload.why: The server is TypeScript that Bun runs directly. The client is code that Vite transforms. One folder per runtime keeps each tool on the files it owns.
payload.body:
The client source sits in a folder of its own at the top of the repository, apart from the server source. The sketch labels folders by role. The card fixes the layout, not the folder names.

**Layout**

```
repo/
├── <server folder>/     TypeScript that Bun runs as it is
├── <client folder>/     one HTML page + one React root component
│                        (Vite and its React plugin transform these)
├── <output folder>/     the built client, not committed
├── <config>             one Vite config, at the top, with absolute paths
└── package.json
```

**Who touches which folder**

```
 <server folder>/                      <client folder>/
        │                                    │
        │ Bun runs it directly               │ Vite transforms it
        │ (no build step)                    │ (JSX -> JS, Fast Refresh)
        ▼                                    ▼
   Bun server process ──── dev ───────▶ Vite in middleware mode,
        │                               inside the same process
        │                                    │
        │                                    │ build step
        │                                    ▼
        │                              <output folder>/
        ▼
   one port: the API, the live stream, and the client
```

In dev, the Bun server asks Vite for each client file and nothing is written to disk (see #werk-client-reload). The build step is the only writer of the output folder.

**Config and types.** Vite reads one config at the top of the repository. The config gives absolute paths, so the server can start Vite from any project directory. The type check covers the client and the server in one run, with JSX compiled by the React automatic runtime.

**Dependencies.** React is a runtime dependency. Vite and its React plugin are build tools, so they are development dependencies until the server ticket starts Vite in middleware mode.

payload.why: The dev half of the flow, with Vite inside the server process, is the rule this card draws.

patch.body:
A stop is a place where the build cannot go on until a person acts. Chat-pane questions are not stops; they are measured on their own (#ms-outcome-interv-chat).

- **Kinds of stop.** A gate that waits for a person to pass it. A ticket blocked until it is unblocked, and a ticket set that failed the blocked-by check. A merge loop that stopped as stuck. A ticket red or conflicted on the main line. A build that reached its retry cap. Each kind is read from the event the log already holds for it.
- **Length of a wait.** From the stop to the next event that moves the work on. The log does not say who acted, so the panel reports the length of the stop, not a person's response time. A stop still open counts up to now and is drawn as a ring.
- **Marks.** One dot per stop, one row per kind, at the length of the wait on a log axis, because a stop lasts minutes or days. The median of the current window per row.
- **Outlier.** A dot above its row's band is amber, and a dot above 1.5 times the band's top is red. A row with too few stops says how many more it needs.
- **Drill-down.** A dot opens the ticket, run or gate where the build stopped, with the reason the log holds.

The kinds in the image are an earlier set. The marks, the band and the median follow the image.

![Waits per kind of stop, coloured against the band](/api/image?name=vi-flow-ms-waits.png)

payload.text: Prototype built in the Flow tab from the board and pipeline logs. Image restored; its row kinds are the earlier set.

criterion.text: During development, hot reload does not work well for the client or for the server, with this layout.
The architecture gets complex: the layout needs extra configuration, folders or build steps to keep working.
Code that the client and the server both need cannot be shared easily across the two folders.
Code in the v0 directory needs something from the prototype, or a check of v0 only works when it runs from outside the v0 directory.
Copying the v0 directory into a new repository is not enough to build and check it there.

payload.why: A test at the command line or in the browser needs a map that holds only the cards its scenario names, so each one runs on a fresh project.

criterion.text: A test reads a card that another test wrote, or a test directory or server is still there after the test ends, including after a failed test.

payload.title: Each test writes to its own copy of every store, removed when the test ends
payload.why: A test that shares a store with another test reads what that test wrote, so its result depends on the order of the run. A copy left behind fills the disk.
payload.body:
A store is anything a test writes that lasts after the write: files, a database, a log. Before a test writes to one, the harness gives the test a fresh, empty copy, and the test puts in exactly the data its scenario names. When the test ends, the harness removes the copy and stops anything that serves it, also when the test fails.

How a project makes a fresh copy depends on what its store is (see #werk-base-test-project for werk).

payload.title: A test never reaches a real external service or the real data of the person who runs it
payload.why: A real service costs money and time and answers differently on each run, and a write to real data damages the work of the person who runs the tests.
payload.body:
Each external service that a test could start or call is replaced by a fake with fixed answers. Every setting that points at real data is removed before the first test. The guard covers every process a test starts, not only the test process, because a child process can inherit the settings of the shell that started the run. A harness that cannot confirm the fake is in place refuses to start.

How a project replaces its services depends on its runtime (see #werk-test-env for werk).

criterion.text: Two tests pass alone and fail together, or a store copy is still there after a test ends.
A test run calls a real external service, or writes to real data of the person who runs it.

payload.why: The fake agent first on PATH and the cleaned environment for every spawned process are how werk meets the rule on Bun.

payload.title: Each werk test runs on a fresh project directory with an empty map

patch.body:
The test harness gives a command-line test, a server test and a browser test the same thing: a fresh directory with a git repository and an empty map. The test writes its map with werk commands and reads the exit code and output of each command. A browser test serves that map on a port of its own. The harness removes the directory and stops the server when the scope of the test ends.

The map of a project is the fold of its own log (see #pr-log), so a fresh project is a fresh map.
patch.why: In werk the store a test writes is a project: a directory with a git repository and a map log. So the fresh copy that #werk-test-store asks for is a fresh project.

payload.why: A fresh project is how werk gives each test its own copy of the store.

payload.title: The coverage check judges each pure file on its own, and a pure file with no test fails
payload.why: A single percentage over the whole project mixes pure and I/O lines, so well-tested I/O code can hide an untested pure file. And a file that no test loads is missing from the coverage report, so a check that reads only the report never sees it and lets it pass.
payload.body:
Only pure code gets a coverage number (#werk-test-scope). The check therefore works from an explicit list of the pure files in the project, not from every file the report happens to contain.

**Each file on its own.** The coverage run writes a report with one entry per file that a test loaded. The check reads the report and compares each listed file, by itself, with the line threshold that #werk-test-runner sets. One file far above the threshold cannot lift another one that is below it.

**A missing file is 0%.** A coverage tool records a file only when a test loads it. A pure file with no test is not in the report at all. The check treats a listed file with no entry as 0%, so it fails. Without this rule the file would pass because nothing measured it.

**Edge case.** A listed file with no executable lines, for example a file of type declarations, passes.

**Keeping the list current.** The change that adds a new pure file also adds it to the list, so the check sees the file from its first commit.

**Output.** The check prints one line per listed file with its percentage, and exits 1 when any file is under the threshold.

payload.why: Only pure files get a coverage number, so the check judges only the files on the pure list.
The threshold and the coverage report come from the runner and the coverage script that #werk-test-runner sets.

criterion.text: A pure file with no test, or a pure file under the threshold, passes the coverage check; or keeping the pure list current costs more than the bugs it catches.
A check gives a different verdict on a fresh clone than on a working checkout, or the install before each check makes the checks too slow to run often.

patch.body:
A store is anything a test writes that lasts after the write: files, a database, a log. Before a test writes to one, the harness gives the test a fresh, empty copy, and the test puts in exactly the data its scenario names. When the test ends, the harness removes the copy and stops anything that serves it, also when the test fails.

The source code of the project is a store too, for a test that must edit it, for example to check a hot reload. Such a test edits a copy of the code and runs the app from that copy. The checkout stays clean when the test fails.

How a project makes a fresh copy depends on what its store is (see #werk-base-test-project and #werk-test-app-copy for werk).

payload.title: A hot reload test edits a copy of the werk app, never the checkout
payload.why: The hot reload and client reload tests must edit the server and client source to see a reload. An edit to the checkout would stay behind, and leave it dirty, when a test fails.
payload.body:
The harness copies the server source, the client source and the build and type configuration into a temporary folder, and runs the app from there.

The installed packages are not copied. The copy links to each package of the checkout, except the Vite dependency cache: each copy keeps its own. A cache shared by two app roots makes Vite optimize the dependencies again and reload the page, which a reload test would read as its own result.

The browser harness starts one werk server per test from such a copy, on a copy of the fixture project. It removes the setting that points at a real project log, so a test server never takes the lock of a real project.

payload.why: The copy of the app is how werk meets the rule that a test which edits the code edits a copy.
The client reload test edits client source in the copy, so the copy must hold the client and run Vite inside the server as that card says.

criterion.text: A failed hot reload test leaves the checkout dirty, or a reload test fails because of the copy itself, for example a Vite page reload that no edit caused.

patch.body:
A stop is a place where the build cannot go on until a person acts. Chat-pane questions are not stops; they are measured on their own (#ms-outcome-interv-chat).

- **Kinds of stop.** A gate that waits for a person to pass it. A ticket held in blocked by a failed check, held as stuck, held because a cited card changed, or blocked with no check. A merge loop that stopped. A merge that was red on the main line, or that conflicted with it. A build that reached its retry cap.
- **Where the kind comes from.** The structured facts the build writes with each stop: the gate events, the check that holds a blocked ticket, how the merge loop ended, the merge result and its conflict flag, and the build's end at the cap. The reason text never decides the kind, so rewording a reason changes no row. A move written before those facts existed has only its reason, and for that move alone the start of the reason decides the kind.
- **Length of a wait.** From the stop to the next event that moves the work on. A red merge lasts until the ticket moves on from building. The log does not say who acted, so the panel reports the length of the stop, not a person's response time. A stop still open counts up to now and is drawn as a ring.
- **Marks.** One dot per stop, one row per kind, at the length of the wait on a log axis, because a stop lasts minutes or days. The median of the current window per row.
- **Outlier.** A dot above its row's band is amber, and a dot above 1.5 times the band's top is red. A row with too few stops says how many more it needs.
- **Drill-down.** A dot opens the ticket, run or gate where the build stopped, with the reason the log holds.

The kinds in the image are an earlier set. The marks, the band and the median follow the image.

![Waits per kind of stop, coloured against the band](/api/image?name=vi-flow-ms-waits.png)

payload.title: Read the kind of stop from the start of the reason text
payload.why_not: A reason is prose for a person. A reworded reason drops its stops from the panel, and three kinds of blocked ticket read as one.

payload.title: Structured facts only, with no fallback for older moves
payload.why_not: The moves written before the structured facts existed would drop out, and with them every set-check stop the log holds so far.

patch.body:
Each external service that a test could start or call is replaced by a fake with fixed answers. Every setting that points at real data is removed before the first test. The guard covers every process a test starts, not only the test process, because a child process can inherit the settings of the shell that started the run. A harness that cannot confirm the fake is in place refuses to start.

There is one fake per service, and every harness uses it: the command-line tests, the server tests and the browser tests. A second fake in one harness drifts from the first, and the two harnesses then test different behaviour. A fake with no script for the current test fails at once with an error. It never invents an answer, so a test that needs replies must install its script first.

How a project replaces its services depends on its runtime (see #werk-test-env for werk).

A unit test run isolates every test from the machine it runs on. Two things must not leak in. The first is the real agent: starting it costs money and time, and its answers change between runs. The second is the real project log: a test must never write to the map that a person is working in.

The run sets this up once, before the first test. It removes every variable that points at a real project, so a test has no way to reach the real log. It also puts the fake agent first in the program search list (the PATH variable), so a program lookup for the agent finds the fake before the real one.

Changing PATH inside the running test process is not enough. Bun's process spawn, its program lookup and its shell read the environment that the test process started with, not the environment as the setup edited it. A test that starts an agent without passing an environment of its own would still find the real agent. So the run also makes spawn, program lookup and the shell default to the cleaned environment. A process started by a test harness inherits the same cleaned environment.

The browser test server checks the same rule at start-up and refuses to start when the fake agent is not first in the search list. A leak then fails at once, not later as a surprise bill or a changed map. The browser harness uses the same fake agent as the command-line tests. With no script installed, that fake exits with an error.

payload.title: The fake agent keeps a permission ask open while the rest of its script plays
payload.why: A test must script a permission ask followed by a stall, repeated tool calls or a crash, all before anybody answers. A fake that blocks until the ask is answered cannot play those steps.
payload.body:
An ask step prints the permission request and does not wait for the answer. The next steps of the script play at once: a pause, a tool call, or a crash. The turn waits for its open asks only just before it prints its final result.

When the fake runs with an input channel, the answer comes from that channel. With no input channel, the ask is denied at the end of the turn. A crash with an ask open exits with no tool result and no final result, as a real agent that dies does.

Each pause adds a 20 ms margin, so a test never measures a silence shorter than the script asks for.

payload.why: The scripted asks exist to test the behaviour that #werk-mc-asks defines: an ask that names its tab and still stops you while the agent goes on.

criterion.text: A test cannot script an ask followed by a stall, a tool call or a crash, or the fake behaves differently from the real agent when an ask is open.

payload.title: A scripted edit outside the temporary project fails
payload.why: The fake agent writes real files on the machine that runs the tests, so a script with a wrong path must not change anything outside the project of its test.
payload.body: An edit step names a path relative to the temporary project. A path that leads outside the project fails the step, and the fake writes nothing there.

payload.why: A test writes only to its own copy of the store, and the temporary project is that copy.

payload.title: Each launch of the fake agent records the arguments it was given
payload.why: A test must check what werk asked the agent, not only what the agent answered.
payload.body: Each time werk starts the fake agent, the fake records the arguments of that launch in the temporary project. A test reads the record to check that werk started the agent with the right request.

payload.why: The record lives in the fresh project of the test, so no other test reads it.

patch.body:
The harness gives each temporary project one script, and the fake agent reads it at launch. The fake is found first in the program search list under the name of the real agent (see #werk-test-env).

A script is an ordered list of steps and an exit code. A step is an event, printed as one line of the output stream of the agent, or an edit, a file written in the project. The fake plays the steps in order and then exits with the code of the script. One list for both kinds keeps an event and an edit in the order a real agent makes them.

An edit stays inside the project (#werk-test-fake-edit-inside). Each launch is recorded, so a test can read what the agent was asked (#werk-test-fake-launch-log). An ask step does not block the steps after it (#werk-test-fake-ask-open).

payload.why: The fake is reached through the program search list that #werk-test-env sets up.

criterion.text: A scripted edit changes a file outside the temporary project of its test.
A test cannot tell from the record which arguments werk gave the fake agent, or reads a record left by another test.
A test needs an agent behaviour that an ordered list of events and edits cannot express, or the order of events and edits differs from what a real agent does.

patch.body:
Addresses:

- `/map/<id>` — the map with that card open. `/map` opens the home card.
- `/flow` and `/flow/<id>` — Flow, scoped to the whole map or to that card's subtree.
- `/graph`, `/diagram`, `/board` — the other views.

The card id in an address is URL-encoded, so an id with a colon, such as an option or a source id, makes a valid address.

Back and Forward move through these addresses. A switch between views adds one entry. In Flow, a row click that goes one level deeper adds one entry, so Back goes up one level (#vi-flowtab-click).

Filters, sort order, and the Subtrees row setting stay out of the address. They are display settings, not places.

A `#id` link in a card or in the chat opens `/map/<id>` from any view. An old address `/#id` opens `/map/<id>`.

The server answers every view address with the app.

The open-card line in the chat (#werk-card-blind) names the card in the current address: the map card, or the Flow scope. A view with no card in its address keeps the last card named.

Addresses:

- `/map/<id>` — the map with that card open. `/map` opens the home card.
- `/flow` and `/flow/<id>` — Flow, scoped to the whole map or to that card's subtree.
- `/graph`, `/diagram`, `/board` — the other views.

The card id in an address is URL-encoded, so an id with a colon, such as an option or a source id, makes a valid address. An address that names a card that is not in the map, or is removed, opens a page that says so.

Back and Forward move through these addresses. A switch between views adds one entry. In Flow, a row click that goes one level deeper adds one entry, so Back goes up one level (#vi-flowtab-click).

Filters, sort order, and the Subtrees row setting stay out of the address. They are display settings, not places.

A `#id` link in a card or in the chat opens `/map/<id>` from any view. An old address `/#id` opens `/map/<id>`.

The server answers every view address with the app.

The open-card line in the chat (#werk-card-blind) names the card in the current address: the map card, or the Flow scope. A view with no card in its address keeps the last card named.

payload.title: The root view of the map is the page of the card #root, the same as any card page
payload.why: The root card differs from other cards only in that it has no parent, so a special root page would be a second page shape to learn.
payload.body: The map opens on the card #root (see #vi-routes for its address). Its page has the shape of every card page (#vi-onview): the detail on top, the cards that refine #root below. The root view lists nothing else. A source that no card cites, or a card outside the refines tree, does not appear on it.

payload.title: A synthetic root page that lists every card that refines nothing, and every source that no card cites
payload.why_not: It gives the root a page shape that no other card has, and it treats a parentless card as a top-level decision. The root card is a normal card with no parent.

payload.why: The map address with no card opens the home card, and #vi-routes names that address.
The refines link decides which cards sit below #root, and the supported_by link decides which sources a card cites.

criterion.text: Change this when a reader needs a source that no card cites, or a card outside the refines tree, and cannot reach it from the map.

payload.title: The grader scores one scope line: does the diff build something the ticket does not ask for?
payload.why: A builder pass that fixes a failure builds whatever the failure names. Without a scope line, a diff can grow past its ticket and decide questions that other cards and other tickets own.
payload.body: Beside the delivery lines and the contradiction lines (#lp-prod-judge), the grader scores one scope line per ticket. The line fails when the diff builds a behaviour that no acceptance criterion and no story of the ticket asks for. The gap names each such behaviour, so the next pass removes it. A contradiction line never asks for a missing part of a card, so a contradiction line cannot push a diff out of scope.

payload.title: The implement prompt tells the builder to stay in scope, and nothing judges it
payload.why_not: The builder is the agent that goes out of scope, so its own rule does not catch it. The grader already reads the diff against the ticket.

payload.why: The scope line reads the ticket's acceptance criteria and stories, which the implement step hands to each pass.
A story the ticket lists is in scope, so the line needs the ticket's story list.

criterion.text: I read the scope gaps of the next runs. Change this if the line fails diffs that a criterion does ask for, or misses a diff that builds an unasked behaviour.

payload.text: Duplicates #vi-onview (the page shape) and #werk-cli-show (show already prints each incoming refines row with its rollup). New facts: the ghost mark on a sub-card, no sub-card section on a leaf, options listed apart. These belong on #werk-cli-show, not as a child of #vi-onview. Proposal: discard this ghost and add those facts to #werk-cli-show.

payload.title: A builder pass gets the index of decided cards, and searches the map before it decides what no cited card gives
payload.why: The cited cards and their closure miss decisions that sit in another branch of the map. A builder that cannot see such a card decides the question again and contradicts it.
payload.body: Beside its input, each pass gets the id and the title of every decided card in the map. Before the pass decides a question that no cited card answers, it searches the titles, the whys and the bodies of the map for the terms of the question, and reads every card that matches. A decided card that answers the question binds the pass the same as a cited card. Only a search that finds no answer leads to a proposed card (#st-build-missing-decision).

payload.title: Add the refines children of every card in the cited closure to the input
payload.why_not: It finds a decision only when that decision is a child of a closure card. A decision two branches away stays out of reach, and the input fills with cards that do not apply to the ticket.

payload.title: Keep the input as it is and add the missing depends_on edges where a gap shows
payload.why_not: It repairs one case after it fails, and the next missing edge opens the same gap.

payload.why: The search runs before the proposal that #st-build-missing-decision defines, and an empty search is what allows that proposal.

payload.title: `werk search` prints the index of decided cards, or the cards whose words match every term
payload.why: A builder searches the whole map before it decides a question, and the CLI is the only interface it has to the map.
payload.body:
```
werk search ["term" ...] [--status decided|open|proto] [--under <id>]
```

- With no term, `werk search` prints the index: one line per decided card, with the id and the title. A builder pass gets this output as its map index (#st-build-implement-search).
- Each term is a case-insensitive pattern, and terms repeat. A card matches when every term occurs in its title, its why, its body, or the why-not of one of its options.
- One line per match: the id, the status, and the title. The cards with the most hits come first.
- `--status` keeps only the cards with that status. With no term, the default is decided. With a term, every status matches.
- `--under` keeps only the refines subtree of that card.
- A ghost or a removed card never matches.

payload.why: The index and the search are the two operations that #st-build-implement-search gives each builder pass.

payload.title: A sub-card is a tile in a grid: title, why line, meta row, rollup bar
payload.why: The sub-cards section is where a reader picks the next card to open, so each tile must show enough to rank a branch without opening it.
payload.body:
The section heading gives the count of sub-cards, and the count of proposed sub-cards when there are any. The tiles fill a grid with as many columns as the width holds. Real sub-cards come first, in log order. Proposed sub-cards come last.

```
  12 below · 2 proposed
  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  ▌ A link list shows the card id …   │ ▌ A stale card's page shows its …   │
  ▌ Each linked card is one row: its  │ ▌ The reader meets a stale mark on  │
  ▌ #id in a lighter colour, then …   │ ▌ the card page, so the page must … │
  ▌ #vi-onview-links  3 below  I decide○ ▌ #vi-onview-stale  you decide      │
  ▌ ███████████████░░░░               │ ▌                                   │
  └───────────────────────────────────┘ └───────────────────────────────────┘
```

A tile is one link to the page of its sub-card, so nothing inside the tile is a link. From top to bottom, a tile holds the title, the why line, a meta row and the rollup bar. The title renders a backtick span as code (#vi-title-code). The why line is plain words: every Markdown marker is dropped, so a reference reads as #id but does not link (#werk-reflink). The meta row holds the id, the count of cards below when there are any, the count of evidence when there is any, and the who label: "you decide", "I decide" or "build it first". The unchallenged ring sits next to the who label (#werk-contract-guess). A pulsing planning mark joins the meta row while a plan of that subtree runs. The bar is the rollup bar of #rollup. A leaf has no bar.

The left border carries the status colour: decided, open, proto or source. A stale sub-card takes the stale colour in place of the status colour. A postponed sub-card carries grey stripes (#vi-onview-postponed). A proposed sub-card has a blue border and a blue background (#al-diff-render).

An option uses the same tile under Options. It is not a sub-card, because its link is alternative_to, not refines.

payload.title: Measure shows the pipeline measures as panels, one question per panel

patch.body:
Measure shows the measures of #ms-self, grouped by cost, failures and waits.

**Rules for every panel.**
- **One question.** The question is the panel title.
- **Transform first.** A panel shows a fold over the logs, not raw events: per unit of size, a distribution (median, 90th percentile, maximum), a window, or a ratio.
- **Legend.** Every panel names its marks, its lines and its band.
- **Colour marks the outlier.** A mark outside the reference band has its own colour, so a person finds it without a click or a hover.
- **Drill-down.** A mark opens the items behind it: the tickets, cards, and transcripts.
- **Reference band.** Each panel compares against its own history (#vi-flow-ms-ref).
- **Live.** A panel redraws when the pipeline log or the decision log gets an event.
- **Look.** The panel images on the child cards show layout and marks, with made-up data. The type, colours and spacing follow the visual system of the rest of the tool.

A panel that compares two pipeline variants waits for the replay set (#ms-replay).

payload.title: The Measure tab shows the share of one-card diagram redraws that stayed local

patch.body:
Each finished run of the diagram job writes one ended event to the pipeline log (#ms-store). The event holds the result (updated, unchanged or failed), the declared outcome and its reason (#vi-sysdiag-declare), the decided cards whose change started the run, the wall time and the cost.

The gauge counts only updated runs that exactly one card started. A run that batched several cards cannot say what one card does, and an unchanged or failed run made no redraw. Beside the share, the gauge shows the count of batched, unchanged and failed runs, so a small sample is visible.

Under the gauge, a list shows each restructure in the window, with its reason and the card that started it. A click on the card opens it on the map. A person reads this list for the second half of the test: does each reason point at the card that moved a boundary.

The threshold, window and minimum sample come from #vi-sysdiag-localrate. If that card names no threshold, the gauge shows the share in grey with no state. With a threshold, colour follows the state: red fires, green holds, grey not enough data.

The gauge counts every run. Runs belong to the diagram, not to a card.

payload.why: The waits show as a panel in the waits group of the Measure tab that this card defines.

patch.body:
A wait starts when a chat-pane turn leaves a hanging question for the person, and ends when the person answers it or moves on. #ms-outcome-interv-chat-q defines both ends.

Record the conversation, the card the map was at, the start, and the end.

**Numbers.** The median wait per conversation and the total wait per day. A wait that is still open shows its age.

**Where it shows.** A panel in the waits group of the Measure tab, over its time window: the median wait, the wait today, the open waits and the oldest one, a total for each of the last 7 days, and one row per conversation. It counts every wait, with or without a card.

**Where the data comes from.** Button waits come from the chat history of each conversation. A resolved question wait comes from the ask history, which records when a structured question went up and which conversation asked it. An open question wait comes from the live ask queue, because the ask history gets a line only when the ask resolves. Asks resolved before the history held those two facts have no wait.

A chat-pane wait is not an intervention per ticket, and it raises no alert by the rule of #lp-trend-alert.

The tab is called Flow. It reads the log and shows what is counted from map cards: stats on the card status loop, breakdowns and totals for each subtree, and a flat list of all map cards. Each view is its own card under this one. Measures of the pipeline and the tool sit in Measure (#vi-measure).

It replaces the foldable sections at the top of the home card (#vi-flowtab-home).

patch.body:
The section heading gives the count of sub-cards, and the count of proposed sub-cards when there are any. The tiles fill a grid with as many columns as the width holds. Real sub-cards come first, in log order. Proposed sub-cards come last.

```
  2 below
  ┍────────────────────────────────────┐ ┍────────────────────────────────────┐
  ┃ Status and staleness are two axes… │ ┃ A backtick span in a card title …  │
  ┃ A stale decided card is still      │ ┃ A title holds ids and flags, and   │
  ┃ decided. One row cannot say both.  │ ┃ they read as code everywhere.      │
  ┃ #ro-axes  2 below  I decide ○      │ ┃ #vi-title-code  I decide           │
  ┃ ██████████████████████▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒░░░░ │ ┃                                    │
  ┕────────────────────────────────────┘ ┕────────────────────────────────────┘
```

In the preview, the heavy left edge stands for the status colour, ○ is the unchallenged ring, and █ ▒ ░ are the decided, open and proto parts of the rollup bar.

The marks are those of #vi-onview-look. A tile differs from the page of its card in three ways. First, the tile is one link to that page, so nothing inside it is a link. The why line renders inline Markdown: code, bold, italic and strike look the same as on the page. A link and an image show as their text, and a reference reads as #id but does not link (#werk-reflink). Second, the tile shows the title and the why line, and no body. Third, it has no tag row: one meta row holds the id, the count of cards below when there are any, the count of evidence when there is any, the who label with its ring, and the planning mark. The status shows only as the edge colour.

An option uses the same tile under Options. It is not a sub-card, because its link is alternative_to, not refines.

payload.why: A rule that checks a write, such as the one for a rederive, needs to know which cards are stale. The marks come from the order of the events, and the fold already reads that order.
payload.body: The folded map that a write checks against holds the stale and postponed marks, with their traces (see #vi-prop). A rule reads the folded map and nothing else. No rule reads the log itself, so the marks are derived in one place, and every rule and every view sees the same marks. See #pr-log-refuse for how a write checks its events.
