payload.title: A postponement pauses the links that existed when it happened
payload.why: The paused mark goes every distance, over refines children and depends_on dependents. A card linked after the postponement was written against the current text, the same as for a stale mark.
payload.body:
The walk over the links runs once, at the postponement, over the links in the map at that moment. It follows refines children and depends_on dependents, as a change does (#vi-edges), and goes on past the first hop (#pr-wf-paused).

A card linked after the postponement takes no paused mark (#vi-prop-bornstale). It waits only when its basis is open, which holds for the postponed card itself (#map-wait). A card linked to a paused card is not blocked, because the content of a paused card is still true (#pr-wf-paused). The new card shows no sign of the pause above it.

```
 at the postponement          linked after it

 P  postponed (open)          N1 --depends_on--> P    waits, no mark (P is open)
 ^                            N2 --depends_on--> C1   no mark, can be decided
 | depends_on                 N3 --depends_on--> C2   no mark, can be decided
 C1 paused
 ^
 | depends_on                 P is decided again: the marks on C1 and C2 clear.
 C2 paused                    N1, N2 and N3 had none, so nothing changes.
```

payload.why: takes the rule that a link made after a change carries no mark from it
takes the two link types that a mark follows

payload.title: A card linked later to a paused card inherits the paused mark

payload.title: A paused card is still a basis that holds
payload.why: Paused means the content is still true. A card that depends on a paused card can be decided on it, so a postponement never blocks work that only reads its content.
payload.body:
The decide check needs a basis that is decided and not stale (#werk-contract-facts, #map-wait). A paused mark does not fail it: the content under the mark still holds, and only the build of that card waits (#pr-wf-paused). A review mark on a source does fail it.

A card whose basis is the postponed card itself still waits, because that card is open, not decided.

payload.why: takes the rule that an open or stale basis makes the card wait
takes the basis fact that this card says a paused basis meets

payload.title: A card on a paused basis waits like a card on a stale basis
payload.why_not: A postponed card is still true, so the card would wait on content that holds. A postponement would then block work that only reads that content.

criterion.text: Postpone a card, then decide a card that depends on a paused downstream card. The decide passes. If it waits on the paused mark, revisit.

payload.title: A mark's trace names the reopen reason, and a paused trace names the path
payload.why: The reader decides what to do with a marked card from its trace. The reopen reason says whether the content is still true, and a paused mark far from its origin needs the cards between to be followed back.
payload.body:
A mark from a reopen carries its reason: postponed, invalidated or rejected (#pr-wf-paused). Invalidated is the reason of a reopen that names none. An amend is a kind of change, not a reopen reason, so a mark from an amend says amended and carries no reason.

A stale mark sits one hop from the change (#vi-prop), so its trace is one link long. A paused mark can sit any distance away (#pr-wf-paused-reach), so its trace also names each card the postponement passed through, nearest to the changed card first, and the link type of the last hop. The staleness listing and the card page print the same trace.

```
 STALE, one hop                        PAUSED, any distance

 B  reopened or amended                P  postponed
 ^                                     ^
 | depends_on                          | depends_on
 A  marked                             C1
                                       ^
 STALE from #B, invalidated, <date>    | refines
   <text typed at the change>          C2
   A -> B: <the link reason>           ^
                                       | depends_on
 STALE from #B, amended, <date>        C3  marked
   (an amend has no reopen reason)
                                       PAUSED from #P, postponed, <date>
                                         via C1, C2 (nearest to P first)
                                         last hop: depends_on
```

payload.why: takes the three reopen reasons and the paused mark that reaches every distance
takes the walk that puts a paused mark at any distance, so the trace needs a path

payload.title: A stale trace names the full path too
payload.why_not: A stale mark sits one hop from the change, so the path is the one link the trace already shows.

criterion.text: Postpone a card three hops upstream and open the paused card. Its trace lists the cards between and the last link type. If it shows only the origin, revisit.

payload.title: An amend at the end of a review marks the next hop, and its trace says amended
payload.why: A review that changes the card is a change too, so the cards next to it need a mark and a trace. The review sentence is the why that the reader of the trace sees.
payload.body:
A review is the check of one stale card against the change that made it stale (#rederive-reason). It ends in a confirm or an amend. The review records its outcome and one sentence that says why.

A confirm clears the marks on the reviewed card and changes nothing else. An amend clears the marks on the reviewed card that are older than it, and puts a stale mark on its direct dependents and direct children. The trace of each reads: amended, the reviewed card as the cause, and the sentence of the amend (#vi-prop-trace-reason). An amend is a change like any other, so it spreads one hop only (#vi-prop).

```
 B amended --> A stale --review--> confirm   A clears. D1, D2 and E unchanged.
                            |
                            +----> amend     A clears (marks older than the amend)
                                             D1  stale   depends_on A
                                             D2  stale   child of A
                                             E   unchanged: it depends on D1,
                                                 two hops from A

 trace on D1:   STALE from #A, amended, <date>
                  <the sentence of the amend>
                  D1 -> A: <the link reason>
```

payload.why: takes the two endings of a review, confirm and amend
takes the rule that an amend is a change kind that the trace names amended, not a reopen reason

payload.title: An amend after a review marks every card downstream

criterion.text: Review a stale card and amend it. Its direct dependents and children go stale with the trace amended and the review sentence. A card two hops away stays clear. If it goes stale, revisit.

A mark from a reopen carries its reason: postponed, invalidated or rejected (#pr-wf-paused). Invalidated is the reason of a reopen that names none. An amend is a kind of change, not a reopen reason, so a mark from an amend says amended and carries no reason.

A stale mark sits one hop from the change (#vi-prop), so its trace is one link long. A paused mark can sit any distance away (#pr-wf-paused-reach), so its trace also names each card the postponement passed through, nearest to the changed card first, and the link type of the last hop. The staleness listing and the card page print the same trace.

Example. Seven cards:
- X is "We charge per seat".
- Y is "The invoice shows the seat count". It depends on X.
- Z is "The invoice PDF has a seat column". It depends on Y.
- P is "Invoices are in EUR only".
- Q is "Invoice prices use the EUR format". It depends on P.
- R is "The tax line rounds to the euro cent". It is a child of Q.
- S is "The PDF footer states the currency". It depends on R.

What happens:
1. X is reopened with no reason and the text "Charging moves to usage." Y goes stale. Its trace says invalidated and shows that text.
2. The review of Y ends in an amend with the sentence "The invoice now shows usage units." Y clears. Z goes stale. Its trace says amended, with no reopen reason, and shows the sentence (#vi-prop-amended).
3. P is postponed. Q, R and S are paused. The trace on Q names no cards between. The trace on R names Q. The trace on S names Q and R, in that order, and depends_on as the last hop.

```
 Y --depends_on--> X           Q --depends_on--> P
 Z --depends_on--> Y           R --refines-----> Q
                               S --depends_on--> R

 STALE, one hop                PAUSED, any distance

 X  reopened                   P  postponed
 ^                             ^
 | depends_on                  | depends_on
 Y  stale, then amended        Q  paused
 ^                             ^
 | depends_on                  | refines
 Z  stale                      R  paused
                               ^
                               | depends_on
                               S  paused

 trace on Y:                          trace on S:
 STALE from #X, invalidated, <date>   PAUSED from #P, postponed, <date>
   Charging moves to usage.             via Q, R (nearest to P first)
   Y -> X: <the link reason>            last hop: depends_on

 trace on Z:
 STALE from #Y, amended, <date>
   (an amend has no reopen reason)
   The invoice now shows usage units.
   Z -> Y: <the link reason>
```

payload.title: Find lists open and proto cards, and leaves out a postponed card too
payload.why: An agent looks for a card it can work on now. A card in proto is still work. A card reopened as postponed waits, the same as the cards it pauses.
payload.body:
The find operation lists real cards whose status is open or proto, in the refines subtree of one card, breadth first, the card itself included. An option, a source and an excerpt are never listed. With no card named, it reads each tree of the map.

It leaves out a card that carries a paused or a stale mark (#pr-wf-paused), and a card that carries the postponed mark (#pr-wf-postponed). A card reopened as rejected is open again and can be worked on, so find lists it. A removed card and a ghost are not in the map, so find never lists them.

```
 Product            open                   listed  (the card itself)
 +-- Sign-up        open                   listed
 +-- Billing        proto                  listed
 +-- Login          decided                left out: not open or proto
 +-- Export         open, paused           left out: marked paused
 +-- Reports        open, stale            left out: marked stale
 +-- Archive        open, postponed        left out: carries the postponed mark
 +-- Search         open, reopened as      listed:  rejected means work again
                    rejected
```

takes the postponed mark that find leaves out, and when it ends

payload.title: Find lists paused and postponed cards too, with their mark

ops.new: **Title**

ops.old:
- A plain sentence with a subject and a verb. More words are fine when they make it easier to read.
- One idea. A second clause moves down to the why.
- High level: no mechanism, no tool or subagent names, no "now".
- Name the members of a small set, not a slogan: "Four link types: refines, depends_on, supported_by, alternative_to".
ops.new:
- A plain sentence with a subject and a verb. More words are fine when they make it easier to read.
- One idea. A second clause moves down to the why.
- High level: no mechanism, no tool or subagent names, no "now".
- Name the members of a small set, not a slogan: "Four link types: refines, depends_on, supported_by, alternative_to".
- No count that a later change can make wrong, unless the title also names every member. "Named steps in sequence, grouped by stage" stays true when a step is added. "Seven steps" does not.
- It states this card's own rule and names no other decision. "Removal checks the actor the same way as accept" ties the card to a second card that can change on its own.

ops.old: **Why**
ops.new: **Why**

ops.old:
- Two or three short sentences. A reader who stops here understands about 80% of the card.
- It gives the reason in plain causal steps, not as an aphorism.
- No card references and no commands. Those go in the body.
ops.new:
- Two or three short sentences. A reader who stops here understands about 80% of the card.
- It gives the reason in plain causal steps, not as an aphorism.
- No card references and no commands. Those go in the body.
- It does not repeat the body. The body adds the detail.

ops.old: **Body**
ops.new: **Body**

ops.old:
- Short paragraphs and bullet lists. One item or one option per bullet.
- References to other cards, examples, and ASCII diagrams go here.
- A general overview. It does not repeat the titles of subcards, because the tree shows them.
- Every paragraph helps a reader decide or act. A paragraph that does not is cut.
- A rejected alternative is an option node, not prose.
ops.new:
- Short paragraphs and bullet lists. One item or one option per bullet.
- References to other cards, examples, and ASCII diagrams go here.
- A general overview. It does not repeat the titles of subcards, because the tree shows them.
- Every paragraph helps a reader decide or act. A paragraph that does not is cut.
- A rejected alternative is an option node, not prose.
- It states the problem, then the answer: "To avoid X, the map does Y". A decided card records the answer, not the question.

ops.old: **Every layer**
ops.new: **Every layer**

ops.old:
- No coined phrases. "Fans out a calm mark" becomes "puts a grey mark on the cards that depend on it".
- When a layer is too long, its content moves down one level: title, then why, then body, then a subcard.
ops.new:
- No coined phrases. "Fans out a calm mark" becomes "puts a grey mark on the cards that depend on it".
- When a layer is too long, its content moves down one level: title, then why, then body, then a subcard.
- Every term is plain English or a term that another card defines. A term that the card adds is defined in plain words where it first appears. A reader who must ask "what does this mean?" has found a term that breaks this rule: "the actor claim is the nearest check", "one read size", "cards give the edges".
- A reader understands the card from its own text. It does not need a past state of the product, a removed card, or the conversation that wrote it.

payload.title: A card about a mechanism shows one worked example and a picture of it
payload.why: A rule about what changes when someone acts is hard to follow in the abstract. A short example with named things, and a picture with the same names, shows the reader what happens step by step.
payload.body:
A mechanism card says what happens when a person or a program acts: a mark spreads, a card moves, a check refuses. Its body carries one worked example after the rule.

The example names a few concrete things with short names and plain titles, such as X "We charge per seat" and Y "The invoice shows the seat count". A bullet list gives the starting situation, one thing per bullet. Numbered steps give the events, one action and its result per step. The steps include the case where nothing happens, when the rule has one.

An ASCII picture in a code block follows the example. It uses the same names, symbols and states as the example, so each line of the picture matches a step. Every number and every symbol in the picture has a label.

The example shows the rule as it holds now, from the side of the person who uses it: what they do and what they see. It does not set two versions of the rule side by side. It does not depend on a past state of the product that the reader cannot see any more. An example that was the evidence for the decision goes on a source node beside the card, with enough context to read it months later.

A card that names a thing or fixes a layout, and describes no change over time, needs no example.

payload.title: The example sets the rule before and after the change side by side
payload.why_not: The reader must hold two versions in mind and find the difference. The card describes one current rule, and the log holds the old one.

payload.title: The example is a prose paragraph
payload.why_not: A paragraph hides which action causes which result. A list reads one step at a time.

criterion.text: A mechanism card with an example and a picture still leaves me asking what happens when I act

payload.why: takes the rule that a card's evidence sits on nodes beside it

payload.title: Find lists open and proto cards, and leaves out a postponed card too
payload.why: An agent looks for a card it can work on now. A card in proto is still work. A card reopened as postponed waits, the same as the cards it pauses.
payload.body:
The find operation lists real cards whose status is open or proto, in the refines subtree of one card, breadth first, the card itself included. An option, a source and an excerpt are never listed. With no card named, it reads each tree of the map.

It leaves out a card that carries a paused or a stale mark (#pr-wf-paused), and a card that carries the postponed mark (#pr-wf-postponed). A card reopened as rejected is open again and can be worked on, so find lists it. A removed card and a ghost are not in the map, so find never lists them.

Find never lists a decided card. An agent that lacks context about a decision looks for it with the search operation, which reads decided cards (#st-build-implement-search).

```
 Product            open                   listed  (the card itself)
 +-- Sign-up        open                   listed
 +-- Billing        proto                  listed
 +-- Login          decided                left out: found by the search operation
 +-- Export         open, paused           left out: marked paused
 +-- Reports        open, stale            left out: marked stale
 +-- Archive        open, postponed        left out: carries the postponed mark
 +-- Search         open, reopened as      listed:  rejected means work again
                    rejected
```

payload.why: takes the paused mark that find leaves out
takes the postponed mark that find leaves out, and when it ends
takes the rule that missing context about a decision is found by searching decided cards, not by find

payload.title: Find lists paused and postponed cards too, with their mark
payload.why_not: An agent that looks for work it can do now would receive work that waits, and would have to filter it again.

payload.title: Find lists decided cards too, so one operation covers work and context
payload.why_not: Most cards of a map are decided, so the list of work to do would drown in them. Search already finds decided cards by their words.

criterion.text: Postpone a card and mark another stale, then run the find operation on their parent. Neither is listed, no decided card is, and an open, a proto and a rejected card are. If a marked or decided card is listed, revisit.

payload.title: Every agent that can write to the map reads the werk agent instructions, in any project
payload.why: An agent follows only the rules it reads. A build pass runs in the project's own repository, and the project's own instruction files know nothing about the map. So werk gives its instructions to each agent it starts.
payload.body:
Werk keeps one instruction text for agents: how to keep the map current, how to propose and word a card, and how to tag who decides. The text is about any project werk works on, not about werk itself. Werk adds it to the system prompt of every agent it starts that can write to the map: the chat pane agent, each build pass, and the plan writers. The text names the werk command line by the path werk runs from, so its commands work in any repository.

An agent with a narrow contract does not get the text, because the text would contradict that contract. A sample agent may not write to the map. The diagram agents edit the product diagram, and the text forbids that. A model call with no tools cannot act on the map at all.

When the project is werk itself, its own instruction file already includes the text, so werk does not add it a second time.

payload.why: takes that a build runs in the project's own repository, where werk's files are not
takes that the wording rules reach an agent only through its prompt

payload.title: Every claude process that werk starts reads the instructions
payload.why_not: A sample agent and the diagram agents have narrow contracts. The text tells them to write the map and not to touch the diagram, which contradicts their job.

payload.title: Each project carries the map rules in its own instruction file
payload.why_not: A project's own files do not know the map, and a copy in every project drifts away from the rules werk ships.

criterion.text: A build pass or the chat agent proposes a card that breaks the wording rules it was given

payload.title: A change to a decided card cannot leave it missing a required fact
payload.why: A decided card needs four facts. Removing its last option would leave it without one, and nothing would notice. But a card decided before a fact became required lacks that fact already, so it must still be able to receive it.
payload.body:
The map checks the four facts of a decided card whenever a change could leave one missing (#werk-contract-facts). The check cannot treat every change alike. A card decided before a fact became required lacks that fact already, and the change that adds it must go through.

- A change to the title, the why, the body, a depends_on link or the parent: the card must hold all four facts after the change (#map-frozen). A card decided before a fact became required waits for that fact at its next such change.
- Any other change, such as recording who decides, a waiver, a kill criterion, a link to a source or the removal of an option: refused only when it removes a fact the card had. So a missing fact can always be added.
- Removing a card that this card depends on is not a change to this card, so the check does not refuse it.

```
 Q  decided, who: you, one option O, a kill criterion

 remove O                         refused   Q would have no option
 add option O2, then remove O     allowed   Q still has an option
 record a second kill criterion   allowed   it adds a fact, removes none
 edit the body of Q               allowed   all four facts still hold

 R  decided before kill criteria were required, no kill criterion

 edit the body of R               refused   R lacks the kill criterion
 record a kill criterion on R     allowed   it adds the missing fact
```

payload.why: takes the list of fields whose change is an amend, and the two cases where an amend fails
takes the four facts that a decided card must keep
takes the rule that a failed check prints the command that adds the fact, so that command must go through

payload.title: Every change to a decided card needs every fact
payload.why_not: On a card decided before the contract, each command that adds a fact is refused because another fact is still missing, so the card can never be fixed.

payload.title: Check only edits of the words of a decided card
payload.why_not: Removing the last option, or changing who to you, would leave a decided card without a required fact, and no check would see it.

criterion.text: Remove the only option of a decided you card: refused. Record a kill criterion on a card decided without one: allowed. If either result flips, revisit.

payload.title: A waiver of a contract fact needs a written reason
payload.why: A waiver leaves a required fact empty on purpose. Without a written reason, a reader later cannot tell a deliberate waiver from a forgotten fact.
payload.body:
The decide check lets a card go without a basis, or without a weighed option, when the author waives that fact (#werk-contract-facts). Every escape hatch of a check leaves a written reason (#pr-gate), so a waiver does too.

- The basis waiver says why no decided card is a basis, for example that the card is the root of a tree.
- The option waiver says why no option was weighed against the card (#werk-contract-guess).
- A waiver with an empty reason is refused.
- The reason is stored with the waiver and prints wherever the card prints.
- Who decides is not waivable. A kill criterion that names no metric already carries its reason.

```
 T  no basis, who: me

 decide                              refused   no basis
 waive the basis, no reason          refused   a waiver needs a reason
 waive the basis: "root of a tree"   allowed
 decide                              passes    T prints "basis waived: root of a tree"

 U  who: you, no option weighed

 decide                              refused   no option
 waive the option, no reason         refused   a waiver needs a reason
 waive the option: "no real choice"  allowed
 decide                              passes    U prints "option waived: no real choice"
```

payload.why: takes the rule that every escape hatch leaves a written reason
takes the basis fact and the option fact that a waiver can leave empty
takes the option waiver, which is a stated fact stored on the log

payload.title: A waiver is a bare flag with no reason
payload.why_not: A waiver would then leave nothing to read, and a deliberate waiver looks the same as a forgotten fact.

payload.title: Only the basis waiver needs a reason
payload.why_not: The option waiver hides the same kind of gap. A card with no option and no reason cannot be told from a card whose option was lost.

criterion.text: Waive the basis and the option of a card with an empty reason: both refused. With a reason: both pass, and the card prints the reason. If an empty reason passes, revisit.

payload.title: The live dot on a ticket card sits in its top-left corner
payload.why: A ticket card on the board is narrow, and its row already holds the title and small counts. A dot in that row takes a full slot and pushes the title and the counts aside. A dot in the corner takes no slot, so the row keeps its full width.
payload.body:
A building ticket with a live agent session pulses (see #vi-board). The pulse is a small dot. To keep the card row at full width, the dot is pinned to the card's top-left corner, outside the row.

The dot must not cover the title. So only the first line of the title moves a few pixels to the right. The other lines of the title and the counts keep their place.

```
+------------------------------+
|*  Import ticket files from   |   * = the live dot, pinned to the corner
| the plan folder           2  |   2 = a count next to the title
+------------------------------+
```

When the session ends, the dot goes away and the first line of the title moves back to the left edge.

payload.title: The note route is the person's channel, so it needs the token and writes the person's note
payload.why: A note from the person goes to the agent's inbox as an instruction. A caller that can write such a note can speak to the agent in the person's name. The token proves the request comes from the person's own page, and the agent never holds the token.
payload.body:
**Problem.** The note route appends a note to a card's thread and copies the reply prompt to the clipboard. The inbox shows the agent the notes that the person wrote. If the agent, or any other local process, could write a note through the route as the person, it could give the agent instructions that look like the person's.

**Answer.** The note route is a request that writes to the log. So it needs the synchronizer token, like every other write (see #werk-serve-trust). A request with the token comes from the person's page, so the route records the person as the author of the note.

The agent writes its notes from the command line, not through the route (see #werk-chat). The command line records the agent as the author. The agent never holds the token, so the agent cannot reach the route.

**Example.**

- The card #x.
- The person's page, which holds the token.
- The agent, which has a shell and no token.

1. The page posts a note "split this card" on #x with the token. The route writes it. The author is the person.
2. The agent posts a note to the route from its shell with no token. The server refuses it. The log does not change.
3. The agent writes its answer on #x from the command line. The author is the agent.
4. The inbox shows the agent the note from step 1 only.

```
 page (token) ---- note route ----> log: #x "split this card"   author: person
 agent (no token) - note route --X  refused, log unchanged
 agent ----------- command line --> log: #x answer             author: agent
```

payload.title: A card link always shows its id with a # in front
payload.why: A reference can be written in three ways, but a reader needs to see one shape for a link. When every link reads the same, the reader can tell card links from other words at a glance.
payload.body:
A reference can be written with the #, without it, or inside a code span (see #werk-reflink). To give all three forms one look, the map renders every link the same way: the id with a # in front, in a monospace face.

Example: the text `al-diff`, a bare al-diff, and #al-diff all show as #al-diff, and each opens the card al-diff.

The rule changes only the label of a link. Text that does not become a link keeps the exact form it was written in, as #werk-reflink says.

payload.title: A ticket that a person stops waits in ready until a person starts it again
payload.why: A person stops a build because it goes the wrong way. If the merge loop picks the ticket again at once, the same build starts again and the stop changes nothing. So the ticket stays in ready, and only a person can release it.
payload.body:
A stop returns a building ticket to ready (#werk-board-control). The merge loop then ends that one build and keeps the ticket's branch. The other builds go on.

To keep the stop in effect, the ticket is held. A held ticket is a ticket in ready that the merge loop does not pick when it fills a free build slot (#st-build-parallel). The hold ends in one of two ways:

- A person triggers the ticket on the board.
- A person starts the merge loop again, which is the trigger for the whole run.

A ticket that a stopped merge loop returned to ready is not held (#st-build-stop-ready). Only a person's stop of one ticket holds it.

A held ticket cannot build, so the run can end with it still in ready (#st-build-stuck-park). The end report names each held ticket and the tickets that wait on it.

**Example**

- The run holds tickets A "Add the export command" and B "Show the seat count".
- A and B are in building. Nothing else is in ready.

1. A person drags A into ready. The merge loop ends A's build. B builds on.
2. A build slot is free. The merge loop does not pick A, because A is held.
3. B merges. Nothing else can build or merge, so the run ends. The report names A as held.
4. Later, the person triggers A. A builds from its kept branch.

```
step  ready      building   done
 0    -          A  B       -
 1    A(held)    B          -        <- person stops A
 2    A(held)    B          -        <- free slot; A is not picked
 3    A(held)    -          B        <- run ends; report: A held
 4    -          A          B        <- person triggers A

A = "Add the export command"   B = "Show the seat count"
(held) = in ready, skipped by the merge loop until a person starts it
```

payload.title: A discard drops the notes of each ghost that it drops
payload.why: A correction of a ghost is a discard, then a new proposal with the same id. Notes on the old ghost talk about words that are gone. If they stay, the person reads a stale thread beside the new words and cannot tell which words a note was about.
payload.body:
A correction of a ghost frees its id for a new proposal (see #werk-propose-new). Each card has a thread of notes (see #werk-chat). Notes are kept by id, so without a rule the old notes come back on the new ghost.

To avoid this, a discard clears the thread of every ghost that it drops. A ghost that the discard leaves in place keeps its thread. The notes stay in the log, so the person can still read them in the inbox. A note written on the id after the new proposal starts a new thread.

Example:

- X is a ghost card, "Export is its own command".
- N1 is a note on X: "Say what the export writes."

1. The person writes N1 on X. The thread of X shows N1.
2. The agent discards X. X leaves the map, and its thread is empty. N1 stays in the log.
3. The agent proposes X again with new words. The thread of X is still empty.
4. The person writes N2 on X. The thread of X shows N2 only.

```
step  map          thread of X     log
1     X (ghost)    N1              N1
2     -            (empty)         N1
3     X' (ghost)   (empty)         N1
4     X' (ghost)   N2              N1, N2

X  = the first proposal of the id
X' = the second proposal of the same id, with new words
-  = no node with the id in the map
```

payload.title: A node's place in the tree is set only when it is proposed or moved
payload.why: A node must sit in one place, so the tree and every rollup count it once. If a plain link could also set the place, a node could get a second parent, and the checks that a move runs would not run. So one operation sets the place at creation, one changes it later, and a link never touches it.
payload.body:
The place of a node is the link to its parent. For a card, a source and an excerpt that link is refines (see #vi-edges). For an option it is alternative_to to its card (see #ro-optparent).

To keep one place per node, the map sets that link in two operations only:

- The proposal of a node names its parent. The place is part of that one change (see #pr-log-one-event).
- A move replaces the parent link with a new one. A person asks for it, and the agent runs it (see #vi-levels).

The link operation adds only the links that are not a place: depends_on and supported_by. A link of type refines or alternative_to is refused, and the message names the move.

Example:

- P "Pricing" and Q "Billing" are cards.
- A "We charge per seat" is proposed under P.
- A:opt0 "We charge per account" is proposed under A.

1. The proposal of A places it: A refines P.
2. The proposal of A:opt0 places it: A:opt0 alternative_to A.
3. A link from A to Q of type refines is refused. A stays under P only.
4. A move of A to Q replaces the place: A refines Q, and A no longer refines P.
5. A link from A to P of type depends_on is accepted. It does not change where A sits.

```
  after step 2         step 3                       after step 5

  P        Q           P        Q                   P        Q
  │                    │        ▲                   ▲        │
  A                    A ──✗────┘ refines, refused  ┊        A
  └ A:opt0             └ A:opt0                     └┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┤ depends_on
                                                             └ A:opt0

  │  = refines, the place of a card
  └ A:opt0 = alternative_to A, the place of an option
  ┄  = depends_on, not a place
  ✗  = the link operation refuses this link
```

payload.title: A builder session runs only while the board log says it started and its process is still alive
payload.why: A builder runs in its own process and can die without a word, for example when a person kills it by hand. A flag in a log alone then says it still runs, and the ticket pulses forever. So the board also checks the process itself, and keeps the agent's many lines out of the board log so that log stays a short record of ticket state.
payload.body:
The pulse and the live preview (#vi-board) mean that a builder session runs right now. The board needs a test for "runs now" that a dead process cannot fool.

**When a session runs.** The board log records when a session starts and when it ends (#vi-board-state). The start names the builder process. A session counts as running only while both hold:

- the board log has a start for it and no end yet;
- the named process is still alive.

When a builder process exits without writing its end, the server writes the end for it (#vi-board-details). A process that dies with no one to see it — killed from a terminal, or started before a server restart — fails the second test, so its ticket stops pulsing at once.

**Where the agent's lines go.** Each session writes the agent's stream to its own session log, one line per event with its time. The start in the board log names that session log. The live preview reads it (#vi-board-details). The board log holds no agent line: one board event per agent line would bury the few ticket moves under thousands of lines that every fold must read.

**Example.**

- Ticket T "r/01" sits in building.
- Session S is the build of T. Its process is P.
- The board log holds "S started, process P, session log L".

1. The agent writes 200 lines. They go to L. The board log does not change. T pulses, and the preview shows the lines of L.
2. A person kills P from a terminal. Nothing writes an end for S.
3. The board reads the log: S has no end. It checks P: P is dead. S does not run, and T stops pulsing.
4. T stays in building until the stop is handled (#werk-board-control). L stays on disk; the preview drops it once T leaves building (#vi-board).

```
board log                 process P     session log L    T on the board
---------                 ---------     -------------    --------------
S started (P, L)          alive         200 lines        pulses, preview of L     (step 1)
(no change)               killed        (no change)                               (step 2)
still no end for S        dead          (no change)      no pulse                 (step 3)

running = "started, no end"  AND  "process alive"
```

payload.title: Each part of a reply stays under the message that asked for it
payload.why: A person can send a second message while a reply still streams. The pane draws that message at once. If the pane adds each new part of the reply at the bottom, the rest of the first reply reads as the answer to the second message.
payload.body:
To keep a reply under its own message, every message the person sends gets a turn name when the browser sends it. A turn is one message from the person and the whole reply to it, up to the line that ends it with duration and cost (see #werk-progress).

The agent of a conversation runs one turn at a time. The server keeps the turns that are sent and not yet ended, in the order they were sent. Each part of the agent's reply belongs to the oldest of these turns. The end line closes that turn, and the next turn starts. The live channel carries the turn name with each part, and the pane adds the part to that turn.

Two edge cases:

- The agent exits before it ends its turns. Each open turn gets the exit as its end, so no turn waits forever.
- A part arrives for a turn that this page did not send, for example after a reload. The pane starts a new turn for it.

Example:

- Message A "Summarise the open cards" is sent. Its reply streams.
- Message B "Also list the ghosts" is sent while the reply to A streams.

1. The pane draws A, then the first part of reply A under it.
2. The person sends B. The pane draws B below reply A. The server holds B, because A has not ended.
3. A second part of reply A arrives. The pane adds it under A, above B.
4. The end line of A arrives. A closes, and the agent starts B.
5. The first part of reply B arrives. The pane adds it under B.

```
server order: [A, B]        pane
                            A  Summarise the open cards
  part 1 -> A                 a1
  part 2 -> A                 a2     <- step 3: lands above B
  end    -> A  (A closed)     12s · $0.04
                            B  Also list the ghosts
  part 1 -> B                 b1     <- step 5
```

payload.title: A plan writer proposes a card only for an answer that changes the finished product
payload.why: A proposed card asks a person to judge it before it counts. An answer about the order of the work leaves the finished product the same. The tickets already hold that answer, and a person sees and changes it on the ticket board.
payload.body:
A plan writer answers two kinds of question that no card settles:

- A **product answer** changes what the finished subtree does, or how it is built inside. Examples: a refund rounds down to the cent, or two features share one storage table.
- A **delivery answer** changes only how the work reaches that result: which ticket comes first, how one feature splits into tickets, or what a ticket waits for.

To keep the cards a person must judge to real decisions, a writer returns only product answers as card records (see #st-spec-answers). A delivery answer stays in the spec and in the tickets: the order is the tickets' blocked_by (see #st-ticket), and a person sees it on the ticket board (see #vi-board).

The test: imagine the subtree finished with the answer, and finished without it. If the two results are the same, the answer is a delivery answer and gets no card.

Example:

- Subtree S "Customers get refunds".
- Answer A: "A refund rounds down to the cent."
- Answer B: "The refund form ticket waits for the refund API ticket."

1. The writer applies the test to A. Without A, a refund can round up, so the result differs. A is a product answer.
2. The writer returns A as a card record. The plan proposes it under S.
3. The writer applies the test to B. With B or without it, the finished refunds work the same. B is a delivery answer.
4. The writer puts B in the refund form ticket's blocked_by. No card record holds B.

```
answer  same result without it?   goes to
------  -----------------------   --------------------------------
A       no  (rounding differs)    card record -> proposed under S
B       yes                       blocked_by of the refund form ticket
```

The rule covers the plan writers only. A person may still put a delivery decision on the map when it has a reason beyond one plan, for example when an earlier step makes a later one testable.

payload.title: The printed card shows the words of its options, excerpts and sources
payload.why: The agent reads a card only in its printed form. If the printed card names an option or an excerpt but not its words, the agent must run one more query for each. It skips those queries, and then it reopens a choice that was already rejected for a reason.
payload.body:
To give the agent the same proof that a person sees on the card's page (see #vi-detail), `werk show` prints the proof with its words, not only the ids.

The printed card ends with up to three sections, after the links:

- **Options**: each option that is `alternative_to` the card, with its title and its why-not reason.
- **Say**: each excerpt that the card is `supported_by`, with its speaker and its verbatim words.
- **Ev**: each source that the card is `supported_by`, with its title and its finding.

The link types come from #vi-edges. An item that is still a ghost carries the word `proposed` (see #werk-propose-new). A section with no items is not printed.

Example:

- Card `price` "We charge per seat".
- Option `price:opt0` "We charge per project", why-not "Projects vary in size too much".
- Excerpt `price:ex0`, speaker you, words "Seats are what the buyer counts".
- Source `src-survey` "Buyer survey", finding "8 of 10 buyers budget per seat". It is a ghost.

1. The agent runs `werk show price`.
2. The output prints the card, its links, and then the three sections.
3. The agent reads the rejected option and its reason without a second query.

```
card price  [decided]
We charge per seat
  ...links...
Options
  price:opt0  We charge per project
    why not: Projects vary in size too much
Say
  price:ex0  you: "Seats are what the buyer counts"
Ev
  src-survey  Buyer survey  proposed
    finding: 8 of 10 buyers budget per seat
```

payload.title: A merge never removes an entry from the list of pure files
payload.why: Each branch adds its own pure files to the list in the change that writes them. A merge that keeps only one side drops the other side's files from the coverage check. Those files then pass with no test, and no output shows the loss.
payload.body:
The coverage check judges only the files on the explicit list of pure files (see #werk-test-pure-list). Two branches that each add a pure file both edit that list, often at the same place. Version control then reports a conflict on the list.

**The answer.** The resolution keeps every entry from both sides. The list is a set: the order of its entries has no effect on the verdict, and each file appears once. A file leaves the list only when the file is deleted or stops being pure, in a change that says so. A merge never removes an entry as a side effect.

**Example.**

- The main line has the list `[a, b]`.
- Branch X adds the pure file `x`. Its list is `[a, b, x]`.
- Branch Y adds the pure file `y`. Its list is `[a, b, y]`.

1. Branch X merges into the main line. The list is `[a, b, x]`.
2. Branch Y merges next. Both sides changed the same place, so the merge conflicts on the list.
3. The resolution keeps both entries. The list is `[a, b, x, y]`.
4. The coverage check prints one line each for `a`, `b`, `x` and `y`.

```
main   [a, b] --------+-- [a, b, x] --+-- [a, b, x, y]
                      |               |
X      [a, b, x] -----+               |
                                      |
Y      [a, b, y] ---------- conflict -+   keep x AND y
```

A resolution that keeps `[a, b, y]` passes every check, because `x` is no longer judged. The coverage output after a merge is the test: it holds one line for every pure file of both branches.

payload.title: A dispute refuses an excerpt
payload.why: A dispute says that the evidence may be wrong. The words of an excerpt are an exact copy of one message, and the quote check proved it. A doubt about an excerpt is a doubt about how the citing card reads those words, so the card is the thing to change.
payload.body:
A dispute on a source flags every card that cites the source for review (see #vi-srcnode). An excerpt is a different kind of node from a source (see #werk-excerpt-event). It holds a pointer into a transcript, not a finding.

To keep a proven quote from being marked as doubtful, a dispute on an excerpt fails. The refusal names the reason: the words are the transcript's. The excerpt and its citing card stay as they were.

When the citing card reads the quote wrongly, the person reopens or edits that card. When the message itself was mistaken, the decision built on it is reopened in the same way. The excerpt stays, because the message was said.

Example:

- X "We charge per seat" is a decided card.
- X:ex0 is an excerpt that X cites. Its text is the message "charge per seat".
- S is a source that X also cites.

1. The person disputes X:ex0. The dispute fails and says that an excerpt's words are the transcript's. X gets no flag.
2. The person disputes S. X gets a flag for an evidence review.
3. The person decides that X reads X:ex0 wrongly. The person reopens X. X:ex0 does not change.

```
  dispute X:ex0 ──✕ refused: "the words are the transcript's"
                     X: no flag

  dispute S ──────▶ X  flagged for review   (S ◀─supported_by── X)

  reopen X ───────▶ X  open                 (X:ex0 unchanged)

  ✕ = the operation fails, nothing enters the log
```

payload.title: A pure file's coverage counts only the lines that its own test file runs
payload.why: A test for one pure file often calls other pure files too. Those calls run lines in the other files, so a file can reach the threshold with no test of its own. When its own tests are deleted, the check still passes and nobody sees the loss.
payload.body:
The per-file coverage check (see #werk-test-pure-list) compares each listed pure file with the threshold. To stop a caller's test from hiding a missing test, the check counts a line as covered only when the file's own test file runs it.

**Own test file.** The test file that sits next to the pure file and has the same name with a test suffix. One pure file has one own test file.

**How the run works.** The coverage run runs each own test file alone, with coverage on, and keeps only the result for its pure file. The results join into one report, and the per-file check reads that report. Lines that another file's test runs do not count. The ordinary test run still runs the whole suite, so no test is lost from it.

**A missing own test file.** A listed pure file with no own test file counts as 0%. The check names the test file that is missing.

**Example.**

- Pure file R renders text. Its own test file is R-test.
- Pure file K finds card links. R calls K. Its own test file is K-test.
- R-test runs every line of K, because R calls K.

1. The coverage run runs K-test alone. K-test runs all lines of K. K is at 100%.
2. Someone deletes K-test. R-test still runs every line of K.
3. The coverage run runs R-test alone and counts only R's lines from it. No run counts K's lines.
4. K has no own test file, so the check sets K to 0%, names K-test as missing, and fails.

```
step  run          lines it may count   K's result
----  -----------  -------------------  ------------------------
1     K-test       K                    100%   pass
2     (K-test deleted)
3     R-test       R only               K not counted
4     check        -                    0%     fail: K-test missing

R-test --calls--> R --calls--> K
   |                            ^
   +-- K lines run, NOT counted-+
```

payload.title: Every real card has a chain of real parents up to the root
payload.why: A real card under a ghost has no place in the map until someone accepts the ghost, and a discard of the ghost leaves it with no parent. A loop of parents never reaches the root, so the tree cannot draw those cards and an accept walk never reaches a real card. So a change to the tree that breaks the chain is refused before it is written.
payload.body:
A card sits in the tree by its refines link to its parent (see #vi-edges). An accept walks up from a ghost to the first real card (see #werk-propose-new). Both depend on one fact: from every real card, the parent links go up through real cards only, end at the root, and never repeat a card.

To keep that fact, a change to the tree refuses in two cases, and says which one:

- **A real card under a ghost.** A ghost is a proposed card that nobody has accepted. A real card cannot take a ghost as its parent. A ghost under a ghost, or a ghost under a real card, is allowed.
- **A loop.** A card cannot take as its parent a card that already sits below it.

The same refusal holds for every operation that sets a parent: the link operation with the refines type, a move, and a drag in the map. A ghost proposed under its parent is checked the same way.

Example:

- X "We charge per seat" is a real card under the root.
- G "The invoice lists each seat" is proposed under X. G is a ghost.
- Y "Seats are counted each month" is a real card under X.

1. The agent moves Y under G. The move is refused: Y is real and G is a ghost. Y stays under X.
2. Eryk accepts G. G is real now.
3. The agent moves Y under G. The move succeeds.
4. The agent moves X under Y. The move is refused: Y already sits below X, so the move closes a loop.
5. The agent moves Y back under X. The move succeeds: X does not sit below Y.

```
  step 1             step 3             step 4
  root               root               root
   └ X                └ X                └ X  ──move under Y──✗ loop
      ├ G (ghost)        └ G                 └ G
      └ Y ─move─✗          └ Y                  └ Y

  (ghost) = proposed, not accepted     ✗ = refused, nothing written
```

payload.title: A ticket card on the board cuts a long title short with an ellipsis
payload.why: A long title makes one ticket card many times taller than the others. Then a column holds fewer tickets and a person cannot scan it. A fixed height keeps every card the same size, and the full title stays one step away.
payload.body:
To keep columns easy to scan, the board card shows the title up to two lines. A longer title stops at the end of the second line with an ellipsis. Pointing at the title shows it in full. The drawer header always shows the full title (see #vi-board-details).

Example:

- A ticket with the title "Import ticket files from the plan folder and skip ids that already exist on a second run".
- A column narrow enough that this title needs four lines.

1. The board card shows the first two lines and an ellipsis.
2. A person points at the title. The full title shows in a tooltip.
3. A person clicks the card. The drawer header shows the full title.

```
+-----------------------------+
| Import ticket files from    |
| the plan folder and skip... |
+-----------------------------+
```

payload.title: A judge agent can only read, and it cannot ask for more tools
payload.why: A judge must not change the code that it judges. If a judge could ask for a write tool, a model would decide each ask, and a write can look reasonable for the ticket. A fixed list of read tools makes the limit certain and costs no model call.
payload.body:
A judge agent is the grader (#lp-prod-judge) or a reviewer (#lp-prod-review). A judge reads the diff of a pass and returns a judgement. A builder agent asks for a tool when it needs one, and the overseer sends that ask to a classifier (see #lp-overseer-asks). A judge does not use that route.

To keep a judge from changing the code, the loop starts each judge with a fixed tool list:

- tools that read a file, search the text of files, and find files by name;
- the git operations that show a diff, the commit history, and one commit.

The judge session has no way to ask for another tool. The agent runtime refuses every other tool call at once, and the judge continues without it. No ask reaches the overseer, so the classifier never runs for a judge. The overseer still watches a judge session for silence and for loops, the same as a builder session.

**Example**

- B: the builder session of pass 2. It can ask for any tool.
- G: the grader session of pass 2. It has the read list only.
- O: the overseer of the build pass.

1. B asks to run the test command. O sends the ask to the classifier. The classifier allows it, and B runs the tests.
2. G reads the diff and two source files. Each call is on its list, so it runs with no ask.
3. G tries to edit a test file. The runtime refuses the call. O sees no ask.
4. G returns its scores. The edit did not happen, so G judged the code that B wrote.

```
  B --ask: run tests--> O --> classifier --allow--> B runs tests
  G --read diff------> on list --> runs, no ask
  G --edit test------> not on list --> refused by the runtime
                                       (O sees nothing)
  G --scores---------> loop
```

payload.title: The cards-cited check counts only accepted cards of the planned subtree
payload.why: A proposed card is not in the map until a person accepts it. The plan itself proposes cards under the subtree it plans, so counting them would make the plan fail its own check. A proposed card counts after it is accepted, on the next run of the checks.
payload.body:
The cards-cited check needs the set of decided cards in the planned subtree (#st-ticket-set-checks). To keep that set to what the person agreed to, the check reads the subtree root and the cards under it through accepted cards only. A proposed card is not in the map (see #werk-propose-new). It does not count, also when it is proposed with the status decided. A card under a proposed card is also proposed, so it does not count either.

This matters because the plan proposes its own new answers as cards under the subtree root (see #st-spec-answers). Those answers wait for the person. The tickets of the same plan run do not have to cite them.

**Example**

- R "Invoices" is the subtree root. It is decided.
- A "The invoice shows the seat count" refines R. It is decided and accepted.
- P "Round the seat count up" refines R. The plan proposed it, with the status decided. Nobody accepted it.
- The tickets cite R and A.

1. The checks run. The set is R and A. The cards-cited check passes. P is not in the set.
2. The person accepts P.
3. The checks run again. The set is R, A and P. The check fails and names P, because no ticket cites it.

```
step 1                 step 3 (after P is accepted)
R  decided   cited     R  decided   cited
├─ A decided cited     ├─ A decided cited
└╌ P proposed  -       └─ P decided NOT CITED  -> fail

├─  accepted refines link
└╌  proposed card: not counted
```

payload.title: A plan archives each open ticket that the new ticket set leaves out
payload.why: The ticket writer rewrites a needed open ticket in place, under its own number. So a ticket that the writer does not carry into the new set is a ticket that the current spec does not need. A broken rewrite is different: the writer kept the ticket, so the plan holds it instead of archiving it.
payload.body:
A plan must decide which open tickets the current spec no longer needs (#st-plan-archive). To avoid a second judge beside the ticket writer, the plan reads the answer from the new ticket set.

- **Open** means ready or blocked (#werk-board-control). The plan looks only at open tickets of its own subtree. A ticket that started to build is not the plan's to change (#st-plan-extend).
- **Left out** means the writer does not carry the ticket into the new set under its number. The writer either marks the number as dropped or writes no file for it. The plan archives the ticket, with the reason that #st-plan-archive sets.
- **Kept but broken** means the writer rewrote the ticket, and the rewrite fails its own checks (#st-ticket-own-checks). The plan does not archive it, and the old text does not stay buildable. The plan moves the ticket to blocked, with the failed check as the reason. An agent fixes the ticket and clears the reason.

Example:

- Subtree X has three open tickets: 3 "Show the seat count", 4 "Charge per seat", 5 "Export the invoice".
- Ticket 6 "Refund a seat" is in building.
- The spec of X changes. Export is no longer in it.

1. The plan runs. The writer rewrites 3 and 4 under their own numbers, and leaves 5 out.
2. The rewrite of 3 passes its own checks. Ticket 3 stays in ready with its new text.
3. The rewrite of 4 has no acceptance criteria. Ticket 4 moves to blocked, with that failed check as the reason.
4. Ticket 5 is archived, with the reason that the current spec of X no longer needs it.
5. Ticket 6 does not change, because it started to build.

```
            before plan     new set            after plan
  3  ready  ------------>  3 (passes)    -->  3  ready, new text
  4  ready  ------------>  4 (fails)     -->  4  blocked: no acceptance criteria
  5  ready  ------------>  (left out)    -->  5  archived: X no longer needs it
  6  building              (not the plan's) -> 6  building
```

payload.title: A quote matches only words that a person or the agent wrote, never text that the tooling added
payload.why: The tooling around a conversation adds text to a turn: the line that names the open card, expanded command prompts, reminders, tool calls and tool results. An excerpt names a speaker. A quote taken from added text would claim that the speaker said words that nobody in the conversation wrote.
payload.body:
To keep an excerpt true to its speaker, the quote operation searches only the messages that a person typed or that the agent wrote as its reply (see #werk-excerpt). Text that the tooling added never counts as a match, even when it sits in the same turn as the person's words.

Added text is any text that no person and no agent reply wrote:

- the line that tells the agent which card is open,
- a command or skill prompt that the tooling expands into the turn,
- a reminder that the tooling injects into the turn,
- a tool call and its result.

A quote whose text occurs only in added text fails, and the quote operation writes nothing. A rule that lives in added text has its own source, such as a card or a prompt file. Cite that source instead.

**Example**

- Card X "Export is its own command".
- The person types "make export its own command".
- The tooling adds the line "[the map is now at #X]" and the reminder "Write short sentences." to the same turn.
- The agent reply contains a tool result that repeats "Write short sentences.".

1. The agent quotes "make export its own command" for X. The text occurs once, in the person's words. The excerpt is written, with the person as speaker.
2. The agent quotes "Write short sentences." for X. The text occurs in the reminder and in the tool result, both added text. The quote fails. Nothing is written.
3. The agent quotes "the map is now at" for X. The text occurs only in the open-card line. The quote fails. Nothing is written.

```
turn of the conversation              searched?   quote result
------------------------------------  ---------   ---------------------------
[the map is now at #X]                no          step 3: fails
Write short sentences.                no          step 2: fails
make export its own command           yes         step 1: excerpt, speaker = person
agent reply text                      yes
  tool result: Write short sentences. no          step 2: fails

no  = added by the tooling, never a match
yes = written by a person or the agent
```

payload.title: A refused decide lists every missing fact in one refusal
payload.why: A check that stops at the first missing fact costs one failed attempt for each fact. The agent also cannot see how far the card is from decided. One full list lets the agent fix the card in one pass.
payload.body:
To avoid one failed decide per missing fact, the contract check tests every fact before it answers. When one or more facts are missing, the refusal names all of them together. It names them in the order of #werk-contract-facts. Each entry is the fix message of #werk-contract-fix for that fact. A fact that holds does not appear.

**Example**

- Card X "We charge per seat" has the decider you.
- X has a depends_on link to a decided card, so its basis holds.
- X has no option and no kill criterion.

1. The agent tries to decide X. The check finds two missing facts.
2. The refusal lists the option fact first, then the kill criterion, each with its fix.
3. The agent records an option and a kill criterion on X.
4. The agent tries to decide X again. All facts hold, and X becomes decided.

```
decide X  (attempt 1)
  who       ok
  basis     ok
  options   MISSING  -> fix: record an option
  kill      MISSING  -> fix: record a kill criterion
  => refused, 2 entries in one refusal

record option on X, record kill on X

decide X  (attempt 2)
  who ok | basis ok | options ok | kill ok
  => X is decided
```

payload.title: Each test runs with the globals that its own code expects
payload.why: Server code and client component code expect different globals. One test run can hold both kinds of test in one process. A global that a setup changes for one kind of test then changes for the other kind too, and that test fails for a reason outside its own code.
payload.body:
A global is a function or an object that the runtime gives to all code without an import: the network function, streams, timers, a document. Server code expects the globals of the runtime. Client component code expects a browser-like environment with a document.

To keep the result of each test about its own code, a harness meets three conditions:

- A test sees the globals that its own code expects.
- A setup that adds an environment for one kind of test puts back each runtime global that it replaced.
- A test that builds something in a shared environment removes it when it ends, also when the test fails.

How a project meets these conditions depends on its stack. A card for the stack names the environment and when the harness sets it up (see #werk-test-dom for werk).

**Example**

- D: a browser-like environment. A setup registers D one time, before any test file loads. D brings its own network function.
- C: a component test. It renders a button into the document of D.
- S: a server test. It calls the network function to reach a local test server.

1. The setup registers D. D replaces the runtime network function with its own.
2. The setup puts the runtime network function back. The document of D stays.
3. C renders the button, checks it, and removes it. The document is empty again.
4. S calls the network function. S gets the runtime function and reaches the local server.
5. Without step 2, S gets the network function of D. That function follows browser rules, so S fails for a reason outside its own code.

```
step  network function   document of D    who uses it
----  ----------------   -------------    -----------
 1    D's  (replaced)    empty            setup
 2    runtime (put back) empty            setup
 3    runtime            button -> empty  C
 4    runtime            empty            S -> local server: OK
 5    D's  (no step 2)   empty            S -> fails
```

payload.title: A fence tag picks its grammar by any common name, and a tag with no grammar renders plain
payload.why: Card writers tag a fence the way they do in any Markdown file, so the same language arrives under several names. A wrong grammar colours the wrong tokens, and that misleads more than no colour. So an unknown tag gets no colour, but the code still shows in full.
payload.body:
To avoid a missed colour for a common tag, each grammar of the highlighter (see #werk-codeblock) answers to the usual names of its language, in any letter case. Examples: `sh`, `shell` and `zsh` select the shell grammar. `tsx` and `typescript` select the script grammar. `jsonc` selects the JSON grammar.

To avoid a broken card, a tag with no grammar, or no tag at all, never fails the render. The fence renders in the same box with the same sideways scroll. The code shows as plain escaped text with no colour.

When a fence has a tag, the tag shows as a small label in the corner of the box. The label shows for a known tag and for an unknown tag.

payload.title: An accept takes a ghost card's evidence with it, and a discard keeps evidence that another card still cites
payload.why: A card that commits without its evidence shows no proof, and its links to that evidence stay held. A source can support many cards, so one card that goes must not delete what another card cites. An excerpt or a source that no card cites any more is an orphan that no view reaches.
payload.body:
A ghost card often arrives with ghost evidence: a source it cites, or an excerpt quoted for it. The card is supported_by each one. The accept and the discard must each decide what happens to that evidence (see #werk-propose-new for ghosts, the accept and the discard).

**Accept.** The accept makes real every ghost source and ghost excerpt that the accepted card is supported_by. The same holds for each ghost refines parent that the accept commits with it. A real source stays as it is.

**Discard.** The discard drops a ghost excerpt of each card it drops, because an excerpt is quoted for one card (#werk-excerpt). It drops a ghost source only when no remaining card, real or ghost, cites it. A source that another card cites stays, as it does for a removal (see #werk-remove).

Example:

- C "We charge per seat", a ghost card.
- C:ex0, a ghost excerpt quoted for C.
- S "Pricing survey", a ghost source. C and D both cite S.
- D "The invoice shows the seat count", a second ghost card.
- T "Churn study", a ghost source. Only C cites T.

1. The person discards C. C and C:ex0 leave the map. T leaves, because no card cites it now.
2. S stays a ghost, because D still cites it.
3. The person accepts D. D and S become real together. D shows S as its proof at once.

```
before                       after discard C       after accept D

C (ghost) --> C:ex0 (ghost)  (gone)                (gone)
C (ghost) --> T (ghost)      (gone)                (gone)
C (ghost) --> S (ghost)      S (ghost)             S (real)
D (ghost) --> S              D (ghost) --> S       D (real) --> S

-->  supported_by
```

payload.title: A page redraws each chat thread from its transcript every time its live channel connects
payload.why: The live channel keeps nothing for a page that is not connected. A block that the agent finishes while the page is away never reaches that page by the channel. The transcript holds every finished block, so a read of it on each connect closes the gap.
payload.body:
The live channel is the open stream on which the server pushes new blocks to a page. A page that reloads, opens in a second browser tab, or loses the channel (a laptop sleep, a server restart) misses every block sent while it was not connected.

To close that gap, the page reads each conversation's whole transcript every time its live channel connects, the first connect included. It redraws the thread from that read. The transcript holds only finished blocks, and a streamed block shares its id with its finished form (see #werk-progress). So the read never removes a block that still streams: the streamed block stays, and its finished form replaces it when it arrives. Each conversation tab reads its own transcript (see #werk-multichat).

Example:

- A conversation tab `T`. Its transcript holds `B1` (the person's message "Rename X") and `B2` (the agent's reply, finished).
- The page shows `B1` and `B2`. The agent starts to stream `B3`.

1. The laptop sleeps. The live channel drops.
2. The agent finishes `B3` and `B4`. The server writes both to the transcript. No page receives them.
3. The laptop wakes. The live channel connects again. The page reads the transcript of `T` and draws `B1` to `B4`.
4. The agent starts to stream `B5`, and the channel drops and connects again. The read returns `B1` to `B4`. The page keeps the streamed `B5`.
5. The finished `B5` arrives with the same id. It replaces the streamed `B5`.
6. The channel connects again with no missed block. The read draws the same thread, and nothing changes on screen.

```
step  live channel   transcript of T      pane of T
----  ------------   ------------------   ---------------------------
 0    open           B1 B2                B1 B2 [B3~]
 1    dropped        B1 B2                B1 B2 [B3~]
 2    dropped        B1 B2 B3 B4          B1 B2 [B3~]      (stale)
 3    connects       B1 B2 B3 B4  -read-> B1 B2 B3 B4
 4    connects       B1 B2 B3 B4  -read-> B1 B2 B3 B4 [B5~]
 5    open           B1 B2 B3 B4 B5       B1 B2 B3 B4 B5
 6    connects       B1 B2 B3 B4 B5 -read-> B1 B2 B3 B4 B5  (no change)

[Bn~]  block Bn while it streams, not yet in the transcript
-read->  the page reads the whole transcript and redraws the thread
```

payload.title: A reader of the server lock sees a whole lock or none, never a half-written one
payload.why: A starting server reads the lock to find the pid of the holder. If it reads the lock while another process writes it, it finds no pid. Then it takes a live lock for a stale one, and two servers share one directory.
payload.body:
The lock holds the pid and the port of the server (see #werk-onelock). The lock changes at two moments: a start takes it, and the holder records its port after the listen succeeds. A second start can read the lock at either moment.

To avoid a half-written read, every change to the lock is complete before any reader can see it:

- When a start takes the lock, the lock appears whole, or not at all. When two starts take it at the same moment, only one succeeds.
- When the holder records its port, a reader sees the old lock or the new lock, never a mix and never an empty file.

Example:

- Server A holds the lock: pid 100, no port yet.
- The listen of A succeeds on port 4211.
- Start B reads the lock at the same moment.

1. A writes the new lock, pid 100 and port 4211, out of sight of readers.
2. A puts the new lock in place in one step.
3. B reads the lock. It sees pid 100 with no port, or pid 100 with port 4211.
4. Pid 100 is alive in both cases. B waits, then refuses to start.
5. B never sees an empty lock, so B never removes the lock of A as stale.

```
  A: lock {pid 100, no port}     B: reads lock
          |                               |
  1 A writes {pid 100, port 4211} aside   |
          |                               |
  2 A swaps it in, one step  ---------  3 B sees {100, no port}
          |                               or {100, 4211}
          v                               |
  A: lock {pid 100, port 4211}   4 pid 100 alive -> B waits, refuses

  never:  B sees {}  ->  "stale"  ->  two servers
```

payload.title: An excerpt points at one spoken message by its position in the transcript and a character span
payload.why: A reader checks an excerpt by opening the same transcript later and finding the same characters. A position that changes with a filter, or a message that nobody said, makes that check fail or mislead. So the pointer counts every line of the file and names only words the person or the agent said.
payload.body:
See #werk-excerpt for the parts of a pointer: session, message position, span and speaker.

A pointer must land on the same characters every time a reader follows it. To make that hold, each part has one fixed meaning:

- **Session**: the conversation whose transcript holds the quote.
- **Message position**: the place of the message among all lines of the transcript, counted from zero. Hidden lines count too, so a view that hides tool calls or results does not move the pointer.
- **Span**: the start and end character of the quote inside the text of that one message. A quote never crosses from one message into the next.
- **Speaker**: the person or the agent, as the transcript records it on that message.

Only a spoken message can hold a quote. A spoken message is text that the person typed or the agent wrote. Tool calls, tool results and text that the harness injects are never spoken messages. A tool result can hold a copy of the quoted words, for example a printed earlier conversation. Harness text puts words in the person's mouth that the person never typed. Text that occurs only in such lines gives no match.

payload.title: An excerpt holds only the words that the quote matched, and those words never change
payload.why: An excerpt is proof of what someone said in a conversation. If an agent could write or edit its words, a reader could not tell a real quote from a paraphrase. So the quote check is the only way in, and nothing can change the words after it.
payload.body:
To keep every excerpt a true copy of the transcript, the map gives an excerpt three guards:

- Only the quote operation creates an excerpt. A plain add of an excerpt refuses, because it has no transcript match behind it.
- The words of an excerpt never change. A retitle or a text edit refuses on an excerpt, before and after the accept. A note on the excerpt is still allowed, because a note does not touch the words.
- The quote creates the excerpt and its supported_by link from the citing card as one change (see #pr-log-one-event). The two accept or discard together (see #werk-propose-new). So there is never an excerpt that supports no card.

An excerpt is its own node kind beside the card (see #map-card). It is not a source: a source holds a finding that a person can dispute, and an excerpt holds only words.

Example:

- Card X "We charge per seat" is decided.
- Conversation C holds the message "seats are the unit we bill".

1. The agent quotes "seats are the unit we bill" from C for X. The quote finds the text, and ghost excerpt X:ex0 appears with a held link from X.
2. The agent tries to retitle X:ex0 to "we bill per seat". The retitle refuses.
3. Eryk accepts X:ex0. The excerpt and its link go live together.
4. The agent tries to edit the text of X:ex0. The edit refuses again.
5. The agent tries to add an excerpt X:ex1 by hand, with no quote. The add refuses.

```
step 1   X ··held··> X:ex0 "seats are the unit we bill"   (ghost)
step 2   retitle X:ex0          -> refused
step 3   accept X:ex0
         X ──supported_by──> X:ex0 "seats are the unit we bill"   (live)
step 4   edit X:ex0             -> refused
step 5   add X:ex1 by hand      -> refused

··held··>  a link that waits for the accept
──>        a live link
```

payload.title: `werk add` gives a card with no `--status` the status open
payload.why: Every card in the map needs a status, because the find operation, the search index and the rollup sort cards by status. A card with no status falls out of all three. Most new cards are open, so open is the safe default.
payload.body:
`werk add <id> --title "..."` with no `--status` flag proposes a card with the status open. `--status proto` proposes it as proto. The form of the command is on #werk-cli-add.

An option, a source and an excerpt get no default status. Status is a property of a card only, and the decide check and the rollup read it only on cards.

payload.title: The fake agent lives as long as the agent it stands in for
payload.why: A chat agent and a build pass both read their messages from an open input stream. The chat agent answers many messages, and a build pass answers one and ends. A fake with the wrong life hangs a test or hides a bug in how werk ends a pass.
payload.body:
A chat agent and a build pass take their input the same way, so the fake cannot tell them apart by how it is started. werk tells the fake which kind of agent it stands in for (see #st-build-seam-role-env).

- **Chat agent.** One conversation lives across many messages (see #werk-onechat). Each message is one turn: the fake records it, plays the next scripted reply, and waits. It ends when its input closes.
- **Any other agent.** One pass does one unit of work and exits (see #lp-stateless). The fake reads the first message, plays one reply, and exits with the code of the script. A permission answer that arrives on the input is part of that reply, not a new turn (see #werk-test-fake-ask-open).

Example:

- C is a chat agent. Its script has two replies, R1 and R2.
- B is a build pass. Its script has one reply, R1, with one permission ask, and exit code 0.

1. A test sends message M1 to C. C plays R1 and waits.
2. The test sends M2 to C. C plays R2 and waits.
3. The test closes the input of C. C exits.
4. werk sends the prompt P to B. B plays R1 and prints the ask A.
5. werk sends the answer to A. B does not start a new turn. B finishes R1 and exits with 0.

```
C (chat)                      B (build pass)
M1 --> R1, wait               P  --> R1 ... ask A
M2 --> R2, wait               answer A --> (same turn)
input closed --> exit         R1 done --> exit 0
```

payload.title: A page fetches the whole map each time its live channel connects
payload.why: The server learns about a log write from a watch on the log's directory. A write that comes before the watch is live, or while the server is down, sends no push. A fetch on each connect draws that write anyway, so the watch needs no timer behind it.
payload.body:
A watch is a request to the operating system: tell the server when a file in the log's directory changes. The watch starts on its own thread and gives no signal when it is live. So a write in that moment, or a write while the server is stopped, sends no push to the pages (see #werk-write-changed for the push and the fetch it starts).

To avoid a page that misses such a write, the page fetches the whole map every time its live channel connects: on the first load, and on every reconnect after the server restarts. The server starts the watch before it accepts a connection, so every write before the connect is in that fetch, and every write after it sends a push. No timer polls the log.

Example:

- Card X "We charge per seat" is in the log.
- A page shows X. The server is stopped, so the page's live channel is down.
