1. A command appends card Y "The invoice shows the seat count". No server sees the write.
2. The server starts. It starts the watch, then it accepts connections.
3. The page's live channel connects again. The page fetches the map and draws X and Y.
4. A command appends card Z. The watch sees it, the server pushes changed, and the page fetches and draws X, Y and Z.
5. Nothing is written. No push comes, and the page fetches nothing.

```
step   log        server              page
----   --------   -----------------   -----------------------------
 1     X Y        stopped             shows X   (channel down)
 2     X Y        watch, then listen  shows X
 3     X Y        live                connect -> fetch -> shows X Y
 4     X Y Z      watch sees Z        changed -> fetch -> shows X Y Z
 5     X Y Z      live                no push, no fetch
```

In the picture, "connect" is the live channel opening, "changed" is the push, and "fetch" reads the whole map.

payload.title: A quote must occur exactly once in the transcript
payload.why: An excerpt points at one span of one message. When the quoted text occurs twice, the program must pick one occurrence, and the citer did not choose it. A repeat inside one message is as much a guess as a repeat across two messages.
payload.body:
See #werk-excerpt for the rule that a quote fails instead of guessing. This card fixes what counts as one match: one occurrence in the whole transcript, not one message that holds the text.

The quote operation counts every occurrence of the text in every message. It writes an excerpt only when the count is one. Otherwise it fails, writes nothing to the log, and says which case it found:

- no exact match;
- a match in more than one message, with the number of messages;
- more than one match inside one message, with the number of matches.

The citer then quotes more of the sentence until the text is unique.

Example:

- M3 is the message "We pick a grid."
- M7 is the message "the grid wins, and the grid is faster."

1. The citer quotes "pick a grid". It occurs once, in M3. The excerpt points at M3, span 3 to 14.
2. The citer quotes "grid". It occurs in M3 and in M7. The quote fails and names 2 messages.
3. The citer quotes "the grid". It occurs only in M7, but two times. The quote fails and names 2 matches in M7.
4. The citer quotes "the grid is faster". It occurs once, in M7. The excerpt points at M7, span 19 to 37.

```
M3  "We pick a grid."
M7  "the grid wins, and the grid is faster."

quote                 M3  M7   result
"pick a grid"          1   0   excerpt  M3 span 3-14
"grid"                 1   2   fails: 2 messages
"the grid"             0   2   fails: 2 matches in M7
"the grid is faster"   0   1   excerpt  M7 span 19-37

M3, M7 columns: number of occurrences of the quote in that message
span: start and end character offset in the message text
```

payload.title: Only one start at a time may remove a stale lock
payload.why: A start reads the lock, sees a dead holder, and then removes the lock. These are two steps. A second start that read the same stale lock can remove a fresh lock that a third start took in between, and then two servers share one log.
payload.body:
A stale lock is a lock whose holder process is dead (see #werk-onelock). The lock itself is taken in one step that fails when a lock exists (see #werk-onelock-hardlink). The removal of a stale lock is not one step, so it needs its own protection.

To avoid the race, a start takes a second, short-lived lock, the guard, before it removes a stale lock. The guard is taken in the same one-step way as the lock and holds the pid of its holder. Under the guard, the start reads the lock again. It removes the lock only if the lock still names a dead process. Then it drops the guard and tries to take the lock again. A start that finds the guard taken waits one poll interval and tries again.

A guard whose holder is dead is removed like a stale lock. That removal has no guard of its own. It goes wrong only if a start dies inside the short removal step and two other starts race over its guard.

Example:

- The lock names pid 7. Pid 7 is dead.
- Start A and start B both read the lock and see that it is stale.
- Start C begins a moment later.

1. A takes the guard. B tries to take the guard, finds it taken, and waits.
2. A reads the lock again. It still names pid 7, so A removes it and drops the guard.
3. C finds no lock and takes it. The lock now names pid 9, which is alive.
4. B takes the guard and reads the lock again. Pid 9 is alive, so B keeps the lock and drops the guard.
5. B waits for pid 9 like for any live holder, and then refuses. One server serves the log.

Without the guard, B removes the lock of pid 9 in step 4 and takes its own. C and B then both serve.

```
            lock            guard
start     | pid 7 (dead) | free
step 1  A | pid 7 (dead) | A        B: guard taken -> wait
step 2  A | (none)       | free     A: pid 7 dead -> remove
step 3  C | pid 9 (live) | free     C: take lock
step 4  B | pid 9 (live) | B        B: pid 9 alive -> keep
step 5  B | pid 9 (live) | free     B: wait, then refuse

lock  = the server lock; (none) = no lock file
guard = the guard; free = nobody holds it
```

payload.title: A reference links only to a card that the map can open
payload.why: A link must always open a card. A removed card has no page in the map, so a link to it opens nothing. Its reference therefore stays plain text until the card comes back.
payload.body:
Only a known id becomes a link (see #werk-reflink). To keep every link able to open a card, a known id is the id of a card that is in the map now. A card that is removed, or that went out with a removed parent, is not known (see #werk-remove). The text that names it does not change. Only the way the text renders changes.

A restore makes the card known again. Every reference to it links again, with no edit to the text.

Example:

- Card `pricing` "We charge per seat" is in the map.
- Card `pricing-seats` "The invoice shows the seat count" refines `pricing`.
- Card `invoice` has the body "see #pricing-seats".

1. A reader opens `invoice`. The reference `#pricing-seats` is a link. A click opens `pricing-seats`.
2. A person removes `pricing`. The removal takes `pricing-seats` out with it.
3. The reader opens `invoice` again. The body still reads "see #pricing-seats", but as plain text with no link.
4. A person restores `pricing`. `pricing-seats` comes back with it.
5. The reader opens `invoice`. `#pricing-seats` is a link again.

```
step  cards in the map          body of invoice        renders as
1     pricing                   "see #pricing-seats"   link
        +- pricing-seats
2-3   (none: both removed)      "see #pricing-seats"   plain text
4-5   pricing                   "see #pricing-seats"   link
        +- pricing-seats

+-  = refines (the child sits under the parent)
```

payload.title: A removal frees nothing: the card's links wait, and its id stays taken
payload.why: A removal only hides a card, and every event about it stays in the log. So a link of a removed card cannot be lost, and it comes back when both of its ends are in the map again. A new card cannot take the id, because the old card's history would fold into the new card.
payload.body:
#werk-remove says that a restore returns a card and its edges. This card states what happens when the two ends of a link leave and come back at different times, and what happens to the id while the card is out.

- **A link waits.** A link is out of the map while one or both of its ends are out. It is not deleted. It is back in the map at the moment when both ends are in the map again. The order of the removals and the restores has no effect on the result, because each removal is undone on its own (see #werk-remove-restore-undo).
- **The id stays taken.** While a card is out, an add with the same id refuses and names the restore as the way back. The log still holds every event of the old card under that id (see #pr-log). A new card with that id would get the old card's links and history.

Example:

- Card `login` depends_on card `session`.
- Both cards are decided and in the map.

1. A person removes `login`. The link `login -> session` leaves the map with it.
2. A person removes `session`.
3. A person restores `login`. The link stays out, because `session` is still out.
4. An agent tries to add a new card with the id `session`. The add refuses and names the restore.
5. A person restores `session`. The link `login -> session` is back in the map, as it was before step 1.

```
step   login   session   link login -> session
0      in      in        in
1      out     in        waits
2      out     out       waits
3      in      out       waits
4      in      out       waits   (add 'session' refuses)
5      in      in        in
```

payload.title: An id inside a longer token is not a reference
payload.why: Card ids hide inside other text: command flags, doubled markers, joined ids, and escaped characters. If that inner part linked, the reader would see a link that the writer did not mean. So the whole token links, or none of it does.
payload.body:
A reference starts only where a token starts. #werk-reflink already keeps a URL fragment and a path out, by the word character or slash before the #. Four more characters join the text to a token before it, so the text after them is not a reference:

- a second `#`: a doubled marker or a heading-like run.
- a hyphen: the end of a command flag or a hyphenated word.
- a colon: the inside of a longer id, such as the option part of an option id.
- an ampersand: an escaped character, which is never a card id.

A longer token that is itself a known id still links whole (see #werk-reflink).

Example:

- The map holds the card al-diff.
- A note on a card holds four pieces of text: `--al-diff`, `##al-diff`, `&al-diff` and `see #al-diff`.

1. The note renders `--al-diff`. A hyphen comes before `al-diff`. It stays text.
2. The note renders `##al-diff`. A second # comes before `#al-diff`. It stays text.
3. The note renders `&al-diff`. An ampersand comes before `al-diff`. It stays text.
4. The note renders `see #al-diff`. A space comes before the #. It links to al-diff.

```
text           character before the id   result
-------------  ------------------------  ------
--al-diff      -  (hyphen)                text
##al-diff      #  (second #)              text
&al-diff       &  (ampersand)             text
see #al-diff   space                      link -> al-diff
```

payload.title: A card with no decider needs the option fact
payload.why: A card with no who may be yours to decide. If the option fact waited for who, a bare card would fail twice, once before who is set and once after.
payload.body:
The option fact of #werk-contract-facts applies when who is you, and also when who is not set. A card with who set to me or prototype needs no option. A refused decide lists every missing fact at once (#werk-contract-all-missing), so a bare card sees the option fact in its first refusal.

The cost is small. If who later becomes me, the option fact no longer applies, and the check does not refuse the card for it.

Example:

- X "We charge per seat" has a title and a body.
- X has no who, no basis, no option and no kill criterion.

1. The agent tries to decide X. The check refuses it and names four missing facts: who, basis, option, kill criterion.
2. The agent sets who to you, adds a basis, an option and a kill criterion.
3. The agent tries to decide X again. The check passes. X is decided.
4. Had the agent set who to me in step 2, it could skip the option. The check passes without it.

The same bare card X, without and with this rule:

```
option fact waits for who          option fact applies with no who

decide X  -> refused               decide X  -> refused
   missing: who, basis, kill          missing: who, basis, option, kill
set who=you, basis, kill           set who=you, basis, option, kill
decide X  -> refused               decide X  -> decided
   missing: option
add option
decide X  -> decided

2 refusals                         1 refusal
```

The left column is what the check does when it tests the option fact only for who=you.

payload.title: A command accepts a card id with or without a leading hash sign
payload.why: Cards, notes and tickets write a reference as a hash sign and an id. An agent copies that text into a command as it is. If the command treats the hash sign as part of the id, it finds no card and the agent spends a turn on the retry.
payload.body:
A reference in text has the form `#id` (see #werk-reflink). An agent that copies it into a command gives `#auth`, not `auth`.

Every argument that names a card takes `#auth` and `auth` as the same id. This holds for the positional ids of every verb (`show`, `link`, `status`, `reopen`, `accept`, and the others) and for every flag whose value is a card id, such as `--parent` and `--under`. The command removes one leading `#` and nothing else.

An argument that holds text keeps its hash sign. `--title`, `--why`, `--body`, `--why_not` and a note's text are text, so `--why "see #auth"` stays as written.

No card id starts with a hash sign, because an `add` with `#auth` creates the card `auth`.

payload.title: A log change tells every open view to read the whole map again
payload.why: The signal carries no cards and no events, only the fact that the log grew. Each view then reads the map the same way it reads it on first load. So a view has one way to get the map, and it cannot drift from the log.
payload.body:
To keep every open view in step with the log, the server watches the log. When the log grows, the server sends a bare signal on the live channel to every open page. The signal holds no data. Each page then reads the whole fold again and redraws it (see #pr-log for the fold).

A page never patches its copy of the map from the signal. There is one read path: the full read of the fold. This rule covers the map only. The chat stream carries its own blocks (see #werk-progress).

Example:

- Tab T1 and tab T2 show the map. Both show card #a.
- The agent adds card #b from the command line.

1. The add appends one event to the log.
2. The server sees the log grow and sends the signal to T1 and T2.
3. T1 reads the whole fold again. It now shows #a and #b.
4. T2 does the same and shows #a and #b.
5. Nothing else changes in the log. The server sends no signal, and no tab reads again.

```
  agent           log            server             T1, T2
    |  add #b      |               |                   |
    |------------->| (1) +1 event  |                   |
    |              |-- grows ----->|                   |
    |              |               |-- (2) signal ---->|  no data
    |              |<------------- (3)(4) read fold ---|  each tab
    |              |-- #a, #b ---------------------->  |  redraw
```

Numbers match the steps. "signal" is the bare push on the live channel. "read fold" is the same full read a page does on first load.

payload.title: Each agent that the pipeline starts carries its role outside the prompt
payload.why: One fake agent stands in for every agent in a test, so it must know which job each launch does. The prompt text changes often, so a fake that reads the prompt gives the wrong reply after a wording change. A role value in the environment of the launch stays fixed, and the real agent ignores it.
payload.body:
To pick a reply, a test fake must know which job a launch does: chat, build, grade, review, or another. The fake cannot see the caller. It sees only its own launch. One fake plays every agent at both test seams (see #werk-v0-seams), and the grader, the reviewers and the classifiers of a build are fakes too (see #st-build-seam).

So the pipeline puts a role name in the environment of every agent process it starts. A role name is a short fixed word for the job, such as builder or grader. The pipeline sets it in production and in tests alike. The real agent does not read it, so the value changes nothing in production. The fake reads it and picks the reply that the test scripted for that role. A new kind of agent gets a new role name when it is added.

Example:

- A test scripts reply R1 for the role builder and reply R2 for the role grader.
- The builder prompt opens with "Implement the ticket". The grader prompt opens with "Grade the change".

1. The pipeline starts the builder with the role builder. The fake reads builder and plays R1.
2. The pipeline starts the grader with the role grader. The fake reads grader and plays R2.
3. A later change rewords the builder prompt to "Build the ticket". The role stays builder. The fake still plays R1, and no test changes.

```
pipeline                      fake agent            script
--------                      ----------            ------
start(role=builder,
      "Build the ticket") --> reads role=builder -> R1
start(role=grader,
      "Grade the change") --> reads role=grader  -> R2

role=   the role name in the environment of the launch
R1, R2  the replies the test scripted for each role
```

payload.why: takes the rule that every write to the log needs the token, and that the agent never holds the token, from werk-serve-trust
takes the scheduler that fills free build slots from ready, which is what skips a held ticket, from st-build-parallel
takes the return to ready after a merge loop stops, which this card keeps distinct from a person's stop, from st-build-stop-ready
takes the rule that the run ends when nothing can build or merge, and reports what waits, from st-build-stuck-park
takes the rule that each card has a thread of notes from werk-chat
takes alternative_to as the only link from an option to its card
takes the rule that the place of a new card is part of the one event that adds it
takes the move as the way a person corrects the place of a card
takes the session start and end events in the board log from vi-board-state
takes the server's end for a builder that exits while live, and the summarised preview lines, from vi-board-details
takes the end line with duration and cost that closes a turn in the pane from werk-progress
takes from #st-ticket that blocked_by holds the delivery order and the planner decides it, so a delivery answer has a place outside the map
takes from #vi-board that a person sees each ticket and its blockers on the board, so a delivery answer stays visible without a card
takes the three kinds of proof a card carries from vi-detail
takes the alternative_to and supported_by link types that select each section from vi-edges
takes the ghost state that the proposed mark shows from werk-propose-new
takes the fact that an excerpt is its own kind of node, with fixed words, distinct from a source, from #werk-excerpt-event
takes what a dispute does, a review flag on every card that cites the evidence, from #vi-srcnode
takes the rule that a refines link places a card in the tree under one parent from vi-edges
takes the drawer header that shows the full title from vi-board-details, so the board card can cut it short
takes the reviewers as the second kind of judge agent, next to the grader
takes the classifier route for a builder's ask, which a judge does not use
takes the rule that a proposed card is not in the map until it is accepted from werk-propose-new
takes the fact that the plan proposes its own answers as cards under the subtree root from st-spec-answers
takes the meaning of an open ticket and the reversible archive from werk-board-control
takes the per-ticket checks that a rewrite must pass to stay buildable from st-ticket-own-checks
takes the set of facts and their order from werk-contract-facts
takes the fix message of each entry from werk-contract-fix
takes the rule that a source stays while a card that cites it stays from werk-remove
takes the fact that an excerpt is quoted for the one card that cites it from werk-excerpt
takes the fact that one source node can support many cards from vi-srcnode
takes the rule that each tab is its own conversation, with its own transcript to read, from werk-multichat
takes the ghost stage and the rule that a link proposed with a node accepts or discards with it from werk-propose-new
takes the rule that a node and the link that belongs to it are one change from pr-log-one-event
takes the excerpt as its own node kind beside the card from map-card
takes the add command and its --status flag from werk-cli-add
takes the signal by which werk tells the fake which kind of agent it stands in for from st-build-seam-role-env
takes the rule that one chat conversation lives across many messages from werk-onechat
takes the rule that a build pass does one unit of work and exits from lp-stateless
takes the rule that a permission answer arrives on the input during a turn from werk-test-fake-ask-open
takes the changed push and the fetch of the whole map that it starts from werk-write-changed
takes the one-step take that fails when the file exists, which the guard uses too
takes that a removal takes the card and its refines subtree out of every view, and a restore puts them back, from werk-remove
takes the rule that nothing leaves the log, so a removed id still has its events, from pr-log
takes the rule that each removal is undone on its own, so the restore order does not change the result, from werk-remove-restore-undo
takes the option fact and the rule that a me or prototype card needs no option from werk-contract-facts
takes the written form of a reference, a hash sign before the id, from werk-reflink
takes the rule that one scripted fake stands in for every agent at both test seams
The single shared DOM is the way werk meets the rule that each test sees its own globals.

payload.title: The dot sits inline before the title
payload.why_not: The dot takes a full slot in the card row. The title and the counts get less width on a card that is already narrow.

payload.title: The note route refuses every request that carries an Origin header, so only a local process without a page reaches it
payload.why_not: A shell sends no Origin header, so the agent itself passes the check and can write notes that the inbox shows as the person's. A header check also replaces the token, which the server already chose over header checks.

payload.title: Give the agent the token so that it can write notes through the route
payload.why_not: The agent reads its own environment and transcript, so a prompt that reaches the agent could use the token for any write. The agent already writes notes from the command line, so it gains nothing from the route.

payload.title: Remove the note route from the server
payload.why_not: The chat card keeps the route as the server's way to write a note and fill the clipboard. Removing it changes that card, not this one.

payload.title: A link keeps the form it was written in
payload.why_not: A bare id and a code span then look like plain words or like code. The reader cannot see which words open a card without a hover.

payload.title: A stopped ticket goes back into the queue, and the merge loop builds it again when a slot is free
payload.why_not: The same build starts again on the same path, so the stop undoes nothing.

payload.title: A stop moves the ticket to blocked, with the stop as the blocking reason
payload.why_not: Blocked means an agent holds the ticket for a reason it states or resolves. A person's stop returns the ticket to ready, and a person releases it.

payload.title: The thread carries over to the new proposal of the same id
payload.why_not: The old notes judge words that the person can no longer see. The reason for the correction already lives in the log and the inbox.

payload.title: The link operation adds all four link types, refines and alternative_to included
payload.why_not: A refines link then gives a node a second parent, so the tree shows it twice and its rollup counts it twice. It also skips the check a move runs, which drops each depends_on link that the new place puts in one line.

payload.title: The board log alone says if a session runs
payload.why_not: A builder killed by hand never writes its end. The ticket then pulses until a person notices.

payload.title: One board event per agent line
payload.why_not: The board log then holds thousands of agent lines per session. Every fold of the board must read them to find a few ticket moves.

payload.title: A separate session record per ticket holds the running flag and the process
payload.why_not: The board log already records when a session starts and ends. A second record of the same fact can disagree with it.

payload.title: The pane draws a sent message only when its turn starts
payload.why_not: The person sees no sign that the message was received while the earlier reply runs. Several waiting messages stay invisible.

payload.title: A new message stops the running reply
payload.why_not: It throws away work that the person did not ask to stop. Stopping a turn is a separate action.

payload.title: Propose a card for every answer the writers give, delivery order included
payload.why_not: A delivery card leaves the finished product the same, so the person judges a card that changes nothing on the map. The tickets and the board already show that answer.

payload.title: The printed card lists only the ids and titles of its options and sources
payload.why_not: The agent must run one more query for each item to read its reason, and it does not. The rejected reason is the part that stops a choice from coming back.

payload.title: The proof sections print only when the reader asks for them with a flag
payload.why_not: The agent does not know that it needs the proof until it has read it. The card page shows the proof every time, so the printed card does the same.

payload.title: Fix one order for the merged list, the branch's entries first
payload.why_not: The coverage check reads each entry on its own, so the order changes no verdict. A fixed order adds a rule that a merge can break with no effect on the result.

payload.title: Each pure file declares itself, and the check finds the files, so no shared list exists
payload.why_not: It replaces the explicit list that #werk-test-pure-list decided, which a merge rule cannot change. While that list exists, the union rule keeps it correct.

payload.title: A dispute on an excerpt flags its citing card for review, the same as a source
payload.why_not: The flag questions words that the quote check already proved exact. The real doubt is about the card, and a reopen of the card says that directly.

payload.title: Any test in the suite that runs a line counts it as covered
payload.why_not: A caller's test runs the lines of the files it calls. A pure file then passes with its own tests deleted, and the check cannot see the loss.

payload.title: Allow the link and let the map show the real card at the root until the ghost is accepted
payload.why_not: The place of a real card would then change when someone accepts or discards a ghost. Nobody accepted that change of place.

payload.title: Accept the ghost parent at the same time as a real card is put under it
payload.why_not: That is an accept that the person never gave. The accept gate exists to stop exactly this silent commit.

payload.title: The title wraps in full on the board card
payload.why_not: One long title makes its card many times taller, so the column holds fewer tickets and is hard to scan.

payload.title: A judge asks for tools like a builder, and the classifier denies each write
payload.why_not: The classifier allows an ask that makes sense for the ticket, and a write can look sensible to it. Each ask also costs a model call that a fixed list does not need.

payload.title: The cards-cited check also counts proposed cards that carry the status decided
payload.why_not: The plan proposes its own answers under the subtree root, so every plan with a new answer would fail its own check. Tickets would also have to cite words the person has not accepted.

payload.title: The subagents that the agent instructions name travel with them into every project
payload.why: An instruction to use a subagent that the project does not have fails at the moment the agent needs it. So the definitions go wherever the instructions go.
payload.body:
The werk agent instructions tell an agent to use three subagents: one that decides whether a requirement is worth sampling, one that builds the options of a fork, and one that classifies a module before its tests are written. A project werk works on does not define them, so werk ships their definitions with the instructions. Each agent that reads the instructions also gets the subagents, with every werk command named by the path werk runs from.

Inside a werk checkout, the project already defines the same subagents, so werk adds nothing.

payload.why: takes the sampler subagent as one that is shipped

payload.title: The plan compares each open ticket's cited cards with the new spec to decide what is no longer needed
payload.why_not: This adds a second judge beside the writer, who already read the spec. A ticket's cards can stay in the spec while its slice moves to another ticket, so the comparison keeps a ticket that nothing needs.

payload.why: takes the test-scope subagent as one that is shipped

payload.title: The instructions name a subagent only when the project defines it
payload.why_not: The project never defines them, so the agent loses the sampling and test-scope steps in every project but werk.

payload.title: The plan archives an open ticket whose rewrite fails its own checks
payload.why_not: The writer kept that ticket, so the spec still needs it. An archive hides a needed ticket, and nobody sees that it needs a fix.

criterion.text: A build pass in a target project asks for a subagent that is not there

payload.title: The plan keeps the earlier text of an open ticket whose rewrite fails its own checks
payload.why_not: The earlier text fits the earlier spec. A build from it can deliver work that the current spec no longer asks for.

payload.title: Quote added text too, and name the tooling as its speaker
payload.why_not: Added text is a copy of a rule that already has a source, such as a card or a prompt file. An excerpt of the copy is weaker evidence than a link to that source.

payload.title: Report only the first missing fact
payload.why_not: Each further fact costs one more failed decide. The agent cannot see how far the card is from decided.

payload.title: All tests run in one browser-like environment
payload.why_not: Server code then calls the network, stream and timer functions of the environment, not of the runtime. These behave differently, so a server test can pass or fail for a reason that production never sees.

payload.title: An unknown tag falls back to the nearest known grammar
payload.why_not: A guessed grammar colours the wrong tokens, for example a Python comment read as a shell keyword. Plain text is honest about what the highlighter knows.

payload.title: Only the exact canonical tag selects a grammar
payload.why_not: Writers use `sh` as often as `bash` and `tsx` as often as `ts`. A strict match leaves many ordinary fences without colour.

payload.title: A discard leaves every ghost source and excerpt in place
payload.why_not: An excerpt or a source that only the dropped card cited stays as a ghost that no card reaches. Nobody can find it to accept or discard it.

payload.title: A discard drops every ghost source and excerpt the dropped card cites
payload.why_not: A ghost source that a second card also cites disappears, and that card loses its evidence before anyone judges it.

payload.title: Evidence stays a ghost after the accept, and the person accepts it one node at a time
payload.why_not: The real card shows no proof until extra accepts follow. Its supported_by links stay held, so the card reads as unsupported.

payload.title: The server keeps the blocks it sent and replays the ones a page missed when it connects again
payload.why_not: The server must keep a buffer and a position for every page, and a server restart loses that buffer. The transcript already holds every finished block, and it survives a restart.

payload.title: A page reads the transcript only when it first loads
payload.why_not: A page that loses its live channel and connects again misses every block of the gap. The pane shows an incomplete thread until the person reloads the page.

payload.title: Write the lock in place with an exclusive create
payload.why_not: The file exists empty for a moment after the create. A reader in that moment finds no pid and takes a live lock for a stale one.

payload.title: A reader that cannot parse the lock waits and reads it again
payload.why_not: A reader cannot tell a lock that is being written from a lock that a crash left broken. A broken lock then blocks every start until a person removes it.

payload.title: The message position counts only the spoken messages
payload.why_not: The count then depends on which lines a reader filters out. A change to the filter moves every later pointer to a different message.

payload.title: A quote can come from a tool call or a tool result too
payload.why_not: A tool result can hold a printed copy of the same words, which makes a second, false match. Words in a tool line are not words that anyone said in the conversation.

payload.title: An excerpt is a source with transcript fields
payload.why_not: A source can be disputed and can be written by hand. An excerpt as a source would let a hand-written quote pass as an extracted one.

payload.title: The quote creates the excerpt and its link to the citing card as two separate changes
payload.why_not: A failure between the two leaves an excerpt that supports no card. One change can never be half done.

payload.title: `werk add` refuses a card with no `--status`
payload.why_not: Almost every new card is open, so the flag adds words to nearly every call and catches no real mistake.

payload.title: The fake treats every launch with an open input stream as a chat agent
payload.why_not: A build pass keeps its input open for permission answers and never closes it. A fake that waits for the next message never exits, and the test hangs until its time limit.

payload.title: Two fakes: one for the chat agent, one for build passes
payload.why_not: The command-line tests and the browser tests use one fake agent. Two fakes need two script forms and two launch records, and a test that runs both kinds reads two places.

payload.title: Poll the log on a timer as well as watch it
payload.why_not: A poll adds a second trigger and an interval to tune. The fetch on each connect already covers every write the watch can miss, so the poll adds no coverage.

payload.title: A repeat inside one message takes its first occurrence
payload.why_not: The span then points at a place the citer never chose. That is the guess that extraction exists to prevent.

payload.title: The citer names which occurrence to take, by its position
payload.why_not: The citer must count occurrences by eye, which is the memory-based step that extraction removes. Quoting more of the sentence gives the same result and keeps the quote readable.

payload.title: Remove the stale lock only if its content still matches what the start read
payload.why_not: The compare and the remove are still two steps. A fresh lock can arrive between them, so the race stays.

payload.title: Rename the stale lock to a private name, then check what was moved
payload.why_not: A rename moves whatever lock is there at that moment, so it can move a fresh lock. Putting that lock back is a second race.

payload.title: Use an operating-system file lock that the kernel releases when the holder dies
payload.why_not: The runtime offers no portable advisory file lock. Without one, the server needs a native module, and the project has no dependencies.

payload.title: A reference to a removed card renders in a separate removed style, such as grey text with a removed label
payload.why_not: A removed card is out of every view, and a marked reference puts it back into view as noise. The removed list already shows what is out and lets a person restore it.

payload.title: A removal deletes the links of the removed card
payload.why_not: A restore then cannot give back the map as it was. A person must find and add each link again by hand.

payload.title: A removed card's id is free for a new card
payload.why_not: The log still holds the old card's events under that id. The fold then mixes the old links and history into the new card.

payload.title: The option fact waits for who
payload.why_not: A bare card that becomes yours is refused a second time, for an option the first refusal did not name. The agent needs two passes for one card.

payload.title: A command refuses an id with a hash sign and prints the id without it
payload.why_not: The agent learns nothing it can act on except to retry. Every copied reference costs one failed command and one more turn.

payload.title: A command removes a leading hash sign from every argument, text included
payload.why_not: A title, a why or a note may start with a hash sign on purpose, for example a reference at the start of a sentence. Changing text would corrupt what the agent wrote.

payload.title: Send the new events or the new fold on the live channel
payload.why_not: The page then gets the map two ways, from the full read and from the push. The two can disagree, and a page that misses one push keeps a wrong map.

payload.title: The fake picks a reply by a pattern on the prompt text
payload.why_not: Each change to a prompt's wording breaks the tests that match it. Two jobs whose prompts share words get each other's replies.

payload.title: The pipeline passes the role as a command-line argument
payload.why_not: The real agent rejects an argument it does not know, so production launches fail.

payload.title: The fake picks a reply by the order of launches
payload.why_not: The order of agents that run at the same time is not fixed, so a reply can go to the wrong job.

payload.title: Every decided card in the ticket's dependency closure is a delivery line: does the diff do what this card says?
payload.why_not: A ticket builds one slice of a subtree, and its closure reaches the subtree's root card. The grader then fails a correct slice for work that later tickets build, and the builder cannot close that gap.

payload.title: The cards that the ticket cites are delivery lines, and the other cards in its closure are contradiction lines
payload.why_not: A ticket often cites a broad card, such as the root of a subtree, so a cited card still asks one slice for work it does not do. The ticket's acceptance criteria already state the exact scope that the ticket claims.

payload.title: A card with no defined decider requires an alternative option
payload.why: A card with no who may be yours to decide. If the option waited for who, a bare card would fail twice, once before who is set and once after.
payload.body:
A card that you decide needs an alternative option that was weighed, or a written reason that none was (#werk-contract-facts). The same rule holds for a card whose who is not set yet. A card whose who is me or prototype needs no option.

| who | needs an alternative option |
|---|---|
| you | yes, or a written reason that none was weighed |
| not set yet | yes, so that a bare card is not refused a second time |
| me or prototype | no |

A refused decide lists every missing fact at once (#werk-contract-all-missing), so a card with no who sees the missing option in its first refusal.

The cost is small. If who later becomes me, the card no longer needs an option, and the check does not refuse it for one.

Example:

- X "We charge per seat" has a title and a body.
- X has no who, no basis, no option and no kill criterion.

1. The agent tries to decide X. The check refuses it and names four missing facts: who, basis, option, kill criterion.
2. The agent sets who to you, adds a basis, an option and a kill criterion.
3. The agent tries to decide X again. The check passes. X is decided.
4. Had the agent set who to me in step 2, it could skip the option. The check passes without it.

```
 option waits for who               option required with no who

 decide X  -> refused               decide X  -> refused
    missing: who, basis, kill          missing: who, basis, option, kill
 set who=you, basis, kill           set who=you, basis, option, kill
 decide X  -> refused               decide X  -> decided
    missing: option
 add option
 decide X  -> decided

 2 refusals                         1 refusal
```

payload.why: takes the option fact and the rule that a me or prototype card needs no option
takes the rule that one refusal lists every missing fact, which is why a bare card sees the option at once

A project's map does not hold werk's own cards, so an agent in that project cannot open a card id that points into werk's map. Every rule that the instructions or a shipped subagent relies on is written out in the text, in plain words, where it is used. An example names no real card. It uses a made-up id, such as #checkout-retry.

The rule holds for werk's own map too. The text reads the same in every project, and a change to a werk card does not change what an agent is told until the text changes with it.

payload.title: A corrected ghost keeps the thread of notes that led to its new words
payload.why: A ghost is corrected by a discard and a new proposal with the same id, and the notes on it are the reason for the correction. If the thread were cleared, the person would lose why the words changed. A marker in the thread shows where the new words begin, so each note is read against the words it was about.
payload.body:
A thread of notes belongs to a card id, not to one proposal of it (see #werk-chat). A discard of a ghost removes the card from the map, and it leaves the thread of the id in place. When the same id is proposed again, the new ghost carries that thread. So the notes that asked for the correction stay beside the card they led to.

The thread shows a marker at each point where the id was proposed again. A note above a marker was about the earlier words. A note below it is about the new words. A reader never has to guess which words a note meant.

A card that is discarded and never proposed again leaves its thread out of sight. The person can still read the notes they typed in the inbox. An id that someone reuses for an unrelated card carries the old thread, so a new idea gets a new id.

Example:

- X is a ghost card, "Export is its own command".
- N1 is a note on X: "Say what the export writes."

1. The person writes N1 on X. The thread of X shows N1.
2. The agent discards X. X leaves the map. N1 stays in the thread of the id.
3. The agent proposes X again with new words that answer N1. The new ghost X shows N1, then a marker "proposed again".
4. The person writes N2 on X. The thread shows N1, the marker, then N2.

```
step  map          thread of X
1     X (ghost)    N1
2     -            N1                  (kept, out of sight)
3     X2 (ghost)   N1 | proposed again
4     X2 (ghost)   N1 | proposed again | N2

X  = the first proposal of the id
X2 = the second proposal of the same id, with new words
|  = the marker: notes above it were about the earlier words
-  = no node with the id in the map
```

payload.why: takes the rule that each card has a thread of notes, kept by the card id

payload.title: A discard clears the thread of the ghost
payload.why_not: The notes that asked for the correction are the reason for the new words. Clearing them hides why the card changed, and the person loses the thread that led to it.

payload.title: An excerpt points at one spoken message in a conversation, and through its session at the wider context
payload.why: A reader must open the same message later and find the same characters. A position that moves with a filter, or a message that nobody said, breaks that. The session and the time lead on from the quote to the wider conversation around it.
payload.body:
A pointer must lead a reader to the same characters every time, and from there to the conversation around them. Each part has one fixed meaning:

- **Conversation**: the conversation whose chat log holds the quote. The chat log sits in the project beside the decision log, so the quote check can read it.
- **Session**: the id of the agent session of that conversation. From it, a reader or an agent opens the raw transcript of the session, when that file is still on disk, and reads the context around the quote. This is how an agent answers "what is this card about".
- **Message position**: the place of the message among all lines of the chat log, counted from zero. Hidden lines count too, so a view that hides tool calls or results does not move the pointer.
- **Span**: the start and end character of the quote inside the text of that one message. A quote never crosses from one message into the next.
- **Speaker**: the person or the agent, as the chat log records it on that message.
- **Time**: when the message was written.

Only a spoken message can hold a quote. A spoken message is text that the person typed or the agent wrote. Tool calls, tool results and text that the tooling adds are never spoken messages. A tool result can hold a printed copy of the quoted words. Tooling text puts words in the person's mouth that the person never typed. Text that occurs only in such lines gives no match.

The excerpt also keeps the quoted words as its own text. The chat log and the transcript are files on one machine and are not part of the project history. On another machine, or in a fresh clone, both can be missing. The card then still shows the words, the speaker and the time.

Example:

- Card X is "We charge per seat".
- Conversation "pricing" has session 6ae61be7.
- Message 12 is typed by the person: "seats are the unit we bill".
- Message 13 is a tool result that prints message 12 again.

1. The agent quotes "seats are the unit we bill" for X. The pointer is: conversation pricing, session 6ae61be7, message 12, span 0 to 26, speaker person, and the time of message 12.
2. A reader opens the chat log of pricing, takes line 12 and cuts the text at the span. The reader finds the same words.
3. An agent asks what X is about. It follows the session id to the raw transcript, if the file exists, and reads the messages around message 12.
4. Message 13 holds the same words, but it is a tool result. It is not a spoken message, so it never counts.

```
 excerpt of X                         chat log of "pricing"
 conversation  pricing  ----------->  line 11  person   ...
 message       12       ----------->  line 12  person   "seats are the unit we bill"   <- span 0..26
 time          t12                    line 13  tool     (prints line 12 again)          <- never a match
 session       6ae61be7 ---+
                            |         raw transcript (when on disk)
                            +------>  the same session, with the messages around line 12
```

payload.title: The message position counts only the spoken messages
payload.why_not: The count then depends on which lines a reader filters out. A change to the filter moves every later pointer to a different message.

payload.title: A quote can come from a tool call or a tool result too
payload.why_not: A tool result can hold a printed copy of the same words, which makes a second, false match. Words in a tool line are not words that anyone said in the conversation.

payload.title: A dispute marks the cards that cite a source for review, and makes none of them stale
payload.why: Evidence can be doubted while every decision stays as it was. A stale mark says that a decision changed, and none did. A review mark says only that the ground of a decision is in doubt.
payload.body:
A dispute says that one source may be wrong. It puts a review mark on every card that cites the source (see #vi-edges for the supported_by link). It reaches those cards only, one hop. It makes no card stale or paused, and it changes no status. Clearing the dispute removes the source's review marks. The marks belong to the source, so they do not clear one card at a time.

A reader who meets a review mark asks one question: does this card still hold if the evidence is wrong? If it does, the reader clears the dispute. If it does not, the reader reopens the card, and the ordinary rules of a change take over (see #vi-prop).

The map has three marks, and they come from different operations. A change to a card marks cards that depend on it or sit under it (see #vi-prop). A postponement marks every card downstream (see #pr-wf-paused). A dispute marks the cards that cite the evidence.

Example:

- Billing is the root card.
- P is "We charge per seat". It cites the source S.
- Y is "The invoice shows the seat count". It depends on P.
- W is "The invoice has a seat limit line". It is a child of Y.
- Z is "The invoice PDF has a seat column". It depends on Y.
- T is "Seat prices are per month". It cites S.
- S is the source "Pricing study: per-seat billing".

1. P is amended. Y goes stale. W and Z stay clear, because a change marks one hop.
2. P is reopened as postponed. Y, W and Z all go paused, at any distance. P itself stays open.
3. S is disputed. P and T get a review mark. Y, W and Z stay clear: Y depends on P, not on S, and a dispute never passes through a depends_on link.
4. A person writes a note on P. No card is marked.
5. The dispute of S is cleared. The review marks on P and T go.

```
 Billing
  +-- P  "We charge per seat"               --supported_by--> S
  +-- Y  "The invoice shows the seat count" --depends_on-->   P
  |    +-- W  "The invoice has a seat limit line"   (child of Y)
  +-- Z  "The invoice PDF has a seat column" --depends_on-->  Y
  +-- T  "Seat prices are per month"        --supported_by--> S

  S  source "Pricing study: per-seat billing"

  operation                       marks            reach                       mark
  P amended or reopened           Y                direct dependents/children  stale
  P reopened as postponed         Y, W, Z          every distance              paused
  S disputed                      P, T             the cards that cite S       review
  note on P                       none             -                           none
  dispute of S cleared            clears P, T      -                           review gone
```

payload.why: takes what each link type carries: supported_by flags for review, depends_on carries a change
takes the rule that a change marks one hop, which a dispute is set against
takes the postponement mark that reaches every distance, which a dispute is set against

payload.title: A dispute makes the citing cards stale
payload.why_not: Stale means that a card it stands on changed. Doubt about evidence is not a change, and a stale mark would send the reader along the dependency chain for what may be a false alarm.

payload.title: A dispute reaches every card downstream of the citing cards, like a postponement
payload.why_not: Only the cards that cite the evidence stand on it. The cards further down stand on decisions that have not changed, so a mark there would claim a doubt nobody has.

criterion.text: Dispute a source that two cards cite. Both cards get a review mark, no card becomes stale or paused, and a card that depends on a citing card stays clear. If any of those fails, revisit.

payload.title: A dispute reopens the citing cards, so a review mark is a reopen
payload.why_not: A reopened card is open, so it stops being a basis and its dependents wait or go stale, which spreads a doubt that may be a false alarm. It would also look like any other open card, and the reader would lose the sign that the card is decided and its evidence is in doubt.

payload.title: A doubted source is handled by listing the cards that cite it and reopening each one by hand
payload.why: A source can turn out wrong while every decision that cites it still holds. Only a person can tell which decisions fall with the source. So the map lists who cites the source and leaves each decision to be reopened or kept, with no mark of its own.
payload.body:
A source may turn out to be wrong. To avoid a third kind of mark, the map keeps no state for a doubted source. A person asks what cites the source, and the answer is the cards with a supported_by link to it. For each of those cards the person asks one question: does this card still hold if the evidence is wrong? If it holds, the person does nothing. If it does not, the person reopens the card, and the ordinary rules of a change take over (see #vi-prop).

Example:

- S is the source "Pricing study: per-seat billing".
- P is "We charge per seat". It cites S.
- T is "Seat prices are per month". It cites S.
- Y is "The invoice shows the seat count". It depends on P.

1. The person learns that S is wrong, and asks what cites S. The answer is P and T. No card is marked.
2. The person reviews P. P does not hold without S, so the person reopens P. Y goes stale, one hop.
3. The person reviews T. T holds on other grounds, so the person leaves it decided. Nothing happens to T.
4. If nobody reviews a card, nothing marks it. The list of citing cards is the only record of the doubt.

```
  S  source "Pricing study: per-seat billing"
  ^   ^
  |   +--supported_by-- T  "Seat prices are per month"     (reviewed: kept)
  +--supported_by------ P  "We charge per seat"            (reviewed: reopened)
                        ^
                        +--depends_on-- Y  "The invoice shows the seat count"   (stale)

  action             result            mark
  ask what cites S   P, T              none

payload.title: Each part of a reply stays under the message that asked for it
payload.why: A person can send a second message while a reply still streams. The pane draws that message at once. If the pane adds each new part of the reply at the bottom, the rest of the first reply reads as the answer to the second message.
payload.body:
To keep a reply under its own message, every message the person sends gets a turn name when the browser sends it. A turn is one message from the person and the whole reply to it, up to the line that ends it with duration and cost (see #werk-progress).

The agent of a conversation runs one turn at a time. The server keeps the turns that are sent and not yet ended, in the order they were sent. Each part of the agent's reply belongs to the oldest of these turns. The end line closes that turn, and the next turn starts. The live channel carries the turn name with each part, and the pane adds the part to that turn.

A message whose turn has not started shows a waiting mark under it: "waits for the reply above". The mark tells the person that the message arrived and has no answer yet. It goes away when the turn starts.

Two edge cases:

- The agent exits before it ends its turns. Each open turn gets the exit as its end, so no turn waits forever, and no waiting mark stays.
- A part arrives for a turn that this page did not send, for example after a reload. The pane starts a new turn for it.

Example:

- Message A "Summarise the open cards" is sent. Its reply streams.
- Message B "Also list the ghosts" is sent while the reply to A streams.

1. The pane draws A, then the first part of reply A under it.
2. The person sends B. The pane draws B below reply A, with the waiting mark. The server holds B, because A has not ended.
3. A second part of reply A arrives. The pane adds it under A, above B.
4. The end line of A arrives. A closes, the agent starts B, and the waiting mark under B goes away.
5. The first part of reply B arrives. The pane adds it under B.

```
server order: [A, B]        pane
                            A  Summarise the open cards
  part 1 -> A                 a1
  part 2 -> A                 a2     <- step 3: lands above B
  end    -> A  (A closed)     12s · $0.04
                            B  Also list the ghosts
                               ○ waits for the reply above   <- steps 2 to 4
  part 1 -> B                 b1     <- step 5
```

○ is the waiting mark. a1, a2 and b1 are parts of a reply.

payload.why: takes the end line with duration and cost that closes a turn in the pane from werk-progress

payload.title: The pane draws a sent message only when its turn starts
payload.why_not: The person sees no sign that the message was received while the earlier reply runs. Several waiting messages stay invisible.

payload.title: A new message stops the running reply
payload.why_not: It throws away work that the person did not ask to stop. Stopping a turn is a separate action.

payload.title: Mockup: a second message sent while a reply streams, in five steps
payload.body:
A static mockup of the chat pane. Message A "Summarise the open cards" is sent. Message B "Also list the ghosts" is sent while reply A still streams. Each step shows the pane as it was before turn names (left) and with turn names (right). An amber outline marks the parts that arrive in that step. The "reply A" and "reply B" labels exist only in the mockup.

Step 1: message A is sent, and the first part of reply A streams. Both panes are the same.

![Step 1: A and the first part of reply A](/api/image?name=werk-chat-turn-id-step1.png)

Step 2: message B is sent while reply A streams. Both panes draw B at once. On the right, B shows the waiting mark.

![Step 2: B is sent, with the waiting mark on the right](/api/image?name=werk-chat-turn-id-step2.png)

Step 3: a tool call and the rest of reply A arrive. On the left they land under B and read as the answer to B. On the right they land above B.

![Step 3: the rest of reply A lands above B on the right](/api/image?name=werk-chat-turn-id-step3.png)

Step 4: reply A ends, and reply B starts. On the left, reply B runs on from reply A. On the right, the waiting mark goes away, and reply B starts under B.

![Step 4: reply B starts under B on the right](/api/image?name=werk-chat-turn-id-step4.png)

Step 5: both replies are done. On the right, the chat reads as two question-and-answer pairs. On the left, B has three parts under it, and only the last one answers it.

![Step 5: the finished chat](/api/image?name=werk-chat-turn-id-step5.png)

ops.old:

1. Reorder tickets within ready.
2. Archive a ticket. A ready, blocked or building ticket shows this action; a merging or done ticket does not. Archiving a building ticket ends its build and keeps its branch. 3. Trigger the build of a ready ticket inside an active run. Either press the trigger icon, or drag the ticket into building.
4. A triggered build cannot be stopped in place. A person ends it by archiving its ticket (action 2), and nothing else returns a building ticket to ready.

payload.title: The server restarts a build whose process died, as a fresh pass
payload.why: A build runs in its own process, apart from the server, so a server restart does not stop it. But the build process itself can die: a kill, a crash, a machine sleep. Nothing inside that process can see its own death, so the server, which already checks whether each build process is alive, writes the end and starts a fresh pass from the work already committed on the ticket's branch.
payload.body:
**The problem.** A ticket whose build process died sits in building with no pulse (#vi-board-session-file). Nobody starts it again, so the run stops until a person sees it.

**The answer.** The server is the watcher. It looks for a dead build at two moments: when a build process it started exits, and when the server itself starts. A build counts as dead when the board log has a start for it, no end, and its process is gone. For each one the server does three things. It writes the end, with died as the reason. It starts a fresh pass of the same ticket, from the last commit on the ticket's branch, with the death as the last failure in the brief (#lp-stateless). The fresh pass counts against the ticket's retry cap, so a build that dies on every pass still stops (#st-build-silence-act treats a silent pass the same way).

A pass does not resume the agent's own conversation. Work the dead pass did not commit is lost: at most one pass of work. The session id stays in the session log for a person who wants to read what the dead pass did.

While the server is down, nothing watches. A build keeps running without the server; a build that dies in that time is found when the server starts again.

**Example.**

- Ticket T "r/03" sits in building. Its branch has two commits from earlier passes.
- Pass 3 runs in process P. It has edited files and not committed them.

1. A person closes the laptop lid. P dies. The server is down too.
2. The person starts werk. The server reads the board log: pass 3 of T started, has no end, and P is dead.
3. The server writes the end of pass 3: died. The edits that pass 3 did not commit are gone.
4. The server starts pass 4 of T from the second commit. The brief says that pass 3 died.
5. Pass 4 is the last pass the retry cap allows. If it dies too, T stops with died as the reason, and the server starts nothing more.
6. A build whose process is alive is left alone, whether this server started it or an earlier one did.

```
board log for T            process     server action
-----------------          -------     -------------------------------------
pass 3 started (P)         P alive     none                          (before step 1)
no end                     P dead      (server is down)              (step 1)
no end                     P dead      write end: died               (steps 2-3)
pass 4 started (P2)        P2 alive    started from commit 2         (step 4)

dead = started, no end, process gone
fresh pass = new agent, last commit of the branch, death in the brief, counts against the cap
```

payload.why: takes the test for a dead build: a start with no end and a process that is gone
takes the rule that a fresh pass is a new agent with the last failure in the brief, so no conversation needs resuming
takes the rule that a fresh pass after an abnormal end counts against the retry cap
takes the fact that the overseer is a timer inside the build process, so it cannot restart that process

payload.title: The overseer restarts a dead build

payload.why_not: A pass is stateless by design: the branch is the memory. A resumed conversation brings back a long context and a half-done step whose files may not match what the agent remembers. The gain is at most one pass of uncommitted work.

payload.title: A merge never removes an entry from the list of pure files
payload.why: Each branch adds its own pure files to the list in the change that writes them. A merge that keeps only one side drops the other side's files from the coverage check. Those files then pass with no test, and no output shows the loss.
payload.body:
A pure file is a file with no live part, such as a child process, a socket or an open file. A bug in it never announces itself, so the coverage check holds it to a line-coverage threshold (see #werk-test-scope). The check judges only the files on the explicit list of pure files (see #werk-test-pure-list). Two branches that each add a pure file both edit that list, often at the same place. Version control then reports a conflict on the list.

**The answer.** The resolution keeps every entry from both sides. The list is a set: the order of its entries has no effect on the verdict, and each file appears once. A file leaves the list only when the file is deleted or stops being pure, in a change that says so. A merge never removes an entry as a side effect.

**Example.**

- The main line has the list `[a, b]`.
- Branch X adds the pure file `x`. Its list is `[a, b, x]`.
- Branch Y adds the pure file `y`. Its list is `[a, b, y]`.

1. Branch X merges into the main line. The list is `[a, b, x]`.
2. Branch Y merges next. Both sides changed the same place, so the merge conflicts on the list.
3. The resolution keeps both entries. The list is `[a, b, x, y]`.
4. The coverage check prints one line each for `a`, `b`, `x` and `y`.

```
main   [a, b] --------+-- [a, b, x] --+-- [a, b, x, y]
                      |               |
X      [a, b, x] -----+               |
                                      |
Y      [a, b, y] ---------- conflict -+   keep x AND y
```

A resolution that keeps `[a, b, y]` passes every check, because `x` is no longer judged. The coverage output after a merge is the test: it holds one line for every pure file of both branches.

payload.title: A pure file's coverage counts only the lines that its own test file runs
payload.why: A test for one pure file often calls other pure files too. Those calls run lines in the other files, so a file can reach the threshold with no test of its own. When its own tests are deleted, the check still passes and nobody sees the loss.
payload.body:
The per-file coverage check (see #werk-test-pure-list) compares each listed pure file with the threshold. To stop a caller's test from hiding a missing test, the check counts a line as covered only when the file's own test file runs it.

**Own test file.** The test file that the project names for a pure file by one fixed convention. One pure file has one own test file, and the check finds it by that convention.

**How the run works.** The coverage run runs each own test file alone, with coverage on, and keeps only the result for its pure file. The results join into one report, and the per-file check reads that report. Lines that another file's test runs do not count. The ordinary test run still runs the whole suite, so no test is lost from it. The cost is one coverage run for each pure file on the list, so the coverage run grows with the list.

**A missing own test file.** A listed pure file with no own test file counts as 0%. The check names the test file that is missing.

**Example.**

- Pure file R renders text. Its own test file is R-test.
- Pure file K finds card links. R calls K. Its own test file is K-test.
- R-test runs every line of K, because R calls K.

1. The coverage run runs K-test alone. K-test runs all lines of K. K is at 100%.
2. Someone deletes K-test. R-test still runs every line of K.
3. The coverage run runs R-test alone and counts only R's lines from it. No run counts K's lines.
4. K has no own test file, so the check sets K to 0%, names K-test as missing, and fails.

```
step  run          lines it may count   K's result
----  -----------  -------------------  ------------------------
1     K-test       K                    100%   pass
2     (K-test deleted)
3     R-test       R only               K not counted
4     check        -                    0%     fail: K-test missing

R-test --calls--> R --calls--> K
   |                            ^
   +-- K lines run, NOT counted-+
```

payload.title: A plan archives each open ticket that the new ticket set leaves out
payload.why: The ticket writer rewrites a needed open ticket in place, under its own number. So a ticket that the writer does not carry into the new set is a ticket that the current spec does not need. The plan reads this from the new set and keeps no second judge beside the writer.
payload.body:
A plan must decide which open tickets the current spec no longer needs (see #st-plan-archive). To avoid a second judge beside the ticket writer, the plan reads the answer from the new ticket set.

- **Open** means ready or blocked (see #werk-board-control). The plan looks only at open tickets of its own subtree. A ticket that started to build is not the plan's to change.
- **Left out** means the writer does not carry the ticket into the new set under its number. The writer either marks the number as dropped or writes no file for it.

The plan archives each ticket that is left out, with the reason that #st-plan-archive sets. The archive is reversible, so a mistake costs one restore.

Example:

- Subtree X has three open tickets: 3 "Show the seat count", 4 "Charge per seat", 5 "Export the invoice".
- Ticket 6 "Refund a seat" is in building.
- The spec of X changes. Export is no longer in it.

1. The plan runs. The writer rewrites 3 and 4 under their own numbers, and leaves 5 out.
2. Tickets 3 and 4 stay on the board with their new text.
3. Ticket 5 is archived, with the reason that the current spec of X no longer needs it.
4. Ticket 6 does not change, because it started to build.

```
            before plan     new set            after plan
  3  ready  ------------>  3 (carried)   -->  3  ready, new text
  4  ready  ------------>  4 (carried)   -->  4  ready, new text
  5  ready  ------------>  (left out)    -->  5  archived: X no longer needs it
  6  building              (not the plan's) -> 6  building
```

payload.title: The plan compares each open ticket's cited cards with the new spec to decide what is no longer needed
payload.why_not: It makes the plan a second judge next to the writer, and the two can disagree about the same ticket. The writer already knows which tickets the new spec needs.

payload.title: A plan blocks an open ticket whose rewrite fails its own checks
payload.why: The writer kept the ticket, so the spec still needs it. If the plan archived it, the work would drop out of the plan. If the plan kept the earlier text, the ticket would build a version that the spec has changed. So the ticket stays on the board, blocked, until an agent fixes it.
payload.body:
A plan changes open tickets in place (see #st-plan-extend). The writer can rewrite a ticket and get it wrong, so that the rewrite fails the checks of a single ticket (see #st-ticket-own-checks). The ticket then has old text on the board and a broken new text beside it.

The plan does not archive the ticket, because the writer kept it. It does not keep the old text buildable, because the spec changed. It moves the ticket to blocked, with the failed check as the reason. An agent fixes the ticket and clears the reason (see #werk-board-control).

Example:

- Open tickets 3 "Show the seat count" and 4 "Charge per seat" are in ready.
- The spec changes. The writer rewrites both under their own numbers.

1. The rewrite of 3 passes its own checks. Ticket 3 stays in ready with its new text.
2. The rewrite of 4 has no acceptance criteria. The plan moves ticket 4 to blocked, with that failed check as the reason.
3. The old text of 4 is no longer on the board as buildable text.
4. An agent writes the acceptance criteria and clears the reason. Ticket 4 returns to ready.

```
            before plan     new set            after plan
  3  ready  ------------>  3 (passes)    -->  3  ready, new text
  4  ready  ------------>  4 (fails)     -->  4  blocked: no acceptance criteria
                                               agent fixes 4 --> 4  ready
```

payload.why_not: The writer kept the ticket, so the spec still needs it. An archive drops the work from the plan, and a restore would bring back the old text.

payload.why: A second set of tickets beside an unfinished first set, or a plan that changes tickets under a running build, creates races that nobody decided. Resume continues the same work. A restart ends it first, so there is only ever one set of unfinished tickets for a subtree.
payload.body:
A subtree has **unfinished work** when one of its tickets is ready, blocked, building or merging. The work can be running, or it can have stopped for any reason: the builder was killed, the machine slept, or a person paused it. A ticket that is done stays in the main line and is not unfinished.

When a person presses Build on a subtree with unfinished work, the press does not start a second run. The board offers two actions:

- **Resume** is the default. It starts the merge loop again over the same tickets, and the loop continues where it stopped (see #st-build-run-mechanics).
- **Restart** is a separate action that asks for confirmation. The confirmation says what it does: it cancels every running build and keeps their branches, it archives every unfinished ticket of the subtree, and it keeps the done tickets. Then a new plan and run start from the current spec. The archives are reversible (see #werk-board-control).

The restart is always possible, and it is never the default or an accident.

Example:

- Subtree X "Invoices" has five tickets. 1 and 2 are done. 3 is building, and its builder was killed when the laptop crashed. 4 is ready. 5 is blocked.
- A person presses Build on X.

1. The board shows "Unfinished work: 3 building (process dead), 4 ready, 5 blocked". The buttons are **Resume** and **Restart…**.
2. The person presses Resume. The merge loop starts again. 3 builds on from its branch, and 4 and 5 follow.
3. Or the person presses Restart…. The confirmation lists: cancel the build of 3 and keep its branch, archive 3, 4 and 5, keep 1 and 2.
4. The person confirms. Tickets 3, 4 and 5 are archived. A new plan writes tickets from the current spec, and a new run builds them.
5. Later the person restores 4. It returns to the board as it was.

```
  Build pressed on X
       |
       v
  unfinished work?  -- no --> plan, then run
       |
      yes
       v
  +---------------------------+
  | Unfinished: 3 building    |
  | (process dead), 4 ready,  |
  | 5 blocked                 |
  |  [ Resume ]  [ Restart... ]|
  +---------------------------+
      |                 |
      v                 v
  merge loop       confirm: cancel 3 (keep branch),
  starts again     archive 3, 4, 5, keep 1, 2
  over 3, 4, 5            |
                          v
                   new plan, new run
```

payload.why: takes the rule that starting the merge loop again resumes the same tickets
takes the board log that says which run holds a ticket and whether its process still runs

payload.title: A press on a subtree that already has a plan extends that plan in place and resumes its run
payload.why_not: A plan then changes tickets under a running build, and two plans can write to one subtree at once. No rule says who wins, so tickets and builds can race.

payload.title: A press on a subtree with unfinished work is refused, and only resume is possible
payload.why_not: A person who changed the spec and wants a clean rebuild would have no way to get one.

payload.title: A press on a subtree with unfinished work restarts it at once, with no choice
payload.why_not: A person who presses Build by habit cancels running builds. The archive is reversible, but the cancelled build work is lost.

criterion.text: Press Build on a subtree with a killed build. The board offers Resume and Restart, and neither runs alone. Restart asks for confirmation and archives only unfinished tickets. If a press starts a second run, revisit.

payload.title: A subtree with unfinished work shows Resume and Restart where it shows Build
payload.why: A person decides to build from the map, and checks a stuck run on the board. If only one place offered the choice, the other place would offer a second press that starts a second run. So both places show the state of the work and offer the same two actions.
payload.body:
The Build button of a map card (see #werk-board-build-subtree) and the plan card on the board (see #vi-board-plan) show the same state of one subtree and offer the same actions. The behaviour of Resume and Restart is set in #werk-board-restart. This card sets where the controls sit.

| State of the subtree | Map card | Plan card on the board |
|---|---|---|
| No unfinished work | **Build** | none, or the done state |
| Unfinished work, running | the running indicator, a link to the plan card, no button | the running state and the stop |
| Unfinished work, not running (killed, paused, stopped) | **Resume**, and **Restart…** as a smaller second action | the stopped state with its reason, **Resume** and **Restart…** |

Both places open the same confirmation for a restart. The map card never shows Build while unfinished work exists, so a press cannot start a second run.

Example:

- Subtree X "Invoices" has unfinished tickets 3, 4 and 5. Its builder was killed.
- The map card of X and the plan card of X are both on screen.

1. The map card shows **Resume** and a smaller **Restart…**. The plan card shows "stopped: builder killed, 3 unfinished tickets" with the same two actions.
2. The person presses **Resume** on either. The merge loop starts again over the same tickets.
3. Both cards change at once. The map card shows the running indicator. The plan card shows building and the stop.
4. All tickets reach done. The map card shows **Build** again, and the plan card shows done.

```
 map card "Invoices"                    plan card on the board
 +----------------------+              +---------------------------------+
 | [ Resume ] Restart…   |              | Invoices   stopped: builder      |
 | unfinished: 3 tickets |              | killed     3 unfinished tickets  |
 +----------------------+              | [ Resume ]  [ Restart… ]         |
   shown instead of Build              +---------------------------------+

 no unfinished work -> Build    running -> indicator + stop    not running -> Resume, Restart…
```

payload.why: takes what resume and restart do, and the confirmation of a restart
takes the Build button of a map card, which the Resume action replaces while unfinished work exists
