payload.title: A subtree shows Build, Resume or Restart by the state of its work, and a run above it disables them
payload.why: A person decides to build from the map, and checks a stuck run on the board. If only one place showed the state, the other place would offer a press that starts a second run. So both places show the state, offer the same actions, and disable them while a run is in progress on the subtree or above it.
payload.body:
The Build button of a map card (see #werk-board-build-subtree) and the plan card on the board (see #vi-board-plan) show the same state of one subtree and offer the same actions. What Resume and Restart do is set in #werk-board-restart. This card sets which control each state shows, and when it is disabled.

A run is **in progress** when its process is alive (see #vi-board-state). A run in progress on a subtree, or on any ancestor of it, disables every start action of that subtree. A disabled control stays on screen and says which run blocks it, with a link to that run's plan card. A person who looks for the button finds it and sees why it does not work.

| State of the subtree | Map card | Plan card on the board |
|---|---|---|
| A run is in progress on it or on an ancestor | **Build**, **Resume** or **Restart…** disabled, with the blocking run named | the running state and the stop, on the plan card of the run itself |
| Unfinished work, no run in progress | **Resume**, and **Restart…** as a smaller second action | the stopped state with its reason, **Resume** and **Restart…** |
| No unfinished work, no run in progress | **Build** | none, or the done state |

Both places open the same confirmation for a restart. The map card never shows an enabled Build while unfinished work exists, so a press cannot start a second run.

Example:

- Billing "Billing" is the parent of X "Invoices".
- A run is in progress on Billing.
- X has unfinished tickets 3, 4 and 5 from an earlier run that was killed.

1. A person looks at the map card of X. **Resume** and **Restart…** are disabled, with the text "Blocked by the run on Billing", linked to the plan card of Billing.
2. The run on Billing ends. Both controls of X become enabled.
3. The person presses **Resume**. The merge loop starts again over 3, 4 and 5. The map card of X shows the running state, and its controls are disabled.
4. All tickets reach done. The map card shows **Build**, enabled.

```
 Billing    run in progress                 X "Invoices"  (child of Billing)
 [ Build ] disabled: it is running           [ Resume ] [ Restart… ]   both disabled
                                             Blocked by the run on Billing ->

 Billing run ends                            X:  [ Resume ] [ Restart… ]   enabled
 press Resume on X                           X:  running  (its own controls disabled)
 every ticket done                           X:  [ Build ]   enabled
```

payload.why: takes what resume and restart do, and the confirmation of a restart
takes the Build button of a map card, which Resume replaces while unfinished work exists
takes the run started event and the process that says whether a run is in progress

payload.title: Only the map card carries the start actions
payload.why_not: A person who finds a stuck run on the board sees a stopped plan and has nothing to press there. The board is where a stuck run shows.

payload.title: Only the plan card on the board carries the start actions
payload.why_not: A person decides to build from the map. The map would still show Build for a subtree with unfinished work, and a press there would start a second run.

payload.title: A press on a subtree under a running ancestor starts its own run
payload.why_not: Two runs would write overlapping ticket sets and build against the same code at the same time, and no rule says which one wins.

payload.title: The start actions of a blocked subtree are hidden
payload.why_not: A person who looks for the button cannot tell if it is missing or broken. A disabled control that names the blocking run answers the question.

criterion.text: Start a run on a parent subtree and look at the map card of a child. Its start controls are disabled and name the parent run. End the run: they are enabled. If a press on the child starts a second run, revisit.

payload.title: The start of a run refuses while a run is in progress on its subtree or an ancestor
payload.why: An agent starts runs from the command line, not from a button. If only the board disabled the start, an agent could still start a second run, and two runs would write overlapping tickets and build against the same code. So the rule sits where every run starts, and the board only shows what it refuses.
payload.body:
A run is **in progress** when its process is alive (see #vi-board-state). Every way to start a run checks the same rule before it starts: a run in progress on the same subtree, or on any ancestor of it, makes the start fail. The refusal names the blocking run and where to find it. The same refusal holds for a resume, a restart and a plan over that subtree. The board shows the same fact as a disabled control (see #vi-board-plan-controls).

A restart ends the unfinished work of a subtree first (see #werk-board-restart). The command line has its own restart. It must say that it ends the unfinished work, and it prints each running build it cancels and each ticket it archives, so an agent cannot restart by accident. A run on a descendant of the subtree is not covered by this rule.

Example:

- Billing "Billing" is the parent of X "Invoices".
- A run is in progress on Billing.
- An agent starts a run on X from the command line.

1. The start is refused. The message says "a run is in progress on Billing" and points to its plan card. Nothing starts, and nothing is written to X.
2. The run on Billing ends.
3. The agent starts the run on X again. It starts. X has no unfinished work, so a new plan and run begin.
4. The agent starts the run on X once more while it is in progress. The start is refused: a run is in progress on X.
5. The run on X stops, and 3 unfinished tickets stay. The agent asks to restart. The command line prints "ends the unfinished work: cancel the build of 3, archive 3, 4 and 5" and waits for the agent to say it means it.

```
 start run on X
      |
      v
 run in progress on X or on an ancestor?
      |                         |
     yes                        no
      v                         v
 refused: names the        unfinished work on X?
 blocking run                |            |
                            yes           no
                             v            v
                   resume, or a confirmed   plan, then run
                   restart that lists
                   what it ends
```

payload.why: takes what resume and restart do, and what a restart archives
takes the run started event and the live process that says whether a run is in progress

payload.title: Only the board disables the start, and the command line does not check
payload.why_not: An agent works through the command line. It could start a second run that the disabled button would have blocked.

payload.title: The command line refuses only a second run of the same run id
payload.why_not: A run on a child subtree and a run on its parent have different ids, so both would start and write overlapping tickets and builds.

payload.title: A start that is blocked waits and starts when the blocking run ends
payload.why_not: The person cannot see why nothing builds, and the queued start can run long after the person has changed the spec. A refusal says what is wrong now.

criterion.text: Start a run on a parent subtree, then start a run on its child from the command line. The start is refused and names the parent run. If the second run starts, revisit.

payload.text: Checked against the current server code. A start that reads an empty or half-written lock fails to parse it and exits, so it refuses to start. That failure is safe, not the shared-directory case in the why. The open gap is different: the check for a lock and the write of the lock are two steps, so two starts in the same moment can both pass. The exclusive create on #werk-onelock-lockfile closes that gap.

payload.title: A start takes the lock in one step that fails when a lock already exists
payload.why: If a start first checks for a lock and then writes one, two starts at the same moment can both find no lock and both run. One create step that fails when the file already exists lets only one of them win. The loser then reads the lock to decide whether to wait or to take over a stale one.
payload.body:
The lock is a file in the same directory as the log, so a log in another directory has its own lock. It holds the pid and the port of the holder (see #werk-onelock).

To avoid two starts that both find no lock, a start creates the lock file in one step that fails when the file exists. Exactly one start succeeds. A start whose create fails reads the lock. A dead pid means a stale lock: the start removes it and creates again. A live pid means a running server: the start polls until that server exits, and refuses at the end of the wait. A lock that does not parse counts as held during the wait, because its holder can be between the create and the write. If it still does not parse at the end of the wait, it counts as stale, because its holder died between the two.

The removal of a stale lock has no guard. Two starts that read the same stale lock in the same moment can both run. That needs two starts within milliseconds of each other right after a crash, and the lock accepts that risk.

Example:

- No server runs. Starts B and C begin at the same moment.
- Later, B is killed with no clean exit. Start D begins.

1. B creates the lock. The create succeeds. B runs.
2. C creates the lock. The create fails, because the file exists.
3. C reads the lock. It is empty, because B has not written yet. C waits and reads again.
4. C reads pid B. B is alive. C polls until the wait ends, then refuses.
5. B is killed. The lock stays and still names pid B.
6. D creates the lock. The create fails. D reads pid B, and B is dead.
7. D removes the stale lock, creates it again, and runs.

```
  B: create ──> ok ──────────────> lock {pid B}   B runs
  C: create ──> exists
     read ──> {} (not parsed) ──> wait, read again
     read ──> {pid B}, B alive ──> poll ... refuse

  B killed: lock {pid B} remains, B dead
  D: create ──> exists ──> read {pid B}, dead ──> remove ──> create ──> ok   D runs

  {}      = empty lock, not parsed yet
  {pid B} = lock that names the pid of B
```

payload.why: takes the guarantee that a hot reload never starts the server a second time in one process, so the holder never meets its own lock

payload.title: Write the lock aside and move it into place in one step
payload.why_not: A start that finds a lock it cannot parse waits and reads it again, so a partly written lock does no harm. The extra step protects nothing.

payload.title: A second, short-lived lock guards the removal of a stale lock
payload.why_not: The race it closes needs two starts within milliseconds of each other right after a crash. The guard lock has its own stale case to handle.

payload.title: An operating-system file lock that the kernel releases when the holder dies
payload.why_not: The runtime has no built-in call for it, and the project takes no dependencies.

criterion.text: Two servers on one .werk directory, seen even once after this lock exists, kill it: the unguarded removal of a stale lock is then the first suspect.

payload.title: `werk add` refuses a card with no `--status`
payload.why_not: A new card is nearly always open, so the agent would type the same flag every time. A refusal costs a failed call for no gain, and open is the safe default.

payload.why: The label rule gives one look to the reference forms that this card defines as links.

payload.text: Decided (who: me). The test preload registers one happy-dom window, puts back the runtime network, stream and timer globals, and empties the document after every test. A guard test checks that a server test reaches a local server with the runtime fetch, and that each test starts with an empty document. Without the restore step, Bun.serve fails: the DOM's Response replaces the runtime one.

payload.title: A removal deletes each link and a restore adds each one back
payload.why_not: A removal is one event and a restore is its exact inverse, so the log holds no event per link. A replay on restore cannot add a link whose other end is still out, so it must hold that link until both ends are in. That is the waiting rule with more code around it. A replay that builds its list at restore time can also bring back a link that a person cut on purpose. The only gain is that the log shows each lost link as its own event.

payload.text: Decided as written. The accept and the discard now follow it. Before this, both read supported_by in the wrong direction: an accept never took a cited source, and a discard of a ghost source took the ghost cards that cite it.

payload.title: The grader asks, for every decided card the ticket depends on, whether the diff builds all of that card
payload.why_not: A ticket builds only one part of a subtree. The cards it depends on, directly or through other cards, reach up to the card at the top of the subtree, and that card describes the whole subtree. The grader would then fail a correct ticket for parts that later tickets build, and the builder has no way to fix that.

payload.title: The client builds its screens from one UI component system
payload.why: An agent writes most of the client. It writes faster and more consistently when it picks from a small set of known components than when it styles each screen by hand. The set must still let a screen change one component's look without a fork of the library.
payload.body:
To keep screens consistent and cheap for an agent to write, the client uses one component system for buttons, inputs, dialogs, menus, tabs, tooltips and layout.

The system must meet four criteria. First, a small, fixed set of components, each with a documented contract, so an agent does not invent a new variant per screen. Second, a way to change one component's look or behaviour without a fork. Third, direct support for React, see #werk-stack-framework. Fourth, no style work at run time: styles come from static CSS, not from JavaScript that computes styles on each render.

Accessibility (keyboard focus, roles, screen reader labels) comes from the system, not from each screen.

payload.why: The component system must support React, the framework that #werk-stack-framework chose.

payload.title: shadcn/ui: Radix primitives styled with Tailwind, copied into the client as source
payload.why: Agents know it better than any other React component set. The client owns each component file, so a change is an edit, not an override. Tailwind compiles to static CSS. The risk: owned source drifts if each screen edits a component instead of passing a variant.

payload.title: Radix Themes: a fixed set of styled components, set through props and CSS variables
payload.why: The set is small and the contract is strict: size, colour and variant are props, and a theme sets the rest through CSS variables. It uses plain static CSS and no Tailwind. A look outside the props needs a CSS override, which is harder than an edit to owned source.

payload.title: Mantine: a large styled library with CSS modules
payload.why: It has the most ready components, including hooks for forms and hotkeys, and it styles with static CSS modules. The set is large, so an agent has more ways to do one thing.

payload.title: MUI or Chakra: styled libraries that compute styles in JavaScript
payload.why_not: Both compute styles in JavaScript on each render, through Emotion. That costs time on every render and fails the static CSS criterion. MUI also has a very large component set.

payload.title: The client builds its screens from shadcn/ui components

patch.body:
To keep screens consistent and cheap for an agent to write, the client builds every button, input, dialog, menu, tab, tooltip and layout from one component set: shadcn/ui. Each component is a Radix primitive, which gives keyboard focus, roles and screen reader labels, styled with Tailwind. React support comes from #werk-stack-framework.

The component files are copied into the client as its own source, not installed as a package. So the set is small and fixed, each component has a documented contract, and a change to a component's look or behaviour is an edit to one file, not a fork of a library. Tailwind compiles to static CSS, so no style work runs in the browser on each render.

To keep the set from drifting, a screen changes a component only through its variants and its class names. A new look that more than one screen needs becomes a new variant in the shared component file. A screen never edits a shared component for its own case.
patch.why: An agent writes most of the client. It writes faster and more consistently when it picks from a small set of known components than when it styles each screen by hand. shadcn/ui is the React component set that agents know best, and the client owns its source, so a change is a plain edit.

patch.why_not: Its set is small and its contract is strict, but a look outside its props needs a CSS override against styles the client does not own. Agents also know it less well than shadcn/ui, so they guess more about its props.
It styles with static CSS, but its set is large and comes with its own hooks for forms and hotkeys. An agent then has several ways to build the same screen, which defeats a small fixed set.

criterion.text: Revisit when a tested agent pipeline that builds client screens with these components gives poor results, or its agents misuse the component syntax: they invent props or variants that do not exist, mix in other styling methods, or edit shared components for one screen.

payload.title: A pipeline change tells open views to read only the measures again
payload.why: The pipeline log holds build measures, not cards. A change to it cannot change the map, so a full map read would be wasted work. It sends its own signal, and each view reads only the measures.
payload.body:
The server watches the pipeline log next to the map log. When the pipeline log grows, the server sends a bare measure signal on the live channel. The signal holds no data, the same as the map signal. Each page then reads the measures again and redraws the Measure panels. It does not read the map.

Example:

- Tab T1 shows the map. Tab T2 shows Measure.
- A build step ends and appends one event to the pipeline log.

1. The server sees the pipeline log grow and sends the measure signal to T1 and T2.
2. T1 has no Measure panels open. Nothing changes on T1.
3. T2 reads the measures again and redraws its panels.
4. Neither tab reads the map. The map log did not change.

```
  build        pipeline log     server             T1 (map)   T2 (Measure)
    |  step ends    |              |                   |            |
    |-------------->| (+1 event)   |                   |            |
    |               |-- grows ---->|                   |            |
    |               |              |-- (1) measure --->|----------->|
    |               |              |                   | (2) idle   |
    |               |<------------------------ (3) read measures ---|
```

Numbers match the steps. "measure" is the bare signal. A change to the map log still sends the map signal, and that full read also refreshes the measures.

criterion.text: Merging the two signals back is a two-line change. Revisit if the Measure view starts to read the map.

payload.title: werk's client is built from components on one framework
payload.why: Hand-written rendering grows with every screen, and each screen solves layout, state and live updates in its own way. A component framework gives every screen one way to do this. An agent then changes one small part at a time, and a change in one part does not break another.

ops.old: A new implementation is built on this stack from scratch — this card is not a migration plan, and nothing here asks anyone to port the current frontend.
ops.new: To keep every screen a set of small parts that an agent can write and change on its own, werk builds its client from components on one framework, not from hand-written rendering. The client renders the one-view-per-card layout (#vi-onview).

ops.old: Two separate choices, each decided on its own card:

framework    React + Vite              #werk-stack-framework
    hydration    islands as a pattern      #werk-stack-hydration
Runtime (Bun, bun --hot) was already decided at #werk-hmr. Progressive loading is an API shape decision, not a framework feature — see #werk-stack-api.
ops.new: The choice of framework (#werk-stack-framework) and the pattern that decides which parts run in the browser (#werk-stack-hydration) are separate decisions. The server runtime and its hot reload come from #werk-hmr. Progressive loading is a shape of the API, not a framework feature (#werk-stack-api).

payload.why: Archive in the drawer as the only way to end a build follows the board actions that this card defines.

payload.title: v0's packages and checks sit at the root of v0's own repository, not in a directory inside the prototype's repository
payload.why: One card puts v0 in a directory of the prototype's repository and another puts it in a new repository, and only one location can hold.
payload.body: v0 has its own package list, lockfile, compiler configuration and test configuration, and nothing in it imports from the prototype, as #werk-base-dir requires. These files sit at the root of the new repository that #werk-base-repo names, because a separate repository is the only layout in which no build can start from or merge into the prototype's tree, and every project builds in a repository of its own (#st-build-target). Every check runs inside that repository and installs the locked packages first when they are missing. The part of #werk-base-dir that places v0 in a directory of the prototype's repository does not hold.

payload.title: The fake agent's launch record holds the role name next to the arguments
payload.why: A test must check which job werk asked for, and the role travels in the environment, not in the arguments.
payload.body: Each launch of the fake agent records its arguments and the role name from its environment. A test reads the record to check that werk started each kind of agent with the right role and the right request.

payload.title: The control that starts an empty conversation sits in the tab strip, next to the fork control
payload.why: The fork card asks for a second, explicit way to start empty, and the tab strip is where a person already starts a conversation.
payload.body: The tab strip has two controls at its end: '+' forks a conversation at the open card, and a separate control starts a conversation with no parent session. The empty start is never the default of any gesture.

payload.title: werk's agent roles are chat, spec writer, ticket writer, builder, grader, reviewer, classifier, step author and binder
payload.why: Every agent werk starts carries a role, and the fake needs one fixed word per job to pick its reply.
payload.body: Each kind of agent that werk starts has one role name: chat for a conversation, spec writer and ticket writer for the plan, builder for a build pass, grader, reviewer for each of the five review areas, classifier for the overseer's loop check, and step author and binder for the held-out set. The names live in one list of entries. A new kind of agent adds one entry.

payload.title: `werk ticket-check` names a missing input and prints no usage text
payload.why: A missing folder, spec or root and a wrong flag both exit 2, so the exit code alone cannot tell them apart. The message tells them apart: a call whose flags were right needs the name of what is missing, not the form of the command again.
payload.body:
Two kinds of call exit 2 before any check runs. A call with a missing or unknown flag, or with no folder argument, prints its problem and then the usage line. A call whose flags are right but whose folder, spec file or root card is not there prints one line that names that input, and no usage line. Nothing goes to standard output in either case, so no failure line or count line can be read as a result.

Example, in a project whose map has no card "nope":

1. `werk ticket-check tickets --root map` prints "--spec is required" and the usage line. Exit 2.
2. `werk ticket-check tickets --root map --spec none.md` prints 'no spec file "none.md"'. Exit 2.
3. `werk ticket-check tickets --root nope --spec spec.md` prints 'no node "nope"'. Exit 2.
4. `werk ticket-check tickets --root map --spec spec.md` with every input present runs the checks. Exit 0 or 1.

```
call ──> flags right? ──no──> problem + usage line ──> exit 2
             │yes
             v
   folder, spec, root there? ──no──> 'no <input> "<name>"' ──> exit 2
             │yes
             v
        run the checks ──> exit 0 (pass) or 1 (a check fails)
```

payload.why: It takes the rule that a call which could not run the checks is a third outcome, apart from a pass and a failed check.

payload.title: The builder loop ends its own build when it reads that its ticket is archived
payload.why: A build can run from the merge loop or from a single build command, and only the builder loop is present in both. When the builder loop reads the board itself, an archive ends every build the same way, with no second process that has to notice it.
payload.body:
While a build runs, its builder loop reads the board about once a second. When it finds its ticket archived, it stops the agent of the pass that runs, commits nothing of that pass, runs no checks, records no retry, and ends. The worktree folder goes and the branch stays. A merge loop that started the build reads the ended build as a person's stop: nothing of it merges.

Example:

- Ticket T "Draw the board" is in building. Its pass 2 agent runs.
- A person archives T on the board.

1. The board log gets the archive. T leaves the columns.
2. Within about a second, the builder loop of T reads the board and sees T archived.
3. It stops the pass 2 agent. The session ends, so T stops pulsing.
4. The builder loop ends. Branch werk-build/T stays. Nothing merges.
5. Case where nothing happens: the person cancels the confirmation. No event, and the build goes on.

```
board log            builder loop of T            agent of pass 2
---------            -----------------            ---------------
T archived  ---->    reads board (~1 s): archived
                     stop  -------------------->  killed
                     no commit, no checks
                     worktree removed, branch kept
```

payload.why: It adds an ending to the builder loop that st-build-ticket defines.

payload.title: A test run drops every werk, agent and git setting, and gets a fresh home folder
payload.why: A setting can point at a real map, a real repository or the person's agent account under many names, and a list of single names misses the next one. Removing whole families by their name prefix, and replacing the home folder, covers the names that do not exist yet.
payload.body:
To keep a test away from real data, the unit test run removes every environment variable whose name starts with WERK_, CLAUDE, ANTHROPIC_ or GIT_. These name the map log, the agent's configuration and account, and the repository that git works on. The run also sets the home folder to a fresh empty folder, so no tool reads the person's own configuration files from it. Every other variable stays, so the tools the tests need still run.

Example:
- the person's shell has WERK_LOG pointing at their map, CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR pointing at their agent setup, and HOME as their home folder.

1. The run starts. WERK_LOG and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR are gone, and HOME is a new empty folder.
2. A test reads WERK_LOG. It finds nothing, so it cannot write to the person's map.
3. A variable that matches no prefix, such as LANG, stays as it was. Nothing happens to it.

```
 shell environment            test run environment
 WERK_LOG=~/proj/.werk/... -> (removed)
 CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.cl.. -> (removed)
 GIT_DIR=~/proj/.git       -> (removed)
 HOME=/Users/p             -> HOME=<fresh empty folder>
 LANG=en_US.UTF-8          -> LANG=en_US.UTF-8   (kept)
```

payload.why: It takes the rule that every setting pointing at real data is removed before the first test, and names which settings those are.

payload.title: The fake agent finishes writing an event before it plays the next step
payload.why: The output stream of a process can hold a line back in a buffer while the process goes on. If the fake wrote a file while its last event still waited in that buffer, a reader could get the event after the file was already on disk, and the order of the script would be lost.
payload.body:
To keep the order of a script visible to the reader, the fake agent plays an event step in two parts: it writes the line to its output stream, and it waits until the stream has taken the whole line. Only then does it play the next step.

Example:

- Event E1 "first", edit F "edited.txt", event E2 "second".

1. The fake writes E1 and waits until the stream has taken it. edited.txt does not exist.
2. The reader gets E1. edited.txt is still absent, if the script holds the fake here.
3. The fake writes edited.txt.
4. The fake writes E2. The reader gets E2, and edited.txt is on disk.

With no edit between two events, nothing changes: the reader gets the two events in order.

```
fake:    write E1 --wait--> write F --> write E2 --wait--> exit
reader:            get E1 (F absent)               get E2 (F present)
```

The wait covers the stream only. A test that must see the disk at E1 before F is written still holds the fake after E1, because the reader can be slower than the fake.

payload.why: The fake that this rule shapes is the one that the test run puts first in the program search list.

payload.title: A settled ask prints its tool result, and the turn ends at its first result event
payload.why: A test must see when an ask settles and whether it was allowed. A real agent shows both by the tool result it prints after the answer. A denial is an answer like an allow, so it ends neither the turn nor the agent.
payload.body:
To show a settled ask the way a real agent does, the fake prints a tool result for it at the moment it settles. The tool result carries the id of the ask. An allowed ask gives a plain result. A denied ask gives an error result that says the tool was refused, and the script goes on.

The end of the turn is the first scripted event of type result. A script with no such event ends its turn after its last step. At that point the fake waits for every open ask, then prints the result or exits.

A crash is its own step that holds an exit code. The fake exits with that code at once and prints nothing more.

Example:

- Ask A: a permission request for Bash, with id r1.
- Script S: ask A, a pause of 100 ms, a tool call, a final result.

1. The fake prints the request for A and goes on.
2. It stays silent for at least 120 ms, then prints the tool call.
3. It reaches the final result and waits for A.
4. The answer allow arrives. The fake prints the tool result for r1, then the final result.
5. With no input channel, step 4 is a denial: the tool result for r1 is an error, and the final result follows.
6. If S has a crash step in place of the tool call, the fake exits with its code after step 1, and nothing follows.

```
request r1 --> pause 120 ms --> tool call --> [wait for r1] --> tool result r1 --> result
request r1 --> crash(1) --> exit 1        (no tool result, no result)
```

payload.why: A test must see when an ask settles and whether it was allowed. A real agent shows both by the tool result it prints after the answer. A denial is an answer like an allow, so it ends neither the turn nor the agent.

payload.title: Each reviewer's role name carries its quality area
payload.why: The five reviewers of a pass run at the same time, so a test cannot tell them apart by launch order or by prompt text. A test must still script a finding for one area only. A role name per area lets the fake give each reviewer its own reply.
payload.body:
The reviewer is one kind of agent, with one entry among the roles. Its role name is the word reviewer, a dash, and the key of its quality area: reviewer-design, reviewer-tests, and so on. The fake treats every area as a reviewer for its lifetime: one pass.

Example:

- A test scripts reply F, one HIGH finding, for reviewer-security, and a reply with no finding for the other four areas.

1. The pass starts five reviewers at once. Each carries reviewer-<area>.
2. The security reviewer plays F. The other four play the empty reply.
3. The pass fails at the review, and the failure names the security finding.

```
reviewer-design     -> no finding
reviewer-tests      -> no finding
reviewer-security   -> F (HIGH)  -> pass red at review

reviewer-<area>   the role name of one reviewer
F                 the reply the test scripted for that area
```

payload.why: takes the five quality areas that each get one reviewer

payload.title: All five reviewers carry the one role name reviewer
payload.why_not: The fake could not give one area a finding and the others none, because nothing else tells the five apart.

payload.title: A pasted image travels inside the chat message, and the server stores it
payload.why: The composer sends one request per message. Carrying the image bytes in that request means a message and its images arrive together or not at all, and no image is stored for a message that never reached the server.
payload.body:
To send a message with images in one step, the page reads each pasted image in the browser and puts its bytes, encoded as text, into the same request as the message text, the open card and the tab. The server checks each image's type and size, writes it to the attachments folder of the project, and gives the agent the path of the file (see #werk-shots for the folder and the limits).

Example:

- The person pastes one screenshot and types "Why is this red?".

1. The composer shows the token [Image #1] and a chip.
2. Enter sends one request with the text and the image bytes.
3. The server stores the file and the agent's turn names its path as [Image #1].
4. A request whose image has a wrong type stores nothing and starts no turn.

```
page --(text + image bytes + card + tab)--> server --(store file)--> attachments/
                                              |
                                              +--(turn text with [Image #1] = path)--> agent
```

payload.why: takes the attachments folder, the image types and the size cap from werk-shots

payload.title: A turn sent with no card open says that the map shows the whole tree
payload.why: Every turn starts with a line about the open card, so the agent always knows what the person looks at. With no card open, a missing line would leave the agent on the card that the last turn named.
payload.body:
When the person sends a message from the map's whole tree, the first line of the turn says that no card is open and the map shows the whole tree. The next turn sent with a card open then says the map is now at that card, because the open card changed.

Example:

1. The map shows the whole tree. The person sends "What is left open?". The turn starts with [no card is open: the map shows the whole tree].
2. The person opens the card "The open card lives in the location hash" and sends a second message. The turn starts with [the map is now at #map-hash — The open card lives in the location hash].
3. The person sends a third message from the same card. The turn starts with [still on #map-hash — The open card lives in the location hash].

payload.why: takes the now-at and still-on lines that name the open card on every turn from werk-card-blind

payload.title: The browser test run finds the held-out browser tests beside its own specs
payload.why: The binder writes its tests into a folder of their own, outside the folder of the browser specs. A browser test run that looks only in the spec folder finds no test there and exits red, so every held-out browser step reads red whatever the product does.
payload.body: The browser test runner looks for specs in two folders: the folder of the browser specs, and the folder where the binder of the held-out set writes its tests. A held-out test that names its own file then runs with the same harness, the same fake agent and the same fixture project as a spec of the product.

payload.why: takes the folder of the binder tests that the binder writes

payload.text: Ticket werk/109 carries held-out steps written for the earlier rule: a drag from building back to ready stops the build, a building ticket has no archive, and a stop by hand returns the ticket to ready. This card, as accepted on 2026-10-22, refuses that drag and makes archive the one way to end a build. Build werk/109 keeps the refusal. The stale steps need rewriting against this card.

payload.title: The held-out binder and step author do not get the agent instructions
payload.why: Neither agent decides anything the map records. The step author has no tools, and the binder only turns written steps into tests, so rules about writing cards would be noise in their prompts.
payload.body: Among the agents a build starts, the builder pass is the one that writes the map: it proposes a card for each decision that no card makes. So the builder gets the agent instructions in its system prompt. The read-only judges cannot write the map. The held-out step author writes steps from the brief with no tools at all. The held-out binder turns those steps into test code and has no decision of its own to record. None of these three gets the text. An agent that later gains a reason to propose a card joins the builder.

payload.why: takes that the binder only turns written steps into tests
takes that the builder proposes a card for a decision no card makes

payload.title: Every build agent with tools gets the instructions, the binder too
payload.why_not: The binder has nothing to record on the map, and a longer prompt about card wording pulls it away from its one job.

payload.title: The agent instructions are added after the agent's own system prompt, not in its place
payload.why: An agent still needs its own base prompt and the project's instruction files to do its work. The werk text adds the map rules on top of them, so nothing the agent already reads is lost.
payload.body: To keep the agent's tool rules and the project's own instructions, werk appends its text to the end of the system prompt of the agent it starts. The agent then reads three things in order: its own base prompt, the project's instruction files, and the werk text.

payload.title: The agent instructions replace the agent's system prompt
payload.why_not: The agent would lose its base rules for tools and the project's own instruction files, and the werk text does not restate them.

payload.why: takes that the wording rules reach an agent only through its prompt

payload.title: A fork of a tab that has no session yet starts empty
payload.why: A fork copies the parent's session at the moment the tab opens. A tab that has sent no message has no session, so there is nothing to copy. The new tab then starts a session of its own, the same as an empty conversation.
payload.body:
The fork point is taken when the tab opens, not when its first message goes out. So a later turn in the parent never leaks into the fork.

Example:

- tab A, homed on "#map", has sent no message, so it has no session.
- tab B is forked from A at "#fold".

1. B opens. A has no session, so B records no parent.
2. B sends its first message. Its agent starts a new session, with no history.
3. A sends a message later. B does not see it.

    A (no session) ──fork──> B (parent: none) ──first message──> new session

payload.why: The new tab still keeps the home card that this card defines, even with no parent session.

payload.title: The empty-conversation control always opens a new tab, also on a card that has a tab
payload.why: An empty conversation is a deliberate new topic. Switching to the tab that already sits on the card would hide the control's whole effect. So only a fork switches to an existing tab.
payload.body:
A Shift+click and the '+' fork the active tab. When a tab already has the clicked card as its home, they switch to that tab instead. The empty control does not check this: it opens a tab with no parent every time, at the open card.

Example:

- tab main, homed on "#map".

1. The person presses '+' on "#map". The pane switches to main. No tab opens.
2. The person presses the empty control on "#map". A second "#map" chip opens, with no parent session.

    [#map]  +  ∅   --'+'-->  [#map]          (no change)
    [#map]  +  ∅   --'∅'-->  [#map] [#map]   (new, empty)

payload.why: The empty control is the explicit second choice that this card keeps beside the fork.

payload.title: The command line's start-up finishes before a long verb runs, so a hot reload can start
payload.why: Bun's hot reload does not run while the program's first evaluation still waits on something it loaded later. The serve verb runs until the server stops, so a start-up that waits for the verb's end would block every reload.
payload.body:
The start-up of the command line loads the verbs and starts the chosen verb. It does not wait for the verb's result as part of its own evaluation. The exit code is set when the verb ends, from a callback. So the first evaluation finishes at once, and a later edit of any module reloads it in the same process (see #werk-hmr for the runtime and the guard).

Example:

- The server runs under hot reload. The chat child C runs a turn.

1. The start-up loads the verbs, starts the serve verb, and finishes.
2. An agent saves an edit to a server module. Bun evaluates the modules again.
3. The serve verb finds the live server on the global object and swaps in the new request handler. C keeps its turn.
4. The person stops the server. The serve verb ends, and the callback exits with its code.

Nothing reloads in step 2 if the start-up waits for the verb: the reload waits for an evaluation that never ends.

payload.why: takes the reload that evaluates the start-up again and swaps the handler, which this rule lets start

Example:

edit:      evaluate again -> swap handler    (C keeps its turn)

```

payload.why: takes the reload that evaluates the start-up again and swaps the handler, which this rule lets start

payload.title: Each conversation session is one line in an append-only conversations log beside the map log
payload.why: The list of conversations must outlive the server that started them, and a restart gives the first tab a new session under the same tab name. One line per reported session keeps every past session listable, where one file per tab would overwrite the old session.
payload.body:
To let any process list and read every conversation of the project, the server appends one line to a conversations log in the same folder as the map log each time a tab's agent reports a session id it has not reported before. A line holds the tab name, the session id, the home card when the tab has one (see #werk-mc-split), and the parent session when the tab is a fork (see #werk-mc-fork). The list folds the lines into one conversation per session id, in the order the sessions first appeared. A reference to a conversation resolves, in order, as an exact session id, a home card, a tab name, or a session id prefix. A reference that matches two conversations is refused as ambiguous, and one that matches none is refused as unknown.

Example. Tab main starts and its agent reports session s-1. A fork tab with home card #map-hash reports session s-2. The server restarts, and tab main reports session s-3.

1. The log gains three lines: main s-1, the fork s-2 with home #map-hash and parent s-1, main s-3.
2. The list prints three conversations. Both s-1 and s-3 show the tab name main.
3. A reference to #map-hash resolves to s-2.
4. A reference to main is refused as ambiguous: it matches s-1 and s-3.
5. A reference to s-9 is refused as unknown. Nothing is printed.

payload.why: The log records each conversation under the home card that this card gives it.
The log is the store from which the list and the read operations of this card find a conversation by its session id.
