1. The log gains three lines: main s-1, the fork s-2 with home #map-hash and parent s-1, main s-3.
2. The list prints three conversations. Both s-1 and s-3 show the tab name main.
3. A reference to #map-hash resolves to s-2.
4. A reference to main is refused as ambiguous: it matches s-1 and s-3.
5. A reference to s-9 is refused as unknown, and nothing is printed.

```
conversations log                     list
main  s-1                             main  s-1
fork  s-2  home #map-hash  parent s-1 fork  s-2  #map-hash
main  s-3                             main  s-3
```

payload.why: The log records each conversation under the home card that this card gives it.
The log is the store from which the list and the read operations of this card find a conversation by its session id.

payload.title: One folder per tab, holding a file with the tab's current session id
payload.why_not: A tab name outlives its session: the first tab keeps its name across a restart and gets a new session, so the file would be overwritten and the earlier session would drop out of the list.

payload.title: A step past the last chip goes to the first, and a step before the first goes to the last
payload.why: Stepping is the secondary way to switch tabs, used to cycle through a short strip. A step that stops at an end does nothing on the next press, so the person must check where they are. A wrap always moves, the way browser tab stepping does.
payload.body:
To keep every step press useful, the strip treats its chips as a ring. The next step from the last chip focuses the first chip, and the previous step from the first chip focuses the last chip. A strip with one chip stays where it is. A step keeps each tab's own map position, so the map moves to the card of the chip that gets focus.

Example, with three chips in insertion order:

- chip 1 "the map", at card fold
- chip 2 "#fold", at card log
- chip 3 "#log", at card map-hash

1. Chip 3 has focus. The person steps to the next chip. Chip 1 gets focus, and the map moves to fold.
2. The person steps to the previous chip. Chip 3 gets focus again, and the map moves to map-hash.
3. Only chip 1 is open. A step in either direction leaves chip 1 focused, and nothing moves.

```
 next:     [1] -> [2] -> [3] --+
            ^                  |
            +------------------+
 previous: the same ring, the other way
```

payload.why: The step that wraps is the secondary tab key that this card defines.

payload.title: A step stops at the first and the last chip
payload.why_not: A press at an end then does nothing, so the person must look at the strip before each step. Browser tab stepping wraps, so a stop also breaks a habit the person already has.

criterion.text: Step past the last chip several times in daily use. If the wrap lands on a tab you did not mean to open, change to a step that stops at the ends.

payload.title: The silence clock starts at the agent's first event
payload.why: An agent process takes time to start before it writes anything, and that time grows under load. Counting it as silence cancels a healthy agent when the silence limit is short. A start that never ends is still caught, by the wall-clock limit of the session.
payload.body:
The silence limit measures the time between two events of a session. Its clock starts when the agent writes its first event, and starts again at each event after that. Before the first event, only the wall-clock limit of the session applies.

Example, with a silence limit of 50 ms:

- Agent A "starts slowly": it takes 300 ms to start, then writes its first event, then nothing for 10 s.
- Agent B "runs a long tool call": it writes a tool call event at 300 ms, then nothing for 1 s, then the result.

1. A starts. 300 ms pass with no event. Nothing happens: the clock has not started.
2. A writes its first event. The clock starts.
3. 50 ms pass with no event and no tool call in flight. The overseer cancels A for silence.
4. B writes its tool call event. The clock starts, but a tool call is in flight, so the overseer waits.
5. B writes the result 1 s later. Nothing happens to B.

```
time (ms)   0        300        350               1300
A           start....event------X cancelled for silence
B           start....tool call=======in flight=====result
            .... = start-up, no clock   ---- = clock runs   ==== = tool call in flight
```

payload.why: A clock that runs while a tool call is in flight waits, as the in-flight rule says.
A cancel for silence after the first event starts a fresh pass, as that card says.

payload.title: A green build of one ticket moves the ticket to merging with its branch
payload.why: A ticket whose build is green has nothing left to do in building. If it stayed there, the board would show finished work as work in progress, and a second build would start it again. In merging, the next merge loop of its subtree finds it and merges its branch first.
payload.body:
A person can build one ticket on its own, outside a run. When that build goes green, the ticket leaves building and goes to merging, and the board records the branch that holds the green work. The build does not merge the branch itself. The merge loop owns every change to the main line, so the next run of the merge loop on the ticket's subtree takes the ticket from merging and merges its branch before it starts any other ticket. A build that stays red at the retry cap leaves the ticket in building.

Example, with ticket 3 "The thing is done" in ready:

1. The person builds ticket 3. Pass 1 goes green. Ticket 3 moves to merging, with its build branch.
2. The person builds ticket 3 again. The build refuses: ticket 3 is in merging, not in ready.
3. The person starts the run of the subtree. The merge loop merges the branch of ticket 3 first.
4. A build of a ticket that stays red at the cap: the ticket stays in building, and nothing moves.

```
ready --build--> building --green--> merging --merge loop--> done
                    |
                    +-- red at the cap: stays in building
```

payload.why: The hand-off relies on the merge loop to take a ticket from merging and merge its branch before any other ticket.
The hand-off moves the ticket between the building and merging columns that this card defines.

payload.title: The unit tests run on parallel workers, with a per-test time limit that allows for the shared load
payload.why: A test run in one process takes most of the time that the build loop gives one check, so a slow machine fails the check for time alone. Parallel workers cut the run to about a third. But the workers compete for the machine, and a test that starts many processes then runs past a short per-test limit.
payload.body: To keep the unit test run well inside the time limit of one check, the test command runs the test files on four workers at the same time. Each test gets a default limit of 15 seconds instead of the runner default of 5 seconds. A test that needs more still sets its own, longer limit. The limit is not a gate on speed: a test that hangs still fails, only later.

payload.why: takes the rule that a check is one command whose run the loop ends at a time limit

payload.title: The idle limit and the check interval come from the server's environment
payload.why: A test must see a swept session in milliseconds, but the serve command's flags set only the conversation, the tool allowlist and the lock. An environment value changes the timing without a new flag on the command.
payload.body:
The server reads two optional values when it starts. WERK_IDLE_MS is the idle limit: how long a parked conversation may stay idle before its process is killed. It defaults to 30 minutes. WERK_IDLE_CHECK_MS is the time between two idle checks. It defaults to 60 seconds, or to the idle limit when that is shorter. A value that is not a positive whole number is ignored, and the default holds.

Example: a server starts with WERK_IDLE_MS=300. A conversation is parked and has no open turn. About 300 ms later, the next check kills its process. With no value set, the same conversation keeps its process for 30 minutes.

```
WERK_IDLE_MS        unset -> 1800000 ms (30 min)
WERK_IDLE_CHECK_MS  unset -> min(60000, idle limit)
```

payload.why: The defaults are the 30-minute limit and the at-most-one-minute check that this card sets.
The values are not flags because this card limits the serve flags to the conversation, the allowlist and the lock.

payload.title: An un-park keeps a live process, and resumes a stopped one at once
payload.why: A parked conversation whose process still runs has lost nothing, so a restart would only cost time. A conversation whose process was stopped must be back before the person types, so the resume starts at the click and not at the next message.
payload.body:
The page tells the server each time a conversation is parked or un-parked. Only the server knows whether the conversation's process still runs. To avoid a second process for one conversation, an un-park of a conversation with a live process changes nothing on the server. To avoid a wait at the next message, an un-park of a conversation with no live process and a known session starts a new process at once, on that session with the resume option. A conversation with no session yet starts nothing, and its first message starts a fresh process as before. Any later process of a conversation that has a session also resumes that session.

Example: conversations A and B, and B has session s-b.
1. B is parked. Its process still runs. The person clicks B in the '…' menu. B's chip comes back, and no process starts.
2. B is parked again and stays idle past the idle limit. The check kills its process.
3. The person clicks B in the menu. The server starts a process with the resume option and s-b.
4. A has never sent a message and is un-parked. No process starts.

```
un-park B
  live process?  yes -> keep it            (step 1)
                 no  -> session known?  yes -> start: --resume s-b   (step 3)
                                        no  -> start nothing          (step 4)
```

payload.why: A stopped process exists only because this card's idle check kills a parked one, and its reopen resumes.
The new process resumes the stored session id that this card proves resumable.

payload.title: A tab's background agents are the last list of background tasks its agent reported
payload.why: Claude Code resends its whole list of background tasks each time one starts or ends. Reading the last list, not counting starts and ends, cannot drift when one event is missed. A child that exits takes its background tasks with it.
payload.body: To tell a finished main turn from an idle tab, the conversation manager keeps the number of background tasks that the agent's last task list named. A tab runs while a turn is open or that number is above zero. When the child exits, the number drops to zero.

payload.why: The count is how a tab knows the background agent that this card says must keep it running.

payload.title: A child that exits without werk stopping it marks its tab dead until the tab's next child starts
payload.why: Werk stops children on purpose, by the idle sweep and at shutdown, and those exits must not read as deaths. Any other exit needs a decision from the person, so the mark and the line in the other panes stay until a new child replaces the dead one.
payload.body:
A child is dead when it exits and werk did not stop it. A stop by the idle sweep, or by the server as it shuts down, is not a death. To keep the mark honest, a death also drops the open asks and the background agents of that child: nobody can answer them any more. The mark stays until the next child of that tab starts, on the next message or on an un-park. While it stays, every other tab's pane shows one line under its chat log that names the dead tab and gives the error.

Example:
- tab #fold "Fold the cards from the log", in the background, with an ask open
- tab #log, in focus

1. The agent of #fold exits with code 1. The #fold chip turns red, and the ask leaves its ask bar.
2. The #log pane shows the line: #fold died: the agent exited with code 1.
3. The person focuses #fold. Its own pane shows the error at the end of its turn, and no line.
4. The person sends a message in #fold. A new child starts, the chip is no longer red, and the line leaves every pane.
5. The idle sweep stops a parked tab's child. Nothing turns red, and no line shows.

```
  #log pane (in focus)                 tab strip
  +-----------------------------+      [ #log ] [ #fold (red) ]  ... (red)
  | chat log                    |
  | #fold died: exited code 1   |  <-- one line per dead tab that is not in focus
  | ask bar of #log only        |
  +-----------------------------+
```

payload.why: The idle sweep of that card is the exit on purpose that this card does not count as a death.
An ask leaves its own tab's ask bar when the child dies, because that card keeps each ask on its own tab.

payload.title: The grader reads every scenario of a follow-up ticket in full, as a story of the ticket
payload.why: A follow-up ticket delivers held-out scenarios, not spec stories, so its story list is empty. The scope line then sees only each scenario's title, and it calls the behaviour that the scenario steps ask for out of scope. The next pass removes that behaviour, the delivery line fails, and no pass can satisfy both lines.
payload.body:
A follow-up ticket asks for red held-out scenarios word for word. Its acceptance criteria name each scenario by its title only. To keep the scope line from judging a scenario by its title, the grader gets the full Given, When and Then text of each scenario in the place of the ticket's stories. A behaviour that any line of a scenario names is in scope. A behaviour that no scenario line and no criterion names is still out of scope.

Example:

- A follow-up ticket asks for the scenario "G2 opens after the last merge and opens again after a later merge".
- One of its lines reads "When the person approves G2".

1. The builder adds the operation that approves G2.
2. The scope line reads the scenario line about the approval, and the operation passes as in scope.
3. The builder also adds a new export command. No scenario line names an export, so the scope line fails and names it.

```
follow-up ticket ──> grader
  criteria: scenario titles      ─┐
  stories:  full scenario text   ─┴─> scope line: in scope if a criterion or a scenario line names it
```

payload.title: Turn the scope line off for a follow-up ticket
payload.why_not: A follow-up pass can still grow past its scenarios and decide questions that other cards own, which is the reason the scope line exists.

payload.why: The grader reads each scenario as Given, When and Then lines, the form that card gives a held-out step.
The scenario text takes the place of the story list, which that card defines and leaves empty for a ticket with no spec story.

payload.title: A held-out step written before its source card changed is rewritten before it can file a follow-up
payload.why: A step author writes steps from the decided cards as they read at one moment. A later change to a card can leave a step that asks for behaviour the card now forbids. When that step goes red, it files a follow-up that no builder can finish without breaking the card.
payload.body:
A held-out step is true only while the cards it came from read the same. To keep an outdated step from filing work against a decided card, each steps file records which cards, at which version, its steps were written from. Before the held-out set runs on a merged tree, every step whose source card changed since then goes back to the step author. The author rewrites the step from the current card, or drops it when the card no longer asks for that behaviour. A step never files a follow-up while its source card is newer than the step.

Example:

- Card B "A person stops a build only by archiving its ticket" replaced the earlier rule that a drag back into ready stops a build.
- Step S "A person stops a build by a drag back into ready" was written from B before that change.

1. The held-out set is about to run. S records B at its old version, and B has a newer one.
2. The step author reads the current B. B forbids the drag, so the author drops S.
3. The held-out set runs without S, and no follow-up asks for the drag.
4. A step whose source cards did not change runs as before.

```
steps file:  S  ← written from B (version 1)
map:         B  now at version 2
                 │
before run:  version 1 ≠ version 2 → step author rewrites or drops S
run:         only fresh steps run; only a fresh red step files a follow-up
```

payload.why: The step author that writes a step from the cards is the one that rewrites it when a card changes.
A step to rewrite is one Given, When and Then step, in the form that card gives it.

payload.title: Check each red step against the decided cards before the follow-up is filed
payload.why_not: It catches the conflict only after the run went red, and it asks a model to compare a step with every card. A changed card version is a fact that needs no judgement.

payload.title: Put a step that contradicts a card in front of the person as a question
payload.why_not: The person would rewrite a step that the step author can rewrite from the current card, and the run would wait for the answer.

payload.title: A pass that ends on a spec gap does not count against the retry cap
payload.why: The decision pass starts only on the pass after a spec gap shows. When the gap shows on the last pass the cap allows, the cap stops the ticket first. The person then sees a stuck ticket with no question on it, and the passes spent fixing symptoms are lost.
payload.body:
To make sure a spec gap always gets its decision pass, a failed pass whose cause is a spec gap (#ms-fail-cause) is not counted toward the retry cap, the same as a merge conflict (#st-build-conflict). A grader gap that says a person must settle a question counts as a spec gap too. The decision pass that follows always runs. Once the ticket cites the proposal from that pass, every later failed pass counts as usual, so a ticket gets one free pass per open question, not an unbounded number.

Example:

- Ticket T has a cap of 5 passes.
- Pass 5 fails on the grader. The builder of the next pass would name the cause spec gap.

1. Pass 5 fails. Its cause is a spec gap, so the count of counted passes stays at 4.
2. Pass 6 is a decision pass. It proposes a card for the question and builds on it.
3. Pass 6 fails on a check. The cause is a builder error, so the count goes to 5, and the cap stops T.
4. If pass 5 had failed with a builder error instead, the count would reach 5 at step 1 and the cap would stop T there.

```
pass:     1   2   3   4   5(spec gap)   6(decision)
counted:  1   2   3   4   4             5 → cap
```

payload.why: Whether a failed pass is free depends on the cause that card says the next pass names.
It follows the rule that a merge conflict does not count against the cap.

payload.title: Stop the ticket and ask the person as soon as a pass names a spec gap
payload.why_not: It parks the ticket and every ticket that needs it until the person is back, which is the cost the decision pass exists to avoid.

payload.title: Raise the retry cap
payload.why_not: More passes that fix symptoms do not answer the question behind them, and a gap on the last pass still meets the cap.

payload.title: A red held-out run files one follow-up ticket for each ticket whose steps went red
payload.why: A held-out run covers the steps of every done ticket in the subtree. When every red step goes into one follow-up ticket, that ticket mixes unrelated work from many tickets. One hard step then holds back every easy one, and the cap stops them all together.
payload.body:
Each held-out step belongs to the ticket whose steps file holds it. To keep one hard step from blocking unrelated fixes, a red run groups its red steps by that ticket and files one follow-up ticket per group. Each follow-up cites the cards of its own source ticket, and it has its own retry cap. A source ticket that already has an open follow-up gets no second one; its new red steps wait for the next run.

Example:

- Tickets P and Q are done. Run R turns step P.2 red, and steps Q.1 and Q.4 red.

1. R files follow-up F1 with step P.2, citing the cards of P.
2. R files follow-up F2 with steps Q.1 and Q.4, citing the cards of Q.
3. F2 stops at its cap. F1 still builds and merges.
4. A later run turns Q.1 red again while F2 is open. No new ticket is filed for Q.

```
run R:  P.2 ✗   Q.1 ✗   Q.4 ✗
         │        └───┬───┘
         ▼            ▼
        F1 (P)       F2 (Q)      ✗ = red step, (X) = source ticket
```

payload.why: A red step on the merged tree is what files a follow-up, and the merge stands, as that card says.

payload.title: One follow-up ticket for every red step of the run
payload.why_not: It mixes unrelated work. One step that no builder can finish stops the fixes for every other step at the same cap.

payload.title: One follow-up ticket for each red step
payload.why_not: Steps of one ticket often share one cause, so one ticket per step builds the same fix many times and gives merge conflicts between the follow-ups.

payload.why: The source ticket of a step comes from the held-out set that card keeps per ticket of the subtree.

The next pass already reads the failure and the code to fix it, so it knows the cause with no extra session. Only flakiness needs no judgement: the same check on the same commit either passes again or does not. A check that passes again says nothing about the diff, so it does not cost the ticket a pass.

ops.old: The cause names are those of #ms-fail.
ops.new: The cause names are those of #ms-fail.

ops.old:
- **Flaky.** A red check runs once more on the same commit. Green on the rerun gives the cause flaky. The pass stays red: the rerun classifies, it does not change the verdict.
- **Check infrastructure.** The check reports a crash, a timeout, or a missing tool before the code ran. The check run sets this cause itself, with no judgement, and the check is not run again. A stop by the person is not a check infrastructure fail.
- **Every other cause.** The next pass names one cause of the last failure, with one sentence of reason, at the end of its work. Conflict applies only to a fail from the merge loop.
- **No next pass.** A fail at the retry cap has no next pass, so its cause stays unknown.
ops.new:
- **Flaky.** A red check runs once more on the same commit. Green on the rerun gives the cause flaky, and the pass goes on as if the check was green: a flaky check does not cost the ticket a pass. The flaky cause stays on the pass record, so the count of flaky checks still shows.
- **Check infrastructure.** The check reports a crash, a timeout, or a missing tool before the code ran. The check run sets this cause itself, with no judgement, and the check is not run again. A stop by the person is not a check infrastructure fail.
- **Every other cause.** The next pass names one cause of the last failure, with one sentence of reason, at the end of its work. Conflict applies only to a fail from the merge loop.
- **No next pass.** A fail at the retry cap has no next pass, so its cause stays unknown.

ops.old: The cause is stored on the pass that named it, and the report attributes it to the pass before. A cause the check run set comes before a cause the next pass names.
ops.new: The cause is stored on the pass that named it, and the report attributes it to the pass before. A cause the check run set comes before a cause the next pass names.

payload.title: A flaky check keeps the pass red, and the rerun only sets the cause
payload.why_not: A check that passes again on the same commit says nothing wrong about the diff. Keeping the pass red spends a retry on noise, and the next builder edits test settings to stop the noise instead of building the ticket.

payload.why: The wrap is how the previous-chip and next-chip step keys behave, and #werk-mc-keys defines those keys as the secondary way to switch tabs.

payload.title: Each reviewer's role name carries its quality area
payload.why: The reviewers of a pass run at the same time, one per quality area, so a test cannot tell them apart by launch order or by prompt text. A test must still script a finding for one area only. A role name per area lets the fake give each reviewer its own reply.
payload.body:
A reviewer's role name is the word reviewer, a dash, and a short fixed word for its quality area (see #lp-prod-review for the areas): reviewer-design, reviewer-security, and so on. A new area gets a new role name when it is added. Every reviewer still lives for one pass, like every agent that is not a chat agent (see #werk-chat-fake-role).

Example:

- A test scripts reply F, one HIGH finding, for reviewer-security. It scripts reply E, with no finding, for every other area.

1. The pass starts one reviewer per area, all at once. Each carries its own reviewer-<area> name.
2. The fake reads reviewer-security and plays F. The other reviewers play E.
3. The pass fails at the review, and the failure names the security finding.
4. If the test scripts E for every area, no reviewer finds anything, and the pass goes green at the review.

```
reviewer-design           -> E
reviewer-maintainability  -> E
reviewer-tests            -> E
reviewer-security         -> F (HIGH)  -> pass red at review
reviewer-performance      -> E

reviewer-<area>   the role name of the reviewer for one area
F                 the scripted reply with one HIGH finding
E                 the scripted reply with no finding
```

payload.why: takes the quality areas that each get one reviewer
takes the rule that every agent other than a chat agent lives for one pass

payload.title: All reviewers carry the one role name reviewer
payload.why_not: The fake could not give one area a finding and the others none, because nothing else tells the reviewers apart.

payload.title: A fork of a tab with no session opens an empty tab
payload.why: A fork copies the session of the tab it comes from, and a tab that has never sent a message has none. Opening the tab anyway keeps the fork gesture working on every tab. The new tab then behaves like an empty conversation on the clicked card.
payload.body:
A fork copies the session of the tab it comes from. A tab that has sent no message, and is not itself a fork, has no session. To keep the fork gesture from failing on such a tab, the fork opens the new tab anyway, on the clicked card, with no parent session. Its first message starts a new session with no history. The new tab keeps its home card (see #werk-mc-split).

A tab that is itself an unsent fork still has a session to copy: the one it will resume. A fork of that tab copies the same session, so it does not start empty.

Example:

- tab A, homed on "#map", has sent no message and is not a fork.
- tab B is a fork of A at "#fold".

1. The person forks A at "#fold". Tab B opens with home "#fold" and no parent session.
2. B sends its first message. Its agent starts a new session, with no history.
3. The person forks a tab that already has a session. Nothing changes from the normal fork: the new tab copies that session.

    A "#map" (no session) --fork--> B "#fold" (parent: none) --first message--> new, empty session
    C "#map" (session s1) --fork--> D "#fold" (parent: s1)   --first message--> copy of s1

payload.title: Refuse the fork and ask for a first message
payload.why_not: The gesture fails on the newest tab, which is where a person most often starts. The person must type a throwaway message only to be able to fork.

payload.title: Copy the parent's session when the fork sends its first message
payload.why_not: The fork then holds parent turns from after the moment it opened, so its fork-point notice points at the wrong message. A tab that never gets a session still leaves the fork with nothing to copy.

payload.title: The agent instructions are added after the agent's own system prompt, not in its place
payload.why: An agent needs its own base prompt, which holds the rules for its tools. The werk text holds only the map rules and does not restate those tool rules. So werk adds its text at the end and removes nothing.
payload.body:
To keep the agent's own rules for its tools, werk appends its text to the end of the agent's system prompt. It never replaces that prompt. The project's own instruction files load the same way as without werk.

Example:
- Project P has an instruction file that says "Run the tests before a commit".
- Werk starts a build pass in P.

1. The agent starts with its own base prompt, which holds the rules for its tools.
2. Werk adds the map rules at the end of that prompt.
3. The agent reads the instruction file of P, as it does without werk.
4. The agent follows all three. For an agent that does not get the werk text, step 2 does not happen.

```
 system prompt                    project context
+--------------------------+     +-------------------------------+
| 1 base prompt: tool rules|     | 3 instruction file of P:      |
| 2 + werk map rules       |     |   "Run the tests before a     |
+--------------------------+     |    commit"                    |
                                 +-------------------------------+
 1, 2, 3 = the steps above. "+" = added at the end, nothing removed.
```

payload.title: The agent instructions replace the agent's system prompt
payload.why_not: The agent would lose the base rules for its tools, and the werk text does not restate them.

payload.why: takes that each agent is a started Claude Code process, which comes with its own base prompt and reads the project's instruction files

payload.title: A separate control in the tab strip starts an empty conversation in a new tab
payload.why: A fork brings the parent's history, which is wrong for an unrelated topic. One press must give a clean conversation. It always opens a new tab, because a switch to an existing tab would show an old conversation instead.
payload.body:
A fork carries the parent's whole history (see #werk-mc-fork). That is wrong for an unrelated topic. To give that topic a clean start, the tab strip has a second control next to '+' (see #werk-mc-open for '+'). The empty control opens a new tab at the open card, with no parent session. The first message in that tab starts a session with no history. No other gesture starts a conversation empty.

The empty control never switches to an existing tab. A fork switches to a tab that already has the card as its home. The empty control opens a new tab every time, also on that card. The new tab still takes the open card as its home and its chip label (see #werk-mc-split).

Example:

- tab "main", home card "#map", active. The map shows "#fold".
- tab "fold", home card "#fold".

1. The person Shift+clicks a link to "#fold". The pane switches to tab "fold". No tab opens.
2. The person goes back to "main". The map shows "#fold" again.
3. The person presses the empty control. A second "#fold" chip opens and becomes active. Its conversation has no history.

    start:              [#map*] [#fold]           +  ∅
    Shift+click #fold:  [#map]  [#fold*]          +  ∅   (switch, no new tab)
    ∅ on #fold:         [#map]  [#fold] [#fold*]  +  ∅   (new tab, no history)

    *  the active tab
    +  the fork control
    ∅  the empty control

payload.why: The fork stays the normal start. This control is the explicit second choice that the fork decision keeps for an unrelated topic.
The control sits at the end of the tab strip that this card defines.
The empty tab still takes the open card as its home card and chip label.

payload.title: Fork, then clear the context
payload.why_not: It takes two steps for one intent, and the person must know that the clear lives in the context popover. The fork first copies the parent's session, and the clear then throws it away.

payload.title: The empty control switches to a tab that already has the card as its home
payload.why_not: The press then shows an old conversation with its history. That is the opposite of what the person asked for.

payload.title: The product's browser test run also finds the tests in the binder's folder
payload.why: The binder writes its browser tests into a folder of its own, outside the folder of the product's browser specs. A test run that looks only in the spec folder finds no test there, so a held-out browser step never goes green, whatever the product does. When the product's own run finds the binder's tests, a held-out test gets the same server, fake agent and fixture project as a product spec.
payload.body:
To let a held-out browser test run, the product's browser test run looks for tests in two folders: the folder of the product's browser specs, and the folder where the binder writes its tests (#lp-heldout-binder). A held-out test then runs with the same harness as a product spec: a real server on a copy of the fixture project, with the fake agent first on the program search list (#werk-test-visual).

The binder's folder exists only in the temporary checkout where the binder works (#lp-heldout-mechanics). A builder's checkout has no such folder, so a builder's browser test run finds only the product specs.

Example:

- Step S1 "The list updates while the person types a search".
- The binder writes the test for S1 as one file in its folder.

1. The binder starts the browser test run on that one file. The run finds the file in the binder's folder, starts the real server on a copy of the fixture project, and runs the test. S1 ends green or red, by what the product does.
2. A builder starts the browser test run in its own checkout. That checkout has no binder folder. The run finds the product specs only, and no held-out test runs.

```
  binder's temporary checkout          builder's checkout
  ---------------------------          ------------------
  spec folder     product specs        spec folder     product specs
  binder folder   S1 test              (no binder folder)
        |                                    |
        v                                    v
  browser test run, both folders       browser test run, both folders
        |                                    |
        v                                    v
  S1: green or red                     product specs only
```

S1 = one held-out step. "spec folder" = the folder of the product's browser specs. "binder folder" = the folder where the binder writes its tests.

payload.why: takes the folder of its own where the binder writes its tests, outside of which a write voids its report
takes the browser harness that a held-out test shares: a real server on a copy of the fixture project, with the fake agent first
takes the temporary checkout of the binder, so the binder's folder never exists in a builder's checkout

payload.title: The binder writes its own browser test settings inside its folder
payload.why_not: The settings must repeat how the product starts its server, its fake agent and its fixture project. A copy that differs from the product's harness makes a held-out step fail for a harness reason, and that reads as a product failure.

payload.title: Each conversation session is one line in an append-only conversations log beside the map log
payload.why: A tab keeps its name when it gets a new session, for example when its stored session no longer resolves at a restart. A store that keeps one current session per tab then overwrites the old session, and that conversation drops out of the list. One line per new session keeps every past session listable.
payload.body:
To keep every past session listable, the server appends one line to a conversations log in the same folder as the map log. It appends the line each time a tab's agent reports a session id that the log does not hold yet. A line holds the tab name, the session id, the home card when the tab has one (see #werk-mc-split), and the parent session when the tab is a fork (see #werk-mc-fork). No line is ever rewritten. The list of conversations folds the lines into one entry per session id.

A plain restart resumes the same session and adds no line (see #werk-resume). A tab gets a new session under its old name only when its stored session no longer resolves at a start, or when the server starts the first tab fresh on purpose. In those cases the old session stays in the log.

Example. These things exist:

- Tab main, whose agent reports session s-1.
- Tab map-hash, a fork of s-1 with home card #map-hash, whose agent reports session s-2.

1. Tab main reports s-1. The log gains the line main s-1.
2. Tab map-hash reports s-2. The log gains the line map-hash s-2, home #map-hash, parent s-1.
3. The server restarts and tab main resumes s-1. The log gains nothing, because it holds s-1 already.
4. At the next restart s-1 no longer resolves, so tab main reports a new session s-3. The log gains the line main s-3.
5. The list shows three conversations: s-1, s-2 and s-3. Both s-1 and s-3 carry the tab name main.

```
step  event                          line appended to the conversations log
1     main reports s-1          -->  main      s-1
2     map-hash reports s-2      -->  map-hash  s-2  home #map-hash  parent s-1
3     restart, main resumes s-1 -->  (none: s-1 is in the log already)
4     restart, s-1 is gone,
      main reports s-3          -->  main      s-3

list:  s-1 (main)   s-2 (map-hash)   s-3 (main)
```

payload.why: The log records each conversation under the home card that this card gives it.
The list and read operations of this card find each conversation in this log.
A fork is its own session with a parent session, as this card decides, so a log line records that parent.
A restart resumes the stored session and adds no line; only the fallback to a new session that this card defines adds one.

payload.title: One folder per tab, holding a file with the tab's current session id
payload.why_not: A tab name outlives its session: when the stored session no longer resolves, the tab gets a new session under the same name, the file is overwritten, and the earlier session drops out of the list.

payload.title: The command line does not wait for a verb that runs until stopped, so a hot reload can run
payload.why: Bun's hot reload waits until the program's first evaluation ends. The serve verb runs until the server stops. A start-up that waited for serve would never end, so no edit would ever reload.
payload.body:
The start-up of the command line starts a verb that runs until someone stops it, such as serve, and does not wait for it. The verb reports a failure, and sets the exit code, from a callback when it ends. So the first evaluation ends at once, and a later edit of any module reloads it in the same process (see #werk-hmr for the runtime and the guard). A short verb, such as add or show, may still be awaited, because it ends before anyone edits a file.

Example:

- The server runs under hot reload. The chat child C runs a turn.

1. The start-up loads the verbs, starts the serve verb, and ends.
2. An agent saves an edit to a server module. Bun evaluates the modules again.
3. The serve verb finds the live server on the global object and swaps in the new request handler. C keeps its turn.
4. The person stops the server. The server stops its children and exits.

If the start-up waited for serve, nothing would reload in step 2. The reload waits for an evaluation that never ends, and the edit has no effect until a restart.

```
start-up:  load verbs -> start serve -> end      (no wait on serve)
edit:      evaluate again -> swap handler        (C keeps its turn)
stop:      server stops C -> exit
```

payload.title: The silence clock starts at the agent's first event
payload.why: An agent process takes time to start before it writes anything, and that time grows under load. Counting it as silence cancels a healthy agent when the silence limit is short. A start that never ends is still caught by the wall-clock limit of the session.
payload.body:
The silence limit measures the time between two events of a session. Its clock starts when the agent writes its first event, and starts again at each event after that. Before the first event, only the wall-clock limit of the session applies (see #al-sample-budget).

Example, with a silence limit of 60 s and a wall-clock limit of 600 s:

- Agent A "starts slowly": under load it takes 90 s to start. It writes its first event, then stops.
- Agent B "runs a long build": it writes a tool call event at 5 s. The build runs for 300 s, then the result comes.
- Agent C "never starts": it writes no event at all.

1. 90 s pass with no event from A. Nothing happens: the clock of A has not started.
2. A writes its first event at 90 s. Its clock starts.
3. 60 s pass with no event and no tool call in flight. At 150 s the overseer cancels A for silence.
4. B writes its tool call event at 5 s. Its clock starts, but a tool call is in flight, so the overseer waits.
5. B writes the result at 305 s. Nothing happens to B.
6. C writes nothing. At 600 s the wall-clock limit cancels C.

```
time (s)  0        90       150          305           600
A         start....event----X
B         start=tool call (5 s)==========result
C         start........................................X
          .... = start-up, no clock running
          ---- = silence clock running
          ==== = tool call in flight, overseer waits
          X    = cancelled: A for silence, C at the wall-clock limit
```

payload.why: A clock that runs while a tool call is in flight waits, as the in-flight rule says.
A cancel for silence after the first event starts a fresh pass, as that card says.
Before the first event, the wall-clock limit that this card caps is the only stop for an agent that never starts.

payload.title: The builder loop ends its own build when it reads that its ticket is archived
payload.why: A build can run from the merge loop or from a single build command, and only the builder loop is present in both. When the builder loop reads the board itself, an archive ends every build the same way, with no second process that has to notice it.
payload.body:
While a build runs, its builder loop reads the board about once a second. When it finds its ticket archived during a pass, it stops the agent of that pass, commits nothing of the pass, runs no checks, records no retry, and ends. An archive that comes while the checks or the grader of the last pass run also ends the build: nothing of the build merges, even a pass that ended green. In every case the worktree folder goes and the ticket's branch stays.

A merge loop that started the build merges nothing of it and goes on with its other tickets. The archive ends one build. It is not a stop of the merge loop, so no other ticket moves back to ready.

Example:

- Ticket T "Draw the board" is in building. The agent of its pass 2 runs.
- Ticket U "Save the log" builds beside T in the same merge loop.
- A person archives T on the board.

1. The board log gets the archive. T leaves the columns.
2. Within about a second, the builder loop of T reads the board and sees T archived.
3. It stops the pass 2 agent. The board no longer shows T as running.
4. The builder loop of T ends. The branch of T stays. Nothing of T merges.
5. The merge loop goes on. U builds and merges as before.
6. Case where nothing happens: the person cancels the confirmation. No event is written, and the build of T goes on.

```
board log            builder loop of T              agent of T, pass 2
---------            -----------------              ------------------
T archived  ---->    reads board (~1 s): archived
                     stop  ---------------------->  stopped
                     no commit, no checks
                     worktree removed, branch kept
                          |
                          v
                     merge loop: T merges nothing; U goes on
```

~1 s: the time between two reads of the board.

payload.why: It adds an ending to the builder loop that st-build-ticket defines.
It says how the merge loop of st-build-run treats a build that an archive ended: nothing of it merges, and the loop goes on.

payload.title: A turn sent with no card open says that the map shows the whole tree
payload.why: Every turn starts with a line about the open card, so the agent always knows what the person looks at. With no card open, a missing line would leave the agent on the card that the last turn named.
payload.body:
A turn sent from the map's whole tree has no open card to name. To keep the first line on every turn, the line then says that no card is open and that the map shows the whole tree. The next turn sent with a card open says that the map is now at that card, because the open card changed. See #werk-card-blind for the now-at and still-on lines.

Example:

- The whole tree: the map page with no card open.
- Card A: #werk-chat "The composer sends a live agent turn".

1. The map shows the whole tree. The person sends "What is left open?". The turn starts with [no card is open: the map shows the whole tree].
2. The person opens card A and sends a second message. The turn starts with [the map is now at #werk-chat — The composer sends a live agent turn].
3. The person sends a third message from card A. The turn starts with [still on #werk-chat — The composer sends a live agent turn].
4. The person goes back to the whole tree and sends nothing. No turn goes out, so no line goes out.

```
turn   map shows     first line of the turn
----   -----------   ------------------------------------------
1      whole tree    [no card is open: the map shows the whole tree]
2      card A        [the map is now at #werk-chat — ...]   (card changed)
3      card A        [still on #werk-chat — ...]            (same card)
```

payload.title: The command line's start-up does not wait for the verb, so a hot reload can run
payload.why: Bun's hot reload waits until the program's first evaluation ends. The serve verb runs until the server stops. A start-up that waited for its verb would never end under serve, so no edit would ever reload.
payload.body:
The start-up of the command line loads the verbs and starts the chosen verb. It does not wait for the verb's result as part of its own evaluation. When the verb ends, a callback exits with the verb's exit code. So the first evaluation ends at once, and a later edit of any module reloads it in the same process (see #werk-hmr for the runtime and the guard).

Example:

- The server runs under hot reload. The chat child C runs a turn.

1. The start-up loads the verbs, starts the serve verb, and ends.
2. An agent saves an edit to a server module. Bun evaluates the modules again.
3. The serve verb finds the live server on the global object and swaps in the new request handler. C keeps its turn.
4. The person stops the server. The serve verb ends, and the callback exits with its code.

If the start-up waited for the verb, nothing would reload in step 2. The reload waits for an evaluation that never ends.

```
start-up:  load verbs -> start serve -> end      (no wait on serve)
edit:      evaluate again -> swap handler        (C keeps its turn)
stop:      serve ends -> callback -> exit with serve's code
```

payload.title: An un-park keeps a live process, and resumes a stopped one at once
payload.why: A parked conversation whose process still runs has lost nothing, so a restart would only cost time. A conversation whose process was stopped must be back before the person types, so the resume starts at the click and not at the next message.
payload.body:
The page tells the server each time a conversation is parked or un-parked. Only the server knows whether the conversation's process still runs. To avoid a second process for one conversation, an un-park of a conversation with a live process changes nothing on the server. To avoid a wait at the next message, an un-park of a conversation with no live process and a known session starts a new process at once, and that process resumes the session (see #werk-resume). A conversation with no session yet starts nothing on un-park. Its first message starts a fresh process.

Example: conversations A and B. B has the session s-b. A has never sent a message.
1. B is parked. Its process still runs. The person clicks B in the '…' menu. B's chip comes back, and no process starts.
2. B is parked again and stays idle past the idle limit. The idle check kills its process (see #werk-mc-reap).
3. The person clicks B in the menu. The server starts a process at once, and it resumes s-b. The person types into a conversation that is already running.
4. A is un-parked. No process starts. A's first message starts a fresh process.

```
un-park B
  live process?  yes -> keep it, start nothing              (step 1)
                 no  -> session known?
                          yes -> start now, resume s-b      (step 3)
                          no  -> start nothing              (step 4)
```

payload.why: A stopped process exists only because the idle check of that card kills a parked one, and its reopen resumes.
The new process resumes the stored session id that this card proves resumable.

payload.title: Resume a stopped process at the next message
payload.why_not: The person types into a conversation that has no process. The message then waits while the process starts and the session loads, which is the slowest moment to wait.

payload.why: A follow-up ticket asks for each of its scenarios line by line, so every Given, When and Then line is part of what the ticket asks for. The scope line must judge the diff against that whole request. A scenario title names only a small part of the behaviour that its lines ask for.

payload.title: The unit tests run on parallel workers, with a per-test time limit that allows for the shared load
payload.why: Run in one process, the unit tests take most of the time that the build loop gives one check, so a slow machine fails the check for time alone. Parallel workers make the run shorter. But the workers compete for the machine, so a test that starts many processes in sequence runs past a short per-test limit.
payload.body:
To keep the unit test run well inside the time limit of one check, the test command runs the test files on four worker processes at the same time. Each test gets a default limit of 15 seconds, not the runner default of 5 seconds. A test that needs more still sets its own, longer limit.

The longer limit does not hide a slow test or a frozen test. A test that hangs still fails, only 10 seconds later. A check that runs past its own time limit is a fail of the check infrastructure, not of the code (#ms-fail-cause), so the run time of the whole suite is the number to protect.

payload.why: The unit test run is one check: one command whose exit code is the verdict.
A check that runs past its time limit fails as check infrastructure, not as code. That is the fail this card keeps the test run away from.

payload.title: Run the test files in one process, with the runner default per-test limit
payload.why_not: The run in one process takes most of the time limit of one check. A slower machine or a few more tests then fail the check for time alone, with no fault in the code.

payload.title: A green build of one ticket moves the ticket to merging with its branch
payload.why: A ticket whose build is green has nothing left to do in building. If it stayed there, the board would show finished work as work in progress, and a second build would start it again. In merging, the next merge loop of its subtree finds it and merges its branch first.
payload.body:
A person can build one ticket on its own, outside a run. When that build goes green, the ticket leaves building and goes to merging, and the board records the branch that holds the green work. The build does not merge the branch itself. The merge loop owns every change to the main line (#st-build-run). The next run of the merge loop on the ticket's subtree takes the ticket from merging and merges its branch before it starts a new build. A build that stays red at the retry cap leaves the ticket in building.

Example, with ticket 3 "The export writes one file per order" in ready:

1. The person builds ticket 3. Pass 1 goes green. Ticket 3 moves to merging, with its build branch.
2. The person builds ticket 3 again. The build refuses: ticket 3 is in merging, not in ready.
3. The person starts the run of the subtree. The merge loop merges the branch of ticket 3 before it starts any build.
4. The person builds ticket 4, and every pass stays red until the retry cap. Ticket 4 stays in building, and nothing moves.

```
ready --build--> building --green--> merging --merge loop--> done
                    |
                    +-- red at the retry cap: stays in building
```

payload.title: A pasted image travels inside the chat message, and the server stores it
payload.why: The composer sends one request per message. Carrying the image bytes in that request means a message and its images arrive together or not at all. No image is stored for a message that never reached the server, or for an image the person removed before sending.
payload.body:
To send a message and its images in one step, the page reads each pasted image in the browser. It puts the image bytes, encoded as text, into the same request as the message text, the open card and the tab. Nothing goes to the server at paste time. The server checks every image's type and size before it stores any of them. Then it writes each image to the attachments folder and gives the agent the path of each file (see #werk-shots for the folder, the types and the size cap).

Example:

- The person pastes a 2 MB screenshot and a 25 MB screenshot, and types "Why is this red?".
- The person removes the second chip, because it is over the size cap, and presses Enter.

1. Each paste shows a token, [Image #1] and [Image #2], and a chip. The server has no file yet.
2. Removing chip 2 drops its bytes from the page. The server never sees them.
3. Enter sends one request with the text and the bytes of image 1.
4. The server checks image 1, stores it, and the agent's turn names its path as [Image #1].
5. Had the person sent both images, the server refuses the whole request: it stores no image and starts no turn.

```
paste --> page keeps the bytes (chip + [Image #N])      server: nothing yet
Enter --> page --(text + image bytes + card + tab)--> server
                                                       | check every image (type, size)
                                                       |   one bad -> refuse: no file, no turn
                                                       v
                                       store each file --> attachments/
                                                       |
                                                       +--(turn text: [Image #1] = path)--> agent
```

payload.title: A tab counts its background tasks from the last full list its agent sent
payload.why: The agent sends its whole list of background tasks each time one starts or ends. Werk keeps the length of the last list, so one lost event cannot leave a wrong count. A count of starts and ends would stay wrong after one lost event, and the tab would never read as idle again.
payload.body:
A background task is a subagent or a shell command that the agent starts and that runs on after its turn ends. Claude Code, the agent that werk runs in each tab, sends the full list of these tasks each time one starts or ends. To avoid a count that drifts after one lost event, werk does not add up starts and ends. It replaces the tab's count with the length of each new list. This count is what keeps a tab with a finished turn marked as running (see #werk-mc-bgagents). When the tab's child process exits, its tasks end with it, and the count goes to zero.

Example:
- tab #fold "Fold the cards from the log"
- task A, a subagent that reviews a card
- task B, a shell command that runs the tests

1. The agent starts task A and sends the list [A]. The count is 1.
2. The agent starts task B and sends [A, B]. The count is 2.
3. The turn ends. The count is 2, so #fold still shows as running.
4. Task A ends, but werk loses the list [B]. The count stays 2.
5. Task B ends, and the agent sends []. The count is 0, and #fold is idle. The lost list in step 4 leaves no error.
6. Any other event from the agent leaves the count as it is.
7. If the child exits while a task runs, the count goes to 0 at once.

```
  list from the agent       count   #fold chip
  [A]                       1       running
  [A, B]                    2       running
  (turn ends)               2       running
  [B]  -- lost --           2       running
  []                        0       idle

  count = number of tasks in the last list received
  child exits               0       (dead or idle, never running)
```

payload.why: The count is how a tab knows the background agent that this card says must keep it running.

payload.title: The page uploads each image when it is pasted, and the message carries only its path
payload.why_not: An image is stored for every paste, also for a chip the person removes or a message never sent. The chip must wait for the upload before it can show the image, and a send in that wait has no path to carry.

payload.why: takes the verbs that register themselves, which the start-up loads before it starts one

payload.title: Each conversation session is one line in an append-only conversations log beside the map log
payload.why: A tab keeps its name when it gets a new session, for example when its stored session no longer resolves at a restart. A store that keeps one current session per tab then overwrites the old session, and that conversation drops out of the list. One line per reported session keeps every past session listable.
payload.body:
To keep every past session listable, the server appends one line to a conversations log in the same folder as the map log. It appends the line each time a tab's agent reports a session. A line holds the tab name, the session id, the home card when the tab has one (see #werk-mc-split), and the parent session when the tab is a fork (see #werk-mc-fork). No line is ever rewritten. The list of conversations folds the lines into one entry per session id, so a second line for a session the log holds already adds no entry.

A plain restart resumes the same session, so the list keeps one entry for it (see #werk-resume). A tab gets a new session under its old name only when its stored session no longer resolves at a start, or when the server starts the first tab fresh on purpose. In those cases the old session stays in the log.

Example. These things exist:

- Tab main, whose agent reports session s-1.
- Tab map-hash, a fork of s-1 with home card #map-hash, whose agent reports session s-2.

1. Tab main reports s-1. The log gains the line main s-1.
2. Tab map-hash reports s-2. The log gains the line map-hash s-2, home #map-hash, parent s-1.
3. The server restarts and tab main resumes s-1. The list still shows one entry for s-1.
4. At the next restart s-1 no longer resolves, so tab main reports a new session s-3. The log gains the line main s-3.
5. The list shows three conversations: s-1, s-2 and s-3. Both s-1 and s-3 carry the tab name main.

```
step  event                          line appended to the conversations log
1     main reports s-1          -->  main      s-1
2     map-hash reports s-2      -->  map-hash  s-2  home #map-hash  parent s-1
3     restart, main resumes s-1 -->  (no new entry: s-1 is in the log already)
4     restart, s-1 is gone,
      main reports s-3          -->  main      s-3

list:  s-1 (main)   s-2 (map-hash)   s-3 (main)
```

payload.why: The log records each conversation under the home card that this card gives it.
The list and read operations of this card find each conversation in this log.
A fork is its own session with a parent session, as this card decides, so a log line records that parent.
A restart resumes the stored session, so its line adds no new entry; only the fallback to a new session that this card defines adds one.

payload.title: One folder per tab, holding a file with the tab's current session id
payload.why_not: A tab name outlives its session: when the stored session no longer resolves, the tab gets a new session under the same name, the file is overwritten, and the earlier session drops out of the list.

payload.why: The wrap is how the previous-chip and next-chip step keys behave, and #werk-mc-keys defines those keys as the secondary way to switch tabs.

payload.title: A red held-out run files one follow-up ticket for each ticket whose steps went red
payload.why: A held-out run covers the steps of every merged ticket. When all red steps go into one follow-up ticket, that ticket mixes unrelated work. One step that no builder can finish then uses up the retry cap of the whole follow-up, and the easy fixes stop with it.
payload.body:
Each held-out step comes from the brief of one ticket, its source ticket. To keep one hard step from blocking unrelated fixes, a red held-out run groups its red steps by source ticket and files one follow-up ticket per group. Each follow-up cites the cards of its own source ticket and has its own retry cap. A red step that an open follow-up already carries files nothing again.

Example:

- Tickets P and Q are merged. Run R turns step P.2 red, and steps Q.1 and Q.4 red.

1. R files follow-up F1 with step P.2. F1 cites the cards of P.
2. R files follow-up F2 with steps Q.1 and Q.4. F2 cites the cards of Q.
3. F2 stops at its cap. F1 still builds and merges.
4. A later run turns Q.1 red again while F2 is open. F2 already carries Q.1, so nothing is filed.

```
run R:  P.2 ✗   Q.1 ✗   Q.4 ✗
         │        └───┬───┘
         ▼            ▼
        F1 (P)       F2 (Q)      ✗ = red step, (X) = source ticket
```

payload.title: One follow-up ticket for every red step of the run
payload.why_not: It mixes unrelated work. One step that no builder can finish stops the fixes for every other step at the same cap.

payload.title: One follow-up ticket for each red step
payload.why_not: Steps of one ticket often share one cause, so one ticket per step builds the same fix many times and gives merge conflicts between the follow-ups.

payload.why: A step author writes a ticket's steps from that ticket's brief, so each step has one source ticket to group by.
A follow-up is a new ticket with its own retry cap, so a group that stops at its cap stops only its own steps.

payload.title: A fork of a tab with no session opens an empty tab
payload.why: A fork copies the session of the tab it comes from, and a tab that has never sent a message has none. Opening the tab anyway keeps the fork gesture working on every tab. The new tab then behaves like an empty conversation on the clicked card.
payload.body:
A fork copies the session of the tab it comes from. A tab that has sent no message has no session of its own. To keep the fork gesture from failing on such a tab, the fork opens the new tab anyway, on the clicked card, with no parent session. Its first message starts a new session with no history. The new tab keeps its home card (see #werk-mc-split).

This holds also for a tab that is itself a fork and has sent no message: it has no session of its own yet, so a fork of it starts empty too.

Example:

- tab A, homed on "#map", has sent no message.
- tab C, homed on "#map", has sent a message, so it has session s1.

1. The person forks A at "#fold". Tab B opens with home "#fold" and no parent session.
2. B sends its first message. Its agent starts a new session, with no history.
3. The person forks C at "#fold". Nothing changes from the normal fork: tab D opens with parent s1, and its first message continues from a copy of s1.

    A "#map" (no session) --fork--> B "#fold" (parent: none) --first message--> new, empty session
    C "#map" (session s1) --fork--> D "#fold" (parent: s1)   --first message--> copy of s1

payload.title: Refuse the fork and ask for a first message
payload.why_not: The gesture fails on the newest tab, which is where a person most often starts. The person must type a throwaway message only to be able to fork.

payload.title: A child that exits without werk stopping it marks its tab dead until the tab's next child starts
payload.why: Werk stops children on purpose, and those exits must not read as deaths. Any other exit needs a decision from the person, so the mark and the line in the other panes stay until a new child replaces the dead one.
payload.body:
A child is dead when it exits and werk did not stop it. Werk stops a child on purpose in three cases: the idle sweep of a parked tab, a restart for a new model or a cleared context, and the shutdown of the server. None of these is a death. A crash that werk retries on its own is not a death yet: the tab is dead only when that retry also fails, or when the failure is one that a retry cannot fix (see #werk-crashmsg).

A death also drops the open asks and the background agents of that child, because no process is left to answer them. The mark stays until the next child of that tab starts, on the next message or on an un-park. While it stays, the dead tab's chip blinks red (see #werk-mc-asks-dot), and the dead-child bar of every other tab's pane shows one line that names the dead tab and gives the error.

Example:
- tab #fold "Fold the cards from the log", in the background, with an ask open
- tab #log, in focus

1. The agent of #fold exits with code 1, and the failure is not one to retry. The #fold chip blinks red, and the ask leaves the #fold ask bar.
2. The #log pane shows the line: #fold died: the agent exited with code 1.
3. The person focuses #fold. Its own pane shows the error at the end of its turn, and no line.
4. The person sends a message in #fold. A new child starts, the chip stops blinking red, and the line leaves every pane.
5. The idle sweep stops the child of a parked tab. Nothing turns red, and no line shows.

```
  #log pane (in focus)
  +--------------------------------+
  | chat log                       |
  | #fold died: exited with code 1 |  <-- dead-child bar: one line per dead tab not in focus
  | ask bar: asks of #log only     |
  +--------------------------------+
  tab strip:  [ #log ]  [ #fold * ]

  *  = the chip dot blinks red: the child of #fold is dead
```

payload.why: Each ask lives in the ask bar of its own tab, so a death clears that tab's bar and no other.
The idle sweep stops a parked child on purpose, so its exit is not a death.
A model change restarts the child on purpose, so its exit is not a death.
A context clear restarts the child on purpose, so its exit is not a death.
A crash gets one automatic retry first, so the tab is dead only when the retry also fails or is not made.
A dead tab shows on its chip as the red blink of the chip dot.

The next pass already reads the failure and the code to fix it, so it knows the cause with no extra session. Only flakiness needs no judgement: the same check on the same commit either passes again or does not. A check that fails and then passes on the same commit gives no stable verdict on the diff, so it does not cost the ticket a pass.

ops.old: The cause names are those of #ms-fail.
ops.new: The cause names are those of #ms-fail.

ops.old:
- **Flaky.** A red check runs once more on the same commit. Green on the rerun gives the cause flaky. The pass stays red: the rerun classifies, it does not change the verdict.
- **Check infrastructure.** The check reports a crash, a timeout, or a missing tool before the code ran. The check run sets this cause itself, with no judgement, and the check is not run again. A stop by the person is not a check infrastructure fail.
- **Every other cause.** The next pass names one cause of the last failure, with one sentence of reason, at the end of its work. Conflict applies only to a fail from the merge loop.
- **No next pass.** A fail at the retry cap has no next pass, so its cause stays unknown.
ops.new:
- **Flaky.** A red check runs once more on the same commit. Green on the rerun gives the cause flaky, and the green rerun is the verdict of that check. The pass goes on to the next check, the grader and the review, so a flaky check alone never costs the ticket a pass. The pass record keeps the flaky cause, so the fail report counts flaky checks on green passes too. Red on the rerun leaves the pass red, and the next pass names the cause.
- **Check infrastructure.** The check reports a crash, a timeout, or a missing tool before the code ran. The check run sets this cause itself, with no judgement, and the check is not run again. A stop by the person is not a check infrastructure fail.
- **Every other cause.** The next pass names one cause of the last failure, with one sentence of reason, at the end of its work. Conflict applies only to a fail from the merge loop.
- **No next pass.** A fail at the retry cap has no next pass, so its cause stays unknown.

ops.old: The cause is stored on the pass that named it, and the report attributes it to the pass before. A cause the check run set comes before a cause the next pass names.
ops.new: The cause is stored on the pass that named it, and the report attributes it to the pass before. A cause the check run set comes before a cause the next pass names.
Example:
- Ticket T has the checks type check, unit test and lint, in that order, and a retry cap of 5.

1. Pass 2 runs the checks. The type check is green and the unit test is red.
2. The unit test runs once more on the same commit. It is green, so its cause is flaky.
3. Lint, the grader and the review run on pass 2. All pass, so pass 2 is green and T is built in 2 passes.
4. If the rerun had been red, pass 2 would be red, it would count against the cap, and pass 3 would name the cause.

```
pass 2:  type check ✓  unit test ✗ → rerun ✓ (flaky)  lint ✓  grader ✓  review ✓   → pass 2 green
pass 2:  type check ✓  unit test ✗ → rerun ✗                                       → pass 2 red, pass 3 names the cause

✓ green   ✗ red   → leads to
```

The line fails when the diff builds a behaviour that no acceptance criterion and no story of the ticket asks for. The gap names each such behaviour, so the next pass removes it. A contradiction line never asks for a missing part of a card, so a contradiction line cannot push a diff out of scope.

The line fails when the diff builds a behaviour that no acceptance criterion and no story of the ticket asks for. payload.why: A held-out step tests the product against what its cards say. The cards keep changing after the steps are written, so a step is a fair test only while it says what its cards say now. Keeping the steps in step with the cards makes every red step point at work the map still asks for.

criterion.metric: follow-up tickets that stop at the retry cap while a red step contradicts a decided card

payload.why: A failed pass that ends on a spec gap costs the ticket no retry, so the decision pass that answers the gap always gets to run, even after the last counted pass. Every other failed pass still counts, so the cap still stops a ticket that keeps failing for a reason a decision cannot fix.

payload.title: A red held-out run files one follow-up ticket for each ticket whose steps went red
payload.why: A red run groups its red steps by the ticket they came from, and files one follow-up ticket for each group. Each follow-up builds, fails and stops on its own, so one step that no builder can pass does not hold back the fixes for other tickets.
payload.body:
Each held-out step comes from the brief of one ticket, its source ticket. To keep one hard step from blocking unrelated fixes, a red held-out run groups its red steps by source ticket and files one follow-up ticket per group. Each follow-up cites the cards of its own source ticket and has its own retry cap. A red step that an open follow-up already carries files nothing again.

Example:

- Tickets P and Q are merged. Run R turns step P.2 red, and steps Q.1 and Q.4 red.

1. R files follow-up F1 with step P.2. F1 cites the cards of P.
2. R files follow-up F2 with steps Q.1 and Q.4. F2 cites the cards of Q.
3. F2 stops at its cap. F1 still builds and merges.
4. A later run turns Q.1 red again while F2 is open. F2 already carries Q.1, so nothing is filed.

```
run R:  P.2 ✗   Q.1 ✗   Q.4 ✗
         │        └───┬───┘
         ▼            ▼
        F1 (P)       F2 (Q)      ✗ = red step, (X) = source ticket
```

payload.why: A red step on the merged tree is what files a follow-up, and the merge stands, as that card says.
The source ticket of a step comes from the held-out set that card keeps per ticket of the subtree.

payload.title: One follow-up ticket for every red step of the run
payload.why_not: It mixes unrelated work. One step that no builder can finish stops the fixes for every other step at the same cap.

payload.title: One follow-up ticket for each red step
payload.why_not: Steps of one ticket often share one cause, so one ticket per step builds the same fix many times and gives merge conflicts between the follow-ups.

criterion.text: Revisit when a decision pass runs and the pass after it names a spec gap again for the same question: then the free pass buys no answer, and a person must take the question.

criterion.metric: share of follow-up tickets that hit a merge conflict with another follow-up filed by the same held-out run

criterion.text: A wrong role name fails the build's own tests at once, and a change back touches one naming rule and the tests that script reviewer replies.
Switching to replace is one flag on the agent start. A test that shows an agent losing its tool rules, or a werk rule conflicting with the base prompt, is enough to switch.

payload.title: The product's browser test run also finds the tests in the binder's folder
payload.why: The binder is the agent that turns each held-out step into a browser test, and it writes those tests into a folder of its own. The product's browser test run looks in that folder as well as in its own spec folder, so a held-out test runs on the same server, fake agent and fixture project as a product spec. A run that looked only in the spec folder would find no held-out test, and a held-out browser step would never go green, whatever the product does.
payload.body:
The binder is the agent that turns each held-out step into a browser test, without ever changing the product (#lp-heldout-binder). It writes those tests into a folder of its own. To let them run, the product's browser test run looks for tests in two folders: the folder of the product's browser specs, and the binder's folder. A held-out test then runs with the same harness as a product spec: a real server on a copy of the fixture project, with the fake agent first on the program search list (#werk-test-visual).

The binder's folder exists only in the temporary checkout where the binder works (#lp-heldout-mechanics). A builder's checkout has no such folder, so a builder's browser test run finds only the product specs.

Example:

- Step S1 "The list updates while the person types a search".
- The binder writes the test for S1 as one file in its folder.

1. The binder starts the browser test run on that one file. The run finds the file in the binder's folder, starts the real server on a copy of the fixture project, and runs the test. S1 ends green or red, by what the product does.
2. A builder starts the browser test run in its own checkout. That checkout has no binder folder. The run finds the product specs only, and no held-out test runs.

```
  binder's temporary checkout          builder's checkout
  ---------------------------          ------------------
  spec folder     product specs        spec folder     product specs
  binder folder   S1 test              (no binder folder)
        |                                    |
        v                                    v
  browser test run, both folders       browser test run, both folders
        |                                    |
        v                                    v
  S1: green or red                     product specs only
```

S1 = one held-out step. "spec folder" = the folder of the product's browser specs. "binder folder" = the folder where the binder writes its tests.

payload.why: takes the folder of its own where the binder writes its tests, outside of which a write voids its report
takes the browser harness that a held-out test shares: a real server on a copy of the fixture project, with the fake agent first
takes the temporary checkout of the binder, so the binder's folder never exists in a builder's checkout

payload.title: The binder writes its own browser test settings inside its folder
payload.why_not: The settings must repeat how the product starts its server, its fake agent and its fixture project. A copy that differs from the product's harness makes a held-out step fail for a harness reason, and that reads as a product failure.

payload.title: The binder's folder sits inside the product's spec folder
payload.why_not: The product's run would find the tests with no change to its settings. But the binder's folder would then sit inside the product's tree. The check that voids a binder's report when it writes outside its own folder would have to treat that one subfolder as the binder's, and a builder could see the folder in the spec tree.

payload.title: The binder names its own folder when it starts the browser test run
payload.why_not: The product's settings would never know the held-out set. But the binder's override must keep the product's harness: the server, the fake agent and the fixture project. A later change to how the settings choose tests would break the binder's run with no clear error.

criterion.text: A builder's browser test run finds a held-out test, or a held-out browser step fails because the run did not find its test.
