criterion.text: Archive a building ticket during a merge loop run. Revisit if any part of that ticket merges afterwards, if its branch is gone, or if another ticket of the run moves back to ready.
Revisit when an edit to a module under the running serve verb no longer reloads in the same process, or when the runtime's hot reload no longer waits for the first evaluation to end.
Un-park conversations in daily use. If the eager resume leaves idle processes that nobody types into, or a conversation ever runs two processes, change to a resume at the next message.

payload.title: A tab counts its background tasks from the last full list its agent sent
payload.why: The agent sends its whole list of background tasks each time one starts or ends. Werk keeps only the length of the last list, so the count always equals what the agent reported last, and werk never has to match the end of a task to its start.
payload.body:
A background task is a subagent or a shell command that the agent starts and that runs on after its turn ends. Claude Code, the agent that werk runs in each tab, sends the full list of these tasks each time one starts or ends. Werk replaces the tab's count with the length of each new list. It does not add up starts and ends, so it keeps no record of which task is which. This count is what keeps a tab with a finished turn marked as running (see #werk-mc-bgagents). When the tab's child process exits, its tasks end with it, and the count goes to zero.

Example:
- tab #fold "Fold the cards from the log"
- task A, a subagent that reviews a card
- task B, a shell command that runs the tests

1. The agent starts task A and sends the list [A]. The count is 1.
2. The agent starts task B and sends [A, B]. The count is 2.
3. The turn ends. The count is 2, so #fold still shows as running.
4. Task A ends, and the agent sends [B]. The count is 1.
5. Task B ends, and the agent sends []. The count is 0, and #fold is idle.
6. Any other event from the agent leaves the count as it is.
7. If the child exits while a task runs, the count goes to 0 at once.

```
  list from the agent       count   #fold chip
  [A]                       1       running
  [A, B]                    2       running
  (turn ends)               2       running
  [B]                       1       running
  []                        0       idle
  child exits               0       dead or idle, never running

  count = number of tasks in the last list received
```

payload.why: The count is how a tab knows the background agent that this card says must keep it running.

payload.title: Count each task start up and each task end down
payload.why_not: Werk must then match each end to its start by task id, and an event it skips leaves the count wrong until the child exits. The full list gives the same number with no matching.

payload.why: The count is what keeps a tab with a finished turn in the running state that this card defines.

payload.title: A tab's pane shows a line while a background agent of that tab still runs
payload.why: A background agent can run on after its turn ends, so the pane looks finished while work goes on. A line pinned to the bottom of the tab's pane shows the agent while it runs, and the tab's live marker keeps the tab running. So the work never ends unseen.

ops.old: Decided: the marker lives in the tab's own chat pane, not on the tab chip. A permanent line pinned to the bottom of that pane, present only while a background agent is running there, gone once it finishes.
ops.new: Claude Code shows its own marker while a background agent runs, and that marker does not reach werk's pane. To keep the agent visible, werk pins one line to the bottom of the tab's own chat pane while at least one background agent of that tab runs (#werk-mc-bg-line places it). The line goes when the last background agent ends. The line sits in the pane, not on the tab chip.

ops.old: The card's live indicator (#werk-mc-live) counts a background agent as 'running' too. A tab whose main turn already finished but that still has a background agent going must not read as idle.
ops.new: The tab's live marker counts a background agent as running too (see #werk-mc-live). So a tab whose turn has ended does not read as idle while its background agent works (#werk-mc-live-bgcount gives the count).

Example:

- tab #fold "Fold the cards from the log"
- agent R, a background subagent that reviews a card

1. A turn in #fold starts R, and the turn ends. The #fold pane shows the line, and the #fold chip still shows running.
2. R ends. The line goes, and the chip shows idle.
3. A turn that starts no background agent shows no line at any time.

```
 #fold pane                         tab strip
 +------------------------------+
 | chat log                     |   [ #fold (running) ]
 | (turn ended)                 |
 |------------------------------|
 | background line  <-- R runs  |
 +------------------------------+

 background line = shown while at least one background agent of the tab runs
 (running)       = the live marker of the tab chip
```

payload.title: A separate control in the tab strip starts an empty conversation in a new tab
payload.why: A fork brings the parent's history, which is wrong for an unrelated topic. One press must give a clean conversation. It always opens a new tab, because a switch to an existing tab would show an old conversation instead.
payload.body:
A fork carries the parent's whole history (see #werk-mc-fork). That is wrong for an unrelated topic. To give that topic a clean start, the tab strip has a second control next to '+' (see #werk-mc-open for '+'). The empty control opens a new tab at the open card, with no parent session. The first message in that tab starts a session with no history. The only other empty start is a fork of a tab that has no session yet (see #werk-mc-fork-nosession).

The empty control never switches to an existing tab. A fork switches to a tab that already has the card as its home. The empty control opens a new tab every time, also on that card. The new tab still takes the open card as its home and its chip label (see #werk-mc-split).

Example:

- tab "main", home card "#map", active. The map shows "#fold".
- tab "fold", home card "#fold".

1. The person Shift+clicks a link to "#fold". The pane switches to tab "fold". No tab opens.
2. The person goes back to "main". The map shows "#fold" again.
3. The person presses the empty control. A second "#fold" chip opens and becomes active. Its conversation has no history.

```
start:              [#map*] [#fold]           +  ∅
Shift+click #fold:  [#map]  [#fold*]          +  ∅   (switch, no new tab)
∅ on #fold:         [#map]  [#fold] [#fold*]  +  ∅   (new tab, no history)

*  the active tab
+  the fork control
∅  the empty control
```

payload.why: The fork stays the normal start. This control is the explicit second choice that the fork decision keeps for an unrelated topic.
The control sits at the end of the tab strip that this card defines.
The empty tab still takes the open card as its home card and chip label.
Takes the one other case where a gesture starts a conversation empty: a fork of a tab with no session.

payload.title: Fork, then clear the context
payload.why_not: It takes two steps for one intent, and the person must know that the clear lives in the context popover. The fork first copies the parent's session, and the clear then throws it away.

payload.title: The empty control switches to a tab that already has the card as its home
payload.why_not: The press then shows an old conversation with its history. That is the opposite of what the person asked for.

payload.title: A pasted image travels inside the chat message, and the agent reads it from a stored file
payload.why: The page sends each image inside the message request, so a message and its images reach the server together or not at all, and nothing is stored for an image the person removed. The server writes each image to a file and the agent opens that file, so the model sees the image itself and never the encoded bytes.
payload.body:
To send a message and its images in one step, the page keeps each pasted image in the browser until the person sends. The send is one request with the message text, the open card, the tab, and the bytes of each image. The request is plain text, so the bytes travel encoded as text (base64), but only between the page and the server. Nothing goes to the server at paste time.

The server checks every image's type and size before it stores any of them. Then it turns the text back into bytes and writes each image to the attachments folder as an image file (see #werk-shots for the folder, the types and the size cap). The agent never gets the image bytes. Its turn names the path of each file, and the agent opens the file with its own file read. That read gives the model the image itself, not text, so one image costs a few thousand tokens (see #img-subagent).

Example:

- The person pastes a 2 MB screenshot and a 25 MB screenshot, and types "Why is this red?".
- The person removes the second chip, because it is over the size cap, and presses Enter.

1. Each paste shows a token, [Image #1] and [Image #2], and a chip. The server has no file yet.
2. Removing chip 2 drops its bytes from the page. The server never sees them.
3. Enter sends one request with the text and the encoded bytes of image 1.
4. The server checks image 1 and writes it as a PNG file. The agent's turn says [Image #1] is that path.
5. The agent reads the file and sees the screenshot as an image.
6. Had the person sent both images, the server refuses the whole request: it stores no image and starts no turn.

```
paste --> page keeps the bytes (chip + [Image #N])         server: nothing yet
Enter --> page --(text + base64 bytes + card + tab)--> server
                                                         | check every image (type, size)
                                                         |   one bad -> refuse: no file, no turn
                                                         v
                                         decode, write file --> attachments/shot.png
                                                         |
                                                         +--(turn text: [Image #1] = path)--> agent
                                                                                              |
                                                         agent reads shot.png --> image block <+

base64 = the image bytes written as text; it exists only on the page-to-server hop
```

payload.title: The page uploads each image when it is pasted, and the message carries only its path
payload.why_not: An image is stored for every paste, also for a chip the person removes or a message never sent. The chip must wait for the upload before it can show the image, and a send in that wait has no path to carry.

payload.why: takes that a file read gives the model a native image block of a few thousand tokens, which is why the agent gets a path and not the bytes

payload.title: The page uploads each image when it is pasted, and the message carries only its path
payload.why_not: It stores a file for every paste, also for a chip the person removes or a message never sent, and a send must wait until each upload ends. Both costs are small: the attachments folder is outside version control, and the chip can show the wait.

payload.title: A pasted image uploads at once, and the message carries only its path
payload.why: The page uploads each image when it is pasted, so the server checks it at once and a wrong type or an oversized image shows on its chip before the send. The message then carries only paths, and the agent opens each file, so the model sees the image itself and never the bytes.
payload.body:
To show a bad image before the person sends, the page uploads each image the moment it is pasted. The server checks the type and the size cap, writes the image to the attachments folder as an image file, and answers with the file's name (see #werk-shots for the folder, the types and the cap). The chip shows a spinner until that answer, then the thumbnail that the server serves. A refused image shows its reason on its chip and is not part of the message.

The send is one request with the message text, the open card, the tab, and the path of each stored image. Enter waits while an upload still runs, so a message never goes out without the path of a chip it shows. The agent never gets the image bytes: it opens each path with its own file read, which gives the model the image itself, not text (see #img-subagent).

A chip that the person removes leaves its file in the attachments folder. That folder is outside version control, so the cost is disk space only.

Example:

- The person pastes a 2 MB screenshot and a 25 MB screenshot, and types "Why is this red?".

1. Paste 1 shows a chip with a spinner and the token [Image #1]. The server stores the file and answers with its name. The chip shows the thumbnail.
2. Paste 2 shows a chip and the token [Image #2]. The server refuses it: it is larger than 20 MB. The chip shows that reason, and nothing is stored.
3. The person removes chip 2. The token [Image #2] goes from the composer.
4. Enter sends one request with the text and the path of image 1.
5. The agent's turn says [Image #1] is that path. The agent reads the file and sees the screenshot as an image.
6. Had the person pressed Enter during step 1, the send waits until the upload of image 1 ends, then goes out with its path.

```
paste 1 --(image bytes)--> server: check, store --> attachments/shot-1.png
        <--(name)--------- chip: spinner -> thumbnail
paste 2 --(image bytes)--> server: over 20 MB -> refuse, store nothing
        <--(reason)------- chip: shows the reason; the person removes it
Enter   --(text + path of shot-1 + card + tab)--> server --(turn: [Image #1] = path)--> agent
                                                                                        |
                                                agent reads shot-1.png --> image block <+
```

payload.title: The page sends the image bytes inside the message request, and nothing is uploaded at paste time
payload.why_not: A wrong type or an oversized image shows only when the person sends, and one bad image refuses the whole message. The chip has no stored file to show as a thumbnail. Its only gain is no file for a removed chip, which costs disk space alone.

payload.why: takes that a file read gives the model a native image block of a few thousand tokens, which is why the message carries a path and not the bytes

payload.why: The whole tree is the home card's own page, so a card is always open and the usual open-card line always has a card to name. A separate line for no card open would describe a state that the map does not have.

ops.old: A turn sent from the map's whole tree has no open card to name. To keep the first line on every turn, the line then says that no card is open and that the map shows the whole tree. The next turn sent with a card open says that the map is now at that card, because the open card changed. See #werk-card-blind for the now-at and still-on lines.
Example:

- The whole tree: the map page with no card open.
- Card A: #werk-chat "The composer sends a live agent turn".

1. The map shows the whole tree. The person sends "What is left open?". The turn starts with [no card is open: the map shows the whole tree].
2. The person opens card A and sends a second message. The turn starts with [the map is now at #werk-chat — The composer sends a live agent turn].
3. The person sends a third message from card A. The turn starts with [still on #werk-chat — The composer sends a live agent turn].
4. The person goes back to the whole tree and sends nothing. No turn goes out, so no line goes out.

```
turn   map shows     first line of the turn
----   -----------   ------------------------------------------
1      whole tree    [no card is open: the map shows the whole tree]
2      card A        [the map is now at #werk-chat — ...]   (card changed)
3      card A        [still on #werk-chat — ...]            (same card)
```

- Card A: #werk-chat "The composer sends a live agent turn".

payload.title: Component tests share one DOM in each test process
payload.why: Server tests and React component tests run in the same test process and need different globals, and React finds a DOM only if one exists when it first loads.

ops.old: This is the way werk meets #werk-test-globals. One DOM window is registered before any test file loads, so React finds a DOM when it first loads. Each component test unmounts what it rendered.

ops.old: This is the way werk meets #werk-test-globals. One DOM window is registered before any test file loads, so React finds a DOM when it first loads. ops.new:
This is the way werk meets #werk-test-globals. A test process is one running copy of the test runner, and every test file in it shares its globals. In each test process, one DOM window is registered before any test file loads, so React finds a DOM when it first loads. The network, stream and timer globals of the runtime are put back after the registration, so a server test in the same process uses the real network function, not the one of the DOM. Each component test unmounts what it rendered.

The rule holds for any number of test processes. A unit run on parallel workers (#werk-test-runner-parallel) has one test process per worker, and each worker registers its own DOM in the same way. No DOM is shared between two workers, and none needs to be: a test file runs inside one worker only.

payload.title: A tab that needs the person shows a line in every other pane, in the color of the reason
payload.why: A person reads one pane at a time, and a blink on a small chip is easy to miss, but a line in the pane they read is not. One pattern for every reason is learned once, and its color tells the person what the tab needs before they switch to it.
payload.body:
To keep a tab that needs the person from going unseen, every such tab shows the same two signals. Its chip dot blinks, and the attention bar of every other tab's pane shows one line that names the tab and the reason. The attention bar is the row of the pane between the chat log and the ask bar (see #werk-mc-tabs for the order of the pane). The dot and the line share one color, and the reason sets it:

- Dead, red: the agent exited and werk did not stop it (see #werk-mc-live-dead). The line gives the error.
- Permission, yellow: a tool call waits for an allow or a deny (see #werk-approve-bar). The line names the tool.
- Question, blue: the agent asked a question that the person answers in a form (see #werk-mc-askqa). The line gives the question.
- Offer, green: a next-action button waits for a click (see #werk-mc-asks-offer). The line gives the action.

A line stays while its reason holds. It goes when the person answers or clicks, when the agent withdraws the ask, or when the next child of a dead tab starts. A tab with two reasons shows only the more urgent one, in the order of the list. A click on a line focuses that tab. The tab in focus shows no line for itself, because its own pane already shows the ask or the error.

Example:

- tab #log, in focus
- tab #fold, whose agent asks to run Bash
- tab #map, whose agent asks "Which layout?"

1. The #fold chip dot blinks yellow. The #log pane shows the line "#fold waits for permission: Bash".
2. The #map chip dot blinks blue. A second line shows under the first: "#map asks: Which layout?".
3. The person clicks the #map line. #map gets focus, and its own pane shows the question form. Its pane shows the #fold line, and no line for #map.
4. The agent of #fold exits with code 1 before anyone answers. Its ask is dropped, and its line turns red: "#fold died: exited with code 1".
5. A tab whose agent runs and asks nothing shows no line, and its dot does not blink.

```
  #log pane (in focus)
  +--------------------------------------+
  | chat log                             |
  | [Y] #fold waits for permission: Bash |  <-- attention bar: one line per tab
  | [B] #map asks: Which layout?         |      that needs the person
  | ask bar: asks of #log only           |
  +--------------------------------------+
  tab strip:  [ #log ]  [ #fold (Y) ]  [ #map (B) ]

  [R] (R) = red, dead        [Y] (Y) = yellow, permission
  [B] (B) = blue, question   [G] (G) = green, offer
  [x] = color of the line    (x) = color of the blinking chip dot
```

A crash that werk retries on its own is not a death yet: the tab is dead only when that retry also fails, or when the failure is one that a retry cannot fix (see #werk-crashmsg).

payload.title: Every build opens a card obligation, and the pass closes it with a card or with the cards it followed
payload.why: The obligation is data in the log, so a pass that changes code and leaves the map untouched shows as an open obligation. A pass that made no new decision closes it by naming the cards its choices came from, so it never writes a card only to meet a quota.

ops.old: The CLI command that starts a build appends the obligation to the log, before any code is written.
ops.new: The CLI command that starts a build appends the obligation to the log, before any code is written.

ops.old: The agent then places it: the title, the why, the parent in the refines tree, the depends_on. The CLI cannot choose the parent, because knowing what a decision refines is judgment. So the pipeline creates the demand and the agent satisfies it.
ops.new: When the pass writes a card, the agent places it: the title, the why, the parent in the refines tree, the depends_on. The CLI cannot choose the parent, because knowing what a decision refines is judgment. So the pipeline creates the demand and the agent satisfies it.

ops.old: Nothing here can drift, because the obligation is data in the log rather than a line in a prompt. An unsatisfied one is visible in the map.
ops.new: Nothing here can drift, because the obligation is data in the log rather than a line in a prompt. An unsatisfied one is visible in the map.

ops.old: One obligation means at least one card for the pass, not exactly one. A pass that weighs three decisions writes three.
ops.new: A pass closes the obligation in one of two ways. It proposes one card for each decision that no card gives: a pass that makes three decisions writes three. Or, when every choice in its diff came from a cited card or from a card its search found, it records "no new decision" and names those cards. The grader checks that record against the diff the same way it checks the cited cards. A choice in the diff that none of the named cards gives fails the pass as an unrecorded decision. A list of values, a configuration, or the inside of one helper is not a decision, so it is never a reason to write a card.

Example:

- Card A "Each agent carries its role outside the prompt".
- Ticket T "Show the role in the launch record", which cites A.
- Pass P builds T.

1. The build starts. The log gets obligation O for P, and the map shows O open.
2. P adds the role to the launch record. Every choice comes from A. P records "no new decision" and names A. O closes.
3. The grader reads the diff. Each choice traces to A, so the pass goes on.
4. P also picks a new file format that A does not give, and names only A. The grader fails the pass as an unrecorded decision. The next pass proposes a card for the format, and that card closes O.
5. P exits with neither a card nor a record. O stays open on the map.

```
build starts ──> obligation O (open)
                      │
pass P ──┬── a decision no card gives ──> proposes card C ──> O closed by C
         └── every choice from cards ──> "no new decision: A" ──> O closed
                                               │
                       grader: a choice in the diff that A does not give ──> pass fails

O = the card obligation of one build   A = a card the pass names   C = a card the pass proposes
```

payload.title: The builder prompt says that a list of values or one helper's internals is not a card
payload.why_not: The builder already reads that rule, and the quota overrides it. A rule in a prompt drifts, which is the reason the obligation is data in the log.

payload.title: A chat reply names the map operation, not the command line that runs it
payload.why: The person reads a reply in the chat pane and acts in the map, not in a terminal. A full command line with its path and flags tells them nothing they can use. The name of the operation, such as decide or accept, tells them what comes next.
payload.body: To keep a reply readable, the chat agent names an operation by its plain name when it tells the person what to do next or what it did, for example "Next: decide #checkout-retry". The agent still runs the full command itself. A full command line appears in a reply only when the person must run it in a terminal.

payload.why: The reply this card shapes is the streamed agent turn that the composer starts.

payload.title: `werk followed` closes a card obligation with the cards the pass followed
payload.why: A pass that made no new decision must still close its obligation, and the log must say which cards its choices came from. One verb writes that record, so a pass never writes a card only to close the obligation.
payload.body:
```
werk followed <obligation-id> --cards <card-id>,<card-id>...
```

- The command closes one card obligation with the record "no new decision", and names the cards the pass followed. It appends one event to the log and prints `<obligation-id> closed: no new decision, follows #a, #b`. Exit 0.
- `--cards` takes one card id or more. Each must be a decided card in the map. A ghost, a removed card or an unknown id is refused, and the message names it. Exit 1, and nothing is written.
- An unknown obligation is refused. An obligation that is already closed, by a card or by an earlier record, is refused, and the message names what closed it. Exit 1.
- The record is a fact in the log, not a proposal, so it needs no accept. The grader checks it against the diff (#st-build-card).

Example, with obligation `build-7` open and card `role-env` decided:

```
werk followed build-7 --cards role-env           build-7 closed: no new decision, follows #role-env   exit 0
werk followed build-7 --cards role-env           build-7 is already closed by a record               exit 1
werk followed build-8 --cards draft-card         draft-card is not a decided card                    exit 1
werk followed build-8                            --cards is required                                 exit 1
```

payload.why: The command writes the no-new-decision record that closes an obligation, as that card defines it.

payload.title: A flag on an existing verb closes the obligation
payload.why_not: The record is its own event, with its own checks on the named cards. A flag on a verb with another job mixes two operations in one form and hides the record in a place no pass looks.

criterion.text: Run werk followed on an open obligation with one decided card, then on the same obligation again, then with a ghost card. If the first does not close it, or either of the other two writes anything, revisit.

payload.title: A reply shows the full command line for each map operation

criterion.text: Reopen if a person must copy a command out of the chat to finish a step that the map cannot do.

payload.title: A conversation keeps its model and its context fill across a server restart
payload.why: The model choice and the context size belong to the conversation, not to the server process. Both are saved next to the conversation's session, so a restart resumes the same model and shows the same fill. Without it, every restarted conversation falls back to the default model and reads a wrong window size.
payload.body:
A conversation's model and advisor are launch settings of its agent process. When the server restarts, the process is gone and so is anything held only in memory. To avoid a silent fall back to the default model, the conversation saves its model, its advisor and its last context fill beside its session, and reads them when it is rebuilt.

The context window depends on the model, so the pie never uses one fixed size. Before a turn reports the real window, the size comes from the model: a model marked as one-million-token has a million, any other has two hundred thousand. When a turn ends, the window is read from the usage entry of the conversation's own model, not from the advisor's entry, which can list first and has a smaller window. A model switch resets the size to the new model's window until the next turn reports it.

Example:

- Conversation A "Opus, no advisor", at 150,000 tokens of a 200,000 window.
- A server restart.

1. The server starts. A is rebuilt from disk and reads its saved model, advisor and fill.
2. The pane shows Opus without advisor and a pie at 75%, before A sends anything.
3. A conversation with no saved settings starts on the default model with an empty pie.

```
model switch / turn end ──> saved beside session
server restart ──> rebuild A ──> read saved ──> pane: Opus, 150k / 200k
```

See #werk-model-select for the choices, #werk-context-pie for the pie, #werk-resume for the session that comes back, and #werk-mc-fork-notice for how a fork inherits them.

payload.why: the settings are saved beside the session that a restart resumes
the saved fill and window are what the pie shows

payload.title: Recover the model from the CLI's own session file

payload.title: The plan scope is the subtree plus every decided card it depends on, followed down and never up
payload.why: A decision two links away, under a card the subtree links, reached the planner only as a title, and the planner filled the gap itself. Following every dependency, and every card below it, hands the planner each decision the subtree rests on. Stopping at parents and at undecided or postponed cards keeps the scope to what the subtree needs.

ops.old: The plan stage reads two sets of cards in full: the subtree, and every card a subtree card links. Both sets are the scope.

A link is one of two things:
1. A depends_on edge from a subtree card.
2. A #card-id reference in a subtree card's title, why, or body.
Only one hop. A linked card's own links are not followed. They stay in the map index, by id and title.

The scope rules apply to linked cards the same as to subtree cards:
- An open or proto linked card stops the run before any agent call.
- Every linked card must be cited by at least one ticket.
The prompt keeps the two sets apart: the subtree first, then the linked cards under their own heading.

ops.new: The plan stage reads every card in the scope in full. The scope starts with the subtree. Then, until nothing new comes in, each card in the scope adds every card it depends on, together with that card's own subtree. The walk never goes from a card to its parent, because the way up leads to the whole map.
Only decided cards are in the scope. The walk stops at an open, proto, stale or postponed card and does not go below it. To keep a feature out of a build, postpone it.

The scope has two tiers. The first tier is the subtree and every card that a subtree card links: a depends_on target, or a #card-id written in its title, why or body. An open or proto card in the first tier stops the run before any agent call, and every first-tier card must be cited by at least one ticket. The second tier is the rest of the scope. It is context: no ticket must cite it, and it never stops a run. The prompt keeps the tiers apart, the first tier first.

Example. The subtree is #app "The app", with one child, #app-login "Login by magic link".

- #app-login depends on #mail "Mail goes through one provider".
- #mail sits under #infra "Infrastructure", next to #cdn "Static files on a CDN".
- #mail has two children: #mail-retry "A failed send retries three times", and #mail-bounce "Bounces unsubscribe the address", which is open.
- #mail-retry depends on #queue "Jobs run on one queue".

1. The scope starts with #app and #app-login. Both are first tier.
2. #app-login depends on #mail. #mail comes in as first tier, because a subtree card links it. #mail-retry comes in with it as second tier.
3. #mail-retry depends on #queue. #queue comes in as second tier.
4. #mail-bounce is open. It stays out, and the run does not stop, because it is second tier.
5. #infra and #cdn stay out. The walk never goes from #mail up to #infra.

```
#infra                        out: a parent is never followed
 ├─ #cdn                      out
 └─ #mail                     tier 1 (linked by #app-login)
     ├─ #mail-retry           tier 2 ──depends_on──▶ #queue   tier 2
     └─ #mail-bounce (open)   out, no stop
#app                          tier 1 (subtree)
 └─ #app-login                tier 1 ──depends_on──▶ #mail
```

payload.title: Every change to werk passes the production checks before it merges and again on a clean machine after
payload.why: An agent writes most of werk's code, and nobody reads every line. Automated checks are the only review that runs on every change. They run twice: before the merge on the builder's machine, so a red change never reaches the main line, and after the merge on a clean machine, so a pass does not depend on local state.
payload.body:
werk gives each production check name a real command: the linter for lint (#werk-lint), the type checker for typecheck (#werk-typecheck), and the test commands that #werk-test already decides for test, test:coverage and e2e.

A change to werk merges through the merge loop, not through a hosted pull request. The merge loop runs the checks on the main line plus the change, and merges only on green. A hosted CI service then runs the same checks after the merge, from a clean install (#werk-ci).

This card is the requirement, not a choice. No alternative was weighed against having checks.

payload.why: werk fills the five check names that this card defines.
The merge loop of this card is werk's gate before a merge.
The test, test:coverage and e2e checks are the harness that this card decides.

payload.title: Biome lints and formats all of werk's code with one configuration
payload.why: An agent runs the linter after every edit, so the linter must be fast and its fixes must apply without a person. Biome lints and formats TypeScript, JSX and JSON as one program with one configuration file. So there are no overlapping rules between two tools, and one command fixes what it can.
payload.body:
To keep the code in one style without a person reviewing every line, the lint check runs Biome over the server, the client and the tests. Biome reports style problems and likely bugs, and it rewrites the files it can fix. The formatter and the linter share one configuration, so a format fix never breaks a lint rule.

The rule set is Biome's recommended set plus its React rules, which check hook dependencies and hook order (React comes from #werk-stack-framework). A rule turns off only in the shared configuration, with a reason beside it. A comment that turns a rule off for one line also needs a reason.

Biome's type-aware rules are fewer than those of typescript-eslint. The type checker (#werk-typecheck) covers the type errors. The one known gap is a promise that nobody awaits. If that gap causes a real bug, the option to add ESLint for type-aware rules only is the fallback.

payload.why: The React rule set is on because the client is React.

payload.title: ESLint with typescript-eslint, and Prettier for formatting
payload.why_not: It is two programs with two configurations and a set of plugin packages, and the lint and format rules overlap until a third package turns the overlap off. A type-aware run is slow on every agent edit. Its one real gain is the full set of type-aware rules, such as a promise that nobody awaits.

payload.title: Oxlint for linting, with a separate formatter
payload.why_not: It is as fast as Biome, but linting and formatting are two programs with two configurations. Biome gives the same speed with one program.

payload.title: No linter: the type checker and a formatter only
payload.why_not: The type checker does not find unused code, wrong hook dependencies or a style that drifts across files. An agent copies the style of the code it reads, so drift grows with every change.

criterion.text: A change of linter is one configuration file and one automated rewrite of the code. Revisit when an unawaited promise causes a real bug that Biome did not report.
werk must become a product that agents change without a person reading every line. Checks stay as long as that holds.

payload.title: The TypeScript compiler checks all of werk's code in strict mode as a separate check
payload.why: Bun and Vite remove the types from TypeScript and run the code without checking it. So a type error runs until it breaks at runtime. A separate pass of the TypeScript compiler, in strict mode, finds the error before the merge.
payload.body:
To catch type errors that the runtime never reports, the typecheck check runs the TypeScript compiler over the server, the client and the tests. The compiler only checks. It writes no output, because Bun runs the server source and Vite builds the client (#werk-stack-layout).

Strict mode is on, and so is the rule that a read from an array or a map can return nothing. The second rule finds the most common runtime error in code that an agent writes: a lookup that is assumed to succeed. A type that says nothing (any) is not allowed. The linter (#werk-lint) reports it.

One configuration covers all the code. A part that needs other settings, such as browser types for the client, gets its own configuration that extends the shared one, and the check runs all of them.

payload.why: Bun, the runtime from this card, runs TypeScript without a type check, so a separate check is needed.
The check covers the server and client folders that this card lays out, and writes no output because each runtime builds its own.

payload.title: No separate type check: the editor and the runtime find type errors
payload.why_not: Bun and Vite never check types, and an agent does not look at an editor. A type error then reaches the main line and shows only when the code runs.

payload.title: The default strict mode, without the check on array and map reads
payload.why_not: Strict mode alone types a read from an array or a map as always present. A missing key then fails at runtime, which is the error the check exists to catch.

criterion.text: A change of strictness is one setting. Revisit if the check on array and map reads makes agents add empty guards more often than it finds real bugs.

payload.title: werk ships as one executable file per platform, with the runtime and the built client inside
payload.why: A user should install werk without first installing a runtime of the right version. Bun compiles the server, its packages, the Bun runtime and the built client into one executable file. So the user gets one file that starts werk, and every user runs the same Bun version that the checks ran on.
payload.body:
To make werk installable with nothing else on the machine except the Claude Code command line, each release builds one executable file per platform. The file holds the server code, the packages it imports, the Bun runtime, and the client that Vite built (#werk-stack-layout). werk serves the client from inside the file, so no folder is unpacked next to it.

The platforms are macOS and Linux, each on ARM and Intel processors. Windows is out until a user needs it. The Claude Code command line stays a separate install, because werk starts it as a child process and the user logs in to it.

A file of this kind is large: tens of megabytes, most of it the runtime. That is the cost of not asking the user to install Bun.

A user installs the file through one channel (#werk-dist-channel). A release builds the files only from a commit that passed every check (#werk-release).

payload.why: It uses the compiled executable of Bun, the runtime that this card chose partly for that reason.
It puts the client that Vite builds into the output folder of this card inside the executable.

payload.title: An npm package that runs on a Bun the user installs
payload.why_not: The user installs a second runtime before werk. Each user then has a different Bun version, and werk's behaviour depends on it: a fix in one Bun version is a break in another. The checks never ran on the user's version.

payload.title: An npm package built to run on Node
payload.why_not: werk runs on Bun and uses Bun's server and test APIs. A Node build is a second runtime to test and support, for a gain of no install step only for users who already have Node.

payload.title: A container image
payload.why_not: werk starts the local Claude Code command line and edits the user's own repository. A container needs the repository mounted, the Claude login passed in, and the git settings copied. Each is a step where the install can go wrong.

criterion.text: The release check installs the file on a clean machine of each platform, starts werk, opens the map and runs one chat turn. If that fails on a platform and a fix needs changes to werk's code, fall back to the npm package.

payload.title: Users install and update werk through a Homebrew tap
payload.why: Homebrew is on most macOS developer machines and runs on Linux too. It downloads the right file for the platform, checks its checksum, puts it on the path, and updates it with the user's other tools. So werk needs no installer or update command of its own.
payload.body:
To install werk with one command and update it the same way as other tools, werk publishes a Homebrew formula in a tap: a git repository of formulas that werk's project owns. The formula points at the executable files of a release (#werk-dist) and at their checksums. A release updates the formula (#werk-release).

Each release also attaches the files for direct download, for a machine without Homebrew. A direct download gets no automatic update.

macOS marks a file that a browser downloads as untrusted, and refuses to start an unsigned one. Homebrew does not set that mark, so the tap needs no Apple signing. Signing becomes necessary only if direct download becomes the main channel.

payload.title: An npm package that downloads the right executable for the platform
payload.why_not: It needs Node and npm on the machine only to install a file that does not use them. The pattern also needs one package per platform and a wrapper package that picks one.

payload.title: An install script that the user downloads and runs from the shell
payload.why_not: werk would need its own update command and its own checksum check, which Homebrew already gives. The user also runs a script from the network without a review step.

criterion.text: A second channel reads the same release files, so adding one is a small change. Revisit when users without Homebrew ask for werk.

payload.title: GitHub Actions runs every check again on a clean machine after each merge to the main line
payload.why: The merge loop runs the checks on the builder's machine, where installed packages, local files and a warm cache can hide a problem. A run on a clean machine starts from the lockfile alone, so it finds what only a new user would hit. It runs after the merge, so it adds no wait to the merge loop.
payload.body:
To prove that the main line works from a clean state, each push to the main line starts a GitHub Actions run. The run installs the locked packages, runs every production check, builds the executable for one platform (#werk-dist), and starts it once to see that werk serves its map. The run is the gate for a release (#werk-release), not for a merge.

A red run is handled like a red held-out step: the merge stands, and the failure becomes a follow-up ticket. A pull request that a person opens gets the same run, and merges only on green.

**Example**

- Ticket T "Card titles wrap at the card edge"
- Commit M, the main line after T merges

1. The builder finishes T. The merge loop runs the checks on the main line plus T. If one is red, nothing merges and CI never starts.
2. All checks are green. T merges, and the main line moves to M.
3. The main line is pushed to GitHub.
4. GitHub Actions starts on a clean machine: install, lint, typecheck, test with coverage, end-to-end, build, start.
5. Green: M can be released. Red: a follow-up ticket gets the failure, and M cannot be released.

```
 builder's machine                    GitHub Actions (clean machine)
 ─────────────────                    ──────────────────────────────
 T done                                  
   │                                     
   ▼                                     
 checks on main+T ──red──▶ no merge      
   │ green                               
   ▼                                     
 merge: main = M ──── push M ────────▶ install from lockfile
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                       every check, build, start
                                         │
                              green ◀────┴────▶ red
                                │                 │
                         M can be released   follow-up ticket,
                                             M cannot be released
```

payload.why: It runs after the merge loop of this card merges, and a red run becomes a follow-up ticket as a red held-out step does.
It runs the production checks that this card names.
It builds and starts the executable that this card defines.

payload.title: Hosted CI on a pull request is the gate before every merge
payload.why_not: The merge loop already merges on green checks. A hosted gate adds a push, a wait for a remote machine and a second queue to every ticket, and the merge loop then stops whenever the service is slow or down.

payload.title: No hosted CI: the merge loop's checks are the only run
payload.why_not: Every check then passes only on a machine that has already built werk. A package missing from the lockfile, or a test that reads a local file, shows up first on a user's machine.

payload.title: Git hooks run the checks before each commit
payload.why_not: An agent commits many times per ticket, and the merge loop already checks before each merge. A hook repeats the same run on every commit, and a commit can skip it.

criterion.metric: share of main-line runs that are red while the merge loop's checks on the same commit were green

payload.title: A person releases a version by tagging a green commit on the main line
payload.why: The merge loop merges many tickets a day, and a subtree is often half built. A release on every merge would ship half-built features and a new version every hour. A person picks the commit, and GitHub Actions does every step after that, so a release is one action.
payload.body:
To ship only states of werk that a person chose, a release starts when a person puts a version tag on a commit of the main line. The tag is refused unless that commit's clean-machine run is green (#werk-ci).

The tag starts a GitHub Actions run. It builds the executable for each platform (#werk-dist), attaches the files and their checksums to a GitHub release, and updates the Homebrew formula to the new version (#werk-dist-channel). The release notes list the cards that became decided since the previous tag.

The version follows semantic versioning: a major number for a change that breaks the map files or a command, a minor number for a new feature, a patch number for a fix.

payload.why: A tag is accepted only on a commit whose clean-machine run from this card is green.
The release updates the Homebrew formula that this card defines.

payload.title: Every green merge to the main line is a release
payload.why_not: The main line moves once per ticket, and a subtree is often half merged. Users would get a new version every hour, some with half of a feature.

payload.title: A tool computes the next version from a change note in each ticket
payload.why_not: Each ticket must carry a change note that an agent writes, and the version then follows the notes, not a person's choice of what is ready.

criterion.text: The tag only starts the release run, so a change of trigger is a change to one workflow. Revisit when releases happen less often than once a month because nobody tags.

payload.title: A person or an agent can start work on werk from the repository and the map alone
payload.why: An agent starts every session with no memory, and a new person starts with no context. Both need the same three things: how to run the project, where each decision is recorded, and which command does each task. When the repository answers these, nobody has to ask, and an agent does not guess.
payload.body:
werk's repository gives every newcomer, human or agent, one path in. The README says what werk is and how to install and start it. The agent instruction file says how to work on the code (#werk-devex-agents). The map holds every decision and its reason (#werk-devex-docs). One list of task commands covers everything a person or an agent runs (#werk-devex-tasks), on a pinned tool version (#werk-devex-toolver).

This card is the requirement, not a choice. No alternative was weighed against it.

criterion.text: werk is built mostly by agents that start each session cold. The requirement holds as long as that is true.

payload.title: One agent instruction file, AGENTS.md, holds only what an agent cannot learn from the code or the map
payload.why: Each line in an instruction file is read at the start of every agent session, so a long file costs attention and drifts from the code. A short file that says how to run, check and find things stays true. AGENTS.md is read by most agent tools, so werk is not tied to one of them.
payload.body:
To give every agent the same short start, werk's repository has one instruction file at its root, AGENTS.md. A tool that reads a file under another name, such as Claude Code with CLAUDE.md, gets a file of one line that imports AGENTS.md. No content lives in the second file.

The file holds what the code and the map cannot say: how to start werk in development, which task command runs each check (#werk-devex-tasks), where the server and the client code live, and the rule that a decision goes on the map, not into the file. It includes the shared werk agent instructions (#werk-agent-instructions), so the rules for the map are written once.

A line goes into the file only after an agent got the same thing wrong more than once. A rule that a program can check becomes a check, and leaves the file. The file has no list of modules or files: the code is the record of its own layout.

payload.why: The file includes the shared instruction text that this card defines.
A rule that a program can check moves out of the file into a check, as this card requires.

payload.title: CLAUDE.md as the only instruction file
payload.why_not: It ties werk's own repository to one agent tool, and werk must become a product that runs outside that tool.

payload.title: An instruction file in each folder, beside the code it describes
payload.why_not: Each file is a second description of its folder, and a change to the code does not update it. With many files, an agent cannot tell which one is out of date.

payload.title: A full guide to the code in the instruction file: modules, data flow and conventions
payload.why_not: The agent reads all of it in every session, and it goes out of date with each refactor. The agent can read the code itself for its layout, and the map for its reasons.

criterion.text: The file is short and one edit changes it. Revisit when agents ask the same question about the code in more than one session, which shows a missing line.

payload.title: The map is werk's design documentation, and the code points to the card that explains it
payload.why: A design document beside the map would be a second record of the same decisions, with no staleness marks, so it drifts without a sign. The map already holds each decision, its reason, its rejected options and what depends on it. So the only prose outside the map is the README for users, and a code comment names a card id when it needs to say why.
payload.body:
To keep one record of every decision, werk's design lives on the map and nowhere else. The repository has a README with what werk is, how to install it, and how to start it. It has no folder of design or architecture documents.

A code comment says why only when the reason is not visible in the code. If a card holds that reason, the comment names the card id and does not copy the reason. A card never names a file or a function, so the link goes one way: from the code to the card. A rename in the code then breaks no card.

A term that werk uses is defined on the card that introduces it. An agent that meets an unknown term finds its card on the map.

payload.title: A docs folder with architecture and design documents
payload.why_not: Each document repeats decisions that the map records, and nothing marks it when one of those decisions changes. An agent then reads a document that contradicts the map and cannot tell which one is right.

payload.title: Architecture decision records as numbered files in the repository
payload.why_not: They record the same thing as a decided card, with no link between dependent decisions and no mark when a decision they rest on changes.

payload.title: A glossary file of werk's terms
payload.why_not: Each term gets a second definition beside the one on its card. When the card changes, the glossary keeps the old meaning.

criterion.text: A person new to werk tries to find how one feature works, from the README, the map and the code only. If they cannot find the overview they need, add a document for that one gap.

payload.title: Every task a person or an agent runs on werk is a make target, and the Makefile lists them all
payload.why: The checks are already make targets, so the Makefile is the one place a newcomer looks. When every other task is a target too, one list holds everything that can be run, and an agent never has to guess a tool's flags. A target with a one-line description prints in the help list, so the list cannot drift from the Makefile.
payload.body:
To give one entry point for every task, the Makefile has a target for each task, not only for the checks: start werk in development, run each production check, run all checks in the order the merge loop runs them, fix what the linter and the formatter can fix, build the executable, and print the list of targets. A target with no arguments prints that list.

Each target calls a script in the package file, which holds the real command. So a change of tool is an edit to one script, and the target name stays the same, as for the checks (#lp-checks-scripts).

The fix target exists so that an agent repairs style problems with one call before it runs the checks, instead of fixing each lint error by hand.

payload.why: It extends the make-target form that this card sets for checks to every other task.
The fix target runs the automatic fixes of the linter and formatter that this card chooses.

payload.title: Make targets for the checks only, package scripts for every other task
payload.why_not: A newcomer then has two lists to read, and must know which kind of task is in which list.

payload.title: A dedicated task runner such as just or Task
payload.why_not: It is one more tool to install on every machine and in CI, while make is already on macOS and Linux and the checks already use it.

criterion.text: A target is a few lines and moves easily. Revisit if agents call package scripts or tools directly more often than the targets.

payload.title: The repository pins one Bun version, and every task stops on a different one
payload.why: Bun ships breaking changes in minor releases, so the same code can pass on one version and fail on another. A version pinned in the repository makes every machine, CI and the release build run the same Bun. A task that stops with a clear message on a wrong version turns a confusing failure into a one-line fix.
payload.body:
To make a check mean the same thing on every machine, the repository holds a file with the exact Bun version. GitHub Actions installs that version (#werk-ci), and the release build compiles with it (#werk-dist). Every make target compares the installed version with the pinned one first. On a mismatch it stops and prints both versions and how to install the pinned one.

An upgrade of Bun is a ticket of its own: it changes the pinned version, and the merge loop's checks decide whether it merges.

payload.why: Bun is the runtime that this card chose, and its fast breaking-change cadence is the reason for the pin.
The version check runs at the start of each make target that this card defines.

payload.title: A version manager such as mise or asdf installs the pinned version
payload.why_not: Every person and every CI machine must install the version manager first, which is one more tool to set up before werk.

payload.title: No pin: any recent Bun runs werk
payload.why_not: A check can then pass on the builder's Bun and fail in CI or in the release build, and the failure does not say that the version is the cause.

criterion.text: The pin is one file and one check. Revisit if Bun keeps compatible behaviour across minor releases for a year.

payload.title: werk's repository configures Claude Code for speed and safety, and never for a rule
payload.why: Claude Code is a temporary harness, so a rule that lives in its configuration stops working when werk runs outside it. The configuration may still make an agent faster and safer inside it: fewer permission questions, the subagents the instructions name, and quick feedback after an edit. Every rule the configuration helps with is also enforced by a check or by the werk command line.
payload.body:
To keep werk's rules working outside Claude Code, the Claude Code configuration in werk's repository holds no rule of its own. It holds four things: which commands an agent may run without a question (#werk-cc-perms), a hook that gives feedback after an edit (#werk-cc-hooks), the subagent definitions (#werk-cc-subagents), and nothing more (#werk-cc-skills).

The test for any new entry: if Claude Code ignored it, would a rule break? If yes, the rule belongs in a check or in the werk command line, and the entry may only repeat it earlier.

payload.why: It applies to werk's own repository the reason this card gives: a hook does not run outside the harness.
A rule that the configuration helps with is enforced by the checks that this card requires.

payload.title: Claude Code hooks and settings enforce werk's development rules
payload.why_not: A hook runs only inside Claude Code. An agent in another harness, a script, or a person at the terminal never meets the rule, and the rule fails without a sign.

criterion.text: It holds while the Claude Code harness is temporary for werk. If werk becomes a Claude Code plugin only, the configuration may hold rules.

payload.title: werk's repository configures Claude Code for speed and safety, and never for a rule
payload.why: Claude Code is a temporary harness, so a rule that lives in its configuration stops working when werk runs outside it. The configuration may still make an agent faster and safer inside it: fewer permission questions, the subagents the instructions name, and quick feedback after an edit. Every rule the configuration helps with is also enforced by a check or by the werk command line.
payload.body:
To keep werk's rules working outside Claude Code, the Claude Code configuration in werk's repository holds no rule of its own. It decides which commands run without a question (#werk-cc-perms), gives feedback after an edit (#werk-cc-hooks), and defines the subagents that the instructions name (#werk-cc-subagents). A repeated workflow becomes a command, not a skill (#werk-cc-skills).

The test for any new entry: if Claude Code ignored it, would a rule break? If yes, the rule belongs in a check or in the werk command line, and the entry may only repeat it earlier.

payload.title: Claude Code hooks and settings enforce werk's development rules
payload.why_not: A hook runs only inside Claude Code. An agent in another harness, a script, or a person at the terminal never meets the rule, and the rule fails without a sign.

criterion.text: It holds while the Claude Code harness is temporary for werk. If werk becomes a Claude Code plugin only, the configuration may hold rules.

payload.title: The shared Claude Code settings allow the task commands and werk's own command line, and personal entries stay out
payload.why: An agent that stops for a question on every check run is slow, and a person who approves the same command many times stops reading the questions. The commands an agent runs on every ticket are safe and few: the make targets and the werk command line. Allowing exactly those in the shared settings removes most questions, and a person's own tools never reach another person's machine.
payload.body:
To cut the questions that carry no risk, the Claude Code settings file that the repository shares allows every make target (#werk-devex-tasks) and the werk command line, and nothing else. A command outside that list goes to the permission engine of Claude Code, as in every other project werk runs.

An entry for a person's own tools, such as a cloud command line or a chat service, goes into the personal settings file that git ignores. The shared file holds no such entry.

The shared file allows no command that writes outside the repository or reaches the network, so a person can accept the repository's settings without reading every line.

payload.why: It allows the make targets that this card defines.
A command outside the allow list goes to the Claude Code permission engine that this card relies on.

payload.title: No shared settings: each person approves commands on their own machine
payload.why_not: Every person and every new worktree asks the same questions about the same safe commands, and an agent waits for each answer.

payload.title: The shared settings skip every permission question
payload.why_not: An agent can then delete files outside the repository or send data over the network with no person in the loop, on every machine that checks out werk.

criterion.text: The list is a few lines. Revisit when the same question about a command outside the list comes up in most sessions.

payload.title: One hook formats and lints each file right after an agent edits it
payload.why: An agent that learns about a lint error only when the checks run must find the file again and fix it in a second pass. A hook after each edit fixes the format at once and shows the remaining lint errors while the file is still in the agent's context. The lint check still runs before every merge, so a skipped hook breaks nothing.
payload.body:
To give lint feedback at the moment of the edit, the shared Claude Code settings have one hook. After an agent writes or edits a source file, the hook runs the formatter and the linter (#werk-lint) on that file only, applies the safe fixes, and returns the errors that remain to the agent. On one file it finishes in well under a second.

The hook does not block the edit and does not run tests or the type check. Those are slower and run in the checks of the merge loop.

**Example**

- File F, a client component that an agent just edited
- The edit leaves wrong indentation and an unused import

1. The agent saves F.
2. The hook formats F, which fixes the indentation, and removes the unused import as a safe fix.
3. No error remains, so the hook returns nothing and the agent goes on.
4. If an error remained, such as a missing hook dependency, the agent reads it in the hook output and fixes it in its next edit.
5. If the hook did not run at all, the lint check before the merge reports the same errors.

```
 agent edits F ──▶ hook: format + lint F ──▶ errors left?
                                              │       │
                                             no      yes
                                              │       │
                                         agent goes   agent reads the error
                                         on           and fixes F
                       (hook skipped) ──▶ lint check before the merge reports it
```

payload.why: The hook runs the formatter and linter that this card chooses.

payload.title: No hooks: the agent sees lint errors only when the checks run
payload.why_not: The agent fixes each lint error in a second pass, after the file has left its attention, and the merge loop sends more tickets back for style alone.

payload.title: A hook runs every check when the agent ends its turn
payload.why_not: The tests and the end-to-end run take minutes, so every turn ends with a long wait, also in a chat turn that changed no code. The merge loop already runs the same checks once per ticket.

criterion.text: One hook entry, removed in one edit. Remove it if it makes an edit wait noticeably or if its output distracts the agent from the task.

payload.title: A subagent that werk ships has one definition, and werk's own repository links to it
payload.why: werk ships some subagent definitions into every project, and its own repository needs the same subagents. Two copies drift: a fix lands in one and the other keeps the old prompt. When the repository's subagent folder links to the shipped files, werk's own agents always run the prompt that users get.
payload.body:
To keep one prompt per subagent, each subagent that werk ships with its agent instructions (#werk-agent-subagents) is defined once, in werk's source, beside the instruction text. The Claude Code subagent folder of werk's repository holds a link to each of these files, not a copy. A check fails if a shipped subagent has no link, or if the folder holds a file under a shipped subagent's name that is not a link.

A subagent that only werk's own development uses, and that werk does not ship, is a plain file in that folder.

A subagent definition holds a prompt only. A step that a program can do is a werk command that the prompt names.

payload.why: It keeps one copy of the subagent definitions that this card ships into every project.
A definition holds a prompt only, and its steps are commands, as this card requires.

payload.title: Two copies, the shipped one and the repository's one, kept the same by hand
payload.why_not: A fix to one copy does not reach the other, and nothing shows the difference. werk's own agents then test a prompt that users do not get.

payload.title: A setup step copies the shipped definitions into the repository's subagent folder
payload.why_not: Every checkout and worktree needs the setup step before an agent works, and a copy made before a change is out of date until someone runs it again.

criterion.text: Links are easy to replace. Revisit if links fail on a platform or in a tool that werk must support.

payload.title: werk's repository has no project skills or MCP servers, and a repeated workflow becomes a command
payload.why: A skill is a prompt file that runs only in Claude Code, and its steps are rules that no program checks. A workflow that agents repeat is cheaper and safer as a make target or a werk command: it runs the same way every time, in any harness, and a person can run it too.
payload.body:
To keep every workflow runnable outside Claude Code, werk's repository defines no Claude Code skills and no MCP servers of its own. When agents repeat the same sequence of steps, the sequence becomes a make target (#werk-devex-tasks) or a werk command, and the agent instruction file names it (#werk-devex-agents).

A person may use their own personal skills while working on werk. The repository does not depend on them, and no card or instruction names one.

payload.why: A workflow is a program, not a prompt file, as this card requires.
A repeated workflow becomes a make target that this card defines.

payload.title: Project skills for werk's common workflows, such as adding a card or running a build
payload.why_not: The steps live in prompt text that an agent may skip or change, and the skill runs only in Claude Code. The same workflow as a command runs the same way every time and in any harness.

payload.title: TypeScript 7, the native compiler, checks all of werk's code in strict mode as a separate check
payload.why: Bun and Vite remove the types from TypeScript and run the code without checking it, so a type error runs until it breaks at runtime. A separate pass of the TypeScript compiler, in strict mode, finds the error before the merge. TypeScript 7 is the compiler rewritten in Go, about ten times faster than the JavaScript version, so the check stays cheap enough to run after every agent change.
payload.body:
To catch type errors that the runtime never reports, the typecheck check runs the TypeScript 7 compiler over the server, the client and the tests. The compiler only checks. It writes no output, because Bun runs the server source and Vite builds the client (#werk-stack-layout). werk does not call the compiler from its own code, so the compiler's programmatic interface, which is not stable in TypeScript 7.0, does not matter.

Strict mode is on, and so is the rule that a read from an array or a map can return nothing. The second rule finds the most common runtime error in code that an agent writes: a lookup that is assumed to succeed. A type that says nothing (any) is not allowed. The linter (#werk-lint) reports it.

One configuration covers all the code. A part that needs other settings, such as browser types for the client, gets its own configuration that extends the shared one, and the check runs all of them.

payload.title: No separate type check: the editor and the runtime find type errors
payload.why_not: Bun and Vite never check types, and an agent does not look at an editor. A type error then reaches the main line and shows only when the code runs.

payload.title: The default strict mode, without the check on array and map reads
payload.why_not: Strict mode alone types a read from an array or a map as always present. A missing key then fails at runtime, which is the error the check exists to catch.

payload.title: TypeScript 6, the last compiler written in JavaScript
payload.why_not: It is about ten times slower on a full check, and werk needs none of what it still has over TypeScript 7: werk calls no compiler interface from its own code and emits no output.

criterion.text: A change of strictness or compiler version is one setting. Revisit if the check on array and map reads makes agents add empty guards more often than it finds real bugs, or if a tool werk adopts needs the TypeScript 6 compiler interface.

payload.title: Measurement on the werk prototype: TypeScript 7.0.2 full check and the array and map read rule (Oct 2026)
payload.finding: On the prototype code base (about 80 server modules plus the browser scripts), a full TypeScript 7.0.2 check in strict mode takes 0.42 s of wall time. It reports 4 errors, so the prototype's typecheck check is red today. Turning on the rule that a read from an array or a map can return nothing adds 394 errors. Most are in a few modules that index arrays in loops: 68 in one geometry module, 20 to 25 in each of several test files. The count is the cost of adding the rule to existing code, not to code written under it from the start.

payload.title: The shared Claude Code settings allow the task commands and werk's command line, except the operations that only a person may do
payload.why: An agent that stops for a question on every check run is slow, and a person who approves the same command many times stops reading the questions. The make targets and the werk command line are safe and run on every ticket, so the shared settings allow them. Accepting, removing and restoring a card are a person's decisions, so these still ask.

ops.old: To cut the questions that carry no risk, the Claude Code settings file that the repository shares allows every make target (#werk-devex-tasks) and the werk command line, and nothing else. A command outside that list goes to the permission engine of Claude Code, as in every other project werk runs.
ops.new: To cut the questions that carry no risk, the Claude Code settings file that the repository shares allows every make target (#werk-devex-tasks) and the werk command line. An ask rule in the shared file wins over an allow rule in a personal file, so a personal entry cannot turn these questions off. A command outside the list goes to the permission engine of Claude Code, as in every other project werk runs.

payload.title: Spike on the werk prototype: Bun 1.4.1 compiles werk into one executable that runs with no checkout (Oct 2026)
payload.finding: The prototype server, its client files and its prompt files were compiled with Bun 1.4.1 into one executable and run from an empty git repository, with the source folders moved away. It added and showed cards, served the client from inside the file (byte counts equal to the source files), kept a live event stream open and survived a client disconnect, and started a fake Claude Code child that called the executable back to propose a card. Size per platform: 63 MB on macOS ARM (26 MB compressed), 70 MB macOS Intel, 82 MB Linux Intel and ARM; the werk code adds almost nothing to the runtime. A native build takes under a second; all other platforms cross-build from one Mac. The first build crashed at start, because the code read a folder of its own modules and its client files from disk at run time. Seven files changed to make it run: every file the code reads became a file listed at build time, and every place where werk starts itself, in a child process or in an agent prompt, had named the runtime and a source path instead of the executable. About forty messages shown to a person still printed the source form of the command. A file imported both as code and as an embedded file is refused by the compiler. The executable has only an ad-hoc signature and is not notarized.

ops.old: To make werk installable with nothing else on the machine except the Claude Code command line, each release builds one executable file per platform. The file holds the server code, the packages it imports, the Bun runtime, and the client that Vite built (#werk-stack-layout). werk serves the client from inside the file, so no folder is unpacked next to it.
ops.new: To make werk installable with nothing else on the machine except the Claude Code command line, each release builds one executable file per platform. The file holds the server code, the packages it imports, the Bun runtime, and the client that Vite built (#werk-stack-layout). werk serves the client from inside the file, so no folder is unpacked next to it.

Inside the executable there is no source folder, so two rules hold from the first line of code. werk reads no file of its own from a folder at run time: every client file, prompt and module that the code loads is listed when the executable is built. And werk never starts itself through a runtime and a source path: a child process, an agent prompt, and a command shown to a person all name the executable that is running. The same code then runs from a checkout and from the executable, with no second branch.

payload.title: The agent builds named options side by side, each in its own worktree, for the person to compare
payload.why: A person often cannot choose between versions described in prose, but chooses at once between versions they can look at. So the options are named first, by the person or the agent, and each one is built on its own copy of the project. Separate copies keep one option's changes out of another option's result.
payload.body:
To compare options that only show their difference when built, the person asks for them by name, or the agent names them before it asks a question (#al-two). Each option gets one agent and one throwaway worktree, and the agents run at the same time. Each agent leaves a screenshot and a patch, and its worktree is deleted (#al-ephem). The person compares the results and picks one, or asks for another option.

Example. The brief is "Show the open card's sub-cards".

- Option A "A grid of tiles".
- Option B "A compact list".

1. The person asks the agent to build A and B to compare them.
2. werk starts two agents, each in its own worktree made from the current main branch.
3. Agent A builds the grid, and agent B builds the list. Neither sees the other's changes.
4. Each agent leaves a screenshot and a patch on its option, and its worktree is deleted.
5. The person opens both screenshots and picks A. Option B stays as a rejected option, with its screenshot as the reason.
6. If agent B fails or runs past its time limit, option B shows the error, and option A still completes.

```
brief + A "A grid of tiles"  ──▶ agent A ──▶ worktree A ──▶ screenshot A + patch A ─┐
                                                                                    ├─▶ person picks
brief + B "A compact list"   ──▶ agent B ──▶ worktree B ──▶ screenshot B + patch B ─┘
                                 (A and B run at the same time; worktrees deleted after)
```

payload.why: Every comparison shows at least two contrasting options, as this card requires.

A program that learns which commands exist by listing a folder finds an empty list inside the executable, and stops.
