payload.title: The agent builds options only when their difference cannot be read in prose
payload.why: A built option costs an agent run and often a worktree, and most choices are rules that two sentences state fully. A build pays only when the person must see the result to judge it, such as a layout, a wording or a timing.

ops.old: Plan-or-code is not a setting. It is a per-item call, made at the moment the fork is found. Two tests, both must pass before any sampling run:

1. **The fork lives in an artifact you have to look at.** Layout, wording, timing, feel. If two sentences of prose make the fork clear — as they did for this card's own plan-vs-code options — the samples show nothing you cannot read. Write the options and ask (#al-two).
2. **The agent cannot predict the pick.** If the manifests would agree, there is no fork and the run is pure cost.
When both pass, the substrate is the cheapest artifact where the fork becomes visible: plan text, then running code, then a screenshot. Climb only as far as needed.

ops.new: Before the agent builds options (#al-build-options), it asks whether two sentences of prose make the difference between them clear. If they do, a build shows nothing new: the agent writes the options and asks (#al-two). If they do not, the difference lives in something the person must look at, such as a layout, a wording or a timing, and the agent builds the options.

A build goes only as far as the difference needs. A static mockup in an output folder comes first. A running build in its own worktree comes only when an option must change the project's code (#al-sample-build-isolation).

Example. Two questions reach the agent.

- Q1 "Where does the remove button sit on a card?", with option A "in the top right corner" and option B "at the bottom of the card".
- Q2 "Does a removed card keep its id?", with option A "the id stays taken" and option B "the id is free again".

1. For Q1, two sentences do not show which one looks right, so the agent builds A and B.
2. A mockup shows the difference, and neither option needs a change to the project's code, so each mockup goes to its own output folder and no worktree is made.
3. The person opens both mockups and picks one.
4. For Q2, two sentences state each option fully, so the agent builds nothing. It writes A and B and asks.

```
question ──▶ do two sentences show the difference?
               ├─ yes ──▶ write the options and ask                     (Q2: nothing built)
               └─ no  ──▶ must an option change the project's code?
                            ├─ no  ──▶ one mockup per option, in an output folder   (Q1)
                            └─ yes ──▶ one build per option, in its own worktree
```

payload.title: One reading of an I/O module names its behaviours, and each doubt is settled against the source or by a person
payload.why: A list of named behaviours needs one careful reading of the module, not several. A doubt is either about what the code does, which the source answers, or about what it should do, which only a person decides.

ops.old: The recipe for #werk-test-scope's step 4, reusable on any project's I/O modules.

**1. Write one brief for every target module together.** Ask for named behaviours that would break the tool if wrong, one sentence each, small enough to read in one sitting. One shared brief costs one sampling run instead of one per module.
**2. Run a handful of independent samples against it.** Use the sampling runner (#al-sample-runner) — each sample reads the real code and writes its own list; none may ask a question.
**3. Convergence is the list.** Where the samples agree almost word for word, that agreement is the behaviour, with no further check needed. Most of a real module's list settles this way.

**4. A fork is a fact question or a design question — tell them apart before you touch it.** A fact question asks what the code already does. Settle it by reading the source and citing the exact lines, never by asking a person to guess at running code. A design question asks what the code should do, and nothing decides that but a person with real contrast in front of them, per #al-two.

**5. Write the resolved list back onto one card per module,** each item at the responsibility level per #werk-test-scope's step 5, with any resolved fork kept as its own card so the reasoning survives even after the behaviour sounds obvious in hindsight.
Applied to werk today, as evidence: #werk-test-behaviours:src0.

ops.new: The recipe for finding the behaviours of an I/O module (#werk-test-scope), in any project.

One agent reads the module and the code that calls it, against one brief: name what breaks the tool if this is wrong, one sentence each. It writes each behaviour as a responsibility, not as a location.

Where the agent is unsure, it writes the doubt down as a question and sorts it. A fact question asks what the code already does: the agent reads the source and settles it. A design question asks what the code should do: only a person decides it, with at least two contrasting options in front of them (#al-two).
The settled list becomes the module's named test cases. A design question that stays open becomes a card.

Example. The module is the manager of the chat agent's process.

1. The agent reads it and writes six behaviours, such as "a crash never loses the message in flight".
2. It is unsure whether a restart sends the waiting message again. That is a fact question. The source shows that it does, so the behaviour goes on the list.
3. It is unsure whether an idle process should stop after 30 or after 60 minutes. That is a design question, so it becomes a card with both options for the person.
4. The seven behaviours become the module's named test cases.

```
module ──▶ one reading ──▶ behaviours ─────────────────────────────────▶ named test cases
                     └──▶ doubts ──┬─ fact question ──▶ read the source ──┘
                                   └─ design question ──▶ card with options ──▶ person decides
```

payload.why: A design question goes to the person with at least two contrasting options, as this card requires.

payload.title: Three independent readings of the module, and the list is where they agree
payload.why_not: Four runs produced lists, but none showed a behaviour that one careful reading would miss, and each run cost three agent runs.

ops.old: **1. Classify the module by one question.** Does a wrong line throw, hang, or crash — or does it quietly produce a result that looks correct? A quiet wrong answer is pure. A loud failure is I/O.

ops.old: **2. Pure code gets a number.** A pure module is a plain function of its input, cheap to call from a test, and a bug in it never announces itself. Set a high line-coverage threshold. Testing it is cheap and missing a bug in it is expensive, so a hard number belongs here.

payload.title: Panel: which unit tests fail, and how many of those failures are timeouts?
payload.why: A test that fails only when the machine is busy looks like a code bug and costs a pass to chase. The panel counts, per test, how many runs it failed in and how many of those failures were a time limit, so a test that breaks on load shows as that and not as a defect.
payload.body:
Every run of the unit test command leaves one record: when it ended, how many tests ran, and the tests that failed. A failure is a timeout when the runner ended the test on its time limit, or when the failure message names a time limit. The panel reads these records.

- **Marks.** One bar per run, oldest first: red when a time limit broke a test in that run, amber for any other failure, grey for a clean run. Four tiles show the runs in the window, the share of runs with a timeout, the share with any failure, and the number of tests that failed.
- **Table.** One row per test that failed in the window, with the share of runs it failed in, how many of those failures were a timeout, and its last failure with the first line of its message. Rows with timeouts come first.
- **Outlier.** A run with a timeout is red, and a timeout puts a dot on the panel in the rail. A plain failure does not: it is a defect to fix, not a measure to watch.
- **Drill-down.** A bar names the tests that failed in that run.
- **Scope.** The panel counts runs on one machine's checkout. The checks of a build run in their own worktree and are not counted.

Example, with three recorded runs:

- Run A "A clean run".
- Run B "One test hit its time limit": "A classifier that times out counts as not looping" failed on the time limit.
- Run C "A timeout and a plain failure": the same test timed out again, and "A plain assertion" failed.

1. The panel shows 3 runs, 2 with a timeout, 2 with any failure, and 2 tests that failed.
2. The table lists the classifier test first: failed in 2 of 3 runs, both on a time limit.
3. The plain assertion is second: failed in 1 of 3 runs, no timeout.
4. A window with only clean runs shows grey bars, no table row, and no dot in the rail.

```
runs   A    B    C        bar: [ok] [timeout] [timeout]
       .    T    T
table  classifier test   2 of 3   timeouts 2
       plain assertion   1 of 3   timeouts 0
```

payload.why: The runs it counts are runs of the unit test command that this card chooses, with its time limit per test.
It is one measure of the pipeline's own failures: a failure that moves with load, not with the code.

payload.title: One werk server works on many projects, and only the UI is shared between them
payload.why: werk is a tool for any project, and werk itself is one of those projects. A person moves between projects many times a day, so one place lists them and switches between them. Each project keeps its own map, chats, agents and history, so work in one project never touches another.
payload.body:
A project is a folder with a git repository and a map. The person adds a project once, and it stays on the list until they remove it (#werk-projects-list). The UI, its code and its display settings are shared (#werk-projects-display). Everything that belongs to the work is kept per project: the map, the conversations, the running agents and the history.

Every feature of werk works in every project. No feature is limited to werk's own repository.

werk v0 (#werk) has this too.

payload.title: One server process holds every project, so one code reload reaches all of them
payload.why: A change to werk's code must apply to every project, not only to werk's own. With one process, one hot reload replaces the code that serves every project. A process per project would need a reload in each process and a proxy in front of them.
payload.body:
There is one werk server per machine, on one port. It holds one context per project: the map, the conversations, the agents and the builds of that project. A hot reload in dev mode replaces the code for every context at once, and the live agent sessions of every project survive it (see #werk-hmr).

Starting werk in a folder while a server already runs does not start a second server. It adds the folder to the list, opens that project in the browser, and exits.

payload.why: a hot reload that keeps live agent sessions is what lets one reload update every project safely
dev mode is the hot reload that this card extends to every project

payload.title: One server process per project, behind a shared UI
payload.why_not: A code change needs a reload in every process, and the UI needs a proxy to reach each one.

payload.title: A project keeps its agents running while the person looks at another project
payload.why: A switch changes only what the browser shows. An agent turn can run for minutes, so stopping it on a switch would waste the work and keep the person in one project.
payload.body: Chats, builds and other background work of a project continue when the person switches to another project. The switcher marks each project that has a running agent turn.

payload.why: work can continue out of view because the one server process holds every project's agents at the same time

payload.title: The project list is stored once per user, outside every project
payload.why: The list belongs to the person, not to a project, so no project folder holds it. A project stays on the list until the person removes it. Removing a project never deletes its map.
payload.body:
Remove takes a project off the list. The folder and its map stay as they are, so adding the folder again brings back the same map. If the project has a running agent turn, werk names the running turns and asks for confirmation, then stops them and removes the project. Without a running turn, remove needs no confirmation.

A listed folder that was moved or deleted shows as missing. It does not open, and the person can remove it. werk never removes a project from the list by itself.

payload.why: remove must stop the running turns that a project keeps while out of view

payload.title: A project is named by its folder name
payload.why: The name shows in the switcher and in the address, so it must be short and readable. The folder name is the name the person already uses for the project.
payload.body: When two projects have the same folder name, the later one adds its parent folder name in brackets, for example "api (work)". A project has no other name, and there is no rename.

payload.why: names are unique only within the stored list, so a clash is found against it

payload.title: Adding a project opens the operating system's folder dialog
payload.why: A browser cannot give the server the full path of a folder, so the server opens the folder dialog itself. The server runs on the same machine as the browser, so the dialog appears in front of the person.
payload.body:
The last row of the switcher is "Add project…". It opens the macOS folder dialog. A folder with no map gets an empty map. A folder with no git repository cannot be a project yet: werk says that git is required and offers to initialise a repository there. It initialises the repository only when the person agrees.

When the list is empty, opening werk shows one page with the same "Add project…" action.

payload.why: an added folder goes onto the stored list

payload.title: A path field that autocompletes from the server's file system
payload.why_not: It is needed only when the server runs on another machine, and werk does not support a remote server. On one machine the folder dialog is faster.

payload.title: In dev mode, werk's own checkout is always on the project list
payload.why: In dev mode the person builds werk with werk, so werk's own map must always be one click away. The entry is the checkout whose code is running, not the folder where the server started.
payload.body: The entry is added each time werk starts in dev mode. It is not written to the stored list, so it is gone when werk runs outside dev mode. It cannot be removed. The rule holds for any dev mode: the mode that runs werk from its own source.

payload.why: the entry is added on top of the stored list, without being written into it
dev mode is what decides whether the entry is present

payload.title: Display settings are shared by all projects, and each project keeps its own open card and view
payload.why: Theme, panel widths, filters and sort order are how the person likes to read any map, so they follow the person across projects. The open card and the current view name a place in one map, so each project remembers its own.
payload.body: Switching to a project opens the card and the view that were open the last time the person was in that project. A project opened for the first time opens its home card on the map.

payload.why: the open card and the view are the parts of the address that each project remembers

payload.title: Keep every display setting per project
payload.why_not: The person would set the same theme, widths and filters again in each project.

payload.title: A project switcher sits at the left of the sticky header
payload.why: The project is the widest scope in werk, so it sits before the breadcrumbs, which move within one map. It shows in every view, so the person always knows which map they edit.
payload.body:
The header shows the current project's name with a menu arrow. The menu lists every project, then a divider and "Add project…".

Example:

- Projects: "werk" (dev mode, an agent turn is running), "checkout", and "api" (its folder was deleted).

1. The person opens the menu. The "werk" row has a busy dot. The "api" row is grey and says missing.
2. The person points at "checkout". A × appears on that row. The "werk" row never shows a ×.
3. The person clicks "checkout". The map of checkout opens. The agent turn in werk continues.
4. The person clicks "api". Nothing opens, because the folder is missing.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [werk ▾]  root › werk › map       Map Flow … │  ← sticky header
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ● werk      ~/Projects/werk                  │  ● = an agent turn is running
│   checkout  ~/Projects/checkout         ×    │  × = remove (shows on hover)
│   api       ~/work/api  (missing)       ×    │  missing = the folder is gone
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────    │
│ + Add project…                               │  opens the folder dialog
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

payload.why: the menu shows the stored list, its remove and its missing state
each row shows the project name
the busy dot shows the turns that run out of view
the last row starts the add
the dev-mode entry has no remove
the switcher sits before the breadcrumbs in the same sticky header

payload.title: Agents call the CLI by the plain name werk, in every project
payload.why: werk gives its instructions and subagents to agents in every project, so the text must name the CLI the same way everywhere. A path into werk's own source exists only in werk's repository.
payload.body:
Every instruction, subagent and permission rule writes the CLI as `werk`. werk keeps a launcher named `werk` in a folder of its own and puts that folder first on the PATH of every agent it starts. In dev mode the launcher runs the CLI of the checkout whose code is running, so each call uses the current code. In production it runs the installed program. The person's own terminal does not get it.

A `werk` command writes to the map of the nearest folder at or above the current folder that has a map. With no such folder it fails with an error. An agent starts in its project's root folder, so its commands reach its own project's map.

payload.why: the instructions that name the CLI go to agents in every project
each agent belongs to one project of the one server, and its commands must reach that project's map

payload.title: Write the absolute path of the running CLI into the prompt
payload.why_not: The text then differs per machine and per mode, and every prompt and subagent file needs a placeholder. One plain name reads the same everywhere.

payload.title: Put the project name first with no prefix: /<project>/map/<id>
payload.why_not: A project named like a view, such as map or board, would make the address mean two things.

payload.why: the project part of every address is the project name
v0 includes working on many projects from one server

payload.title: Run one werk instance per project, each on its own port
payload.why_not: Each instance needs its own port, browser tab and code reload, and nothing lists the projects or switches between them.

criterion.text: I use werk on at least two real projects for a week, and switching between them never mixes their state.

ops.old: The card has one color per state. Creating: the plan's agents run, and the card pulses and shows the step that runs now, spec writer, ticket writer, or checks. payload.title: A search that starts with # matches card ids only, and the exact id comes first
payload.why: A person who knows a card's id wants that card, not every card whose text mentions the word. Restricting the match to ids and ranking the exact id first puts the wanted card on top, so Enter opens it.
payload.body:
The map search box reads a leading # as the id form of a reference, the same form a card uses to link another card (see #werk-reflink). With the #, it compares the query to card ids only: the exact id ranks first, then ids that start with the query, then ids that contain it. Without the #, the search matches ids, titles, reasons and findings.

Example. The map holds the card werk-stack, its options werk-stack:opt0 and werk-stack:opt1, and a card vi-werk-stack-notes.

1. A person types #werk-stack. The list shows werk-stack first, then werk-stack:opt0 and werk-stack:opt1, then vi-werk-stack-notes. Enter opens werk-stack.
2. A person types werk-stack without the #. The list also shows every card whose title or reason holds the word.
3. A person types #nothing-like-this. No id matches, and the list stays closed.

```
 search: #werk-stack
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ 1 werk-stack            exact id     │  <- Enter opens this
 │ 2 werk-stack:opt0       id prefix    │
 │ 3 werk-stack:opt1       id prefix    │
 │ 4 vi-werk-stack-notes   id contains  │
 └──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

payload.why: takes the # form of a card reference from it

criterion.text: Type the # form of a known id in the map search box and check that Enter opens that card.

payload.title: A search result names the card by its id and shows its kind by color
payload.why: The word card or option on every result row repeats a fact that the id suffix and a color can carry, and hides the id that a person can paste into a reference. The row shows the id instead, and one color tells the kinds apart.
payload.body: Each row in the map search results shows the title, then the card id in a small monospace label. The kind of the result (card, option, source, excerpt) is shown by color, not by a word. The color scheme is still to choose.

payload.why: the id on the row is the form a # search matches

payload.title: The id label carries the kind color
payload.why: Card ids stay grey and only options, sources and excerpts get color, so the rows that are not cards stand out and the list stays quiet.
payload.body:
Card ids are grey, option ids orange, source ids purple, excerpt ids dim. A row has no stripe and no dot.

![The id label carries the kind color](/api/image?name=vi-jump-row-opt1.png)

payload.title: Each row has a left stripe in the grid tile color
payload.why: The stripe matches the grid tiles and shows each card's status at a glance, but one stripe then carries both status and kind, and the reader must learn eight colors.
payload.body:
A card row takes its status color: green, amber, red or blue. An option row is orange, a source row purple, an excerpt row grey. The id label is grey.

![Each row has a left stripe in the grid tile color](/api/image?name=vi-jump-row-opt2.png)

payload.title: A colored dot before the title shows the kind
payload.why: A dot is the calmest mark to read, but elsewhere in the map a dot means status, so a reader takes this dot for status too.
payload.body:
The dot is grey for a card, orange for an option, purple for a source, dim for an excerpt. The id label is grey.

![A colored dot before the title shows the kind](/api/image?name=vi-jump-row-opt3.png)

payload.title: A search result shows a dot in the card's status color and the card id

patch.body:
Each row in the map search results shows a dot, the title, and the card id in a small grey monospace label at the right edge. The dot uses the status colors of the counts (see #vi-counts): green for decided, amber for open, blue for proto. A stale card's dot is red, whatever its status.

A postponed card's dot is split along a diagonal like a slash: the upper-left half keeps its status color and the lower-right half is grey (see #pr-wf-postponed for the mark). So a postponed card still shows its status.

An option, a source or an excerpt has no status. Its dot takes the color of its kind: orange for an option, purple for a source, grey for an excerpt. The id suffix names the kind too.

Example. A search for werk-stack finds these:

- werk-stack, decided
- werk-stack-bun, open
- werk-stack-test, decided and stale
- werk-stack-deploy, open and postponed
- werk-stack:opt0, an option

1. werk-stack gets a green dot.
2. werk-stack-bun gets an amber dot.
3. werk-stack-test gets a red dot. Stale wins over decided.
4. werk-stack-deploy gets a dot half amber, half grey.
5. werk-stack:opt0 gets an orange dot.

```
 ●  werk runs on Bun                werk-stack         ● green  = decided
 ●  Bun runs the TypeScript         werk-stack-bun     ● amber  = open
 ●  Tests run on the Bun runner     werk-stack-test    ● red    = stale
 ◩  werk ships as one binary        werk-stack-deploy  ◩ amber / grey = open, postponed
 ●  Node with a build step          werk-stack:opt0    ● orange = option
```

![The status dot on each search result](/api/image?name=vi-jump-row-dot-status.png)
patch.why: A person scanning results wants to know which card is settled and which is not, and wants the id to paste into a reference. A dot in the status color answers the first, as dots do everywhere else in the map, and the id label answers the second, so the kind word on the row goes.

payload.why: takes the status colors of the dot from it
takes the postponed mark that the split dot shows

payload.title: A dot before the title in the card's status color

patch.body:
The screenshot shows the layout. The card body above gives the colors.

![A dot before the title](/api/image?name=vi-jump-row-dot-status.png)
patch.why: The dot means status here as it does in the counts, so the reader learns no new meaning, and the row stays calm.

patch.why_not: Coloring the id shows the kind but not the status, and the status is what a person scanning results needs.
A stripe shows status, but a full-height bar on every row is louder than a dot, and in the counts a dot already carries status.

criterion.text: Search the map for a mix of decided, open, stale and postponed cards and check that each dot reads at a glance.

payload.title: The search box in the header opens any card by its id or its words
payload.why: A person often knows a word or an id but not where the card sits in the tree. Typing it into one box in the header and pressing Enter opens the card from any view, so nobody has to walk the tree to find it.
payload.body:
The search box sits in the header row next to the view tabs (see #vi-layout). As a person types, a list opens below the box. A result is any card, option, source or excerpt whose id, title, reason or finding holds the typed text, with case ignored. The list shows at most twelve results, in map order. A query that starts with # matches ids only (#vi-jump-hash). Each row names its result (#vi-jump-row).

The keyboard drives the list. The down and up arrows move the selection, Enter opens the selected result in the map view, and Escape clears the box and closes the list. A click on a row opens it too. Opening a result clears the box.

Example. The map holds the card werk-stack, titled "werk runs on Bun with no dependencies", and its option werk-stack:opt0, titled "Node with a build step".

1. A person types bun. The list shows werk-stack, because its title holds the word. The first row is selected.
2. The person presses the down arrow. The selection moves to the next row.
3. The person presses Enter. The map opens the selected card, and the box clears.
4. A person types qqq. Nothing matches, and the list stays closed.
5. A person presses Escape. The box clears and the list closes.

```
 header:  [ crumbs ]  [ counts ]  [ tabs ]  [ bun          ✕ ]  LIVE
                                            ┌──────────────────┐
                                            │▶ row 1 (selected)│  ↓ ↑  move the selection
                                            │  row 2           │  Enter  open it in the map
                                            │  …  up to 12     │  Esc    clear and close
                                            └──────────────────┘
```

criterion.text: Type a word from a card's title in the search box, press Enter, and check that the map opens that card.

payload.why: opens a result at the map address of that card

payload.title: The view tabs in the header switch the left pane between the views of the map
payload.why: One map has several views, and a person moves between them many times in a session. One row of tabs in the header is always on screen and marks the view in use, so a switch is one click from anywhere.
payload.body:
Each view has one tab, and the tab of the view in use is highlighted. A click on a tab opens that view at its own address (see #vi-routes), so Back returns to the view before. The map view opens at the card that was last open on the map. The Flow view keeps its last scope. Every other view opens at the root. The view in use is remembered per project, so a reload opens it again.

Example. A person reads the card "Checkout retries" on the map.

1. The person clicks the Board tab. The board opens at the root, and the Board tab is highlighted.
2. The person clicks the Map tab. The map opens at "Checkout retries" again.
3. The person clicks the Map tab while the map is open. Nothing changes.

```
 [ Map ] [ Graph ] [ Board ] [ Flow ]      ▔▔▔ = the view in use
   ▔▔▔
 click Board  ->  [ Map ] [ Graph ] [ Board ] [ Flow ]    board at the root
                                     ▔▔▔▔▔
 click Map    ->  [ Map ] [ Graph ] [ Board ] [ Flow ]    map at "Checkout retries"
                    ▔▔▔
```

payload.why: opens each view at the address that vi-routes gives it

criterion.text: Click each tab, then Back, and check that each view opens at its own address and Back returns to the view before.

payload.title: The screen is split into a left pane for the views and a right pane for the chat
payload.why: A view redraws while the reply streams in, so the view and the chat stay in sight side by side. Each pane keeps its own controls, so neither moves when the other changes.

ops.old: Two panes sit side by side.
ops.new: Two panes sit side by side.

ops.old:
**Left pane: the map.** A sticky header over a scrolling body.
1. Breadcrumbs, one row (#vi-crumbs-place).
2. A row with the whole-map counts, the view tabs, a jump-to-card search box, and a live marker.
3. The body is the view the tab picks. The views and their addresses are in #vi-routes.
ops.new: **Left pane: the views.** A sticky header over a scrolling body. payload.title: A chat lets a person talk to a live agent that changes the map in the same turn
payload.why: Decisions settle in conversation, and a map that someone fills in afterwards misses them. The agent in the chat sees the open card and writes to the map while it replies, so what the talk settles is on the map when the turn ends.

ops.old: Typing in the composer and pressing Enter sends the message to the server. The request carries the text, any pasted images, the open card from the location hash, and the active conversation tab.

The server hands the message to that conversation's agent. The agent runs it as a live turn, and the reply streams back over the SSE channel. #werk-pane describes the pane, and #werk-chat-stdin the claude child behind it.
The agent reads a card's thread and writes a note to it from the command line.

ops.new: To turn talk into decisions with no copy step, a person talks to a live agent in a chat, and the agent writes what the talk settles into the map during the same turn.

A message goes to the agent with the card the person has open, so "this card" needs no id (#werk-onechat). The agent runs the message as a live turn: it reads the code and the map, runs commands, and writes cards and notes. Its reply streams into the chat while it works, and the map redraws each time the agent writes to it. A reply stays under the message it answers, also when the person sends again before it ends (#werk-chat-turn-id). Each conversation has its own agent process (#werk-chat-stdin), and a person can keep more than one (#werk-multichat). The composer shows what can be typed, such as commands (#werk-chat-cmdmenu).
The page never writes to the map itself. Every change comes from an agent turn, and only a request that carries the server token from a local address can start one (#werk-serve-trust).

Example. The map holds the card "Checkout retries", which says two tries.

1. The person opens "Checkout retries", types "Make it three tries", and presses Enter. The message goes out with that card.
2. The agent turn starts. The reply streams in while the agent reads the card.
3. The agent changes the card. The map redraws, and the card says three tries.
4. A page on another site sends a message to the server. It has no token, so no turn starts and the map does not change.

```
 person ──(message + open card)──▶ server ──▶ agent turn
   ▲                                           │
   │                                           ├─ reads code and map
   └──── reply streams into the chat ◀─────────┤
                                               └─ writes ──▶ map redraws
```

payload.title: The stage panel switches its unit between dollars, tokens and wall time
payload.why: The stage that costs the most money is not always the stage that takes the most time, and a slow stage holds up every ticket behind it. One switch on the same chart answers both questions with the same lines, legend and drill-down.
payload.body:
A switch above the chart sets the unit of every line and of the legend: dollars, tokens, or wall time. Dollars is the default. The stages, the period, the outlier band and the drill-down stay the same in each unit; the band is computed again from the points in the chosen unit.

In wall time, a point is the sum of the time that the steps of that stage ran and ended inside that point's span. A ticket that waits in a column, for a person or for its turn, adds no stage time: a wait for a person is measured on its own (see #vi-flow-ms-waits). In tokens, a point is the sum of every token kind. Its hover title shows the breakdown, because a cache read costs about a tenth of a fresh input token, so tokens can rank stages differently from dollars (see #ms-cost).

Example. In one week the build stage cost $40 over 6 hours, and the grader cost $12 over 9 hours.

1. The panel opens in dollars. The build line is the highest.
2. The person switches to wall time. The grader line is now the highest, and the legend shows 9 h beside it.
3. The person clicks a point of the grader line. The drill-down lists the same tickets as in dollars, each with its time.
4. A ticket waits two hours in the todo column. No stage line rises for those two hours.

```
 unit:  ( $ )  tokens   time          ( ) = the unit in use

 $  │   build ●───●            time │        grader ●───●
    │  grader ●───●                 │   build ●───●
    └──────────────                 └──────────────
      wk 1   wk 2                     wk 1   wk 2
```

payload.why: takes the dollars, the token breakdown and the wall time of each step from it
leaves the time a ticket waits for a person to that panel

payload.title: The effort panel switches its unit between dollars, tokens and wall time
payload.why: A ticket can grow costly without growing slow, or slow without growing costly, and each is a different sign of rot. One switch on the same chart shows the trend of each unit with the same dots, lines and drill-down.
payload.body:
A switch above the chart sets the unit of every dot: dollars, tokens, or wall time. Dollars is the default. Each dot stays one finished ticket, adjusted for the ticket's size in every unit. The reference band, the alert line and the current median are computed again from the dots in the chosen unit, so an alert in one unit says nothing about another.

In wall time, a dot is the time that the ticket's builder passes, checks, grader and reviews ran. Time the ticket waited in a column adds nothing. In tokens, a dot is the sum of every token kind, and its hover title shows the breakdown, because a cache read costs about a tenth of a fresh input token (see #ms-cost).

Example. Ticket A cost $3 and ran 40 minutes. Ticket B cost $3 and ran 90 minutes, because its checks are slow. Both have the same size.

1. The panel opens in dollars. A and B sit at the same height.
2. The person switches to wall time. B sits above A, and above the band.
3. The person clicks B. The drill-down lists its passes, each with its time.
4. B waited one night in the todo column. Its dot does not count that night.

```
 unit:  ( $ )  tokens   time          ( ) = the unit in use

 $  │  A ●  B ●               time │        B ●   above the band
    │░░░░░░░░░░░ band               │  A ●
    └────────────                   │░░░░░░░░░░░ band
      tickets in build order        └────────────
```

payload.why: takes the tokens and the wall time that the loop records for each ticket from it
takes the dollars and the token breakdown of each step from it

payload.title: A plan's start event lists the scope cards it reads, with their tier and version
payload.why: Two plans of one subtree can differ because their input differed, not because the planner did. With no record of the input, a report cannot tell these cases apart, and cannot relate the cost of a plan to its size. A list of card ids with a position in the decision log is small, and it recovers the exact text that the planner read.
payload.body:
When a plan starts, it appends one event to the pipeline log. The event holds the scope (see #st-spec-linked) as a list. Each entry has the card id, its tier, and the position in the decision log of the last change to that card. The decision log is append-only (#pr-log), so a fold up to that position gives the card text that the planner read.

The event also holds the size of the input: the number of cards in each tier, and the length in characters of the scope text that the prompt holds. The token count of the call is in the cost of the step (#ms-cost), so the event does not repeat it.

Example. A plan of #app reads #app and #app-login in the first tier, and #mail-retry and #queue in the second tier.

1. The plan starts. The event lists four entries, for example #app-login at tier 1, log position 812.
2. The size reads: tier 1 has 2 cards, tier 2 has 2 cards, scope text 9,400 characters.
3. #app-login changes later, at log position 905. A second plan lists #app-login at position 905.
4. A comparison of the two plans shows that #app-login changed between them. When no position differs, the input was the same.

```
plan 1  start  [app@790 t1] [app-login@812 t1] [mail-retry@640 t2] [queue@611 t2]  2+2 cards, 9,400 chars
plan 2  start  [app@790 t1] [app-login@905 t1] [mail-retry@640 t2] [queue@611 t2]  2+2 cards, 9,650 chars
                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the only input that changed
```
@N = position in the decision log. t1, t2 = tier.

payload.why: The list holds the scope and its two tiers that this card defines.
A log position recovers the card text because the decision log is append-only, as this card decides.

payload.title: The event holds a full copy of each scope card's text
payload.why_not: A scope has tens of cards, and every plan would copy them into a log that every fold reads. The decision log already holds each version, so a position recovers the same text.

payload.title: The event holds only the count of cards per tier
payload.why_not: A count shows that the input grew, not which card changed. Two plans with the same count can read different decisions.

payload.title: Each plan keeps a copy of the spec and the tickets it wrote, beside the pipeline log
payload.why: A plan updates the spec and the open tickets of its subtree in place, so the next plan erases what the last one wrote. Without a copy, no one can compare what two plans produced from their inputs. A copy per plan is small text, and it changes nothing that the build reads.
payload.body:
To compare two plans of one subtree, each plan keeps what it wrote. When a plan ends, it copies the spec and every ticket it wrote or changed into one directory beside the pipeline log. The plan's ended event names that directory, in the same way as a transcript file (#ms-store-files).

The copy is a record, not a second source. The build reads only the live spec and tickets (#st-plan-extend). No plan or build reads a copy.

A ticket that the plan did not change is not copied. The copy lists its id and says that it was kept as it was, so a comparison can still show the whole ticket set of that plan.

Git does not track the copies, for the same reason as the other detail files (#ms-store-git). The measures stay in the log when a copy is lost.

Example. #app is planned twice.

1. Plan 1 ends. It writes the spec and tickets 01, 02 and 03. The copy holds all four files.
2. Ticket 01 is built and goes to done.
3. #app-login changes, and plan 2 runs. It changes the spec and ticket 02, and adds ticket 04. Ticket 03 is open and does not change. Ticket 01 is done, so the plan does not touch it.
4. Plan 2's copy holds the spec, 02 and 04, and lists 03 as kept.
5. A comparison of the two copies shows the spec change, the change to 02, and the new 04.

```
plan 1 copy:  spec   01   02   03
plan 2 copy:  spec*       02*  03=  04+
              * changed   = kept as it was   + new   (01 done, not part of plan 2)
```

payload.why: A copy is needed because a plan updates the spec and open tickets in place, as this card decides.
The copy is a detail file beside the log, named by its event, under the rule this card sets.
The copies are not tracked, under the rule this card sets for detail files.

payload.title: Git history of the spec and ticket files is the copy
payload.why_not: Git does not track the ticket files, and two plans between two commits leave only the second in history.

payload.title: Git tracks the copies, beside the pipeline log
payload.why_not: A copy is debugging detail, like a transcript. A comparison of two plans is needed for recent plans, so the repository would grow with every plan for little use.

payload.title: The time a ticket spends in each board column is a measure, folded from the board log
payload.why: Cost says what a ticket cost, not where it waited. A ticket that waits two days in ready and one that builds for two days cost differently but look the same in wall time. The board log already gives every move a time, so this measure needs no new event.
payload.body:
For each ticket, the time in a column runs from the move into that column to the move out of it. A ticket that enters a column more than once adds the visits, and the count of visits is kept beside the total. The time before the first move runs from the event that planned the ticket. Done is not timed. A ticket that is archived stops its clock at the archive.

The measure is a pure fold over the board log (#vi-board-state). A move is a fact about where a ticket is, so the pipeline log holds no copy of it.

Per column, the report shows a distribution: the median, the 90th percentile and the maximum, for the same reason as cost (#ms-cost). A ticket still in a column counts up to now and is marked as open, so a stuck ticket shows before it moves.

Example. Ticket 01 "Login by magic link".

1. 10:00 — planned into ready.
2. 10:30 — to building. Ready: 30 min.
3. 10:42 — a check fails, to blocked. Building: 12 min.
4. 14:00 — a person moves it to ready. Blocked: 3 h 18 min.
5. 14:05 — to building. Ready: 5 min more.
6. 14:15 — to merging. Building: 10 min more.
7. 14:17 — to done. Merging: 2 min.

Totals: ready 35 min in 2 visits, building 22 min in 2 visits, blocked 3 h 18 min, merging 2 min. If step 4 has not happened yet, blocked counts up to now and shows as open.

```
10:00   10:30   10:42                         14:00 14:05 14:15 14:17
  |ready  |build |blocked ....................  |rdy  |build|mrg |done
  [ 30m  ][ 12m ][         3h 18m             ][ 5m ][10m ][2m ]
ready = 30+5 (2 visits)   building = 12+10 (2 visits)   blocked = 198   merging = 2
```
Times in minutes. Each bar runs from the move into the column to the move out.

payload.why: The fold reads the timed moves of the board log that this card defines.
The measure has one row per column that this card defines.
It reports the median, 90th percentile and maximum, the distribution shape that this card sets.

payload.title: The build writes each move into the pipeline log as a step event
payload.why_not: The board log already holds every move with its time. A second copy can disagree with the first, and the board log stays the one record of where a ticket is.

payload.title: The time of the last visit only, not the sum of the visits
payload.why_not: A ticket that goes back to building three times would show only its last pass, and the retries would not show in the time.

patch.body:
A follow-up is a request from the person to change work that a finished build delivered: a done ticket, or a run whose tickets are merged.

**Who records it.** The chat agent that receives the request records it in the same turn, before it starts the work. The record goes into the board log as a fact about the ticket (#vi-board-state). It names the ticket, the class, where the problem was found, and one line of reason. The person can correct a record. A correction is a new record for the same follow-up, and the last one counts.

**Class.**
- **Plan miss.** The build did what the plan said, and the plan was wrong or silent. Example: the login link must last 15 minutes, and no card said so.
- **Build miss.** The plan was right, and the build got it wrong. Example: a card says 15 minutes, and the link lasts 1 minute. A build miss is also an escape (#ms-outcome-escape), so its record also says whether a check could have caught it.

**Where found.** At review, before the person passes the gate of the run, or after merge.

**Early signals of plan misses.** These come before the person sees the build: the cards a builder proposes when no cited card gives a decision (#st-build-missing-decision), and the spec-gap fails of #ms-fail.

**Numbers.** Plan misses and build misses per ticket. Builder proposals per ticket.

**Starting threshold.** Follow-ups per ticket must go down over time. A rise raises an alert by the rule of #lp-trend-alert.

Example. Ticket app/01 "Login by magic link" is done and merged.

1. The person writes in the chat: "the link expires after 1 minute, make it 15".
2. The agent reads #app-login. It says 15 minutes. So the plan was right: a build miss, found after merge. A unit test on the expiry could have caught it.
3. The agent records the follow-up on app/01, then fixes the code.
4. The person reads the record and says the card never said 15. The agent records a correction: plan miss.
5. The person writes "rename the button" about a ticket still in building. That is not a follow-up: the build is not finished, and nothing is recorded.

```
chat turn ──► follow-up app/01  build miss  after merge  check could catch: yes
          ──► correction app/01  plan miss                 (the last record counts)
board log:  [moved done] [merge green] [follow-up] [follow-up correction]
```
patch.why: Plan has no exit code. A request to change the result of a finished build is the clearest sign of what the plan or the build got wrong. The chat agent records each request when the person makes it, because only then are the request and its reason both at hand.

payload.why: The follow-up record is a fact about a ticket, stored in the board log that this card defines.
Builder proposals are the early signal of plan misses, counted per ticket.

payload.title: The person files each follow-up and chooses its class
payload.why_not: The class is exact, but every request costs the person a form, and a request without the form is not counted.

payload.title: A review agent finds and classifies follow-ups later, from the chat, the decision log and git
payload.why_not: It writes late and guesses the request from what is left. A request after the last review is not recorded, and no such agent exists.

patch.body:
An escape is a defect in a ticket that passed the builder loop (#st-build-ticket). It is found in one of four places:

- **The merge loop.** A check is red when the merge loop runs it on the ticket (#st-build-run). A conflict with other work is not a defect of the ticket, so it is not an escape.
- **The held-out set.** A held-out step goes red after the ticket's merge (#st-build-run).
- **At review.** The person finds it before passing the gate of the run.
- **After merge.** The person finds it later.

**Where the facts come from.** The first two are folded from the merge result and the held-out result that the board log already holds for the ticket. A check found them, so a check could catch them: the question is only why it ran so late. The last two are follow-ups with the class build miss (#ms-outcome-followup). Their record says whether a check could have caught the defect.

**Numbers.** Escapes per ticket, split by where they were found.

**Starting threshold.** An escape that a check could have caught adds that check. No window and no threshold.

Example. Three tickets pass the builder loop.

1. app/01 goes red in the merge loop on the unit tests. Escape: merge loop.
2. app/02 merges. A held-out step fails afterwards. Escape: held-out set.
3. app/03 merges. A week later the person reports a wrong expiry time, and the chat agent records a build miss found after merge, which a check could have caught. Escape: after merge.
4. app/04 conflicts in the merge loop. No escape.

```
              merge loop   held-out   at review   after merge
app/01            1
app/02                        1
app/03                                                1 (check could catch)
app/04        (conflict: not counted)
```
patch.why: Each escape is a missing check or rubric line. The place where it was found shows which gate should have caught it. Two places are checks that already leave a result on the ticket, and the other two are follow-ups, so no escape needs a record of its own.

payload.why: Escapes found by the person are the build-miss follow-ups that this card records.
Merge-loop and held-out escapes are folded from the results the board log holds per ticket.

patch.body:
A stop is a place where the build cannot go on until a person acts.

**Kinds of stop.**
- A gate that waits for a person to pass it.
- A ticket held in blocked: by a failed check, as stuck, because a cited card changed, or with no check.
- A merge loop that stopped.
- A merge that was red on the main line, or that conflicted with it.
- A build that reached its retry cap.
- A restart of unfinished work, which ends the tickets of the subtree that had not merged (#werk-board-restart).

A builder's question is not a stop: the overseer answers it, not a person. A gate has no reject: a person who does not accept the result asks for a change, and that is a follow-up (#ms-outcome-followup). A chat-pane question is measured on its own (#ms-outcome-interv-chat).

**Where the kind comes from.** The structured facts that the build writes with each stop: the gate events, the check that holds a blocked ticket, how the merge loop ended, the merge result and its conflict flag, the end of a build at the cap, and the restart flag on each ticket a restart ends. The reason text never decides the kind, so a reworded reason changes no count. A move written before those facts existed has only its reason, and for that move alone the start of the reason decides the kind.

**Length of a wait.** From the stop to the next event that moves the work on. The log does not say who acted, so the length is that of the stop, not a person's response time. A stop still open counts up to now.

**Numbers.** Stops per ticket and per card, by kind, and the total wait.

**Starting threshold.** Stops per ticket must go down over time. A rise raises an alert by the rule of #lp-trend-alert.

Example. Ticket app/02 "Add an item".

1. 10:00 — a check fails in building, and the ticket moves to blocked with the check named. A stop of kind blocked by a failed check starts.
2. 11:30 — the person moves it to ready. The stop ends: 1 h 30 min.
3. 12:00 — the run reaches the gate and waits. A stop of kind gate starts.
4. If the person has not passed the gate yet, the stop counts up to now.

```
app/02   10:00 [blocked: check] ── 1h30 ── 11:30 ready     12:00 [gate] ── open ──► now
stops:   1 x blocked by a check (1h30)   1 x gate (open)
```
patch.why: An autonomous pipeline that often waits for a person is not autonomous. Each stop already leaves a structured fact in the board log or the pipeline log, so the count and the wait time are a fold, and only a restart needs a fact it does not leave yet.

payload.why: Each kind of stop is read from a structured fact in the board log that this card defines.
A restart is a kind of stop, and ends the unfinished tickets as this card defines.
A person's rejection of a gate's result is counted as a follow-up, not as a stop.

patch.body:
Two kinds:

- **A cited card reopened.** A decided card is reopened after a ticket that cites it started to build. The reopen events come from the decision log (#pr-log), and the cards a ticket cites, with the time it cited them, from the ticket's cite records (#st-ticket-watch).
- **Merged code changed.** A later commit changes or reverts a line that a ticket's merge added, within 14 days of that merge. The fold reads the merge commit that the board log records for each ticket (#st-build-run), and asks the repository at the time of the report. Nothing new is recorded at merge time.

**Numbers.** Rework events per ticket, by kind. The 14 days are a first guess.

Example. Ticket app/01 cites #app-login and merges on 1 May as commit 9f2c.

1. 3 May — #app-login is reopened. Rework: a cited card reopened.
2. 6 May — a commit rewrites two lines that 9f2c added. Rework: merged code changed.
3. 20 May — another commit changes a line that 9f2c added. That is past 14 days, so it is not rework.

```
1 May merge 9f2c ─┬─ 3 May reopen #app-login   ── rework (card)
                  ├─ 6 May commit edits 9f2c   ── rework (code)
                  └─ 20 May commit edits 9f2c  ── past 14 days, not counted
```
patch.why: Work that is undone soon after it is done costs twice. Rework shows it even when no one filed a follow-up. Both kinds are folds over records that exist already: the reopen events of the decision log, the cited cards of each ticket, and the merge commit of each ticket.

payload.why: Card reopens are read from the reopen events of the append-only decision log that this card defines.
The cards each ticket cites, and when, come from the cite records that this card defines.
The merge commit of each ticket, which the code fold starts from, is recorded by the merge loop that this card defines.
Rework reads card reopens from the decision log that this card defines.

payload.body:
A stage agent has four inputs: werk's generic instructions, its role prompt, the decided cards, and the code. The project's build rules need a fifth home. Three architectures are on the table (the options of this card): one thin instruction file in the repository, an index file that points to documents the agent opens on demand, or build-rule cards in the map from which werk writes the repository files and picks the rules each role gets.

All three share one rule. A build rule that a program can check becomes a linter, a test or a hook that the agent cannot edit. Prose holds only what no check can hold, and only what an agent cannot infer from the code.

Evidence so far: a context file helps only for practices the agent cannot infer, and overviews or generated files raise cost with no gain in success. Long context degrades every model tested. One production report replaced a large instruction file with a short index over checked documents. No study evaluates rules kept as decisions in a map.

ops.new:
- The chat pane receives each turn's cost and token use when the turn ends. It appends one step-ended event for the turn at that moment.
- The event names the conversation and the card that was open on that turn (#ms-cost).
- A turn that runs while no card is open names no card. The report counts it in its day.
- Subagents that a turn starts are part of that turn's cost.
- A background task that the turn started can finish after the turn ends and wake the agent again, with no new message from the person. Each wake ends with its own result, and appends the turn's next part: an event with only the responses since the part before. A part is known by its conversation, its turn and its number, so the live record and a later backfill never count one twice. The report adds the parts into one turn.

Example. A turn starts two subagents in the background and ends at 10:00 for $2. At 10:09 one subagent finishes and wakes the agent, which reads the report for $1. At 10:20 the other wakes it for $0.50.

1. 10:00 — part 0: $2.
2. 10:09 — part 1: $1, only the responses after 10:00.
3. 10:20 — part 2: $0.50.
4. A backfill later finds all three parts in the log and adds nothing.
5. The report shows one turn on the open card, $3.50.

```
prompt ──► result 10:00 ─ wake ─► result 10:09 ─ wake ─► result 10:20
           part 0  $2             part 1  $1             part 2  $0.50
report:    1 turn, $3.50
```

patch.body:
A person writes one short instruction file with the commands and the non-standard rules, and one glossary of domain words. Every stage agent loads both in full. Werk does not write or read them on its own.

![A person writes the instruction file and the glossary; every stage agent loads both whole; linters, tests and hooks block bad output](/api/image?name=st-build-howto-opt0.png)

The always-loaded instruction file is an index of about 100 lines. It points to documents on architecture, conventions, decision records and domain words. An agent opens a document only when its task touches that area. A check in continuous integration flags a document that is stale or that no index entry links to.

![The index loads into every stage agent; the agent opens only the documents its task needs; a freshness check flags stale or unlinked documents](/api/image?name=st-build-howto-opt1.png)

Each build rule is a card, with options, reasons and depends_on edges to the cards about what to build. A changed rule marks its dependents stale. Werk writes the instruction file and the glossary in the repository from the decided cards, so the files never drift from the map. Each stage agent gets only the rule cards for its role.

payload.title: Every stage agent starts with the titles of all build-rule cards in its prompt
payload.why: An agent cannot follow a build rule that it does not know exists. The titles are short, so all of them fit in every prompt, the way a table of contents does. The agent then reads the full card only when its task touches that rule. Werk adds the titles itself, so no agent has to remember to look.
payload.body:
This applies if build rules are cards in the map (#st-build-howto). The titles act as the index, and the cards act as the documents that the agent opens on demand.

To find the build-rule cards, werk needs a mark that is the same in every project, because werk's prompts are the same in every project. The options of this card are two kinds of mark: a position (a second top card beside the root) or a label on each card.

A card is a build rule when a user of the product would not notice a change to it. A card that a user would notice is a requirement, even when it names a technology.

Example:
- Requirement R "An order export holds every order"
- Build rule B "Tests run against a real database, never a mock"
- Build rule C "Domain word: an order is one checkout, not one item"

1. A builder pass starts on a ticket for R. Werk adds the titles of B and C to its prompt.
2. The ticket writes a query, so the builder opens B and reads it in full. It writes the test against a real database.
3. The builder does not open C, because its title answers the question. It names the type Order for one checkout.
4. If no build-rule card exists, the prompt holds no title list, and nothing else changes.

```
prompt of a builder pass
+------------------------------------------+
| werk instructions     (same everywhere)  |
| builder role prompt   (same everywhere)  |
| build-rule titles:    B, C               |  <- added by werk
| ticket for R                             |
+------------------------------------------+
        |  opens B in full when the task needs it
        v
   B Tests

patch.why_not: A hand-written file records no reason for a rule and no link to the requirement it serves, so a changed requirement leaves the rule silently wrong. Loaded whole into every stage, the file also grows into a long list that agents half-follow.

patch.body:
A stage agent has four inputs: werk's generic instructions, its role prompt, the decided requirement cards, and the code. The project's build rules are a fifth: its commands, conventions, domain words and test policy. To give them reasons and links like any other decision, the build rules are cards in the project's map. A build rule depends on the requirements it serves, so a changed requirement marks the rule stale.

The map is the only source: a hand edit to those files is overwritten, and a change goes through a card.

Generated or generic rules do not help an agent, so a build-rule card is decided with an option weighed against it, like any other card.

payload.title: In v0, a new conversation starts empty from a control in the tab strip, with the open card as its home card
payload.why: The chat card says a person can keep more than one conversation, but the cards that define forking, parking and the tab strip are not decided. v0 needs one plain way to start a second conversation, so it starts an empty one and leaves the rest for later.
payload.body:
A person can keep more than one conversation (see #werk-chat). To make that possible without the undecided tab features, v0 gives the tab strip one control that starts a new conversation. The new conversation gets its own agent process (see #werk-chat-stdin) and an empty session. Its home card is the card open when it starts, and the home card is its tab label (see #werk-mc-split).

Each tab is a chip in the tab strip. A click on a chip switches the chat pane to that conversation and shows its newest message (see #werk-mc-tab-bottom). A tab whose agent died, or that has a running background agent, shows it as #werk-mc-live-dead and #werk-mc-bgagents say. Every conversation stays on the strip; v0 has no close, no park and no idle sweep.

Forking a session, reading a sibling conversation, parking a tab and keyboard shortcuts for tabs are not in v0.

Example:

- The map shows card A "We charge per seat". Conversation C1 has A as its home card.

1. The person opens card B "The invoice shows the seat count" and presses the new-conversation control.
2. A new tab C2 appears with the label B. Its agent starts with an empty session.
3. The person sends a message in C2. The turn names B as the open card.
4. The person clicks C1. The pane shows the newest message of C1.

```
tab strip:  [ A ]  [ B ]  [ + ]
             C1     C2     new conversation, empty, home card = open card
```

payload.title: v0 writes every build step to the pipeline log and builds no report over it
payload.why: The builder loop needs a record of each pass, its gate and its cause, and a test of the loop reads that record. The pipeline log is the one decided place for it. The reports and views over it are not in v0, so v0 writes the facts and reads them only where the loop itself needs them.
payload.body:
Each project has one append-only pipeline log (see #ms-store). v0 writes to it the start and end of every plan step, builder pass, check, grader run, reviewer run, merge and held-out run, with the wall time, the cost and token breakdown, the result, and for a red step its gate and cause (see #ms-fail, #ms-fail-cause). The transcripts and full check output are files beside it, named by its events (see #ms-store-files).

The builder loop reads the log only where a rule needs it: the retry cap reads which failed passes count (see #st-build-cap-spec-gap), and the next pass reads the last failure. The fail report command, the Measure view, the trend report and the plan-turn cost of chat turns are not in v0.

Example:

- Ticket T has the checks type check and unit test.

1. Pass 1 starts. The log gets a pass start for T.
2. The unit test is red, and its rerun is red too. The log gets the check end with the gate unit test and the result red.
3. Pass 2 starts and names the cause builder error. The log records the cause on pass 2.
4. A test of the builder loop reads the log and finds two passes, one red with its cause.

```
pipeline log
  pass 1 start  T
  check end     T  unit test  red
  pass 1 end    T  red
  pass 2 start  T  cause of last fail: builder error
```

payload.title: Where the operating system has no supported folder dialog, a project is added by starting werk in its folder
payload.why: The folder dialog that adding a project opens is a macOS dialog, and werk also ships for Linux. Starting werk in a folder already adds that folder to the list, so that path works on every platform with no new mechanism.
payload.body:
Adding a project opens the operating system's folder dialog (see #werk-projects-add). On a machine where werk has no supported dialog, the Add project action does not fail silently. It shows that the dialog is not available, and says that starting werk in the project's folder adds the project (see #werk-projects-one-process). The git check and the offer to initialise a repository apply the same way on that path.

In tests the dialog is an external program, so a fake with a scripted folder path stands in for it, as for every external service (see #werk-test-external).

Example:

- A person runs werk on Linux. The server already runs.

1. The person presses Add project. The menu says the folder dialog is not available here and shows how to add a folder by starting werk in it.
2. The person starts werk in the folder of project P. The running server adds P to the list and opens it in the browser.
3. On macOS, Add project opens the folder dialog as before.

```
Add project
  macOS  -> folder dialog -> folder added
  Linux  -> "no folder dialog here: start werk in the folder"
            werk started in folder P -> running server adds P
```

payload.why: A pass records its steps in the pipeline log that this card defines.

ops.new: One fresh agent per pass. Give it the brief, the decision, the rubric, and the last failure. It does one unit of work and exits. The repository is the memory.

ops.new: This changes the engine's shape: no agent lives longer than one pass.

ops.old: **How a pass works:**
ops.new: **How a pass works:**

ops.old:
1. The loop makes one worktree from a snapshot of the working tree.
2. Pass n starts a fresh `claude -p` in the worktree. The prompt holds the brief, the decided cards in its depends_on closure, and the last failure: the failed command and the end of its output, cut to about 4,000 characters.

payload.title: v0 gives the ticket command list, move, archive and restore, and no import
payload.why: An agent must move a ticket between ready and blocked with a reason and archive one, and the board needs the same operations; import only serves ticket files written before plans were recorded, which v0 never has.
payload.body: The command line in v0 carries four ticket operations: list prints the board, move puts a ticket in blocked or ready and needs a reason, archive keeps the ticket's column and reason, and restore puts an archived ticket back where it was. The board's own controls append the same events. Import is left out, because a v0 project has no ticket files from before the plan recorded its tickets. See #werk-cli-build for the command forms and #werk-cli-ticket-restore for the restore.

payload.title: The server holds a per-project context from its first slice, and the project list adds contexts later
payload.why: Building the server for one project and reshaping it for many later would be one change that crosses every server module; a context per project from the start keeps the later project slice small.
payload.body: The first server slice already keeps the map, and later the conversations, agents and builds, inside one context object per project, with exactly one context open: the project the server starts in. The slice that adds the project list, the switcher and the folder dialog only creates and removes contexts. See #werk-projects-one-process for one server holding every project.

payload.title: A pure file's own test file sits beside it, with .test before the extension
payload.why: The coverage check must find each pure file's own test file without a second list to keep current. A name that follows from the pure file's own name and folder gives exactly one candidate, and a person or an agent who writes a pure file knows where its test goes.
payload.body:
The coverage check counts a line of a pure file only when the file's own test file runs it, and it finds that test file by one fixed convention. The convention: the own test file is in the same folder as the pure file, and its name is the pure file's name with .test put before the extension. A pure file with no file at that place has no own test file, so the check counts it as 0% and names the expected test file.

Example.

- Pure file F: a parser in the server folder, with the name parse.ts.
- Its own test file: parse.test.ts in the same folder.

1. The coverage check reads F from the list of pure files and looks for parse.test.ts beside it.
2. The file exists. The check runs it alone and counts only F's lines.
3. Someone moves the test into a separate test folder. The check finds no file beside F, sets F to 0%, and names parse.test.ts as missing.

```
server folder/
  parse.ts        pure file F, on the list
  parse.test.ts   own test file of F   -> counted
tests/
  parse.test.ts   not beside F         -> not counted, F is 0%
```

payload.why: It names the fixed convention by which that card's check finds a pure file's own test file.

payload.title: A call the command line cannot read exits 2, and a verb that fails with an error exits 1
payload.why: An agent reads the exit code before the output. A code that separates a wrong call from a failed operation tells it whether to fix the command or to look at the map.
payload.body:
The command line reads a call in two steps: it finds the verb by name, then it reads the arguments against the positionals and flags that the verb registered. A call that fails either step never reaches the verb. That covers no verb, an unknown verb, an unknown flag, a missing value, a value on a switch, a missing argument and an extra argument. Each of them exits 2. With no verb or an unknown verb, the command line prints the help. With a wrong argument, it prints the verb and the reason, and points at the help.

A verb that fails with an error exits 1 and prints its verb name and the message. Otherwise the process exits with the code that the verb returns.

Example:

- The verb show takes one card id.

1. werk shw auth: no verb shw. The help prints, and the exit code is 2.
2. werk show: the id is missing. The line 'werk show: show needs <id>' prints, and the exit code is 2.
3. werk show auth, and the log cannot be read: the verb fails. Its message prints, and the exit code is 1.
4. werk show auth, and the card prints: the exit code is 0.

```
call -> find verb --no--> help,   exit 2
             |
           read args --wrong--> reason, exit 2
             |
           run verb --error--> message, exit 1
             |
           exit with the verb's own code
```

payload.why: takes the callback that exits with the verb's code, and adds the codes for a call that never reaches a verb

payload.title: A Markdown link or image renders only for a web, mail or in-app address
payload.why: Card text and agent replies come from many hands, and a link that runs script on click is a way into the page. Escaping stops raw tags, but a Markdown link builds its own tag, so its address needs its own check.
payload.body:
The renderer turns a Markdown link or image into an anchor or an image only when its address starts with http:, https:, mailto:, a slash, a # or a dot. Any other address, such as one that starts with javascript: or data:, leaves the whole Markdown span as the escaped text it was written in. The reader still sees what the writer typed, and nothing on the page can run it.

Example:

- A note holds two links: [docs](https://example.com) and [run](javascript:alert(1)).

1. The note renders [docs](https://example.com). The address starts with https:. It becomes a link labelled docs.
2. The note renders [run](javascript:alert(1)). The address starts with javascript:. It stays as the text [run](javascript:alert(1)).

```
written                        address starts with   renders as
-----------------------------  --------------------  -------------------------
[docs](https://example.com)    https:                link "docs"
[run](javascript:alert(1))     javascript:           text, exactly as written
```

payload.title: Any address becomes a link, after escaping
payload.why_not: Escaping keeps quotes inside the attribute, but a javascript: address still runs script when a reader clicks it.

payload.title: A scripted edit is read from the folder the fake agent was started in
payload.why: A build pass works in a worktree of the target repository, not in the folder of the map. A real agent edits the folder it was started in, so the fake reads each edit path from that folder, and the edit lands where a test of the build looks for it.
payload.body:
To keep an edit where the agent's work is, the fake treats the folder that werk starts it in as the project of the edit. A chat agent starts in the project folder, so its edits land there. A build pass starts in its worktree, so its edits land in the worktree and reach the branch of the pass.

A path that leads outside that folder fails the launch at once with an error that names the path, and the fake writes nothing. A path through a link that points outside the folder fails the same way.

Example:

- P is the temporary project folder. T is a worktree of the target repository.
- The script of the builder role has one edit: "src/a.txt".

1. werk starts the builder in T. The fake writes T/src/a.txt.
2. A script edit "../x.txt" from T fails. The fake exits with an error and writes no file.

```
started in T          edit path      result
------------          ---------      ------
T                     src/a.txt  --> T/src/a.txt written
T                     ../x.txt   --> error, nothing written
```

payload.why: takes the rule that the fake edits files the way a real agent does, inside the build's own repository

payload.title: Each launch of a role plays the next reply that the script holds for that role
payload.why: A build runs many fresh passes of the same role, and a test must give each pass a different reply, for example a red first pass and a green second one. Counting the earlier launches of the role picks the reply without reading the prompt and without depending on the order of other roles.
payload.body:
The script holds a list of replies and an exit code for each role. A role other than chat plays one reply per launch: the first launch of the role plays the first reply, the second launch plays the second, and so on. A chat agent plays its replies in order, one per message, inside one launch.

A launch that finds no reply left for its role, or no entry for its role, exits at once with an error that says how many replies the role has. The fake never repeats or invents a reply.

Example:

- The script of the builder role has two replies: R1 "edit, then fail the checks" and R2 "fix the code".
- The script of the grader role has one reply: G1.

1. Pass 1 starts as builder. The fake plays R1.
2. The grader starts. The fake plays G1. The builder count does not change.
3. Pass 2 starts as builder. The fake plays R2.
4. Pass 3 starts as builder. No reply is left, so the fake exits with an error.

```
launch   role      earlier launches of the role   plays
------   ----      ----------------------------   -----
1        builder   0                              R1
2        grader    0                              G1
3        builder   1                              R2
4        builder   2                              error
```

payload.why: takes the rule that each pass is a fresh agent launch, so one test sees many launches of the builder role
takes the role in the environment as the key that groups the launches
takes the rule that a fake with no answer for a launch fails at once and never invents one

payload.title: Every command that reads the map reports each set-aside log line with its line number
payload.why: A bad line that nobody sees stays in the log forever, and the map quietly misses what it said. Each command already folds the whole log, so it can name each set-aside line at no extra cost, and the agent or the person sees it on the next command they run.
payload.body:
The fold sets aside a log line that breaks a map rule (see #pr-log-refuse). To make that line visible, every command that folds the map prints one warning line for each set-aside line on its error output, before its own result. The warning names the line number in the log, counted from 1, and the rule the line breaks. The command still does its work and exits as it would without the bad line.

Example:

- Line 2 of the log links #root under a card #ghost-town that does not exist.
- Line 3 proposes the card #after under #root.

1. The agent shows #after. The command prints the warning for line 2, then the card.
2. The card #after shows its parent #root, because line 3 still folds.

```
log                                   error output
1 added    #root                      werk: log line 2 set aside: unknown node #ghost-town
2 linked   #root > #ghost-town   ✗
3 proposed #after under #root         standard output
                                      card after [open] proposed ... parent: root
✗ = set aside by the fold
```

payload.title: Each fold time is one line in a file beside the log
payload.why: The kill criterion on the fold needs a history of fold times to check. A local file beside the log keeps that history next to the map it measures, and a failed write of it must never stop a read of the map.
payload.body:
Every read of the map folds the whole log and times the fold (see #pr-log-snapshot). The time goes into a file in the same folder as the log, one line per fold. A line holds when the fold ran, how many log lines it read, how long it took in milliseconds, and the name of the command that read the map. A fold over part of the log is not a read of the map and writes no line. If the line cannot be written, the read still returns the map.

Example:

1. The agent runs a show. The fold of 400 log lines takes 1.2 ms. One line is added: the time, 400 lines, 1.2 ms, show.
2. The agent runs an add. Its fold adds a second line, named add.

```
.werk/
  log.jsonl          the decisions
  fold-times.jsonl   {at, lines: 400, ms: 1.2, via: show}
                     {at, lines: 400, ms: 1.1, via: add}
```

payload.title: A command finds the log in the nearest .werk folder above where it runs
payload.why: An agent runs commands from any folder of the project, not only from its top. If each folder could start its own log, one project would split into several maps without anyone noticing.
payload.body:
