A command looks for a folder named .werk in the folder where it runs, then in each folder above it, and uses the log inside the first one it finds. When no folder above has one, the command uses a new .werk folder where it runs. A setting in the environment can name a different log file, so a test or a build agent can point at a map elsewhere.

Example:

1. The project has /p/.werk/log.jsonl. The agent runs a show in /p/src/map. The command finds /p/.werk and reads that log.
2. The environment names /tmp/other/log.jsonl. The same show reads that file instead.

```
/p/.werk/log.jsonl   <── found
/p/src/              ↑ not here
/p/src/map/          ↑ the command runs here
```

payload.why: takes the .werk folder as the one place that holds a project's map

payload.title: A discard drops the ghost options of each card it drops
payload.why: An option exists only as a choice weighed against one card. When that card leaves, the option points at nothing, and no view can reach it to accept or discard it.
payload.body:
A discard drops a ghost card and its ghost descendants (see #werk-propose-new). Each of those cards can have ghost options linked to it by alternative_to. The discard drops each of them with its card. A real option stays as it is.

Example:

- C "We charge per seat", a ghost card.
- C:opt0 "We charge per account", a ghost option of C.

1. The person discards C. C and C:opt0 leave the map together.
2. If C:opt0 had been accepted before, it would stay.

```
before                          after discard C
C (ghost) <── C:opt0 (ghost)    (gone)
<── alternative_to
```

payload.why: takes the rule that an option belongs to one card through its alternative_to link

payload.title: An accept or a discard writes one event for each node it takes, in one write
payload.why: Each node that becomes real or leaves is its own fact, so a reader of the log sees exactly which nodes one click took. Writing them together keeps the click whole: either every node goes, or none does.
payload.body:
An accept can take several nodes: the ghost parents above the card, and its ghost options and evidence. A discard can take the descendants and the evidence that only they cite. The command writes one accept or discard event for each of these nodes, all in one write, so a failure leaves none of them in the log. The order of the events is the order the map rules need: a parent becomes real before its child, and a child leaves before its parent.

Example:

- M "Seats are the unit", a ghost under the real card R.
- L "We charge per seat", a ghost under M, with the ghost source S.

1. The person accepts L.
2. The log gets three events in one write: M accepted, L accepted, S accepted.

```
before                 log, one write          after
R                      accepted M              R
└ M (ghost)            accepted L              └ M
  └ L (ghost) ─> S     accepted S                └ L ─> S
```

payload.why: takes the write that appends all of its events or none

payload.title: The rule against a cycle applies to the refines tree only
payload.why: A loop of parents never reaches the root, so the tree cannot draw it. A loop of depends_on links does no such harm, because a change marks only the next hop, so two cards that each use the other are allowed.
payload.body:
A write refuses a refines link that would make a card its own ancestor. Two cards may depend on each other: when one changes, the other is marked, and the mark stops there.

Example:

- A "Prices are per seat" and B "Invoices count seats", two cards.

1. The agent links A depends_on B, then B depends_on A. Both links are written.
2. The agent links A refines B, then tries B refines A. The second link is refused as a cycle.

```
A ──depends_on──> B ──depends_on──> A    ✓ allowed
A ──refines────> B ──refines────> A      ✗ cycle
```

payload.why: takes the rule that a change marks only the next hop, so a depends_on loop cannot mark without end

payload.title: The number in `werk ticket restore <number>` is the full ticket id, `<subtree-id>/NN`
payload.why: Each subtree numbers its tickets from 01, so a bare NN can match a ticket in every planned subtree. Only the full id names one ticket, so the restore never has to guess or ask.
payload.body: Form: `werk ticket restore <subtree-id>/NN [--actor you]`, for example `werk ticket restore werk/27`. A leading # is accepted, as for a card id. A bare `27` is not a ticket on the board, so it exits 1 and appends nothing, the same refusal as any number not on the board. `werk ticket move` and `werk ticket archive` take the same full id.

payload.why: It takes the ticket id form <subtree>/NN that the board log uses for every ticket.

payload.title: A board event is named for its record and its action, and a ticket event carries the ticket id
payload.why: The board log holds ticket events and run events in one file. A name that starts with the record it changes lets a reader, such as the fold of the columns, take its own events and pass over the rest without a list of every other event.
payload.body:
Each line has the decision log shape: a sequence number, a time, the actor, a type and a payload. The type is the record, a dot and the action in the past tense: `ticket.planned`, `ticket.moved`, `ticket.archived`, `ticket.restored`. Every ticket event has the ticket id in its payload. A planned event also carries the title and the ids of the tickets it waits for. A moved event carries the target column and, when the mover gives one, the reason. An archive and a restore carry only the id, because the column and the reason stay on the ticket.

Example line: `{"seq":4,"at":"2026-10-25T10:00:00Z","actor":"you","type":"ticket.restored","payload":{"id":"werk/27"}}`

payload.why: It keeps the event shape of the append-only decision log that pr-log defines.

payload.title: A held-out step that runs through a screen no merged ticket has built is not run, not red
payload.why: A step author writes browser steps from the brief, so a step can open a card page or a chat pane that a later ticket builds. Such a step fails on the missing screen, not on the ticket's code, and the follow-up it files asks a builder to build another ticket's work or to change nothing. The step can only say something once the ticket that builds the screen is merged.
payload.body:
To keep a red step pointing at merged code (see #st-heldout-merged-only), a step that needs a screen, a route or a pane that no merged ticket provides ends as not run (see #st-heldout-notrun). It files no follow-up. G2 still waits for it, and the held-out run after each later merge tries it again, so the step goes green or red once the ticket that builds the screen merges.

The ticket's own behaviour is still checked on the main line: its unit tests pin the same paths at the seam the ticket builds, such as the renderer for a ticket that renders card text.

Example:

- Ticket R "Card text renders Markdown with live card links" builds the renderer and is merged.
- Ticket P "A card page shows the card as a hero box" builds the card page and is still blocked.
- Step S of R: "When the person opens the card notes-test in the map, then the body shows four links".

1. R merges. The held-out run binds S. No merged ticket serves a card page, so S ends as not run, with a grey badge on R. No follow-up is filed.
2. P merges. The next held-out run tries S again on the card page that P built.
3. S passes: S is green. Or S fails on the rendered body: S is red, and one follow-up for R is filed.

```
merge:   R            P
S:       not run  ->  green | red -> follow-up for R
                 (no screen)   (screen now on the main line)
```

payload.why: the not-run result, which files no follow-up and keeps G2 waiting, that a step through an unbuilt screen receives

payload.title: Build the missing screens inside the follow-up ticket
payload.why_not: The screens are the scope of other planned tickets that are still blocked on their own dependencies, so the follow-up would build the server, the client and the card page out of order, touch their modules, and collide with those tickets when they build.

payload.title: A ticket moves only along a move that a decided card names, and the fold refuses every other move
payload.why: The board log takes moves from a person, an agent, the builder loop and the merge loop, and each card names only the moves of its own actor. A move that no card names has no owner and no meaning on the board, so refusing it by default keeps the columns true to what the loops do.
payload.body:
To keep a ticket's column a fact that some card explains, the board allows exactly these moves and refuses the rest, both at a write and in the fold:

| From | To | Who makes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| blocked | ready | an agent, when it resolves the reason (#werk-board-control) |
| ready | blocked | an agent or a failed set check, with the reason (#st-ticket-partial) |
| ready | building | a trigger, only with no open blocker (#st-build-parallel) |
| building | merging | a green build (#st-build-ticket-hand-off) |
| building | ready | a stopped loop or a build red at its cap (#st-build-stop-ready) |
| building | blocked | a stuck ticket (#st-build-stuck-park) |
| merging | building | a red check in the merge queue (#werk-board-columns) |
| merging | ready | a stopped loop (#st-build-stop-ready) |
| merging | blocked | a ticket at its conflict limit (#st-build-stuck-park) |
| merging | done | a merge (#werk-board-columns) |

A blocked ticket never moves straight to building, and a done ticket never moves. An archived ticket does not move until it is restored. The command line makes only the agent's moves, from ready or blocked to ready or blocked; the moves into building, merging and done belong to the loops.

Example. Ticket werk/03 "Export writes one file" waits for nothing.

1. A plan puts werk/03 in ready.
2. An agent moves it to blocked, reason "needs a decision". Allowed.
3. A trigger asks for building. Refused: blocked to building is not a move.
4. An agent moves it to ready. Allowed. The trigger moves it to building. Allowed.
5. A move from building to done is refused: a ticket reaches done only from merging.

```
blocked <──> ready ──> building ──> merging ──> done
   ^           ^          │  │  ^      │ │ │
   │           └──────────┘  │  └──────┘ │ │
   ├─────────────────────────┘           │ │
   │           ^─────────────────────────┘ │   (merging -> ready)
   └───────────────────────────────────────┘   (merging -> blocked)
```
Each arrow is one allowed move. A pair of columns with no arrow is refused.

payload.title: Allow only the moves between neighbouring columns, plus the return to ready
payload.why_not: It refuses building to blocked and merging to blocked, which a stuck ticket needs, so the merge loop could not park a stuck ticket as the decided cards say.

payload.title: Allow any move, and let each loop keep to its own moves
payload.why_not: A bug in one loop could then move a ticket to done with no merge, and the fold would show it as merged. Refusing by default makes such a line visible as set aside.

payload.why: It takes the agent's moves between ready and blocked and the rule that only a loop moves into building, merging and done.
It takes the moves from building and merging to blocked for a stuck ticket.
It takes the moves from building and merging back to ready when a loop stops.
It takes the moves through merging to done and the return from merging to building.
It takes the rule that a blocked ticket cannot move to building.
It takes the rule that a ticket starts only when every ticket in its blocked_by list is done.

payload.title: A second planned event for an open ticket rewrites its title and blockers, and keeps its column, reason and archive
payload.why: A plan over the same subtree again rewrites its open tickets under their own ids, so the board log must take a second planned event for an id it already holds. Only the words of the ticket change; where the ticket stands is a fact of the board, and a plan does not move a ticket.
payload.body:
To let a plan extend a subtree (#st-plan-extend) without a second ticket set, a planned event for an id already on the board is a re-plan, with the same event type and payload as the first plan. When the ticket is open, in ready or blocked, the fold replaces its title and its blocked_by list and keeps its column, its reason and its archive state. When the ticket is in building, merging or done, the fold sets the event aside and a write refuses it, because only the loops change such a ticket.

Example. Ticket werk/04 "Import reads orders" is in blocked with the reason "waits for werk/02".

1. A second plan writes werk/04 as "Import reads orders and refunds", waiting for werk/02 and werk/03.
2. The fold shows werk/04 with the new title and both blockers, still in blocked with its old reason.
3. Ticket werk/05 is in merging. A planned event for werk/05 is refused, and werk/05 keeps its title.

```
board.jsonl                               board
3 ticket.planned werk/04 "Import..."     werk/04  blocked  "Import reads orders"
5 ticket.moved   werk/04 -> blocked
9 ticket.planned werk/04 "...refunds"    werk/04  blocked  "Import reads orders and refunds"
9 ticket.planned werk/05  (merging)  ✗   werk/05  merging  (unchanged)
```
The number is the event's sequence number. ✗ = refused.

payload.title: A separate re-planned event type for a rewrite
payload.why_not: It adds a second event with the same payload as planned, so every reader of the board log must handle two names for one fact. The smaller interface reuses planned.

payload.title: Refuse every second planned event for an id
payload.why_not: A plan could not rewrite an open ticket under its own id, which the decided plan extension requires.

payload.why: It takes the rule that a second plan rewrites only the open tickets, in ready or blocked, under their own ids.

payload.title: The board fold reads only the board events whose payload a writer defines, and passes over the rest
payload.why: The board log names many ticket and run events, but most of them have no writer yet, so nothing says what their payload holds or what they change on a ticket. A fold that guesses those payloads makes a data shape that the real writer must then follow or break. Passing over an event until its writer exists keeps the fold true and is easy to extend.
payload.body:
To avoid a guessed data shape, the fold of the board log applies an event only when the change that writes that event also defines its payload and its effect on the board. Every other line of the board log is kept and passed over, so a later fold that knows it reads it from the first event (#pr-log-snapshot).

The first fold reads the events that place a ticket: planned, moved, archived and restored (see #vi-board-state-event-names for their payloads). It gives each ticket its id, title, blocked_by list, column, reason and archive state, in the order the tickets were first planned. Reordered, build started, pass, build ended, merge, steps, held-out result, follow-up and every run event join the fold with the change that first writes them.

Example. The board log holds three lines.

1. ticket.planned werk/01 "Login". The fold puts werk/01 in ready.
2. build.started werk/01, written by a later build loop. The fold passes over it; werk/01 stays in ready.
3. ticket.moved werk/01 to blocked, reason "needs a decision". The fold puts werk/01 in blocked with that reason.

```
board.jsonl                       fold
1 ticket.planned  werk/01  ──>  werk/01 ready
2 build.started   werk/01  ··   (passed over, kept in the log)
3 ticket.moved    werk/01  ──>  werk/01 blocked "needs a decision"
```
──> = applied. ·· = passed over.

payload.title: Fold every named ticket and run event now, with payloads chosen for the fold
payload.why_not: No writer exists for most of those events, so each payload is a guess. A wrong guess either binds the later writer or leaves events in the log that a corrected fold reads differently.

payload.why: It relies on every read replaying the log from the first event, so an event passed over now is read by a later fold.
It folds the planned, moved, archived and restored events whose names and payloads that card gives.

payload.text: werk/45 is the third follow-up for the same five werk/15 paths (after werk/43 and werk/44). The renderer already gives each path the right HTML, and web/md.test.ts pins all five. The steps fail only because no merged ticket serves a card page or a chat pane. Until this card is accepted, the held-out run files the same follow-up again after each merge.

payload.title: `werk ticket list` prints each column's tickets in plan order, the archived tickets last, and every set-aside board log line
payload.why: An agent needs to read the board before it moves a ticket, and a plain text list in the order of the columns reads the same in a terminal and in an agent's context. A board log line that the fold left out must show somewhere, or the board quietly misses what it said.
payload.body:
Form: `werk ticket list`. It takes no ticket and appends nothing.

**Output.** For each column, left to right (blocked, ready, building, merging, done), a heading line with the column name, then one indented line per ticket in that column: the id, the title and, in parentheses, the reason of its last move when it has one. An empty column prints no heading. Archived tickets come last under the heading `archived`, each with the column it left and its reason. An empty board prints `The board has no tickets.`

**Set-aside lines.** Before the board, the error output gets one line for each board log line the fold left out: `werk ticket list: board log line 3 set aside: not valid JSON ...` for a line that is not an event, `werk ticket list: board log event 7 set aside: <rule>` for an event that breaks a move rule. The list still exits 0.

Example:

```
blocked
  werk/03  Export writes one file  (needs a decision)
ready
  werk/02  Import reads orders
archived
  werk/04  Refunds  (from ready)
```

payload.why: It prints the board that the fold gives: each ticket's column, title, reason and archive state, in plan order.
It names each set-aside line with its place in the log, as the fold lists it.

payload.title: Print the board as JSON
payload.why_not: Every other werk command prints plain text for an agent and a person to read, and no reader of the board needs a machine format yet.

payload.title: Until a werk server serves a page, a browser test mounts the renderer's output in a routed page
payload.why: A browser test of rendered card text needs a page to open, but the server, the card page and the chat pane can be unbuilt when the renderer merges. Mounting the renderer's own HTML and style sheet in a page that the test serves itself still checks what only a browser shows: the fonts, the colours, the scroll, the script that must not run and the link that must navigate.
payload.body:
To check rendered text in a real browser before any screen exists, the test intercepts every address at a test-only origin and answers each card address with a page that holds the renderer's HTML for that card and the renderer's style sheet. A card link is then a real navigation to the card's address, and the test reads the address and the card the page holds. A chat message or a tile summary is mounted the same way, in a plain wrapper. No request leaves the browser. Once a werk server serves the card page and the chat pane, the same paths run against that server instead.

Example:

- Card notes-test has the body 'See #al-diff'.
- Card al-diff exists in the map.

1. The test opens the test origin at the address of notes-test. The page holds the rendered body.
2. The test clicks the link #al-diff. The browser goes to the address of al-diff, and the test origin answers with the page of al-diff.
3. The test asks for a card that has no body in the test. The test origin answers 404, and nothing reaches the network.

```
browser --GET /map/notes-test--> test origin --> page(rendered body + style sheet)
   |  click #al-diff
   +----GET /map/al-diff-------> test origin --> page(al-diff)
                                  (unknown id -> 404, no network)
```

payload.why: the rendered card text and links that the mounted page shows and the test checks
no request of the test reaches a real service, so the test origin answers every address itself

payload.title: Build the server and the card page inside the ticket that renders card text
payload.why_not: The server, the card page and the chat pane are the scope of other tickets, so building them here would collide with those tickets and build out of order.

payload.title: A browser test file ends in .e2e.ts, and only the browser runner loads that suffix
payload.why: Two runners share one repository, and each must find only its own files. The unit runner loads every file that ends in .test or .spec, so a browser test named with either suffix would run under the unit runner and crash there. A suffix of its own keeps the two sets apart by name alone, wherever the file sits.
payload.body:
To keep the unit runner and the browser runner apart, a browser test file ends in .e2e.ts, and the browser runner loads only files with that suffix. The unit runner loads only .test and .spec files, so it never sees a browser test, and it needs no list of folders to skip. A unit test file ends in .test.ts, beside the code it tests.

A misnamed file fails loudly, not quietly. A browser test named .spec.ts is loaded by the unit runner, and the browser runner's test function throws there. A unit test placed in the browser folder still runs under the unit runner, because the folder does not matter. The guideline step that chose it: the answer safest when it turns out wrong, then the smallest interface (one suffix, no folder list in the unit runner's settings).

Example:

- File rendered-text.e2e.ts "The rendered card text in a real browser".
- File md.test.ts "The renderer turns a reference into a link".

1. A person runs the unit tests. The unit runner loads md.test.ts and skips rendered-text.e2e.ts.
2. A person runs the browser tests. The browser runner loads rendered-text.e2e.ts and skips md.test.ts.
3. An agent names a browser test page.spec.ts. The unit runner loads it, and the run goes red with an error from the browser runner's test function.

```
              unit runner        browser runner
md.test.ts        runs              skipped
x.e2e.ts          skipped           runs
page.spec.ts      runs -> red       skipped
```

"unit runner" = the in-process test runner. "browser runner" = the runner that drives a real browser.

payload.title: Browser tests keep the .spec.ts suffix, and the unit runner is limited to the server and client folders
payload.why_not: A unit test written outside the listed folders is skipped with no error, so a wrong placement goes unseen. It also adds a folder list to the unit runner's settings that every new top-level folder must update.

payload.title: Browser tests keep the .spec.ts suffix, and the unit test command names the folders it reads
payload.why_not: The same quiet skip of a misplaced unit test, and the folder list moves into the test command, where a coverage run and a plain run can drift apart.

payload.why: takes the browser runner and the browser test files whose names this card sets

payload.title: An archive of a ticket that is already archived is refused and appends nothing
payload.why: An archive keeps the ticket's column and reason so that one restore undoes it. A second archive would add nothing to undo and would make the log say twice what happened once. A refusal mirrors the refusal of a restore on a ticket that is not archived.
payload.body:
To keep one archive for each restore, the board refuses an archive of a ticket that is already archived, both at a write and in the fold, and the log gets no line for it. Only a restore ends an archive (see #st-ticket-restore).

Example. Ticket werk/04 "Refunds" is in blocked with the reason "needs a decision".

1. An agent archives werk/04. Allowed. It stays in blocked, archived.
2. An agent archives werk/04 again. Refused: werk/04 is already archived. The log is unchanged.
3. An agent restores werk/04. Allowed. It is back in blocked with "needs a decision".
4. An agent restores werk/04 again. Refused: werk/04 is not archived.

```
board.jsonl                      werk/04
1 ticket.planned                 ready
2 ticket.moved -> blocked        blocked "needs a decision"
3 ticket.archived                blocked, archived
  ticket.archived  ✗             (no line written)
4 ticket.restored                blocked "needs a decision"
  ticket.restored  ✗             (no line written)
```
The number is the event's sequence number. ✗ = refused.

payload.why: The refusal keeps the one-to-one pairing of archive and restore that the restore event relies on to undo an archive exactly.

payload.title: `werk ticket` exits 2 on a call it cannot read and 1 on a change the board refuses
payload.why: An agent that calls the verb must tell a mistake in its own call from a rule of the board. A wrong call needs a fixed call; a refused change needs a different change. Two exit codes let the agent react without reading the message.
payload.body:
Exit 2, with the usage line on the error output, when the call itself is wrong: an unknown subverb, a missing ticket id, a column on a subverb that takes none, a move to a column other than blocked or ready, a move with no reason or an empty reason, a ticket id given to list, or an actor other than `you` or `agent`. The actor is the agent when the call names none. Exit 2 is the same code the command line gives for any call it cannot read.

Exit 1 when the call is well formed but the board refuses the change: a ticket not on the board, a move that the move rules refuse, an archive or a restore that the board refuses. Exit 0 when the event is appended. Every refusal, exit 1 or 2, appends nothing.

Example, on a board where werk/03 is in ready:

1. `werk ticket move werk/03 blocked` exits 2: no reason.
2. `werk ticket move werk/03 done --reason x` exits 2: an agent moves only to blocked or ready.
3. `werk ticket restore werk/03` exits 1: werk/03 is not archived.
4. `werk ticket move werk/03 blocked --reason "needs a decision"` exits 0 and appends one event.

payload.why: The exit 1 for a refused restore, and the actor that defaults to the agent, come from the restore verb's form.
The moves that exit 1 are the ones the move rules refuse.

payload.title: A move, archive or restore that `werk ticket` appends prints one line with the ticket's column after it
payload.why: An agent that changes the board needs to see where the ticket stands now, without a second call to list the board. One short line with the column is enough to confirm the change and costs little context.
payload.body:
After the event is appended, the verb prints one line on the standard output, read from the board as it stands after the change. A move and a restore print `<id> is in <column>`. An archive prints `<id> archived from <column>`, the column the ticket keeps while it is archived. A refused call prints nothing on the standard output (see #werk-cli-build-ticket-exits).

Example, with werk/04 in blocked:

1. `werk ticket archive werk/04` prints `werk/04 archived from blocked`.
2. `werk ticket restore werk/04` prints `werk/04 is in blocked`.
3. `werk ticket move werk/04 ready --reason "decided"` prints `werk/04 is in ready`.

payload.why: The line after an archive names the column the ticket keeps, which the restore puts it back in.
A refused call prints no line because the exit code alone reports the refusal.

payload.title: `werk kill <id>` records one kill criterion, and one flag names its form
payload.why: A criterion takes one of four forms, and each form needs different words. One flag per form lets the command refuse a call that names no form, two forms, or a form without its words.
payload.body:
```
werk kill <id> --metric "<metric>" --source "<source>" --threshold "<threshold>" --window "<window>"
werk kill <id> --manual "<the test the author runs>"
werk kill <id> --no-metric "<the reason no metric applies>"
werk kill <id> --revisit
```

One call adds one criterion to the card, open, decided or proposed (#kill-shape). A metric needs all four of its words. A manual test and a no-metric reason need their text, and an empty text is refused. Revisit at any time needs no words. A call with no form, or with two forms, is refused and names the four forms.

The printed card lists every criterion in the order it was recorded, one line each.

payload.why: the four forms of a criterion, and the words each form needs
a criterion is recorded on an open card before the decide, one call per criterion

payload.title: A removal event names only the card, and the fold works out what the removal takes
payload.why: Every read replays the log from the first event, so the map just before a removal is the same on every read. The set of nodes that the removal takes is then the same on every read too, and the event does not need to list it. The fold keeps that set with the removal, so the restore brings back exactly the same nodes.
payload.body:
To keep a removal one short event, the event holds the id of the card it names, and a flag when the children move up instead. The fold works out the rest at that point of the log: the refines subtree, the options and excerpts, the sources that only those cards cite, and the children that move up. The fold keeps that set with the removal. The restore that names the card brings back exactly that set, whatever changed in the map between the two events.

Example:

- Card `auth` "Login is by magic link", with the children `auth-mail` and `auth-expiry`.
- Option `auth:opt0` "Passwords" is an alternative to `auth`.

1. A person removes `auth`. The log gets one line, and the line names `auth` only.
2. The fold reads the line and takes `auth`, `auth-mail`, `auth-expiry` and `auth:opt0` out of the map.
3. A person restores `auth`. The log gets one line that names `auth` only. The fold brings back the same four nodes.
4. A person restores `auth-mail`. No removal names `auth-mail`, so the restore refuses and the log gets no line.

```
log line          the fold
removed  auth     out: auth, auth-mail, auth-expiry, auth:opt0
restored auth     in:  auth, auth-mail, auth-expiry, auth:opt0
```

payload.title: The removal event lists every node that it takes
payload.why_not: The line repeats what the fold works out by itself, and a hand-edited list can disagree with the map. The restore must then choose between the list and the map.

payload.why: The fold replays the whole log on every read, so the set that a removal takes is the same on every read.

payload.title: `werk ticket` writes the board with move, archive and restore, and a listing of the board waits for a reader that needs it
payload.why: The board log needs a command an agent can use for each change it makes to a ticket: a move with its reason, an archive, and the restore that undoes an archive. A printed listing of the board changes nothing on it, and no rule of the board log needs one yet, so it adds a command and an output format that nothing depends on.
payload.body:
To keep the command line of the board as small as the board log needs, `werk ticket` has three subverbs that each append one event: `move <id> blocked|ready --reason "..."`, `archive <id>` and `restore <id>`, each with `[--actor you]`. A listing of the board, `werk ticket list`, joins the command line with the change whose reader first needs to read the board as text; until then an agent reads where a ticket stands from the one line each write prints (see #werk-cli-build-ticket-done-line).

A call to `werk ticket list` is an unknown subverb: it exits 2 with the usage line and appends nothing (see #werk-cli-build-ticket-exits).

The guideline chose it by the smallest interface: the move, archive and restore are the writes the board refuses or accepts, and a listing is a read that no rule asks for.

payload.title: Build every subverb of the `werk ticket` form at once, the listing included
payload.why_not: It adds a listing and its output format that no rule of the board log needs yet, and a later reader may need a different shape.

payload.title: Build only `werk ticket restore`, and keep move and archive as rules of the fold
payload.why_not: An agent then cannot move a ticket with a reason or archive one, so the refusal of a move without a reason has no command to refuse, and no archive exists for a restore to undo.

payload.why: The restore subverb is the restore verb that this card defines.
The move and archive subverbs make the agent moves and the archive that this card allows.
An unknown subverb, such as the listing, exits 2 under the exit rules of this card.

payload.title: A ticket event names its payload fields id, title, blocked_by, to and reason
payload.why: A writer and the fold of the board log must agree on the names inside each payload, or a line that one writes the other cannot read. Short names that say what a field holds keep each line readable in the log file.
payload.body:
Every ticket event names its ticket in `id`. A planned event carries `title` and `blocked_by`, the list of ticket ids it waits for. A moved event carries `to`, the column the ticket moves to, and `reason` when the mover gives one; the column it leaves is not written, because the fold already knows it. An archived and a restored event carry only `id`.

Example: `{"seq":5,"at":"2026-10-25T10:00:00Z","actor":"agent","type":"ticket.moved","payload":{"id":"werk/03","to":"blocked","reason":"needs a decision"}}`

payload.why: The payload sits in the event shape of the append-only log that this card defines.

payload.title: A block of a body is a paragraph between blank lines, and a fenced code block is one block
payload.why: The cover rule and the quote check compare an op's old text with the blocks of the body, so both need one fixed way to cut a body into blocks. Blank lines are where Markdown already separates paragraphs, lists and headings. A blank line inside a code fence is part of the code, so it does not cut.
payload.body:
To give every op one unit to quote, the body splits at each run of blank lines, outside a code fence. Each block is compared with an old text after the spaces and line breaks at its two ends are trimmed. Two equal blocks are two blocks: each needs its own op.

Example. A body has three parts:
- P, the paragraph "We charge per seat."
- L, a list of two lines, "- monthly" and "- yearly", with no blank line between them.
- F, a code fence that holds one blank line.

What happens:
1. The body cuts into three blocks: P, L and F.
2. L is one block, because no blank line separates its two lines.
3. F is one block, because its blank line is inside the fence.
4. An op list that names P and L but not F is refused, and the refusal prints F.

```
 We charge per seat.        block 1  (P)
                            <- blank line: cut
 - monthly                  block 2  (L)
 - yearly
                            <- blank line: cut
 ```sh                      block 3  (F)
 werk show x
                            <- blank line inside the fence: no cut
 werk accept x
 ```
```

payload.why: A block is the unit that the three tags mark, as the diff look gives it

payload.title: A removal names a card, ghost or real, and never an option, a source or an excerpt
payload.why: An option, a source and an excerpt sit beside a card and leave the map with it, so a removal of one of them alone would leave its card with a hole that no restore of the card can fill. A proposed card is in the map as a ghost, and a ghost can sit under a real card, so a removal of the real card takes the ghost too. A removal that names a ghost is then the same operation, and it keeps the ghost restorable where a discard drops it.
payload.body:
To keep every removal undoable by the restore of one card, the card that a removal names must be of kind card. The removal of an option, a source or an excerpt refuses and says that it goes with its card. The card can be real or a ghost.

A discard and a removal of a ghost differ in what comes after. A discard ends the proposal: the ghost leaves the map and no restore brings it back. A removal hides the ghost: a restore brings it back as a ghost, still waiting for its accept.

Example:

- Card `auth` "Login is by magic link" is real.
- Option `auth:opt0` "Passwords" is an alternative to `auth`.
- Card `auth-mail` "The link expires after one use" is a ghost under `auth`.

1. A person removes `auth:opt0`. The removal refuses, because an option goes with its card. The log gets no line.
2. A person removes `auth-mail`. The ghost leaves the map.
3. A person restores `auth-mail`. The ghost is back under `auth`, still proposed.
4. A person discards `auth-mail`. The ghost leaves the map, and no restore names it.

```
step  named        result
1     auth:opt0    refused (an option goes with its card)
2     auth-mail    out (ghost, restorable)
3     auth-mail    in  (ghost, proposed)
4     auth-mail    discarded (no restore)
```

payload.why: It takes the ghost: a proposed card sits in the map, and a discard drops it for good.
It takes the rule that options, sources and excerpts are nodes beside a card, not cards.

payload.title: A reparent of a card with children needs a parent, and a reparent of a card with no children is a plain removal
payload.why: A reparent moves the children up to the parent of the removed card. A card with no parent has nowhere to send them, and a removal that left them with no parent would break the rule that every real card has a chain of parents up to the root. A card with no children has nothing to move, so the reparent changes nothing and the removal is the same as one without it.
payload.body:
To keep every real card under a chain of real parents, a reparent of a card that has children and no parent refuses, and the log gets no line. The person then removes the card with its subtree, or first places the children under another card.

A reparent of a card with no children is accepted. It takes the card, its options and its excerpts, as a removal without reparent does, and it records no move. Its restore then puts nothing back under the card.

Example:

- Card `root` "We build software with agents" has no parent and has the child `stages`.
- Card `auth` "Login is by magic link" sits under `root` and has no children.

1. A person removes `root` and moves its children up. The removal refuses, because `root` has no parent. The log gets no line.
2. A person removes `auth` and moves its children up. `auth` leaves the map. No child moves.
3. A person restores `auth`. `auth` is back under `root`.

```
step  removal              children   result
1     root, move up        stages     refused (no parent)
2     auth, move up        none       out, no move
3     restore auth         none       in
```

payload.why: It takes the rule that every real card has a chain of real parents up to the root, which a parentless reparent would break.
It takes the moved children that a restore puts back, which is empty when nothing moved.

payload.title: `werk remove`, `werk restore` and `werk removed` take a card out, bring it back, and list what is out
payload.why: Three verbs give the person, and an agent the person asked, the removal, its restore and the list of what is out. Each refusal leaves the log unchanged, so a wrong call costs nothing.
payload.body:
Form: `werk remove <id> [--reparent] --actor you`, `werk restore <id> --actor you`, `werk removed`

**remove.** It appends one removal event that names the card (see #werk-remove-restore-undo-event-names-card). `--reparent` moves the direct children up to the card's parent and takes only the card. It prints `<id>: removed`, then one line `  and <id>  <title>` for each other node that left, then one line `  moved <child>  <title>  up to <parent>` for each child that moved.

**restore.** It appends one restore event that names the card a removal named. It prints `<id>: restored`, the same `and` lines, and one line `  moved <child>  <title>  back under <id>` for each child that goes back.

**removed.** It prints the lines of each removal in the log order, as `remove` printed them, or `no card is removed` when nothing is out.

**Actor.** `remove` and `restore` refuse without `--actor you`, exit 1 and append nothing. The flag states that the person asked for the call; the ✕ in the map is the normal path.

**Refusal.** A call that breaks a removal rule prints the rule, exits 1 and appends nothing: a node that is not a card, a reparent with no parent, a restore of a card that no removal names, or a restore under a parent that is still out.

payload.why: The verbs carry the removal, the reparent and the list of what is out that this card defines.
restore carries the inverse of one removal that this card defines.
remove refuses a node that this card says a removal cannot name.
remove --reparent refuses a parentless card as this card says.

payload.title: A removal and its restore are two event types of their own, `node.removed` and `node.restored`
payload.why: The log is read by the fold and by a person, and a removal and a restore mean opposite things. When each meaning has its own event type, the fold keeps one branch per meaning and a reader sees the fact in the type alone. A flag on another event would hide a removal inside an event that reads as something else.
payload.body:
To keep one branch of the fold per meaning, a removal is the event type `node.removed` and a restore is the event type `node.restored`. The removal carries the id of the card it names, and a flag `reparent` only when the children move up. The restore carries the id of the card that a removal named, and nothing else. What each event takes and brings back is worked out by the fold (see #werk-remove-restore-undo-event-names-card).

The names follow the pattern of the other node events in the log: `node.` then a past-tense verb. The guideline step that chose it is the smallest interface: two events with one id each, and one optional flag.

Example:

- Card `auth` "Login is by magic link", with the child `auth-mail".
- Card `root` is the parent of `auth`.

1. A person removes `auth` and moves its children up. The log gets one line: type `node.removed`, id `auth`, reparent true.
2. A person restores `auth`. The log gets one line: type `node.restored`, id `auth`.
3. A person removes `auth` again, without the move. The log gets one line: type `node.removed`, id `auth`, and no flag.

```
step  type           payload
1     node.removed   id auth, reparent true
2     node.restored  id auth
3     node.removed   id auth
```

payload.title: A removal is a status on the card, set by the existing status event
payload.why_not: A status event already means a move through open, decided and reopened. A removal in it would give one event type two meanings, and the restore would need the earlier status kept somewhere to undo it.

payload.title: One event type for both, with a direction field that says out or in
payload.why_not: One type with two meanings needs a second test in the fold and in every reader of the log. Two types with one id each give the smaller interface.

payload.why: takes what a removal event holds: the id of the card and the reparent flag, and nothing more
takes the rule that each meaning in the log gets its own event type, so the fold keeps one branch per meaning

payload.title: A removal and its restore are two event types of their own, `node.removed` and `node.restored`
payload.why: The log is read by the fold and by a person, and a removal and a restore mean opposite things. When each meaning has its own event type, the fold keeps one branch per meaning and a reader sees the fact in the type alone. A flag on another event would hide a removal inside an event that reads as something else.
payload.body:
To keep one branch of the fold per meaning, a removal is the event type `node.removed` and a restore is the event type `node.restored`. The removal carries the id of the card it names, and a flag `reparent` only when the children move up. The restore carries the id of the card that a removal named, and nothing else. What each event takes and brings back is worked out by the fold (see #werk-remove-restore-undo-event-names-card).

The names follow the pattern of the other node events in the log: `node.` then a past-tense verb. The guideline step that chose it is the smallest interface: two events with one id each, and one optional flag.

Example:

- Card `auth` "Login is by magic link", with the child `auth-mail`.
- Card `root` is the parent of `auth`.

1. A person removes `auth` and moves its children up. The log gets one line: type `node.removed`, id `auth`, reparent true.
2. A person restores `auth`. The log gets one line: type `node.restored`, id `auth`.
3. A person removes `auth` again, without the move. The log gets one line: type `node.removed`, id `auth`, and no flag.

```
step  type           payload
1     node.removed   id auth, reparent true
2     node.restored  id auth
3     node.removed   id auth
```

payload.title: A removal is a status on the card, set by the existing status event
payload.why_not: A status event already means a move through open, decided and reopened. A removal in it would give one event type two meanings, and the restore would need the earlier status kept somewhere to undo it.

payload.title: One event type for both, with a direction field that says out or in
payload.why_not: One type with two meanings needs a second test in the fold and in every reader of the log. Two types with one id each give the smaller interface.

payload.why: takes what a removal event holds: the id of the card and the reparent flag, and nothing more
takes the rule that each meaning in the log gets its own event type, so the fold keeps one branch per meaning

payload.title: The fold keeps removed nodes, each removal's record and the waiting links apart from the live map
payload.why: Every view, rollup and stale mark reads the live nodes and the live links. If a removed card stays among them with a flag, each of those reads must skip it, and one read that forgets leaks a removed card into the map. Kept apart, a removed card is outside every derivation by default, and a restore only moves it back.
payload.body:
To keep a removed card in no view, no rollup and no stale mark by default, the fold holds three things beside the live nodes and the live links. `removed` holds each node that is out, under its id, with all of its fields as they were. `removals` holds one record for each removal still in force, under the id of the card it named. The record lists every node the removal took, the named card first, and, for a reparent, the children that moved up and the parent they moved to. `waiting` holds each link with an end out (see #werk-write-remove-links).

A node is in exactly one of the live nodes and `removed`. A link is in exactly one of the live links, the links with a ghost end, and `waiting`. A restore reads the record of its removal, moves each taken node back, puts each moved child back under the card, and drops the record. Then every waiting link with both ends in goes live again. A node with a removed id still counts as taken for an add.

The guideline steps that chose it are deny by default and the least privilege: a read that knows nothing of removals sees none of them.

Example:

- Card `login` depends_on card `session`.
- Card `session` has the child `session-ttl`.

1. A person removes `session`. `session` and `session-ttl` move into `removed`. `removals` gets one record under `session` that lists both. The link `login -> session` moves into `waiting`.
2. The map view and the rollup read the live nodes. They see `login` only.
3. A person restores `session`. Both nodes move back, the record leaves `removals`, and the link goes live.

```
step  live nodes                    removed               waiting
0     login, session, session-ttl   -                     -
1     login                         session, session-ttl  login -> session
3     login, session, session-ttl   -                     -
```

payload.title: A removed node stays among the live nodes with a removed flag
payload.why_not: Every view, rollup, stale mark and link read must then test the flag. A read that forgets it shows a removed card, which is the unsafe failure. Kept apart, a forgotten test cannot happen.

payload.title: A restore works out again from the log what its removal took
payload.why_not: The map changes between the removal and the restore, so the set worked out at the restore can differ from the set that went out. A record kept at the removal gives back exactly what left.

payload.why: takes the rule that a link with an end out waits and comes back when both ends are in, and that a removed id stays taken
takes the rule that the fold works out the set a removal takes and keeps it with the removal
takes the pattern of a held link list beside the live links, which the fold already uses for ghost ends

payload.title: An inbox note written before its id was proposed again says it was about earlier words
payload.why: The inbox prints each note under the title the id has now. A note written before a discard and a new proposal was about the earlier words, so under the new title it reads as a comment on words it never saw. A label on that note tells the reader to read it against the earlier words.
payload.body:
To avoid a note that reads as if it were about the new words, the inbox labels each note that the thread places above a "proposed again" marker. The inbox has no markers of its own, so the label carries the same fact on the note's own line.

Example:

- X is a ghost card, "Export is its own command".
- N1 is a note the person typed on X: "Say what the export writes."

1. The person writes N1 on X. The inbox prints N1 under "Export is its own command", with no label.
2. The agent discards X and proposes X again as "Export writes every order as one file". The inbox prints N1 under the new title, with the label "on earlier words, proposed again since".
3. The person writes N2 on the new X. The inbox prints N2 with no label.
4. A note on an id that was never proposed again gets no label.

```
inbox line                                           label
[N1] #X  Export writes every order as one file       (on earlier words, proposed again since)
[N2] #X  Export writes every order as one file       -

N1, N2 = log positions of the two notes
-      = no label: the note is about the words shown
```

payload.why: takes the inbox, which prints the notes typed in the map under their card

payload.title: A new change that names a removed node refuses and names the restore
payload.why: A link or an edit made while a node is out would change a card that no view shows, so nobody sees the change before it takes effect. A restore must give back the map as it was at the removal, and a change made in between breaks that. A refusal that names the restore keeps the way back in one step.
payload.body:
To keep a restore exact, every new write that names a node that is out of the map refuses, and the log gets no line. That covers a new link to or from the node, an add under it as the parent, a change to its words or its who field, a kill criterion, a move to decided, and an accept or a discard. The refusal names the card whose restore brings the node back. A link that existed before the removal waits, as #werk-write-remove-links says; only a new one refuses.

Example:

- Card `auth` "Login is by magic link" has the child `auth-mail` "The link is sent by mail".
- Card `billing` "We charge per seat" is in the map.

1. A person removes `auth`. Both cards leave the map.
2. An agent links `billing` depends_on `auth-mail`. The link refuses: `auth-mail` is removed with `auth`, restore `auth` first.
3. An agent adds a card under `auth`. The add refuses and names the restore of `auth`.
4. A person restores `auth`. The same link now succeeds.

```
step  write                          result
2     link billing -> auth-mail      refused (restore auth first)
3     add card under auth            refused (restore auth first)
4     link billing -> auth-mail      in
```

payload.title: A new change that names a removed node waits until the restore
payload.why_not: The change would take effect on a card nobody can see, and the restore would then bring back a card that differs from the one that left. A wrong id also gives no error, because every write to an unknown-looking id could be a wait.

payload.why: takes the rule that a restore gives back exactly what the removal took, which a change made while the node is out would break

payload.title: The printed card shows a pending change as one inline diff, with removed text in [- -] and added text in {+ +}
payload.why: An agent and a terminal have no blue highlight, so the printed card needs plain-text marks for a change. Marks inside the text keep the change one diff that reads in one pass, and not an old copy beside a new copy.
payload.body:
To show a staged change in plain text, the printed card keeps its current words and adds a pending-change section below them. The title and the why each print on one line: the old text in [- -], then the new text in {+ +}. The body prints block by block in the order of the ops. A kept block prints plain, a reworded block prints its old text in [- -] followed by its new text in {+ +}, a new block prints in {+ +}, and a removed block prints in [- -]. A removed block whose old text is not a block of the body carries the note "(not a block of the body)", so a quote that the body does not hold is never read as a real removal.

Example. A card has the title "We charge per seat" and two blocks, A "Seats are counted monthly." and B "Invoices go out on the 1st.". A proposal sets the title to "We charge per active seat", keeps A, and rewords B to "Invoices go out on the 5th.".

1. The header of the printed card says it has a pending change.
2. The title, the why and the body print as they are now.
3. The pending-change section prints the title line and the body, as in the picture.
4. After an accept or a discard, the section is gone.

```
pending change:
  title: [-We charge per seat-]{+We charge per active seat+}
  body:
    Seats are counted monthly.                                          <- A, kept

    [-Invoices go out on the 1st.-]{+Invoices go out on the 5th.+}      <- B, reworded
```

payload.why: The printed change is one diff with marks inside the text, never a before and an after, as this card requires.
The printed marks stand in for the highlight and the strikethrough this card gives the map, block by block in the same way.

payload.title: Each conversation has its own chat log file beside the decision log, with one JSON line per message
payload.why: The quote must find a conversation's messages from its name alone, and must skip every line that nobody said. One file per conversation, named after the conversation, gives the first. A kind on every line gives the second, so the quote never has to guess what a line is.
payload.body:
To let the quote read one conversation without a search, the chat log of conversation N is the file chats/N.jsonl in the folder that holds the decision log. A conversation name is letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores, and does not start with a dot, so a name never points outside that folder.

Each line of the file is one JSON object for one message. It holds the speaker (person or agent), the time the message was written, the session id of the agent session, the kind of the line, and the text. The kind is one of four values: spoken for text that the person typed or the agent wrote, tool_call, tool_result, and tooling for text that the tooling adds. Only a spoken line can hold a quote. A line that is not valid JSON, or has an unknown kind, still counts for the message position, and never holds a quote.

Example:

- Conversation "pricing" has the file chats/pricing.jsonl.
- Line 0 is spoken by the person: "do we bill per seat?"
- Line 1 is a tool_result that prints "seats are the unit we bill".
- Line 2 is spoken by the agent: "seats are the unit we bill".

1. The agent quotes "seats are the unit we bill" from pricing. The quote opens chats/pricing.jsonl.
2. Line 1 holds the words, but its kind is tool_result. It does not count.
3. Line 2 holds the words and is spoken. The excerpt points at message 2.
4. The agent quotes from a conversation "../x". The quote refuses the name and reads no file.

```
.werk/log.jsonl              the decision log
.werk/chats/pricing.jsonl    the chat log of "pricing"
  0  person  spoken       "do we bill per seat?"
  1  agent   tool_result  "seats are the unit we bill"   <- never a match
  2  agent   spoken       "seats are the unit we bill"   <- message 2

0, 1, 2: the message position, counted over every line
```

payload.why: takes the parts of a pointer and the rule that only a spoken message holds a quote, which each line of the chat log must record

payload.title: The build-rule title list holds only decided cards
payload.why: An open or proposed card under the build-rules card is not yet a rule that anyone agreed to. If its title reached every stage agent, the agents would follow a rule the person may still reject. A decided card further down still counts, because its own decision holds.
payload.body:
To keep agents from following a rule nobody has agreed to, the title list that a stage agent starts with holds only the decided cards under the build-rules card. A proposed card and an open card stay out. A decided card below an open one stays in, one level up in the list, because the list follows the decided cards only. Options and sources are not rules and never appear.

Example:
- Build rule B "Tests run against a real database", decided
- Build rule D "Use one log per service", open, under the build-rules card
- Build rule E "Each log line is JSON", decided, under D

1. A builder pass starts. Its prompt lists B and E.
2. D stays out, because it is open.
3. The person decides D. The next pass lists B, D and E, with E under D.
4. With no decided card under the build-rules card, the prompt holds no list.

```
build-rules card            title list in the prompt
  B  decided   ----------->  - B
  D  open      (left out)    - E
    E decided  ----------->
```

payload.why: takes the statuses a card moves through, and that a proposed or open card is not yet agreed

payload.title: A quote writes one log event of its own type, which holds the excerpt, its pointer and the citing card
payload.why: A plain add of an excerpt refuses, and an add carries no supported_by link. So the quote needs an event that only it writes, and that holds the excerpt and its link together. A separate event type also lets the map rules check the pointer of every excerpt in one place.
payload.body:
To keep the excerpt and its link one change, the quote writes one event of type excerpt.quoted to the decision log. Its payload holds the excerpt id, the quoted words as the excerpt's title, the id of the citing card, and the pointer (see #werk-excerpt-pointer). The fields are card, conversation, session, message, start, end, speaker and said_at. The time field is said_at, not at, because at on a log event is the time the event was written, and the excerpt keeps the time the message was said.

The excerpt id is the citing card's id with :ex and the first free number, as in X:ex0, then X:ex1.

Example:

- Card X "We charge per seat" is decided.
- Message 2 of conversation pricing, spoken by the agent at 10:02, is "seats are the unit we bill".

1. The agent quotes "seats are the unit we bill" from pricing for X.
2. The log gets one excerpt.quoted event with id X:ex0, title "seats are the unit we bill", card X, conversation pricing, message 2, start 0, end 26, speaker agent, said_at 10:02.
3. The fold makes ghost X:ex0 and the held supported_by link from X in the same step.
4. A second quote for X gets the id X:ex1.

```
log line   type excerpt.quoted
           id X:ex0  title "seats are the unit we bill"  card X
           conversation pricing  message 2  start 0  end 26
           speaker agent  said_at 10:02
fold       X ··held supported_by··> X:ex0 (ghost)
```

payload.why: takes the parts of the pointer that the event carries

payload.title: The quote writes a proposed node event and a link event
payload.why_not: Two events can be half written, which leaves an excerpt that supports no card, and the plain add of an excerpt must refuse.

payload.title: A chat log line names its parts speaker, at, session, kind and text
payload.why: The chat pane writes the chat log and the quote reads it, so both must use the same field names. A short fixed name for each part lets a reader cut a quote out of a line without a guess. A missing or non-text field reads as empty text, so one damaged line never stops a quote.
payload.body:
Each line of a chat log is one JSON object with five fields: speaker (person or agent), at (the time the message was written), session (the id of the agent session), kind (spoken, tool_call, tool_result or tooling), and text. A field that is missing, or is not text, reads as empty text. The line still counts for the message position (see #werk-excerpt-chatlog).

Example:

1. The line {"speaker":"agent","at":"10:02","session":"6ae61be7","kind":"spoken","text":"seats are the unit we bill"} is a spoken message that a quote can match.
2. The line {"speaker":"agent","kind":"spoken","text":"we bill per seat"} has no at and no session. A quote of it still matches, and the excerpt keeps an empty time and an empty session.
3. The line {"kind":"spoken","text":42} has no text. It counts for the position and never matches.

```
speaker   at      session    kind     text
agent     10:02   6ae61be7   spoken   "seats are the unit we bill"   <- can match
agent     ""      ""         spoken   "we bill per seat"             <- can match, empty time and session
""        ""      ""         spoken   ""                             <- counts, never matches
```

payload.why: takes the parts of a pointer that each line must record: speaker, time, session

payload.title: A chat log line names its parts speaker, at, session, kind and text
payload.why: The chat pane writes the chat log and the quote reads it, so both must use the same field names. A short fixed name for each part lets a reader cut a quote out of a line without a guess. A damaged line still counts for the position, but it cannot give an excerpt with a broken pointer.
payload.body:
Each line of a chat log is one JSON object with five fields: speaker (person or agent), at (the time the message was written), session (the id of the agent session), kind (spoken, tool_call, tool_result or tooling), and text. A field that is missing, or is not text, reads as empty text, and the line still counts for the message position (see #werk-excerpt-chatlog).

A pointer needs its speaker, time and session (see #werk-excerpt-pointer). So when the one match of a quote is in a spoken line with an empty speaker, at or session, the quote refuses, names the missing part, and writes nothing.

Example:

1. The line {"speaker":"agent","at":"10:02","session":"6ae61be7","kind":"spoken","text":"seats are the unit we bill"} is a spoken message. A quote of it gives an excerpt.
2. The line {"speaker":"agent","kind":"spoken","text":"we bill per seat"} has no at and no session. A quote of it refuses: the pointer needs its session.
3. The line {"kind":"spoken","text":42} has no text. It counts for the position and never matches.

```
speaker   at      session    kind     text
agent     10:02   6ae61be7   spoken   "seats are the unit we bill"   <- excerpt
agent     ""      ""         spoken   "we bill per seat"             <- refused: no session
""        ""      ""         spoken   ""                             <- counts, never matches
```

payload.why: takes the parts of a pointer that each line must record: speaker, time, session

payload.title: Two occurrences of a quote that overlap count as two
payload.why: An occurrence is a place where the quoted text starts. Two places that share characters are still two places, and the citer did not say which one to take. If an overlap counted once, the program would pick the first place, which is a guess.
payload.body:
To count occurrences without a guess, the quote counts every character position where the quoted text starts in a spoken message, also when two of those occurrences share characters.

Example:

- Message 4 is spoken: "aaa".

1. The citer quotes "aa". It starts at position 0 and at position 1. The quote fails and names 2 matches in message 4.
2. The citer quotes "aaa". It starts only at position 0. The excerpt points at message 4, span 0 to 3.

```
message 4   a a a
            0 1 2       character positions

"aa"    starts at 0 and at 1   -> fails: 2 matches in message 4
"aaa"   starts at 0            -> excerpt, span 0-3
```

payload.why: takes the span as a start and end character in one message, which defines an occurrence by its start

payload.title: Count only occurrences that do not overlap, from left to right
payload.why_not: The count then says one where the text starts at two places, and the excerpt points at the first of them, which the citer did not choose.

payload.title: The map refuses an excerpt whose span is not as long as its words
payload.why: The span and the words of an excerpt describe the same characters. If their lengths differ, a reader who cuts the chat log at the span finds other words than the excerpt shows. The map refuses that excerpt, so a pointer and its words always agree.
payload.body:
To keep the pointer and the kept words the same text, the map refuses an excerpt when the end of its span minus the start is not the number of characters of its words. The message, start and end must also be whole numbers from zero. The quote always writes a span that passes, so the check stops only a damaged or hand-made log line.

Example:

- Excerpt X:ex0 holds the words "seats are the unit we bill", 26 characters.

1. A log line gives X:ex0 the span 0 to 26. The map takes it.
2. A log line gives X:ex0 the span 0 to 20. The map refuses it, and X:ex0 does not appear.

```
words "seats are the unit we bill"   26 characters
span 0-26   26 = 26   -> excerpt
span 0-20   20 ≠ 26   -> refused
```

payload.why: takes the span as the start and end character of the quoted words in one message

payload.title: `werk quote <card> <conversation> "text"` takes the words as an argument or with --text, and prints the excerpt id and its pointer
payload.why: An agent that quotes must know how to pass the words and what the command answers. The words may be written as the last argument or with a --text flag, so either habit works, but never both at once, so the command never has to choose. The answer names the new excerpt and where it points, so the agent can cite it without a second read.
payload.body:
Form:

```
werk quote <card-id> <conversation> "the words"
werk quote <card-id> <conversation> --text "the words"
```

The card id may carry a leading hash sign. The conversation is the name of its chat log (see #werk-excerpt-chatlog); a session id or a card id does not resolve a conversation here. Exactly one of the two forms of the words is given: with neither, the command refuses with "needs the text to quote"; with both, it refuses with "give the text once, as an argument or with --text". The write is made as the agent, like every other write an agent makes.

On success the command prints one line and exits 0. On a refusal it prints the reason on the error stream, writes nothing and exits 1.

Example:

- Card X "We charge per seat" exists.
- Message 2 of conversation pricing is "the seat is the unit; seats are the unit we bill".

1. The agent runs werk quote X pricing "seats are the unit we bill". It prints: X:ex0: proposed, supports X: conversation pricing, message 2, span 22..48
2. The agent runs werk quote X pricing --text "per seat". The same rules apply, and a match gives X:ex1.
3. The agent runs werk quote X pricing "per seat" --text "per seat". It refuses, and nothing is written.

```
werk quote X pricing "seats are the unit we bill"
  -> X:ex0: proposed, supports X: conversation pricing, message 2, span 22..48
       X:ex0  the excerpt id     2  the message position     22..48  the span
werk quote X pricing "a" --text "a"   -> refused, exit 1, nothing written
```

Both forms are kept because the safest choice, when a caller uses either habit, is that the call works; a call with both refuses by default.

payload.title: Take the words only with --text
payload.why_not: A caller that writes the words as the last argument fails, though nothing about its quote is wrong. The safest answer when a caller uses either habit is to accept both.

payload.title: Take the words only as the last argument
payload.why_not: A caller that uses --text fails, though nothing about its quote is wrong. Keeping both forms costs one refusal for the case where both are given.

payload.why: The command runs the verbatim quote operation that this card defines.
The conversation argument is the chat log name that this card defines.
The printed id is the excerpt id that this card defines, and the line reports the event it writes.

payload.title: A ticket's number is the number at the start of its file name
payload.why: A blocked_by entry is a number, so each ticket file needs a number that other tickets can name. The file name already orders the tickets in a folder, so the number comes from it and the format needs no sixth header line.
payload.body: The ticket checks read a ticket's number from the digits at the start of its file name: the file 02-reopen.md is ticket 2. A file whose name does not start with a number is still checked, but no blocked_by entry can name it. See #st-ticket-set-checks for how a blocked_by number must match a ticket in the set.

payload.why: The number exists so that the blocked_by check can match each blocked_by entry to a ticket in the set.

payload.title: A blocked_by cycle is one failure that names every ticket on it
payload.why: A cycle is one fault in the order, so one failure line reports it, and the person fixes it in one place. The line still names every ticket on the cycle, because each of them must not start to build.
payload.body:
The blocked_by check reports each cycle once. The failure belongs to the ticket file that sorts first on the cycle, and its message lists every ticket file on the cycle. A ticket that names itself as a blocker is a cycle of one. The failure carries the whole list, so a plan can block each ticket on it (see #st-ticket-partial).

Example. Three tickets in one folder:

- 01-reopen.md, blocked_by: 3
- 02-mark.md, blocked_by: 1
- 03-show.md, blocked_by: 2

1. The check follows the blocked_by entries: 1 needs 3, 3 needs 2, 2 needs 1. That is one cycle.
2. It prints one line, owned by 01-reopen.md, that names all three files.
3. A fourth ticket, 04-list.md with blocked_by: 2, is not on the cycle. It gets no line of its own.

```
01-reopen.md --needs--> 03-show.md --needs--> 02-mark.md --needs--> 01-reopen.md
                                                 ^
04-list.md --needs-------------------------------+   (not on the cycle: no line)

output:  01-reopen.md: blocked_by: blocked_by: a blocked_by cycle: 01-reopen.md, 02-mark.md, 03-show.md
```

payload.why: The failure names every ticket on the cycle because each ticket that a failed set check names goes to blocked.

payload.title: A sample agent starts with no build-rule titles
payload.why: A sample agent only plans one option of a fork and records its picks. It may not write to the map, and it does not get the werk agent instructions. The title list tells the agent to open a rule's card through the map, so it belongs with those instructions and goes to the same agents.
payload.body:
To keep a sample agent's contract narrow, werk adds the build-rule title list only to the agents that get the werk agent instructions: the chat agent, each build pass and the plan writers. A sample agent, a diagram agent and a model call with no tools start with their own prompt alone.

Example:
- Project P has two build-rule cards, B "Tests run against a real database" and C "An order is one checkout".

1. A build pass starts in P. Its prompt holds its own prompt, the werk agent instructions, then the titles of B and C.
2. A person samples the options of an open card in P. Each sample agent's prompt holds its own prompt only.
3. If the build-rules card of P has no children, the build pass gets no title list, and the sample agent still gets nothing.

payload.why: takes the set of agents that get the werk agent instructions, and the narrow contract of a sample agent
