payload.title: The person writes a note on a node's thread from the map, and the server appends it in the person's name
payload.why: A ghost is corrected through the notes on its thread, so the person must be able to write there. An agent turn writes in the agent's name, so a note that went through the chat could not show that the person wrote it, and the inbox could not find it. The page therefore sends the note itself, behind the same token that guards every other write.
payload.body:
A ghost is corrected through its thread: the person says what is wrong, and the agent answers, discards and proposes again (see #werk-propose-new-discard-thread). For that, the person must be able to write on the thread of any node in the map: a card, a ghost, an option, a source or an excerpt.

To give the person that thread with no agent between them and the log, the card page has a note box under the thread. A press of its button sends the text to the server. The server checks the synchronizer token and the Host of the request (see #werk-serve-trust), then appends one note in the person's name to the thread of the open id. Without the token, it refuses and appends nothing. Like accept and remove, the note box is a control that appends an event (see #werk-write). It changes no words of a card, so a frozen ghost takes notes too. The agent reads these notes in the inbox, and its own notes come from the command line.

A thread entry shows who wrote it: "you" for the person, "agent" for the agent. Each open page draws the thread again when the log grows, so a note that the agent writes appears on the page with no reload.

Example:

- G is a ghost, "Retry sends a new link".
- N1 is the person's note "No, retry must reuse the same link".
- N2 is the agent's note "Understood, I will correct it".

1. The person opens G, types N1 in the note box and presses the button. The log gets N1 in the person's name. The thread shows N1, marked "you".
2. The agent reads N1 in its inbox and writes N2. The page draws the thread again: N1, then N2, marked "agent".
3. A page on another site sends a note with no token. The server refuses it. The log and the thread stay as they were.

```
 person ── note box + token ──▶ server ── token and Host ok? ──▶ log: note by "you"
                                   │ no
                                   └──▶ refused, nothing written
 agent  ── say (command line) ─────────────────────────────────▶ log: note by "agent"
 log grows ──▶ every open page reads the thread again ──▶ N1 (you), N2 (agent)
```

"note box" = the text box and its button under the thread. "token" = the synchronizer token that the served page holds.

payload.why: takes the synchronizer token and the Host check that guard the note write
takes the rule that a control in a view appends an event and never edits the drawn card
takes the thread of notes and the inbox that reads the notes the person typed
takes the signal on a log change that makes an open page draw the thread again

payload.title: The person writes a note through the chat composer, and the agent writes it to the thread
payload.why_not: The agent writes every note in its own name, so the thread cannot show that the person wrote it, and the inbox cannot tell the person's notes from the agent's. It also needs a running agent for every note.

payload.title: A card that a postponement reaches by two paths gets one paused mark, along the shortest path
payload.why: A paused trace names each card between the postponed card and the marked card. When two paths reach one card, the trace can name only one of them, and the shortest one has the fewest cards to follow back. One mark per postponement keeps the card from listing the same pause twice.
payload.body:
To keep one pause from reading as two, the walk from a postponed card marks each card once, the first time it reaches it. The walk goes one hop at a time, so the first path to reach a card is a shortest one, and the trace shows that path.

Example. Four cards:
- P is "Invoices are in EUR only".
- Q is "Invoice prices use the EUR format". It depends on P.
- R is "The tax line rounds to the euro cent". It is a child of Q, and it also depends on P.
- S is "The PDF footer states the currency". It depends on R.

What happens:
1. P is postponed. Q is paused, one hop from P.
2. R is paused, one hop from P, over its depends_on link. Its path over Q is two hops, so that path is not used.
3. S is paused, two hops from P. Its trace names R only.
4. Nothing is marked twice. A card that no path reaches gets no mark.

```
 Q --depends_on--> P        hop 1: Q, R
 R --depends_on--> P        hop 2: S
 R --refines-----> Q        (not used: R is already marked at hop 1)
 S --depends_on--> R

 trace on S:  PAUSED from #P, postponed, <date>
                via #R (nearest to #P first)
                last hop: depends_on
```

payload.why: The walk that this card bounds to one mark per card is the walk over the links of that moment, at any distance.
The path this card picks is the path that the paused trace names.

payload.title: A confirm names each depends_on target whose link reason the reviewer read
payload.why: A confirm must show that each outgoing link reason was checked, and the program cannot see a reading. So the confirm lists the targets of the links it read, and the program compares that list with the links that were there before the change.
payload.body:
To keep a confirm from clearing a mark unread, the confirm carries the list of depends_on targets whose reasons the reviewer read. The list must hold every target whose link was made before the newest stale mark on the card. A link made after that change needs no entry. A target with no depends_on link from the card is refused. A refusal names each unread link with its reason, and gives the confirm again with the full list.

Example. Four cards:
- A is "We charge per seat".
- B is "The invoice shows the seat count". It depends on A.
- D is "Invoices are in EUR".
- C is "The invoice PDF has a seat column". It depends on B and on D.

What happens:
1. B is reopened and decided again. C goes stale.
2. A confirm of C that lists B only is refused. The refusal names the link C to D and its reason.
3. A confirm of C that lists B and D passes. C clears.
4. A link from C made after step 1 would not need to be listed.

```
 C --depends_on--> B --depends_on--> A
 C --depends_on--> D

 confirm C [B]      refused: the reason of C -> D is not confirmed
 confirm C [B, D]   C clears
```

payload.why: The confirm that this card gives a list of read links is the review ending that rederive-reason defines.
A link made after the change needs no entry in the list, as vi-prop-bornstale sets.

payload.title: A mark holds only while the link it passed over is the same link
payload.why: A mark says that a link was written against text that has changed. A link made later was written against the new text, so it has nothing to review, even when it joins the same two cards. A restore is the exact undo of a removal, so it brings back the old link and the mark on it.
payload.body:
To keep an old mark off a link that nobody wrote against the old text, each link keeps the moment it was made, and a mark records the links it passed over. The mark holds while each of those links is in the map and was made at the same moment.

A link removed and made again is a new link, so the mark does not come back. A child that a removal moves up to the grandparent sits on a new refines link, so a mark from the old parent does not follow it. A restore puts the child back on its old link, and the mark comes back with it (see #werk-remove-restore-undo). A link made again with a new reason is the same link, so its mark stays.

Example. Three cards:
- A is "We charge per seat".
- B is "The invoice shows the seat count". It depends on A.
- K is "The seat count is rounded up". It is a child of B.

What happens:
1. A is reopened. B goes stale.
2. The link B to A is removed. B clears.
3. The link B to A is made again. B stays clear: the new link was written against the reopened A.
4. B is decided and later reopened. K goes stale.
5. B is removed, and K moves up under the parent of B. K clears.
6. B is restored. K is back under B on its old link, and K is stale again.

```
 B --depends_on--> A          K --refines--> B
 step 1  reopen A             B stale
 step 2  unlink B -> A        B clear
 step 3  link B -> A again    B clear (new link)
 step 5  remove B, K moves up K clear (new link)
 step 6  restore B            K stale (old link back)
```

payload.why: takes the rule that a link made after a change carries no mark from it
takes the rule that a removed link drops the mark
takes the rule that a restore undoes the whole removal, the moved children too

payload.title: A card reads as one mark: stale first, then postponed, then paused, then waiting
payload.why: A card tile has room for one mark word, and a reader acts on the most urgent one. Stale needs a review, a postponed card is the one whose work stops, and a pause only waits on another card. Waiting is the weakest: it is shown only when the card has no other mark, because a marked card already says what to do first.
payload.body:
To keep one card from showing two calls to act, the card shows the first of these that holds: stale, postponed, paused, waiting. Each mark keeps its own trace on the card page, so nothing is hidden: only the one word on the card is chosen.

Example. Three cards:
- P is "Invoices are in EUR only".
- Q is "Invoice prices use the EUR format". It depends on P.
- X is "We charge per seat". Q also depends on X.

What happens:
1. P is postponed. Q reads paused. P reads postponed.
2. X is reopened. Q also goes stale. Q reads stale, and its page shows both traces.
3. Q is confirmed after X is decided again. Q reads paused.
4. P is decided again. Q has no mark.
5. A new open card N that depends on the open X reads waiting. Once N gets a mark, it reads as that mark.

```
 Q --depends_on--> P   (postponed)
 Q --depends_on--> X   (reopened)

 marks on Q          word shown
 paused              paused
 paused + stale      stale
 none                (no word)
```

payload.why: takes the waiting state that this order ranks last
takes the postponed mark that the postponed card carries itself

payload.title: A reopen and a confirm are events of their own, and an amend is the accept of a proposal
payload.why: The fold derives every mark from the order of events, so each change that puts or clears a mark must be one event in the log. A reopen and a confirm have nothing else to ride on. An amend already goes through a proposal and its accept, so a second event for it would record the same change twice.
payload.body:
A reopen is one event, `node.reopened`. It names the card, the reason and the text. A reopen that names no reason is read as invalidated.

A confirm is one event, `node.rederived`. It names the card and the list of depends_on targets whose reasons the reviewer read (see #vi-prop-confirm-names).

An amend has no event of its own. The accept of a proposal on a decided card is the amend: it clears the stale marks of the card and marks the next hop with the change amended. The proposal carries the review sentence that the trace shows. An accept of a proposal on an open card marks nothing, because no card can be decided on an open card.

Example. Two cards:
- Y is "The invoice shows the seat count".
- Z is "The invoice PDF has a seat column". It depends on Y.

What happens:
1. A reopen event on Y. Y is open. Z is stale.
2. Y is decided again. Z is still stale.
3. A proposal on the decided Y, with the sentence "The invoice now shows usage units.", then its accept. Z gets a second stale mark, amended, with that sentence.
4. A confirm event on Z that names Y. Z clears.

```
 log:  reopened(Y) ─ decided(Y) ─ proposed(Y) ─ accepted(Y) ─ rederived(Z, [Y])
 Z:    stale         stale        stale         stale x2       clear
```

payload.why: takes the rule that a change to a decided card is an amend through a proposal
takes the amend's sentence and the next-hop mark it leaves
takes the list of read link targets that a confirm carries
takes the rule that every change is one event in the append-only log

payload.title: `werk rederive --confirm` lists the link targets read, and `werk propose --review` carries an amend's sentence
payload.why: A confirm must name the depends_on targets whose reasons the reviewer read, and an amend must carry the sentence its trace shows. Both are plain text on the command line, so the agent, a script and a person give them the same way.
payload.body:
```
werk rederive <id> [--confirm <id>,<id>...] [--status decided]
werk propose <id> ... [--review "..."]
```

- `--confirm` takes the target ids separated by commas. A refusal prints the command again with the full list.
- `werk rederive` on a card with no stale mark writes nothing, says so, and exits 0. With `--status decided` it still decides the card.
- `--status` takes only decided.
- `--review` is read only when the proposal is on a decided card. The trace of each card that the amend marks shows it.

payload.why: takes the confirm event with its target list and the proposal that carries the review sentence
takes the propose command that this card adds one flag to

payload.text: Build werk/52: a held-out scenario expects message position 3 for the third chat-log line (tool result, person, agent). This card counts from zero, so the build gives 2. The build follows this card. If one-based counting is wanted, amend this card; otherwise the scenario's number is wrong.

payload.title: Every place that shows an excerpt shows its stored message position, counted from zero
payload.why: A pointer's message position can be read as a count from zero or as a line number from one, and the two differ by one. If the printed card, a test and a scenario each pick their own reading, a reader opens the wrong line of the chat log. One number, the stored one, everywhere removes the doubt.
payload.body:
To avoid two readings of one pointer, the printed card, the quote's own report and every test or scenario that names a message position use the stored position, which counts every line of the chat log from zero (see #werk-excerpt-pointer). No view adds one to it, and nothing shows a second, one-based line number beside it. A scenario that says the third line of a chat log is at position 3 is wrong: that line is at position 2.

Example:

- Conversation "logs" has a chat log of three lines.
- Line 0 is a tool result, line 1 is spoken by the person, line 2 is spoken by the agent: "we keep one log per conversation and never rewrite it".

1. The agent quotes "one log per conversation" from logs. The quote skips line 0, because a tool result is not spoken, and matches line 2.
2. The quote reports message 2 and span 8..32.
3. The printed excerpt shows message: 2.
4. A reader opens the chat log, counts lines from zero, takes line 2 and cuts characters 8 to 32. The reader finds the quoted words.

```
 chat log of "logs"                        printed excerpt
 line 0  tool    (hidden, still counted)    message: 2   <- the same number
 line 1  person  how do we store a chat?    span: 8..32
 line 2  agent   we keep one log per ...  <-+
```

The guideline step that chose it: the smallest interface and the fewest changed decided cards. The pointer already stores a zero-based position, so one number, shown as stored, adds no second field and changes no decided card.

payload.title: The message position counts lines from one
payload.why_not: It changes a decided card and every pointer already written, and it still leaves a reader who counts from zero, as a program does, one line off.

payload.title: The excerpt stores a position from zero and shows a line number from one
payload.why_not: Two numbers for one pointer are a larger interface, and a reader must know which of the two to use to open the chat log.

payload.why: takes the stored message position, counted from zero with hidden lines included, that every view must show unchanged

payload.title: `werk find` prints one line per card it can work on, with the id, the status and the title
payload.why: An agent reads the list of work and then opens one card from it. The same line shape as a search match lets the agent read both lists the same way, and the status tells open work from a prototype that is still in progress.
payload.body:
```
werk find [<id>]
```

With an id, `werk find` reads the refines subtree of that card, the card itself first, breadth first. With no id, it reads each tree of the map in turn. See #werk-find-scope for which cards it lists.

One line per card: the id, the status and the title, separated by two spaces. When no card is listed, it prints one line that says there is no open or proto card to work on, and names the card when an id was given. An id that is not in the map is refused with exit code 1.

Example. The map holds Billing (decided), under it Refunds (reopened as rejected) and Seats (decided), and under Seats a card Trial (open).

1. `werk find` prints `refunds  open  Refunds go back to the card`, then `trial  open  A trial seat is free`.
2. `werk find seats` prints only the Trial line.
3. `werk find refunds` prints only the Refunds line, because the card itself is read first.
4. `werk find missing` prints an error and exits 1. Nothing is listed.

```
 Billing     decided          (not listed)
 +-- Refunds open (rejected)  line 1: depth 1
 +-- Seats   decided          (not listed)
     +-- Trial open           line 2: depth 2
```

payload.why: takes which cards find lists and in what order

payload.title: The printed rollup line names the card count and only the other counts that are not zero
payload.why: An agent reads the printed card line by line, and a row of zeros hides the one count that matters. The card count is always there, so the reader still knows the size of the branch. A ghost card belongs to no rollup, so it prints no rollup line.
payload.body:
The rollup prints as one line: the card count first, then open, proto, decided, unchallenged and stale in that order, each only when it is above zero (see #rollup for what each count holds). The same text sits in brackets after each incoming refines row. A ghost card, and the refines row of a ghost child, print no rollup.

Example:

- Card `price` "We charge per seat", decided, with two children.
- Child `seats` is open. Child `tiers` is decided and stale.

1. The agent prints `price`.
2. The rollup line reads `subtree: 3 cards, 1 open, 2 decided, 1 stale`. The proto and unchallenged counts are zero, so they do not print.
3. The row of `seats` reads `(1 card, 1 open)`.

```
card price  [decided]
We charge per seat
subtree: 3 cards, 1 open, 2 decided, 1 stale    <- 3 = price + 2 children
  <- refines  seats  ...  (1 card, 1 open)
  <- refines  tiers  ...  (1 card, 1 decided, 1 stale)
```

payload.why: takes the six counts and the subtree they cover from rollup
takes the rule that a ghost is in no rollup from werk-propose-new

payload.title: A start that finds a live lock waits five seconds for the holder to exit, then refuses
payload.why: A server that is stopping still holds its lock for a moment, so a restart right after a stop would refuse at once without a wait. A wait of a few seconds covers that stop, and it is short enough that a person who started a second server by mistake sees the refusal quickly. A test sets a shorter wait in the environment, so a refusal does not cost it five seconds.
payload.body:
A start whose create of the lock fails reads the lock again every tenth of a second. It stops waiting when the lock is free or stale, and it refuses when five seconds pass and the holder is still alive. A setting in the environment changes the length of the wait; a value that is not a whole number of milliseconds is ignored and the five seconds hold.

Example:

- Server A holds the lock. Start B begins.

1. B fails to create the lock and reads pid A. A is alive.
2. B reads the lock again every tenth of a second.
3. Case one: A exits after two seconds and removes its lock. B creates the lock and runs.
4. Case two: A is still alive after five seconds. B refuses and names the pid and the port of A.

```
  t=0s   B: create -> exists, read {pid A}, alive
  t=0.1s B: read {pid A}, alive   ... every 0.1s
  t=2s   A exits, lock gone -> B: create -> ok, B runs      (case one)
  t=5s   A alive -> B refuses: pid A, port of A            (case two)
```

payload.title: A start that finds a live lock waits five seconds for the holder to exit, then refuses
payload.why: A server that is stopping still holds its lock for a moment, so a restart right after a stop would refuse at once without a wait. A wait of a few seconds covers that stop, and it is short enough that a person who started a second server by mistake sees the refusal quickly. A test sets a shorter wait in the environment, so a refusal does not cost it five seconds.
payload.body:
A start whose create of the lock fails reads the lock again every tenth of a second. It stops waiting when the lock is free or stale, and it refuses when five seconds pass and the holder is still alive. A setting in the environment changes the length of the wait; a value that is not a whole number of milliseconds is ignored and the five seconds hold.

Example:

- Server A holds the lock. Start B begins.

1. B fails to create the lock and reads pid A. A is alive.
2. B reads the lock again every tenth of a second.
3. Case one: A exits after two seconds and removes its lock. B creates the lock and runs.
4. Case two: A is still alive after five seconds. B refuses and names the pid and the port of A.

```
  t=0s    B: create -> exists, read {pid A}, A alive
  t=0.1s  B: read {pid A}, A alive    ... again every 0.1s
  t=2s    A exits, lock gone -> B: create -> ok, B runs    (case one)
  t=5s    A still alive -> B refuses, names pid and port   (case two)

  {pid A} = the lock, naming the pid of A
```

payload.why: takes the rule that a setting only a test needs comes from the environment, not from a flag

payload.title: The
payload.why: The
payload.body:
The ✓ needs a way to reach the server that a page from another site cannot use. To give it one, the page sends one POST to the address /api/accept, beside the address that takes a note. The body is a JSON object with one field, id: the node the ✓ sits on. The request carries the synchronizer token of the page (see #werk-serve-trust).

The server commits what an accept from the command line commits for that id: a ghost with its ghost parents, its ghost options and its ghost sources (see #werk-propose-new-carry), or the pending change of a real card. It appends one accept event per node, in the person's name, and answers with the sequence number of the last event and the list of ids it accepted. A refusal answers with an error text and appends nothing: 405 for a method other than POST, 403 for a missing or wrong token, 400 for a body that is not a JSON object with a text id, and 422 for an id with nothing to accept. The page shows that error text under the card.

Example:

- C is a decided card, "Retry sends a new link".
- E is a ghost excerpt that supports C.

1. The person opens C and presses the ✓ on E. The page sends id E with its token. The server appends the accept of E and answers 200 with the list [E]. The link from C to E goes live with no second request.
2. The person presses the ✓ on E again from an old page. E has nothing pending. The server answers 422 with the reason, and the log stays as it was.
3. A page on another site sends id E with no token. The server answers 403 and writes nothing.

```
 page ── POST /api/accept {id: E} + token ──▶ server
                                               │ token ok, E pending?
                                     yes ──────┴────── no
                                      ▼                 ▼
               log: accept E (by "you")          422 + reason, nothing written
               reply 200 {seq, ids: [E]}
```

"token" = the synchronizer token that the served page holds. "seq" = the sequence number of the last event written. "ids" = every node the accept committed.

payload.why: The
The
The

payload.title: The ✓ sends one token-guarded request with the node id, and the server answers with the ids it accepted
payload.why: The ✓ must commit the same events as an accept from the command line, and only the served page may send it. One request that names the node lets the server work out what the accept takes along, so the page never needs to know which ghost parents or options go with it. The answer lists those ids, so a refusal or a partial result is visible on the page.

payload.why: The request carries the press of the ✓ that this card places on a pending node.
The request is a write, so it carries the synchronizer token and a loopback Host.
The server commits the same set of nodes that an accept takes along.

payload.title: The server renders each chat text to HTML, and a streamed update carries the whole block so far
payload.why: Only the server knows which ids the map can open, so only the server can decide which reference in a chat text becomes a link. A streamed update that holds the whole block so far renders on its own, also when a code fence in it is not closed yet. The page then replaces the block with each update and never joins pieces of text.
payload.body:
To keep the links in the chat the same as on a card, the server renders the person's message and every block of the reply with the same Markdown renderer and the ids of the cards the map can open now (see #werk-reflink-inview). The page draws the HTML it gets and renders nothing itself.

A reply block reaches the page as a series of updates with one block id (see #werk-progress). Each update while the block streams carries the text of the block up to that moment, rendered. The finished block carries the final text under the same id, so it replaces the last update in its place.

Example:

- The map holds the card `al-diff`.
- The agent replies with a block that ends in a code fence tagged json.

1. The first update holds "Here it is:" and an open fence with `{"card": "al-diff", "depth": `. The page shows a box labelled json with that code.
2. The next update holds the same text plus `2}`. The page replaces the block, and the box holds the longer code.
3. The finished block arrives with the closed fence. The page replaces the block a last time, and the box shows the complete code with JSON colours.
4. An update for a block id the page has not seen adds a new block under the others. Nothing is replaced.

```
 agent text so far         server                      page
 "Here … {"card": … "  ──▶ render(text, open ids) ──▶  [m1:0] box json  (step 1)
 "Here … 2}"           ──▶ render(text, open ids) ──▶  [m1:0] replaced   (step 2)
 finished "Here … ```" ──▶ render(text, open ids) ──▶  [m1:0] replaced   (step 3)
```

[m1:0] is the block id. Each arrow is one update on the live channel.

payload.why: takes the block id that a streamed block shares with its finished form
takes the set of ids the map can open, which the renderer links

payload.title: A chat message is one request with the person's words, and its answer is the message as HTML
payload.why: The page draws the person's message from the answer, so the message shows the same links as the reply, rendered once by the server. The words alone are enough for the agent to answer, so the request carries nothing else.
payload.body:
To send a chat message, the page makes one request to the server with the words the person typed and the token of the page (see #werk-serve-trust). The server hands the words to the chat agent and answers with the message rendered as HTML. A request with no words, or with only spaces, is refused and reaches no agent.

The reply does not come in the answer. It streams on the live channel of the page as the agent writes it.

Example:

1. The person types "Compare #al-diff with #old-idea" and sends it. The map holds al-diff, and old-idea is removed.
2. The server answers with the message as HTML: #al-diff is a link, #old-idea is plain text.
3. The page adds the message to the thread.
4. The person sends a message of three spaces. The server refuses it, and the thread does not change.

```
 page ──(words + token)──▶ server ──(words)──▶ chat agent
   ◀──(message as HTML)──┘                       │
   ◀──────────── reply on the live channel ◀──────┘
```

payload.why: takes the token that every request which starts an agent must carry

payload.title: The chat agent starts at the first message, and again at the first message after it exits
payload.why: A server that a person only reads needs no agent, so it starts none. An agent that has exited reads no more input, so the next message starts a new one rather than go nowhere.
payload.body:
The chat of a project has one agent process (see #werk-chat-stdin). The server starts it when the first message arrives, and every later message goes to the same process. When the process exits, the server forgets it. The next message starts a new process and goes to that one.

Example:

1. The server starts. No agent runs.
2. The person sends "hello". The agent starts and reads "hello".
3. The person sends "again". The same agent reads it. No new agent starts.
4. The agent exits.
5. The person sends "once more". A new agent starts and reads it.

```
 message:   hello   again        once more
 agent:     [start ── A ──── exit]  [start ── B ...
```

A and B are the two agent processes.

payload.why: takes the one agent process per conversation that this card starts and restarts

payload.title: A held-out step that needs a command-line operation no merged ticket has built is not run, not red
payload.why: A step author writes steps from the brief, so a step can start a build pass, a chat or a sample that a later ticket builds. Such a step fails because the command line does not know the operation, not because of the ticket's code. Each follow-up it files can only build another ticket's work or change nothing, so the same follow-up comes back after every merge.
payload.body:
To keep a red step pointing at merged code (see #st-heldout-merged-only), a step whose path starts an operation of the command line that no merged ticket provides ends as not run (see #st-heldout-notrun). It files no follow-up. G2 still waits for it, and the held-out run after each later merge tries it again. The ticket's own behaviour stays checked on the main line by its unit tests at the seam it builds, such as the prompt builder for a ticket that builds agent prompts.

Example:

- Ticket R "Every agent werk starts gets the agent instructions" builds the prompt builder and is merged.
- Ticket B "A build pass runs on one ticket" builds the operation that starts a build pass, and is still blocked.
- Step S of R: "When the person starts a build pass on a ticket, then its prompt begins with the build agent's own instructions".

1. R merges. The held-out run binds S. The command line answers that it has no such operation, so S ends as not run, with a grey badge on R. No follow-up is filed.
2. B merges. The next held-out run tries S again through the operation that B built.
3. S passes: S is green. Or S fails on the prompt: S is red, and one follow-up for R is filed.

```
merge:   R                    B
S:       not run       ->     green | red -> follow-up for R
         (no operation)       (operation now on the main line)
```

payload.why: the not-run result, which files no follow-up and keeps G2 waiting, that a step through a missing operation receives

payload.title: Build the missing operation inside the follow-up ticket
payload.why_not: The operations that start a build pass, a chat and a sample are the scope of other planned tickets that are blocked on their own dependencies. A follow-up would build them out of order, touch their modules, and collide with those tickets when they build.

criterion.metric: follow-up tickets filed for a step whose held-out run failed only because the command line did not know the operation

payload.title: A chat message is a POST to the chat address with a text field, and the answer holds an html field
payload.why: The page and the server must agree on one address and one set of field names, or a message never reaches the agent. The chat gets its own address beside the note address, so a request can only start a chat turn and can write nothing else. A refusal names its cause, so the page can show it.
payload.body:
The request of a chat message (see #werk-reflink-chat-request) goes to the address /api/chat with the method POST. Its body is JSON with one field, text: the words the person typed. The token of the page travels in the same header as on every other write (see #werk-serve-trust). The answer to a sent message has the status 200 and the JSON body {"html": ...}: the message as HTML, with a link only for an id the map can open. Every refusal reaches no agent and has a JSON body {"error": ...} with one sentence: status 405 for another method, 403 for a missing or wrong token, 400 for a body that is not JSON or a text that is empty or holds only spaces. Example: 1. The page sends POST /api/chat with the body {"text": "Compare #al-diff"} and the token. The server answers 200 with {"html": "

Compare …

"}. The page adds the message to the thread. 2. The page sends {"text": " "}. The server answers 400 with {"error": "a chat message needs a text"}. No agent starts, and the thread does not change. 3. A page on another site sends the same body with no token. The server answers 403. Nothing happens. 4. A GET to /api/chat gets 405. ``` page ── POST /api/chat {text} + token ──▶ server ── token ok, text not blank? ──▶ chat agent ◀────────── 200 {html} ────────────────┘ │ no ◀────────── 403 / 400 {error} ─────────────┘ ``` The guideline step that chose it: the least privilege and the smallest interface. One address that takes one field can start a chat turn and nothing else.

payload.title: Send chat messages to the same write address as notes, with a kind field
payload.why_not: One address with two meanings is a larger privilege: a wrong kind field sends the person's words to the wrong place, a chat turn or the log.

payload.title: Send chat messages up a second live channel that stays open in both directions
payload.why_not: The live channel only goes from the server to the page. A two-way channel is a second connection to guard with the token and to reconnect, for a message that one request carries.

payload.why: takes the token header and the loopback Host check that every request which starts an agent must pass
gives the address and fields to the request whose words and HTML answer that card defines

payload.title: Each reply update on the live channel holds only the block id and the block as HTML
payload.why: The page draws only HTML that the server rendered, so an update needs nothing but the place it goes and the HTML to put there. Raw text in the update would invite the page to render it a second way, with links the server did not check. A finished block that matches no streamed block still needs an id of its own, or it would replace a block it does not belong to.
payload.body:
Each update of a reply block goes out on the live channel of every open page as one event. The event name says whether the block still streams or is finished, on the two channels that carry a reply (see #werk-progress). Its data is JSON with two fields: id, the block id, and html, the whole block so far rendered with the ids the map can open (see #werk-reflink-chat-render). The page puts the html in the block with that id, or adds a new block when it has no block with that id. A finished block normally takes the id of the streamed block it completes. When no streamed block of its kind waits, for example when the agent sent no stream events for it, the finished block gets the id of its message, a colon, the letter f and the count of finished blocks in the stream so far. That id matches no streamed block, so the block is added and replaces nothing. Example: - The agent writes message m1 with one text block, and then message m2 whose finished block came with no stream events. It is the third finished block of the stream. 1. A delta event with {"id": "m1:0", "html": "

Here

"} arrives. The page adds block m1:0. 2. A chat event with {"id": "m1:0", "html": "

Here it is.

"} arrives. The page replaces block m1:0. 3. A chat event with {"id": "m2:f3", "html": "

Done.

"} arrives. The page has no block m2:f3, so it adds one under m1:0. Nothing is replaced. ``` event data page delta {id: m1:0, html:

Here

} [m1:0] added (step 1) chat {id: m1:0, html:

Here it is.

} [m1:0] replaced (step 2) chat {id: m2:f3, html:

Done.

} [m2:f3] added (step 3) ``` The guideline step that chose it: the smallest interface. Two fields carry everything the page needs.

payload.title: Send the raw text of the block beside its HTML
payload.why_not: A second field is a larger interface, and a page that holds the raw text can render it again without the server's list of cards the map can open.

payload.title: Give a finished block with no streamed match the plain index id of its message
payload.why_not: Every finished block sits at index 0, so the plain index id can equal a streamed block of the same message and overwrite it with a different block.

payload.why: takes the two reply channels and the message and block index id that a streamed block and its finished form share
takes the fact that every finished block arrives at index 0, which is why an unmatched block needs an id of its own
takes the rule that each update carries the whole block so far, rendered by the server

payload.title: werk runs in dev mode when its Vite config sits in the source it runs from
payload.why: Dev mode is the mode that runs werk from its own source. Only a source checkout holds the Vite config, and a compiled executable never does. So the presence of that config tells the two apart with no flag and no setting.
payload.body: To decide whether to start Vite inside the server, werk checks for the one Vite config at the top of the source it runs from (see #werk-stack-layout). When the config is there, werk runs from a checkout: the server starts Vite in middleware mode and transforms the client on each request (see #werk-client-reload). When the config is not there, werk runs outside dev mode and serves the client that the build step wrote. No environment variable or command-line flag switches the mode.

payload.why: takes the definition of dev mode as the mode that runs werk from its own source
takes the one Vite config at the top of the repository that marks a source checkout

payload.title: Outside dev mode, the server reads the built client from a folder named client beside the running program
payload.why: Outside dev mode no Vite runs, so the server needs the files that the build step wrote, at a place it can find from any project directory. The running program is the one fixed point, so the build puts the client beside it. A request can name only a file inside that folder, so a crafted address cannot read another file on the machine.
payload.body: The build step runs the Vite build into the output folder first, then compiles the executable, and the client folder sits next to the executable. Outside dev mode the server answers a client address with the file of the same path inside that folder, and answers 404 for an address that leaves the folder or names no file. A view address gets the folder's page, filled by the server. This places the output folder on disk; #werk-dist asks for the client inside the executable, and that card decides how the files move inside it.

payload.why: takes the test that tells a run outside dev mode from a run in dev mode

payload.title: The server fills the client's one page at two marked places, the head and the view
payload.why: The page is the one HTML file that Vite transforms, but the token, the title and the first card exist only on the server. Two named comments in the page mark where they go, so the server fills them with a text replace and the first paint holds the card before any script runs.
payload.body:
The client page holds two HTML comments, one in the head and one in the body of the left pane. For each view address the server takes the page as Vite or the build gave it, puts the synchronizer token and the page title in place of the head comment, and puts the server-rendered card in place of the view comment. The islands then mount into that markup.

Example. The page holds a head comment and a view comment. A browser opens the map address of card checkout, titled "Ship the checkout".

1. The server reads the page. Result: the page with both comments.
2. The server replaces the head comment. Result: the token meta tag and the title "Ship the checkout".
3. The server replaces the view comment. Result: the card checkout as server-rendered HTML.
4. A view with no card, such as the board. Result: the view comment becomes empty, and the island draws the view.

```
page (from Vite)            filled page (to the browser)
<head>                      <head>
  [head comment]   --(2)-->   token meta tag, title
<main>                      <main>
  [view comment]   --(3)-->   card HTML  (empty for a view with no card, step 4)
```

payload.why: takes the one HTML page of the client folder that the server fills
takes the synchronizer token that goes into the head of the page

payload.title: A view's address enters the client with the view it opens
payload.why: The list of view addresses names views that do not exist yet. An address with no view behind it shows an empty or placeholder pane, and that placeholder is a screen nobody decided. So each address is added by the work that builds its view, and the client answers only the addresses of views it has.
payload.body:
To avoid placeholder screens, the client and the server know only the addresses of views that are built. An address of a view that is not built yet is answered like any other address that is not a view address: not found. The work that builds a view adds its address, its page title and its tests in the same change.

Example. The address list holds the map address and the board address. The map view is built; the board view is not.

1. A browser opens the map address of card checkout. Result: the app, with the card checkout.
2. A browser opens the board address. Result: not found, because no board view exists.
3. The board view is built. Result: the same change adds the board address, and step 2 now gives the app with the board.

```
address        view built?   answer
/map/<id>      yes           the app, card open        (1)
/board         no            not found                 (2)
/board         yes           the app, board open       (3)
```

Guideline step that chose it: the smallest interface, and the safest when wrong. An address added later costs one change; a placeholder view that ships stays as an undecided screen.

payload.title: Answer every listed view address with the app now, with an empty or placeholder pane for a view not built yet
payload.why_not: It ships a screen that no card decides, and its tests pin a placeholder that the real view must then remove. It gives a larger interface than the views that exist.

payload.why: The list of view addresses and the rule that the server answers each with the app come from it; this card says when each address is added.

payload.title: A follow-up whose every step needs an unbuilt command-line operation closes with no code change
payload.why: A follow-up ticket can hold only held-out steps that start a build pass, a chat or a sample before any merged ticket built that operation. No change inside the follow-up can make those steps pass, and the behaviour behind them is already checked by unit tests at the seam an earlier ticket built. Each further builder pass costs a run and ends on the same finding.
payload.body:
To stop a follow-up from looping on work that belongs to another ticket, a builder pass on it checks two facts. First, each of its steps starts an operation that the command line does not provide on the main line. Second, the seam behind each step has unit tests that state the step's outcome, and those tests pass on the main line. When both facts hold, the pass ends with no code change, and the grader scores each acceptance criterion as met: the step is not run (see #st-heldout-notrun), not failed. The steps stay in the held-out set, G2 still waits for them, and the held-out run after each later merge tries them again. A step that goes red once its operation exists files a new follow-up then (see #st-heldout-followup-per-ticket). When a step lacks a passing unit test at its seam, the pass writes that test, and does not close on the first fact alone.

The guideline chose this answer by no data deleted and easiest to undo: no step leaves the held-out set, and a later red result files a fresh follow-up. It also needs no new link between tickets, which is the smallest interface.

Example:

- Ticket R "Every agent werk starts gets the agent instructions" built the prompt builder and merged, with unit tests for each prompt.
- Follow-up F holds R's steps S1 "a build pass starts with the instructions" and S2 "a sample agent gets no instructions".
- Ticket B "A build pass runs on one ticket" and ticket P "Samples run" build the operations, and neither has merged.

1. A builder pass on F finds that the command line has no operation that starts a build pass or a sample. Fact one holds.
2. It finds a passing unit test at the prompt builder for S1 and for S2. Fact two holds.
3. The pass ends with no code change. The grader scores both criteria as met. F closes.
4. B merges. The held-out run tries S1. S1 is green: nothing happens. S1 is red: a new follow-up for R is filed.
5. If step 2 had found no unit test for S2, the pass writes one at the prompt builder, and F closes with that test as its change.

```
F (follow-up)         builder pass               later merges
 S1 --needs--> [no build-pass op]  ok   \
 S2 --needs--> [no sample op]      ok    >-> F closes, no code change
 S1, S2 unit tests at the seam     pass /
                                                 B merges -> S1 tried: green | red -> new follow-up
ok   = fact one holds for the step
pass = fact two holds for the step
```

payload.title: Block the follow-up on the tickets that build the missing operations
payload.why_not: It needs a new blocking link from a follow-up to tickets of other subtrees, and the follow-up then waits with nothing to build. When those tickets merge, the held-out run rechecks the steps by itself and files a new follow-up for a red one, so the blocked ticket adds a second record of the same wait.

payload.title: Archive the follow-up as not needed
payload.why_not: An archive says that the spec no longer needs the ticket, and that is false: the steps must still pass. It also takes the open wait off the board, so the person no longer sees it.

payload.why: the not-run result that lets the grader score a step through a missing operation as met, not failed
the new follow-up that a step files when it goes red after its operation merges, which makes closing safe

payload.text: Follow-up ticket werk/57 repeats held-out step 12.1, which expects message position 3 for the third chat-log line. The merged tree gives 2, as the decided pointer rule says. Every other part of the step passes. Step 12.1 stays red until this card is accepted and the step is rewritten to position 2.

Ticket werk/57 pass 2 is a decision pass on this question: is the third chat-log line at message position 2 or 3? This card already answers it with 2, and the code and tests follow it. Accept this card to settle it, and the held-out step that expects 3 must then be rewritten. Discard it and pick opt0 or opt1 if positions should read from one.

payload.title: A card page lists every neighbour of the card, under one heading for each link type and direction
payload.why: A reader of one card must see where it sits and what it rests on without opening another card. The card read already gives the id and title of every neighbour, so the page draws all of them. A page that drew only the sub-cards and the evidence hid the parent, the dependencies and the options.
payload.body:
To show every neighbour, the card page puts one list under the hero for each link type and direction that the card has. Each row shows the other card's id, its title and the link's reason, and a pending mark while the link is held because one end is a ghost (see #vi-onview-links for the row). A list with no rows is left out.

The headings, from this card's side:

- Refines: the parent card.
- Depends on, and Depend on this card.
- Alternative to: the card that an option competes for.
- Options: the options that compete for this card.
- Evidence, and Cited by.

The children stay in the sub-card tiles and get no second list.

Example. Card I "The invoice shows the seat count" refines Root, depends on S "We bill per seat" with the reason "Counts seats", and has option O "Flat fee".

1. The person opens I. The page shows Refines with Root, Depends on with S and "Counts seats", and Options with O.
2. The person opens S. The page shows Depend on this card with I.
3. The person opens Root. Root has no parent and no dependencies, so it shows no Refines and no Depends on list, only I as a sub-card.

```
page of I                      page of S
---------------------------    ---------------------------
I  The invoice shows ...       S  We bill per seat
REFINES     #root Root         DEPEND ON THIS CARD
DEPENDS ON  #S We bill ...                 #I The invoice ...
            Counts seats
OPTIONS     #O Flat fee
```

In the picture, each capital word is a list heading, and the line under a row is the link's reason.

payload.why: takes the row form of a link list: the id, the title and the link's reason
takes the card read, which gives the ids and titles of every neighbour of one card

payload.title: A move between view addresses happens inside the page, so the chat pane stays open
payload.why: The chat pane holds a live stream and an in-flight turn, and a page load cuts both. So a plain click on a link to a view address changes the address and the view without a page load, and Back and Forward do the same. A link that the browser must follow itself still loads a page.
payload.body:
To keep the chat pane alive across every move, the client changes the address in the browser history and redraws only the view. A plain click on a link to a view address on the same server adds one history entry and opens that view. A click with a modifier key, a click with another button, a link that opens a new tab, and a link to another site load as usual. Back and Forward open the view of the history entry they reach.

The view and the page title read one page state: the open address and the last card read for it. Each move starts a new card read. Only the newest read may land, so a slow read of an earlier card never covers a later card.

Example. The page shows card retry, titled "Retry a failed payment once". Its body links to card root, titled "Ship the checkout".

1. The person clicks the link to root. Result: the address becomes the map address of root, one history entry is added, and the view shows root. The chat pane keeps its stream.
2. The person presses Back. Result: the address becomes the map address of retry, and the view shows retry. No page load.
3. The read of root is slow and lands after step 2. Result: nothing happens, because a newer read started.
4. The person clicks the link to root with the command key held. Result: the browser opens root in a new tab, and this page does not change.

```
 history            view          chat pane
 [retry]            retry         open
   | (1) click
 [retry][root]      root          open   (no page load)
   | (2) Back
 [retry] root       retry         open   (no page load)
   (3) late read of root  ->  dropped
```

payload.why: takes the view addresses and the rule that Back and Forward move between them
takes the chat pane whose live stream a page load would cut

payload.title: The card read of an id that the map does not hold carries the page that says so
payload.why: The view draws the HTML that the server renders for a card, and the server already renders a not-found page for a first page load. When a later card read of an unknown or removed id carries that same page, the view draws one answer however it got it, and the client keeps no second copy of the not-found page.
payload.body:
To keep one not-found page, the server writes it and the client only draws it. The card read of an id answers with whether the map holds the card, the card's data when it does, and the server-rendered HTML in both cases: the card when the map holds it, the not-found page when it does not. A malformed id is still refused.

Example. The map holds card root, titled "Ship the checkout", and no card nobody.

1. A card read of root. Result: found, the card data of root, and the HTML of root.
2. A card read of nobody. Result: not found, no card data, and the page that says no card nobody is in the map.
3. The view draws the HTML of either answer. Result: the same not-found page as a first load of the map address of nobody.
4. A card read with a malformed id. Result: refused as a bad request, and the view does not change.

```
 card read      found   card data   HTML
 root   (1)     yes     root        card root
 nobody (2)     no      none        not-found page  == first load of /map/nobody (3)
 bad id (4)     refused
```

payload.why: takes the rule that an address of a card not in the map opens a page that says so

payload.title: The composer stashes its draft each time the page goes away
payload.why: A reload that a client edit forces gives the composer no warning it can wait for. The browser signals every page that goes away, whatever the cause, so a stash at that signal covers the forced reload and a manual reload too. The stash sits in the tab's session storage, so each tab keeps its own draft.
payload.body:
To keep a draft through a reload that nobody can predict, the composer does not stash on each keystroke and does not wait for a reload event. It writes the draft to the tab's session storage under one fixed key when the browser signals that the page goes away. When the page loads again, the composer starts with the stashed draft. A sent message empties the draft, so the next stash is empty.

Example. Tab A and tab B show the app. The person types "check the retry" in tab A and "draft two" in tab B.

1. A client edit that cannot apply in place reloads tab A. Result: the page-away signal stashes "check the retry" in tab A's storage, and the reloaded composer shows it.
2. Tab B reloads too. Result: tab B shows "draft two", because each tab has its own session storage.
3. The person sends the message in tab A, then reloads it. Result: the composer is empty.
4. The person closes tab A. Result: the browser drops tab A's session storage, and nothing else changes.

```
 tab A: "check the retry" --page goes away (1)--> storage A --load--> composer A
 tab B: "draft two"       --page goes away (2)--> storage B --load--> composer B
 send in A (3) -> draft "" -> next stash ""
```

payload.why: takes the rule that the composer draft survives the reload in the browser's session storage

payload.title: The one conversation of a werk server is named main, and its chat log is the main chat log
payload.why: A quote names the conversation whose chat log holds the words, so the conversation needs a name before its first message is written. A server holds one conversation at a time, so one fixed name is enough, and it does not change when the agent restarts.
payload.body:
To give a quote a conversation to name, the chat of a werk server writes every message of its one conversation to the chat log of the conversation named main, in the folder that holds the decision log. The name stays the same across a new agent process and across a server restart, so one chat log holds the whole conversation, and each line still records the session that wrote it.

Example:

- The project keeps its decision log in the .werk folder.

1. The person sends "Make it three tries". The chat log .werk/chats/main.jsonl gains the open-card line and the person's words.
2. The agent replies. The finished reply goes to the same file.
3. The agent exits, and the next message starts a new agent with a new session. Its lines go to the same file, with the new session id.
4. The agent quotes the reply from step 2 with the conversation name main. The quote finds it in that file.

```
.werk/log.jsonl            the decision log
.werk/chats/main.jsonl     the chat log of the conversation "main"
  0  werk    tooling  [the map is now at #retry — ...]   (step 1)
  1  person  spoken   Make it three tries                 (step 1)
  2  agent   spoken   Done: three tries.                  (step 2, session s-1)
  3  werk    tooling  [the map is now at #retry — ...]   (step 3, session s-2)
```

payload.why: takes the rule that a quote points at one message of a named conversation's chat log, which needs a conversation name

payload.text: Ticket werk/62 applies this card. No verb starts a build pass or a sample. Each of the 4 steps has a passing unit test at the agent-launch seam. The chat step also passes through the chat server. The pass changed no code.

payload.title: A card added with no parent sits under the root
payload.why: The map draws only the cards in the tree below the root. A card with no parent would be in the log but on no page, so a person would never see it. Placing it under the root makes every new card visible at once, and the person moves it lower by request.
payload.body:
To avoid a card that is in the log but on no page of the map, an add of a card that names no parent places the card under the root, in the same added event (see #pr-log-one-event). The root page then lists it with the other cards below the root (see #vi-onview-root).

The rule holds for cards only. An option and a source sit beside a card and never in the tree, so they take no parent. The root itself takes no parent, and neither does a card added to a map that has no root yet.

Example:

- The map holds the root card Root and nothing else.
- No server runs.

1. The agent adds card S We

payload.why: takes the rule that every card has a chain of parents up to the root, which a card with no parent breaks
takes the rule that the root page lists only the cards in the tree below the root
takes the rule that the parent of a new card is part of its one added event

payload.title: An add of a card with no parent is refused
payload.why_not: Nearly every card has an obvious place, so the agent would type the root for most top-level cards. A refusal costs a failed call, and the root is a safe place the person can move the card from.

payload.title: A card added with no parent sits under the root
payload.why: The map draws only the cards in the tree below the root. A card with no parent would be in the log but on no page, so a person would never see it. Placing it under the root makes every new card visible at once, and the person moves it lower by request.
payload.body:
To avoid a card that is in the log but on no page of the map, an add of a card that names no parent places the card under the root, in the same added event (see #pr-log-one-event). The root page then lists it with the other cards below the root (see #vi-onview-root).

The rule holds for cards only. An option and a source sit beside a card and never in the tree, so they take no parent. The root itself takes no parent, and neither does a card added to a map that has no root yet.

Example:

- The map holds the root card "Root" and nothing else.
- No server runs.

1. The agent adds card S "We charge per seat" and names no parent. The added event names the root as the parent of S.
2. The server starts and the person opens the map. The root page shows a tile for S.
3. The agent adds option S:opt0 "Flat fee" with no parent. The option gets no parent, and it shows on the page of S once it is linked to S.
4. The agent adds card T "Seats are counted each month" and names S as its parent. T sits under S, and nothing changes at the root.

```
  after step 1         after step 4
  root                 root
   └ S (ghost)          └ S (ghost)
                           └ T (ghost)
  S:opt0 ··· beside S, not in the tree

  └ = sits under (a refines link)   (ghost) = proposed, not accepted
```

payload.why: takes the rule that every card has a chain of parents up to the root, which a card with no parent breaks
takes the rule that the root page lists only the cards in the tree below the root
takes the rule that the parent of a new card is part of its one added event

payload.title: An add of a card with no parent is refused
payload.why_not: Nearly every top-level card belongs under the root, so the agent would name the root on most adds. A refusal costs a failed call, and the root is a safe place from which the person moves the card.

criterion.text: I add a card with no parent and check that the root page lists it

payload.title: Every chat event on the live channel names its turn, and the start and the end of a turn are events of their own
payload.why: The pane puts each part of a reply under the message that asked for it, and removes the waiting mark when that message's turn starts. So the pane needs the turn of every part, and it needs to hear when a turn starts and when it ends. A tool call is not text, so it travels as its own fields, which the pane can fold into one line.
payload.body:
To let the pane place every part without a guess, each chat event that the server puts on the live channel carries the turn name. A streamed block and a finished block keep their own events (see #werk-reflink-chat-frame). A tool call is a tool event with the call id, the tool name and the input as text. A tool result is a tool-result event with the call id, the output and an error flag. The state of the agent (thinking, or the running tool, and the tokens so far) is a status event. A turn event says that a turn started, that it ended with its duration and cost, or that it ended because the agent exited. The person's message goes to the server with its words, its turn name and the open card. A turn name is letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores, so it cannot carry markup into the page. Example: - Message A "Rename the card" with turn name t1. - Message B "And its parent" with turn name t2, sent while A streams. 1. The person sends A. A turn event says t1 started. 2. A tool event for t1 names the call Bash. A tool-result event for t1 gives its output. 3. The person sends B. No turn event comes, because t1 is still open. The pane shows the waiting mark under B. 4. A chat event for t1 carries the finished reply. The pane puts it under A, above B. 5. A turn event says t1 ended after 12 seconds for 0.04 dollars. A second turn event says t2 started. The waiting mark under B goes away. 6. The agent exits during t2. A turn event says t2 ended because the agent exited. ``` event turn data pane turn t1 started A (1) tool t1 Bash, input A [Bash · 1 call] (2) tool-result t1 output A [Bash · 1 call] (2) B ○ waits (3) chat t1

Done.

A ... Done. (4) turn t1 ended, 12s, $0.04 A ... 12s · $0.04 (5) turn t2 started B (mark gone) (5) turn t2 exited B ended (6) ○ the waiting mark. (n) the step of the example. ```

payload.why: takes the status channel with the thinking state, the running tool and the tokens, and the end line with duration and cost
takes the two events of a text block, which this card extends with the turn name
takes the need to show each call with its input and output, which the tool and tool-result events carry

payload.title: A reply part that arrives with no open turn opens a turn that the server names
payload.why: Every part on the live channel names a turn, but the agent can write when no message waits for an answer. The server has no page-given name for that part, so it gives the turn a name of its own. A name that no page uses cannot match a message, so every page starts a new turn for it.
payload.body:
To keep the rule that every part belongs to a turn, a part that arrives while no sent turn is open opens a new turn. The server names it agent, a dash and a count of such turns since the server started: agent-1, agent-2. The turn starts with that part, and it ends like any other turn, at the end line or at the exit of the agent. A message that the person sends while that turn is open waits behind it.

Example:

- No message is open. The agent writes "Background build done." on its own.
- The person sends message A with turn name t5 a moment later.

1. The part arrives with no open turn. The server opens turn agent-1, and a turn event says agent-1 started.
2. The part goes out under agent-1. No page sent agent-1, so each page starts a new turn for it at the bottom.
3. The person sends A. Turn agent-1 is still open, so A shows the waiting mark.
4. The end line closes agent-1. Turn t5 starts, and the mark under A goes away.

```
 open turns        event                      pane
 []                part, no turn              -                                  (1)
 [agent-1]         turn agent-1 started       agent-1: Background build done.   (2)
 [agent-1, t5]     A sent                     A  ○ waits                         (3)
 [t5]              end agent-1, start t5      A  (mark gone)                     (4)

○  the waiting mark.  (n)  the step of the example.
```

payload.why: takes the turn event that announces the start of the turn the server opens

payload.title: The chat log keeps the open-card line, the person's words, each finished block, and each tool call and its result
payload.why: A later reader of a conversation needs what the agent was told, what it said, and what it did. A streamed token is only an early form of a finished block, so a copy of it would repeat the block. A tool call with its input is the record of an action, and only its own kind keeps it from ever counting as a quote.
payload.body:
To keep the whole conversation readable later, the chat writes one chat log line for each of these, in the order they happen: the open-card line that starts a turn, with the kind tooling; the person's words, spoken by the person; each finished text block of the agent, spoken by the agent; each tool call, with the kind tool_call; each tool result, with the kind tool_result. A tool call line holds the tool name, a space, and the call's input as JSON. A streamed token, a status update and a turn start or end write no line (see #werk-excerpt-chatlog for the kinds).

Example:

- The person sends "Make it three tries" with #retry open.

1. The turn starts. The log gains a tooling line with the open-card line, and a spoken line by the person.
2. The agent streams "Done". Each token goes to the pane only.
3. The agent runs Bash with the command werk show retry. The log gains a tool_call line.
4. The output comes back. The log gains a tool_result line.
5. The block "Done: three tries." finishes. The log gains a spoken line by the agent.

```
 #  speaker  kind         text                                         step
 0  werk     tooling      [the map is now at #retry — ...]             (1)
 1  person   spoken       Make it three tries                          (1)
 -  -        -            D, Do, Don, Done   (tokens: no line)        (2)
 2  agent    tool_call    Bash {"command":"werk show retry"}          (3)
 3  agent    tool_result  card retry [decided] ...                     (4)
 4  agent    spoken       Done: three tries.                           (5)

#  the message position in the chat log.  (n)  the step of the example.
```

payload.why: takes the four kinds of a chat log line and the rule that only a spoken line can hold a quote
takes the chat log of the one conversation that these lines go to
takes the rule that a streamed token is ephemeral and a finished block is kept

payload.title: A chat log line waits until the agent names its session, and an agent that exits first leaves its lines with no session
payload.why: A new agent names its session only in its first output, but the open-card line and the person's words are written before that. A line written at once would have no session, and a quote of it would refuse. An agent that exits before it names a session never will, and its lines must still reach the log.
payload.body:
To give every line of the chat log the session of the agent that heard it, the chat holds each line of a fresh agent in memory until that agent names its session. Then it writes the held lines with that session, in order, and writes each later line at once. If the agent exits before it names a session, the chat writes the held lines with an empty session, so no message is lost. A quote of such a line refuses (see #werk-excerpt-chatlog-fields).

Example:

1. The person sends "Hi". A new agent starts. The open-card line and "Hi" wait in memory.
2. The agent names its session s-1. Both lines go to the log with s-1.
3. The agent replies. The reply goes to the log with s-1 at once.
4. The agent exits. The person sends "Again". A new agent starts, and the two new lines wait.
5. That agent exits before it names a session. The two lines go to the log with an empty session.

```
 #  text                            session   written at
 0  [the map is now at #root ...]   s-1       step 2 (held from 1)
 1  Hi                              s-1       step 2 (held from 1)
 2  Hello.                          s-1       step 3
 3  [still on #root ...]            ""        step 5 (held from 4)
 4  Again                           ""        step 5 (held from 4)
```

payload.why: takes the rule that each line of the one chat log records the session that wrote it
takes the session field of a line and the refusal of a quote whose line has an empty session

payload.title: A turn sent with an id that the map does not hold names the id and says the map holds no such card
payload.why: The page can send an id that is gone by the time the turn starts, for example after a removal in another turn. A refused message would lose the person's words. A line that names the id and says it is not in the map keeps the turn going and tells the agent the truth.
payload.body:
To keep a message from being lost when its open card is not in the map, the turn still goes out. Its open-card line names the id and says that the map holds no card with this id, in place of the compact block. The next turn on the same id gets the usual one-line reminder.

Example:

- The page has #old-retry open. Another turn removed that card.

1. The person sends "Why was this removed?". The turn starts with [the map is now at #old-retry — the map holds no card with this id], then the words.
2. The person sends again with the same id. The turn starts with the one-line reminder on #old-retry.

```
 turn   open id       first line of the turn
 1      #old-retry    [the map is now at #old-retry — the map holds no card with this id]
 2      #old-retry    [still on #old-retry — ...]
```

payload.why: takes the now-at line and the still-on reminder that this card fills for an id the map does not hold

payload.title: The home view has the address /, and the map address with no card opens the card #root
payload.why: The home is the first screen, so it takes the shortest address. The map address with no card keeps its own meaning, the page of the root card, so the home and the root page are two places that Back and Forward can move between.
payload.body:
A person who opens the server with no path sees the home view. The address / names it. The map address with no card opens the page of #root, the same as the map address with the id root.

Example. The map has the cards #root and #how.

1. The person opens /. The home view shows #root and #how side by side.
2. The person clicks the title of #root. The address becomes the map address of root, and the root page opens.
3. The person presses Back. The home view opens again.
4. The person opens the map address with no card. The root page opens, not the home.

```
 /              home: #root | #how
 /map           page of #root
 /map/root      page of #root
 /map/<id>      page of <id>
```

payload.why: the home address joins the list of view addresses that the routes card keeps
the map address with no card opens the root page that this card defines

payload.title: The server computes the header, the search results and the home view, and the page reads them as small replies
payload.why: The path, the counts and the search results need the whole folded map, and the server already holds it. A reply with only the rows the header shows keeps the page from loading every card to compute them.
payload.body:
To avoid sending the whole map to the page, each header part is one read from the server. The read of an open card carries its path from the root and the counts of its subtree, beside the card itself. The search read takes the typed text and returns at most twelve rows, each with the id, the title, the dot color and whether the card is postponed. The home read returns the two columns ready to show.

Example. The person opens the card "Checkout retries".

1. The page reads the card. The reply holds the card, its path Home › Checkout › Checkout retries, and its counts.
2. The person types #check in the search box. The page sends the text. The reply holds the matching rows, exact id first.
3. The person clears the box. The page sends nothing.

```
 page                         server
  | -- card read (id) ------->  |  card + path + counts
  | -- search read (text) --->  |  up to 12 rows
  | -- home read ------------>  |  #root column | #how column
```

payload.why: the replies stay small because the page loads only what it shows
the search read returns the rows that the search box lists
the card read carries the counts that the header strip shows

payload.title: The header row says writing while the agent streams its reply text
payload.why: A text block is neither thinking nor a tool call. Without its own state, the header row keeps the last state, and it can say that a tool runs while the agent writes its answer. A third state, writing, tells the person what the agent does at that moment.
payload.body:
The agent is in one of three states in the header row above the composer: thinking during a thinking block, running a tool during a tool call, and writing during a text block. The state changes when a new block starts. The tokens so far in the turn show with every state.

Example:

- The person sends "Make it three tries".

1. A thinking block starts. The header row says thinking.
2. A tool call to Bash starts. The header row says running Bash.
3. A text block starts. The header row says writing.
4. The turn ends. The header row shows the duration and the cost.

```
 block      header row
 thinking   ● thinking · 3s · 120 tokens       (1)
 tool_use   ● running Bash · 5s · 180 tokens   (2)
 text       ● writing · 7s · 260 tokens        (3)
 end        12s · $0.04                         (4)

●  the pulse of a live turn.  (n)  the step of the example.
```

payload.why: takes the status event with thinking or running, the seconds and the tokens, and adds one state to it

payload.title: The browser keeps the last place on the map, once for each project
payload.why: The last open card and view belong to one person in one browser, so the server does not need to know them. The browser storage keys the place by the project name, so two projects never overwrite each other.
payload.body:
The page holds the project name it shows. Each move on the map, to the home or to a card, writes that address to the browser storage under a key that holds the project name. A Map tab click and a reload with no place in the address read it back. A project with no stored place opens the home.

Example. Two projects, shop and werk.

1. In shop, the person opens the card "Checkout retries". The browser stores its map address under shop.
2. The person clicks the Board tab. The stored place does not change.
3. The person clicks the Map tab. The map opens at "Checkout retries".
4. The person opens werk for the first time. Nothing is stored under werk, so the home opens.

```
 browser storage
  place of shop  ->  map address of checkout-retries
  place of werk  ->  (none, so the home opens)
```

payload.why: each project keeps its own open card and view
the storage key holds the project name, which is its folder name

payload.title: A turn name holds at most 100 characters and does not start with a dot
payload.why: The server copies a turn name into every event of the turn and into the page. A name with no length limit lets one request make every later event large. A name that starts with a dot reads like a hidden file name or a relative path, and no page needs one.
payload.body:
To keep a turn name small and plain, the server takes a turn name of 1 to 100 characters. Each character is a letter, a digit, a dot, a dash or an underscore, and the first character is not a dot. A message with any other turn name is refused, and no turn starts.

Example:

1. The page sends turn name t1. The server takes it.
2. The page sends turn name .t1. The server refuses the message.
3. The page sends a turn name of 101 characters. The server refuses the message.

```
 turn name          result
 t1                 taken      (1)
 .t1                refused    (2)
 xxx...x (101)      refused    (3)
```

payload.why: takes the characters a turn name may hold and adds a length limit and a first character

payload.title: The page names each turn it sends from the time and a count of its own messages
payload.why: Two pages, or one page after a reload, can send at the same time, and a name that two turns share would put a reply under the wrong message. The time of the page load and a count of the messages it sent give a name that no other page makes in practice, with no request to the server first.
payload.body:
To give each sent message a turn name before the server answers, the page builds the name itself: the letter t, the current time in milliseconds in base 36, a dash, and the count of messages this page has sent. The name has only the characters that a turn name allows. A turn that the server names itself starts with agent, so a page name never matches it.

Example:

- The page loads and sends its first message.

1. The person sends "Hi". The page names the turn t followed by the time, then -1.
2. The person sends "Again" a second later. The name ends in -2, and its time part is larger.

```
 message   turn name
 Hi        tmgx1k2p0-1     (1)
 Again     tmgx1kzz3-2     (2)

t  the prefix.  mgx1k2p0  the time in base 36.  -1  the count of messages this page sent.
```

payload.why: takes that the page sends a turn name with each message, and the characters that name may hold
the paused count in the card read counts each card in the subtree that carries the paused mark this card defines

payload.title: The page names each turn it sends from the time and a count of its own messages
payload.why: Two pages, or one page after a reload, can send at the same time, and a name that two turns share would put a reply under the wrong message. The time of the send and a count of the messages the page sent give a name that no other page makes in practice, with no request to the server first.
payload.body:
