To give each sent message a turn name before the server answers, the page builds the name itself: the letter t, the time of the send in milliseconds in base 36, a dash, and the count of messages this page has sent. The name has only the characters that a turn name allows. A turn that the server names itself starts with agent, so a page name never matches it.

Example:

- The page loads and sends its first message.

1. The person sends "Hi". The page names the turn t followed by the time, then -1.
2. The person sends "Again" a second later. The name ends in -2, and its time part is larger.

```
 message   turn name
 Hi        tmgx1k2p0-1     (1)
 Again     tmgx1kzz3-2     (2)

t  the prefix.  mgx1k2p0  the time of the send in base 36.  -1  the count of messages this page sent.
```

payload.why: takes that the page sends a turn name with each message, and the characters that name may hold

payload.title: A message that the server refuses leaves the thread, and its words go back to the composer
payload.why: The pane draws a sent message at once, before the server answers. If the server refuses it, no turn ever starts for it, so a waiting mark under it would wait for ever. The person still needs the words, so they go back to the composer with the reason for the refusal.
payload.body:
To keep the thread true and the words safe, a message that the server refuses, or that never reaches the server, is taken out of the thread. The composer shows the error. If the composer is empty, it gets the words of the refused message back, so the person can send them again. If the person has typed something new since, the composer keeps the new text.

Example:

- The server token in the page is out of date.

1. The person types "Make it three tries" and sends it. The message shows in the thread at once, and the composer empties.
2. The server answers that the token is wrong. The message leaves the thread.
3. The composer shows the error and holds "Make it three tries" again.

```
 step   thread                    composer
 (1)    Make it three tries ○     (empty)
 (2)    (empty)                   (empty)
 (3)    (empty)                   Make it three tries
                                  ! the server answered 403

○  the waiting mark.  !  the error line.  (n)  the step of the example.
```

payload.why: takes that the pane draws a sent message at once and marks it while its turn has not started

payload.title: A chat message with no open card, or an empty one, names the home card
payload.why: The map has no state with no card open, so a message with no card can only come from a page that left the field out. Naming the home card keeps the turn going with the same lines as any other turn. A card field that is not text at all is a broken request, so the server refuses it.
payload.body:
To keep every turn on a card, the server reads the open card of a chat message this way. A missing card or an empty card names the home card. A card that is text names that card. A card of any other type, such as a number, refuses the message, and no turn starts.

Example:

1. A message arrives with no card. Its turn starts on the home card.
2. A message arrives with card "". Its turn starts on the home card.
3. A message arrives with card retry. Its turn starts on #retry.
4. A message arrives with card 3. The server refuses it.

```
 card field   turn starts on
 (none)       home card        (1)
 ""           home card        (2)
 "retry"      #retry           (3)
 3            refused          (4)
```

payload.why: takes that the whole tree is the home card's page, so a turn with no other card names the home card

payload.title: The compact card block puts each fact of the card on its own labelled line
payload.why: The agent reads the block as plain text at the start of a turn. One labelled line per fact lets it find the status or the parent links at a glance, and a fact that the card does not have is left out, not written as empty.
payload.body:
To make the open card easy for the agent to read, the compact block that starts a turn on a changed card has these lines, in this order. The first line names the card by id and title. The second line holds the kind, the status and the person who decides, joined by a dot; a proposed card shows proposed as its status. Then come a why line, a children line and a depends on line. Each of the last three is left out when the card has nothing for it. The children and depends on lines name each card by id and title, separated by semicolons.

Example:

- Card #retry "Checkout retries", decided, who you, with one child #retry-wait and one dependency #checkout.

1. The person opens #retry and sends a message. The turn starts with the block below.
2. The person sends again on #retry. The turn starts with the one-line reminder, and no block.

```
[the map is now at #retry — Checkout retries]                     (1) id and title
kind: card · status: decided · who: you                           (1) state line
why: A failed charge often succeeds a moment later.               (1) left out if empty
children: #retry-wait — Wait between tries                        (1) left out if none
depends on: #checkout — Checkout charges once per order           (1) left out if none

[still on #retry — Checkout retries]                              (2)
```

payload.why: takes that a turn on a changed card carries the full card and every other turn the one-line reminder

payload.title: A collapsed run of tool calls names the latest call by its tool and the first line of its main input
payload.why: The tool name alone does not say what a call did: five Bash calls read the same. The command, the path, the pattern or the address is the part of the input a person recognises. One short line keeps the collapsed run to one row.
payload.body:
To make the one line of a collapsed run say what the agent does, the line shows the tool name of the latest call, then the first non-empty input field among command, file path, path, pattern, url, query and description, in that order. Only the first line of that field shows. A line longer than 80 characters is cut to 79 and ends with an ellipsis. A call with none of these fields shows the tool name only. The count of calls in the run follows.

Example:

1. The agent runs Read on src/a.ts. The line says Read src/a.ts · 1 call.
2. The agent runs Bash with the command werk show retry. The line says Bash werk show retry · 2 calls.
3. The agent runs a tool with no such field, called Task. The line says Task · 3 calls.

```
 run after step   collapsed line
 (1)              ▸ Read src/a.ts · 1 call
 (2)              ▸ Bash werk show retry · 2 calls
 (3)              ▸ Task · 3 calls

▸  the closed run; a click opens every call with its input and output.  (n)  the step.
```

payload.why: takes that a run of tool calls collapses into one line that shows the latest call and a count

payload.title: A message that waits behind a running turn ends with the agent's exit and is not sent again
payload.why: When the agent exits, a message that waits behind the running turn has already gone to that agent, and the agent took it with it. Sending it again to a new agent would start work that the person did not ask for at that moment, and an agent that exits at once would get the same message again and again. So the message ends with the exit, and the person decides whether to send it again.
payload.body:
To keep every start of agent work in the person's hands, an exit of the agent ends every open turn: the running turn and each turn that waits behind it. The server does not keep a waiting message for the next agent. The next agent starts only when the person sends a new message. Nothing is deleted: the words stay in the thread and in the chat log (see #werk-chat-log-parts).

The pane tells the two ends apart. A turn that started and lost its agent says that the agent exited before the reply ended. A turn that never started says that the agent exited before this message got an answer, so the person knows that the message was not answered and can send it again.

The rule comes from the first step of the guideline: the answer that is safest when it turns out wrong. A message that is not sent again costs one more send. A message that is sent again by itself can start work at the wrong moment, or repeat for ever on an agent that cannot start.

Example:

- Message A "Rename the card" runs.
- Message B "And its parent" waits behind A.

1. The agent exits during A. A turn event says A ended because the agent exited. A second turn event says the same for B.
2. Under A, the pane says the agent exited before the reply ended. Under B, the waiting mark goes away, and the pane says the agent exited before this message got an answer.
3. No agent runs. The person sends B again. A new agent starts, and B runs as a new turn.

```
 open turns   event              pane
 [A, B]       agent exits        A  ... the agent exited before the reply ended          (1, 2)
 []                              B  the agent exited before this message got an answer    (1, 2)
 [B']         person sends B     B' And its parent                                        (3)

(n)  the step of the example.  B'  the new turn of the words of B.
```

payload.title: Send each waiting message again to a new agent after the exit
payload.why_not: It starts agent work with no action of the person, and an agent that exits at once gets the same message in a loop. It is less safe when it turns out wrong, and harder to undo than one more send by hand.

payload.title: Take a waiting message out of the thread and give its words back to the composer, as for a refused send
payload.why_not: The message reached the agent, so it was not refused, and taking it out of the thread hides that it was sent. It also needs a new event to the page, which is a larger interface than one more end line.

payload.why: The exit of each open turn reaches the page as the turn event that says the turn ended because the agent exited.
Each message goes as one line to the stdin of the conversation's own agent, so a message that waits is already in the agent that exits.

payload.title: Each header read is a GET request with no token, and its reply is one JSON object with one named field
payload.why: The header reads need an address and a reply shape that the page and the server agree on. A read changes nothing, so a GET with no token is the least privilege that works, and one named field per reply keeps the interface as small as the view needs.
payload.body:
The home read and the search read each have one fixed address under the server's API prefix. Both are GET requests, and neither carries the synchronizer token, because a read changes nothing and starts nothing (see #werk-serve-trust). The search read takes the typed text in a query parameter named q. The home reply is an object whose html field holds the two columns as server-rendered HTML. The search reply is an object whose rows field holds the list of rows. The read of an open card keeps its own address and adds its path and counts to its reply.

The guideline step that chose it: the least privilege that makes the ticket work, then the smallest interface.

Example. The map has the cards #root, #how and #checkout.

1. The page opens the home. It sends GET /api/home. The reply is { html: the two columns }.
2. The person types #check. The page sends GET /api/search?q=%23check. The reply is { rows: [the row of #checkout] }.
3. The person clears the box. The page sends nothing.
4. A page from another site sends the same GET. It reads nothing, because the browser keeps the reply from that site.

```
 page                                   server
  | -- GET /api/home ----------------->  |  { html }          (1)
  | -- GET /api/search?q=%23check ---->  |  { rows: [...] }   (2)
  (1) home read   (2) search read, at most twelve rows
```

payload.title: Send the search text in a POST with a JSON body
payload.why_not: A POST reads as a change, so the token rule would make every keystroke carry the token for no gain. A GET with no token is the smaller privilege.

payload.title: Fold the home and the search results into the reply of the card read
payload.why_not: The search runs on every keystroke and the home has no card. One reply for all three is a larger interface than each view needs.

payload.why: The reads carry no token because the token rule exempts a request that changes nothing.
The search read returns the rows that the search box of the header lists.
The home read returns the two columns that the home view shows.

payload.title: The served page carries the project name in its head, beside the synchronizer token
payload.why: The browser keys the stored place by the project name, so the page needs that name before it decides where a reload with no place opens. The server already fills the page head with the token at each serve, so the name rides along with no extra request.
payload.body:
The server names the project by its folder (see #werk-projects-names). When it serves the page, it writes that name into a meta tag in the page head, next to the meta tag that holds the synchronizer token. The page reads both tags when it starts. A reload with no place in the address reads the stored place under that name before the first draw, so it never draws the home first and then jumps.

The guideline step that chose it: the smallest interface, since the head is already filled at each serve and no new read is added.

Example. One server holds the projects shop and werk.

1. The browser opens shop. The page head holds the token and the name shop.
2. The page reads the name shop and the place stored under it, the map address of checkout-retries. The map opens there.
3. The browser opens werk. The page head holds the name werk. Nothing is stored under werk, so the home opens.

```
 served page head                 browser storage
  token: <random>                  place of shop -> /map/checkout-retries
  project: shop   ---- key ---->   place of werk -> (none, home)
```

payload.title: Read the project name with a separate request when the page starts
payload.why_not: It adds a read, and a reload with no place in the address must wait for it or draw the home first and then jump.

payload.title: Key the stored place by the server address instead of the project name
payload.why_not: One server holds many projects at one address, so two projects would share one key and overwrite each other's place.

payload.why: The name the head carries is the folder name that names the project.
The name goes into the page head the same way the synchronizer token does.

payload.title: The full-path overlay opens right under the breadcrumb line, layered over the rest of the header
payload.why: An overlay drawn on top of the breadcrumb line hides the line the pointer rests on and takes the pointer from it. Opening the overlay just below the line keeps the line visible and under the pointer, while the overlay still floats over the header and pushes nothing.
payload.body:
The overlay with the whole path starts at the bottom edge of the breadcrumb line and is layered over the header row below it and over the view. It belongs to the same hover area as the line, so the pointer can move from the line down into the overlay and click a segment there without the overlay closing. The line itself stays visible and its segments stay clickable while the overlay is open.

The guideline step that chose it: the answer that is safest when it turns out wrong, since nothing the person points at is hidden.

Example. The open card is Card d, four levels under #root.

1. The line shows … › Card b › Card c › Card d.
2. The person rests the pointer on the line. The overlay opens under it: Home › Root › Card a › Card b › Card c › Card d.
3. The person moves the pointer down into the overlay. The overlay stays open.
4. The person clicks Card a in the overlay. Card a opens.
5. The pointer leaves both the line and the overlay. The overlay closes.

```
 header row 1  | … › Card b › Card c › Card d        |  <- line, stays visible (2)
               +-------------------------------------+
               | Home › Root › Card a › Card b › ... |  <- overlay (2), over row 2
 header row 2  | (covered while the overlay is open) |
```

payload.title: Draw the overlay on top of the breadcrumb line
payload.why_not: The overlay hides the line under the pointer and takes the pointer events from it, so the line is no longer what the person points at.

payload.why: The overlay opens below header row 1, which holds the breadcrumbs.

payload.title: A new agent hears the whole open card on its first turn
payload.why: When the agent exits, the next message starts a new agent that has heard nothing of the conversation. A one-line reminder names a card that this agent was never shown, so it would know the id and title but not the card. The whole card costs a few lines once per agent, and an agent that misses the card works blind.
payload.body:
To keep a new agent from working on a card it was never shown, the first turn that a new agent hears always starts with the compact card block of the open card, also when the open card is the same as on the last turn of the agent before it. Every later turn of that agent follows the usual rule: the whole block when the open card changed since its last turn, the one-line reminder when it did not. The last card heard belongs to one agent, not to the conversation, so it starts empty with each new agent.

The rule comes from the first step of the guideline: the answer that is safest when it turns out wrong. A block that the agent did not need costs a few lines. A reminder that the agent cannot resolve leaves it blind to the card, which is the failure that the reminder exists to prevent.

Example:

- The page has #retry "Checkout retries" open.

1. The person sends "Make it three tries". A new agent starts. The turn starts with the whole block of #retry.
2. The person sends "And log each try". The turn starts with [still on #retry — Checkout retries].
3. The agent exits. The person sends "Why did it stop?". A new agent starts. The turn starts with the whole block of #retry again.
4. The person sends "Go on". The turn starts with the one-line reminder.

```
 turn   agent   open card   first line of the turn
 1      a-1     #retry      [the map is now at #retry — Checkout retries] + block   (1)
 2      a-1     #retry      [still on #retry — Checkout retries]                    (2)
 -      a-1     exits
 3      a-2     #retry      [the map is now at #retry — Checkout retries] + block   (3)
 4      a-2     #retry      [still on #retry — Checkout retries]                    (4)

a-1, a-2  the first and the second agent.  (n)  the step of the example.
```

payload.title: The last card heard belongs to the conversation, so a new agent gets the reminder when the card did not change
payload.why_not: A new agent starts with no memory of the conversation, so the reminder names a card it was never shown. That is the blind state that the reminder is meant to prevent, and it is the less safe answer when it turns out wrong.

payload.why: takes the rule that a turn on a changed card gets the whole block and every other turn the one-line reminder
takes the rule that an exit ends the agent and the next message starts a new one

payload.text: The example's line 3 shows [still on #root ...] for the turn of a new agent. Per #werk-chat-fresh-agent-card, a new agent hears the whole block, so that line reads [the map is now at #root ...]. The session rule of this card is not affected; the line text in the example should change if the card is proposed again.

payload.title: An agent's removal is a staged change, and its accept takes the card out
payload.why: An agent never removes a card itself, so its removal must wait on the card like an edit does. One accept event then ends the review and takes the card out, so a restore of the card undoes it the same way as a removal the person made.
payload.body:
To let an agent propose a removal without performing it, the proposal operation also stages a removal of one card, with or without the reparent. The card keeps its words and shows the pending removal in red (see #werk-remove-red). A proposal stages one thing: a removal, or a change to the words, never both.

The accept of a pending removal is the same accepted event as any accept. The fold then takes the card out with the same rules as a removal the person made (see #werk-remove), and the removal is listed under the card, so a restore of the card brings it back. A discard drops the pending removal and the card stays.

Example:

- Card legacy "Legacy importer" is decided and has no children.

1. An agent proposes the removal of legacy. The log gets one proposed event. The card stays in the map, drawn in red.
2. The person clicks the ✓ on legacy. The log gets one accepted event. The card leaves the map.
3. The person restores legacy. The card is back, with no pending change.
4. Had the person not clicked, nothing would change: the card waits in red.

```
step  event       legacy
1     proposed    in the map, red (pending removal)
2     accepted    out of the map
3     restored    in the map, no pending change
```

payload.why: It stages the removal that this card defines, which an agent must propose and never perform.
It uses the proposed, accepted and discarded events that this card defines.

payload.title: Use a log
payload.why: w
payload.body: b

payload.title: Use an append-only log

payload.body: New body text

payload.why: new why

payload.title: T3
Z

payload.text: This card is test data. A review subagent of build werk-67 wrote log lines 12570 to 12578 by mistake, because WERK_LOG pointed at this map. The accept at line 12571 says actor you, but the person did not make it. Remove this card when you want it gone.

payload.title: `werk retitle` and `werk edit --why --body` replace the words of an open card with one event each
payload.why: An open or proto card has no card that depends on it, so its words can change directly. Each change is one more event in the log, so the map shows only the new words and the log keeps the old ones.
payload.body:
```
werk retitle <id> <title>       or: werk retitle <id> --title <title>
werk edit <id> [--why <text>] [--body <text>]
```

- The title comes once: as the argument or with `--title`. Both together are refused.
- Each command prints `<id>: retitled` or `<id>: edited` and adds one event at the end of the log.
- On a ghost the words are frozen. The command refuses and says to discard the ghost and propose it again (#werk-propose-new).
- On a decided card the words are frozen. The command refuses and prints the proposal that stages the change instead (#map-frozen).
- `--why` and `--body` may go with `--who`, `--no-basis` and `--unchallenged` in one edit. On a decided card the whole edit is refused when it changes words.

Example: #a "Use a log" is open.
1. `werk retitle a "Use an append-only log"` prints `a: retitled`. The log has one more line.
2. `werk show a` prints only "Use an append-only log". The earlier line of the log still holds "Use a log".
3. #a is decided. `werk retitle a X` is refused, and nothing is written.

```
 log                                  show a
 +---------------------------------+  +--------------------------+
 | n    proposed  #a "Use a log"   |  | #a "Use an append-only   |
 | n+1  accepted  #a               |->|     log"                 |
 | n+2  retitled  #a "Use an ..."  |  +--------------------------+
 +---------------------------------+
 n = the line of the add; each command adds one line at the end
```

payload.why: The refusal on a decided card comes from the rule that a decided card changes only through a proposal.
The refusal on a ghost comes from the rule that a ghost is frozen.
Each word change is one event at the end of the log, and the fold shows the latest words.

payload.title: `werk retitle` and `werk edit --body` replace the words of an open card with one event each
payload.why: An open or proto card has no card that depends on it, so its words can change directly. Each command writes one event at the end of the log, so the map shows only the new words and the log keeps the old ones.
payload.body:
```
werk retitle <id> <title>
werk edit <id> --body <text>
```

- The title is the second argument, once.
- Each command prints `<id>: retitled` or `<id>: edited` and adds exactly one event at the end of the log.
- A body edit is an edit of its own. Given with `--who`, `--no-basis` or `--unchallenged`, it is refused and nothing is written, so one command never writes two events.
- On a ghost the words are frozen. The command refuses and says to discard the ghost and propose it again (#werk-propose-new).
- On a decided card the words are frozen. The command refuses and prints the proposal that stages the change instead (#map-frozen).

Example: #a "Use a log" is open.
1. `werk retitle a "Use an append-only log"` prints `a: retitled`. The log has one more line.
2. `werk show a` prints only "Use an append-only log". The earlier line of the log still holds "Use a log".
3. `werk edit a --body "The fold reads the log from the top."` prints `a: edited`. The log has one more line, and show prints the new body under the new title.
4. `werk edit a --body X --who you` is refused, and nothing is written.
5. #a is decided. `werk retitle a X` is refused, and nothing is written.

```
 log                                     show a
 +------------------------------------+  +----------------------------+
 | n    proposed  #a "Use a log"      |  | #a "Use an append-only log"|
 | n+1  accepted  #a                  |->|  The fold reads the log    |
 | n+2  retitled  #a "Use an ..."     |  |  from the top.             |
 | n+3  body      #a "The fold ..."   |  +----------------------------+
 +------------------------------------+
 n = the line of the add; each command adds one line at the end
```

payload.why: The refusal on a decided card comes from the rule that a decided card changes only through a proposal.
The refusal on a ghost comes from the rule that a ghost is frozen.
Each word change is one event at the end of the log, and the fold shows the latest words.
A body edit shares the edit command with the records that the edit command card defines, and is refused beside them.

payload.title: A ghost card cannot take its proposed parent as a depends_on basis
payload.why: A proposed card already sits under its proposed parent, so a depends_on link to that parent repeats the refines link, the same as for a real card. A ghost exception would let a link to an ancestor go live on accept, and the map would hold the very link that the rule keeps out. The basis of a ghost through a depends_on link is a card in another subtree; its proposed parent already counts as a basis once decided.
payload.body:
The question: does the ban on a depends_on link to an ancestor or a descendant also hold while the card is a ghost? The answer: yes. A link from a ghost to its proposed parent, or to any card above or below it, is refused at the link and appends nothing. A held link from a ghost goes only to a card in another subtree, and that link goes live when the ghost is accepted, with no second link event.

Example:
- "Storage" is a real card under the root.
- "Engines" is a real card under the root.
- "Use SQLite" is a ghost under "Engines".

1. A link from "Use SQLite" to "Engines" as its basis is refused: "Engines" is above it. The log does not change.
2. A link from "Use SQLite" to "Storage" as its basis is held. Show lists it as held, and "Storage" lists it as from a ghost.
3. The person accepts "Use SQLite". The link is live. The log holds one link event for it.

```
  root
  ├── Storage  ◀───────(2) depends_on, held, live after (3)──┐
  └── Engines  ◀──✗ (1) refused: ancestor                    │
        └── Use SQLite (ghost) ───────────────────────────────┘
```

Chosen by the guideline: safest when wrong and deny by default. It changes no decided card; the other answer narrows a decided rule.

payload.title: A ghost may take its proposed parent as a depends_on basis
payload.why_not: It narrows a decided rule with an exception for one state, and on accept it puts into the map an ancestor link that the rule refuses for every real card. It is the less safe answer if it turns out wrong, because live ancestor links then need a migration to remove.

payload.why: A link naming a ghost is held and goes live with its card on accept, which is the link this card limits to other subtrees.
A ghost loses nothing by the refusal only because a decided parent counts as a basis.

payload.title: A root that is not decided is no basis for the cards under it
payload.why: A new card goes under the root by default, and a fresh project starts with a root that nobody has decided. If that root were a basis, every new card would wait on it, and the decide check would tell the agent to decide the root, which has no basis of its own. So a root that is not decided counts as no basis, and a card under it must name a depends_on link or a written reason that none applies.
payload.body:
A card stands on its parent and on its depends_on targets. While its parent is the root and the root is not decided, the parent drops out: the card does not wait on the root, and the root does not hold its basis fact. Once the root is decided, it is a basis for each card under it again. A parent that is not the root still makes its open children wait (see #map-wait).

Example:

- The map holds the root "Root", not decided, and the decided card B "Jobs run in order" under it.
- The agent adds card Q "Jobs wait in a queue" with no parent, so Q sits under the root.

1. The agent decides Q. The check refuses it and names the missing basis with the depends_on link command, not with a decide of the root.
2. The agent links Q to B with depends_on, and records who, an option and a kill criterion. The decide passes.
3. The agent removes the link from Q to B. The check refuses it, because the open root does not hold the basis of Q.
4. The person decides the root. A new card under the root now has its basis from the root, and nothing waits.

```
 root (open)            root (decided)
  ├ B (decided)          ├ B
  └ Q ──depends_on──▶ B   └ Q    basis: root

 Q's basis = B only      Q's basis = root, plus B if linked
 ──▶ = depends_on link   ├ └ = sits under the root
```

payload.why: takes the basis fact, of which this card names the one parent that does not count
takes the rule that a card waits on an open basis, from which this card excepts an open root
takes the rule that a card with no parent sits under the root, which makes the open root the parent of every new card

payload.title: Showing a removed card says that it is removed and names the restore
payload.why: A removed card is out of the map, but its id stays taken and every event about it stays in the log. A reply that says only that the card is not in the map reads as if the id was never used. Naming the removal tells the reader that the card can come back, and how.
payload.body:
When a show names a card that is out of the map, it prints no card and fails, as for an unknown id. The message says which removal holds the card and names the restore that brings it back. For the card that the removal named, the message says that the card is removed. For a card that went out with another card, the message says that it is removed with that card, and the restore names that card. A card that a removal with the reparent option moved up stays in the map, and its show prints it as usual, with no word of the removal.

Example:

- Card storage "Storage" has the child cache "Cache".
- cache has the child eviction "Eviction".

1. A person removes cache. cache and eviction leave the map.
2. A show of cache fails and says: #cache is removed; restore #cache to bring it back.
3. A show of eviction fails and says: #eviction is removed with #cache; restore #cache to bring it back.
4. A show of an id that no card ever had fails and says that no such node is in the map.

```
show cache     -> #cache is removed; restore #cache ...
show eviction  -> #eviction is removed with #cache; restore #cache ...
show nope      -> no node #nope in the map
```

payload.why: The message names the restore because a removed card's id stays taken and the card can come back, as that card says.

payload.title: The held-out runner may stay silent for 3 minutes before it counts as stuck
payload.why: The held-out runner starts the product and runs long test commands that print nothing until they finish. A 60-second silence limit cancelled most held-out runs before any test ran, and each cancelled run filed a follow-up ticket for a step that never failed. A longer limit for this one agent keeps the 60 seconds for the builder, where silence is a better sign of a stuck session.
payload.body: The silence limit for the held-out runner is 3 minutes, not 60 seconds. The same 3 minutes is the time a running tool call of the held-out runner may use no CPU before the overseer calls it frozen (see #lp-overseer-inflight). The builder, the planner and every other agent keep the limits of #lp-overseer-silence.

payload.why: It raises the frozen-call limit of #lp-overseer-inflight for the held-out runner to the same 3 minutes.
The held-out runner it applies to is the one #st-validate-heldout runs after each merge.

payload.title: The held-out runner may stay silent for 3 minutes before it counts as stuck
payload.why: The held-out runner starts the product and runs long test commands that print nothing until they finish. With a 60-second limit, the overseer cancels most held-out runs before any test result arrives, so the held-out set stays red for a reason that is not in the code. A longer limit for this one agent keeps the 60 seconds for the builder, where silence is a better sign of a stuck session.
payload.body: The silence limit for the held-out runner is 3 minutes, not 60 seconds. The same 3 minutes is the time a running tool call of the held-out runner may use no CPU before the overseer calls it frozen (see #lp-overseer-inflight). The builder, the planner and every other agent keep the limits of #lp-overseer-silence.

payload.why: It raises the frozen-call limit of #lp-overseer-inflight for the held-out runner to the same 3 minutes.
The held-out runner it applies to is the one #st-validate-heldout runs after each merge.

ops.old: When a ticket's merge fails because git cannot merge it, the next build of that ticket starts fresh from the main line's tip, not from the ticket's old branch. The builder gets the conflict output as its last failure. That pass does not count against the retry cap (#st-build-run-mechanics).
ops.new: When a ticket's merge fails because git cannot merge it, the next build of that ticket starts fresh from the main line's tip, not from the ticket's old branch. The builder gets the conflict output as its last failure. That pass does not count against the retry cap (#st-build-run-mechanics).

ops.old: A red check on the merged tree is still the ticket's own failure and still counts.
ops.new: A red check on the merged tree is still the ticket's own failure and still counts.

ops.old: A ticket whose merge conflicts three times in a row stops the merge loop as stuck, so a conflict that never resolves cannot run without end.
ops.new: A ticket whose merge conflicts ten times in a row stops the merge loop as stuck, so a conflict that never resolves cannot run without end. The limit is high because up to three tickets build at once. A ticket that adds a line to a file that most tickets change, such as the list of commands, can lose the race to the main line several times before it merges.

payload.title: A ready, blocked or building ticket can be archived, and a merging or done ticket cannot
payload.why: Archiving is how a person ends a running build, because nothing else returns a building ticket to ready. So the board must accept an archive of a building ticket. A merging ticket is in the merge queue's hands and a done ticket is merged code, so an archive of either is refused.
payload.body:
To let a person end a running build, the board accepts an archive from three columns: ready, blocked and building. It refuses an archive of a merging or a done ticket, both at a write and in the fold, and the log gets no line for it. The archived ticket keeps its column and reason, so a restore puts it back where it was (see #st-ticket-restore). The builder loop of an archived building ticket ends its own build (see #werk-board-control-archive-ends-build). The narrower reading, that only a ready or blocked ticket can be archived, is wrong: it leaves a person no way to end a build in place.

Example. Ticket werk/05 "Save the log" is in building. Ticket werk/06 "Draw the board" is in done.

1. A person archives werk/05. Allowed. It stays in building, archived, and its build ends.
2. An agent archives werk/06. Refused: a done ticket cannot be archived. The log is unchanged.
3. A restore of werk/05 puts it back in building.

```
column     archive
blocked    allowed
ready      allowed
building   allowed  (the build ends)
merging    refused  x
done       refused  x
```
x = refused, no line written.

payload.why: Takes from it that a ready, blocked or building ticket shows the archive action and a merging or done ticket does not.
Takes from it that an archive of a building ticket ends that ticket's build.

payload.title: Only a ready or blocked ticket can be archived
payload.why_not: A person could then not end a running build, since nothing else moves a building ticket back to ready.

payload.title: The command menu lists the slash commands that the agent names when it starts
payload.why: Only the agent knows its whole set of commands: its built-in ones, the project's and the user's own, and those of its plugins. The agent names that set in the first line it writes when it starts, so the server keeps that list and the menu reads it. Before the agent's first start the list is empty, and the menu stays closed.
payload.body:
To avoid a second, partial copy of the agent's command folders, the server keeps the command names from the start line of the most recent agent, and the composer asks the server for them each time a word starting with a slash opens the menu. The menu shows the names that start with the typed text, case ignored.

Example:

- The project has a chat agent that names the commands review, recall and compact when it starts.

1. The person opens the map and types /re before sending any message. No agent has started, so the server holds no names, and no menu opens.
2. The person sends a first message. The agent starts and names its three commands.
3. The person types /re. The menu shows /review and /recall.
4. The person presses Arrow Down and Enter. The word /re becomes /recall and a space.

```
agent start line --(review, recall, compact)--> server keeps the names
composer: /re --(ask for names)--> server --(3 names)--> menu: /review, /recall
```

payload.why: takes that the agent is a spawned claude child speaking stream-json, whose start line carries its command names

payload.title: The server reads the command and skill folders of the project and the user itself
payload.why_not: It repeats the agent's own lookup, misses the built-in and plugin commands, and drifts when the agent changes where it looks. Its only gain is a menu before the first message.

criterion.text: Open a fresh map and type a slash before the first message. If an empty menu there is a real hindrance, read the command folders as the fallback does.

payload.title: The server tells an image's type from its own first bytes
payload.why: The page and the file name can both be wrong: a renamed file or a browser that guesses keeps its claimed type. Each of the four image types starts with a fixed signature, so the server reads those bytes and trusts nothing else. The agent then always opens a real image, and the served file always gets the right type.
payload.body:
To keep a file of another kind out of the attachments folder, the upload is one write request with the image's bytes as they are and the page's token. The server reads the whole body, and drops the bytes past the size cap while it counts them, so an oversized image costs no memory and the page still gets an answer. It then checks the size, then the signature of the first bytes. A stored image gets a name made of the time it came in, a random part, and the extension of the type the signature showed. The answer is that name, or the reason for the refusal, which the chip shows.

Example:

- The person pastes three files: shot.png, a real PNG of 2 MB; logo.png, an SVG file with a PNG name; and big.png, a PNG of 25 MB.

1. shot.png starts with the PNG signature and is under the cap. The server stores it as 2026-10-25T10-11-12-345Z-bf34ecf0.png and answers with that name.
2. logo.png starts with text, not with any of the four signatures. The server refuses it: the file is not a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP image. Nothing is stored.
3. big.png is over 20 MB. The server reads it to the end, keeps none of it, and refuses it with its size.

```
bytes --> size over 20 MB? --yes--> refuse: the image is 25.0 MB
              | no
              v
          first bytes match PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP? --no--> refuse: not an image
              | yes
              v
          store as <time>-<random>.<ext> --> answer: the name
```

payload.title: The server trusts the type that the page sends with the upload
payload.why_not: A renamed file or a wrong browser guess would store a file of another kind as an image, and the agent's read of it would fail or give text. Reading four fixed signatures costs nothing.

payload.why: takes that the upload is a write, so it carries the synchronizer token and a loopback Host

payload.title: A conversation keeps its session, model and context fill in one settings file beside its chat log
payload.why: The session, the model, the advisor and the fill all describe the same conversation, and a server can hold more than one conversation. One file per conversation, named after its chat log, keeps the five values together, so one write never leaves a resumed session on a model it did not run with.
payload.body:
To resume a conversation as it was, the server keeps one small settings file in the same folder as the conversation chat log, with the same name and a different extension. The file holds the session id from the agent init event, the model, the advisor or none, the used tokens of the latest assistant message, and the window size. The server rewrites the whole file when the agent reports its session, when a turn ends, at a model switch and at a clear. It reads the file once, when the conversation starts. This file replaces a single shared session file for the whole folder, because a single file cannot tell two conversations apart.

A missing or broken file, or a model and advisor pair that the selector does not offer, gives the default choice with an empty fill and no session. A dead session clears only the session id and keeps the model and the fill.

Example:

- Conversation main, with chat log main and settings file main.
- The agent reports session s-1 on Opus, no advisor, and a turn ends at 150,000 of 200,000 tokens.

1. The init event arrives. The file now holds s-1 and Opus.
2. The turn ends. The file now holds 150,000 used and a 200,000 window.
3. The server restarts. It reads the file, starts the agent on Opus resuming s-1, and the pie shows 75%.
4. No file exists. The agent starts fresh on the default choice and the pie is empty.

```
chats/main.jsonl   the chat log (one line per message)
chats/main.json    the settings: session s-1, model Opus, advisor none, used 150000, window 200000
                   written at init, turn end, switch, clear; read at start
```

payload.why: the stored session id is the one a restart resumes
the used tokens and the window are the two numbers the pie shows

payload.title: The pane reads the chat settings, switches the model and clears the context through three separate requests
payload.why: The selector and the pie need the settings before the first turn, and a switch or a clear must be able to say no while a turn runs. Separate requests let the pane read the settings at mount, and let a refusal come back as an answer the pane can show. The live channel tells every open page when the settings change, so a second page stays in step.
payload.body:
The pane has three requests to the server. A settings read answers the model, the advisor, the used tokens and the window, and never the session id. A model switch names one choice of the selector by its pinned model id and its pinned advisor id or none, and the server refuses a pair the selector does not offer. A clear takes no value. A switch and a clear both carry the synchronizer token, answer the settings after the change, and answer a conflict with the reason when a turn runs.

After a switch or a clear, the live channel sends a model event with the new settings to every open page, and a clear also sends a cleared event so each page empties its chat. The server does not push the fill after each turn. Instead, a page reads the settings again when a turn ends, because the fill changes only then.

Example:

- Two open pages, A and B, on conversation main, at Sonnet + Opus advisor.

1. A person picks Opus on page A while idle. The server stops the child, answers the new settings, and both A and B show Opus.
2. A person picks Sonnet on page A while a turn runs. The server answers a conflict, and A shows the reason and keeps Opus.
3. A turn ends. A and B read the settings again, and both pies show the new fill.
4. A person clears the context on page B. Both pages get the model event and the cleared event, and both pies show 0%.

```
page A --switch--> server --(idle) stop child, save--> answer: settings
                          --(turn runs)----------------> answer: conflict + reason
server --model event, cleared event--> page A, page B
turn ends --> each page --settings read--> server
```

payload.why: a switch and a clear refuse while a turn runs instead of stopping the child
the advisor value of a switch is the pinned Opus id, not the alias
a switch and a clear change state, so they carry the synchronizer token

payload.title: A clear empties the pane and ends the session, and the chat log on disk keeps every line
payload.why: A clear must make the agent forget the conversation, but the chat log on disk is also where every excerpt of the conversation points. Deleting that file cannot be undone and leaves earlier quotes with nothing to point at. So a clear ends the agent session and empties each open pane, and the file stays as it is.
payload.body:
To give the agent a fresh context without losing the record, a clear forgets in two places and keeps one. The agent forgets: the stored session id goes, so the next message starts a new session with an empty context. The pane forgets: the live channel tells every open page to empty its shown chat. The chat log on disk keeps every line, old and new, because an excerpt points at a message in it and a quote check reads it. The chosen answer is the one that deletes no data and is easiest to undo.

The pane reaches the chat settings at three addresses: a settings read is GET /api/chat/settings, a model switch is POST /api/model, and a clear is POST /api/clear.

Example:

- Conversation main, with chat log main, one finished turn that says hello, and the pie at 10%.
- Page A and page B are open on it.

1. A person clicks Clear context on page A while idle. The server drops session s-1, sets the fill to 0 and stops the child.
2. Page A and page B empty their chat, and both pies show 0%.
3. The chat log main still holds the hello line, so an excerpt of it still matches.
4. The person sends again. The child starts with no resume, as a new session s-2, and its lines go after the old ones in chat log main.
5. A person clicks Clear context while a turn runs. The server refuses, and nothing changes.

```
POST /api/clear --(idle)--> session: s-1 -> none   fill: 10% -> 0%   child: stopped
                            pages A, B: chat emptied
                            chat log main: hello ... (kept)  + later lines of s-2
POST /api/clear --(turn runs)--> refused, nothing changes
```

payload.title: A clear deletes the chat log file of the conversation
payload.why_not: It deletes data that cannot come back, and an excerpt that points at an earlier message of the conversation loses the words it points at.

payload.title: A clear writes a marker line into the chat log, and readers skip every line before it
payload.why_not: It adds a new line kind that every reader of the chat log must learn, and the pane does not read the chat log at all, so the marker serves no reader.

payload.why: the three requests whose addresses this card names, and the cleared event that empties each page
an excerpt points at a message in the chat log, so the log must keep it after a clear

payload.title: The werk server runs the cited-card watch when it starts and each time the decision log grows
payload.why: The watch must see every change, from any writer, before a build starts. The server already follows the decision log for the open pages, so it runs the watch at the same moment. A change written while no server ran is caught when the next server starts, because the watch compares versions and does not need to see each event live.
payload.body:
To avoid a second process that follows the log, the server that serves a project runs the watch of the cited cards. It runs once when the server opens the project, and again each time the decision log grows. The watch is idempotent: a ticket already in blocked with the same reason gets no second move, so a run with nothing new writes nothing.

The server writes each move to blocked, and each cards-cited failure, as one line on its error output. A failure line is written again only when the set of failures changes. A failed run writes its error and does not stop the server.

Example. Ticket app/01 is in ready and cites #app-login at log position 40. No server runs.

1. A person retitles #app-login from the command line. The log grows to position 41. Nothing watches, so app/01 stays in ready.
2. The server starts. The watch runs once: #app-login changed after position 40, so app/01 moves to blocked with the reason that names #app-login and the new words.
3. A note is written on #app-login. The log grows, and the watch runs again. A note does not count, so nothing moves and the server writes nothing.

```
log position:  40 plan    41 retitle    (server start)    42 note
app/01:        ready      ready         blocked           blocked (no new move)
watch runs:    -          -             yes               yes
```

payload.why: the watch runs when the log changes, the same trigger that tells open views the map changed
a failed watch run must not stop the server

payload.title: An image goes up with a POST to the image address and comes back with a GET to the same address by its name
payload.why: The page and the server must agree on one address and one answer shape, or a pasted image never gets its chip. One address for the upload and the read keeps the interface small: the upload carries the token because it writes, and the read carries only the stored name because it changes nothing. A refused image answers its own status with one sentence, so the chip shows the reason as it is.
payload.body:
The upload (see #werk-chat-image-inline-sniff) is a POST to /api/image. Its body is the image bytes as they are, and the token of the page travels in the same header as on every other write (see #werk-serve-trust). A stored image answers 200 with {"name": ...}. A refused image answers 422 with {"error": ...}: one sentence, which the chip shows. The status 422 says that the request was well formed and its content was refused, so the page tells a refused image apart from a refused request, such as 403 for a missing token.

The read is a GET to /api/image with the stored name in the query parameter name. It carries no token. It answers the file with the type that its extension names, or 404 for any name that is not a stored image (see #werk-crash).

Example:

- The person pastes shot.png, a real PNG of 2 MB, and big.png, a PNG of 25 MB.

1. The page sends POST /api/image with the bytes of shot.png and the token. The server answers 200 with {"name": "2026-10-25T10-11-12-345Z-bf34ecf0.png"}.
2. The chip asks GET /api/image?name=2026-10-25T10-11-12-345Z-bf34ecf0.png and shows the thumbnail.
3. The page sends POST /api/image with the bytes of big.png. The server answers 422 with {"error": "the image is 25.0 MB; the limit is 20 MB"}. The chip shows that sentence.
4. A request asks GET /api/image?name= with no name. The server answers 404 and keeps running.

```
page --POST /api/image (bytes + token)--> server --stored-->  200 {name}   (1)
                                                 --refused--> 422 {error}  (3)
chip --GET /api/image?name=<name>------> server --found-->    200 image    (2)
                                                 --no such--> 404          (4)
```

payload.why: gives an address and statuses to the upload whose body and checks that card defines
takes that the upload is a write and carries the token, and that the read needs none
takes that any name which is not a stored image answers 404 and never harms the server

payload.title: A chat message names each image by its token number and stored name, and the server turns each name into a path
payload.why: The page knows a stored image only by the name that the upload answered, and the agent needs a full path to open the file. The server holds the folder, so it builds each path, and a name that it never stored cannot reach the agent. The answer shows each image under its number, so the sent message looks like what the person sent.
payload.body:
A chat message (see #werk-reflink-chat-wire) holds one more field, images: a list with one entry per sent chip. Each entry has n, the number of its token, and name, the name that the upload answered. A message with no image leaves the field out. The server turns each name into the path of the file in the attachments folder, and the turn maps each token to its path (see #werk-shot-chip).

The server answers 400 with one sentence, and starts no agent, when the field is not a list, when an entry lacks a whole token number of 1 or more or a name, or when a name is not a stored image. The HTML of the answer holds the person's words, then one figure per image: the image from the image address, captioned with its token.

Example:

1. The person sends "Why is this red? [Image #1]" with one stored image. The page sends {"text": "Why is this red? [Image #1]", "images": [{"n": 1, "name": "2026-10-25T10-11-12-345Z-bf34ecf0.png"}], ...}.
2. The server finds the file and the turn says [Image #1] = the full path of that file. The answer HTML shows the words, then the image captioned [Image #1].
3. A request names {"n": 1, "name": "secret.png"}, which the folder does not hold. The server answers 400 with "no stored image is named secret.png", and no agent starts.

```
page --{text, images: [{n: 1, name}]}--> server --name -> path--> turn: [Image #1] = <path>   (2)
     <--200 {html: words + figure [Image #1]}--
     --{images: [{n: 1, name: unknown}]}--> server --> 400 {error}, no agent                  (3)
```

payload.why: adds the images field to the chat request and the figures to its HTML answer, which that card defines
takes the token-to-path header that the server builds from the names, and that the sent message shows each image under its number

payload.title: The attachments folder sits beside the map log, ignores every file in it, and is read only by a plain file name
payload.why: Each project keeps its own images, so the folder belongs beside that project's map log. An ignore file inside the folder that matches every file keeps each screenshot out of version control, and the project's own ignore file does not change. A name that can only be one plain file name cannot reach a file outside the folder.
payload.body:
The folder is named attachments and sits in the .werk folder beside the map log. The server makes it when it stores the first image, together with a version-control ignore file whose one pattern matches every file in the folder, the ignore file too.

A stored name starts with a letter or a digit and holds only letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores, with no two dots in a row. Any other name finds no image: an empty name, a dot name, a name with a slash, or a traversal such as ../log.jsonl. Its read answers 404 (see #werk-crash).

Example:

1. A project has a map log and no attachments folder. The person pastes a PNG. The server makes the folder and the ignore file, and stores the image there.
2. A status of version control in the project shows no new file.
3. A request asks for the name ../log.jsonl. The name is not a plain file name, so the server answers 404 and reads nothing.

```
.werk/
  log.jsonl
  attachments/
    .gitignore      (one pattern: *)
    2026-10-25T10-11-12-345Z-bf34ecf0.png
read "2026-...png"   --> the file
read "../log.jsonl"  --> 404
```

payload.why: takes that every name which is not a file inside the folder answers 404

payload.title: The composer reads the command names with a GET to the commands address, with no token
payload.why: The menu needs the names that the server keeps from the agent's start line. A read changes nothing and starts nothing, so it needs no token, and one named field keeps the answer as small as the menu needs.
payload.body:
Each time a word that starts with a slash opens the menu, the page sends GET /api/commands. The answer is 200 with {"commands": [...]}: the names that the server keeps (see #werk-chat-cmdmenu-source). The page keeps the names that start with the typed text.

Example:

1. No agent has started. The person types /re. The page sends GET /api/commands and gets {"commands": []}. No menu opens.
2. After the first message, the person types /re again. The answer is {"commands": ["review", "recall", "compact"]}, and the menu shows /review and /recall.

```
composer: /re --GET /api/commands--> server --> {commands: [...]} --> menu: names that start with "re"
```

payload.why: reads the list of names that card says the server keeps
carries no token because the token rule exempts a request that changes nothing

payload.title: The card menu shows the cards that the map's id search finds for the typed text
payload.why: The header search already ranks card ids for a text that starts with a hash, with the exact id first. The menu reads that same search, so a card ranks the same in the composer and in the header, and only one ranking must stay right.
payload.body:
Each time the word that starts with # changes, the page sends the search read of the header with the word, hash included (see #vi-layout-header-read-wire). The menu lists the id and the title of each row in the order of the reply (see #vi-jump-hash). A pick replaces the word with the hash, the id and a space.

Example:

- The map holds werk, werk-chat and werk-shots.

1. The person types #wer. The page sends the search read for #wer. The menu lists werk first, then werk-chat and werk-shots, each with its title.
2. The person presses Arrow Down and Enter. The word #wer becomes #werk-chat and a space.
3. The person types #zzz. The search finds nothing, and no menu opens.

```
composer: #wer --search read "#wer"--> server --rows--> menu: #werk, #werk-chat, #werk-shots
Arrow Down + Enter --> text: "#werk-chat "
```

payload.why: takes the id-only match and the ranking with the exact id first
reads the search through the address and reply shape that card defines

payload.title: A word with a second slash, hash or backtick after its trigger opens no menu
payload.why: A path such as /src/app starts with a trigger but is not a command. No command name and no card id holds a slash, a hash or a backtick, so such a word can match nothing, and the menu stays closed instead of showing a list that cannot fit.
payload.body:
The composer looks at the word that ends at the caret. When the word starts with a slash or a hash and the rest of it holds a slash, a hash or a backtick, no menu opens.

Example:

1. The person types /src. The command menu opens for src.
2. The person goes on to /src/app. The word holds a second slash, and the menu closes.
3. The person types #a#b. The word holds a second hash, and no card menu opens.

```
/src       --> command menu, query "src"
/src/app   --> no menu (second /)
#a#b       --> no menu (second #)
```

payload.title: A word with a second slash, hash or backtick after its trigger opens no menu
payload.why: A path such as /src/app starts with a trigger but is not a command. No command name and no card id holds a slash, a hash or a backtick, so such a word can match nothing, and the menu stays closed instead of showing a list that cannot fit.
payload.body:
The composer looks at the word that ends at the caret. When the word starts with a slash or a hash and the rest of it holds a slash, a hash or a backtick, no menu opens.

Example:

- The agent named the commands review and recall when it started.

1. The person types /re. The command menu shows /review and /recall.
2. The person goes on to /re/x. The word holds a second slash, and the menu closes.
3. The person types #werk#chat. The word holds a second hash, and no card menu opens.

```
/re          --> command menu: /review, /recall
/re/x        --> no menu (second /)
#werk#chat   --> no menu (second #)
```

payload.why: takes that the command names come from the agent's start line, and a name of that list holds no slash

payload.title: A model switch and a clear refuse from the moment a message is sent until its reply ends
payload.why: A switch and a clear stop the agent process. A message that waits behind a running reply is already queued for that process, so a stop would drop it with no answer. So both refuse while any sent message has no finished reply, and the pane locks the selector and the clear button for the same span.
payload.body:
A turn is open from the moment the person sends its message, not only from the moment the agent starts on it (see #werk-chat-turn-id for the order of open turns). A model switch or a clear is refused while any turn is open. The pane disables the model selector and the Clear context button for the same span: while a reply streams, and while a sent message still shows its waiting mark. The server refusal stays the real guard, so a second page that did not see the message gets a conflict answer with the reason.

Example:

- Conversation main, idle, on Sonnet + Opus advisor.
- Message A "Summarise the open cards" and message B "Also list the ghosts".

1. The person sends A. The selector and Clear context go grey.
2. The person sends B while reply A streams. B shows its waiting mark. The controls stay grey.
3. Reply A ends. The agent starts B. The controls stay grey.
4. Reply B ends. No turn is open. The selector and Clear context work again.
5. A second page, open before step 1, picks Opus during step 2. The server answers a conflict, and nothing changes.

```
send A        reply A streams     send B (waits)     reply B streams     B ends
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
controls: grey from send A ................................ until B ends -> active
server:   switch/clear -> conflict anywhere in this span
```

payload.why: the open turns, from send to end line, are the span in which a switch and a clear refuse
the switch and the clear requests and their conflict answer are what this card says when to refuse

criterion.text: A person who loses a queued message after a switch, or who finds the controls locked with no reply pending, shows the span is wrong; the fix is a small code change.

payload.title: Only an agent that exits before it names its session is retried or replayed
payload.why: A crash before the agent names its session means no message reached it, so starting it again repeats nothing. After the agent names its session or writes any part of a reply, it may already have run tools or edited files, and a second run would do that work twice. So only the first kind of exit is retried or replayed, and the second kind ends the open turns and leaves the next send to the person.
payload.body:
To retry without repeating work, the chat sorts each exit of the agent that werk did not cause into early or late. An exit is early when the agent wrote nothing of a turn before it: no init event with its session id and no part of a reply. An error result that comes before any output counts as nothing written, so it is not a finished turn. Only an early exit goes to the crash rules: the dead-session replay, the one retry, or the stop for a failure that a retry cannot fix (see #werk-crashmsg and #werk-fullerr). A late exit is never retried. The stored session id stays, the open turns end, and the oldest one shows the whole error output. The rule comes from the first step of the guideline: the answer that is safest when it turns out wrong. A late exit that is not retried costs one more send. A late exit that is retried can run a tool or an edit a second time.

Example:

- Conversation main, with stored session s-1, and the message A "Rename the card".

1. The agent exits with a login error before its init event. The exit is early. No retry runs, and the pane shows the error and asks the person to fix it.
2. The agent exits with an unknown error before its init event. The exit is early. One retry runs on s-1 with message A.
3. The agent names s-1, edits a card, then exits with an error. The exit is late. Nothing runs again, s-1 stays stored, and turn A ends with the whole error.
4. The agent names s-1 and finishes reply A, and later exits with no error while idle. The exit is late, and no turn is open, so nothing shows.

```
spawn ──> [no init, no reply part] ──exit──> early: dead-session replay | retry once | fix first
      ──> init s-1 / reply part ───exit──> late:  open turns end, whole error, s-1 kept, no rerun
```

payload.title: Retry any exit while a turn is open, early or late
payload.why_not: A late exit may come after the agent ran a tool or edited a file, so a retry with the same message can do that work twice; the guideline picks the answer that is safest when it turns out wrong.

payload.title: Call an exit early only when it comes before the init event, and ignore reply parts
payload.why_not: It gives the same answer in every normal run, because the init event comes first, but a reply part that arrives without an init event would then be repeated by a retry; counting any output as written is the safer reading.

payload.why: a late exit is a death of the child, and the dead mark and its line come from that card
an early exit that a retry cannot fix stops by the rule of that card

payload.title: The pane reads the open asks and sends each answer through two separate requests
payload.why: A page that opens while an ask waits must still show it, so the open asks need their own read. An answer must reach exactly one ask, and a second answer to the same ask must change nothing, so the server refuses an answer to an ask that is no longer open instead of sending it to the agent.
payload.body:
The pane reaches the asks at two addresses. A read of the open asks is GET /api/chat/asks, and it returns every ask that waits for the person. An answer is POST /api/ask with the id of the ask, a decision (allow, always, deny, or answer for a question) and, for a question, the labels picked for each question.

The server refuses an answer with a conflict status when the ask is not open: it has its answer already, or its agent exited. It also refuses always on an ask with no widening suggestion, and answer on an ask that is not a question. A refused answer sends nothing to the agent.

Example:

- Conversation main. Its agent asks to run the call X "rm build". The ask has the id a-1.
- Page P opens after the ask arrived.

1. Page P reads the open asks and gets a-1. It shows the ask bar for X.
2. The person clicks Allow once. The pane sends the answer allow for a-1. The server writes the allow to the agent and closes a-1.
3. A second click, or a second page, sends allow for a-1 again. The server refuses it with a conflict, and the agent gets nothing.
4. No ask waits. A read of the open asks returns an empty list.

```
GET  /api/chat/asks                 -> [a-1]
POST /api/ask {a-1, allow}          -> 200, agent gets allow for a-1, a-1 closed
POST /api/ask {a-1, allow} (again)  -> 409 conflict, agent gets nothing
```

payload.why: the buttons and the one-answer rule whose clicks these requests carry
the question answer whose picked labels the answer request carries
an answer changes state, so it needs the synchronizer token

payload.title: The live channel carries an ask event when an ask waits and an answered event when it closes
payload.why: Every open page of a conversation must show an ask the moment it arrives, and must remove it the moment any page answers it. Otherwise a second page keeps showing buttons for an ask that is already closed. One event for each change keeps every page in step without a new read.
payload.body:
To keep each page's ask bar in step with the server, the server sends two kinds of event on the live channel that a page already holds. An ask event carries the whole ask: its id, the tool, the call, the CLI's reason, and the rule that Always allow would add. An ask-answered event carries only the id of an ask that closed, by an answer from any page or by the exit of its agent. A page that opens later reads the open asks once and then follows the events.

Example:

- Conversation main. Page P1 and page P2 are open on it.

1. The agent asks to run the call X. The server sends ask with id a-1 to P1 and P2. Both show the bar for X.
2. The person clicks Deny on P1. The server sends ask-answered with id a-1 to P1 and P2. Both remove the bar.
3. No ask waits and nothing closes. The server sends no ask event.

```
agent asks X   --> ask {id: a-1, tool, call, reason, rule} --> P1, P2 show the bar
Deny on P1     --> ask-answered {id: a-1}                  --> P1, P2 remove the bar
```

payload.why: the bar whose contents the ask event carries
the pending ask on its tab, which the events keep current in every page

payload.title: A question's answer is logged with its own decision, answer, not as a deny
payload.why: The answer to a question travels to the agent as a refusal, because the permission channel has no field for an answer. If the ask log recorded it as deny, a count of refusals would include every normal reply to a question and mislead anyone who reads the log to decide which rules to widen. So the log names a fourth decision, answer, beside allow, always and deny.
payload.body:
To keep a picked answer from counting as a refused call, the ask log writes the decision answer for a question that the person answered. A question that the person declined is written as deny, because the person refused it. An answer widens nothing, so its line lists no added rules.

Example:

- The agent asks Q "Which database?" with the options A Postgres and B SQLite.

1. The person picks A and clicks Submit answer. The agent gets the refusal reason For "Which database?": Postgres. The log line has the decision answer and no added rules.
2. The agent asks the same question again, and the person clicks Decline. The log line has the decision deny.
3. The agent asks to run the call X, and the person clicks Deny. The log line has the decision deny, as before.

```
Submit answer on Q --> agent: refusal reason 'For "Which database?": Postgres' --> log: decision answer
Decline on Q       --> agent: refusal                                         --> log: decision deny
Deny on call X     --> agent: refusal                                         --> log: decision deny
```

payload.why: the ask log and its decision field, to which this card adds the value answer

payload.title: The allow file holds one entry per conversation, each with its own rules and folders
payload.why: Always allow choices must apply only in the conversation where the person gave them, and they must survive a restart. One file keyed by conversation keeps each conversation's choices apart while a relaunch reads only its own entry. Rules and folders stay in two lists because the agent receives them as two different start options: allowed tools and added directories.
payload.body:
To keep Always allow choices apart per conversation, the allow file in the project's werk folder is one JSON object. Each key is a conversation name. Each value holds two lists: rules, the tool rules the CLI suggested, and dirs, the folders it suggested to add. An Always allow click adds the suggestion of its ask to the entry of its own conversation, and each rule or folder appears once. A relaunch of a conversation's agent reads only that conversation's entry and starts the agent with its rules as allowed tools and its folders as added directories. A missing file, or a file that is not a JSON object, counts as no choices.

Example:

- Conversation main. Its agent asks to run the call X "npm test", with the suggestion rule R "Bash(npm test:*)".
- Conversation fork-a has no choices.

1. The person clicks Always allow on X. The entry main gets R. The live agent of main allows R at once.
2. The agent of main asks for X again. The CLI allows it without an ask.
3. The server restarts. The agent of main starts with R allowed. The agent of fork-a starts with no rule.
4. The person clicks Always allow on X again in main. R is already in the entry, so the entry does not change.

```
allow file: { "main": { "rules": ["Bash(npm test:*)"], "dirs": [] } }
relaunch main   --> allowed tools: Bash(npm test:*)
relaunch fork-a --> no entry --> nothing allowed
```

payload.why: the rule that Always allow choices are kept per conversation, which the file's keys carry out
the mechanism that writes the file and merges it into the live process in one step

payload.title: A plus button at the end of the tab strip starts an empty conversation on the open card
payload.why: A person needs one visible control to open a second conversation. While forking waits, a new conversation starts with no history, so a plain button is enough. The open card becomes the new conversation's home card, so the button needs no other input.
payload.body:
The tab strip ends with a + button. A press starts a new conversation whose home card is the card open in the map, adds its chip at the end of the strip and moves the focus to it. The new conversation starts no agent until its first message, and that agent starts with an empty session.

Example: the map shows #retry "Checkout retries", and the strip holds one chip, main.

1. The person presses +. A chip #retry appears after main and takes the focus. No agent runs yet.
2. The person sends a message in #retry. Its own agent starts and gets #retry as its home card.
3. The person presses + again on #retry. A second chip #retry-2 appears.
4. The person clicks main. Nothing starts; main shows its own thread.

```
[ main ][ #retry ][ #retry-2 ][ + ]
   1        2          3        4
1 the first conversation, with no home card
2 started on #retry, its own agent
3 a second start on the same card gets a number
4 the button that starts the next one on the open card
```

payload.why: each conversation the button starts gets its own agent process, which that card requires

ops.old: Two sources show a tool call that is still running:
ops.new: Three sources show a tool call that is still running:

ops.old:
1. The tool-call stream. A call that has started and has no result yet is in flight. The overseer knows the tool, its input, and its start time.
2. The operating system. A shell call is a process tree. For each process the overseer reads the CPU time, the state, the output written, and the open files and network connections.
ops.new:
1. The tool-call stream. A call that has started and has no result yet is in flight. The overseer knows the tool, its input, and its start time.
2. The operating system. A shell call is a process tree. For each process the overseer reads the CPU time, the state, the output written, and the open files and network connections.
3. The agent's event stream. While a call is in flight the agent itself is quiet, so any new event on the stream comes from the work in flight: a message of a subagent, or the start of another call.

ops.old: Together they tell working from frozen:
ops.new: Together they tell working from frozen:

ops.old:
| CPU time | Output | Open connections | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| grows | any | any | working |
| flat | grows | any | working |
| flat | flat | one, to a host that does not answer | frozen on I/O |
| flat | flat | none | frozen on a wait that never ends, such as a promise that never resolves |
ops.new:
| CPU time | Output | Open connections | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| grows | any | any | working |
| flat | grows | any | working |
| flat | flat | one, to a host that does not answer | frozen on I/O |
| flat | flat | none | frozen on a wait that never ends, such as a promise that never resolves |

ops.old: "Flat" means no change for 60 seconds, the same starting value as #lp-overseer-silence. The first runs show whether it needs to change.
ops.new: "Flat" means no change for 60 seconds, the same starting value as #lp-overseer-silence. The first runs show whether it needs to change. Output covers the output of the process tree and any new event on the stream. A subagent call runs inside the agent's own process and has no process tree of its own, so its events on the stream are the only sign that it works. Every new event starts the flat window again.

ops.old: A frozen call is cancelled. The agent gets the cancel as the call's result, with the evidence, and continues.
ops.new: A frozen call is cancelled. The agent gets the cancel as the call's result, with the evidence, and continues.

ops.old: The watch covers every agent session that can run a tool, not only the builder: the grader, the reviewers, and the held-out binder (#lp-heldout-binder) too. The binder is the session that needs it most. It runs the whole held-out suite, often end-to-end browser tests, and that run prints nothing for minutes. Without the watch, the silence limit cancels it mid-run and every step comes back not run.
ops.new: The watch covers every agent session that can run a tool, not only the builder: the grader, the reviewers, and the held-out binder (#lp-heldout-binder) too. The binder is the session that needs it most. It runs the whole held-out suite, often end-to-end browser tests, and that run prints nothing for minutes. Without the watch, the silence limit cancels it mid-run and every step comes back not run.

ops.old: A test runner with a per-test timeout catches most frozen tests first. The overseer catches what the runner does not: a hang outside any test, a runner with no timeout, or a command that is not a test.
ops.new: A test runner with a per-test timeout catches most frozen tests first. The overseer catches what the runner does not: a hang outside any test, a runner with no timeout, or a command that is not a test.

payload.title: Skip subagent calls in the frozen-call check, and let the session's wall-clock limit stop a hung subagent
