payload.why_not: A hung subagent then runs to the session's wall-clock limit, though its events on the stream already show whether it works.

payload.title: Count only the stream events that carry the id of the running subagent call
payload.why_not: It needs each event matched to its call and gives the same reading: while a call runs, the agent itself writes nothing, so every new event comes from the work in flight.

criterion.text: Revisit when a subagent that loops, writing events but making no progress, holds a session open until its wall-clock limit instead of being cancelled.

payload.why: v0 writes the one append-only pipeline log that #ms-store defines.
A red step in the log carries the gate and the cause that #ms-fail requires.
Who sets the cause of a red step comes from #ms-fail-cause.
Transcripts and full check output sit beside the log as #ms-store-files says.
The retry cap reads the log to skip a pass that ended on a spec gap, as #st-build-cap-spec-gap requires.

criterion.text: A report over the log is additive: it reads events that v0 already writes, so adding one later changes nothing that exists.

payload.title: With one conversation per project, a dead agent is marked in its own chat header row
payload.why: The tab chip and the other panes' dead-child bar that mark a dead agent belong to the postponed multichat, so v0 needs one place for the mark.
payload.body: A child that exits without werk stopping it marks its conversation dead until the next child starts. With one conversation per project and no tabs, the mark sits in the chat header row of that conversation, beside the turn state, and the pane shows the whole error. No other pane shows a line for it. The next message starts a new child and clears the mark.

payload.title: Each pipeline agent runs on the model that its role needs
payload.why: Most of the pipeline's cost comes from the agents that run many times per ticket: builder passes, reviewers and held-out runs. Opus stays where one mistake spreads to every later step or where a result is judged: the plan and the grader. The builder gets Sonnet with Opus as an advisor for the difficult parts, and the narrow or mechanical roles get Sonnet alone.
payload.body:
To keep cost down without weakening the gates, the pipeline picks the model of each agent from its role, not from one default.

| Role | Model |
| --- | --- |
| Spec writer, ticket writer | Opus |
| Grader | Opus |
| Builder | Sonnet, with Opus as advisor |
| Reviewers of each quality area | Sonnet |
| Held-out binder, step author | Sonnet |
| Overseer classifiers | Sonnet |

A role that is not in the table, such as the chat agent, keeps the default model of its own setting. The chat agent's model is chosen in the chat header (see #werk-model-select).

A weak builder result does not pass unseen: the grader and the checks still judge it on Opus. A weak plan has no such gate after it, so the planners stay on Opus.

payload.why: It picks the model from the role name that every pipeline agent carries.
It reuses the model choices that #werk-model-select offers, Sonnet with an Opus advisor among them.
It keeps Opus on the grader because the builder loop of #st-build-ticket relies on the grader to catch a weak pass.

payload.title: Every pipeline agent runs on Opus
payload.why_not: The roles that run many times per ticket, builder passes, reviewers and held-out runs, carry most of the cost, and their work does not need the strongest model when a gate on Opus checks it.

payload.title: The grader runs on Sonnet with an Opus advisor
payload.why_not: The grader is the gate that catches a weak Sonnet build. A weaker gate passes gaps that come back later as rework, and it saves little, because the grader is a small share of the cost.

payload.title: The builder stays on Opus, and only the reviewers and the held-out roles move to Sonnet
payload.why_not: Builder passes are the largest pipeline cost after the chat, so keeping them on Opus leaves most of the saving out.

criterion.text: Revisit when the share of tickets that go green on the first pass, or the share of tickets that reach the retry cap, gets clearly worse than in the runs with an Opus builder.

payload.why: v0's own pipeline picks each agent's model from its role, as #st-model-per-role sets.

payload.title: A plan's copy also keeps the answer records that each writer returned
payload.why: Two plans of one subtree can differ in the decisions their writers proposed, and the proposed cards alone do not show which plan wrote which answer.
payload.body: When a plan ends, its copy folder beside the pipeline log holds the spec and the tickets it wrote or changed, and also the list of answer records that the spec writer and the ticket writer returned. A comparison of two plans then shows which answers each plan added. The copy is a record only: no plan or build reads it, and git does not track it.

payload.title: In v0, every recorded kill criterion shows the state recorded, in the neutral look
payload.why: v0 records kill criteria but watches none of them, so it has no fired or unmonitored state to show, and the word monitored would claim a watch that does not run.
payload.body: The kill criteria section on a card page shows a state chip on each row. Because v0 builds no scheduled check, no event trigger and no review-date trigger, every criterion's chip reads recorded, with the neutral border. The fired and unmonitored looks arrive with the watch that sets those states.

payload.title: A pipeline session's cost includes every subagent and fork it started
payload.why: A session's own record holds only its main thread. Workers and subagents that it starts write separate records, so a cost read from the main record alone understates the builder and the held-out binder by about half. Summing the whole tree when the step ends, and writing the sum to the log, keeps the figure after the transcripts expire.
payload.body:
Problem: a pipeline session may start worker forks and subagents. Each one bills on its own and writes its own record, apart from the session's record. The step-end cost then counts only the main thread.

Answer: when a pipeline session ends, the cost is the sum of the main thread and every subagent and fork under it. The step-end event holds that sum, split by token kind, and the count of responses it covers. Cost and tokens follow the rule of #ms-cost. A response that appears in two records counts once.

A past session is rebuilt the same way from the transcripts that its temporary worktree left behind (#ms-cost-history). The worktree is found by the id of the build.

Example.
- Builder session of ticket T ("build one ticket")
- Two worker forks that the builder started
1. The builder's main thread costs $3. The step ends and the old figure is $3.
2. Each fork cost $2 in its own record. The sum is $7.
3. The step-end event now holds $7 with a count of 3 records.
4. A rerun of the backfill finds the event and adds nothing.

```
session T ─┬─ main thread  $3
           ├─ fork 1       $2   ──► step-end event: $7, 3 records
           └─ fork 2       $2
```

payload.why: The sum is written to the pipeline log as the cost of the step-end event.
A past session is rebuilt from transcripts by the backfill rule of this card.

payload.title: Keep the main-thread cost and mark pipeline cost as a lower bound
payload.why_not: The stage panel then keeps understating the builder and the held-out binder, the two largest pipeline stages, and nothing in the panel says by how much.

payload.title: The total cost is the project's own spend: every plan turn and every pipeline session
payload.why: A cost per stage cannot say what the project cost in all. One total that adds plan turns and pipeline sessions, each counted once, answers it and lets every breakdown be checked against it. Spend on other projects is not this project's cost, so it stays out.
payload.body:
The total for a window is the sum of two kinds of event in the pipeline log: plan turns (chat and terminal turns that wrote to the map) and pipeline sessions (builder, grader, reviewers, held-out binder, overseer, spec and ticket writers). A build's own rollup event is not added, because it repeats its sessions. Every breakdown of cost adds up to this total. A session with no price for its model counts as zero and is listed beside the total.

Sessions on this machine that belong to other projects are not read and not counted.

```
total = plan turns + pipeline sessions
      = chats + terminal turns + (builder + binder + reviewers + grader + others)
```

payload.why: A pipeline session counts at the tree sum that this card defines, so the total is not low.
Plan turns enter the total as the events that this card writes.

payload.title: Show a grey remainder line with other Claude Code spend on the machine
payload.why_not: The remainder would be read from transcripts at report time, so it shrinks as transcripts expire and never matches a past report. It is also not a cost of this project.

payload.title: Record every Claude Code session on the machine in the log
payload.why_not: The log would hold work that is not the project's, and a reusable tool would read every other repository of its user.

payload.title: Cost adds up per chat, per ticket and per spec, each from the same events
payload.why: The plan-turn event names its conversation and card, and every pipeline session names its ticket and build. So each unit is a sum over events that exist, and no new recording is needed. Showing all four units answers where the money went for a person who thinks in chats, in tickets or in plans.
payload.body:
Per chat: the turns of one conversation, with its home card and the number of turns. A conversation that started over counts as one chat; its sessions add up.

Per ticket: every session of every build of the ticket, green or red, and the merge loop's sessions. A red build is real cost, so it counts. The held-out binder works for a set of tickets, so it is a row of its own beside the tickets, not split between them.

Per spec: the spec writer and ticket writer sessions, plus the tickets of that spec (see #st-spec).

Per card: as #ms-cost already says.

Each unit shows dollars, tokens by kind, wall time and the count of sessions. Each unit's rows add up to the total of #ms-cost-total, with a row for events that name no unit.

payload.why: Every unit's rows must add up to the total that this card defines.
A ticket's cost uses the session cost that includes subagents and forks.
Per-ticket effort of green builds already exists there; this card adds the red builds.

payload.title: Panel: where did the money go?
payload.why: One total, then bars that split it by the unit a person asks about, answer the question before any trend does. Big bars compare the groups, small bars show each row's share inside its group, and a click opens the sessions behind a row.
payload.body:
Marks. A header shows the total for the window (#ms-cost-total). Under it, one group per kind of work: plan chats, terminal turns on the map, and the pipeline with a row for each role (builder, held-out binder, reviewers, grader, overseer, writers). A group's big bar is its share of the largest group. A row's small bar is its share inside the group. Each row shows dollars and percent of the total.

Units. A selector switches the rows between roles, chats, tickets, specs and cards (#ms-cost-rollup). The total stays the same in every unit.

Legend. Each group has one plain line saying what its rows are. A row names its session count on hover.

Outlier. A row whose cost in the window is above the median to 90th percentile band of the same row in earlier windows is drawn in the outlier colour (#vi-flow-ms-ref).

Drill-down. A row opens the chats, tickets or transcripts behind it. A card opens on the map.

Window. The window of #vi-measure-scope sets the range.

Example.
- Window "last 30 days", unit "role"
- Group "Pipeline" with rows builder and reviewers
1. The header reads the total of both groups.
2. The pipeline group's big bar is full, because it is the largest.
3. The builder row's small bar shows its share of the pipeline group.
4. A click on the builder row lists its tickets, largest first. With no sessions in the window the group shows no rows.

```
$TOTAL  (window)
Pipeline          ████████████████ $a · p%
  builder         ████████ $b · q%      [q = b / a]
  reviewers       ████ $c · r%
Plan chats        ████████ $d · s%
  #root           ███ $e · t%
```

payload.why: The header shows the total that this card defines.
The unit selector switches between the units that this card defines.
The outlier colour uses the reference band that this card defines.

payload.title: Past pipeline sessions are rebuilt from transcripts when the log has no tree sum for them
payload.why: Builds from the last weeks ran before the log recorded the cost of subagents and forks. Their transcripts are still on disk, so the same tree sum can be written for them now. Transcripts expire after 30 days, so the rebuild is worth running once, soon.
payload.body:
For each past session event in the log, the backfill finds the transcripts of the build's temporary worktree by the build's id, sums the main thread and every subagent and fork (#ms-cost-tree), and appends a correction event. The original event stays in the log. The fold takes the latest cost for a session. A session with no transcript left keeps its old figure and is listed as not rebuilt.

A rerun skips a session that has a correction. The window starts at the oldest build with a surviving transcript.

```
log:  session event  $3   (main thread only)
disk: main $3 + fork $2 + fork $2
log:  + correction   $7   ← the fold reads this one
```

payload.why: The correction event holds the tree sum that this card defines.

payload.title: Panel: where did the money go, and how does the split change by day?
payload.why: One total, then a stacked bar for each day that shows each part's share of that day's cost, answers where the money went and whether the split shifts. Bars of equal height compare days that cost very different amounts. A click on a segment opens the sessions behind it.
payload.body:
Header. The total for the window (#ms-cost-total), and each part's dollars and share of the total, as one line per part.

Chart. One bar for each day in the window. Every bar has the same height, 100% of that day's cost. A segment is one part, and its height is the part's share of that day. A segment shows its dollars on hover, with the day's total. A day with no cost has no bar.

Parts. The unit selector sets what a segment is: role, chat, ticket, spec or card (#ms-cost-rollup). The default is role, with plan chats, terminal turns, builder, held-out binder, reviewers, grader, overseer and writers. In a unit with many rows, the six largest rows over the window get their own segment and the rest form one segment, other. A part keeps the same colour and the same place in the stack on every day.

Legend. One line per part with its cost over the window. A click hides or shows that part, and the bars then re-scale to 100% of what is shown. The legend is always open.

Outlier. A part whose share on the last day is above the median to 90th percentile band of its earlier days gets a heavier outline (#vi-flow-ms-ref), once it has ten days.

Drill-down. A segment opens the chats, tickets or transcripts of that part on that day. A card opens on the map.

Window. The window of #vi-measure-scope sets the range.

Example.
- Parts: builder, reviewers, plan chats
- Monday: builder $30, reviewers $10, plan chats $10
- Tuesday: builder $10, reviewers $10, plan chats $80
1. Monday's bar reads builder 60%, reviewers 20%, plan chats 20%.
2. Tuesday's bar reads builder 10%, reviewers 10%, plan chats 80%. The bar is as tall as Monday's, and the hover shows $100 against $50.
3. A click on Tuesday's plan chats segment lists the chats of that day, largest first.
4. A click on the legend entry "reviewers" hides it, and the two other segments of each bar re-scale to 100%.

```
100% ┤ ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒    ░░░░░░░░    P = plan chats  ▒
     │ ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒    ░░░░░░░░    R = reviewers   ░
     │ ░░░░░░░░    ░░░░░░░░    B = builder     █
     │ ████████    ████████
     │ ████████    ░░░░░░░░
  0% ┼──────────────────────
       Mon $50      Tue $100
```

payload.why: The header shows the total that this card defines.
The unit selector switches between the units that this card defines.
The outlier outline uses the reference band that this card defines.

payload.title: A criterion may name a fallback option and a minimum sample
payload.why: A row links to the rejected option the criterion falls back to, and a metric states its smallest sample. Without a stored field for each, the row has nothing to show.
payload.body: Every form of criterion may carry the id of a rejected option. A metric criterion may carry a minimum sample size. The trigger chip is not stored: a metric reads as a metric trigger and every other form as a review date.

payload.why: The new fields extend the criterion forms that #kill-shape defines.

payload.title: A command that werk prints starts with the executable's own file name
payload.why: A person runs a printed command in a shell. The executable can have any file name after a download or a rename, so a fixed word would name a program that is not on their path. The file name that is running is always right.
payload.body: A printed command is a fix that werk shows a person, such as the next step after a refused change, or the usage line. When werk runs from the executable, the command starts with that file's own name. When werk runs from a checkout, there is no executable, so it starts with werk. An agent prompt and a child process use the full command that one shared helper gives, and never a runtime and a source path.

payload.title: Panel: where did the money go in this window?
payload.why: A total, then bars that split it by the unit a person asks about, answer where the money went before any trend does. Big bars compare the groups, small bars show each row's share inside its group, and a click opens the sessions behind a row. How the split changes by day is on the stage chart.
payload.body:
Header. The total for the window (#ms-cost-total).

Groups. One group for each kind of work: plan chats, terminal turns on the map, and the pipeline. A group's big bar is its share of the largest group. Each row inside it has a small bar for its share of the group, its dollars, and its percent of the total. Rows of the pipeline group are the roles: builder, held-out binder, reviewers, grader, overseer, writers.

Units. A selector switches the rows between roles, chats, tickets, specs and cards (#ms-cost-rollup). The total stays the same in every unit. In a unit with many rows, the six largest get their own row and the rest form one row, other, with its count.

Legend. Each group has one plain line that says what its rows are. A row shows its session count on hover.

Outlier. A row whose cost in the window is above the median to 90th percentile band of the same row in earlier windows of the same length is drawn in the outlier colour (#vi-flow-ms-ref), once it has ten earlier windows.

Drill-down. A row opens the chats, tickets or transcripts behind it. A card opens on the map.

Window. The window of #vi-measure-scope sets the range. For the change by day, see #vi-flow-ms-stage.

Example.
- Window "last 30 days", unit "role"
- Groups: pipeline (builder $60, reviewers $20) and plan chats ($20)
1. The header reads $100.
2. The pipeline group's big bar is full, because it is the largest. Plan chats is a quarter of it.
3. The builder row's small bar is 75% of the pipeline group, and the row reads 60%.
4. A click on the builder row lists its tickets, largest first. A group with no cost in the window shows no rows.

```
$100  (last 30 days)
Pipeline     ████████████████ $80 · 80%
  builder    ████████████     $60 · 60%   [bar = 60 / 80]
  reviewers  ████             $20 · 20%
Plan chats   ████             $20 · 20%
```

payload.why: The header shows the total that this card defines.
The unit selector switches between the units that this card defines.
The outlier colour uses the reference band that this card defines.

payload.title: The stage panel switches its chart between lines and a stacked share of each day
payload.why: Lines show how much each stage cost and when it spiked. They do not show how the split between stages moves, because one spike hides every other line. A stacked bar of equal height for each day shows the share of every stage on that day, so a shift in the split is visible even on a cheap day. One switch on the same chart gives both views with the same legend and drill-down.
payload.body:
A switch beside the unit switch sets the view: lines or share. Lines is the default.

Share draws one bar for each day of the period. Every bar has the same height, 100% of that day's value in the chosen unit (#vi-flow-ms-stage-unit). A segment is one stage and its height is that stage's share of the day. The hover on a segment shows the stage's value and the day's total, so a $50 day and a $100 day stay distinguishable. A day with no value has no bar. A period of 24 hours uses one bar for each hour, because a day would be one bar.

A stage keeps its colour and its place in the stack on every day and in both views. The legend, the click to hide a stage, the command-click to show only one, and the drill-down work as in lines. Hiding a stage re-scales every bar to 100% of the stages still shown. A segment opens the tickets or plan turns of that stage on that day. The outlier rule of the panel marks a stage by its share on the last day, against the band of its earlier days.

Example.
- Stages: build, review, plan. Unit: dollars.
- Monday: build $30, review $10, plan $10. Tuesday: build $10, review $10, plan $80.
1. Lines view: the plan line spikes on Tuesday, and build and review sit near the bottom.
2. The person switches to share. Monday reads build 60%, review 20%, plan 20%. Tuesday reads build 10%, review 10%, plan 80%. Both bars are equally tall.
3. The person hides review. Monday re-scales to build 75%, plan 25%.
4. A click on Tuesday's plan segment lists the plan turns of that day, largest first.

```
 view:  lines  ( share )          ( ) = the view in use

100% ┤ ▒▒▒▒▒▒     ░░░░░░         ▒ plan   ░ review   █ build
     │ ░░░░░░     ▒▒▒▒▒▒
     │ █████      ▒▒▒▒▒▒
  0% ┼─────────────────
     Mon $50      Tue $100
```

payload.why: The share of a day is computed in the unit that this card sets.
The segments are the per-stage dollar costs that this card defines.

payload.title: The stage panel switches its chart between lines, a daily share and a pie of the period
payload.why: Lines show when each stage spiked, but one spike hides every other line. A bar of equal height for each day shows how the split between stages moves. A pie of the whole period shows the final split at a glance. One switch on the same chart gives all three views with the same legend, unit and drill-down.
payload.body:
A switch beside the unit switch sets the view: lines, share or pie. Lines is the default. All three use the unit of #vi-flow-ms-stage-unit and the period of the panel.

Share draws one bar for each day of the period. Every bar has the same height, 100% of that day's value. A segment is one stage and its height is that stage's share of the day. The hover on a segment shows the stage's value and the day's total, so a $50 day and a $100 day stay distinguishable. A day with no value has no bar. A period of 24 hours uses one bar for each hour. The outlier rule of the panel marks a stage by its share on the last day, against the band of its earlier days. A segment opens the tickets or plan turns of that stage on that day.

Pie draws one slice for each stage, sized by its share of the value over the whole period. Slices run clockwise from the top, largest first. A slice of 5% or more shows its percent on the slice. The hover shows the stage's value and percent. A slice opens the tickets or plan turns of that stage in the period. The pie has no outlier mark, because it holds no earlier points to compare with.

A stage keeps its colour in every view. The legend, the click to hide a stage and the command-click to show only one work in every view. Hiding a stage re-scales bars and slices to 100% of the stages still shown.

Example.
- Stages: build, review, plan. Unit: dollars. Period: 2 days.
- Monday: build $30, review $10, plan $10. Tuesday: build $10, review $10, plan $80.
1. Lines view: the plan line spikes on Tuesday.
2. Share view: Monday reads build 60%, review 20%, plan 20%. Tuesday reads build 10%, review 10%, plan 80%. Both bars are equally tall.
3. Pie view: the period total is $150. Plan is 60%, build 27%, review 13%.
4. The person hides review. The pie re-scales to plan 69%, build 31%.

```
 view:  lines   share  ( pie )        ( ) = the view in use

 share                      pie (period)
100% ┤ ▒▒▒▒▒  ░░░░░             ▒ plan    60%
     │ ░░░░░  ▒▒▒▒▒             █ build   27%
     │ █████  ▒▒▒▒▒             ░ review  13%
  0% ┼───────────
     Mon $50  Tue $100
```

payload.why: Shares and slices are computed in the unit that this card sets.
The segments and slices are the per-stage dollar costs that this card defines.

payload.title: The held-out step author, the held-out binder and the overseer classifiers have their own role names
payload.why: The model of an agent comes from its role name, so each kind of agent needs a fixed name that the table and the test fake both read. Three kinds had no name yet.
payload.body: The held-out step author has the role step-author, the held-out binder has the role binder, and the overseer classifiers have the role classifier. Each runs on Sonnet with no advisor.

payload.why: takes the rule that each kind of agent gets a fixed role name

payload.title: The pipeline log has four event types, and one run id joins the events of a plan
payload.why: A fold must pair each step start with its end and group a plan's events without guessing. A fixed set of event types and one shared run id make both exact, and the builder loop and the merge loop add their own types in the same shape.
payload.body: A plan writes four event types: a plan start, a step start, a step end and a plan end. Every event of one plan carries the same run id: the planned subtree's root id, a slash, and the start time of the plan. A step start and its step end are paired by the step name within one run. A step ends as done or failed. A plan ends as done, failed or stopped. Later writers add their own types to the same log and keep the shape of an event: a sequence number, a time, a type and a payload.

payload.why: the step end carries the cost and token breakdown that ms-cost defines

payload.title: Detail files live in fixed folders beside the pipeline log, and git ignores them
payload.why: A later step finds a session file or a plan copy from the event that names it, so the addresses must not vary. Git must ignore the large detail files and track the log, so the ignore rule is written by the first writer, in any project.
payload.body: The pipeline log sits in the project's store folder. Agent session files are one flat folder beside it, one file per session, named by the start time and the role. Each plan's copy is a folder per planned subtree root and per run, holding the spec, the tickets, and each writer's answer records. The store's ignore file lists the session folder and the plan folder, and the first append to the log writes those rules if they are missing. The log itself is never ignored.

payload.why: the ignore rules follow the split of tracked log and untracked detail

payload.title: A session that reports no cost is logged as zero cost and zero tokens
payload.why: A plan must not fail because an agent reported no usage. The cost then reads as zero, so a fold cannot tell an unknown cost from a true zero. That is the accepted price of a log that is always written.
payload.body: When an agent session ends without a cost report, for example when it was stopped, its step end records zero dollars and zero tokens. A measure over the log treats those as real values. A step end with a failed result and zero cost is the sign of a session that reported nothing.

payload.why: the step end of the pipeline log is where the zero is recorded

payload.title: A kept ticket is an open ticket whose file is the same before and after the plan
payload.why: A comparison of two plans needs to list the tickets that stayed as they were. Comparing the file text before and after is exact and needs no judgement from an agent.
payload.body: A ticket is kept when it is ready or blocked, is not archived, and its file has identical text before and after the plan. A done or archived ticket is not part of the plan and is not listed. A changed or new ticket is copied, not listed as kept.

payload.why: the plan extends the open tickets in place, so only open tickets can be kept

payload.title: A session that reports no cost is logged as zero cost and zero tokens
payload.why: A plan must not fail because an agent reported no usage. The cost then reads as zero, so a fold cannot tell an unknown cost from a true zero. That is the accepted price of a log that is always written.
payload.body: When an agent session ends without a cost report, for example when it was stopped or crashed first, its step end records zero dollars and zero tokens. A measure over the log treats those as real values.

payload.why: the step end of the pipeline log is where the zero is recorded

payload.title: A plan copy folder holds the spec, a folder of tickets, and one answer file per writer
payload.why: A reader of two plan copies must find the same item at the same place in each. A fixed layout inside the folder makes a comparison a plain file-by-file diff.
payload.body: The copy folder of one plan run holds the changed spec, a tickets folder with each ticket the plan wrote or changed, and one answers file for the spec writer and one for the ticket writer. The list of kept ticket ids sits in the plan end event, not in a file.

payload.title: A fold of the pipeline log sets aside an event that has no start before it
payload.why: A log is append-only, so a damaged or partial log can hold events that fit no plan. The fold must not guess or fail on them, and a person must still see that they exist.
payload.body: An event of a run with no plan start, and a step end with no open step start of the same name, is left out of the plans. The fold reports it with its sequence number and a plain reason.

payload.title: A later grade of a ticket checks the earlier gaps and regressions, not a fresh reading
payload.why: A grader that reads each pass fresh finds a new small detail every time, so a ticket fails pass after pass on gaps that nobody saw before. When the first grade must name every gap at once and each later grade checks only those gaps plus anything newly broken, the passes move toward green instead of chasing a moving target.
payload.body:
The first grade of a build names every gap it finds on a line in one answer. Each later grade in the same build gets the lines that failed before, with their gaps. A line that failed before fails again only while its gap is still open. A line that passed before fails only for a regression: something that worked at the earlier grade and that the later changes broke. A gap that was already there at the earlier grade and was not named then does not fail a later pass.

A new build of the ticket starts with a fresh first grade.

Example:

- Ticket T "Paste a screenshot" rests on card A "A message carries its images" and card B "The composer shows a menu".

1. Pass 1: the grader fails A, gap: an empty list is still sent. B passes.
2. Pass 2: the builder fixes the empty list. The grader checks A's gap: closed. It checks B for a regression: none. The pass is green.
3. If pass 2 had broken B's menu, B fails as a regression.
4. If the grader now notices a small detail in B that pass 1 already had, B does not fail.

```
pass 1 grade:  A fail (empty list sent)   B pass
                     |
pass 2 grade:  A: is that gap closed?     B: did pass 2 break it?
               yes -> pass                no -> pass
```

payload.why: It changes what each grade of the builder loop of #st-build-ticket checks after the first failed pass.

payload.title: Each grade reads the diff fresh against every line
payload.why_not: In past runs most failed grades named a small gap in a card the diff built, and a fresh reading on each pass found another one, so tickets used up their passes on details.

criterion.text: Revisit when held-out steps or later tickets often find a gap that the first grade of a ticket should have named.

payload.title: On the last counted pass, small gaps in built cards merge and become a follow-up ticket
payload.why: A ticket whose only remaining problems are small gaps in cards it did build would otherwise reach the retry cap and park, with all its work unmerged and every ticket after it waiting. Merging it and filing the gaps as a ticket of their own keeps the work moving and keeps each gap visible on the board.
payload.body:
A small gap is a failed grade line on a decided card that the diff builds, scored one point under a pass, that no person must settle. An unmet acceptance criterion, a behaviour out of scope, an unrecorded decision, a plain contradiction and a gap only a person can settle still fail the pass.

When a pass that would use up the retry cap fails only on small gaps, the pass counts as green. The review still runs on it. If the rest is green, the ticket merges, and a follow-up ticket is filed. The follow-up cites the cards of the gaps, quotes each gap as the grader wrote it, and waits until the ticket is done. Before the last counted pass, a small gap fails the pass as before, so the builder gets every chance to close it first.

Example:

- Ticket T "Paste a screenshot" has a retry cap of 5. Card A is "A message carries its images".

1. Passes 1 to 4 fail. On pass 4 the only failed line is A, score one under a pass, gap: an empty list is still sent.
2. Pass 5 fails on the same line only. Pass 5 is the last counted pass, so it counts as green, and the review runs.
3. The review passes. T merges. Follow-up F "Close the gaps the grader found in T" cites A and quotes the gap.
4. F waits for T, then builds like any ticket.
5. If pass 5 had also missed an acceptance criterion, T would reach the cap and park as before. No follow-up is filed.

```
pass 5 of 5:  checks green -> grade: only small gaps -> review green
                                                         |
                                       T merges ---------+--> F (cites A, quotes the gap)
                                                              waits for T, then builds
```

payload.why: It reads the grade lines, scores and the person flag that #lp-prod-judge defines.
It is the exception to parking a ticket at its retry cap that #st-build-stuck-park describes.

payload.title: A stuck ticket goes back to the planner, which splits it and gives each part a fresh budget
payload.why_not: It adds a plan cost to every stuck ticket and treats the ticket's size as the cause, while the tickets that got stuck were small and failed only on details.

payload.title: Every failed grade line fails the pass, up to the cap
payload.why_not: A ticket with only small gaps left parks at the cap with all its work unmerged, and every ticket after it waits for a person.

criterion.text: Revisit when follow-ups for deferred gaps pile up unbuilt, or when a deferred gap turns out to break a user path.

payload.why: v0's builder loop grades later passes against the earlier gaps and regressions, as #st-grade-converge sets.
v0's builder loop merges small gaps on the last counted pass and files them as a follow-up, as #st-grade-defer sets.

payload.title: A ticket listing line holds the id, the column, an archived flag and the reason
payload.why: A listing that shows the column and the reason lets the person check a move or a restore without reading the board log. Archived tickets stay listed, flagged, with the column they will return to.
payload.body: The listing prints one line per ticket, in the order the board log introduced the tickets. A line holds the ticket id, then its column, then the word archived when the ticket is archived, then a dash and the reason when the ticket has one. An archived ticket shows the column and reason it kept, so a restore is predictable. Archiving a done ticket is refused with a message that says a done ticket cannot be archived.

payload.title: A restore accepts the full ticket id or the number after the slash, and refuses an ambiguous number
payload.why: The full id is long to type, while the number alone is what the person sees on the board. A number that fits two archived tickets would restore the wrong one, so it is refused.
payload.body: A restore first matches the argument against full ticket ids. Otherwise a bare number matches the archived tickets whose id ends in a slash and that number. One match restores that ticket. More than one match restores nothing and fails with a message that names the candidates and asks for the full id.

payload.title: A failure that a retry cannot fix ends with the not-delivered line
payload.why: A person who sends a message needs to know whether it arrived. A login problem, a bad flag or a missing credential fails the same way every time, so the agent never starts a second time. The pane shows the whole error, then says the message was not delivered, so the person fixes the cause and sends it again.
payload.body: Every stop of a send ends with one line under the message: "Your message was not delivered. Send it again." This holds for a failure that a retry cannot fix (login, credential, bad flag or bad argument) and for a failure that a retry did not fix. The pane no longer has a separate fix-first line for the first kind. The whole error stays above the line, with no retry in between.

payload.why: a failure that a retry cannot fix is one where the agent exits before it names its session

payload.title: A failure that a retry cannot fix ends with the not-delivered line
payload.why: A person who sends a message needs to know whether it arrived. A login problem, a bad flag or a missing credential fails the same way every time, so the agent never starts a second time. The pane shows the whole error, then says the message was not delivered, so the person fixes the cause and sends it again.
payload.body: Every stop of a send ends with one line under the message: "Your message was not delivered. Send it again." This holds for a failure that a retry cannot fix (login, credential, bad flag or bad argument) and for a failure that a retry did not fix. There is no separate fix-first line, so this line replaces the one that #werk-fullerr names. The whole error stays above the line, with no retry in between.

payload.why: a failure that a retry cannot fix is one where the agent exits before it names its session

payload.title: The inbox prints every note of the map, grouped by card
payload.why: An agent that writes a note on a card must read the whole thread back from the inbox. A flat list of the person's notes hid the agent's own notes and split one card's notes apart.
payload.body: The inbox prints the notes of every writer, the person and the agent. Notes sit in one group per card, under the card's title. A group holds its notes in log order, and groups come in the order of each group's first note. The start position and the count limit the notes before they are grouped. A note on a ghost card prints like any other.

payload.title: A held-out step that needs a capability no merged ticket has built is not run, not red
payload.why: A step author writes steps from the brief, so a step can need an operation, a screen, a log field or an agent behaviour that a later ticket builds. Such a step fails because the capability is missing, not because of the ticket's code, and the follow-up it files can only build another ticket's work or change nothing, so the same follow-up returns after every merge. Ending the step as not run keeps every red step pointing at merged code.
payload.body:
A capability is anything a step reaches the product through: an operation of the command line, a screen or route, a field or kind of event in the log, a behaviour of an agent. To keep a red step pointing at merged code (see #st-heldout-merged-only), the binder reports the capability a step needs when the main line does not provide it. If that capability belongs to the scope of a ticket that is not merged yet, the step ends as not run (see #st-heldout-notrun). It files no follow-up. G2 still waits for it, and the held-out run after each later merge tries it again.

If the missing capability belongs to the step's own source ticket, the ticket forgot to build it, and the step is red. Only a capability that another ticket owns makes a step not run.

The ticket's own behaviour stays checked on the main line by its unit tests at the seam it builds, such as the prompt builder for a ticket that builds agent prompts.

Example:

- Ticket R "Every agent werk starts gets the agent instructions" builds the prompt builder and is merged.
- Ticket B "A build pass runs on one ticket" builds the operation that starts a build pass, and is still blocked.
- Step S of R: "When the person starts a build pass on a ticket, then its prompt begins with the build agent's own instructions".

1. R merges. The held-out run binds S. The product has no operation that starts a build pass, and B owns it, so S ends as not run, with a grey badge on R. No follow-up is filed.
2. B merges. The next held-out run tries S again through the operation that B built.
3. S passes: S is green. Or S fails on the prompt: S is red, and one follow-up for R is filed.
4. If R itself was meant to build that operation, S is red at step 1.

```
merge:   R                    B
S:       not run       ->     green | red -> follow-up for R
         (capability owned    (capability now on the main line)
          by B, not merged)
```

payload.why: the not-run result, which files no follow-up and keeps G2 waiting, that a step through a missing capability receives

payload.title: Build the missing capability inside the follow-up ticket
payload.why_not: The capability is the scope of another planned ticket that is still blocked on its own dependencies. A follow-up would build it out of order, touch that ticket's modules, and collide with it when it builds.

payload.title: One card for each kind of capability: operation, screen, and each kind found later
payload.why_not: Every kind states the same rule, so the cards drift apart, and a new kind of capability files repeat follow-ups until someone writes its card.

payload.title: A follow-up whose every step needs an unbuilt capability closes with no code change
payload.why: A follow-up that holds only steps for a capability another ticket owns cannot be fixed by any change inside it, and the behaviour behind the steps is already checked by unit tests at the seam an earlier ticket built. Closing it with no change stops the loop of builder passes that each end on the same finding. The steps stay in the held-out set, so a later red result still files a fresh follow-up.
payload.body:
To stop a follow-up from looping on work that belongs to another ticket, a builder pass on it checks two facts. First, each of its steps needs a capability that the main line does not provide and that another unmerged ticket owns (see #st-heldout-unbuilt-capability). Second, the seam behind each step has unit tests that state the step's outcome, and those tests pass on the main line. When both facts hold, the pass ends with no code change, and the grader scores each acceptance criterion as met: the step is not run (see #st-heldout-notrun), not failed. The steps stay in the held-out set, G2 still waits for them, and the held-out run after each later merge tries them again. A step that goes red once its capability exists files a new follow-up then (see #st-heldout-followup-per-ticket). When a step lacks a passing unit test at its seam, the pass writes that test and does not close on the first fact alone.

Example:

- Ticket R "Every agent werk starts gets the agent instructions" built the prompt builder and merged, with unit tests for each prompt.
- Follow-up F holds R's steps S1 "a build pass starts with the instructions" and S2 "a sample agent gets no instructions".
- Ticket B "A build pass runs on one ticket" and ticket P "Samples run" build the operations, and neither has merged.

1. A builder pass on F finds that the product has no operation that starts a build pass or a sample. Fact one holds.
2. It finds a passing unit test at the prompt builder for S1 and for S2. Fact two holds.
3. The pass ends with no code change. The grader scores both criteria as met. F closes.
4. B merges. The held-out run tries S1. S1 is green: nothing happens. S1 is red: a new follow-up for R is filed.
5. If step 2 had found no unit test for S2, the pass writes one at the prompt builder, and F closes with that test as its change.

```
F (follow-up)         builder pass               later merges
 S1 --needs--> [no build-pass op]  ok   \
 S2 --needs--> [no sample op]      ok    >-> F closes, no code change
 S1, S2 unit tests at the seam     pass /
                                                 B merges -> S1 tried: green | red -> new follow-up
ok   = fact one holds for the step
pass = fact two holds for the step
```

payload.why: the not-run result that lets the grader score a step through a missing capability as met, not failed
the new follow-up that a step files when it goes red after its capability merges, which makes closing safe

payload.title: Block the follow-up on the tickets that build the missing capability
payload.why_not: It needs a new blocking link from a follow-up to tickets of other subtrees, and the follow-up then waits with nothing to build. When those tickets merge, the held-out run rechecks the steps by itself and files a new follow-up for a red one, so the blocked ticket adds a second record of the same wait.

payload.title: Archive the follow-up as not needed
payload.why_not: An archive says that the spec no longer needs the ticket, and that is false: the steps must still pass. It also takes the open wait off the board, so the person no longer sees it.

criterion.text: After a run, check the follow-up list: a step filed more than once for a capability another ticket owns, or a step shown as not run after its owning ticket merged, means the rule is wrong.

After a run, check the closed follow-ups: a follow-up that closed with no change while its step stayed red after its capability merged, or one that closed without a passing unit test at the seam, means the rule is wrong.

payload.title: A step that contradicts a card stops the run until a person rules
payload.why_not: A run that waits for a person stalls every ticket that needs a merge behind it, and the question has a safe default by the guideline for a missing decision, so no person is needed to start.

payload.title: A red step is checked against its source cards before it files a follow-up, and a contradiction files a decision follow-up
payload.why: A step that was wrong from the start fails after every build, because no code can satisfy both the step and the card. Checking the step against its source cards before it files keeps such a step out of the build tickets. A contradiction goes to a ticket that judges the step and the card and proposes a card, so no run waits for a person.
payload.body:
A held-out step can contradict a decided card without the card ever having changed: the step author misread the card when it wrote the step. Such a step is red after every build, and each build follow-up it files cannot make it green. A step that is out of date because its card changed is a different case (see #st-heldout-step-fresh).

To avoid a follow-up that cannot succeed, the step author reads every red step against its source cards before the step files anything. The check has two results.

**The step agrees with its cards.** The step files a build follow-up as before (see #st-heldout-followup-per-ticket).

**The step contradicts a decided card.** No build follow-up is filed. A decision follow-up is filed for the source ticket instead. It builds no code at first. It judges whether the card or the step is right, by the guideline of #st-build-missing-decision: the answer that is easiest to undo, and when two are equally safe, the one that changes the fewest decided cards. It then proposes a card with its answer, its reason and the options it weighed. The proposal is an ordinary proposal and an agent never accepts it. The step stays out of the set, as a step not run, until the step author rewrites it from the cards and the proposal. If the judgement changed the card, the follow-up then builds the code that the proposal asks for.

Nothing in this path waits for a person. The person rules on the proposal later, with the effects that #st-build-missing-decision gives for an accept and for a discard.

Example:

- Ticket Q "A quote becomes an excerpt" is merged.
- Card E "A message position counts from zero, hidden lines included".
- Step S "The excerpt's message position is 3". The chat log in S has three lines, so the last line has position 2.

1. The held-out run turns S red.
2. The step author reads S against E. E gives 2, S says 3: a contradiction.
3. A decision follow-up D is filed for Q. No build follow-up is filed.
4. D judges that E is right: it changes no decided card. D proposes a card that confirms E for this case.
5. The step author rewrites S to position 2, citing E and the proposal. S runs again and is green.
6. If S had agreed with E, step 3 would be a build follow-up, as usual.

```
S red -> author reads S against E
           |-- agrees ------> build follow-up for Q
           '-- contradicts -> decision follow-up D -> proposed card P
                                                        |
                              S rewritten from E and P <'  -> S runs again
```

payload.why: It adds a check before the filing that #st-heldout-followup-per-ticket describes, and a second kind of follow-up beside it.
It takes the guideline for the answer and the rules for the proposed card from #st-build-missing-decision.
It shows a step that waits for its rewrite as not run, which files no follow-up and keeps G2 waiting.
The step author reads the red step against its cards and rewrites it.

criterion.source: the pipeline log's follow-up tickets, grouped by held-out step
criterion.metric: held-out steps that file a second build follow-up after the check passed them

payload.title: A follow-up merges only when its own red steps pass on its tree
payload.why: A follow-up's checks never run the step that made it, so it can finish while the step is still red, and the next held-out run files another follow-up. Running those steps in the merge gate makes "done" mean that the step passes. A step that no builder can pass then stops at the retry cap instead of merging and coming back.
payload.body:
A follow-up is built and merged like any ticket, but its job is to turn specific red steps green. The checks of the merge loop test the code, not those steps. A follow-up can therefore merge with its steps still red, and each merge files the next follow-up for the same step.

To avoid that, the merge gate of a follow-up has one more stage. After the checks pass on the temporary tree (run's tree plus the follow-up), the binder runs the follow-up's own red steps on that tree (see #lp-heldout-binder).

- All of those steps pass: the follow-up merges.
- A step ran and is red: nothing merges. The ticket goes back to the builder loop with the failure, and the retry cap applies. The failure names the red steps and what the binder saw. It never shows the step text, because the builder never sees the held-out steps (see #lp-heldout-mechanics).
- A step is not run, because the binder could not run it: it does not block the merge. It is not red (see #st-heldout-notrun).

A follow-up that reaches its cap stops there, unmerged, with the red steps named.

Example:

- Follow-up F carries step S "A quote that is not unique writes nothing".
- F's checks are green.

1. The binder runs S on the temporary tree. S is red.
2. F goes back to the builder with "S red: the log grew by one event". The step text stays hidden.
3. The next pass fixes it. The checks are green and S is green. F merges.
4. If S were red at the cap, F would stop there and the main line would stay as it was.

```
temp tree = run's tree + F
   checks green? --no--> back to builder
        | yes
   F's red steps (binder) --any red--> back to builder (cap applies)
        | all pass or not run
      merge F
```

payload.why: The binder runs the follow-up's red steps and reports them without making one pass.
The failure it sends back to the builder must keep the step text hidden.
A step the binder could not run is not red, so it does not block the merge.

payload.title: Keep the gate as it is and cap the follow-ups filed for one step
payload.why_not: A cap stops the repeat but does not change what done means: a follow-up still merges with its step red, and the cap only decides when the run gives up.

criterion.source: the pipeline log's follow-up tickets, grouped by held-out step
criterion.metric: merged follow-ups whose step is red again at the next held-out run

payload.title: A follow-up merges only when its own red steps pass on its tree
payload.why: A follow-up's checks never run the step that made it, so it can finish while the step is still red, and the next held-out run files another follow-up. Running those few steps in the follow-up's merge gate makes "done" mean that the step passes. A step that no builder can pass then stops at the retry cap instead of merging and coming back.
payload.body:
A follow-up is built and merged like any ticket, but its job is to turn specific red steps green. The checks of the merge loop test the code, not those steps. A follow-up can therefore merge with its steps still red, and each merge files the next follow-up for the same step.

To avoid that, the merge gate of a follow-up has one more stage. After the checks pass on the temporary tree (the run's tree plus the follow-up), the binder runs the red steps that the follow-up carries, and only those, on that tree (see #lp-heldout-binder). The whole held-out set still runs beside the merge queue and never holds a merge back (see #st-heldout-beside). The gate adds a wait only for the few steps of one follow-up.

- Every one of those steps passes: the follow-up merges.
- A step ran and is red: nothing merges. The ticket goes back to the builder loop with the failure, and the retry cap applies. The builder gets the failed step as that card says (see #lp-heldout-feedback).
- A step is not run, because the binder could not run it: it does not block the merge. It is not red (see #st-heldout-notrun).

A follow-up that reaches its cap stops there, unmerged, with its red steps named.

Example:

- Follow-up F carries step S "A quote that is not unique writes nothing".
- F's checks are green.

1. The binder runs S on the temporary tree. S is red.
2. F goes back to the builder with the text of S and what the binder saw.
3. The next pass fixes it. The checks are green and S is green. F merges.
4. If S were still red at the cap, F would stop there and the main line would stay as it was.

```
temp tree = run's tree + F
   checks green? --no--> back to builder
        | yes
   F's red steps (binder) --any red--> back to builder (cap applies)
        | all pass or not run
      merge F
```

payload.why: The binder runs the follow-up's red steps and reports them without making one pass.
The failure it sends back to the builder is the failed step's text, which #lp-heldout-feedback sets.
A step the binder could not run is not red, so it does not block the merge.
It keeps the whole held-out set beside the merge queue and gates only the steps of one follow-up.

payload.title: Keep the gate as it is and cap the follow-ups filed for one step
payload.why_not: A cap stops the repeat but does not change what done means: a follow-up still merges with its step red, and the cap only decides when the run gives up.

criterion.source: the pipeline log's follow-up tickets, grouped by held-out step
criterion.metric: merged follow-ups whose step is red again at the next held-out run

payload.title: Every pipeline agent has one fixed role name
payload.why: The pipeline runs many kinds of agent, and two rules need to tell them apart: which model an agent runs on, and which scripted reply a test fake plays. A fixed name per kind of agent gives both rules the same key, and a name does not change when a prompt is reworded.
payload.body:
A role name is a short fixed word for the job one kind of agent does. The pipeline gives every agent that it starts one role name. The name is a fact about the job, not about the prompt or the model, so a rewording of a prompt or a switch of model keeps the role.

| Role | Job |
| --- | --- |
| spec-writer | Writes the spec over one decided subtree |
| ticket-writer | Splits a spec into tickets |
| builder | Does one implement pass of a ticket |
| grader | Judges the diff against the decided cards |
| reviewer-<area> | Reviews the diff in one quality area, one role per area |
| step-author | Writes the held-out steps from the brief |
| binder | Turns held-out steps into tests |
| classifier | Decides a question about a running agent for the overseer |

The chat agent is not a pipeline agent and has no pipeline role. Each role is defined by the card of its job. A new kind of agent gets a new role name when it is added, and this card then names it. Other rules key on the role: the model of an agent follows from it (#st-model-per-role) and a test fake picks its reply from it (#st-build-seam-role-env).

payload.why: takes the spec-writer and ticket-writer jobs
takes the builder and grader jobs
takes the reviewer job, one per quality area
takes the step-author job
takes the binder job
takes the classifier job that judges progress
takes the classifier job that judges a tool call in flight
picks the model from the role name that this card defines
takes the set of role names that a fake agent reads

payload.title: In v0, each project has one conversation, and the rules written for a tab apply to it
payload.why: Several conversations in tabs are postponed, but some decided chat rules are written for tabs. Reading each tab rule as a rule for the one conversation keeps those rules in v0 without the tab strip.
payload.body:
v0 builds one continuous conversation per project in the chat pane (see #werk-onechat), with no tab strip, no fork and no park (see #werk-multichat, which is postponed).

A rule that names a tab applies to that one conversation. The background line shows in its pane (see #werk-mc-bgagents). The dead mark stays until the next child starts (see #werk-mc-live-dead). A dead child has no other pane in the same project to show a line in, so its error shows in its own pane, and the project switcher marks the project as dead beside the busy mark (see #werk-projects-switcher).

Example:

- Project P "checkout" has its one conversation C.
- The person looks at project Q.

1. The child of C exits with an error that a retry cannot fix.
2. The switcher row of P shows the dead mark.
3. The person opens P. The pane of C shows the error at the end of the turn.
4. The person sends a message in C. A new child starts, and the dead mark goes.

payload.title: Where the server cannot open a folder dialog, a project is added by starting werk in its folder
payload.why: werk ships for macOS and Linux, and the folder dialog is decided for macOS only. Starting werk in a folder already adds that folder to the running server, so it is a path that works on every platform with no new interface.
payload.body: Adding a project opens the operating system's folder dialog (see #werk-projects-add). On a platform where the server cannot open one, for example a Linux machine with no dialog program, the "Add project…" row says so and names the other way in: start werk in the folder. A start in a folder while a server runs adds the folder to the list and opens it (see #werk-projects-one-process). The git check and the empty map work the same on both paths.

payload.title: A pure file's own test file has the same name with a test suffix, in the same folder
payload.why: The coverage check finds each pure file's own test file by one fixed convention, and no card names it. The name beside the file is the one the runner already finds and a person already expects.
payload.body: The coverage check counts only the lines that a pure file's own test file runs (see #werk-reflink-own-test-coverage). The own test file of a pure file is the file in the same folder with the same base name and the test suffix that the unit test runner picks up. A pure file with no such file counts as 0%, and the check names the expected test file.

payload.title: The board log defines every ticket, run and plan event type before any pipeline step writes one
payload.why: The plan, the builder loop, the merge loop and the held-out run all write board events. When each of them adds its own event types to the board fold, they all change one module and cannot build at the same time.
payload.body: To let the pipeline steps build independently, the board log and its fold come first and hold every event type that the board card lists: the ticket events, the run events, and the plan events (plan started, plan step, plan ended). A later pipeline step writes these events through the board log and does not change the fold. A step that needs a new event type changes the board log module in its own ticket.

payload.title: One pipeline agent runner starts every agent of the build pipeline
payload.why: Every pipeline agent needs the same things at launch: its role in the environment, the model of its role, a session log, a wall-clock limit, start and end events in the pipeline log, and the overseer. One runner gives all of them the same launch, so a fix applies to every role at once.
payload.body: The spec writer, the ticket writer, the builder, the grader, the reviewers, the step author, the binder and the overseer classifiers all start through one runner. The runner builds the launch from the role, writes the session log and the pipeline log events, enforces the wall-clock limit, and holds the overseer. A role differs only in its prompt, its tool list and the reply it parses. The chat conversation is not a pipeline agent and has its own child, with the same launch options for its role.

payload.title: The quote operation is built before the chat pane, and the chat pane writes its chat log in the form the quote reads
payload.why: The quote operation needs only a chat log to read, and it is part of the map's write path, so it can be built and tested on a hand-written chat log early. The conversation then writes the same form, so no second reader is needed.
payload.body: The quote ticket defines how a chat log holds a message: its position, its speaker, whether it is spoken, its text, its session and its time. Its tests use a hand-written chat log in a fresh project. The conversation ticket writes each line of the chat log in that form, so a quote of a real conversation works with no change to the quote operation.

payload.title: A launch tells the fake agent its script and its role through two environment variables
payload.why: The fake runs as a separate process that sees only its own launch, so the script and the role must travel in the launch. Variables leave the arguments free for what the real agent takes, and the launch record sits beside the script so a test finds it from the script it installed.
payload.body: The harness names the script file of its temporary project in one variable, and the pipeline names the role in another (see #st-build-seam-role-env). A launch with no script or no role fails at once with an error that names the missing variable. The launch record is a file of one JSON line for each launch and each chat message, kept beside the script file, and a launch counts the earlier launches of its role from that file.

payload.why: The role variable carries the role name that this card's fake reads.
The record of each launch is the file that this card places beside the script.

payload.title: Each fold appends its time to a file beside the log
payload.why: The kill criterion on the fold time needs data, and the time must be kept apart from the log so the log holds map events only. A file of its own keeps the log the only state of the map.
payload.body: Every read of the log appends one line to a measures file in the same folder as the log: the moment, the number of events folded and the milliseconds. A folder that refuses the write does not stop the read.

payload.title: A verb module is a file in the verbs folder, found by scanning the folder
payload.why: The start-up finds verbs without a shared list, so a new verb is a new file and nothing else changes. Test files in that folder are not verbs.
payload.body: The start-up imports every source file in the verbs folder except test files. Each import registers its verb. A second registration of a name replaces the first, so a hot reload of one verb module works.

payload.title: A link prints its reason, marks a held link, and exits 2 for a bad call and 1 for a refusal
payload.why: A reader of a printed card needs each link's reason and needs to tell a held link from a live one. An agent needs to tell a mistyped call from a link the map refused.
payload.body: The printed card shows a link's reason on a line under the link row. A link on a ghost carries a held mark. The link command prints linked on success. A call with missing or bad arguments exits 2. A link that the map refuses exits 1 and prints the broken rule. A depends_on link from a card to itself counts as a link to an ancestor and is refused.

payload.title: The wording rules reach every agent that can write card text
payload.why: The wording card says every session and subagent, while the instruction card keeps the text from agents with a narrow contract. Both hold when the rules go to the agents that write cards, because only they can break the rules. An agent that never writes a card gains nothing from them, and the text would contradict its contract.
payload.body: The wording rules travel inside the agent instructions, so they reach the chat agent, each build pass and the plan writers. A sample agent, the diagram agents, the shipped subagents that never add a card, the grader, the reviewers and the other classifiers do not get them. The first guideline step chose it: it is the least privilege that makes the rules reach every card writer, and it changes no decided card. Every stage agent still gets the titles of the build-rule cards.

payload.title: Put the wording rules into every session, subagent and stage agent
payload.why_not: The shipped subagents, the grader and the reviewers never write card text, and the sample and diagram agents have contracts that the instruction text contradicts. It adds text to every launch for no gain.

payload.why: takes the set of agents that receive the instruction text, and the narrow-contract exclusion

payload.title: The serve verb runs itself again under hot reload, and the child stops when its parent dies
payload.why: A person starts the server with the plain serve verb, and hot reload is a runtime flag, not a setting a running process can turn on. So the verb starts one child with hot reload on, and the child alone holds the lock and the port. A parent that dies leaves no server behind that no one can stop.
payload.body: To avoid a server that runs without hot reload, the serve verb starts a child process with hot reload on and waits for it. The child carries a marker naming its parent, so it never starts a child of its own. The child holds the lock and the port. The parent passes the stop signals to the child and exits with the child's exit code. The child checks that its parent is alive twice a second and stops itself when the parent is gone, so a killed parent never leaves a server that holds the lock. A person who starts the verb under hot reload by hand gets the server directly, with no child.

payload.title: The page carries the token in a meta tag, and a changing request sends it in a request header
payload.why: The page is the one place a same-origin script can read the token and another site cannot. A header is the one place the server can check it before it reads the request body.
payload.body: The served page holds the token in a meta tag named for the werk token. A changing request carries the same token in one request header. The server compares the header with the token it made at its start, after it checks the Host. A tool that makes a changing request fetches the page and reads the meta tag, the same way the page does. The check runs before routing, so a route that is added later is covered without its own check.

payload.title: The inbox lists every note and every proposed-again marker, each at its log line
payload.why: A thread is read against the words each note was about, and the person needs to find an entry by its place in the log. So a note from the agent and a note from the person sit in one thread, and the marker sits at the line where the id was proposed again.
payload.body: A thread entry is a note, written by the agent or by the person, or a marker. The position of an entry is the line of its event in the map log. The inbox prints entries of every id, oldest first, whether or not the id still has a card, and the start position and the count cut the list. A note needs a card that exists in the map, so a discarded id takes no new note until it is proposed again.

payload.why: The marker and the kept thread come from the rule that a thread belongs to the id.

payload.title: Board log events name their ticket, and a retry is a red pass
payload.why: Every board event must name its ticket the same way, so one fold and one write check can read any of them. A retry count needs one definition so every view reports the same number.
payload.body: A ticket event names its ticket by the full id: plan run, slash, two-digit number. A restore names it in a field of its own and records who restored it. A person may type the bare two-digit number; it names a ticket only when exactly one plan run has it, and a number on two plan runs is refused. A ticket's retry count is the number of its passes that ended red. A move to blocked always carries its blocking reason, and a blocked ticket moves only to ready.

payload.title: The lock file is named serve.lock and holds its port after the server listens
payload.why: The lock must sit beside the log and name its holder, but the holder cannot know its port until it listens. A fixed name keeps one lock per log directory. A port of zero marks a holder that has not listened yet.
payload.body: The lock is the file serve.lock in the log's directory. The start writes its pid and a port of zero when it creates the lock, and fills in the real port once the server listens. A reader that sees port zero treats the holder as a live server whose port is not known yet.

payload.title: The token travels in the request header named x-werk-token
payload.why: A header name must be fixed so the page and every tool send the token the same way. The name says what the value is.
payload.body: A changing request carries the token in the header x-werk-token. The page's meta tag is named werk-token. A request with a missing or wrong header is refused with 403.

payload.why: fixes the header name that the carrier leaves open

payload.title: The shape read lists every node with its edges and a per-card rollup, and no full-map read exists
payload.why: The shape must serve the tree, the rollup bars and the graph from one read, and it must never carry a body. A read of the whole map with bodies would bring back the cost that the shape exists to avoid.
payload.body: The graph read answers only the shape query, and a graph read without the shape flag is refused with 400. The shape lists each node with its id, kind, status and marks, and a flag for a proposed node. Each edge carries a held flag when it belongs to a proposed card. Each card has a rollup of its subtree counts: cards, open, proto, decided and stale, with proposed cards left out. The card read answers found with the card, or found false, and each neighbour carries its id, title and a direction, incoming or outgoing.

payload.title: A ticket's number is the leading digits of its file name, and a number held by two files names no ticket
payload.why: A blocked_by entry is a number, so each ticket needs one number that a person can read off its file name. A number two files share would point at an unknown ticket, so it fails instead of picking one.
payload.body: A ticket's number is the digits that start its file name, with leading zeros dropped, so a file named 02-reopen is ticket 2. A file with no leading digits has no number and cannot be a blocker. When two files give the same number, each of them fails the blocked_by check on its file name, and neither counts as a blocker.

payload.why: The numbering feeds the blocked_by check that this card defines.

payload.title: A card whose parent is still out is not restored
payload.why: A restored card under a parent that is out would sit in no tree, and every real card must have a chain of real parents. So the restore refuses and names the parent to restore first.
payload.body: A restore of a card that was removed on its own is refused while the card's parent is out, whether the parent went out by its own removal or with a card above it. The refusal names the parent. Restoring the parent first, then the card, gives the same map as restoring in the other order would, because each removal is undone on its own.

payload.why: Takes the rule that every real card has a chain of real parents up to the root.

payload.title: A kill criterion is recorded in one of four forms, and one call records one
payload.why: A criterion with a missing part cannot be checked, and a bare answer hides why there is no metric. Four forms cover the answers of a decision, and each form names every part it needs.
payload.body: A metric form needs a source, a metric, a threshold, a window and a sample, all non-empty. A manual form holds the test the author runs. A no-metric form holds the reason there is no metric. A revisit form holds nothing, because it says the decision may be revisited at any time. A call that names two forms, or a metric with a missing part, is refused.

payload.why: takes the parts of a metric criterion and the no-metric reasons

payload.title: A real card never takes a ghost as its basis or its weighed option
payload.why: A real card that stood on a proposal nobody accepted would be decided on words that may be discarded. A ghost may stand on a ghost, because both commit as one unit.
payload.body: The contract check counts a basis or an option only when it is real, unless the card being decided is itself a ghost. A decided ghost basis does not make a real card decidable.

payload.why: takes the rule that a ghost commits with its held edges as one unit

payload.title: A decide, a kill criterion and a waiver are recorded as their own log events
payload.why: The log shows each fact in the event type alone, so the fold keeps one branch per meaning. A waiver rides on the edit of its card because it is a record about that card, not a state change.
payload.body: A move to decided is one event type and a kill criterion is one event type. A who, a basis waiver and an option waiver are fields of the edit event, each waiver holding its non-empty reason. A criterion holds the parts of its form: source, metric, threshold, window and sample for a metric, a test for a manual form, a reason for a no-metric form, nothing for a revisit form.

payload.title: Every edit of a decided card is refused, who and waivers included
payload.why: A who or a waiver changed after the decide would change the facts the decide was checked against. A change goes through a proposal, which runs the facts again.
payload.body: The refusal uses the frozen rule. A decided card is never edited, and an event that decides a card twice is refused under the contract rule. A basis that is paused still counts as a basis that holds.

payload.title: The basis and unchallenged flags of the edit take the reason as their value
payload.why: A waiver needs a written reason, so the flag that records it cannot be bare. One flag with a value keeps the flag and its reason together.
payload.body: The edit form takes a reason after the no-basis flag and after the unchallenged flag. A kill call names exactly one form: revisit as a switch with no value, a manual test, a no-metric reason, or a metric with source, threshold, window and sample. The status verb takes only decided and refuses any other status.

payload.title: A refusal names each missing fact by its fact name, then its fix with the card id filled in
payload.why: The agent reads one line per fact and runs the fix, so the line starts with the fact name and ends with a command that completes it.
payload.body: A refusal reads that the card is missing a count of facts, then one entry each for who, basis, option and kill. A basis that waits names a decide for an open basis and a review for a stale one. The option fix of a real card says the added option must be accepted, since a real card counts only a real option. A card shows its waivers and its criteria wherever it prints.

payload.title: A quote is one log event that holds the excerpt's words and its whole pointer
payload.why: The quote must write the excerpt and its link as one change, and the excerpt must be readable on a machine that lacks the chat log. So the one event carries the quoted words and every part of the pointer, and the fold refuses an event that lacks one.
payload.body: The event names the excerpt, the citing card, and the pointer parts: conversation, session, message position, span start and end, speaker and time. The quoted words are the excerpt's title, so a view that prints a title prints the words. The fold stages the excerpt as a ghost with the supported_by link held from the citing card. An event with a missing or malformed pointer part, or a name already taken, is set aside. The quote also refuses before it writes when the matched message has no speaker, time or session, because the pointer would be incomplete.

payload.why: the pointer parts the event must carry

payload.title: A quoted excerpt is decided from the start, so a ghost excerpt shows no open mark
payload.why: An excerpt is a fixed copy of words, not a choice to make. A status of open would count it in the open cards and the unchallenged count, though nobody can decide anything about it.
payload.body: The quote stages the excerpt with the status decided. Accepting it changes only whether it is a ghost. The words never change (see #werk-excerpt-event), so the excerpt has no open state to wait in. The guideline step that chose it: the answer that leaves the open-card counts unchanged.

payload.title: Accept any conversation name and join it to the folder
payload.why_not: A name with a path separator or two dots could read a file outside the chats folder. Deny by default rejects it.
