payload.why: takes the rule that the chat log sits beside the decision log and that only spoken messages hold a quote

payload.title: The server renders the open card, and the page swaps its HTML in
payload.why: The card text needs no state in the browser. A server render keeps it out of React, and a swap on each signal keeps one read path.
payload.body: The left pane's card text, which holds the title, the why, the body and the titles of its sub-cards, is rendered to escaped HTML on the server. The page reads that HTML on each connect and on each bare change signal, and puts it into the body slot. React mounts only where state lives, which is the composer.

payload.why: The swap is the page's one read after each bare change signal.

payload.title: A reworded block prints its changed words marked, not the whole block twice
payload.why: A reworded paragraph of forty words that changes one word would print both copies in full if the whole block were marked. Marking only the changed words lets a reader find the change in one pass.
payload.body:
To show a reworded block in plain text, the printed diff compares the old and the new block word by word. A shared word prints plain, a removed word run prints in [- -], and an added word run prints in {+ +}. A kept block prints plain, a new block prints whole in {+ +}, and a removed block prints whole in [- -]. The title and the why print the same way on one line each.

Example. A block says "Invoices go out on the 1st." and its new text says "Invoices go out on the 5th."

1. The printed block reads: Invoices go out on the [-1st.-] {+5th.+}
2. A block with equal old and new text prints plain.
3. When nothing is shared, the whole old text prints in [- -] and the whole new text in {+ +}.

payload.title: A decided card's option is removed one at a time, and the removal keeps an option
payload.why: Removing an option is the one change that can leave a decided card without a required fact, so an option must be removable on its own, and only while the card keeps another option.
payload.body: A removal names an option of a card in the map and takes that option with its own evidence. The card stays. When the card is decided and the option is its last one while who is you with no waiver, the removal is refused and the card keeps the option. After a second option is added, the first can go. A ghost option is dropped by a discard, not a removal.

payload.title: A follow-up record is its own board event, beside the one that links a follow-up ticket
payload.why: A request after a finished build is a fact about the ticket, and the board already has an event for a follow-up ticket. A separate event keeps the two facts apart, so a fold counts requests without counting tickets.
payload.body: The record holds the ticket, the class, where it was found, the reason, the catchable answer for a build miss, and the number of the record it corrects. The older event that links a follow-up ticket keeps its meaning.

payload.why: adds one event type to the ticket events of the board log

payload.title: A correction points at an original record, and corrections share the numbering
payload.why: A chain of corrections is hard to read, and the last record already wins. Pointing only at an original keeps one rule for what is in force, and one numbering lets the person name any record.
payload.body: A correction of a record that is itself a correction is refused. Originals and corrections take numbers from one sequence per ticket. The list shows each original with the correction in force, and marks it as corrected by that record number.

payload.why: the last correction of a follow-up is the one that counts

payload.title: A Markdown link renders only for a web, mail, site or page address
payload.why: A link written as Markdown can carry any scheme, and some schemes run code when clicked. Allowing a short list keeps every link in a card safe to click, and the refused text stays readable.
payload.body: A Markdown link becomes a link only when its address starts with http://, https://, mailto:, a slash or a hash. Any other address is not a link: the text renders exactly as written, brackets and address included, so nothing is hidden and nothing is clickable.

payload.title: A reference token drops trailing punctuation until it names a known id
payload.why: A reference at the end of a clause is often followed by a full stop or a dash. Without trimming, a known id followed by punctuation would stay plain text, and the reader would see a dead reference.
payload.body: The token after the hash or the bare id may end in a full stop, colon, underscore or hyphen. The renderer removes those characters one at a time until the rest is a known id, and links that. The removed characters stay as text after the link. If no shorter form is a known id, the token stays text.

payload.title: The Markdown renderer is one pure module of three parts, shared by server and client
payload.why: Card text is rendered on the server, and the client shows the result. One module serves both, so card bodies, whys, notes and chat read the same. Splitting it by job keeps each part small and testable.
payload.body: The renderer sits in its own folder beside the server code. One part escapes text, one part highlights code by grammar, and one part reads the Markdown and joins them. It has no dependencies. The server calls it to render card text and the client reuses the same output.

payload.title: A review ends with a confirm list or an amend sentence, and each is typed at the rederive
payload.why: A confirm must name every outgoing link reason it checked, and an amend must carry the sentence the trace shows. Typing both at the rederive keeps the check in the write, so a script and a person meet the same refusal.
payload.body: werk rederive <id> [--confirm <id,id|all>] [--amend "<what changed>"] [--why "..."] [--status decided]. A confirm names the depends_on targets whose reasons were read, or all of them. A missing target refuses the confirm and the refusal prints the list to confirm. An amend takes the place of a confirm and its sentence is the text of the marks it puts on the next hop. A status of decided on a card that is already decided also runs the four-fact check.

payload.why: the confirm and the amend are the two endings of a review

payload.title: A reopen applies to a decided card or a postponed one, and a later reopen ends the earlier postponement
payload.why: A reopen of a card that was never decided has nothing to reopen, and marks would reach cards for a change that never happened. A postponed card is open, yet a later reopen must be able to change its reason, so it is allowed too.
payload.body: A card that is open and carries no postponed mark cannot be reopened. A reopen of a postponed card with any reason ends the postponement: its postponed mark goes and so do the paused marks it caused, then the new reason marks the cards as its own rule says.

payload.title: A review clears the stale marks of a card and leaves its paused marks
payload.why: A paused card is never reviewed, so a review cannot judge a pause. Only a resume ends a pause, so a review that cleared it would hide work that still waits.
payload.body: A confirm and an amend clear only the stale marks of the reviewed card. The paused marks and the postponed mark stay until the postponed card is decided again.

payload.why: only the decide of the postponed card ends a paused mark

payload.title: The stale list names a waiting card when it is unmarked, not decided, and stands on a basis that does not hold
payload.why: A card marked stale already shows why it cannot be decided. A card with no mark and an open or stale basis would otherwise hide in the list, so it prints as waiting with the basis it waits for.
payload.body: A paused or postponed card prints as paused, a card with a stale mark prints as stale, and a decided card with no mark is never listed. Each waiting card names every basis that does not hold, with its state.

payload.why: a card on a basis that is open or stale waits
a postponement's paused marks end at a resume, and a later reopen ends them too

payload.title: A card downstream of a postponement carries the paused mark, and the postponed card carries the postponed mark
payload.why: Two decided cards disagree on the word of the downstream mark: one says every mark reads postponed, while the trace, the list filter and the marks cards all say paused. Naming the downstream mark paused keeps the one word the most cards and the output already use, and the origin still reads postponed.
payload.body: The reason of a reopen and the mark on the reopened card read postponed. The mark on every card downstream of it reads paused, in the trace, in the list of marked cards and in its filter. Only the origin was postponed, and a downstream card was not touched, so the trace names the origin and the cards between to show the distance. Chosen by the guideline step: when answers are equal in safety, change the fewest decided cards. This answer changes one card, the naming card. Renaming the mark to postponed would change the paused cards, the trace card, the list card and the stories.

payload.title: The downstream mark also reads postponed
payload.why_not: It changes the trace card, the list card, the paused cards and the ticket stories, and a trace that says postponed on an untouched card hides which card was postponed.

payload.why: takes the trace that names a paused mark and the cards between

payload.title: A pipeline event is a step start or a step end, and detail files sit in one ignored folder beside the log
payload.why: A fold, a test and the retry cap all read the same record, so its shape must be fixed: one start and one end per step, with the result green or red. Detail files are large and only debugging reads them, so one folder that git ignores as a whole keeps them out of the history.
payload.body: The log is a file named pipeline.jsonl in the folder of the map log. Each line is one event. A step start and a step end share the step's id. Each event names its build, ticket, step kind and time. A build is separate from its ticket, because a ticket that the merge loop sends back builds twice. Every step except a plan step carries the number of its builder pass. An end event carries the wall time, the cost with its token breakdown, and the result, which is green or red. A red end names its gate. A red step with no gate of its own is named by its step kind. The first red step of a pass names the gate of that pass. The next pass states the cause of the last failure and one sentence of reason on its own start event, because only that pass has read the failure (see #ms-fail-cause). A cause is written as a lowercase hyphenated name: builder-error, test-is-wrong, spec-gap, false-finding, check-infrastructure, flaky, conflict. The detail files of a check or an agent session sit in one folder beside the log, with one file per step. The file name is the step id, with every character outside letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore replaced. The folder holds its own ignore rule that matches everything in it, so git tracks the log and none of the detail, in any project and with no edit to the project's own ignore file (see #ms-store-git).

payload.why: takes the one append-only log, one event per line, with a start and an end per step
takes the cause names and who sets each one
takes the rule that git tracks the log and not the detail files

payload.title: Let a closed obligation take a later record that names the proposed card
payload.why_not: The builder must then notice the gap and repeat a step that the grader could do from the log. The pass in that state already wrote the card, so the loop would still spend a pass on a record.

payload.title: A choice that a card proposed by the same build gives is a recorded decision
payload.why: A build can write a card for a choice and later close its obligation by naming other cards. If the grader read only the named decided cards, it would call the choice unrecorded although a card for it exists. Counting the build's own proposals as recorded ends that false failure, so the build never loops on a gap that only the person's accept could close.
payload.body:
A pass checks its "no new decision" record against the diff. The check asks whether a choice in the diff comes from a card that the record names. To avoid failing a choice that the build already wrote down, the cards that this build proposed count as named, whether or not the person has accepted them yet. The grader sees each such card marked as proposed.

A choice that no named card and no proposed card of this build gives still fails the pass as an unrecorded decision, as before.

Example:

- Card A "Each agent carries its role", decided.
- Pass 1 builds a chat log layout that no card gives, and proposes card C for it.
- Pass 2 records "no new decision" and names A only.

1. The grader reads the diff. The role comes from A, and passes.
2. The chat log layout comes from C, which this build proposed. The grader counts it as recorded, and passes.
3. A second new choice with no card still fails the pass.

```
choice in diff --> from a named decided card A ----------> recorded
               --> from a card C this build proposed ----> recorded (C may still wait for the person)
               --> from neither -------------------------> unrecorded decision: the pass fails
```

payload.why: It extends the rule that a build's own proposals count as decided to the check of the record.

payload.title: Let a closed obligation take a later record that names the proposed card
payload.why_not: The builder must then notice the gap and repeat a step that the grader could do from the log. The pass in that state already wrote the card, so the loop would still spend a pass on a record.

criterion.text: A build that proposed a card for a choice and later records no new decision is not failed on that choice; I watch for a ticket that ends in the cap on a gap that its own proposal gives.

payload.title: The link check for shipped subagents runs inside the lint check
payload.why: A check that fails on a missing or copied subagent link must run on every merge. The lint check already runs on every merge and already judges the shape of the repository's files, so it carries this check and the merge loop needs no new check name.
payload.body: The lint check runs the formatter and linter, then a small program that compares the shipped subagents with the subagent folder of the repository. The program lives in its own module for Claude Code tooling, beside the edit hook (#werk-cc-hooks), so no other module changes. It fails when a shipped subagent has no link, or when the folder holds a file under a shipped subagent's name that is not a link (#werk-cc-subagents). A separate make target for it would add a sixth production check that the merge loop does not run (#werk-checks).

payload.why: the link check runs as part of the lint check

payload.title: A shipped subagent is one markdown file that werk reads at run time
payload.why: The repository's Claude Code needs a markdown file with a header, and werk needs the same prompt to ship into other projects. One file read by both keeps a single prompt, and werk names its commands by the path it runs from only when it ships the prompt.
payload.body: A shipped subagent is one markdown file in Claude Code's agent format: a header with name, description and tools, then the prompt. The repository's subagent folder links to it. When werk ships the subagent to another project, it reads the same file, takes the name, description and tools from the header, and replaces the werk command in the prompt with the path werk runs from (#werk-agent-subagents). Inside a werk checkout the link serves the file unchanged, so the command reads as written.

payload.why: the path substitution applies when the definitions travel with the instructions

payload.title: The project list is one file of folder paths in a per-user folder
payload.why: The list must survive restarts and belong to the person, so it sits in a folder of the user, not in a project. Only real folder paths are stored, so two links to one folder are one project. A file that cannot be read is never taken as an empty list, because the next save would erase the person's projects.
payload.body: The per-user folder is the folder named by the WERK_HOME setting when set, otherwise the user's config folder for werk. When the WERK_LOG setting points elsewhere, the per-user folder is a folder beside it, so a test or a second instance never touches the real list. The list is one file that holds the folder paths in order. A save writes a new file and renames it over the old one, so a crash never leaves half a list. A folder is stored by its real path, so a link is resolved before it is stored. A file that does not parse is refused with an error, and nothing is overwritten.

payload.title: A server holds one lock per machine and each project holds its own lock
payload.why: Two servers on one machine would clash on the port, and two servers on one project would share its chat state. One lock per machine stops the first, and a lock in each project folder stops the second, also for a server that was started in another way.
payload.body: The machine lock sits in the per-user folder and holds the pid and the port of the server. A second start reads it to find the running server. Each project context takes the project's own lock in its map folder, with the rule of the one-lock card. A project whose lock another live server holds shows as locked: it is listed, and it does not open.

payload.title: Every page and every API route of a project carries the project's name
payload.why: One server holds many projects, so a route with no project name cannot tell whose map it reads. Putting the name in the address also lets a link or a reload open the same project.
payload.body: A project page is at the path p followed by the encoded project name. Every route that reads or changes one project lives under the projects path with the project name, and a request for a name that is not on the list is refused. The list itself is read and added to at the projects path, and a project is removed with a delete request on its name. The root address redirects to the first project that can open.

payload.title: A second start finds the running server, adds its folder and exits
payload.why: The person starts werk in a folder and expects that folder in the one running server. The start must find the server without a setting, and prove it is allowed to change state.
payload.body: The start reads the port from the machine lock and waits up to 5 seconds for a port, in case the server is still starting. It reads the synchronizer token from the server's page, posts the folder, opens the project in the browser, and exits. The WERK_OPEN setting names the program that opens the browser, so a test opens nothing.

payload.title: Adding a folder asks the person to agree before it creates a git repository
payload.why: A project needs a git repository, but making one in a folder is a change the person did not ask for yet. So the server refuses a folder without a repository, says why, and adds it only after the person agrees.
payload.body: The folder dialog runs on the server, so it works on macOS only, and the WERK_FOLDER_DIALOG setting replaces it for tests. An add of a path that is not a folder is refused as a bad request. An add of a folder with no git repository is refused as a conflict that names the need for a repository. The person agrees, and the add is sent again with a request to create the repository.

payload.title: A removal of a project with running turns needs confirmation, and the dev checkout refuses it
payload.why: A removal that stops a running agent without warning would lose work. The checkout that dev mode adds is not stored, so removing it would be undone at once and only confuse the person.
payload.body: A removal of a project with running agent turns is refused as a conflict that names the turns, and it goes through when the request confirms. A removal of the dev checkout is refused as forbidden.

payload.title: The dev checkout is listed first, and a third clash adds the whole parent path
payload.why: The dev checkout is the one the person builds with, so it comes first. A third folder with one name and a parent name that is also taken still needs a distinct name.
payload.body: The later project with a taken folder name adds its parent folder name in brackets. When that name is taken too, it adds the whole parent path.

payload.why: each project lock follows the one-lock rule
the attach posts with the synchronizer token
an add stores the folder by its real path
the dev checkout is the entry that cannot be removed
the dev checkout entry comes first
the port is read from the machine lock

payload.title: A repository has a main line when it has a branch named main or master
payload.why: A build merges onto the main line, so a target with no such branch cannot take a build. Two names cover the repositories people create.
payload.body: The target check accepts a repository that has a branch named main or master, and refuses any other.

payload.title: The target repository is recorded in the project's board log
payload.why: The target is one fact about the project. The board log is the project's own store, outside the target, and every build command already reads it.
payload.body: Setting the target appends an event to the board log, and the latest event is the current target.

payload.title: A plan keeps its files in one folder per subtree in werk's store, and a plan run replaces it
payload.why: One subtree gives one spec and its tickets, so one folder holds them and the answer files. A fresh run starts from an empty folder, so no file of an earlier run is read as this run's output.
payload.body: The folder holds the spec, the spec writer's answers, the ticket writer's answers and one numbered file per ticket. A ticket's number is the number that starts its file name, from 1 to 99. A ticket file without one is not planned. A spec is valid only with a User stories heading and at least one numbered story. Every answer card is proposed as open. A writer whose answers fail to propose stops the plan before the next writer starts.

payload.why: takes the rule that a record the plan cannot propose ends the plan with an error
takes the rule that the spec holds a numbered list of user stories
takes the rule that tickets merge onto the target's main line
takes the rule that the target is one fact for all build commands of the project

payload.title: A card page address names the project and then the card
payload.why: One server holds many projects, so the address of a card page must say which project it belongs to. A card link in the page keeps the short form, and the page rewrites it when it is followed.
payload.body: The address of a card page is the project address followed by the map and the card id, with the id URL-encoded. A card link written in a card or a tile has the short form, the map and the card id. A click on it opens that card's page in the same project and adds one history entry, so Back returns to the card before. A click with a modifier key follows the link as the browser would. The server answers a read of the open card with the page of the card that the read names, and says that the map has no such card when the id is unknown.

payload.why: The address names the project by its folder name.

payload.title: werk's list of its own files is written when the code is bundled, and the executable does not hot reload
payload.why: A folder listing finds nothing inside the executable, and a checkout has no build step to write a list. If the bundler writes the list into the code, the same code reads it in both places. The executable has no source to reload, so it serves in its own process.
payload.body: To avoid listing a folder while werk runs, the list of command modules is produced by the bundler at the moment it reads the code, in a checkout and in a release build alike. The release build also writes the list of client files and of command modules to a file beside the executables, and its entry module embeds those files and registers them before the command line starts. The Vite dev server is not in the executable; it loads only when dev mode asks for it. A serve in the executable runs in its own process with no hot reload child.

payload.title: The count line writes the postponed ring as postponed
payload.why: One word names the state everywhere the map prints it, so a reader never looks for a difference between paused and postponed. The count line is the only place that still listed the older word.
payload.body: The ring after the stale ring in the count line reads postponed, with its number. It counts the postponed card and every card it pauses, but not a card that is also stale, because stale wins where the kind is shown. The guideline step that chose it: the answer that keeps one word for one state.

payload.title: Keep the word paused in the count line
payload.why_not: Two words for one state, against the rule that postponed names it wherever the map prints it.

payload.why: It takes the single word postponed for the mark.

payload.title: A card page has a named read, a postponed trace section, and a reply for an unknown card
payload.why: The page needs an address to read one card, a place for the postponed trace, and an answer for a card the map lacks. No cited card gives them.
payload.body: The page of one card is read with a GET that names the project and takes the card id in a query parameter named card. The page holds a section that prints the trace of a postponed mark, next to the one for a stale mark. An unknown id is answered with a normal reply whose page says that the map has no such card. The rollup also carries a count of postponed cards, and a count of them for each status, for the hatched slice of the bar. Section headings read Evidence and excerpts, and Sub-cards with their count. The guideline step that chose it: the smallest interface.

payload.why: It takes the rule that the server answers a card read and says when the map has no such card.

payload.title: A person who moves a stuck ticket back to ready gives it a new retry budget
payload.why: The retry cap counts every pass of a ticket across all its builds. A ticket that hit the cap and then gets a fix elsewhere would be parked again at once, with no pass run, so a person's retry would do nothing. A new budget on the person's move lets the retry run, and the cap still stops a loop that no one has looked at.
payload.body:
To avoid parking a retried ticket before it builds, the passes that counted against the cap up to the move no longer count after a person moves a stuck ticket to ready or to building. The passes stay in the ticket's record and in its count of retries. Only the budget starts again, at the full cap.

A ticket held for any other reason keeps the passes it has spent. A ticket that waits on an open ticket, or on a failed set check, is not stuck, and its move does not renew the budget.

Example:

- Ticket T has a cap of 5 passes. Its first build used 5 and parked it as stuck.
- The cause is fixed in the map or in the grader.

1. A person moves T to ready. T has 5 passes on record, and 5 left in its budget.
2. The merge loop builds T. Pass 1 of the new build counts, so 4 are left.
3. T hits the cap again after 5 more passes. It is parked as stuck again, and the next retry starts a new budget again.
4. If T were moved to ready only because the ticket it waited on merged, its spent passes would stay counted.

```
build 1: 5 passes --> stuck (spent 5 of 5)
   person moves T to ready
build 2: budget 5 again (record still shows 5 + n passes)
```

payload.why: It changes the count of passes that the cap is measured against, as the spec-gap rule does.

payload.title: Reset the pass count of a ticket whenever it leaves blocked
payload.why_not: A ticket that waits on an open ticket also leaves blocked, so the reset would hand a ticket that failed its cap a full budget when a neighbour merges, with no person looking at it.

criterion.text: I retry a stuck ticket after fixing its cause and see whether it builds a pass.

payload.title: The page answers an open ask with one POST that names the ask and the choice
payload.why: The page and the server must agree on one address and one set of choices, or a click never reaches the child that waits. One write request carries the token and the choice; a closed ask answers with a status of its own, so a second click is harmless.
payload.body:
Problem: an open ask waits in the child, and the page must answer it once. Answer: the page sends POST /api/projects/<project>/ask with the page's token (see #werk-serve-trust) and a body of the ask's id and a decision: allow, always, deny, decline, or answer with the picks. The picks are a list with one list of labels for each question, and a free-text answer is one more entry in its question's list. The server answers 200 when the answer reached the child. It answers 409 when no such ask is open, for example after a second click, and 400 when the choice does not fit the ask: Always allow with no suggestion, or picks that leave a question without an answer.

The ask log records an answered question form as an allow, and a declined one as a deny, because a picked answer is a normal reply and not a failure (see #werk-approve-log, #werk-mc-askqa).

Example:

- The agent asks Which db? with the options Postgres and SQLite.

1. The page shows the form. The person picks SQLite and clicks Submit answer.
2. The page sends the ask's id, the decision answer and the picks [["SQLite"]]. The server answers 200, and the model reads: For "Which db?": SQLite.
3. A second click sends the same body. The server answers 409 and the child is not written to again.

```
page --POST /ask {id, decision, picks}--> server --200--> child: control_response
second click --------------------------> server --409--> nothing written
```

payload.why: the answer wire carries the choices that werk-mc-askqa defines
the answer wire carries the choices that werk-approve-log defines

payload.title: The board address opens a placeholder page until the board view exists
payload.why: The routes name a board address, but no board view is built yet. The address and the tab work now, so the board can fill the page later without a routing change.
payload.body: The board address opens a page with a heading and no ticket data. The tabs offer the map and the board only, because the graph, the diagram and Flow have no page to open yet.

payload.title: The header reads one index of the map's nodes, with parents and counts, from the server
payload.why: Breadcrumbs, search and counts all need every node's title, status and parent. One read of that index serves all three, so the page never folds the log itself.
payload.body: The index lists each real node in map order with its kind, title, reason, status, stale and postponed flags and parent, plus the counts of every card. A ghost is left out. The page reads it each time it reads the open card.

payload.title: A send names each stored image by its file name, and the server turns it into the path
payload.why: A path that the page sends could point anywhere on the disk. A file name can only point into the attachments folder, so the server checks it and builds the path itself.
payload.body: The upload answers with the stored file's name. The send carries those names in the order of the tokens. The server accepts a name only when it is a file in the attachments folder, refuses the whole send otherwise, and puts the absolute path in the agent's turn. The attachments folder holds its own ignore rule, so it stays outside version control without an edit to the project's files.

payload.title: A quote is its own kind of log event, apart from a card proposal
payload.why: A quote writes an excerpt and its link as one change, and the fold must read it with different rules than a card proposal: the pointer parts are required and the words are the title. A separate event type keeps one fold branch per meaning.
payload.body: The event is named for the quote. Its time part is named for when the message was said, so it is not mistaken for when the quote was written. See #werk-excerpt-event-shape for the parts the event holds.

payload.why: takes the parts the quote event holds

payload.title: Every proposed change to an excerpt refuses, not only a change of its words
payload.why: An excerpt is a fixed copy, so no change has a purpose on it: a status or an owner change would give an open mark or a decider to something nobody can decide. Refusing every change is simpler to state and to check than listing the words that are frozen.
payload.body: A proposal, an accept and a discard of a change on an excerpt all refuse, before and after the accept. A note on the excerpt is not a change and still works. See #werk-excerpt-event for the three guards.

payload.title: A quote takes the citing card, the conversation and the words
payload.why: The citer names the card that the excerpt supports and the conversation whose chat log holds the words, so the program needs no guess for either. The words come last, as an argument or with a flag, so a quote with a leading dash needs no escape.
payload.body: Form: quote <card-id> <conversation> "the words", or the words given with --text. Giving the words both ways, or not at all, refuses. The excerpt gets the citing card's id, a suffix, and the first free number.

payload.why: takes the rule on what a quote must match
takes the chat log that the quote reads

payload.title: A proposed card has no ✕, because discarding is a typed correction
payload.why: A proposed card cannot be removed, only accepted or discarded. A ✕ on it would be a discard button, and discard has no button. So a proposed card shows its ✓ and nothing else.
payload.body: The ✕ is drawn only on a real card. A proposed card shows the ✓ alone; the person discards it by telling the agent. The one-question confirmation of the ✕ therefore covers a real card with no children. A proposed removal on a real card is the case of a pending removal: its ✓ takes the card out, and it has no ✕. The person's ✕ appends the removal at once after one confirmation, while an agent only proposes a removal and waits for the ✓. The confirmation is drawn inside the card, under its buttons. Chosen by deny by default and the least privilege that makes the ticket work.

payload.title: The ✕ on a proposed card discards it
payload.why_not: It adds a discard button, which narrows the rule that discard is typed, and it gives one control two meanings.

payload.why: Discard has no button, so a proposed card gets no ✕.

payload.title: A proposed removal is its own log event, and accept and discard reuse the existing events
payload.why: An agent only proposes a removal, so the log needs a pending removal that a person can accept. Reusing the accept and discard events keeps one ✓ path for every kind of proposal, and the button adds no new kind of change.
payload.body:
A removal proposal is a log event of its own. It names the card and whether its children move up. The card carries a pending removal until the person accepts or discards it, and the card is drawn in red (see #werk-remove-red). An agent's removal command stages this event. A person's ✕ appends the removal at once, after one confirmation.

Accept and discard of a pending removal use the same events as an edit or a ghost. The fold checks for a pending removal first, so an accept takes the card out and a discard only clears the proposal.

The ✓ and ✕ ask the server to accept or remove. A removal request carries the card and whether its children move up. The server refuses with a conflict when the card has no pending proposal, and with a bad-request refusal when the request is malformed. Both requests need the synchronizer token (see #werk-serve-trust). Chosen by the smallest interface: no new accept event, no new route kind.

payload.title: A separate accept event for a removal
payload.why_not: It adds a second accept path and a second ✓ to keep in step with the first, for no new fact.

payload.why: Defines the removal, the reparent and the pending removal this card stages.
Defines the ✓ that asks the server to accept and the check for a pending proposal.

payload.title: Accept and remove are two posts under the project address
payload.why: A button needs one address per action and a body that names the card. Two plain addresses under the project keep the interface small and follow the routes that already change state.
payload.body: The ✓ posts to the accept address of the project with the card id. The ✕ posts to the remove address of the project with the card id and a flag that says whether the children move up. Both need the synchronizer token (see #werk-serve-trust).

payload.why: Both posts change state, so they carry the token

payload.title: A pending removal is one field on the card, holding whether children move up
payload.why: The fold needs one place to read a proposed removal. A single field on the card, set by the proposal and cleared by accept or discard, keeps one ✓ path.
payload.body: A removal proposal sets a pending removal on the card with the move-up flag. Accept applies the removal with that flag. Discard clears the field.

payload.title: The remove command stages a removal when asked to propose
payload.why: An agent only proposes a removal, so the command needs a mode that stages instead of removing.
payload.body: A remove with the propose option appends the removal proposal and prints that a removal was proposed. Without it, the removal applies at once.

payload.title: An option node has a ✕ too, because nothing else can reach it
payload.why: An option sits in no tree, so a wrong one has no other way out. Removal takes it already, so the button only exposes that.
payload.body: A real option node shows the ✕ like a real card. A proposed one shows the ✓ alone.

payload.title: A card with no parent offers only the subtree answer
payload.why: Move-up needs a parent to receive the children. A card with none has nowhere to move them.
payload.body: For a card with children and no parent, the confirmation offers the whole subtree or cancel.

payload.title: A tile shows the proposed badge for any pending change, red for a removal
payload.why: A reader scanning tiles must see which sub-cards wait for a ✓ without opening them, in the same colours as the hero.
payload.body: A tile of a card with a pending edit or removal shows the badge. A pending removal is red, others blue.

payload.why: Takes the red colour for a removal

payload.title: The word menu sits above the composer, and a choice puts the trigger, the choice and one space in the text
payload.why: The composer sits at the bottom of the pane, so a menu below it has no room. Adding a space after the choice lets the person keep typing without a manual gap.
payload.body: The slash menu and the card menu share one place and one look: a list above the composer. Choosing an option replaces the typed word with the trigger, the chosen name and a single trailing space, and puts the caret after that space. Arrows move, Enter or Tab chooses, Escape closes.

payload.title: A trigger word starts after whitespace and holds no second trigger or backtick
payload.why: A trigger inside another token, such as a path or a URL, is not a request for a menu. Closing the menu on a second trigger character keeps text like a/b or a#c plain.
payload.body: The word before the caret opens a menu when it begins with a slash or a hash and the character before it is whitespace or the start of the text. A backtick right before the trigger makes the word begin with the backtick, so no menu opens. A second slash, hash or backtick inside the word closes the menu.

payload.title: The card menu lists id matches first, then title matches, and shows nothing for a bare hash
payload.why: The ticket asks the # menu to match ids and titles, while the header search matches ids only after a hash. The id matches keep the header's order, and title matches fill in after them.
payload.body: The card menu ranks the cards whose id matches by the same rule as the header search after a hash, with the exact id first. Cards whose title holds the typed text follow, and the list is cut at the header search's limit. A bare hash with no text lists nothing. Choosing a card inserts its id with the hash.

payload.why: takes the id match order and the exact-id-first rule, and adds title matches after them
the menu it places lists the commands that this source gives

payload.title: The composer reads the command names with a GET to its project's commands address, with no token
payload.why: The menu needs the names that the server keeps from the agent's start line. A read changes nothing and starts nothing, so it needs no token, and one named field keeps the answer as small as the menu needs.
payload.body:
Each time a word that starts with a slash opens the menu, the page sends a GET to the commands address under the open project, /api/<project>/commands. The answer is 200 with {"commands": [...]}: the names that the project's chat keeps (see #werk-chat-cmdmenu-source), or an empty list when the project has no chat yet. The page keeps the names that start with the typed text.

Example:

1. No agent has started. The person types /re. The page asks the commands address and gets {"commands": []}. No menu opens.
2. After the first message, the person types /re again. The answer is {"commands": ["review", "recall", "compact"]}, and the menu shows /review and /recall.

```
composer: /re --GET /api/<project>/commands--> server --> {commands: [...]} --> menu: names that start with "re"
```

payload.why: reads the list of names that card says the server keeps
carries no token because the token rule exempts a request that changes nothing

payload.title: Push the names to the page over the live channel
payload.why_not: A second channel for one small list is a larger interface than one read when a menu opens.

payload.title: Clear context has its own address, and a refused switch or clear answers busy
payload.why: A clear drops the session and the transcript, which a model pick never does, so one address per action keeps each request's meaning plain. A refusal that names busy lets the pane show why nothing happened.
payload.body: Choosing a model and clearing the context are two separate requests. Both are refused while a turn runs, with a conflict answer that says the agent is busy and why. Asking for either by a plain read is refused as a wrong method. See #werk-model-select and #werk-context-pie.

payload.title: Other tabs learn of a clear and of a model change through live events that carry the new fill
payload.why: A second open tab must not keep a transcript or a pie that the first tab just reset. One event for the clear and a model event that carries the fill keep every tab equal without a re-read.
payload.body: A clear sends an event that tells every tab to drop its transcript. A model change sends an event with the model, the advisor, the tokens in use and the window. See #werk-model-select.

payload.title: Reading a conversation returns its saved settings next to its messages
payload.why: The pane must show the selector and the pie before any message. Giving the settings in the same read as the transcript means one request fills the whole header.
payload.body: A read of a conversation builds it if it is not yet built, so a restart shows the saved model and fill. The answer holds the messages and the settings together. See #werk-model-persist.

payload.title: A model pick is a family name, the server maps it to the pinned id, and Opus with an Opus advisor is refused
payload.why: The pane should not know model ids, so a repin changes one place. An Opus advisor on Opus adds cost and no second opinion, so the pick is refused.
payload.body: The pane sends sonnet or opus and an advisor of none or opus. The server turns the family into the pinned id (see #sonnet-pin and #opus-pin). Opus with the Opus advisor is not a choice and is refused. See #werk-model-select.

payload.why: takes the clear action and its busy guard
takes the fill values that the event carries
takes the pinned Opus id that the family maps to

payload.title: A start line replaces the kept command names, and each name is stored without its leading slash
payload.why: The agent may write its names with or without a slash, and a later start may name none. Storing bare names keeps the menu's matching and the inserted text uniform, and replacing the list on every start keeps it from showing commands the agent no longer accepts.
payload.body: Each start line of the agent replaces the kept list. A name that is not text, or is empty once a leading slash is removed, is dropped. A start line that names no commands sets the list to empty. Before the first start the list is empty. See #werk-chat-cmdmenu-source for where the names come from.

payload.title: A session log line holds its time and the agent's event
payload.why: The live preview shows one line per event with its full time, so each line of the log must carry both. A line in any other shape cannot be summarised.
payload.body: Each line of a session log is one JSON object with two fields: the time of the event, and the agent's stream event as it came. The preview skips a line that is not in this shape. It shows the last 200 events, oldest first.

payload.title: A conversation's saved settings are one file beside its session file
payload.why: The model, advisor and context fill must survive a restart, and a reader must know where they live. One file next to the session file keeps both halves of a conversation's state in the same place, and a clear removes the session without touching the settings.
payload.body: The saved model, advisor and last context fill are written as one JSON file named chat-model.json in the same folder as the session file (see #werk-resume). A missing or broken file means no saved settings, so the conversation starts on the default model with an empty pie. A clear drops the session file and keeps the settings. Chosen as the smallest interface: one new file, no change to the session file's format.

payload.title: Put the settings in the session file
payload.why_not: The session file holds one bare id that the resume path reads as is; adding fields changes its format and risks a wrong id passed to resume.

payload.why: takes the session file's place and format

payload.title: A conversation's saved settings are one file beside its session file
payload.why: The model, advisor and context fill must survive a restart, and a reader must know where they live. One file next to the session file keeps both halves of a conversation's state in the same place.
payload.body: The saved model, advisor and last context fill are written as one JSON file named chat-model.json in the same folder as the session file (see #werk-resume). A missing or broken file means no saved settings, so the conversation starts on the default model with an empty pie. A clear removes the session file, keeps the model and advisor, and resets the fill. Chosen as the smallest interface: one new file, no change to the session file's format.

payload.title: Put the settings in the session file
payload.why_not: The session file holds one bare id that the resume path reads as is; adding fields changes its format and risks a wrong id passed to resume.

payload.why: takes the session file's place and format

payload.title: A build's card obligation is three kinds of log event
payload.why: The obligation must be data in the decision log, so the ticket can read what its builds proposed or followed. A fixed event shape lets the board and the build loop read it the same way.
payload.body: The decision log holds an event that opens the obligation, naming its ticket and the cards the ticket cites. A second event closes it with the cards the pass followed. A card that a build proposes carries the id of its obligation, so the ticket can list it. A ticket with no obligation has no Decisions section.

payload.title: The board is read from two addresses of the project API
payload.why: The client needs the whole board fold and the live log of one ticket. Two read-only addresses keep the log read apart from the board fold, which is small.
payload.body: One address returns the whole board. A second returns the summarised log lines of one ticket, and refuses a request that names no ticket.

payload.why: The log address reads the session log that the board log names

payload.title: The board redraws on a live-channel signal, and a slow poll catches a dead builder
payload.why: A dead process writes nothing to the board log, so the log change signal never fires for it. A slow poll makes the dot stop without a log change.
payload.body: The server sends a board event on the live channel when the board log grows, and the client reads the board again. The client also reads it again every few seconds, so a process that died without an end stops pulsing.

payload.why: The poll exists because the process check cannot be signalled by the log

payload.title: A proposed card that the map no longer holds shows as gone in Decisions
payload.why: A person can discard a proposal. The ticket then still names a card that is not in the map, so it must not link to nothing or be called accepted.
payload.body: Each Decisions entry is a proposal, accepted, or gone. Gone marks a card of a build that the map no longer holds.

payload.title: A relative session log path is read from the project's .werk folder
payload.why: The start event names the session log. A path with no root must mean one place, or the preview reads the wrong file.
payload.body: A session log path in the board log that is not absolute is resolved against the folder that holds the logs.

payload.title: The agent's full task list arrives as one event that carries the list
payload.why: The count needs one event that holds the whole list, so that werk reads its length and nothing else. Any other event leaves the count alone.
payload.body: The agent reports its background tasks as one system event with a list of tasks. Werk replaces its count with the length of that list. An event with no list leaves the count as it is.

payload.title: Show with no id prints the first real card that refines no other
payload.why: A map has one root card, and a person who runs show without an id expects to land on it. A proposed card is not yet in the map, so it is never the root.
payload.body: When no id is given, the printed card is the first accepted card, in the order the cards were added, that refines no other card. If no such card exists, show prints that the map has no card.

payload.title: A build session that is still making progress is not cut off by the wall-clock cap
payload.why: A fixed cap cannot tell a long job from a stuck one, so it kills healthy sessions and throws away work that a new pass must repeat. The progress classifier already judges whether a session moves forward, so its verdict decides whether the cap gives more time. A stuck session still ends on silence, on a looping verdict, or at a ceiling.
payload.body:
A pass in a busy project can need more than the cap: it runs the whole test suite more than once, and other builds share the machine. When the cap ends such a pass, its work is half done, and the next pass pays again for reading and writing the same files.

To avoid cutting off healthy work, the cap becomes a checkpoint. When a session reaches the cap, the overseer reads the last verdict of the progress classifier for that session (#lp-overseer-progress). If the verdict is "not looping", the session goes on for another stretch as long as the cap. A session with no verdict, or with a "looping" verdict, ends at the cap as before. A session never runs more than three stretches in all, so a classifier that is wrong cannot keep a session alive without end. Each extension is an overseer line in the session log with the reason from the verdict (#lp-overseer-mechanics).

The silence limit and the in-flight check still apply in every stretch (#lp-overseer-silence, #lp-overseer-inflight). The extension covers only the build passes that the overseer watches (#lp-overseer-scope).

Example, with a cap of 600 s and a classifier verdict every 300 s:

- Pass A "writes and tests": it edits files and runs the suite, and the verdict at 300 s says "not looping".
- Pass B "repeats one fix": the verdict at 300 s says "looping".
- Pass C "is quiet": it made no tool call since the start, so there is no verdict.

1. At 600 s the cap is reached for all three.
2. A has a "not looping" verdict, so it gets stretch 2. The log shows an extend line with the reason.
3. B was already cancelled at 300 s by its looping verdict, so nothing is left to extend.
4. C has no verdict, so the cap ends it.
5. At 1800 s, A reaches its third stretch. The session ends there even with a "not looping" verdict.

```
time (s)   0        300         600          1200         1800
A          start....verdict:ok..cap->extend..cap->extend..ceiling X
B          start....verdict:loop X
C          start...................cap X

ok = "not looping"   loop = "looping"   X = session ends   extend = another stretch of the cap
```

payload.why: The extension reads the verdict this card defines, and no verdict gives no extension.
The extension is one more overseer act, written as a line in the session log, inside the headless runner.
It covers only the build passes that the overseer watches.

payload.title: Raise the fixed cap for every pass
payload.why_not: A stuck session then waits longer before the cap ends it, and a healthy one that needs more than the new number is still cut off.

payload.title: Each pass runs its checks on the ticket merged with the main line's tip
payload.why: Tickets that build at the same time name their modules by concept, so two of them can still edit one file, and the clash shows only at the merge queue, after a full pass of checks. Merging the tip into the branch before the checks makes the clash a failure of the pass, where the builder is already working. It also makes the checks see the same tree that the merge queue will check.
payload.body:
The overlap rule compares module names only (#st-build-parallel). A module list can miss a shared file, such as the file that lists every command. Two tickets then build to green on their own, and the second one fails to merge. The full build and checks were spent on a tree that never reaches the main line.

To avoid that, a pass merges the main line's current tip into the ticket's branch right after the builder commits and before any check runs. The pass ends in one of two ways:

- **The merge is clean.** The checks, the grader and the review run on the merged tree. The tip becomes the base for the diff that the grader reads, so the grader sees only this ticket's changes. A red check from the combination of this ticket and the main line is now a red check of the pass.
- **The merge conflicts.** The pass fails with the conflict as its failure, and the merge stays open in the worktree. The next pass resolves it as #st-build-conflict-resolve describes. A conflict pass does not count against the retry cap, up to three conflict passes in one build. After that each conflict counts as any red pass.

When the main line has not moved since the build started, nothing is merged.

Example:

- Ticket A "Add the export command" and ticket B "Add the import command". Both add one line to the list of commands. Their module names do not overlap.
- The main line starts at tip T0.

1. A and B build at the same time from T0.
2. A is green and merges. The tip is now T1.
3. B's builder finishes pass 1 and commits. B's branch has no T1.
4. Before the checks, the pass merges T1 into B's branch. Git reports a conflict on the list of commands.
5. Pass 1 ends red with that conflict. B's pass 2 keeps both lines and runs the checks. They are green on the merged tree, and the merge queue accepts B at once.
6. If the tip had not moved at step 3, B would run its checks without a merge.

```
main line   T0 ------- A merges ------> T1
B branch    T0 -- pass 1 commit --+--> merge T1 --> checks --> merge queue
                                  |        |
                                  |        +-- conflict: pass 1 red, pass 2 resolves
                                  +-- tip unmoved: checks run as they are

T0, T1 = tips of the main line   A, B = tickets   checks = checks of the ticket
```

payload.title: Leave the conflict for the merge queue to find
payload.why_not: The conflict shows only after a full build and its checks. The ticket then pays for a pass that finds the clash and a pass that fixes it, and a check that is red only on the combined tree shows up at the merge queue.

payload.why: A conflict that the pass finds is resolved by the next pass, started the way that card defines.
The module-name overlap rule misses shared files, which is why a clash can reach the merge queue.

payload.title: A red check in the merge queue runs once more on the same tree
payload.why: A check that fails and then passes on the same tree says nothing about the ticket, yet a red merge sends the ticket back for a full pass of work. The builder pass already reruns a red check once, so the merge queue applies the same test and keeps the ticket for a real failure only.
payload.body:
Checks that wait on time, on a page, or on a file system are slower and less steady when several builds run on one machine. In the merge queue such a check can fail on a tree that is fine. The queue then sends the ticket back, and a builder pass of several dollars is spent on no real failure.

To avoid that, a red check in the merge queue runs once more on the same merged tree, as #ms-fail-cause does for the builder pass. Green on the rerun is the check's verdict. The cause is flaky, the queue goes on to the next check, and the merge result records the flaky checks. Red on the rerun is the verdict, and the merge is red as before. A check that did not run the code, because it crashed or timed out before the tests started, is not run again. A merge conflict has no check to run again.

Example:

- Ticket T is green on its own, and its merge runs the checks unit test, page test and type check.

1. The queue merges T into a temporary tree. The unit test is green.
2. The page test fails: a heading is not visible within its time limit.
3. The queue runs the page test again on the same tree. It is green, so the cause is flaky and the verdict is green.
4. The type check is green. The main line moves to the merged tree, and the merge record names the page test as flaky.
5. If the page test had been red again, the merge would be red and T would go back to the builder.

```
merge tree --> unit test ok --> page test RED --> rerun on same tree
                                                    |-- ok  -> flaky, go on --> type check --> main line moves
                                                    |-- red -> merge red, ticket goes back

RED = first run fails   ok = passes   flaky = failed once, then passed on the same tree
```

payload.title: Run the merge checks with fewer workers than the build checks

payload.why: It takes the meaning of flaky and the rule that a check on the same tree decides it, and applies them to the merge queue.

payload.title: A red check in the merge queue does not stop the merge, and files a follow-up ticket to fix it
payload.why: The ticket's checks already ran on the ticket merged with the main line's tip, so a check that is red at the merge is rarely the ticket's fault, and most often a flaky check. Merging anyway keeps the work moving, and the follow-up ticket makes every red check, flaky or broken, a visible task that a builder pass fixes. A rerun would hide a flaky check and leave it broken for the next ticket.
payload.body:
A red check at the merge used to send the ticket back to the builder for a full pass of work, at a cost of several dollars, although the ticket was green on its own pass and its branch already held the main line's tip (#st-build-tip-in). A rerun of the red check would save that pass only when the check passes the second time, and it would hide the flaky check, which then fails again for the next ticket.

To avoid both, the merge queue runs every check of the ticket once on the temporary merged tree and never runs a check again. A red check does not stop the merge. The main line moves to the merged tree, and the merge record names each red check. The queue then files one follow-up ticket for that merge. The follow-up names each red check with the tail of its output, cites the cards that the merged ticket cites, and has the red checks as its own checks. It waits on nothing, because the ticket it follows is already merged. The builder pass that takes it decides whether the check or the code is wrong. A flaky check and a broken one get the same treatment.

A merge conflict still sends the ticket back, because there is no merged tree to check (#st-build-conflict). A stage after the checks that fails, such as the held-out gate, still stops the merge. A red check in a builder pass still fails that pass (#ms-fail-cause).

Example:

- Ticket T is green on its own pass, and its merge runs the checks unit test, page test and type check.
- Follow-up F is the ticket that the queue files for the red checks of T's merge.

1. The queue merges T into a temporary tree. The unit test is green.
2. The page test fails: a heading is not visible within its time limit. The queue does not run it again.
3. The type check is green.
4. The main line moves to the merged tree. The merge record names the page test as red.
5. The queue files F "Fix the red checks of T". F names the page test, quotes its output, and lists it as its check.
6. F builds like any ticket. If the page test was flaky, the pass makes it steady. If the code was wrong, the pass fixes the code.
7. If all three checks had been green, no follow-up is filed.

```
merge tree --> unit test ok --> page test RED --> type check ok --> main line moves
                                    |                                   |
                                    +--------- merge record: red -------+--> F (names the page test, waits on nothing)

RED = the check failed on the merged tree   ok = it passed   F = the follow-up ticket
```

payload.why: Every route needs the same place to read the conversation from, so one rule refuses a bad name everywhere. A page that predates tabs sends no name and keeps working on the first conversation.

payload.title: A plan run starts from an empty folder of its own files and keeps the files of tickets the board holds
payload.why: A file of an earlier run must not be read as this run's output, and the text of a ticket on the board must stay for a restore. So a run removes what the board does not hold and nothing else.
payload.body: A ticket's number is the number that starts its file name, from 1 to 99. A ticket file without one is not planned. Two files with the same number are both not planned, because the board holds one ticket for a number. A spec is valid only with a User stories heading and at least one numbered story. Every answer card is proposed as open. A writer whose answers fail to propose stops the plan before the next writer starts. The plan's id in the pipeline log is plan, the subtree id and the start time in milliseconds, joined by hyphens.

payload.body: A builder session runs in the automatic permission mode with the standard allowed tools plus make and git commands. Any other tool needs an approval that nobody gives, so it is denied.

payload.why: The home is a view like the map and the board, so it takes the same tab and the same address form. A project opens on it, because the first screen must show both top cards.

A project no longer reopens on the view it last showed, because that would skip the first screen. The map tab still opens the card last open on the map.
