takes the tab row that switches views, and adds the home tab to it

payload.title: A build's branch is named by its ticket id
payload.why: Two builds of one ticket must find the same branch, so that a red merge or an archive leaves work the next build can reuse. A name made from the ticket id gives that with no lookup.
payload.body: The branch of a build is named by the ticket id, plan run and number. The worktree starts from the main line's tip. An existing branch of that name that sits on top of the tip keeps its commits; any other branch of that name starts again from the tip. Chosen by the guideline step: the answer easiest to undo and that changes the fewest decided cards.

payload.title: A fresh branch name per build, with a timestamp
payload.why_not: A later build could not find the earlier work, so a red merge or an archive would lose the branch the next build should start from.

payload.why: takes the rule that the next build starts from the old branch when it sits on the main line

payload.title: The build's card obligation is one event in the decision log, named by ticket and start time
payload.why: A pass closes the obligation by id, so the id must be unique per build and readable by the pass. Putting it in the decision log keeps it beside the cards that close it.
payload.body: The start of a build appends one obligation event to the decision log. It names the ticket and the cards the ticket cites. Its id is build, then the ticket id with the slash turned to a dash, then the start time in milliseconds, so a second build of the same ticket opens its own obligation. Chosen by the guideline step: the smallest interface, with nothing deleted.

payload.title: The obligation id is the ticket id alone
payload.why_not: A second build of the same ticket would reuse an obligation that an earlier build already closed, so the new build would look done before it starts.

payload.why: takes the rule that every change is one event appended to the decision log

payload.title: A builder session has a total time limit, and a session that runs past it fails its pass
payload.why: The silence rule stops a silent agent, but an agent that keeps writing events can run forever. A total limit, set as a parameter, ends such a session, and the pass counts against the retry cap so a repeat still stops.
payload.body: Each builder session gets a wall-clock limit, a parameter of the build. When a session runs past it, the loop commits what the session left, skips the checks, and records the pass as red at the builder step with the reason. The pass counts against the retry cap, the same as a silenced pass (#st-build-silence-act). The next pass reads the reason in its brief.

payload.why: A timed-out session is handled like a silenced one: edits committed, checks skipped, a pass counted.

payload.title: A pass ended by an archive is marked in its ended event and costs no retry
payload.why: An archive ends a build from outside, so the pass is no evidence about the ticket. The ended event of the pass carries a mark, and the fold leaves that pass out of the retry count and out of the last failure.
payload.body: The ended event of a step or pass that an archive stopped carries an archived mark. The fold of the pipeline log counts no retry for such a pass and does not take it as the last failure. The transcript of the pass stays named by its event (#ms-store-files).

payload.why: An archive records no retry for the pass it stops.

payload.title: The board log records a replan, a mark and a cards-cited result as three events of their own
payload.why: A replan, a cite mark and a re-run set check change a ticket for different reasons. One event for each keeps the fold exact and lets a view say why a ticket moved.
payload.body: A replan rewrites an open ticket in place and records its new title, blockers, cited cards with their versions, and its blocking reason. A mark records one changed cited card, the kind of change and the card version it was seen at. A cards-cited result records the plan and the decided cards that no ticket cites, and blocks no ticket.

payload.why: takes the rule that a cited-card change marks a ticket and a new card re-runs the cards-cited check
takes the rule that a plan rewrites open tickets in place

payload.title: A card version is the position of its latest counted change in the decision log
payload.why: A position in an append-only log is exact and needs no clock. Comparing two positions says whether a counted change came after the plan.
payload.body: The version of a card is the position of the last event that counts as a change to it, and 0 when none does. A note and a change of view do not move it. A ticket records the version of each cited card at the plan; a card whose version is higher than the recorded one has changed.

payload.why: takes the append-only order of the log as the measure of what came after

payload.title: The ticket writer lists the open tickets it drops, each with a reason, in a separate output
payload.why: A ticket that the new spec no longer needs has no text to write. A separate list of drops gives the plan a reason to record, without making the writer produce a ticket file for it.
payload.body: The writer returns the drops as a list of ticket numbers, each with a one-sentence reason. The plan archives each listed open ticket and records the reason. A listed ticket that is not open is ignored.

payload.why: takes the rule that a plan archives an open ticket the spec no longer needs

payload.title: An archive made by a plan records the plan as the actor and states the reason
payload.why: A person must tell a plan's archive from their own, and must see why the ticket left the board before they decide to restore it.
payload.body: The archive event of a plan names the plan as its actor and carries a reason. A restore ends it exactly as it ends a person's archive.

payload.why: takes the restore that undoes the archive

payload.title: A marked ticket cannot return to ready until a plan keeps it
payload.why: Moving a marked ticket to ready by hand would hide that its cited card changed. Only a plan that reads the new versions can clear the mark.
payload.body: While a ticket carries a mark, any move of it to ready is refused. A plan that changes or keeps the ticket records the new versions and clears the marks. The blocking reason joins the set-check reason with one clause for each marked card, naming the card and the kinds of change.

payload.why: takes the rule that ready and blocked moves belong to an agent that states or resolves the reason

payload.title: A plan never changes a ticket that is not open, and never keeps a rewrite that fails its own checks
payload.why: The writer can touch any ticket file. A building, merging or done ticket must stay as it is, and an open ticket whose rewrite fails its checks would leave a broken ticket on the board.
payload.body: When the writer changes the file of a ticket that is not open, the plan restores the old file and reports it. When the writer rewrites an open ticket and the new text fails the ticket's own checks, the plan restores the old text and records no event for that ticket.

payload.why: takes the checks that decide whether a rewritten ticket may stay

payload.title: The server runs the cited-card watch on each change to the decision log, and a read error skips that run
payload.why: The watch must run at the moment of the change, and a half-written log line must not crash the server. The next change runs it again.
payload.body: Each change the server sees in the decision log starts one run of the watch for the project. A failed read of the log or the board ends that run without a mark. The next change starts a new run, so a missed mark is found then.

payload.why: takes the signal that tells the server the log changed

payload.title: A merged ticket has at most one open follow-up of each kind, and a later problem joins it
payload.why: A merged ticket can go wrong in the same code again and again: a second held-out step turns red, or a second decision it was built on changes. A new ticket for each event gives several tickets that change the same code at the same time. One open follow-up per ticket and kind takes each later problem into itself, so one builder fixes them together.
payload.body:
Problem. A merged ticket can need a fix more than once before the first fix is built. Its held-out steps can turn red one run after another, and the decisions it was built on can change one after another. Each event filed its own follow-up ticket, so one merged ticket got four or five open follow-ups. They cite the same cards, touch the same code, and conflict when they merge.

Answer. A merged ticket has at most one open follow-up of each kind. The kinds are the step follow-up, which makes red held-out steps green (#st-heldout-followup-per-ticket), and the rework, which brings the code in line with a decision that changed (#st-build-missing-decision). A follow-up is open until it is done or archived.

When a later problem of the same kind appears, one of three cases holds:
- There is no open follow-up of that kind. A new follow-up is filed.
- The open follow-up is still in ready or blocked. It takes the new problem into itself: its text and its list of steps or changes are written again with both, and no ticket is filed.
- The open follow-up has started to build. Its text does not change under a running builder. A step follow-up files nothing, and the next held-out run after its merge sees the red steps again. A rework files a new ticket, because the change is not in the text the builder reads.

A follow-up that judges a held-out step against a decided card is a different kind and is not covered here.

Example:
- Ticket W is merged. It has held-out steps W.1, W.2 and W.3.
- F is the open step follow-up of W.

1. Held-out run 1: step W.1 is red. No follow-up of W is open, so F is filed with W.1.
2. Held-out run 2, F in ready: step W.2 is red. F takes it. F now carries W.1 and W.2.
3. F starts to build. Held-out run 3: step W.3 is red. F is building, so nothing is filed.
4. F merges. The next held-out run finds W.3 red and files a new follow-up G with W.3.

```
run 1: W.1 red ----------> F (W.1)           file F
run 2: W.2 red ----------> F (W.1 W.2)       F in ready: join
run 3: W.3 red   F building: wait
F merges
run 4: W.3 red ----------> G (W.3)           no open follow-up: file G

F, G = follow-up tickets of W   W.n = held-out step n of W
```

payload.why: The step follow-up that takes later red steps into itself is the follow-up that card files for each source ticket.
The rework that takes later changed decisions into itself is the follow-up that card files for a merged ticket.

payload.title: One rework ticket for each changed card
payload.why_not: Every rework cites all cards of the merged ticket, so tickets for different cards change the same code and conflict. The changes are one problem in one place.

payload.title: Always file a new follow-up for each event
payload.why_not: A merged ticket gets four or five open follow-ups for the same code. They conflict, and each builder pays for a full pass to fix a part of one problem.

payload.title: Change the text of a follow-up that is building
payload.why_not: A builder reads its ticket text once at the start of a pass. A change under it is not seen, and the pass can end green against the old text.

criterion.text: After a run with several red held-out runs or several changed decisions, list the tickets: if one merged ticket still has two open follow-ups of one kind, or joined problems make one follow-up fail its cap more often than separate tickets did, reopen this card.

payload.title: A spec update keeps the number of every story that still holds
payload.why: Tickets that are building, merging or done list story numbers. A renumbered story would leave their stories pointing at the wrong story, and those tickets cannot change.
payload.body: When a plan updates the spec of a subtree, a story that still holds keeps its number. Each new story is numbered after the highest number. A story is dropped only when the cards no longer ask for it.

payload.why: the tickets list story numbers that stay frozen once built

payload.title: A ticket archive keeps its record only when it states a reason
payload.why: A reason is what a person reads before a restore. An archive with no reason has nothing to show, and the restore works the same either way.
payload.body: An archive event that carries a reason records who archived and why. An archive with no reason, such as a person's confirmed archive on the board, records no reason, and the ticket is still archived and restorable.

payload.why: a restore ends an archive whether or not it has a record

payload.title: A follow-up ticket is held to the same checks as any ticket, and its quoted gaps lose file paths
payload.why: A grader gap names a file and line, and a ticket names no file path, so a follow-up that quotes a gap word for word fails its own checks and never reaches the board. Cutting the paths out of the quote keeps the gap readable and the follow-up on the board.
payload.body: A follow-up ticket quotes each gap as the grader wrote it, except that each file path is cut to its bare file name, a gap is shortened to fit the size limit, and the quotes sit once, in the acceptance criteria. The follow-up then runs the checks on one ticket like every ticket. A follow-up that still fails them is not filed and gets no planned event. This is the deny-by-default answer: no ticket skips its own checks.

payload.title: Follow-up tickets are exempt from the no-file-paths and size checks
payload.why_not: An exempt ticket breaks the rule that a ticket names no file paths, and a path goes out of date before the build reaches the ticket.

payload.why: takes the rule it refines from this card

payload.title: The grader replies with one line per criterion, card and scope, and reports regressions itself
payload.why: The loop needs a fixed reply shape to score lines, fail them and tell a regression from a gap.
payload.body: Each line has an id (criterion-N, card-<id>, or scope), a score, a gap, and flags for whether the diff builds the card, whether a person must settle it, and whether it is a regression. A line the reply leaves out scores 0 and fails, also at a later grade, so a silent grader never passes a line. A low score on a line that passed before fails only when the grader flags a regression. Chosen as deny by default.

payload.title: A later grade forgives a line the grader leaves out when it passed before
payload.why_not: A silent grader would pass lines nobody read.

payload.title: A follow-up ticket takes the first free number in its plan and waits for its source ticket on the board
payload.why: The follow-up needs a file, a number and a wait, and no card gives them.
payload.body: The follow-up file is written to the ticket folder of the source's plan under the first free number from 01 to 99, counted over the board and the folder. It copies the source's touches line and checks, has one acceptance criterion per gap, and leaves the blocked_by header empty. The wait on the source is recorded on the board event only, so the file stays valid when the source number is in another plan folder. Smallest interface.

payload.title: The follow-up lists its source in the blocked_by header
payload.why_not: The header holds numbers of the same plan only, and a source can be written by a different number scheme.

payload.why: takes the rule it refines from this card

payload.title: A review finding with a missing or unknown severity is recorded and does not block
payload.why: A reviewer can write a severity the rubric does not name, and a block on every unknown word would fail a pass on a typo.
payload.body: Only CRITICAL and HIGH fail the pass. A finding with any other severity, or none, is recorded as written, or as UNKNOWN. This follows the ticket text.

payload.title: An unknown severity blocks like HIGH
payload.why_not: It fails a pass on a typo and costs a full retry.

payload.why: the scope line is one of the reply lines
a review that does not block lets the pass go on

payload.title: A restarted build runs in its own process group and outlives the server
payload.why: A build that the server restarts must survive a stop of the server, or an interrupt of the server would kill the fresh pass and count as one more death against the cap.
payload.body: The server starts the fresh pass through the public command line of the build, as a separate process in its own process group, and does not wait for it. The build takes a flag that names the dead session. The fresh pass continues the dead build: it keeps the build identity and the card obligation that the first pass opened, and opens no new obligation. The server still learns of the exit, to look for dead builds again.

payload.title: A fresh pass after a death uses the retry cap that the dead build ran with
payload.why: A build started with a custom cap must stop at that cap. A fixed default in the server would let it run too long or stop too early.
payload.body: The start of a build records its retry cap in the board log. The server reads that cap when it restarts a dead build, and passes it to the fresh pass. A start with no recorded cap, from an earlier version, uses the default cap of the build.

payload.title: A death is recorded as a red pass with no cost
payload.why: The board and the measures read passes and steps. A death must show there as a failed pass, so the count of passes and the failure reasons stay true.
payload.body: The end written for a dead build carries died as its reason. The server also records the dead pass as a red pass on the ticket, and as an ended pass step in the pipeline log with died as the reason, zero wall time and no cost, because the dead process cannot report either.

payload.title: The address /map shows the home, and the two top cards open at /map/root and /map/how

patch.body:
The home view shows the root of the requirements and the build-rules card side by side. A card page shows one card. To keep the two apart, the address with no card shows the home, and each card, #root and #how too, opens at its own address.

Example. The map has the cards #root and #how.

1. The person opens /map. The home view shows #root and #how side by side.
2. The person clicks the title of #root. The address becomes /map/root, and the page of #root opens, the same as the page of any card.
3. The person presses Back. The home view opens again.
4. The person opens /map/how. The page of #how opens, not the home.

```
 /map           home: #root | #how
 /map/root      page of #root
 /map/how       page of #how
 /map/<id>      page of <id>
```

What the bare project address opens is in #vi-home-howwhat-open.
patch.why: The home is a view of its own, so it needs an address that no card page uses. The address /map shows it. Every card, the two top cards included, keeps the address /map/<id> and the page of any card, so Back and Forward move between the home and a card page.

payload.why: takes that the page of #root is the page of any card, so it opens at /map/root and not at /map

The home reads the whole map again on every change signal, like any card page. The open card that the chat names on the home is the root card (see #werk-chat-no-card-line).

   1        2          3        4

ops.new: The tab strip ends with a + button. A short press forks the conversation on the open card (see #werk-mc-fork): the new tab keeps the parent's history, takes the open card as its home card and chip label (see #werk-mc-split), and takes the focus. short +:    [#map]  [#fold] [#fold*]         +   (fork, history kept)
empty:      [#map]  [#fold] [#fold] [#fold*] +   (new tab, no history)

*  the active tab
+  a short press forks, a long press opens the menu
```

patch.body:
The tab strip ends with a + button. A short press forks the conversation on the open card (see #werk-mc-fork): the new tab keeps the parent's history, takes the open card as its home card and chip label (see #werk-mc-split), and takes the focus. A fork switches to a tab that already has the card as its home.

A long press, a press held for about half a second, or a right-click opens a small menu above +. It has two rows, each with an icon before its label: "Fork current conversation", in bold because a short press does the same, and "New empty conversation". A fork brings the parent's history, which is wrong for an unrelated topic, so the second row gives a clean start without a second button. "New empty conversation" opens a new tab every time, also on a card that already has a tab, because a switch to an existing tab would show an old conversation. The new tab has no parent session and starts no agent until its first message. That agent starts with an empty session. A click outside the menu closes it and nothing else happens.

Example:

- tab "main", home card "#map", active. The map shows "#fold".
- No tab has "#fold" as its home card yet.

1. The person presses + briefly. "main" forks: a tab "#fold" opens with the history of "main" and takes the focus.
2. The person goes back to "main" and presses + briefly again. The pane switches to the tab "#fold". No tab opens.

```
start:     [#map*]                      +
1 fork:    [#map]  [#fold*]             +   (history kept)
2 press +: [#map]  [#fold*]             +   (switch, no new tab)
4 empty:   [#map]  [#fold] [#fold*]     +   (new tab, no history)

*  the active tab
+  a short press forks, a long press opens the menu
```

patch.body:
The tab strip ends with a + button. A short press forks the conversation on the open card (see #werk-mc-fork): the new tab keeps the parent's history, takes the open card as its home card and chip label (see #werk-mc-split), and takes the focus. A fork switches to another tab that already has the card as its home, and does not fork twice. The tab the person is on is never that other tab: on the home card of the active tab, + forks that tab, so the button never looks dead.

A long press, a press held for about half a second, or a right-click opens a small menu above +. It has two rows, each with an icon before its label: "Fork current conversation", in bold because a short press does the same, and "New empty conversation". A fork brings the parent's history, which is wrong for an unrelated topic, so the second row gives a clean start without a second button. "New empty conversation" opens a new tab every time, also on a card that already has a tab, because a switch to an existing tab would show an old conversation. The new tab has no parent session and starts no agent until its first message. That agent starts with an empty session. A click outside the menu closes it and nothing else happens.

Example:

- tab "main", home card "#map", active. The map shows "#fold".
- No tab has "#fold" as its home card yet.

1. The person presses + briefly. "main" forks: a tab "#fold" opens with the history of "main" and takes the focus.
2. The person goes back to "main" and presses + briefly again. The pane switches to the tab "#fold". No tab opens.
3. The person holds + down. The menu opens. No tab opens yet.
4. The person picks "New empty conversation". A second "#fold" chip opens and takes the focus. Its conversation has no history.

```
start:     [#map*]                      +
1 fork:    [#map]  [#fold*]             +   (history kept)
2 press +: [#map]  [#fold*]             +   (switch, no new tab)
4 empty:   [#map]  [#fold] [#fold*]     +   (new tab, no history)

*  the active tab
+  a short press forks, a long press opens the menu
```

payload.title: Who decides and a waiver on a decided card change only by an amend
payload.why: Who decides and a waiver are facts the decide was checked against. If either changed in place, the cards that stand on the decision would not hear of it. An amend runs the facts again and marks the next hop, so each card next to it is reviewed.
payload.body:
A decided card is frozen in its words and links (#map-frozen). Who decides and a waiver of a fact are frozen in the same way. They are not words, but the decide check read them, and a change to them can change what the card means to the cards that stand on it. A change to either goes through a proposal. Its accept is an amend: the facts run again on the new version, and the next hop is marked (#vi-prop-amended).

The amend can fail in the two cases that #map-frozen names: the change removes a fact, or the card lacks a fact that became required after it was decided. A kill criterion, an option and a source stay free, so a missing fact can always be added first (#werk-contract-amend-scope). A waiver still needs its written reason (#werk-contract-waiver-reason).

Each card that goes stale ends in a confirm or an amend of its own (#rederive-reason). An amend there marks one more hop.

Example. Three cards:
- P is "We charge per seat". It is decided, and who decides is me.
- Q is "The invoice shows the seat count". It depends on P.
- R is "The seat limit counts per workspace". It is a child of P.

What happens:
1. Someone proposes that who decides on P becomes you, with the sentence "The pricing model needs Eryk's judgement." Nothing changes yet. P stays decided, and Q and R stay clear.
2. P has no weighed option and no unchallenged record, so the accept is refused and names what is missing. The option is added, which needs no amend. The accept runs again and passes.
3. P stays decided, now with who decides you. Q and R go stale, and their trace shows amended with that sentence.
4. Q is reviewed and confirmed. It clears. R is reviewed and amended, so the cards that depend on R go stale.
5. A change that leaves who decides and every waiver as they are marks nothing.

```
 P  decided, who: me
 Q --depends_on--> P        R --refines--> P

 proposal: who -> you     P decided (me).  Q clear.  R clear.
 accept, fact missing     refused. P stays as it was.
 add option, accept       P decided (you). Q STALE.  R STALE.
                            trace: amended, "The pricing model needs Eryk's judgement."
 confirm Q                Q clear.
 amend R                  R clear. cards on R STALE.
```

payload.why: takes the rule that a change to a decided card is an amend through a proposal, and the two cases where an amend fails
takes the next-hop mark that an amend leaves and the trace that says amended
takes the confirm or amend that each marked card ends in
takes the facts that an amend runs again, who decides among them
takes the written reason that a waiver carries
takes the rule that a missing fact can always be added, so the amend can be unblocked

ops.new: To keep the excerpt and its link one change, the quote writes one event of a type that only the quote writes. The event names the excerpt, the citing card, and the pointer parts: conversation, session, message position, span start and end, speaker and time. An event with a missing or malformed pointer part, or a name already taken, is set aside. The quote also refuses before it writes when the matched message has no speaker, time or session, because the pointer would be incomplete. payload.title: Each conversation runs in an agent process that werk starts, not in the session that hosts it
payload.why: The host application holds the input of the session it starts, so werk cannot send that session a message. An agent process that werk starts takes its input directly, so every conversation can have a real two-way channel.

ops.old: Conductor spawns its pinned claude binary (2.1.237) from 'conductor-runtime sidecar' with:
claude --output-format stream-json --input-format stream-json --verbose --thinking adaptive --thinking-display
Its fds 0, 1 and 2 are unix sockets to the sidecar, not a tty. A user turn is one JSON line written to that socket. So Conductor never pastes and never simulates keystrokes.
Two consequences for werk.

1. The composer cannot reach a Conductor-owned session. That stdin belongs to the sidecar. The clipboard stays the seam for the session you are in.
2. werk can spawn its own claude child with the same flags and get a real per-node conversation, no paste. Conductor proves the flag set works in production.

The 'conductor message create --session <id>' CLI command does send a user turn, but it targets api.conductor.build. There is no keychain token here and this workspace is CONDUCTOR_IS_LOCAL=1, so it does not reach a local session.

ops.new: A session that a host application started holds its own input, and werk has no way to write to it. So the composer cannot reach such a session. To give each conversation a real two-way channel, werk starts an agent process of its own for the conversation and writes each user turn to that process's input. The clipboard stays the way to hand text to the session the person is working in.
The process werk starts uses the same input and output setup that the host uses for its own sessions, so the setup is known to work in production. The evidence is on the source.

Example:

- Conversation B runs in an agent process that werk started.
- Session A was started by the host application.

1. The person writes a message to B in the pane. werk writes it to B's input and B answers.
2. The person writes a message meant for A. werk cannot write to A's input, so nothing is sent. The person copies the text and pastes it into A.

```
composer ──turn──> werk ──write──> B's input     (process started by werk)
composer ──turn──> werk ──x──> A's input          (held by the host: refused)
clipboard ──paste──> A
```

payload.title: The propose form takes a waiver's reason as the flag's value, as the edit form does
payload.why: A waiver needs a written reason. A flag that accepts a reason and drops it leaves a waiver nobody can read, so the staged change takes the reason with the flag and refuses a bare flag.
payload.body: A change to who decides or to a waiver on a decided card is staged as a proposal. The proposal names the waiver and its reason together, the same way an edit of an open card does. A waiver flag with no reason is refused with a message that shows the form that works. A proposal never accepts a waiver and drops its reason without a word.

payload.why: takes the rule that every waiver carries a written reason

criterion.text: I run propose with a bare waiver flag and see it refused, then with a reason and see it staged

payload.title: The agent reviews every card a change marks, in the same turn
payload.why: A mark only says a card may no longer hold. Most marked cards still hold, and a person should not read each one. So the agent reads each marked card and its link reasons right after the change, confirms the ones that hold, and proposes an amend for the rest.
payload.body:
A change marks the next hop (#vi-prop). Left alone, the marks stay until someone reviews them, and a map with many marks stops being read. To avoid this, the agent that made the change reviews every card the change marked, before the turn ends.

For each marked card the agent reads the card, the changed card, and the reason on each link between them. Then it ends the review in one of the two ways that #rederive-reason defines. A card that still holds gets a confirm, which clears the mark and stops the spread there. A card that no longer holds gets a proposal to amend it. The person accepts or discards the proposal. An amend of a card that the person decides (who: you) is never applied by the agent alone.

A review is not a bulk clear. Each confirm lists the link targets that the agent read (#vi-prop-confirm-names). A card whose basis is still stale or open is skipped, because it waits (#map-wait). A paused mark is left as it is.

Example. Three cards:
- A is "We charge per seat".
- B is "The invoice shows the seat count". It depends on A.
- C is "The invoice PDF has a seat column". It depends on B.

1. The person asks to reword A. A is amended.
2. B depends on A, so B is marked stale. C is not marked, because the mark moves one hop.
3. The agent reads B and the reason of its link to A. The wording change does not touch the seat count, so the agent confirms B. The mark ends. C stays unmarked.
4. Another case: the person changes A to "We charge per active user". The agent reads B, sees that the seat count is now a user count, and proposes an amend of B.
5. When the person accepts the amend, B changes, and C is marked stale. The agent then reviews C in the same way.
6. If the change marks no card, the agent has nothing to review.

```
  A amended ──marks──▶ B ──agent reads B + link reason──┬─ holds ──▶ confirm: mark ends
                                                         └─ differs ─▶ amend proposal
                                                                         │ accepted
                                                                         ▼
                                                              B changed ──marks──▶ C ──▶ review
```

payload.why: The agent ends each review with a confirm or an amend, as #rederive-reason defines.
Each confirm lists the link targets read, so the review cannot clear a mark unread.
A card on a stale basis waits, so the review skips it.

payload.title: Marks stay until a person asks for a review
payload.why_not: The marks pile up with no reader. A map where most cards are red stops telling which ones need attention.

criterion.text: After a change that marks cards, check whether the agent's confirms hold up: a confirmed card that a later change shows was wrong means the review is too loose.
After the change ships, confirm a card while leaving one of its older link targets off the list. The confirm must be refused and name that link.
Run a confirm with a missing target, with an unknown target, and with a full list. Only the full list clears the mark. Run an amend with a sentence and read it in the trace of a marked card.

A waiver flag with no reason is refused with the form that works. The reason is never dropped without a word.

payload.title: A command that werk prints starts with the name of the file that runs it
payload.why: A person copies a printed command into a shell. A downloaded file often has a long name such as werk-darwin-arm64, or the person renames it, so the word werk would name a program that is not on their path. The name of the running file always works when they paste it.
payload.body:
A printed command is a command that werk shows to a person to copy: the next step after a refused change, or a usage line. To avoid a command that fails when pasted, werk starts every printed command with the name of the executable file that is running. When werk runs from a source checkout, there is no executable file, so the command starts with the word werk. An agent prompt and a child process get the full command from one shared source, and never a runtime name with a source path.

Example

- File "werk-darwin-arm64": the file Maria downloaded and did not rename
- File "werk": the file Tom renamed after the download
- Card "checkout-retry": a proposal that waits for accept

Steps

1. Maria runs the file werk-darwin-arm64 and opens a change that werk refuses.
2. werk prints the next step: "werk-darwin-arm64 accept checkout-retry". Maria pastes it and it runs.
3. Tom runs the file werk. werk prints "werk accept checkout-retry". Tom pastes it and it runs.
4. A developer runs werk from a checkout. There is no executable file, so the line starts with "werk".

If werk printed the word werk in step 2, Maria's shell would answer "command not found".

  running file            printed command
  ----------------------  ---------------------------------
  werk-darwin-arm64  -->  werk-darwin-arm64 accept <card>
  werk (renamed)     -->  werk accept <card>
  checkout (no file) -->  werk accept <card>

The install puts the executable on the path under the name werk, so that word works in every shell, and every printed line, prompt and document reads the same. A person who keeps the file under another name makes it work by placing it on the path as werk.

Example

- Command "werk": the executable that the install placed on the path
- Card "checkout-retry": a proposal that waits for accept

Steps

1. Maria installs werk. The shell now finds the command werk.
2. Maria opens a change that werk refuses.
3. werk prints the next step: "werk accept checkout-retry". Maria pastes it and it runs.

  how werk runs     printed command
  ----------------  -------------------------
  installed         werk accept <card>
  from a checkout   werk accept <card>

payload.title: The lint check fails when werk's own copy of a shipped subagent is not a link
payload.why: werk's own agents must run the same subagent prompts that users get, and that holds only while the repository's folder links to the one shipped definition. A forgotten link or a copy made over a link fails without any sign: the agent is missing when called, or it runs an old prompt. A check at the end of the lint check catches both before a merge, and the merge loop needs no new check.
payload.body:
Claude Code reads subagents from one folder of the repository. werk's own repository needs the shipped subagents there, and their one definition lives elsewhere in werk's source, so the folder holds links to it (#werk-cc-subagents). Two mistakes break that, and neither shows. A shipped subagent has no link: the agent instructions name an agent that the repository lacks, and the failure appears when an agent first calls it. A link is replaced by a plain file with the same name: agents run it, but a later fix to the shipped definition never reaches it, so werk's own agents run a prompt that users do not get.

To catch both before a merge, the lint check ends with a small program that compares the shipped subagents with the folder. It fails when a shipped subagent has no entry, when its entry is a plain file, or when its link points to any file other than the shipped definition. A subagent that only werk's development uses is not shipped, and the program ignores it. The check runs wherever the lint check runs: in the merge loop before a merge, on the clean machine after it, and on demand (#werk-checks). The check needs no new check name.

**What the check is not.** It does not run in a project that werk builds. That project has no folder of links, because werk hands the definitions to each agent when it starts the agent (#werk-agent-subagents). It does not judge whether a prompt is good, only that there is one copy of it. It does not stop anyone from making a copy. It makes a copy fail before the merge, so a copy does not stay unseen.

**Example**

- P, the shipped subagent that builds the options of a fork, defined once in werk's source
- F, P's entry in the repository's subagent folder, a link to that definition
- R, a new shipped subagent that someone has just added
- D, a subagent that only werk's development uses, a plain file in the folder

1. An agent saves a rewritten P as a plain file at F. The link is gone.
2. The lint check runs the comparison. F is a plain file, so the check fails with "P is a copy, not a link". The merge stops.
3. The agent restores the link and makes the edit in P's shipped definition. The comparison passes.
4. Someone adds R with no entry in the folder. The check fails with "R has no link".
5. D is a plain file with no shipped definition. The comparison skips it and nothing happens.

```
shipped definitions            repository's subagent folder
   P ------------------------<------ F   link         -> pass
   R                                  (none)          -> fail: no link
   P ------------------------   F'  plain file        -> fail: a copy
                                  D   plain file, not shipped -> skipped
```

payload.why: the link check runs as the last step of the lint check
the merge loop and the clean-machine run call the lint check, so they run this check

payload.title: A separate task for the link check, outside the lint check
payload.why_not: The merge loop runs only the existing production check names, so a separate task does not run before a merge and a copy can merge unseen. Adding it to the merge loop adds one more check name for one small comparison.

criterion.text: The check fails with no real copy or missing link behind the failure, or it never fails because the link is always updated together with every change to a shipped subagent, so it protects against nothing.

payload.title: A shipped subagent is one markdown file that Claude Code and werk both read
payload.why: Claude Code needs a markdown file with a header, and werk needs the same prompt in other projects, where the werk command is not on the command path. One file serves both: the repository links to it, and werk reads it and writes the path into the prompt as it ships it. There is one prompt to fix.
payload.body:
Claude Code reads a subagent from a markdown file: a header that gives the name, a description and the allowed tools, then the prompt. werk ships the same subagents into other projects, and there the prompt cannot say "run the werk command", because werk is not on that project's command path. To avoid two files per subagent, the subagent is defined once, as the markdown file Claude Code reads. The repository's subagent folder links to it (#werk-cc-subagents). When werk ships the subagent, it reads the same file, takes the name, description and tools from the header, and replaces each werk command in the prompt with the full path that werk runs from (#werk-agent-subagents). Inside werk's own checkout the link serves the file unchanged, so the command reads as written.

**Example**

- P "prototyper", a shipped subagent. Its prompt tells it to run werk's command that builds one prototype per option.
- C, Claude Code in werk's own repository
- X, another project where werk starts an agent that needs P

1. C opens P through the repository's link. The file is served as written, and the prompt names the werk command. C runs it.
2. A fix to P's prompt is saved in the one file. C sees the fix at its next call.
3. werk starts an agent in X. It reads the same file and takes the name, description and tools from the header.
4. In the prompt, werk replaces the werk command with the full path of the werk it runs from. The agent in X can run it.
5. A prompt with no werk command passes through unchanged.

```
one file: P (header + prompt)
   |
   |-- link ------------> repository's subagent folder -> C   prompt as written
   |
   '-- read at run time -> header kept, command -> path -> agent in X
```

The repository's subagent folder links to it (#werk-cc-subagents). When werk ships the subagent, it reads the same file and takes the name, description and tools from the header and the prompt from the rest (#werk-agent-subagents). The prompt needs no change for another project, because a command in it starts with the word werk everywhere (#werk-dist-printed-name).

**Example**

- P "prototyper", a shipped subagent. Its prompt tells it to run werk's command that builds one prototype per option.
- C, Claude Code in werk's own repository
- X, a project that werk builds

1. C opens P through the repository's link and runs the werk command in the prompt.
2. A fix to P's prompt is saved in the one file. C sees the fix at its next call.
3. werk starts an agent in X. It reads the same file and takes the name, description and tools from the header.
4. The agent in X gets the prompt as written, from werk at start, and runs the same werk command. X's own subagent folder stays untouched.
5. A header with a tool that the agent may not use is a fault in the one file, so it shows in C first.

```
one file: P (header + prompt)
   |
   |-- link ------------> repository's subagent folder -> C   header + prompt
   |
   '-- read at run time -> name, description, tools, prompt -> agent in X
```

payload.why: the file is read when the definitions travel with the instructions
the prompt needs no rewrite because a command starts with werk in every project
